title: The Book That Changed My Life review – these joyful tales of the power of reading are TV magic | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Wonderful, exuberant stories spill out in these honest tales of lives genuinely transformed by literature – while Queen Camilla has an off-with-their-heads moment
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Wonderful, exuberant stories spill out in these honest tales of lives genuinely transformed by literature – while Queen Camilla has an off-with-their-heads moment
Content: Gleam in her eye … Queen Camilla in The Book That Changed My Life.Photograph: BBC/Blink FilmsView image in fullscreenGleam in her eye … Queen Camilla in The Book That Changed My Life.Photograph: BBC/Blink FilmsTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewThe Book That Changed My Life review – these joyful tales of the power of reading are TV magicWonderful, exuberant stories spill out in these honest tales of lives genuinely transformed by literature  – while Queen Camilla has an off-with-their-heads momentLucy ManganWed 14 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou have to love a documentary in which Queen Camilla reveals that as a teenager one of her favourite books was The Scarlet Pimpernel because “I was sort of obsessed at that time by the guillotine”. ’I’m sorry, what? Could we back up a moment? I have a few more questions I’d like to ask.Alas, she goes on to refer to the tricoteuses in A Tale of Two Cities as “ghastly women”, so hopes of Camilla’s coronation as the end of a very long seditious play by the Shands are ultimately dashed. But if anyone was ever going to be an aristocratic sleeper agent primed to bring down the monarchy from within, it would be Camilla. Clearly born the very gamest of girls, she has a gleam in her eye as she recalls her younger self that still makes you wonder …Anyway. While we wait for the ultimate truth to reveal itself, there is much to divert and – somehow, even in this godforsaken year of 2026 – uplift us in The Book That Changed My Life. Made by the BBC in partnership with the Open University and in collaboration with the Queen’s Reading Room to mark the close of the National Year of Reading, it does a wonderful, if markedly unsentimental, job of illuminating the transformative power of reading. This kind of thing can easily become an emetic horror, but here the stories told by people of coming across, in extremis, books they credit with changing, and in some cases even saving, their lives are told so honestly that all the usual tonal traps for heffalumps remain resolutely undisturbed.View image in fullscreen‘It literally, literally allows you to escape’ … former prisoner Omar Mentesh.Photograph: BBC/Blink FilmsOmar found a copy of Jack Higgins’s bestselling second world war thriller The Eagle Has Landed when he was a teenager serving a two-month sentence in Feltham prison for breaking and entering. A previous inmate had left it behind. “First time I ever read a book was in that place.” Badly injured in an accident as a child and hospitalised for a long time, he had fallen behind in school, started truanting and turned to crime. He read, he says, just well enough “to be in the scene” and breeze past the words he couldn’t understand. “To be out of the cell,” he remembers, “was amazing. It literally, literally allows you to escape.” As his reading improved, “it allowed me to cross over into the new world – the communication, the emotional regulation and understanding and the nuance to be able to be in an environment outside of crime”.Liverpudlian truck driver Peter was born partially deaf and, like Omar, fell behind at school – “One of the worst times in the world” – and left without being able to read. The self-loathing (“thick as two short planks”, he was told) and alienation it brought, especially once his children were born, propelled him to the edge of suicide. His wife persuaded him to start a Read Easy course – one last go at learning this elusive skill. His teacher, Alison, “justgotme”. The first book he read was Harry Potter. He was himself, says Peter, like a boy emerging from under the stairs and becoming a wizard. “Sounds very corny. But it’s true, innit.”View image in fullscreenLike learning magic … truck driver Peter Lloyd.Photograph: BBC/Blink FilmsInterspersing these larger stories are shorter interviews with a variety of (non-celebrity) bookworms from all walks of life. They’re bursts of exuberance, really, going off like fireworks. A woman with pink hair (I apologise for the lack of names – I don’t know if they were added to the broadcast version but my preview didn’t have them), who was sent to a school for maladjusted children, apparently in response to her severe dyslexia, remembers tackling Wuthering Heights “one word, one word, one word” at a time until suddenly the chaos of her classroom fell away and “it’s snowing. I’m on a moor.” A man who didn’t read at all as a child (“books were just things in school”) started working through the classics after one caught his eye, and says here: “I only found out the authors were dead when I tried to email Oscar Wilde.” A fan of The Girl With the Louding Voice remembers being caught reading at a wedding. “In my defence, the bride was late and there’s only so much small talk I can endure.” If you know, you know.And the queen does her bit, delivering anecdotes about “my husband” laughing at Wodehouse as they sit together in the evenings and read – “Quite off-putting! I can’t get back into my book!” – then remembering how she wept throughout her father’s book Previous Engagements, describing the wartime experiences he would never speak about, and always proceeding from “my simple conviction that books make life better”.Omar delivers literacy workshops in prisons now. He started after reading Viktor Frankl’s Man’s Search for Meaning. “Reading … it’s the route out of everything. It’s like abracadabra.”Such magic.The Book That Changed My Life aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionFictionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Try to eat really well, 80% of the time’: nutrition expert says healthy eating is easier than you think | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Christopher Gardner, the author of Food Sense and director of nutrition studies at Stanford, says we have overcomplicated the question of what to eat
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: Christopher Gardner, the author of Food Sense and director of nutrition studies at Stanford, says we have overcomplicated the question of what to eat
Content: ‘You’re much more likely to stick with a healthy diet that has room for a few exceptions than if you hold yourself to being exclusive and restrictive.’Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘You’re much more likely to stick with a healthy diet that has room for a few exceptions than if you hold yourself to being exclusive and restrictive.’Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesDeep diveWell actuallyInterview‘Try to eat really well, 80% of the time’: nutrition expert says healthy eating is easier than you thinkElle HuntChristopher Gardner, the author of Food Sense and director of nutrition studies at Stanford, says we have overcomplicated the question of what to eatWed 14 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinally, some good news: eating well is more straightforward than you think. “There’s a lot of good science out there, and it mostly agrees,” says Stanford University’s director of nutrition studies and professor of medicine Christopher Gardner from his office in Palo Alto – beaming, bronzed and the picture of health.In the age of social media and wellness grift, we’ve overcomplicated the question of what to eat, he says.In 2023, Gardner was invited to serve on the US government’s dietary guidelines advisory committee, reviewing the official guidelines for healthy eating and recommending updates. “It was quite an honour to be asked,” remembers Gardner. It was also “a tonne of work”.View image in fullscreenChristopher Gardner.Photograph: Katherine TaylorGardner was more than up for the task. He has researched nutrition for more than 30 years, regularly advising official bodies on the latest science and conducting his own gold-standard studies on everything from fermented foods to fish oil.But when, after two years of work, the committee submitted its 400-page report, it was summarily dismissed byRobert F Kennedy Jr, the Trump administration’s new health secretary, and his team.Now Gardner’s view is that expert advice is more necessary than ever for navigating the noise around nutrition. His new book,Food Sense, brings together everything he’s learned to give straightforward, science-backed advice on “what to eat and why”.In a surprisingly optimistic interview, Gardener spoke about what’s being missed in the binary of “miracle foods” and “ultra-processed” ones, the politicisation of nutrition science and how science can help us to make better choices at every meal.Answers have been condensed for sense and clarity.Why did you believe this book was needed?I give a lot of talks and, afterwards, people have often said to me: “Thank you for clarifying, and not talking down to me, and being practical, and acknowledging that I have a limited budget or access to healthy food.” Everyone eats, but there’s so much fearmongering and bickering aboutwhatto eat – I thought I could find a way to pull a bunch of this information together, and give everybody a better chance to do their best.Why is there so much debate over how to eat?For a start, there are different kinds of science, and it’s never complete. I’ve done 25 human intervention trials, always trying to answer practical questions. For example, we did a study testing whether real garlic or garlic supplements can lower the bad LDL [low-density lipoprotein] cholesterol. The public’s interest, of course, is: “Is garlic good for you?”, but you can’t design a study that answers such a general question. We have to look at a particular dose, population, duration and outcome.Tell us: are you a single woman? We want to know about your relationship to sexRead moreAs I advanced in my career, I started being invited to serve on nutritionary advisory committees, such as for the American Heart Association and the American Diabetes Association. Reviewing papers with other scientists, we almost always found that we agreed: even if we didn’t have all the data we needed, we had enough to say that people should probably eat this or that. What I kept noticing, again and again, was that it really wasn’t hard to reach consensus.If there’s so much agreement about what we should be eating, why does the advice seem so contradictory?We’ve all seen the headlines saying that “eggs are good for you” – then they’re bad, then they’re good again. If you’d followed the science, it’s more that we thought this one thing about eggs, then we did more studies and found there was more to the story, and, since then, the advice has been pretty consistent – but it’s hard to attract attention with that. If you want to make clickbait, you can say something quite plausible that’s not scientifically accurate.double quotation markI do feel sorry for people with this information overload. They just think: ‘I give up … to hell with it.’I do feel sorry for people with this information overload. They just think, “I give up – I’m going to eat this inexpensive, convenient thing, and to hell with it.” The food industry has done such a good job of passing on responsibility: “We just make what people are asking for, and shame on you if you can’t choose properly.” But how can you choose properly in this context?Your advice in your book is consistent with author Michael Pollan’sfamous 2006 dictum: “Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.” Why has that message failed to land?I love bringing up that quote. I jokingly complain about it all the time: how many citations does he have? None! As a scientist, having to back up everything I say with evidence, I could never get away with that. But when I’m asked to summarise all of the nutrition I have studied and researched, that 20-year-old phrase of seven words really does capture most of what I have found.We’re definitely overcomplicating it. The interest in themicrobiomeis a perfect example: you can now find out the particular microbes in your gut, in theory allowing you to “personalise your diet”. The problem is, there are hundreds of gut microbes, and we have not perfectly classified them all as healthy versus pathogenic.Precision medicine is a really interesting idea, and a goal, but the commercial industry is getting ahead of us: there are now people eating a lot of junk food, then having a “gut shot”. That could help, but you’d be better off eating some veggies, fruit and legumes, and getting that solid foundation that all health professionals agree on first.What do you make of ultra-processed foods, the latest category to be demonised?In the US, 60% of the average diet is now classified as “ultra-processed”.I think Carlos Monteiro, the Brazilian nutritional scientist who coined the term, made a brilliant observation, looking beyond added sugar, added salt, refined grains and saturated fats to the other cosmetic additives in those junk foods; but I think he made a poor choice with the phrasing, “ultra-processed”.My family tried to eat fewer ultra-processed foods for five years. Here’s what we learnedRead moreIf you think about the transition from groats – that’s the hulled oat kernel – to steel-cut oats, to rolled oats, to quick-cooking rolled oats, to oat flour: they are different levels of processing, but each one is still basically just oats. Dr Monteiro was mostly concerned with the cosmetic additives: the artificial flavours or colours, the emulsifiers, the gelling, the foaming – all the things the industry does to food that is like putting lipstick on a pig.I think, as [former FDA commissioner] Dr David Kessler said, that this is more about theformulationthan it is the processing. Even breads or tomato sauces can be demonised as “ultra-processed”, because they have at least one of those additives. But health professionals are more worried about things like cookies’n’cream “high protein” cereals. Those are already junk foods; I’m not sure that additionally demonising them as “ultra-processed” helps consumers.You write that there’s no such thing as a super-food, and even dark chocolate should be considered candy and an occasional treat. What’s one rule that does work for making better overall choices?Try to eat really well, 80% of the time. You’re much more likely to stick with a healthy diet that has room for a few exceptions than if you hold yourself to being exclusive and restrictive. Beyond that, it’s about treating every meal as an opportunity to make good choices. Let’s say you’re the average American, eating sugary breakfast cereals. Immediately, as a nutritionist, I’m going to say eggs are better – but if you’re having eggs with cheese, sausage and bacon, that’s just a saturated fats nightmare.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnother example is coffee. In 2015, it was adopted into the US dietary guidelines as being consistent with better health, even at three to five cups a day. Most people don’t know that. But it’s not mocha-frappa-crappaccino – it’s black coffee, or with small amounts of sweetener and dairy.What have you found to be effective in changing people’s eating habits?The science alone often isn’t enough to convince people to change their eating behaviours, but eating in a way that aligns with your personal values can help, and often it happens to line up with health.If I’m given a choice between a steak or a salad, even if I’m aspiring to eat better, it’s easy to say “I can start tomorrow,” because the only person I’m hurting by choosing the steak is me. But if I understand more about food, I know that my choices are affecting others. It’s not just about cholesterol levels: there are impacts for the person working in a slaughterhouse in dangerous conditions; the production of CO2, and climate change; and the inhumane slaughter of animals.View image in fullscreenThe science alone often isn’t enough to convince people to change their eating behaviours.Photograph: Simon & SchusterThere’s more to nutrition than knowing about the biochemical pathways. If you engage with animal rights, human labour issues, the environment and all the different things that food is connected to, it can be easier to make the behaviour change and maintain it: “I did this for a reason, and I can keep doing it.”Your 2023 study,comparing vegan and omnivore diets in 22 pairs of identical twins, showed wide-ranging, conclusive benefits for the vegan group. Does that mean, in an ideal world, wewould all be vegans?Not necessarily. French fries, Oreos and soda are all vegan, but not nutritious. Also, the term “vegan” can be very polarising. The alternative term “plant-based” is now being used instead, including for packaged foods that aren’t necessarily healthy for you.I’ve lately transitioned to recommending a “whole-food, plant-rich” diet, which I hope will be interpreted as rich in flavour and variety but not exclusively plants, or necessarily vegan. If people would just eat more plants, that would address most issues.Ten years ago, the Culinary Institute of America came up with this concept of the “protein flip”, making vegetables, grains and beans the center of the plate, then adding a little bit of meat: a couple of strips of chicken, not a whole breast. That gets rid of the polarisation, of vegans versus carnivores, and even brings people together. You’d have a bigger global impact getting omnivores to eat half as much meat than you would from doubling the number of vegans.Tell me about your time on the 2025dietaryguidelinesadvisorycommittee. How did you feel when your report was dismissed?Twenty of us volunteered for 10 hours a week, for two years, and produced a 400-page report and a 1,000-page supplementary report. We handed it in in December 2024, just as the administration was handed over to Trump; almost immediately, after Robert F Kennedy Jr took over, he said: “I’m not using any of this.” We were devastated. Like, you’ve got to be kidding me – we had each put in 1,000 hours! We were well aware that we were an advisory committee, and that the government rarely takesallof the advice, but, in more than 20 years, it’s never been completely dismissed.double quotation markPersonally, I have been very vocal: we were slanderedPersonally, I have been very vocal: we were slandered. The government said we had “conflicts of interest”. Technically, that is true: among the 20 of us, there was a long list – for example, one of my 25 studies was funded by Beyond Meat – but many were very benign, and decades ago, all of them had been reported and made public before we did our work. In the committee that replaced us, five of the nine advisers had direct ties to meat and dairy, and stronger conflicts. The hypocrisy was just mind-boggling.Even more heinous, in my opinion, was that they dismissed our report for using a “health equity” lens, which they said was not appropriate for science. We were tasked with doing that: these were the dietary guidelines for all Americans, not white Americans, so we tried to address any possible differences related to race and ethnicity, or socioeconomic position. Because of the limited available data, I remember making only one substantive change on that basis, and it had to do with dairy consumption for non-white people. We didn’t demonise dairy, though I know it pissed off the industry; we simply changed the wording to suggest it wasn’t necessary to a healthy diet, to acknowledge the differences for racial groups. My experience of the government was that there was repression of science, racism and hypocrisy.What do you make of theguidelinesultimately produced byKennedy’s replacement committee?Most of them were fine. They do include recommendations based on solid science, many carried forward from the past: don’t eat too many calories; have veggies, fruit and whole grains; limit added sugar. But in our report, the most consistent finding was to replace red and processed red meat with beans, peas and lentils. The new committee replaced that with advice to prioritise protein at every meal, including red meat, and put a steak alongside the food pyramid. It was a slap in the face.Beans, beans, the magical fruit: how healthy are they really?Read moreBut the difficulties go beyond politics – it’s the food industry, lobbying, marketing, social media, all causing more confusion. Although I wish there was less misinformation, it means I have job security forever.With so many structural barriers to healthy eating, is there any hope for widespread change?I’ve been convinced that people aren’t widely going to go back to scratch-cooking, so I’ve shifted my research to institutional food settings. I think I can have the biggest impact by trying to work with chefs on making the default choices healthier, and improving the menus offered by universities, hospitals, senior centres, prisons and the military.We’re going to see how this plays out over the next decade in schools. The current administration has instructed schools to get rid of all UPFs [ultra-processed foods], but schools will say: “You don’t give us enough money for real food.” The government will have to force the industry to make better options and charge reasonable prices; give the schools more money; or, hopefully, both. It costs a lot more to eat well, and it takes more time, but the obvious answer is that our kids are worth it.I’m actually pretty optimistic. The food environment is so obscene, in so many places, that there is an emerging counter-movement, which I hope my book contributes to.Food Sense: What to Eat and Whyby Christopher Gardner is out now in the US and published in the UK on 15 OctoberExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyDeep diveFoodHealthRobert F Kennedy JrNutritionUltra-processed foodsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remain
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remain
Content: Research workers in a lab in Irkutsk, Russia.Photograph: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/APView image in fullscreenResearch workers in a lab in Irkutsk, Russia.Photograph: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/APAI (artificial intelligence)ExplainerCould AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remainIan SampleScience editorWed 14 Oct 2026 13.34 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his annual speech on threats to the nation, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of the UK’s intelligence service,MI5, warned that AI had the potential to “change the stakes” on existing and even new bioweapons. Here we look at how AI might help in the development of bioweapons and the hurdles that remain.How could AI help people make bioweapons?It depends on who wants to make them. One risk is the rogue, unskilled bad actor or terrorist group that works from a garage laboratory. AI chatbots could help them skill up, by compiling relevant information, planning experiments and troubleshooting problems. It’s likely the work would focus on using existing pathogens and toxins.The other risk comes from well-resourced organisations and nation states that have plenty of skilled scientists, high containment laboratories and all of the equipment and reagents needed to work on bioweapons safely. AI tools could help researchers identify genetic tweaks to make existing pathogens more lethal, for example. This is the more immediate concern, according to Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London. “Here, AI does not remove the need for expertise, it amplifies expertise that is already there,” she says.A more distant risk comes from highly skilled groups using AI to design completely new pathogens and toxins that are resistant to drugs or have no antidotes.Have people tried using AI to make bioweapons?Last year, police in India uncovered a suspected bioterrorism plot in which a doctor and several others drew on AI chatbot queries and AI-driven search, allegedly to help them make ricin, a deadly toxin, using kitchen tools. It is unclear whether the AI’s responses helped, but other accounts suggest the tools can provide relevant and dangerous information.The AI company Anthropic raised further concerns in September when itreportedfive cases of scientists in unnamed countries trying to use its Claude chatbot for what may have been dangerous work on viruses or toxins. One red flag, the company said, was that after being blocked, the scientists found workarounds.UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing InstituteRead moreIn one case, Anthropic said researchers used the chatbot to plan experiments that would introduce mutations in a highly pathogenic bird flu virus to make it adapt and spread more easily in mammals. The work, and the other cases, could signify attempts to make pathogens more dangerous, but such studies are also done in legitimate labs to help researchers spot future pandemics and develop vaccines and drugs to treat disease.What else has raised concerns?A flurry of studies has shown how AI tools can provide potentially dangerous information on bioweapons. In arecent exerciseat MIT, non-science students were asked if they could get an AI chatbot to help them unleash a pandemic. Within an hour, the chatbots listed four potential pandemic pathogens, explained how to make them from synthetic DNA, and supplied names of DNA synthesis companies that were unlikely to screen their orders. It is easier said than done, however.In another case, the Stanford University researcher Dr David Relman described how an AI explained how to modify a pathogen to make it resistant to treatment. Another scientist revealed that an AI chatbot had explained how to use a weather balloon to release biological weapons from the sky.The dual-use nature of biological research can make it hard to distinguish valuable work that could protect health from attempts to develop bioweapons. In 2025, scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratorytrained an AIto predict how exceptionally potent neurotoxins from marine snails latch on to human cells, work that could help in the development of antidotes. But the US government became concerned when Chinese researchers drew on the work to develop their own tool todesign new toxins. The Chinese researchers said the work was aimed solely at developing drugs.In April, scientists raised further concerns when they madethe first viruses designed by AI. The viruses are a particular type that only invade bacteria, and the work could lead to new medicines, but experts warned that it raised “urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions”.What hurdles make it difficult?Most work on bioweapons is beyond the reach of unskilled groups: as well as being highly technical, it is extremely dangerous. While AI chatbots might be prompted to give information on bioweapons, a list of instructions is not enough. “Information is only one part of the problem,” says Lentzos. “Tacit expertise, access to biological materials and equipment, experimental validation, scale-up and delivery all remain substantial barriers.”Sonia Ben Ouagrham-Gormley, the deputy director of the biodefense programme at George Mason University in Virginia says tacit knowledge – the unwritten knowhow that an AI is unlikely to help with – has been key in the success of historical state-run bioweapons programmes.Prof Martin Pačesa at the University of Zurich said access to material was critical. “Any graduate physicist could sketch up plans for a potentially more effective nuclear bomb, but where is he going to get a lump of uranium from? Same for bioweapons. If you have access to material and facilities capable of producing them, then AI is not going to make too much difference if you want to do harm.”What extra measures are needed?Some AI companies are taking steps to prevent people from using their tools to develop bioweapons, but the majority are not announcing what, if anything, they are doing, says Prof Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We have no formal government policies in place in any country yet to protect against this kind of misuse,” he says.He wants formal independent evaluations of new AI models before they are released, with any dangers eliminated before the models are made public. And high-risk biological data, such as information on how pathogens might spread more easily, should be restricted. Meanwhile, companies that make genetic material for researchers must screen orders to ensure they are not for the creation of novel, highly dangerous viruses. Some screening already happens, but it is largely voluntary, and can be sidestepped if researchers use AI to design new, harmful genetic sequences that companies are not checking for.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChatbotsInfectious diseasesMI5AnthropicUK security and counter-terrorismBiologyexplainersShareReuse this content

title: For the future of green politics, look beyond the Green party | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Environmentalists of all political hues must find the language and ideas that turn passion for climate action into impetus, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Environmentalists of all political hues must find the language and ideas that turn passion for climate action into impetus, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Climate protesters outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, London, 6 October 2026.Photograph: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenClimate protesters outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, London, 6 October 2026.Photograph: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionClimate science scepticism and denialFor the future of green politics, look beyond the Green partyZoe WilliamsEnvironmentalists of all political hues must find the language and ideas that turn passion for climate action into impetusWed 14 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTShareThe future of Green politics is under constant discussion after theHolborn and St Pancras byelection, but a much heavier clash – in meaning, symbolism and portent – happened earlier this summer, in King’s Lynn and West Norfolk. The council declared a climate emergency in 2021, along with hundreds of others, and while it was under Conservative control. It is now controlled by independents, and a Reform UK councillor, Austen Moore, moved to scrap the declaration.It was the end of June, and the meeting had to be called off, because of the extreme heat in the King’s Lynn council chamber. A lot of people paused to grimly remark on that irony, but not Moore, who simply rescheduled the motion for the following week, where it was voted down (by 33 to seven). A local scientist and member of Extinction Rebellionliveblogged that debate, adding helpful maps, such as how much of the county was already below the annual flood level – most of it, including King’s Lynn itself. If this all sounds like a cheerful take home, numerous other Reform-led councils have had the same debate and Reform has prevailed. Their arguments can be terrifyingly illiterate. In Kent, councillor Linden Kemkaran asserted that climate change is fine because the worldwas warmer in Roman times, and as “carbon dioxide … is a trace gas essential for life on Earth”, to try to cut carbon emissions would itself be dangerous.If you’re waiting for reality to knock some sense into politics, you will wait too long. There is no heatwave, no flood, no El Niño, no omnicrisis, that will divert rightwing populism from its crusade against action on climate.The question isn’t what the Green party alone could do to create an eco-populist wave of equal volume. A party that could single-handedlyrepresent the 68% of peoplewho want action on climate change doesn’t exist in modern British politics. The question is, how do you turn that strength of feeling into something more concrete, so it isn’t constantly being ram-raided by unshameable, unscientific chancers? Environmentalists in every party, leaders of every party (apart from the Conservatives, who seem hellbent on chasing Reform, despite thestated valuesof their supporters), need to find the language and ideas that turn passion for the environment into impetus.In theirrecent report, Caroline Lucas and the green philosopher Rupert Read make the case for “eco-popularism” rather than eco-populism: a way of thinking that doesn’t try to hotwire its way into people’s emotional circuitry with invigorating binaries, but, rather, describes actions that would genuinely change lives for the better, and therefore be popular.Rightwing populists have a set of arguments against climate action that are taking hold more generally and are self-fulfilling: the more they’re repeated, the more they win at local level, the more people come to believe that these views are generally held. Those narratives are that climate action of any sort – be it ultra-low emission zones, 15-minute cities or, most importantly, net zero – is too expensive at this time; that net zero itself is a luxury belief of the comfortable elite who don’t care about ordinary people’s living conditions (Lucas and Read paraphrase from aNigel Farage columnlast year).This so-called “Manichean” framing, the noble masses betrayed by a corrupt elite, is dog obvious, but to point to Farage and say “you, the guy in receipt of £5m from a non-domiciled crypto billionaire,you’rerepresenting the masses against the elites?” is tempting but fruitless. No case for climate action will take hold unless it addresses the conditions that populists exploit – the cost of living, of course, but also the sense of precariousness and active fear of the future that climate events intensify.A prime minister freezing bus fares or taking the VAT off heating doesn’t address those brute realities and deep anxieties: if anything, it shores up a sense that central government is no longer capable of building the resilience and adaptation a chaotic world demands. People need to know there’s a plan for cheaper, greener energy, food security and extreme weather events. Local, tangible actions should be supported, broadcast and celebrated, in political debate and in the media; a discussion held in abstract terms of global patterns and borderless looming disaster doesn’t just foster despair. It plays back into the hands of populists, whose incredibly proximal enemies – small boats, asylum seekers – and standing street armies create the opposite impression, of agency and might. It doesn’t matter that it’s specious and vindictive – it matters that it lands and there is no answering call to arms. One of the many paradoxes of the climate debate is that the far right talks as though disaster is not real, but acts as though it’s imminent. The left does the opposite, talking of catastrophe but acting as if there’s time to lose.Without a change of direction, even those of us who are constitutionally not susceptible to rightwing populism will still give in to its echo, which is hopelessness. Coherence is desperately needed: to promise defence spending at the expense of heat pumps, or high-quality jobs with the downside of new fossil-fuel exploration, is simply to reinforce a sense of impotence, nationally and individually.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKing’s Lynn and West Norfolk’s debate in July had an interesting pivot from Reform: they had started to magpie the language of “resilience building”, in place of climate action. But they didn’t mean it to describe peat and wildlife restoration, or food cooperatives, or retrofitted housing, or community-owned wind power. They weren’t interested in solar panels or sustainable drainage or civic infrastructure. It was the broadest possible false promise: spend less on climate, therefore less has been spent, therefore your community is more resilient. Councillors from all the other parties united to defeat them, and politics national and local can learn from that unity; but no party can afford to wait for an opponent to unite against.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: In Germany the mood is dark. But the Weimar narrative is a far right trap | Klaus Brinkbäumer | The Guardian
description: The final season of the TV epic Babylon Berlin is taking us back to 1933. Our confidence is falling apart, but that’s where the parallels end, says the German journalist Klaus Brinkbäumer
Author: Klaus Brinkbäumer
Headline: The final season of the TV epic Babylon Berlin is taking us back to 1933. Our confidence is falling apart, but that’s where the parallels end, says the German journalist Klaus Brinkbäumer
Content: Liv Lisa Fries as Charlotte Ritter and Volker Bruch as Gereon Rath in Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Christine Schroeder/X Filme CreaView image in fullscreenLiv Lisa Fries as Charlotte Ritter and Volker Bruch as Gereon Rath in Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Christine Schroeder/X Filme CreaOpinionGermanyIn Germany the mood is dark. But the Weimar narrative is a far right trapKlaus BrinkbäumerThe final season of the TV epic Babylon Berlin is taking us back to 1933. Our confidence is falling apart, but that’s where the parallels endWed 14 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 06.48 EDTShareThere is one experience we in Germany can all find mildly satisfying this autumn, as we watch the dark and terrifyingfinal season of the hit TV series Babylon Berlin. We know everything those fearless (a few of them) or frightened (many more) and opportunistic (the majority) people on the screen do not. We know their future.Made by the public broadcaster ARD, Babylon Berlin has run for over 10 years, brilliantly fictionalising howGermanysleepwalked into nazism and the second world war. The fifth and last season begins in January 1933 with Adolf Hitler appointedReichskanzler.Our funny and beautiful police detective superheroine Charlotte Ritter and the also beautiful, less funny and slightly more dubious detective Gereon Rath – both fictional – are still arguing and falling in and out of love as they chase criminals and Nazis, who are becoming synonymous. Berlin is still singing, dancing. loving. Newspapers are still being printed. Trains still run. The Jewish lawyer Hans Litten – a historical figure – still believes in German laws and German integrity (the real Litten ended up killing himself in Dachau in 1938).Watching the show 93 years after the events being depicted, I constantly want to shout at the screen: turn left here – you can kill Hitler at this dinner, and the Reichstag won’t burn, and it will all end differently. Wake up, I want to scream at the opportunistic majority – don’t you understand what is happening?They don’t, of course. They turn the other way and fail to kill Hitler. Because facts are facts. The dramatists are accurately describing February 1933 as the month in which German society was radically torn apart at an extraordinary speed because of mistakes made by party leaders and others who could still have stopped it all. ⁠View image in fullscreenThe Nazis take hold in Babylon Berlin’s fifth season.Photograph: Frédéric Batier/X Filme CreativeThe timing could hardly be more apt. Babylon Berlin began streaming in 2017, the year the extreme-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) entered the Bundestag for the first time with 12.6 % of the vote. Nine years on, the AfD has become my country’s dominant political force. In September it won 44% of the vote in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and 38.3% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the latter contest, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU dropped to 4.9% and didn’t even garner enough votes to enter the state parliament – an unprecedented humiliation.It is, therefore, quite tempting to watch Babylon Berlin and see ourselves in those historic times. But does it make sense? It does, but not in the way you might expect.There are not millions of desperate unemployed people on today’s German streets, nor paramilitary armies fighting heated battles. There is no Versailles trauma and the last global financial crisis was in 2008. There is no German president systematically replacing parliamentary government with emergency rule.The German men’s football team coach, Jürgen Klopp, recentlyadvised the nation to look at its strengthsrather than constantly stare at what is not working, so let’s start there. Germany has a strong constitutional court system and powerful federal states; it has, with help from its partners, created and maintained European integration, along with an established democratic culture and institutions designed explicitly because of the lessons of Weimar. Our European Germany in 2026 is not Weimar Germany in 1933.But there is another connection between Babylon Berlin and us as German spectators today – an echo that is more subtle and more interesting. It lies in this conviction that everything is falling apart. Here the wonderfully tongue-breaking termselbsterfüllende Prophezeiung(self-fulfilling prophecy) comes into play.Germany excels at the one thing no country should aspire to be good at. We are constantly describing ourselves as a country in terminal decline. Just spend an evening watching political talkshows or listening to people around you, and you will conclude that we are witnessing the final collapse of a failed state.The trains are all late. Bridges and streets are crumbling. Schools are failing and German childrenlagging behind in Pisa rankings.Bureaucracy is suffocating business and taxes are sky-high, plus ineffectively used. Isn’t energy too expensive and our pension system unsustainable? Immigration is out of control. Our digital transformation is a joke. And as for our car industry, that is on its knees. Plus, we lost to Ecuador and Paraguay at the World Cup. And the government cannot agree on how to fix any of this because support for the two big mainstream parties (the centre-right CDU and the centre-left SPD) is shrinking, and coalitions between parties that hate each other have become ever more complicated and fragile.Some of this is true – painfully so.View image in fullscreenAfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund embraces co-leader Alice Weidel after the party won 44% of the vote in the Saxony-Anhalt state elections, September 2026.Photograph: Thilo Schmülgen/ReutersI started writing these lines on a train from Hamburg to Tübingen via Stuttgart which was delayed by two hours. Someone in the hierarchy of Deutsche Bahn (or an AI, of course) then decided that, as we were already this late, the train would terminate in Mannheim. I had to cancel my plans and instead turn around and go back home. This is how you spend a day in modern Germany.Something much larger than my individual problem has arisen, however: our national narrative of failure has developed a disturbing relationship with reality. Germany’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed back above 3 million in September and inflation reached 3.3%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWithin the world of public broadcasting, talk about reform has been imminent for more than a decade – but instead of building the strongest and most robust system possible, which then might actually withstand the shocks, there are simply more meetings, and more reports, and more commissions of inquiry.The biggest problem, though, is Germany’s belief in the enormity of its problems. And this is exactly where Babylon Berlin and its look at 1933 becomes a more relevant companion to 2026 than the “Weimar is back” cry suggests .Democracies become vulnerable when people cease to believe that democracy can deliver. The destruction of Weimar was preceded by such a loss of faith. The circumstances were and are fundamentally different now. But one political mechanism is recognisable: the extreme right has a brief and simple story to tell.Close the borders. Deport those people we don’t know. Ignore Brussels. Stop paying Ukraine. Bring back cheap Russian energy and abolish stupid climate rules. Put Germany first.Our society seems scared and exhausted from years of crisis after crisis, and from the alarming talk of never-ending crises of tomorrow. The AfD understands this and knows how to turn every minor and unresolved problem into evidence that “das System” is rotten. My cancelled train is no longer just that, but proof of national doom. The brilliance of declinism lies in the fact that it is self-confirming. Once you have accepted that the country is collapsing, you see nothing but evidence for it.Would we recognise the end of our democracy if it were happening today, and to us? Or, instead, would we recognise the strength of our democracy if it were not ending?There is a danger in catastrophising so much that we cease to notice resilience, and progress, and that many things work just fine. German angst becomes German cynicism; cynicism turns to contempt; and, finally, contempt will make the AfD’s promise of destruction sound like the renewal we all need.We can and must tell the other, true story, of a country that has found trusted friends and partners and hence a peace that has lasted for 80 years, and economic and political, cultural and scientific successes most nations dream of – even in football (although it has become increasingly difficult to remember those days).This is not 1933 revisited, but it is a serious moment. And a good moment to for a reminder that, in dangerous times, a democratic coalition needs to govern as decisively, effectively and empathetically as it possibly can.Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is a podcast and TV host in Germany and has published nine booksExplore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: Jason Wilcox: ‘best eyes’ at Manchester United or promoted too far and too fast?  | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Director of football is tarnished by his recruitment record and Amorim’s tenure but has received glowing review from Ratcliffe
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Director of football is tarnished by his recruitment record and Amorim’s tenure but has received glowing review from Ratcliffe
Content: Jason Wilcox (left) with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who once said: ‘When I listen to Jason, I get what he’s saying.’Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJason Wilcox (left) with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who once said: ‘When I listen to Jason, I get what he’s saying.’Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedJason Wilcox: ‘best eyes’ at Manchester United or promoted too far and too fast?Director of football is tarnished by recruitment record and Amorim stint but has received glowing review from aboveWill UnwinWed 14 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLisandro Martínez is not naive. At 28, he has experienced plenty in football and knows the causes of success and failure. He has aWorld Cup winner’s medal, whereas Jason Wilcox has overseen the latest period of mediocrity at Manchester United, during which the focus has fallen more onthe team’s performancesthan the wider reasons behind it.Martínez was not solely speaking for himself when, after United’s defeat at Atlético Madrid, he strongly criticised Wilcox. His views are shared by others at United frustrated by the output from above and who “expect” more from a director of football. Wilcox knows he is under pressure because the inadequate results cannot all be pinned on Michael Carrick, who is working with a squad unable to cope with the rigours of challenging at the top of the Premier League and facing Europe’s elite.Manchester United teammates widely share Martínez view that Wilcox is failingRead moreClubs live and die by their recruitment, and United sitting 13th in the Premier League after one win from six matches does not suggest the squad is in rude health. A sporting director, like a referee, goes unnoticed when performing well but it has reached the point at United where players can take no more.Three years at Ajax taught Martínez about football structure. The Dutch clubs mix homegrown players with imports from around the world, many of whom are sold on for large profits. Wilcox would struggle to make the case that any of his recruits, with the possible exception of Senne Lammens, have markedly increased in value. There are many sporting directors more adept at finding undervalued talent. Wilcox was offered the chance to sign Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest a year before the midfieldersigned for Manchester City, but decided against moving for a player who continued to grow in value and was eventually out of United’s price range. If Sir Jim Ratcliffe is so eager to run United as a business, questioning why the outlay on players leads to so little return would be a sensible starting point.Wilcox arrived at Old Trafford in April 2024 after less than a year as the director of football in the Championship with Southampton, who gave him his first executive role in senior football. Before that, the former Blackburn and Leeds winger had worked in youth development, eventually becoming Manchester City’s academy director, and was well respected, but whether this was sufficient grounding for leading United’s football operation was debatable. Wilcox oversaw at City the emergence of a glut of talent, including Phil Foden, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers. Some of those who have dealt with him feel a senior academy position is where his skills lie.A key reason why he was brought back to his native north-west by United was Omar Berrada’s appointment as chief executive. The pair worked together at City and there was a high degree of mutual respect, supported bythe – now tainted– achievements of the club. Wilcox was given the title technical director and was supposed to work under the experienced sporting director Dan Ashworth, who held similar roles at Brighton and Newcastle but lasted only five months under Ratcliffe, earning Wilcox a rapid promotion.View image in fullscreenMichael Carrick with Jason Wilcox after the former United midfielder was named the permanent head coach in May 2026.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesSome United staff in place when Wilcox arrived grew frustrated at the number of former City Football Group appointments being made. United had got plenty wrong over the years but continued to thrive in certain aspects, so trying to turn the club into a copy of one of their fiercest rivals grated.Wilcox was influential in the recruitment of Ruben Amorim, who had a specific way of playing but not the players to carry out his demands.The experiment failed, accelerated by a breakdown in relationship between the head coach and Wilcox, who did not see eye-to-eye on tactics, among other things.When it comes to players there is increasingly a focus on Premier League experience with Wilcox; this summer Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba arrived from top-flight English clubs for a combined £155m. The midfield did require an overhaul, with Casemiro leaving and Manuel Ugarte, currently injured, never reaching the requisite level. That outlay, however, meant there was no money for a left-back or backup striker, leaving fans eager for an explanation. In the defeat at Atlético, Carrick played the 20-year-old centre-back Ayden Heaven out of position to cover Luke Shaw’s latest absence, summing up the shallowness of the squad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGraphic showing Manchester United player purchases under Jason WilcoxRatcliffe, the minority owner, is on record as saying he has a lot of time for Wilcox, “When I listen to Jason speak, I get what he’s saying,” he toldthe Timesin March 2025. “He’s a warm character, he’s got a sense of humour, he knows what he’s talking about.” At matches, the pair can be often found sitting next to one another in discussion. Ratcliffe has displayed a ruthless business approach since investing in United, but removing Wilcox would be one of the more difficult personal decisions. Their relationship is strong and making a change would be bold. With finances likely to be tight in January, the planning at this stage is for next summer and who is best to navigate it.If results continue to be substandard, Ratcliffe and Berrada will be forced to consider their options. Wilcox’s bond with the pair is important but Carrick has a lot more credit in the bank with a fanbase that wields power and has strong reservations over the director of football. Removing Wilcox would be the more widely popular decision but also an acceptance of failure from the top brass. Ratcliffe once said Wilcox had the “best eyes in the club” but he cannot be blinded by the truth.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedJim RatcliffefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president accused US president of picking the other side after four years of war
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Ukrainian president accused US president of picking the other side after four years of war
Content: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham in London.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Pool/APView image in fullscreenUkraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham in London.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Pool/APUkraineVolodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink accessUkrainian president accused US president of picking the other side after four years of warDan Sabbagh,Jessica ElgotandAndrew Rothin KyivWed 14 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by theUS agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.Ahead of a meeting with prime ministerAndy Burnhamin Downing Street, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated ⁠than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, wasno longer working at speeds greater than 100mph.That effectively rendered most of the drones used byUkraineto strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukrainewithout any advance warning from the USfor a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham greeted Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warmly at No 10.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersThe two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death tollRead moreIn brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”The UK is also set to give £17m in funding towards repairs to the protective roof over the destroyed Chornobyl nuclear power plant which was damaged by Russian drone strike last year.The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish Guards in full ceremonial uniform.Musk said the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | EditorialRead moreLimiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.“With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineAndy BurnhamVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and extreme comments | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Party faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist views
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Party faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist views
Content: Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, was filmed calling Asian homeowners ‘parasites’.Photograph: ITVView image in fullscreenAlan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, was filmed calling Asian homeowners ‘parasites’.Photograph: ITVReform UKReform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and extreme commentsParty faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist viewsBen QuinnPolitical correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 15.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 17.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and election candidates for the party were caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from an ITV undercover investigation that aired on Wednesday.Reform leaderNigel Faragehas postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex on Thursday morning as the party tries to contain the fallout expected to come from further revelations in the coming days. That will include revelations from undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters.Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites,” and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.View image in fullscreenChris Whelan resigned from Reform UK on 12 October.Photograph: ITVFeeney won seats on Birmingham city council and Solihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”.Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues.Feeney was filmed with other candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, talking about where a local mosque might be built. After they make extreme racist comments in the discussion, Feeney says: “Oh god, we’re all going to end up in the papers”.Reform donations scandal: the final blow for Farage? – The LatestRead moreChris Whelan announced he had resigned from Reform on 12 October “on personal and health grounds”. Campbell is still in post.Dean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed separately making a range of comments during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection, including when he discussed what he would do with illegal immigrants crossing the Channel.Reform has been attempting to pre-empt the impact from the ITV investigation, which will potentially be at its most damaging when footage from inside Reform’s London HQ airs.The party used a statement issued on Wednesday night to accuse ITV and Hardcash Productions of “extreme methods of deception”.“They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees,” it said.The party said that this came at a time when Farage and other members of Reform were “being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation”.View image in fullscreenDean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed making comments about illegal immigrants during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection.Photograph: ITV“They have not included this in their report, despite being on notice since March this year. There is currently an ongoing police investigation relating to security breaches against Mr Farage, as is well known,” it added.Reform said that not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK, adding: “Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.”The latest crisis to hit the party comes at a time when it has been stalling in the polls and faces problems including the fallout from a different undercover investigation which filmed senior officials discussing a potential way tosecure foreign donations to the party.The outcome is also awaited of a parliamentary standards commissioner investigation into whether Farage should have declared a £5m gift from thecrypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.Bridget Phillipson MP, chair of the Labour party, said: “The extreme racism and appalling behaviour exposed by this investigation is truly sickening. Nigel Farage can’t shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples. Every Reform councillor, council candidate or party member found to have made such despicable comments must be thrown out of Reform UK immediately.”Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on 18 October at 10.20pm on ITV1, ITVX, STV & STV PlayerExplore more on these topicsReform UKLocal governmentNigel FarageLocal politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK hospitality sector to offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people out of work | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Restaurants and pubs such as Nando’s and Fuller’s will create placements for 18- to 24-year-olds under DWP-backed scheme
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Restaurants and pubs such as Nando’s and Fuller’s will create placements for 18- to 24-year-olds under DWP-backed scheme
Content: The scheme is intended to help young people ‘get their first step on the ladder’ and build their careers.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe scheme is intended to help young people ‘get their first step on the ladder’ and build their careers.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesYouth unemploymentUK hospitality sector to offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people out of workRestaurants and pubs such as Nando’s and Fuller’s will create placements for 18- to 24-year-olds under DWP-backed schemeAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBars, clubs and restaurants will offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years in an effort to give them a first step on the ladder into work.The move comes before the publication of a report on Neets by the former health secretary Alan Milburn, who has warned that the number of young people not in work or education in the UKcould rise to 1.25 millionover the next five years unless ministers intervene.His full review into Britain’s crisis in youth unemployment, including recommendations to the government about how to tackle the crisis, is expected soon after the autumn budget on 28 October.Working with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), hospitality businesses including the restaurant chains Wagamama, Nando’s andBurger King, the hotel chain Premier Inn and pub chains including Fuller’s and Mitchells & Butlers will offer Neets aged 18 to 24 placements of up to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.The initiative, which will be launched by Andy Burnham during a visit to a hospitality venue on Thursday, comes after the DWPannounced a similar scheme for retailersincluding Marks & Spencer, Asda, Pets at Home and the John Lewis Partnership last month.The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said the scheme would help young people “get their first step on the ladder” and build their careers. “With the UK employment rate now the second highest in the G7, this will unlock 100,000 jobs and connect young people with employers ready to take them on and help them build a brighter future,” he said.Lucy Powell, the education secretary, is expected to announce a review of school exclusion changes, after research showed that students who are persistently absent from school are nearly four times more likely to end up unemployed and not in education or training.A consultation will gather views on measures to support students at risk of exclusion, improve integration into the classroom and help children stay engaged in the classroom.Powell said: “Absence and exclusion are too often a path to disengagement, with increased risks of becoming Neet. Too many young people who fall out of education risk being permanently left on the sidelines of work and opportunity.”Milburn has signalled that Britain’s benefits system should be overhauled, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships. Ministers are understood to be considering sweeping changes to the welfare system, includingscrapping a critical disability benefitfor under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.Milburn has previously argued that a national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work.The chancellor, John Healey, has indicated a readiness to curtail the government’s rising benefits bill, while McFadden has said there isa moral and economic caseto shake up the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has made demands for cuts to welfare a central plank of her attacks on the government, telling Burnham in prime minister’s questions (PMQs) on Wednesday that he should cut welfare to fund higher defence spending.But ministers will be wary of going head to head with Labour MPs, and will hope to avoid a repeat of thewelfare rebellionthat forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentLabourHospitality industryBurger KingMitchells & ButlersUnemploymentYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel blocks construction of key Gaza base created by Trump peace board | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Israel has not permitted US-led project to house 150 international troops to move forward
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: Exclusive: Israel has not permitted US-led project to house 150 international troops to move forward
Content: Trump, with Board of Peace representatives, shows the group’s founding charter at a meeting at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump, with Board of Peace representatives, shows the group’s founding charter at a meeting at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesUS foreign policyIsrael blocks construction of key Gaza base created by Trump peace boardExclusive: Israel has not permitted US-led project to house 150 international troops to move forwardAram Rostonin WashingtonWed 14 Oct 2026 15.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.In early August, the Board of Peace, the international organization authorized in 2025 by the UN and chaired by the US president, issuedits first construction contract for Gaza: Louisiana-based Arkel International would construct a military outpost for 150 international troops that would be the vanguard of an international stabilization force.Two months later,Israelhas still not permitted the contract to move forward, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Contractors and trucks are not being allowed to cross into Gaza and begin the work. “Israel won’t open the border,” they said.Trump’s Board of Peace plans to grant itself sweeping immunity, documents showRead moreA Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment. The Israeli Defense Forces and the Israeli government declined tocomment.Israel’s war in Gaza is one of the eight wars Trump claims to have resolved. Helisted it again last week in a screedon social media, protesting that it was unfair he had not won the Nobel peace prize.The Board of Peace, formed in the wake of an October 2025 ceasefire inGaza, is central to Trump’s claims to have ended the conflict.Arkel’s planned “mission support site temporary outpost” is decidedly rudimentary: a fortified position of about 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site that was once part of the controversial and now defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, according to the person familiar with the matter. The US-backed GHF operated in Gaza from May 2025 till October 2025 to deliver aid protected by private contractors.The base would host short rotating deployments of a well-armed force of 150 troops in Gaza, the person said. They would come from a larger component of 500 sent already from Morocco and Kosovo.But without this contract, the source said, the rest of the Board of Peace program cannot launch. Israel’s refusal to allow Arkel, the contractor, to build the base, essentially cuts the Board of Peace off at the legs.“You can’t get in without [an international stabilization force (ISF)]. You can’t rebuild,” the person said. “There’s no security. There’s no deliveries of construction equipment. You can’t even start putting utilities. You can’t start putting in basic life-support facilities you know because without the ISF you can’t go in.”The person familiar with the matter said the Board of Peace believes that Israel’s government will let the project proceed after the Israeli elections, which are scheduled for 27 October.The controversial Board of Peace has a unique structure. Trump is designated as chair for life. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is an executive board member, as is real estate developer Steve Witkoff, whom Trump has appointed as a mediator in various international disputes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThough many western democracies have kept their distance from the Board of Peace, 28 countries joined as founding members earlier this year. Kushner has unveiled renderings of a futuristic vision of Gaza, where the city was envisioned as a pristine luxury waterfront resort city with hi-tech skyscrapers looking out over the Mediterranean.On 23 September the group unveiled what it said was a six-month, $2.45bn plan, as the first step towards reconstruction with a 10-year estimated cost of $71bn.There were lofty promises and requests for contributions. “Today we can point to real progress,” announced Witkoff.A US senior adviser to the board, Aryeh Lightstone, announced a new fund would be started. “Your high net-worth donations will go directly to the Palestinian people,” he said. Lightstone has traveled in Trump circles since the president’s first term. He officiated as a rabbi at the 2020 wedding of Trump adviser Stephen Miller to Katie Miller.Israel has continued strikes in Gaza since the October ceasefire, killing about1,400people over that time, according to Gaza health authorities.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyIsraelGazaDonald TrumpPalestineTrump administrationMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Stopping Pip for ADHD or autism would not make big savings, says thinktank | Benefits | The Guardian
