description: Resolution Foundation says ‘crude changes’ to benefits system would probably make it harder for people to work
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Resolution Foundation says ‘crude changes’ to benefits system would probably make it harder for people to work
Content: The number of Pip claimants has gone up rapidly in recent years, particularly among younger people with mental health issues, ADHD or autism.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe number of Pip claimants has gone up rapidly in recent years, particularly among younger people with mental health issues, ADHD or autism.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesBenefitsStopping Pip for ADHD or autism would not make big savings, says thinktankResolution Foundation says ‘crude changes’ to benefits system would probably make it harder for people to workPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorWed 14 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBanning people with anxiety, ADHD or autism from claiming disability benefits would not deliver major financial savings and would probably make it harder for them to get or stay in a job and participate in society, a leading thinktank has warned.TheResolution Foundationsaid any proposals to make certain mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions ineligible for personal independence payments (Pip) would be “crude changes” aimed at hitting unrealistic savings targets.But it warned that Pip was “failing on several fronts” and called for a major overhaul to keep a lid on costs – currently rising at an “unsustainable” rate – and restore public trust in a benefit widely seen as unfair and dysfunctional.Young people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’Read moreAbout £4.4bn a year could be saved if Pip support was better targeted, it said. Cash support could be removed from an estimated one in six working-age Pip claimants (670,000) who report having no extra costs as a result of their disability.However, it added that any reforms should proceed with caution because of the success of Pip in ensuring high numbers of disabled and ill people were able to participate in “economically valuable” activities, such as work, caring, training or volunteering, that they would not be able to do otherwise.Official concern over Pip has soared in recent years, in part because of the rapidly rising number of claimants, particularly among young people, with much of that sharp increase linked to claims for mental health, ADHD and autism.Spending on Pip in England and Wales has risen in real terms by 183% since it was introduced in 2014. This year the bill is expected to be £28bn, rising to £34bn by the end of the decade, according to official forecasts.Attempts by the previous Labour administration under Keir Starmer to push through £5bn of crude savings to Pip collapsed last year amid a rebellion of backbench MPs. His successor, Andy Burnham, has said renewed attempts to reform benefits would not involve “crude cuts”.Welfare officials, who are awaiting anofficial review of Pip by welfare minister Stephen Timmsand the Milburn review of the youth jobs crisis, are understood to beconsidering proposalsto exclude under-25s from the Pip system.Pip has also found itself at the heart of culture war rows, with some, such asthe Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, arguing it should not be paid to claimants with so-called “mild” conditions that were not disabling or likely to incur higher daily living costs.The Resolution Foundation said attempting to link Pip awards to particular conditions was simplistic and impractical as most claimants reported multiple conditions – often combining physical, mental and behavioural conditions.Burnham has a chance to overhaul Pip. Here’s what a truly progressive system could look like | Frances RyanRead moreLindsay Judge, the thinktank’s research director, said: “Pip is a vital benefit for disabled people that enables them to participate in society and live fuller and more active lives. But the current system is failing on several fronts – claimants don’t trust it, awards don’t fully reflect the nature of disability today and spending is rising unsustainably.“As well as continuing to provide cash awards to help with ongoing additional costs, a reformed Pip system should focus on supporting disabled people to participate in society. A system more attuned to people’s needs would also mean that around one in six current Pip recipients who don’t face significant limitations or additional costs because of their disability would no longer qualify for cash support.“There is no perfect system of disability support, but one that better reflects the fact that people often have multiple and fluctuating conditions must target greater support and engagement where it’s needed, and avoid waste where it’s not.”A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “Pip is awarded based on a functional assessment that determines how a condition impacts a person’s day-to-day needs. But as the Timms Review report made clear, Pip is no longer fit for purpose and the recommendations from its final report will lay the foundation for sustainable reform.”Explore more on these topicsBenefitsMental healthNeurodiversityResolution FoundationState benefitsWelfareDisabilitynewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annually | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares
Content: OpenAI is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1.1tn.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1.1tn.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annuallyAccounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last yearRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings,according tothe Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped andhacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this monthone of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.Booming AI salaries have already had asignificant effect on housing pricesin San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIChatGPTAI (artificial intelligence)LondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand was ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Comedian faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Comedian faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women
Content: Russell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenRussell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court.Photograph: Ben Stansall/AFP/GettyUK newsRussell Brand was ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator, court toldComedian faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six womenEmine SinmazWed 14 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand was a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator who boasted about wanting to have sex with 5,000 women, a court has heard.The 51-year-old comedian is accused of having an “insatiable desire” to get what he wanted and treating women as a means to an end.He allegedly ignored one woman’s pleas to stop raping her in an assault that left her bleeding and in pain. He is also accused of having raped another woman as he told her: “Oh come on, don’t be a spoilsport.”Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.Wearing a black pinstripe suit, a black and white shirt and a necktie, Brand stood in the dock at Southwark crown court in London on Wednesday as the prosecution opened its case.The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, told jurors: “The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant’s career. Offending took place in a number of locations: a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle in a bar and at his home address.“Some of the women involved protested and said no, others had no opportunity to protest and no opportunity to react to his advances but that didn’t matter to the defendant. Regardless of who they were and what they said or did, Russell Brand was not deterred.“His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious. He could be nice when he wanted to be – funny undoubtedly, charming, likable even when he wanted something in return, but then demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite, childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met.“He was ruthless, he was calculated and manipulative, and the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator.”She said Brand had told a former flatmate, Mark Pinheiro, that he wanted to sleep with 5,000 women in his lifetime and had strategies to achieve that aim, allegedly saying: “All you have to do is tell them what they need to hear.”The court heard the earliest allegation dated back to the 1999 Labour party conference in Bournemouth, when Brand was not yet famous. He allegedly raped a woman at a hotel after meeting her at a fringe cabaret show where he was performing.He is accused of stripping off his clothes and performing Basil Fawlty-style silly walks like an ostrich before the attack.“She remembers the weight of him on top of her, she couldn’t move, she was finding it hard to breathe, but she recalls trying not to let him kiss her, and saying ‘no’,” the prosecutor said.“She knows that he groped her, was touching her, he grabbed her breasts, he was trying to kiss her, he was putting his fingers in her mouth and doing things with his tongue that were horrible, like a lizard.”Brand allegedly raped her without a condom, before telling her: “Don’t worry, I get tested regularly for STDs, I don’t have anything.” He then behaved as if nothing had happened, wrote down his email address, and said he had to get back to his mother.View image in fullscreenA court artist sketch by Elizabeth Cook of Russell Brand appearing in the dock at Southwark crown court.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAHe denied the allegation in a prepared statement to police, saying he had had sexual encounters in countless locations and scenarios, often with people he had just met.Giving evidence on Wednesday afternoon, Pinheiro, who had also performed in the cabaret, told jurors that Brand had said he was “going to go and get laid” when their final show ended. He added that Brand appeared “discombobulated” the next day and was eager to leave Bournemouth. Pinheiro said Brand eventually told him about having had sex with a woman, and said he made the comment: “I think I may have gone a bit too far.”Under cross-examination by Brand’s defence barrister Ian Winter KC, Pinheiro was questioned about the reliability of his account but insisted he had merely described Brand’s behaviour.Brand’s celebrity status was growing by the time of the second allegation in 2001, as was his “sense of entitlement to have what he wanted whenever he wanted it”, the prosecutor said.The second complainant was working at MTV when she offered to show Brand to the toilets where he allegedly indecently assaulted her. Brand is accused of grabbing the woman by the forearm and trying to pull her into the male toilets. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: “Please, please come in – oh go on.”She was shocked and mentioned what had happened when she returned from the toilet but never formally reported it.The third woman had attended a friend’s birthday at a bar in Soho in London in 2004 when Brand allegedly sexually assaulted her by grabbing and squeezing her breasts with a “big, weird grin” on his face. He then grabbed her arm and pulled her into the toilets where he orally raped her, the court heard. The prosecutor said: “As she was saying: ‘What are you doing? I don’t want to do this,’ he just said: ‘Oh come on, don’t be a spoilsport. You want to.’”The fourth woman was working at a radio station when she alleged that Brand “sloppily and aggressively” kissed her and grabbed her breasts and buttocks in a sexual assault alleged to have taken place in 2004 or 2005.She pushed him away and told him to “fuck off” to which Brand sniggered. “These women meant nothing to him and perhaps he found their protestations amusing, funny?” the prosecutor said.The fifth complainant was a fan of Brand and had gone with a friend to see the comedian perform at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009. According to the woman’s friend, at the end of the show, Brand said: “If I do speak to you and ask you to come to my dressing room, please know I am not doing that to give you an autograph. I will give you an autograph, but it will be on the inside of your uterus.” He said the age range of people he would sleep with was “from 16 to death”.After the show, the woman was invited backstage and later to his dressing room, where she refused to have sex with Brand. But she did perform oral sex on him before giving him her telephone number and leaving.At a later date, she was driven to Brand’s house, where they had consensual sex before he anally raped her in an attack that left her bleeding for a few days, the court heard.The prosecutor said the woman could not speak through the pain. “She asked him to stop, at first quietly and then louder, a number of times, begging. He did not,” Karmy-Jones said. He then ordered her to “clean up the mess you have made”.Brand texted the woman the following year after seeing each other in a chance encounter in Scotland. She said she messaged Brand: “Why are you even messaging me?” and he replied: “Because you’re dirty, and I wanna push you further.”The court heard that she had replied: “I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal”, and she said Brand had replied: “I’m sorry.”The woman, the prosecutor said, spent years blaming herself for what had happened, and became extremely anxious and unwell. The final alleged victim was working at Channel 4 in 2009 when she alleges that Brand sexually assaulted her by placing his head in her groin area. She told her manager about the attack but she felt her complaint was not taken seriously.Karmy-Jones said that Brand had given prepared statements in police interviews, denying all the allegations. He said he had never engaged in nonconsensual sexual activity, and suggested accounts may have been reinvented or imagined after a documentary about his alleged sexual misconduct.Brand’s wife, Laura Gallacher, sat through the evidence on Wednesday morning. Earlier, the pair arrived at court to a crowd of reporters and photographers. “I feel blessed,” Brand told a journalist. “I feel of course concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved. That’s my prayer.”The trial before judge Mr Justice Bennathan continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s new press secretary faces scrutiny over claims to be a lawyer | US news | The Guardian
description: Katie Zacharia describes herself as a lawyer but no public record shows she has been licensed in the US states where she resided
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Katie Zacharia describes herself as a lawyer but no public record shows she has been licensed in the US states where she resided
Content: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia walks out to speak with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenWhite House press secretary Katie Zacharia walks out to speak with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APUS newsTrump’s new press secretary faces scrutiny over claims to be a lawyerKatie Zacharia describes herself as a lawyer but no public record shows she has been licensed in the US states where she residedJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonWed 14 Oct 2026 15.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. But when asked after her inaugural press briefing on Tuesday to name the state where she passed the bar exam, she replied curiously: “when I moved to China”.No public record shows she has ever been licensed to practice law in the US states where she resided, and her answer to reporters’ questions on Tuesday only deepened scrutiny.Zacharia wasn’t registered in 38 states, as well as DC and the Virgin Islands, where the state’s attorney list was publicly available, according to a review from the Guardian.After hershaky and widely panned first briefing, a reporter asked Trump which state Zacharia had passed the bar exam in. The president, who had described Zacharia as an attorney when announcing her appointment, turned to her and asked: “Which state?” She replied: “when I moved to China”.Zacharia’s law degree is real – Pepperdine Universityconfirmedshe graduated from its law school in 2011. But a degree is not a license, and no record has surfaced showing she was admitted to practice, according to the report in Popular Information.In a later statement to the press, Zacharia said she had “practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials”. The White House did not say whether she had passed a bar exam anywhere.Zacharia’sLinkedIn profilelists her as general counsel of Fix California, a conservative group founded by Ric Grenell, a longtime Trump ally and the special presidential envoy for special missions. Zacharia lived in California, but the state bar of California said it had no record of her being licensed in the state.“The State Bar of California has no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black (or Katie in both instances) having been licensed to practice law in California,” a spokesperson for the California state bar said in a statement. Black is her maiden name.“Due to confidentiality laws, the State Bar can only confirm whether someone passed the bar exam, not whether they took the bar exam,” it added.No report alleges that Zacharia has been charged with or has committed an offence.Campaign for Accountability, a non-profit watchdog organization, on Wednesday filed a complaint with the state bar of California, asking it to investigate whether Zacharia misled the public – and potentially violated state law – by describing herself as a lawyer.“In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” said Michelle Kuppersmith, the group’s executive director, in a statement.California law saysanyone “advertising or holding himself or herself out as practicing or entitled to practice law” who is not an active member of the state bar could be punished with a fine of up to $1,000 and up to one year in jail.“There is a difference between having a JD and being a lawyer, you are licensed as a lawyer by saying that you took the bar,” said Richard Painter, a university of Minnesota law professor and the former chief White House ethics lawyer under the George W Bush administration. “Calling yourself an attorney … it’s a misdemeanor at least.”Zacharia’s LinkedIn notes that she was remote while at Fix California. But Painter said that was “not relevant – you need to be a member of the bar”.The profile also says she worked as an associate at the Beijing firm Zhong Lun from 2011 to 2013. Only Chinese citizens can be licensed as lawyers in China, according to Chinese law and legal affairs websiteChina Justice Observer, though foreign staff can work at Chinese firms in other capacities.TheWashington Post,CNNand theindependent newsletter Popular Informationalso found no sign of admission elsewhere, including Texas and Washington DC, where Popular Information said she had worked. The Post found no active or expired admissions under either of her names.The press office of Gavin Newsom, California’s governor,mocked the exchangeon X, asking whether the new press secretary “appears to be a Chinese lawyer”. Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, in the meantime described her briefing performance as “tremendous” and “commanding”.Zacharia was relatively unknown when Trump announced her selection to be his next press secretarylast week, after the departure of Karoline Leavitt earlier this year. In the days since, several outlets have uncovered a series of since-deleted social media posts that promote debunked or baseless conspiracy.In a series of now-deleted social media posts on X, reviewed by the Guardian, Zachariafawnedover Tesla and Space X founder, Elon Musk.On 22 May 2022, the new press secretary described Musk, a tech billionaire and Trump ally, as “based”. She went on to explain the term was applied “when you want to recognize someone for being themselves” and “courageous and unique or not caring what others think”.In another postfrom the same year, Zacharia also responded to one user sharing a widely circulated picture of Musk and Ghislaine Maxwell, the co-conspirator of the late sex-offender Jeffrey Epstein, at the Vanity Fair Oscar party in 2014, where Zacharia wrote “oh please, he already responded to this #oldnews”.Musk has not been charged with any wrongdoing in connection with Epstein, and has denied knowing Maxwell, claiming the photo which pictures her standing close to him is because she “photobombed” him.In other now-deleted posts, also from the same period, Zachariadirectedvarious complimentary messages at Musk. “#IstandwithElon,” she wrote in one. In another shepraised himfor renouncing his support for the Democratic party and saying he would now support Republicans. “Smartest and richest man in the world right here is saying out loud what everyone else is thinking,” Zacharia wrote.However, last year Zacharia questioned whether Musk could have been trusted “from the beginning” while appearing as a guest on conservative commentator Buck Sexton’spodcast.“He’s heavily invested in China. A lot of people were questioning his allegiance to begin with. Where is his allegiance completely?” she asked on the show. In late 2025, Musk and Trump had a public falling out of the president’s sweeping domestic policy legislation. They have since reconciled and Musk, according to the New York Times, is spending record sums to help Republicans retain control of the midterm elections this cycle.The Bulwark previouslyreportedon Zacharia’s since-deleted posts where she called on the administration to “suspend habeas corpus” – the constitutional right to challenge detention before a judge.Meanwhile CNN also found now-deleted social media posts where Zacharia wrote and reshared comments thataccusedprominent political figures and Hollywood elites of pedophilia. This includes longtime Democratic operative John Podesta – who was the notable target of the debunked Pizzagate conspiracy – which alleged that several prominent Democrats were part of a child sex-trafficking ring.Explore more on these topicsUS newsShareReuse this content

title: The eyes have it: Reform politician’s ‘smart glasses’ prompt calls for ban in Westminster | Wearable technology | The Guardian
description: Jason O’Connell’s suspected use of the specs to aid his speech in Senedd reignites debate over AI-enabled devices
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Jason O’Connell’s suspected use of the specs to aid his speech in Senedd reignites debate over AI-enabled devices
Content: Reform UK politician appears to use smart glasses as teleprompter in debateWearable technologyThe eyes have it: Reform politician’s ‘smart glasses’ prompt calls for ban in WestminsterJason O’Connell’s suspected use of the specs to aid his speech in Senedd reignites debate over AI-enabled devicesRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a flowing speech packed full of precise statistics – but Jason O’Connell, aReform UKSenedd member, was not quite the gifted orator he had first appeared. The periodic flashing in his spectacles seemed to give the game away as he spoke for five minutes in the Senedd chamber without a glance at his notes.“Cardiff reviewed 192 roads, following 933 requests, and only four routes have returned to 30mph,” he said as he led the party’s charge to abolish 20mph traffic zones. “£38.3m wasted to implement this policy and up to £8.9bn in an act of economic self-harm.”It was probably no feat of memory – rather, the Reform member for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr was suspected of using smart glasses that turned his lenses into tiny teleprompters.In the days afterwards, Senedd members said the issue of smart glasses – popularised by Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta – needed to be dealt with at pace, with explicit guidance developed on their use.There was no suggestion that O’Connell’s glasses were recording. But it has prompted a fresh debate about the increasingly popular technology, with theHouse of Commonsfacing calls to ban smart glasses at Westminster.The Liberal Democrats wrote to Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, on Wednesday urging him to act amid the “increasing use of smart glasses” on the parliamentary estate. They warned that with Christmas coming, even more people could start using the AI-enabled devices in 2027.Norway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public placesRead moreThe technology has myriad implications. Anna Sabine, the Liberal Democrat spokesperson for culture, media and sport, said smart glasses could lead to debates becoming increasingly “managed”.“How much is the quality of what an MP is saying actually down to what they’re getting through the AI glasses?” she said. “It’s a really interesting question.”She said she had not yet identified anyone wearing smart glasses in parliament but added: “This is the problem: I wouldn’t necessarily know.” A law would help to keep the estate and the work MPs did “private and secure”.Sabine added: “Smart glasses can record video and take photographs discreetly … creating a particular risk to the existing rules on the parliamentary estate [limiting recording and photography].“I am regularly in meetings with documents or talking about important, private matters on behalf of my constituents. I am sure you will agree that the details of such cases should never be at risk of being shared because someone is filming or taking pictures discreetly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Because smart glasses look like ordinary glasses, and increasingly their recording indicator lights can be covered or disabled, filming could easily go unnoticed by security teams, putting private information at risk.”A spokesperson for the UK parliament said it was reviewing its policy on the use of camera-equipped smart glasses, as well as other forms of wearable technology, on the parliamentary estate.The senior deputy speaker of the House of Lords, Lord Ponsonby, told parliament last month that the review “is considering the implications of these emerging technologies and whether additional guidance is required”.He added: “This work will bring together expertise from those responsible for filming and photography policy, physical and information security, privacy and data protection compliance and accessibility and reasonable-adjustment requirements, ensuring that any future approach appropriately balances security, privacy, operational needs and accessibility considerations.”O’Connell has been contacted for comment. On Sunday heposteda picture on X of himself wearing a pair of comedy large pink glasses for a breast cancer charity, with the message: “Trialling some new glasses for the chamber this week. Apparently my last ones caused quite a stir.”Explore more on these topicsWearable technologyWelsh politicsReform UKTechnology policyHouse of CommonsPrivacyWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Throttling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holds
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Throttling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holds
Content: A Ukrainian couple and their baby daughter outside a bombed building in Kyiv on Tuesday.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APView image in fullscreenA Ukrainian couple and their baby daughter outside a bombed building in Kyiv on Tuesday.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APUkraineAnalysisIn Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death tollDan SabbaghDefence and security editorThrottling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holdsWed 14 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.55 EDTShareInUkrainethe situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a Russian missile attack in Kyiv on Wednesday.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersThe immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal withRussia.However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with theunexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.Russia has bombed twobridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy,on a visit to Londonon Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.Explore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeKyivTrump administrationForeign policyVolodymyr ZelenskyyElon MuskanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Baby review – Pearl Mackie is meticulous as an abuse survivor | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Gurpreet Kaur Bhatti’s compassionate solo play follows a young mother’s struggle to get life back on track after time behind bars
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: Gurpreet Kaur Bhatti’s compassionate solo play follows a young mother’s struggle to get life back on track after time behind bars
Content: ‘You believe me, right?’ … Pearl Mackie in Baby.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreen‘You believe me, right?’ … Pearl Mackie in Baby.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewBaby review – Pearl Mackie is meticulous as an abuse survivorBrixton House, LondonGurpreet Kaur Bhatti’s compassionate solo play follows a young mother’s struggle to get life back on track after time behind barsHolly O'MahonyWed 14 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlenty of abuse survivors don’t go on to commit terrible crimes, argues the titular Baby as she attempts to make sense of the cause-and-effect cycle that landed her in prison and saw her precious baby daughter forcibly removed. It’s a line that echoes the more merciless commentary surrounding the case of US death row inmate Christa Pike, whose failed execution last month led to global headlines.Produced by Clean Break, a theatre company built specifically for women in the sightlines of the criminal justice system, Gurpreet Kaur Bhatti’s compassionate solo play offers a holistic, cradle-to-grave look at its character’s life, while spotlighting a broken pipeline. Once you’ve fallen through the cracks and into a gutter of crime and drug dependency, it argues, it’s impossible to climb back out. Survive and you’ll become a number with a case file and a lack of agency, whose remaining years will be spent pinballing between probation officers and case workers.Baby is played meticulously by Doctor Who’s Pearl Mackie, who carries her character from a precocious child who is top of her class – despite playing carer to her mother behind the scenes – to a young woman who, having unknowingly got involved with an older criminal, ends up behind bars, then struggles to get back on track.View image in fullscreenMeticulous … Pearl Mackie.Photograph: Helen MurrayLike Pike, Baby may not fare well in the court of public opinion, but nor would a formal hearing be likely to present her full story, which she relays to us directly. “You believe me, right?” she implores us, eyes wide. We do.Though we see brief flashes of reasonable anger, Baby wears a beaming smile almost permanently under Milli Bhatia’s direction, and it can seem like trauma bounces off her too lightly. I longed for Baby to deliver a more guttural response to her turmoil, like Denise Gough in People, Places and Things, or Sophie Melville in Iphigenia in Splott.Her uncharacteristic sunniness unshackles her from stereotypes, and on Khadija Raza’s buttercup-yellow set, this is seemingly the point. But the details of her roughest ordeals are skipped over too, creating the sense we’re watching the diluted, censored version of a darker story.AtBrixton Houseuntil 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreWomenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I wanted to change the stigma’: Nikita Hand on winning her civil rape case against Conor McGregor | Ireland | The Guardian
description: The popularity of Hand’s book Not the Perfect Victim is the latest twist in a story that puts the spotlight on how society responds to sexual assault allegations
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: The popularity of Hand’s book Not the Perfect Victim is the latest twist in a story that puts the spotlight on how society responds to sexual assault allegations
Content: Nikita Hand. ‘I get so many beautiful messages online. And then I would get the odd hate message, from women and men, just calling me names, horrible names.’Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNikita Hand. ‘I get so many beautiful messages online. And then I would get the odd hate message, from women and men, just calling me names, horrible names.’Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The GuardianIrelandInterview‘I wanted to change the stigma’: Nikita Hand on winning her civil rape case against Conor McGregorRory Carrollin DublinThe popularity of Hand’s book Not the Perfect Victim is the latest twist in a story that puts the spotlight on how society responds to sexual assault allegationsWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNikita Hand had a compelling reason to not pursue a civil rape case againstConor McGregor. She was, in her own view, an imperfect victim.The day of the assault, she had been partying with alcohol and cocaine before contacting McGregor, who took her to a Dublin hotel.Hours later, bruised and stunned, Hand made a report to police, but Irish authorities declined to pursue a criminal case against the mixed martial artist, saying there was no reasonable prospect of a conviction.That left the option of a civil case. But that would strip the hairdresser of anonymity, and pit her against a powerful celebrity who denied wrongdoing and had teams of lawyers and a vast online following. Hand went for it.“I’m not the perfect victim and I never portrayed myself to be,” she said in an interview in Dublin. “But I feel when victims are not perfect, they seem to get blamed. And I really wanted to try to change the stigma around people thinking you have to be a perfect victim to be believed or heard.”The cross-examination in the witness box at Dublin high court in 2024 felt like another violation, but Handemerged victorious: the jury found that McGregor had assaulted her in 2018 and awarded nearly €250,000 in damages.View image in fullscreenWomen at a solidarity demonstration in Dublin after Nikita Hand won her case against Conor McGregor in November 2024.Photograph: Cillian Sherlock/PA“I felt vindicated. It was a really happy, special moment, but at the same time it was a really scary moment. It didn’t take away the fear and the anxiety – to this day I still live with the anxiety and the fear.”Hand, 37, has published a book,Not the Perfect Victim, that chronicles the assault and the aftermath of a case that continues to reverberate on both sides of the Atlantic.Jimmy Fallontriggered an outcry in June after hosting McGregor on The Tonight Show for a softball interview.Fallout from the case continued to play out on social media, said Hand. “I get so many beautiful messages online. And then I would get the odd hate message, from women and men, just calling me names, horrible names.”Hand’s appearance on the Irish bestseller list is the latest twist in a story that has put a spotlight on how the legal system, and popular culture, responds to allegations of sexual assault.Hand said she still struggled with being in the public eye, but was proud of the book. “I feel like I’m in control of my own story now, which I felt like I wasn’t for many years. The night of the assault, I wasn’t in control, another person was controlling my body.”View image in fullscreenRuth Coppinger and Natasha O’Brien take part in a solidarity demonstration in Dublin in 2024 after Nikita Hand won her case against Conor McGregor.Photograph: Cillian Sherlock/PAGrowing up in Drimnagh, a west Dublin suburb, Hand had acquaintances in common with McGregor, who was from nearby Crumlin. While he found fame and fortune in and out of the octagon, she worked in a salon as a colourist.In 2018 she had a partner, a five-year-old daughter and a new house. “Life was good. I was bubbly and loved going out with my friends.”At a Christmas work party she drank, took cocaine and, on a whim, messaged McGregor on Instagram, asking if he knew of any parties. He collected Hand and a friend on the morning of 9 December and took them to the Beacon hotel.Hand later testified that McGregor pinned her down on the bed, put her in a headlock and mock-choked her while raping her.Hand went to the home of her mother, who called an ambulance and insisted that Hand report the assault, regardless of McGregor’s status. “She didn’t care who it was. She just cared about her daughter. She’s seen the bruises on me, she’s seen the state I was in.”Hand was examined at a sexual assault treatment unit and gave a statement to police. When questioned, McGregor said the sex was consensual. In 2020 prosecutors decided to not press charges.After failing to reverse that decision Hand took a civil case. “I did want this person to go to jail for what he had done to me but I had no other option but to take up a civil case. Unfortunately, when you have a civil case and you win it, your perpetrator gets to walk free. But I knew I had to do everything in my power to get some sort of justice.”In June 2024, four months before the trial, three masked intrudersbroke into her home, smashed windows and stabbed her partner. Hand’s lawyers said they believed it was an attack by McGregor supporters, but that McGregor had nothing to do with it.The two-week trial in November 2024 drew intense media attention. The public gallery was packed and Hand was seated almost within touching distance of McGregor. The cross-examination was humiliating, she said. “I found it really degrading. I found it just as bad as the assault itself. Sometimes I feel like victims nearly are on trial rather than the perpetrators. That’s the way we’re kind of made to feel.”McGregorlost an appealin July 2025. Last month a Dublin couple, Samantha O’Reilly and Steven Cummins, werecharged with perjuryafter an investigation by police into evidence filed in McGregor’s appeal.View image in fullscreenNikita Hand in Dublin in September.Photograph: Patrick Bolger/The GuardianHand credits her mother, her partner and the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre with helping her to rebuild her life and to accept that the assault was not her fault. “The shame is leaving me but I do have my really bad days when I can’t leave my apartment. I have severe anxiety.”She is no longer a hairdresser. “I did try to go back to work and it just wasn’t the same. So it will be a complete career change for me. I’d love to work with victims and survivors and help them have a voice.”She wants her daughters – a teenager and a newborn – to grow up in a world where victims are not shamed or blamed. “It doesn’t matter what you wear or how much you drink or even take a drug. No means no and consent needs to be taken more seriously.”Hand said McGregor should not have beenhosted at the White House in 2025or on Fallon’s chatshow. “It’s really upsetting. I can’t understand how he’s still given such a huge platform.”She seldom mentions McGregor by name. “I don’t have any feelings for him. I don’t forgive him. I gave my evidence, he gave his and the jury made their decision. And that’s all there is to it.”Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in NorthernIreland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsIrelandConor McGregorRape and sexual assaultMMAEuropeinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A big responsibility’: Clifton Suspension Bridge master hails £7.6m renovation | Bristol | The Guardian
description: Engineer Tristan Ralph describes task of maintaining and running Bristol structure without public money
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Engineer Tristan Ralph describes task of maintaining and running Bristol structure without public money
Content: ‘I have to make sure it is handed on in just as good a condition or better than I inherited it,’ Ralph said of his job as bridge master.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I have to make sure it is handed on in just as good a condition or better than I inherited it,’ Ralph said of his job as bridge master.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianBristol‘A big responsibility’: Clifton Suspension Bridge master hails £7.6m renovationEngineer Tristan Ralph describes task of maintaining and running Bristol structure without public moneySteven MorrisWed 14 Oct 2026 08.44 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 07.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe job does not give the holder age-old perks such as the right to drive sheep across the great structure, but the title “bridge master” does have a certain ring to it.“I don’t tend to say I’m thebridge masterwhen I’m at a party,” said Tristan Ralph, the current holder of the title. “But people do seem to know and bring it up. It’s a job less ordinary, isn’t it? It’s a Victorian sounding title and people are really, really interested.”There is, however, nothing ceremonial about the title. Ralph is in charge of maintaining and running theClifton Suspension Bridge, a UK feat of engineering, without any public money.“It does feel a big responsibility,” said Ralph. “When the chairman of the trustees rang to say we’d like you to do it, you suddenly feel the pressure. It’s so famous and people inBristol, quite rightly, are proud and almost possessive of it. Bristolians think: ‘It’s our bridge.’”The bridge master – and the not-for-profit charity the Clifton Suspension Bridge Trust – have the task of maintaining the bridge “in perpetuity”. “I’m a temporary custodian,” Ralph said. “When I’m finished, I have to make sure it is handed on in just [as] good a condition or better than I inherited it.”View image in fullscreenThe project took two and a half years and involved hand-painting more than 4,000 original iron chain links and installing energy-efficient lighting.Photograph: Sam Frost/The GuardianRalph, a bridge engineer by profession, was speaking to mark the conclusion ofa large refurbishment projectthat has taken two and a half years and involved hand-painting more than 4,000 original iron chain links and installing an energy-efficient lighting system. It has cost about £7.5m. “It’s been a big job,” he said. “But it’s come pretty much bang on budget, which is rare these days.”That is important because, to many visitors’ surprise, the bridge does not receive public funding. “The upkeep of the bridge, the running of it, the salary costs and everything are all paid only by our toll money,” said Ralph. “People think that we might get something from local or central government. But, no, it’s just the toll money.”Motorised vehicles – including motorcycles – pay £1 to cross the bridge. There is no charge for pedestrians, cyclists or horse riders. As well as being a beautiful structure, it is also a vital part of Bristol and North Somerset’s transport system.View image in fullscreenThe refurbishment was the largest in the bridge’s history.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianRalph said: “It draws the tourists in. We get visitors from hundreds of countries every year but primarily, it’s still a vital piece of local infrastructure. If the bridge wasn’t here, the difference it would make to Bristol traffic would be incredible. We average over 8,000 vehicles a day still. Maintaining it as a transport link is utterly vital.”The end of the refurbishment does not mean Ralph can rest on his laurels and spend more time hobnobbing with members of theBridge Owners Forum.“In a few years, we’ll need to paint the underside of the bridge. The under-bridge gantry unit itself will be replaced over the coming years. So there’s always something. We need to keep on top of things. It’s like your house or your car. If you just ignore it, don’t do things for a couple of years, they start breaking down.”View image in fullscreenThe project came in almost on budget, which is important as the bridge’s upkeep, running and staff costs are all paid using toll money.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianAs in most walks of life, the climate emergency is a challenge Ralph and the trust are having to face. “We were monitoring the bridge daily in the summer with the very hot weather. And maybe if the bridge was being designed today, there would be a little bit more robustness around wind.”The prevailing south-west wind is not usually a problem and the bridge rarely has to close but if it blows directly through the Avon Gorge it can be more difficult. “We need to keep an eye at both the magnitude of any wind events but also their frequency,” Ralph said.The engineer admires the bridge’s designers, including Isambard Kingdom Brunel. “It’s remarkably advanced for its time.”View image in fullscreenThe bridge rarely has to close, but if the wind blows directly through the Avon Gorge it can be difficult.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAEdward Colston’s remains likely to stay at Bristol church that could become community spaceRead moreAnd there is no sign that its days are numbered, largely because the Victorians did not skimp. Ralph said: “There are three layers of chains. The original Brunel design only had two, but because it went from a timber design to a cast-iron deck, they upped it to three.“There’s a little bit of comfort in there. Today there might be pressure to say, well, can you keep it to two, but in Victorian times they did like to add a little bit of meat on the bones.“It doesn’t have a finite life. There’s no end date in our plans. We all just keep it going in the highest standards as we can. It’s in really good condition as long as we keep doing what we need to do, keep our attention on it and don’t let things drift. Forever is a long time but there’s no reason why we have any need to worry at the moment.”Explore more on these topicsBristolHeritageSomersetConstruction industryCommunitiesInfrastructureEngineeringfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My son killed himself after falling victim to an online scam. I heard it happen – and vowed to protect other children | Online abuse | The Guardian
description: Gavin Guffey was 17 when he was targeted by a ‘sextortionist’ on Instagram. His father Brandon has spent four years fighting for justice, and for social media companies to do more to safeguard young users
Author: Anna Moore
Headline: Gavin Guffey was 17 when he was targeted by a ‘sextortionist’ on Instagram. His father Brandon has spent four years fighting for justice, and for social media companies to do more to safeguard young users
Content: ‘He’d just got comfortable in who he was’ … Brandon Guffey with a portrait of his son Gavin.Photograph: Mike BellemeView image in fullscreen‘He’d just got comfortable in who he was’ … Brandon Guffey with a portrait of his son Gavin.Photograph: Mike BellemeHow we surviveOnline abuseMy son killed himself after falling victim to an online scam. I heard it happen – and vowed to protect other childrenGavin Guffey was 17 when he was targeted by a ‘sextortionist’ on Instagram. His father Brandon has spent four years fighting for justice, and for social media companies to do more to safeguard young usersAnna MooreWed 14 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 07.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat were the last words Brandon Guffey said to his son Gavin? Four years on, he still struggles with this question. “That last exchange, it bothers me constantly,” he says. “I think I said, ‘Goodnight, buddy. I love you,’ and he said, ‘I’ll see you in the morning.’ I sincerely hope that’s what I said. The truth is, I’ll never know for certain.”The exchange happened in 2022, on a hot July in Rock Hill, South Carolina, where, just weeks before, Guffey had won the Republican ticket to stand for the state’s House of Representatives. The election was three months away, Guffey’s head was buzzing with politics, and he’d spent that evening at a local event.The house was still when he returned home just before midnight. His wife, Melissa, had gone to bed; his two younger sons, Callahan, 4, and Coen, 16, and both family dogs were sleeping too. The only sounds were the summer cicadas and the frogs calling from the nearby creek – and also the laughter of his 17-year-old-son, Gavin. He was gaming in his bedroom, headset on, talking with friends. It was the long summer break between school and starting college. “I often say Gavin was living his best life at that point,” says Guffey. “He’d just got comfortable in who he was. He wasn’t trying to ‘fit in’ or please anyone. He was looking forward to starting college and pursuing his dream of becoming an art teacher.”View image in fullscreenGuffey with Gavin.Photograph: Courtesy of Brandon GuffeyA call came in on Guffey’s phone. He wishes he’d never taken it. The idea that Gavin might have needed his dad when he was unavailable, talking politics on the porch outside, is almost too much to bear – but in the hour that followed, Gavin’s life hurtled towards darkness.A friend request came in on Gavin’s Instagram from BellaJanet28. They shared friends – their exchange shows that Gavin thought she was a volleyball player from a local college. Guffey still hasn’t been able to bring himself to read the conversation that took place between them, but he knows that BellaJanet28 suggested a game of truth or dare, which led to Gavin sending intimate photos, and then a sextortion attempt. BellaJanet28 demanded money, otherwise the images would be shared with all Gavin’s contacts.At about 1.30am, Guffey saw Gavin on the landing, where they had that last exchange. Moments later, a terrifying sound, a crash, like a bowling ball, boomed from the bathroom, where Guffey found his son lying on the floor. The smell of gunpowder, the blood soaking into his socks, Melissa’s screams, still haunt and horrify him. “I’ll never stop replaying it,” he says. “They’re etched into me for ever.”View image in fullscreenGuffey at a press conference in Washington DC in February 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGuffey is a South Carolina state representative now, and a leading advocate for child online safety. In his own state he has seen through new levels of safeguarding. Just a year after Gavin’s death, through Guffey’s campaigning, “Gavin’s Law” was passed in South Carolina, making sextortion a felony and education about it mandatory in all schools. Last year, Guffey won more sweeping reforms that will require social media companies to activate safety features when users in South Carolina are under 16, including parental permission for the account, and prohibitions on direct marketing, the “infinite scroll”, and automatic video playback, which are all associated with prolonged screen time. He has founded a non-profit,Less Than 3, which campaigns on these issues, and supports affected families; he regularly shares Gavin’s story in schools, churches and community centres.Now Guffey has written a book about it.Tomorrow Needs Youis a hard, harrowing read – and brutally honest. In all sorts of ways, Guffey has blamed himself. Did his career play a part? Most of Guffey’s working life had been spent in business, building up a landscaping supply yard, which he still ran, but in 2020, he had joined the county council and was now moving towards a seat in the statehouse.“It’s a big seat. This was a big race that got a lot of coverage,” he says, “and Gavin had already gone viral in the middle of it.” On a night out, Gavin had spotted the Lamborghini belonging to the basketball player LaMelo Ball, mooned beside it and posted the image on Twitter/X. “I gave him a speech about the Guffey name, and not to mess it up,” says Guffey. (Gavin duly posted an apology – “Sorry Melo, I won’t show my ass like that again” – with two thumbs-up emojis.) “Gavin had seen friends lose college scholarships for something stupid they said on Twitter,” says Guffey. “To him, everything stays online. These images were never going to go away.”Even putting his political career aside, Guffey felt he had failed as a father, as a role model. “Sitting there that night, I was already asking myself, ‘Why couldn’t he come to me? Was he so worried about being vulnerable?’” says Guffey. “It took a tragedy for me to really start diving deep into myself and saying, ‘I’ve been doing this wrong my whole life.’”View image in fullscreenGuffey at a committe hearing for online child sexual exploitation.Photograph: MediaPunch Inc/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsGuffey himself was brought up by a teenage mum, who was tough – she worked three jobs and carried a brick in her handbag – and taught her son to be tough too. “She was scared I didn’t have a male influence, and she pushed me towards that masculine side where ‘boys don’t cry’, you suck it up whatever happens,” he says. “My entire family, this community, that’s the mindset. Man up. Rub some dirt on it.”And then, there was the gun that Gavin had used to act on that terrible, split-second decision. It belonged to Guffey, who had taken it on a recent camping trip for protection, then left it on a high shelf, intending to lock it away. “I didn’t know that the majority of suicides are impulsive,” says Guffey. He has since been told that themedian length oftime between making the decision to take your life and the act itself is only 20 minutes, but when there’s a gun involved, it can be less than three. (Hence the name of his non-profit.) He has got rid of his guns now. “I’d been so focused on protecting my family from outside threats, I didn’t realise the dangers that can come from within the home,” he says. “The tool I had to protect my son ended up being the tool he used to take his life.”At first, the weight of grief and failure felt too much to carry. Guffey says he couldn’t go 15 minutes without feeling he was breaking down. At times, he drank too much – to the stage of passing out on the path outside his home. It was his son Coen taking him aside and saying how hard it was to see his dad like this that served as a wake-up call. “I was trying to numb myself,” he says. “I haven’t cut out drinking but I don’t keep alcohol in my house now. I’ve learned that whatever emotion I feel when I start drinking is just amplified.”That talk with Coen marked a broader turning point. “The only way I could function was to think that two boys were watching to see how I coped, and I was teaching them whether I wanted to or not,” he says. “Dads are great at giving advice. We’re just horrible at following it. So what I’ve tried to do since then is think, ‘What advice would I give to Coen?’, and then try to do that.”View image in fullscreenGuffey: ‘I would love to see no social media for any minor.’Photograph: Mike BellemeThe immediate support from his community helped. From the night it happened, their house, he says, became like a “small city”, filled with people who brought food, took the rubbish out, cared for four-year-old Callahan. “People I was polar opposite of politically just came out to be there,” he says. “Nothing makes you realise how silly half the stuff we fight about is until you experience loss like that.”Meeting Gavin’s friends was another comfort. Just 48 hours after his death, Guffey invited everyone who had known Gavin to a local community space to share their memories. “I knew Gavin as a son,” he says. “I wanted their perspective, a full picture of who he was.” He discovered that when Gavin used to leave the house at 4am – Guffey had always thought he was going to the gym before school – he’d really been picking up friends who’d stayed out too late and were trying to get home. And the reason so many of Gavin’s clothes seemed to get lost – and Guffey’s too, including his hat which had gone missing – was that Gavin had given them away to friends. “I wanted all the stories, no matter how mad or bad,” he says, “and they brought a lot of joy.”Gavin’s phone had quickly provided police with a clear picture of the exchange that had led to his suicide. Guffey’s first impulse was to pull out of the election and throw himself into the pursuit of “BellaJanet28”. Although Meta had closed that Instagram account after a subpoena, someone with the same profile picture and friends list, using the name BellaJanet30, was now contacting Gavin’s family members. It isn’t believed that Gavin had been targeted because of Guffey’s career – it was probably a random approach – but the sextortionist had followed events since and was now demanding money from Melissa, Coen, Gavin’s 14-year-old cousin and Guffey himself, in exchange for the images. One message featured a headline story involving Hunter Biden, superimposed with a picture of Gavin. The implication was clear.View image in fullscreenGuffey with some of Gavin’s artwork.Photograph: Mike BellemeTwo days before what would have been Gavin’s 18th birthday, a little less than a month since his death, Guffey received a message from BellaJanet30 that said,“Did I tell you your son begged for his life?”,with a laughing face emoji. Guffey messaged back, “I will find you. I will end you. You will regret this.”Amid all of this, the prospect of “politics”, of fighting an election and serving the community seemed impossible. “The last thing I wanted to do was handle other people’s problems. I didn’t feel qualified any more,” he says. Guffey told Melissa that he was standing down but her response was unequivocal. “She said,” recalls Guffey, “‘Absolutely not. You’re one of the few people who can actually make a change. Go down there and save the next Gavin.’”In some ways, this mission has saved Guffey, too, and kept him moving forward. Where once, Guffey knew nothing about sextortion – one of the fastest-growing online crimes against children – there are now few who know more.Guffey is a passionate advocate for the repeal of section 230 in the US which gives platforms legal immunity from the content they carry because it is user-generated. “I would love to see no social media for any minor,” he says, “but if the tech companies could be held civilly liable for what they are delivering to children, they would prioritise safety over profits.”The investigation into BellaJanet28 by the FBI and South Carolina law enforcement required new levels of patience, says Guffey. “It was like holding my breath underwater.” The breakthrough came through bank verification numbers that enabled agents to trace financial transactions linked to the account.In January 2025, the suspect believed to be responsible for Gavin’s sextortion, Hassanbunhussein Abolore Lawal, was extradited from Nigeria. Guffey and Melissa attended his first court appearance in Columbia, South Carolina, where he pleaded not guilty to charges including child exploitation resulting in death, cyberstalking and coercion. “I waited for him to come out, so full of rage and anger and anxiety that I cracked a rear molar,” says Guffey. “As soon as he appeared, my wife just broke down and then it became about protecting her, not anger towards him. He wouldn’t look at us.” The pretrial is scheduled for December.View image in fullscreenGuffey with Coen, Callahan and Gavin.Photograph: Courtesy of Brandon GuffeyIn the short time since Gavin’s death, there has been some progress, Guffey believes. “For the first couple of years, I was only getting calls from teens who were going through it, and I’d try to convince them to go to their parents,” he says. “Now I’m getting calls from the parents, whose teens have told them and they’re coming to me for help.” But nothing he does ever feels like enough. “If you were to ask me what I’ve accomplished, I wouldn’t be able to tell you, because it’s go, go, go,” he says. “That is my grieving. Everyone does it differently and this feels like what I should be doing. I have to use that anger sometimes, just to get up, get going and through the days.”Gavin has stayed with him every moment, he says, in a crowd, in an audience when Guffey gives a speech, and at home when he walks through the door. He sees grief as a kind of “weather system … you’re always under it”, Guffey says. “And you carry an umbrella at all times.”Though people often tell Guffey how “strong” he is, that’s not how he feels. “Strength implies choice,” he says. “What I’ve done has been survival. When Gavin died, I made a vow that his death would not be meaningless. My mission until the day I die will be to try and make sure no other teenager feels as trapped, ashamed and hopeless as he did that night.”Tomorrow Needs You by Brandon Guffey (John Wiley, £21.99) is published on 22 October. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may applyIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text theNational Suicide Prevention Lifelineon 988, chat on988lifeline.org, ortext HOMEto 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14.
