title: The best carpet cleaners in the UK – tested on coffee, curry and red wine stains | Homes | The Guardian
description: Whether you’re mopping up after pets or kids, or just want to be prepared for spillages, here are our favourite upright and standalone carpet cleaners for tackling grubby floors at home
Author: Andy Shaw
Headline: Whether you’re mopping up after pets or kids, or just want to be prepared for spillages, here are our favourite upright and standalone carpet cleaners for tackling grubby floors at home
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHomesReviewThe best carpet cleaners in the UK – tested on coffee, curry and red wine stainsWhether you’re mopping up after pets or kids, or just want to be prepared for spillages, here are our favourite upright and standalone carpet cleaners for tackling grubby floors at homeThe best steam cleaners and mops for a sparkling homeAndy ShawWed 14 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve tested a few carpet cleaners in my time, but I have to admit I learned new things putting these eight models through a series of punishing tests. My main takeaway is this: if you have light-coloured carpet, don’t eat curry over it. If you do, and the worst happens, clean it up as quickly as you can, because every second counts.I also learned that no carpet cleaner in this group comes with a magic wand you can wave over a mess to make it disappear. I doubt there’s a machine on earth that can make a single pass over a dollop of tikka masala paste and leave no trace of it behind.Don’t let this put you off, though. All the machines I’ve tested here put up a good fight against a variety of stains. Just be warned that even with the very best carpet cleaner, you’ll need to add time, elbow grease and persistence if you want a carpet that looks as good as it did before the mess hit the floor.At a glanceBest overall carpet cleanerVaxPlatinum SmartWash XL Advanced£379.99 at VaxBest budget carpet cleanerHenryNumatic Henry Wash£219.99 at My HenryBest overall spot washerRug DoctorPortable spot cleaner£152 at HomebaseBest budget spot washerRussell HobbsHot & Cold spot cleaner£83.99 at WayfairWhy you should trust meWhile I’ve spent more time in the past few yearstesting vacuum cleaners(even my kids call me “the Hoover reviewer”, not least because they know how much it annoys me when they use a trademark as a generic term), I’ve also worked with a good number of carpet cleaners. I’ve reviewed enough of them to be known to my neighbours as someone who might have a carpet cleaner on test that they can borrow, particularly when their carpets have been subjected to a teenager’s house party, a toddler with a stomach bug or an incontinent pet.Beyond cleaning, I’ve been testing all sorts of products for more than 30 years, from laptops and printers to smartphones andvideo doorbells.How I testedView image in fullscreenOur tester attempting to remove curry, coffee, red wine, soot and urine from a rug.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianBefore handing me the task of testing carpet cleaners, the Guardian asked a professional for five of the hardest substances to remove from carpet. They came back with curry, coffee, red wine, soot and urine. No way was I going to drop any of that on to my own carpets, so I bought two rugs to test on: a relatively short-pileSeattle washable rug from the Rangeand a longer-pileMarvel shaggy washable rug from Dunelm.I started with the four full-size cleanersspreading measured quantities of the five substances across the two rugs. I was asked to test them with dried-in stains, so I left them overnight. Don’t do this at home; you’ll end up with a foul-smelling house and stains that are very hard to remove.I passed the full-size cleaners over each of the stains multiple times in an attempt to get the mess out. Urine wasn’t that visible, but the curry was particularly bad, leaving the espresso, spoonful of soot and measure of Waitrose’s cheapest red somewhere in between.View image in fullscreenA fluffy assistant inspects the two rugs destined for coffee, curry and more.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWhere the upright cleaning action struggled, I went on to test their built-in spot-removing tools, in an attempt to get deeper into the stains. I also tested all the full-size cleaners on a larger section of my own carpet, to get a feel for their general cleaning abilities.To test the four spot cleaners, I used the same problematic substances, but I cleaned these up as soon as they were spilt, as these devices are designed to be ready to whip into action as soon as a mess is made.Any test products not returned to the manufacturers will be deep-cleaned and donated to theBritish Heart Foundation.The best carpet cleaners in 2026View image in fullscreenThe eight carpet cleaners put to the test for this guide.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianBest overall carpet cleaner:Vax Platinum SmartWash XL AdvancedVaxPlatinum SmartWash XL Advancedfrom£379.99£379.99 at Vax£439 at AmazonWhat we loveCapable all-in-one carpet and spot washer with self-cleaningWhat we don’t loveSeveral passes and still needed on some spillsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£379.99 at Vax£439 at AmazonThe Vax Platinum SmartWash XL Advanced is a great all-rounder. It’s a large upright cleaner that can cover a lot of carpet, with handy spot-washing attachments for tackling upholstery, stairs, accidents and stains.Why we love itIn its upright mode, the SmartWash provided a satisfying clean, lifting dirt easily out of all the carpets I tested it on. Its automatic mode deposits a mix of water and detergent from its upper tank as you push it forwards, while two brush bars in the floor head work the cleaning agents into the carpet fibres. Pulling it back over the stain draws the water back up into a separate waste tank.View image in fullscreenA longer-pile rug after a spot treatment using the Vax Platinum SmartWash XL Advanced.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt also proved to be one of the best spot cleaners, largely thanks to its SpinScrub hand tool. This has a spray, a brush and a funnel, but unlike most cleaners, the brush mechanically rotates as you scrub, providing an extra level of agitation to get deep into the fibres, which was particularly effective on the deeper pile.I was impressed with how it tackled the coffee, red wine and urine stains in its upright mode by repeatedly washing the area, then pulling the dirty water back up again. Some obvious curry and soot marks still remained on both carpet types after I finished, but switching to the spot-washing attachment lifted out even more of these stubborn stains.View image in fullscreenBefore and after cleaning stains on a short-pile rug with the Vax Platinum SmartWash XL Advanced.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWhen you’ve finished cleaning, there’s a solid plastic tray to stand it on, so it won’t drip water on to the floor. This also helps perform a self-clean and collects trapped dirt and hair from the rollers.Vax operates atake-back scheme, recycling an old carpet cleaner for you when you buy a new one from it – just be aware that you’ll need to return your old model at your own expense.Spare partsare available for repairs, and this model comes with an extremely generous six-year guarantee when registered online.It’s a shame that …it needed several passes to remove the toughest stains.Type:uprightWeight:10.1kgHose length:2.5mCable length:9mClean water capacity:3.8lWastewater capacity:2.7lTools included:2-in-1 Antimicrobial tool, SpinScrub hand toolCleaning solution included:250ml pretreatment solution, 500ml Platinum antibacterial solutionWarranty:6 yearsVaxPlatinum SmartWash XL Advancedfrom£379.99£379.99 at Vax£439 at AmazonWhat we loveCapable all-in-one carpet and spot washer with self-cleaningWhat we don’t loveSeveral passes and still needed on some spillsBest budget carpet cleaner:Numatic Henry WashHenryNumatic Henry Washfrom£219.99£219.99 at My Henry£283.18 at NisbetsWhat we loveAffordable, with good results on carpet and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveRequires scrubbing on carpet, so not ideal for whole roomsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£219.99 at My Henry£283.18 at NisbetsDon’t expect any bells and whistles with this blue, liquid-friendly version of the Henry vacuum cleaner. It doesn’t have all the brushes and other paraphernalia that come with some of the more expensive models, but it has a trick up its sleeve – it’s the only one that’s designed to handle significant spills on hard floors.Why we love itThe tools and instructions for carpet cleaning are basic. It comes with a pair of nozzles you can switch between – a wide one for carpet and a narrow one for upholstery and stairs. Both can spray water and detergent from the generous 6l clean water tank, and suck it back up into the vast 9l base, but the carpet-cleaning attachments have no built-in brushes to aid agitation. Instead, the instructions suggest you scrub with your own brush (not supplied) between applications of liquid and suction.View image in fullscreenBefore and after cleaning stains on a longer-pile rug with the Numatic Henry Wash.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianI did this in my testing, and the results were decent – manually scrubbing marks worked a treat on the more solid stains left by soot and curry. It definitely takes more elbow grease than the cleaners that have their own mechanical scrubbing tools, but the end result wasn’t compromised by separating the scrubbing from the tool. I wouldn’t want to do that across the whole of a room-sized carpet, though. The liquids didn’t get the same amount of sluicing that I saw with rivals that integrate their own scrubbing tools, so it wasn’t as effective against wine, coffee and urine.The hard floor tool is half squeegee, half brush. It can deposit water on the floor, scrub it about, then suck it back up again. It worked well in my tests.Numatic vacuum cleaners are about as repairable as cleaners get, with simple construction andspare partswidely available.It’s a shame that …its carpet-cleaning attachments don’t have built-in brushes.Type:cylinderWeight:10.1kgHose length:2.5mCable length:10mClean water capacity:6lWastewater capacity:9lTools included:carpet cleaner, upholstery tool, hard floor cleanerCleaning solution included:noWarranty:up to 3 years whenregistered, depending on retailerHenryNumatic Henry Washfrom£219.99£219.99 at My Henry£283.18 at NisbetsWhat we loveAffordable, with good results on carpet and hard floorsWhat we don’t loveRequires scrubbing on carpet, so not ideal for whole roomsBest overall spot washer:Rug Doctor portable spot cleanerRug DoctorPortable spot cleanerfrom£152£152 at Homebase£160 at ArgosWhat we loveMotorised brush makes cleaning easierWhat we don’t loveBulkier and trickier to store than rival spot cleanersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£152 at Homebase£160 at ArgosRug Doctor might be best known for its industrial-looking upright cleaners, but this larger-than-average spot cleaner fits into the range well. It’s bigger and more powerful than the other spot cleaners here, and comes with wheels and a retractable handle, so it’s still easy to haul around.Why we love itWhile this uses a standard two-tank system for clean and dirty water, it has a key advantage over the other standalone spot washers – a motorised brush on the hand tool. While I didn’t feel that its back-and-forth motion was as effective as the rotary movement you get from the hand tool of the Vax Platinum SmartWash XL Advanced, it still adds an extra dimension to your own scrubbing action.View image in fullscreenBefore and after cleaning stains on a short-pile rug with the Rug Doctor portable spot cleaner.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIn my tests on recently dropped messes, it did a decent job of picking up dirt and clearing stains, performing particularly well on urine, wine and coffee. It benefits from its ability to get detergent and water to the heart of the problem quickly, agitate the fibres and lift dirty liquid away. It also proved effective on soot but struggled to completely remove the problematic curry stain.Rug Doctor has a good range of pre-treatment sprays you can experiment with, and I used itsHeavy Stain Pre-Treatment. You can also fill the clean water tank with warm water, which adds another gear to the cleaning engine.The brand also has a very extensive spare parts department, so local repairers stand a good chance of being able to keep machines going. It also has atake-back schemefor your old cleaner if you’re buying a replacement.It’s a shame that …it wasn’t particularly easy to clean out damp carpet fluff from the handheld funnel.Type:spotWeight:7.6kgHose length:1.5mCable length:4.6mClean water capacity:1.9lWastewater capacity:1.9lTools included:motorised brushCleaning solution included:236ml spot cleanerWarranty:2 yearsRug DoctorPortable spot cleanerfrom£152£152 at Homebase£160 at ArgosWhat we loveMotorised brush makes cleaning easierWhat we don’t loveBulkier and trickier to store than rival spot cleanersBest budget spot washer:Russell Hobbs Hot & Cold spot cleanerRussell HobbsHot & Cold spot cleanerfrom£83.99£83.99 at Wayfair£83.99 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable; compact; heats waterWhat we don’t loveLack of motorised brush requires more elbow grease on stainsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£83.99 at Wayfair£83.99 at AmazonMost of the other spot washers I’ve reviewed here can take warm or cold water, but if you opt for warm, they come with warnings about maximum temperatures. That’s fine, but when you’re speedily filling the tank having just dropped a glass of Rioja on a white carpet, you probably don’t want to be worrying about whether the water is too hot. Russell Hobbs has taken this worry out of the equation with a cleaner that optionally warms water to the right temperature for the device within a minute of switching it on.Why we love itIt’s a simple but effective system. Wait 45 secondsbefore using the device, and the warmed water provides a bit of extra cleaning power without the worry of damaging your device.The machine didn’t come with any carpet cleaning solution, and the manual doesn’t encourage adding anything other than water to it, though you can use low-foaming pre-treatments on stains first, as long as they adhere to the guidelines in the manual. I particularly liked that the water is squirted from the hand tool in the centre of the brush attachment, so it gets right to the heart of the cleaning problem as you’re scrubbing.View image in fullscreenBefore and after cleaning stains on a short-pile rug with the Russell Hobbs Hot & Cold Spot Cleaner.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt performed well in testing and proved particularly effective on curry stains. Some of the coffee and wine stains reappeared as the carpet dried, but these thinner stains diminished with subsequent cleans.It’s a shame that …there’s no motorised tool to help scrub.Type:spotWeight:4.2kgHose length:1.9mCable length:5mClean water capacity:1.5lWastewater capacity:0.8lTools included:stain brush, wastewater toolCleaning solution included:noWarranty:up to 3 years when registered, depending on retailerRussell HobbsHot & Cold spot cleanerfrom£83.99£83.99 at Wayfair£83.99 at AmazonWhat we loveAffordable; compact; heats waterWhat we don’t loveLack of motorised brush requires more elbow grease on stainsThe best of the restView image in fullscreenA versatile all-in-one that can spruce up carpets and tackle stubborn stains: the Shark CarpetXpert HairPro Pet Deep carpet cleaner.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianShark CarpetXpert HairPro Pet Deep carpet cleaner with built-in StainStriker EX300UKSharkCarpetXpert HairPro Pet Deep carpet cleaner with built-in StainStriker EX300UKfrom£349£349 at John Lewis£349 at AmazonWhat we loveVersatile; very capable on pet problems; easy to cleanWhat we don’t loveCan’t clean carpet as deeply as Vax and Rug DoctorView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£349 at John Lewis£349 at AmazonBest for:pet messesThe Shark CarpetXpert has tools for every eventuality. It’s not the cheapest carpet cleaner here, but if you want an all-in-one that will spruce up every carpet in the house and manage every kind of spot clean you can think of, it’s a great option. It’s worth noting, though, that Shark doesn’t recommend using this on wool carpets.View image in fullscreenBefore and after cleaning stains on a short-pile rug with the Shark CarpetXpert HairPro Pet.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianI found this model particularly effective on the liquid messes (urine, wine and coffee) on short-pile carpet, with the follow-up spot-wash tool also working well against the soot. The curry left a visible stain behind, even after the spot wash.For pet owners, two of its five hand tools come with reversible plates, and two can switch between brushes and fins. The fins are good for pet hair and stop the brushes from getting clogged. Two tools have their own mini collection tanks, with filters to separate liquids from solids, to keep the main machine clear of particularly nasty messes. The whole device is particularly easy to clean, with lots of removable parts.It didn’t make the final cut because …its main brush roller struggled to cope with the longer-pile carpet.Type:upright;weight:8.8kg;hose length:2.01m;cable length:6.71m;clean water capacity:2.1l;wastewater capacity:0.85l;tools included:Tough Stain tool, Wide Tough Stain tool, Crevice tool, Pet Extractor, Pet Stain Trapping tool;cleaning solution included:355ml Shark CarpetXpert Deep Clean Pro Formula, 473ml Shark StainStriker OXY Multiplier Formula;warranty:up to 5 yearswhen registered, depending on retailerSharkCarpetXpert HairPro Pet Deep carpet cleaner with built-in StainStriker EX300UKfrom£349£349 at John Lewis£349 at AmazonWhat we loveVersatile; very capable on pet problems; easy to cleanWhat we don’t loveCan’t clean carpet as deeply as Vax and Rug DoctorRug Doctor Deep carpet cleanerRug DoctorDeep carpet cleanerfrom£299.99£320 at Argos£299.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEffective carpet cleaner with thorough washing optionsWhat we don’t loveOnly works when pulled backwards; spot washer doesn’t spinView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£320 at Argos£299.99 at AmazonBest for:lots of very dirty carpetThe thing that makes the Rug Doctor Deep Carpet Cleaner particularly effective is its ability to drop lots and lots of soapy water on the floor, scrub it into the pile, then pick the dirty stuff back up again.On its wettest setting, it literally drenched the carpet in my tests, getting through the clean water tank in minutes. The large volume of liquid deposited, along with the significant agitation, made this particularly good at removing the wine, coffee and urine stains.View image in fullscreenBefore and after cleaning stains on a short-pile rug with the Rug Doctor Deep carpet cleaner.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianIt proved equally effective on long- and short-pile carpet. The curry, in particular, needed significant attention from the spot washing attachment. It also picked up a lot of dirt, doing the best job of all the upright cleaners, though I still had to resort to its handheld tool to finish off the toughest stains.It didn’t make the final cut because …its design only works as you pull it towards you, so you can’t easily go back and forth over problem areas, and the brush on the spot-washing tool doesn’t spin or oscillate, so it takes more effort.Type:upright;weight:14.6kg;hose length:2.4m;cable length:8.5m;clean water capacity:3.8l;wastewater capacity:4.2l;tools included:upholstery tool kit;cleaning solution included:266ml Rug Doctor detergent;warranty:2 yearsRug DoctorDeep carpet cleanerfrom£299.99£320 at Argos£299.99 at AmazonWhat we loveEffective carpet cleaner with thorough washing optionsWhat we don’t loveOnly works when pulled backwards; spot washer doesn’t spinShark EveryMess Portable 3-in-1 Stain Eliminator wet vac & dry vac VX110UKSharkEveryMess Portable 3-in-1 Stain Eliminator wet vac & dry vac VX110UKfrom£199.99£199.99 at Shark£199.99 at John LewisWhat we loveEffective on difficult stainsWhat we don’t loveNo option to douse carpet with soapy waterView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£199.99 at Shark£199.99 at John LewisBest for:spot-cleaning versatilityThe Shark EveryMess Portable is an anomaly in this group because it doesn’t use water. Instead, it comes with a chemical spray, which you use to douse the dirty area. You then use the vacuum suction of the machine to pick up both the cleaning solution and, hopefully, the dirt. Shark advises against using the EveryMess on wool carpets, however.Because it doesn’t rely on water, it can also be used as a dry vacuum or even a mixture of both – drop a bottle of beer, for example, and you could pick up both beer and broken glass. You can also insert your own bag (any size from 8l to 50l) if you want to collect mess straight into something you can easily throw away, though sharp objects may cut through it.View image in fullscreenBefore and after cleaning stains on a short-pile rug with the Shark EveryMess.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe supplied spray-on detergent did a surprisingly good job of lifting out the wine, urine, coffee and soot stains. It wasn’t quite so good on curry, and tough stains may leave you wishing the device could just add a little water to the mix.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s effective on stains, but not everyone prefers cleaning with a chemical spray instead of water.Type:spot;weight:4.9kg;hose length:1.5m;cable length:6m;clean water capacity:N/A;wastewater capacity:1.9l;tools included:Tough Stain tool, Crevice tool, Squeegee tool;cleaning solution included:500ml Shark StainForce Dual-Formula spray;warranty:up to 3 years, depending on retailerSharkEveryMess Portable 3-in-1 Stain Eliminator wet vac & dry vac VX110UKfrom£199.99£199.99 at Shark£199.99 at John LewisWhat we loveEffective on difficult stainsWhat we don’t loveNo option to douse carpet with soapy waterKärcher Spray Extraction cleaner SE 2 Spot Care spot cleanerKärcherSpray Extraction cleaner SE 2 Spot Care spot cleanerfrom£90£90 at Argos£99.99 at AmazonWhat we loveCompact, easy to store and quick to deployWhat we don’t loveLacklustre scrubbing toolView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andy Shaw/The Guardian£90 at Argos£99.99 at AmazonBest for:compact storageWith a similar price and purpose to the Russell Hobbs Hot & Cold spot cleaner, the Kärcher Spray Extraction cleaner SE 2 was a strong contender for the best budget spot cleaner. In some ways it’s superior to the Russell Hobbs, with a more compact design that neatly stores its attachments on board, so there are no loose parts to lose track of. It falls behind slightly, however, because it doesn’t heat the clean water and can only be used with Kärcher detergent.View image in fullscreenBefore and after cleaning stains on a short-pile rug with the Kärcher Spray Extraction cleaner.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianThe softer brush on the scrubbing tool didn’t do it any favours when I was trying to work detergent into any of the stains. While it still coped reasonably well if deployed immediately after a spillage of wine, coffee or urine, it struggled to clear up tougher stains such as curry.It didn’t make the final cut because …the brush is small and soft, not really ideal for the hard scrubbing I needed to remove the trickiest stains.Type:spot;weight:4.3kg;hose length:1.8m;cable length:4.5m;clean water capacity:1.5l;wastewater capacity:0.8l;tools included:stain removal brush, upholstery nozzle;cleaning solution included:100ml Carpet & Upholstery cleaner;warranty:2 yearsKärcherSpray Extraction cleaner SE 2 Spot Care spot cleanerfrom£90£90 at Argos£99.99 at AmazonWhat we loveCompact, easy to store and quick to deployWhat we don’t loveLacklustre scrubbing toolWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenCarpets in homes with pets may need more frequent cleaning.Photograph: Andy Shaw/The GuardianWhat type of carpet cleaner should I buy?That depends on how you plan to use it. Upright cleaners are best for washing all the carpets in your home, and can cover large areas with minimal fuss. Most can be pushed around just like a vacuum cleaner. Many uprights can also spot clean stairs and upholstery with the included handheld attachments, and they’re useful if you need to focus on a small problem area.If you don’t have a lot of carpet, a dedicated spot cleaner can do a similar job. There’s nothing stopping you from using a spot cleaner on a large area of carpet, but it will take more time and require you to get on your hands and knees. Spot washers are smaller, making them more convenient to store and easier to get ready as soon as an accident happens.What’s the difference between a carpet cleaner and a steam cleaner?Most carpet cleaners use clean water and detergent to wash the carpet and have a suction function to take the dirty waste into a separate container. Steam cleaners use water heated to high temperatures to help kill germs and are more often designed for use on hard floors. They don’t tend to suck up excess water afterwards, but because the water is applied as steam, they generally leave less moisture behind.Should I just rent a carpet cleaner?Renting a carpet cleaner is a great idea. Most people won’t need to wash their carpets every week. You could consider buying a spot washer for tackling small accidents, but rent a full carpet washer when you want to clean the whole house.Rug Doctorspecialises in cleaner hire and rents out professional-grade machines. Stock is conveniently managed through retailers including Tesco and B&Q, meaning cleaners are easy to collect and return. Tool hire services such asHSSalso offer carpet cleaners for rent. You may also be able to borrow one from a localLibrary of Things.How often should you clean your carpets?That depends on how quickly they get dirty. If your footfall is relatively low and you don’t have any pets, then a wash every 12-18 months should be fine. If your carpets see a lot of dirt, though, they might benefit from a more regular clean. Washing carpets with mechanical cleaners can cause wear, so you shouldn’t do it more often than you need to.Does it matter what my carpet is made of?Yes. If your carpet is made of delicate or natural materials such as wool, you should check the manufacturer’s guidelines. Some explicitly advise against using their products on particular types of carpet.How do you recycle an old carpet cleaner?Some manufacturers, includingVaxandRug Doctor, operate a take-back scheme, where you can buy a new device and they’ll take the old one you’re replacing and recycle it. Some retailers, includingCurrys,ArgosandB&Q, offer a similar service.If you miss the return window or don’t want to replace your old carpet cleaner, you can take the machine to a council-run recycling centre or another electrical recycling point. Manufacturers help fund the collection and recycling of electrical items through the government’sWaste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) regulations.For more:The best steam cleaners and mops for a sparkling homeThe best vacuum cleaners for hard floors, carpet and pet hairThe best cordless vacuum cleaners – testedAndy Shaw is a consumer and technology journalist with more than 30 years of experience reviewing technology, home and garden gadgets. He just loves testing and comparing things. Cleaning tools are amonghis favourite things to review, because he can get some housework out of the way while also doing his day jobExplore more on these topicsHomesThe FilterGadgetsHygieneInteriorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Was this Mark Zuckerberg’s first – and last – taste of Guinness? | Beer | The Guardian
description: The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half full
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half full
Content: Mark Zuckerberg savours the flavour of a pint of Guinness.Photograph: YouTube/Cheeky PintView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg savours the flavour of a pint of Guinness.Photograph: YouTube/Cheeky PintPass notesBeerWas this Mark Zuckerberg’s first – and last – taste of Guinness?The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half fullWed 14 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Guinness.Age:Arthur Guinness began brewing porter in the 1770s. Guinness draft was first poured in 1959.Appearance:Espresso martini in a pint glass.But it’s beer.It’s stout, yeah. Irish stout.Sort of an old man’s drink, isn’t it?Not these days. Fans of Guinness include Kim Kardashian, Olivia Rodrigo, even the Princess of Wales.That’s just a bunch of celebrities pretending to like Guinness either because they’re visiting Ireland or it’s Saint Patrick’s Day. Or both.Some of them have actually tasted it:Mark Zuckerberg, for example.I wouldn’t have guessedZuckerbergdrinks Guinness.He has drunk it – and apparently for the first time – on a recent instalment of the Irish billionaire John Collison’s Cheeky Pint podcast, which is set in a pub.How did he like it?He didn’t say.What makes you think it was his first time?The look on his face.Did he look as if he was enjoying it?He looked as if he might be allergic to it.What do you mean?At the start of the podcast, while discussing his new Muse AI app, theMetafounder picks up the full pint in front of him and takes a sip.Like a regular person, you mean.Close enough, up to that point. But his subsequent reaction went viral.What did he do?He looked surprised, for a start. Then as if he was having trouble swallowing. He pursed his lips, squirmed in his seat and seemed to be looking around for the nearest exit.Oh my.After that he clutched at his shirt collar a bit. He even tried smiling briefly before realising he’d selected the wrong human facial expression from the dropdown menu. Eventually he managed to power down and reset himself.Did he at leastfinish the pint?He kept at it, but by the 1 hour 20 minute mark he’d only managed about half.Then what happened?There was an apparent break in filming, and when they resumed he had another full pint in front of him.His worst nightmare! Still, I suppose Guinness can manage withoutZuckerberg’s endorsement.You would have thought so – it sells 1.88bn pints a year globally, withsales continuing to rise, while the overall beer market declines. And Guinness 0.0 is the No 1 non-alcoholic beer in the UK.So what made Zuckerberg think he ought to pretend to like it?Well, he didbuy a castle in Irelandlast month for €20m (£17m), so maybe he’s planning on popping down to his local more often?Do say:“Guinness is an acquired taste, and I’m in the process of acquiring it in the same way I’ve acquired many startups and competitors. Was this answer helpful?”Don’t say:“Then, when my new AI model kills everyone, I’ll drink what I like.”Explore more on these topicsBeerPass notesMark ZuckerbergFood & drink industryMetaAlcoholfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: That Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything is a big help to the PM | John Crace | The Guardian
description: One good poll has convinced the Tory leader she is invincible. She was back in her happy place with a scattergun PMQs
Author: John Crace
Headline: One good poll has convinced the Tory leader she is invincible. She was back in her happy place with a scattergun PMQs
Content: Over the conference break, Kemi has undergone a brain wipe. She is back to making it up as she goes along.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenOver the conference break, Kemi has undergone a brain wipe. She is back to making it up as she goes along.Photograph: House of CommonsThe politics sketchPMQsThat Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything is a big help to the PMJohn CraceOne good poll has convinced the Tory leader she is invincible. She was back in her happy place with a scattergun PMQsWed 14 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.36 EDTShareLittle things please little minds. And minds don’t come much smaller than some of those in Westminster. If a researcher had come up with a study that showed one element two points higher in value than countless other experiments, it would almost certainly be marked down either as an outlier or “within the margin of error”. At the very least, no conclusions would be drawn until many other experiments had been conducted which had produced similar results. Serious scientific journals would just laugh at you if you asked them to publish your findings.And yet. In one – just one out of many – recent opinion poll, the Tories have increased their ratings by a couple of points and are now for the first time in years in second place, ahead of Reform. And all of a sudden, Kemi Badenoch is insisting this is incontrovertible proof that the Tories are back in business. All the sins of its 14 years in government have been wiped clean. All hail to Kemi, the new chief. She is the chosen one. And theConservativesare a government-in-waiting.You need a certain amount of self-confidence to make it as a party leader. Not to say a touch of the Panglossian. The ability to insist all is well when it is turning to shit. But you can have too much of a good thing. You must at least be within touching distance of reality. And it appears that once again Kemi has jumped the shark. The one good poll has gone to her head and she now believes she is invincible. Nothing can touch her narcissism.In her early days as Tory leader, Kemi used to crash and burn every week at prime minister’s questions. She considered preparation and research to be beneath her. Instead, she peddled the latest conspiracy theories she had seen on X with a series of scattergun questions. She only started to improve when her minders tried to get her to concentrate for 10 minutes of sustained questions on one subject. Yet over the conference break, Kemi has undergone a brain wipe. She is back in her happy space of making it up as she goes along. No one knows better than Kemi.Sadly for the Tory leader, Kemi’s approach is also Andy Burnham’s happy place. Much more of this and the prime minister is going to look forward to his Wednesday lunchtime encounters in the Commons. Never look an easy win in the eye. Not because he’s word perfect – there are still a lot of unanswered questions about his involvement with the Manchester City owners – but because there’s an engaging openness to him you seldom find in other politicians. A willingness to answer the questions and to appear as if he’s listening. Mr Congeniality.View image in fullscreenBurnham, Mr Congeniality, chose to respond to Kemi in the most hurtful way. With kindness.Photograph: House of CommonsIt’s also a big help to Andy that Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything. Arguments are always so much simpler when your opponents are deluded. Indeed you couldn’t escape the irony of her insisting that it was Burnham who was consistently mistaken about everything. Even the head of MI5, Ken McCallum, had slapped the prime minister down for suggesting hostile actors had interfered with theBrexitreferendum. Kemi can’t bear the fact she might have had the backing of the Russian state in 2016.Burnham chose to respond to Kemi in the most hurtful way. With kindness. No anger. Just a gentle reiteration of the facts. It was incontrovertible that Russia had tried to influence both the 2019 general election and the EU referendum. The evidence was in front of our eyes. Russian bots selling misinformation all over social media. It was a non-story. And far from correcting him, McCallum had gone out of his way to confirm this.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan LiewRead moreWhat the MI5 boss had gone on to say was that it would be better for everyone concerned if we all just dropped the story as it would only give the Russians further encouragement. And who had been keeping the story alive for a third day by bringing it up at PMQs? Take a bow, Kemi. The Tory leader seemingly content to carry on doing the Russians’ dirty work for them. At leastNathan Gill, Reform’s former leaderin Wales, had the sense to get paid for this. Kemi was doing it for free. Andy ended by saying he would be delighted to debate whether Brexit had done more harm than good. Kemi shook her head. This isn’t an argument the Tories are keen to have. Their feeling is Brexit is something we all just have to suck up.After that, Kemi looked a bit lost. Clueless. Scouring her file for something to ask. Instead she just wasted her own and everyone else’s time. First by asking about the budget. As if Burnham was ever going to say: “You know what? Since you’ve asked I might as well give you a heads-up two weeks early.” All Kemi achieved was to make herself look half witted. She ended up sounding a bit hurt. She had hoped that Andy would have spent more time problem-solving than point-scoring. There are days with Kemi when even giving a straight answer comes across as point-scoring.Earlier in the day, Dominic Cummings had been giving evidence to a Lords select committee on how to prevent rogue actors from entering No 10. That should have been a very short session. Just stop morons like Boris Johnson from appointing people like Dom as his special adviser. Curiously this hadn’t occurred to Dom, nor to the dopey peers interrogating him.It was a bizarre hour and a half. The sort that gives you mild PTSD. Your mind goes back to all the damage he did to the country during the Brexit referendum and during his year in No 10 and suddenly the horror floods back. Just when your brain has done its best to forget all about him. To consider him a footnote in history. For the record, Dom is as deluded as ever. His main thesis seemed to be that Boris was right to allow him to do whatever he liked but no one else in No 10 should ever be allowed to do what he did. Some things never change. We are well rid of him.Explore more on these topicsPMQsThe politics sketchKemi BadenochHouse of CommonsConservativesAndy BurnhamLabourBrexitcommentShareReuse this content

title: The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’ | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: There are many reasons to reject this affordability ‘solution’, not least it being complex and fiddly. Just keep things simple
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: There are many reasons to reject this affordability ‘solution’, not least it being complex and fiddly. Just keep things simple
Content: In theory, the rising block tariff means heavier users would pay higher rates for their extra energy units.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenIn theory, the rising block tariff means heavier users would pay higher rates for their extra energy units.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPANils Pratley on financeUK cost of living crisisThe UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’Nils PratleyThere are many reasons to reject this affordability ‘solution’, not least it being complex and fiddly. Just keep things simpleWed 14 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTShare‘My mark of failure or success is whether I can get bills down or not. That’s the only thing I’m in this job to do.” So said Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary,recently, bracing for the hike in energy bills that looks inevitable in January.Industry projectionssuggest £400-ish on an annual basis is on the way, with“stubbornly high”levels for the rest of decade even if wholesale gas prices cool down.So, yes, one can understand why “affordability” is Fahnbulleh’s “top priority”. And,as this newspaper reported last week, there is likely to be an intervention in that direction in chancellor John Healey’s budget this month: £1bn of extra support for poorer households this winter.But the chat in energy-land is about what comes after that – and what Fahnbulleh’s other remarks about covering the costs of the energy system in a “fairer” way seem to be hinting at.Ministers preparing to slash heat pump subsidies to fund defence spendingRead moreWill the government finally get round to designing a co-called“social tariff” for energy– a way to get financial support to the most needy on a more targeted basis than the clunky warm homes discount, the mechanism Healey will be obliged to use?Will Healey, after chopping VAT from electricity for six months, do so permanently and then shift more green levies and other “hidden taxes” of energy transition into general taxation?And is Fahnbulleh also contemplating something very different? Welcome to the idea of the “rising block tariff” (RBT), the unwieldy name for the proposal to give every household an initial block, or allowance, of cheaper gas and electricity to cover “essential” use and then make subsequent blocks more expensive. In other words, heavier energy consumers would pay higher rates for their extra units.Fahnbulleh has got officials in her department to explore an RBT model. And, note, the New Economics Foundation, the thinktank she used to lead,is a proponent.The Joseph Rowntree Foundation is another backer: inits version, the government could fund an RBT with, say, £5bn of public money, allowing bills to fall for most households – but, critically, the biggest savings would flow to light users, who tend to be low-income households. “An RBT would produce greater reductions in bills lower down the income distribution,” it says.What’s not to like? Plenty. There are at least three reasons why an RBT has few fans elsewhere, not even among charities and thinktanks that focus on fuel poverty.First, Citizens Advice regards low energy use as a poor proxy for low income in practice. Traditional electric heaters, with high electricity usage, “are more common in social or private rented homes, where people can’t change their heating system”,it argues.Quite: a progressive-sounding policy could end up being nothing of the sort, especially if second-home owners, by spreading their usage, are winners. If the reply is that an incomes overlay could address tricky cases in both directions, why not just do the data modelling work to design a proper social tariff in the first place?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSecond, a rigid RBT would be an awkward fit with a renewables-heavy system where the most interesting innovations are “flex” tariffs to exploit very windy or sunny hours when wholesale power prices are dirt cheap. There is a danger of baffling consumers by making them mix their blocks with their flexes.Third, a core aim of the energy transition is to drive take-up of electric vehicles, heat pumps and so on. That becomes harder if the message to consumers is that “the more electricity you use, the more you’ll be charged per unit”.Lobby groupElectrify Britaincalls block tariffs “hugely counterproductive” for electrification: “You can’t ask families to go electric and then pursue a policy that would charge them more for doing so.”That feels the killer point: an RBT model cuts across too many other goals. Fahnbulleh should keep things simple: go for a serious social tariff or discount scheme that effectively identifies “vulnerable” energy users. That idea has enjoyed wide support for years. Block tariffs are too complicated and fiddly to administer.Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisNils Pratley on financeEnergy industryEnergy billsFuel povertyPovertyConsumer affairsHousehold billscommentShareReuse this content

title: Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: Tom Watson has said ‘mob rule’ must not decide public contracts. Perhaps he should take a look at his new employer, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: Tom Watson has said ‘mob rule’ must not decide public contracts. Perhaps he should take a look at his new employer, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: The then defence secretary, John Healey, with the Palantir CEO, Alex Karp, after signing an investment deal in London, September 2025.Photograph: Lucy North/PAView image in fullscreenThe then defence secretary, John Healey, with the Palantir CEO, Alex Karp, after signing an investment deal in London, September 2025.Photograph: Lucy North/PAOpinionPalantirPalantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influenceGeorge MonbiotTom Watson has said ‘mob rule’ must not decide public contracts. Perhaps he should take a look at his new employerWed 14 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTShareWhat a world we live in. Imagine: gangs dragging civil servants off commuter trains and beating them up because they handed government data jobs to the wrong contractor – and the government is changing its procurement decisions as a result. Well, OK, it might not have happened yet, but it’s only a matter of time. As the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watsonasks: “Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?” No, I absolutely don’t want the latter, and it’s always good to get ahead of trouble.But then I remember there are two common meanings of mob rule. One is intimidation by crowds of thugs. The other is a pejorative term for democracy. And while I’ve yet to see government procurement practices in the UK determined by pitchforks and flaming torches, democratic transparency could be a genuine threat to certain contractors. One might have hoped that Watson, who oncetook on the Murdoch empire, would have recognised the distinction. But then again, one might have hoped that Watson would not havetaken a jobas a senior vice-president at Palantir.Over the past few years, this US company has been worming its way into the British state. It has landed contracts worth hundreds of millions with the Ministry of Defence, several police forces, the Financial Conduct Authority, the atomic weapons establishment and the NHS. Its superpower, according to adeep investigationby Peter Geoghegan and Lucas Amin in the London Review of Books, is that it is “willing to spend more on securing political access than almost all of its British and continental competitors”. It made abundant use of Peter Mandelson’s company Global Counsel, which seems, in turn, to have madeabundant useof the UK’s remarkably flimsy lobbying laws. Watson is one of more than 30 former UK ministers and officials Palantirnow employs.Recent lobbyist for Palantir had key role in helping Andy Burnham become PMRead morePalantir’s contracts might have been awarded lawfully, but some of us might question the ways in which doors were opened for it. These include anunrecorded meetingbetween Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings and the co-founder of Palantir, Peter Thiel, in Downing Street in 2019. It was invited back to Downing Street when the Covid-19 pandemic began a few months later, and was working in the NHS within days, on a contract for which it chargedonly £1. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan,has criticisedsuch loss-leaders, which can quickly lead to reliance on a company, at which point it can name its price.Another controversial meeting was brokered by Mandelson in 2025, when he was UK ambassador to the US. Keir Starmer visited Palantir’s showroom in Washington, where he met the company’s global and UK chief executives, Alex Karp and Louis Mosley. They talked about defence spending. No 10, Geoghegan and Amin tell us, “refused to say whether Starmer knew that Palantir was a client of Global Counsel, in which Mandelson still held a stake of around a fifth at the time. The meeting was never declared on transparency registers.” A few months later, Palantirsecureda £241m contract with the Ministry of Defence, without an open tender.Now we learn that Martha Dalton, a key player in Andy Burnham’s campaign to win the Makerfield byelection, enabling him to become prime minister, was onunpaid leavefrom the lobbying company she co-founded, Lodestone. Lodestone had done extensive work for Palantir. And the Financial Timesreportsthat Samantha Jones, then the lead non-executive director on the board of the health department, was an adviser to one of Palantir’s partners when the company was bidding for its huge and controversial NHS contract. Now she is permanent secretary in the same department.There have beenrepeatedallegations that some of Palantir’s products arerubbish. But, as the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committeewarns, government agencies can quickly succumb to “vendor lock-in”: once you start using them, it can be very hard to stop.Thiel,has claimed that“the NHS makes people sick”, and that we should “just rip the whole thing from the ground and start over”. The company is deeply embedded in the Trump administration, where it supplies software that helps ICE findundocumented people. It also works for the Israeli government on identifying targets in Gaza. When Karp was confronted by a protester who told him that “Palantir kills Palestinians”,he replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”This is the company handling our critical information. After official denials, itturns outthat NHS England has granted Palantir “unlimited access” to patient data. This is ahuge issue. Identifiable patient data is supposed to be visible only to people directly involved in a patient’s care, or who have received the patient’s informed consent. There arewidespread concernsabout how this and otherdatasetsmight be used.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow Palantir got into the NHS - podcastRead moreSo, as Palantir runs intoever-greater controversy, it’s not hard to see why it might have hired Watson, who, with Burnham, was a minister in Gordon Brown’s government. I wouldn’t presume to speculate about what attracted Watson to the multibillion-dollar company.In July, the government’s ethics and integrity commissionrecommendeda major shake-up, enabling us to see all the encounters between lobbyists and ministers, aides and senior officials. I’ve heard this call many times before. The pattern is always the same: a scandal, followed by a call to action, followed by … little or nothing.Before he became prime minister, David Cameronnotedthat lobbying “has tainted our politics for too long”. He would shine “the light of transparency” on it. Instead, he oversaw an act that was “more loophole than law”. It did nothing to protect us from lobbying by people such as Cameron –pulling strings, once out of office, among his old colleagues, to try to drum up government business for the bankGreensill.You could almost believe that the real purpose of government was to do the bidding of corporations, foreign states and the ultra-rich. You could almost believe that some government ministers may have an eye on future opportunities when they resist effective reform.So this is another key test for Burnham. Will he allow the mob rule of private business to keep dominating our lives, or will he ensure that government is for the people?George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsPalantirOpinionLobbyingTom WatsonAndy BurnhamPeter ThielNHScommentShareReuse this content

title: This civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: Don’t be fooled by its bickering leaders. Their calibrated fake fighting will probably end in coalition, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: Don’t be fooled by its bickering leaders. Their calibrated fake fighting will probably end in coalition, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: Kemi Badenoch is congratulated by Robert Jenrick after winning the Conservative party leadership contest, 2 November 2024.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch is congratulated by Robert Jenrick after winning the Conservative party leadership contest, 2 November 2024.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionConservativesThis civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than everJonathan LiewDon’t be fooled by its bickering leaders. Their calibrated fake fighting will probably end in coalitionWed 14 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTShareKapow! In a warmly received conference speech, Kemi Badenoch turns her fire on Reform UK, describing it as “weird”, and ruling out an electoral pact. Slap! Not to be outdone, her former colleague Robert Jenrick derides Badenoch as a champion of the wealthy, which is quite rich for a guy who looks like he’s just accidentally ingested a bundle of £50 notes through his sphincter. Bosh! Reform’s Richard Tice and Restore’s Rupert Lowe clash online over the result of acouncil byelectionin Derbyshire, in which the Greens profited from a split rightwing vote. “Vote Restore get Islamists,” Tice chides. “Vote Reform, get some random Bangladeshi bloke,” Lowe responds.Meanwhile, theConservativesare back. The Kemibounce is real. The Keminaissance is true. We’ve all got a severe case of the Kemirrhoids. And you may wonder why much of the media are talking about a Badenoch revival in a year where her party lost 563 councillors and 40% of its councils, remains about four points below its apparent nadir of 2024, and in which the leader herself appears incapable of doing a broadcast interview without looking like a restaurant diner who received exactly what she ordered and is inexplicably furious at it. The point is that the Conservatives are a serious party of government again, and thereasonis that we all said so.And even if we take into account Badenoch’s curiouslyresilient personal polling, this does feel like a largely arbitrary volte-face. There was a soft-focus interview in the Financial Times, a warm editorial in the Sun, and generally positive coverage of the Tory conference in the rest of the rightwing press. Tom Tugendhat, the new shadow foreign secretary and once regarded as a party moderate, had a sympathetic platform in the Observer to defend the party’s opposition to net zero and the European convention on human rights.One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy | Jane MartinsonRead moreFrom a safe distance, it is possible to regard these realignments in a fairly optimistic light. The right is tearing itself to shreds, potentially allowing a leftwing alternative – or failing that, Labour – to clean up. And in the continuing scrap between Lowe and Nigel Farage, or the series of aggressive Telegraph editorials aimed atRestore Britain, it is tempting to glimpse a reassertion of basic, consensual values in which, for all our many disagreements, certain voices will always be beyond the pale.Occasionally you will even hear it said on the progressive left that a strong centre-right is a necessary, welcome bulwark against the extremist far right. That while we can disagree strongly and vehemently with Badenoch’s party, we can also recognise the ways in which a moderate right can act as a kind of cordon sanitaire against the nativists, ethnonationalists and race theorists who may otherwise get their hands on the levers of government. All of which would probably be true, if that were actually what was happening. But is it?Let’s start with the Tories, who appear to be rapidly pivoting towards a demographic that one insider has described as “Waitrose Woman”: affluent, socially liberal, turned off by culture-war rhetoric but laser-focused on tax and the economy. “We have done a ton of opinion research over the last 18 months,” a Conservative source told the Mail on Sunday. “You do have to appear reasonable.” Or, as one shadow cabinet ministertold the Guardian: “We have outsourced our toxicity to Reform.”But in the real world, beyond superficial branding, how different are the two platforms? Shadow cabinet member Nick Timothy called Islamic prayers in Trafalgar Squareun-British, “an act of domination”, “straight from the Islamist playbook”, andBadenoch backed him. Badenoch advocates a ban on pro-Palestine marches, but argued Tommy Robinson should not receive the same treatment. Another shadow cabinet member, Katie Lam, advocated mass deportations of legally settled immigrants in order to make Britain a “culturally coherent group of people”.The Conservative police and crime commissioner Donna Jones responded to the masked vigilante protests in Portsmouth byblaming the governmentfor failing to control our borders. Aformer neo-Nazi activistwas selected as a local election candidate for the Tories, and subsequentlyappointed as an adviser. In the Telegraph, Badenoch wrote that anyone committed to net zero targets is no longer welcome in the party.As for Reform, Monday’s announcement that it wouldimmediately suspend the UK asylum systembrought the party further in line with Restore, both of whom advocate ICE-style raids, the stripping of citizenship from people who thought they were here permanently, and the cessation of aid and visas to countries who refuse to take back migrants. Suella Braverman, a former Tory, now says she can “understand why some people are drawn to Restore”, and suggests people of colour cannot be English.Indeed, you can argue that net zero, welfare, tax cuts, Israel, Brexit, defence spending, trans rights, Donald Trump, the obsession with grooming gangs and Islam, immigration and, most importantly, their common enemies, there is barely a sheet of nori to separate the three parties. And yet at the same time we are expected to believe that these parties engaged in an eternal blood feud, rather than three heads of the same army, pursuing different strategies towards a common cause.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRobert Jenrick launches scathing broadside against ‘Kensington Kemi’Read moreNaturally Westminster will fall for this narrative wholesale, focused as it is on divisions over alliances, personalities over ideas. The Conservatives will be allowed to carry on decontaminating their brand without decontaminating their platform. Farage will continue as flag bearer for the movement, sweeping up donor money and airtime. Meanwhile Restore serves an equally important role as the engine of change, the pressure group, the brains trust: shifting the rhetorical window to the right while allowing Badenoch and Farage to look reasonable in comparison.The civil war on the right is in fact a charade, a fake fight being enacted for our benefit. The right bloc is now a single basic substance, responsive and carefully calibrated to the different audiences it needs to capture. Reform, already in informal talks with Restore, can now tailor its offering to the post-industrial north, Midlands and Wales, leaving the rehabilitated Conservatives – the acceptable face of the project – to concentrate on their southern and rural heartlands. And if, after all the bickering and infighting, a coalition should be required? Do we really expect a Conservative party founded entirely on the gain and exercise of power to suddenly turn it down?To those on the left, the idea of a rightwing meltdown feels vaguely reassuring. But in reality nothing here is being repudiated. The personalities may butt heads for our entertainment, but the ideas and politics are largely common among them all. The parts are being divvied out, but ultimately the production remains the same.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsConservativesOpinionReform UKRestore BritainKemi BadenochNigel FarageRichard TiceFar rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Airports’ TSA staff have been stripped of their chairs in the name of ‘professionalism’. Most supermarket staff have never had them. Meanwhile, Donald Trump is seated at his desk – and apparently snoozing, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Airports’ TSA staff have been stripped of their chairs in the name of ‘professionalism’. Most supermarket staff have never had them. Meanwhile, Donald Trump is seated at his desk – and apparently snoozing, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: ‘Please don’t be seated’ … TSA staff have been deprived of their chairs.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Please don’t be seated’ … TSA staff have been deprived of their chairs.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsWhy are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president?Arwa MahdawiAirports’ TSA staff have been stripped of their chairs in the name of ‘professionalism’. Most supermarket staff have never had them. Meanwhile, Donald Trump is seated at his desk – and apparently snoozingWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTShareGreat news for everyone who is soon to fly via a US airport: the Trump administration has just elevated the travel experience. You still risk getting arrested by immigration agents andthrowninto a detention centre, but never mind that! Instead, luxuriate in the fact that none of the poorly paid Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff with whom you interact will be sitting down. The government recentlygot rid of all the chairsat travel document checking stations, arguing that “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism” and strengthens “our security posture and … commitment to hospitality”. Funnily enough, border patrol and customs officers have not adopted the same policy. Perhaps because their job tends to involve being as inhospitable as possible.TSA agents aren’t the only US workers getting sore calf muscles during their shifts. Unlike their European and British counterparts, cashiers at US supermarkets have traditionally been forced tostand while working. The US’s upright obsession seems to be down to a Protestant work ethic and a lack oflabour laws. Sitting apparently conveys laziness to the discerning American consumer. Over the years there have been numerousright-to-sitlawsuits pushing back on mandatory standing but, while things are shifting slightly, seated supermarket cashiers are still unusual. One exception is Aldi, which has beenexpandingaggressively in the US. Cashiersget chairs at Aldibecause (surprise) it’s more efficient when your workers’ feet aren’t aching all the time.While seated cashiers and TSA agents may be looked down on by the US establishment, it’s a different story for high-flyers. Rather than “maintaining a standing posture” to “reinforce professionalism”, the US president often looks as if he issnoozingat his desk. Which, to be fair, is probably because he regularly stays up all night posting extremely important memes on the internet.Having their chairs seized isn’t the only indignity that TSA agents have faced recently: along with other federal employees, they had towork without payfor several weeks during government shutdowns in Trump’s second term. Members of Congress on the other hand? They could continue to collect their generous salaries during the shutdown unless they explicitlychose not to. Americans should not take this injustice sitting down.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I hate golf | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: I’ve been trying to quit the game for years, writes Adrian Chiles. Just when I thought I was out, it pulled me back in …
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: I’ve been trying to quit the game for years, writes Adrian Chiles. Just when I thought I was out, it pulled me back in …
Content: ‘I played the ninth like a master, then went to the charity shop to dump my clubs.’Photograph: jacoblund/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘I played the ninth like a master, then went to the charity shop to dump my clubs.’Photograph: jacoblund/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionGolfI hate golfAdrian ChilesI’ve been trying to quit the game for years. Just when I thought I was out, it pulled me back in …Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTShareIhate golf. A good walk spoiled? The whole day spoiled, more like. As with many cases of hate, it has its roots in love. You see, I just love the feeling of hitting the ball sweetly. If you feel the same way,then you’re into golf; if you don’t, then you’re not. But I am, and from the moment I struck a ball sweetly for the first time, I was hooked. It happened playing my first proper round of golf, off the third tee at the Gower Golf Club. Woomph. Making hardly a sound and barely seeming to make an impact as club hit ball, off it went. And that was me.My logic ran that if I could play like that as an absolute beginner, imagine what I could do with a bit of practice. I strode up to my ball on the fairway and, swinging with great confidence, played an air shot. Missed it completely. Pretending this was but my practice swing, I tried again, and this time made contact with the ball, but mostly with the ground, causing lasting damage to the fairway. The ball advanced all of six inches. Welcome to golf.double quotation markFinally Laura Davies told me to just shut up and hit the effing thingThat a complete novice can hit a proper shot is both the best thing about golf and the worst. It draws you in, giving you great encouragement. But it also drives you nuts when, unaccountably, you suddenly can’t do it. Other skills aren’t like this. Take the piano. To play even just the slow opening bit of Beethoven’s Pathétique Sonata would take years of practice. Nobody ever sat at a piano, with no experience, and on day one played anything resembling Beethoven. Yet in golf, it is kind of possible. And it’s equally possible, moments later, to find yourself quite incapable of doing anything of the sort.Imagine being able to knock out some Beethoven, yet a minute later finding yourself unable to give a recital of Chopsticks. That’s golf. Consider being skilled enough in the kitchen to cook from scratch a starter of butter-poached scallop, followed by beef wellington for the main course. And then finding yourself unable to serve up a scoop of ice-cream out of a tub for pudding. That’s golf.I started playing too late, in my early 30s, so in golfing parlance I was always playing three off the tee. If you don’t get that, don’t worry – you’re not missing much. The point is: you need to start young, hardwiring the sense of what it takes to strike a ball. Any clown, as I found, could hit it sweetly now and then. Repeating the feat, not so much.My latest discovery? You can eat the skin of a kiwifruit – and the benefits are myriad | Adrian ChilesRead moreNaively enough, I set about addressing this by practising and playing and practising and playing for hours and days on end. In most other pursuits, the hours I put in would have seen me reach some level of reliable competence. In piano, I might not have been playing with the London Philharmonic, but I would have got north of grade 5 and been able to hold my own for 15 minutes on one of those uprights they leave lying around in train stations. But that’s not how golf works. At least for me it wasn’t. Any discernible improvement was so haphazard that it only ever felt like a different iteration of failure. While the good shots got slightly better and more numerous, the improvement in the bad shots lagged behind.It didn’t help that I pinned too much on the whole enterprise. I kept telling myself that I took it up because it was the only sport at which I could hope to improve as I got older. So, in my mind, it became nothing less than an exercise in defying the passage of time. I played so much – whatever the weather, on my own, with friends, with strangers – every round demoralising and encouraging me in equal measure. After a bad round it was not unknown for me to go to the driving range and hit hundreds of balls in a futile rage of desperation to put things right.I had hundreds of lessons, which would invariably conclude with me reliably swinging and striking like a champ and fair salivating at the prospect of my next round, which went as pear-shaped as all the others. Overthinking anything is rarely helpful; with the technical aspects of the golf swing, it’s disastrous. Speed, grip, stance, wrist, elbows, hips, shoulders, head and a dozen other things all demand consideration, and that’s just during the backswing.‘The Jackie Robinson of golf’: the forgotten story of Black pioneer Ted RhodesRead moreI once played in a pro-am with those legends of football and golf Kenny Dalglish and Laura Davies. On the first tee, the announcements of their names were rapturously received. Mine less so, but I didn’t care. My only worry was for the safety of the spectators lining the tee. Miraculously, my first tee shot wasn’t terrible. One hand might even have clapped. After that I played like a drain. I bombarded poor Laura with technical questions until her patience snapped and she told me to just shut up and hit the effing thing.The end came one Saturday in Pitlochry. Nine holes on the morning of a friend’s wedding. After eight holes of tragicomic ineptitude, I decided that I was done with golf for ever. I then played the ninth like a master, but I wasn’t to be fooled. By the time I got to the charity shop to dump my clubs, it had closed for the afternoon, so they survived the cull. But in the 20 years since, I’ve played only a dozen times, which is about as much as my shattered self-esteem can take. Playing with no expectation of my game makes it more tolerable, but only a little. In general, it’s nothing less than triggering.I played on Sunday, at the idyllic Langland Bay course on Gower, with three of my closest, most easygoing friends. This is just fun, it’s great to be here, what’s not to love? This is what I said to myself, like a mantra. It worked for a while, until I found that the bad shots appalled me still and, to the bafflement of my friends, the good shots darkened my mood even more. “But you’re playing well!” they protested. Yes, that’s the problem. I fear being drawn back in. And I allow myself no joy at a good shot because I know that it’ll only make the inevitable subsequent crap shot feel so much worse. Nice course, lovely people but, sorry, there’s no going back. I hate golf.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: President Zelenskyy’s allies must show the Russian president that American perfidy won’t alter the course of a war the Kremlin is losing
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: President Zelenskyy’s allies must show the Russian president that American perfidy won’t alter the course of a war the Kremlin is losing
Content: Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in August 2025. ‘Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Donald Trump in August 2025. ‘Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionUkraineThe Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechangingEditorialPresident Zelenskyy’s allies must show the Russian president that American perfidy won’t alter the course of a war the Kremlin is losingWed 14 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareWhen Donald Trump pledged to end the war in Ukrainewithin 24 hoursof re-entering the White House last year, no one with any depth of insight into the conflict believed him. But Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image as a master dealmaker. After a period when it seemed that Kyiv’s European allies had steered the US president away from pro‑Kremlin partisanship, he has reverted to the grotesque view that Ukrainian capitulation is a necessary precondition for peace.These are the perilous circumstances in which President Volodymyr Zelenskyymet Andy Burnhamon Wednesday in Downing Street. In recent days, the US president has called for a change of government in Ukraine. He claimed that apartial ceasefirehad been agreed, while Russia escalated its bombardments. According to Mr Zelenskyy, the latest missile strikes have come without the intelligence warnings from the US that have, in the past, facilitated self-defence. There have been reports of Ukrainian soldierslosing accessto the Starlink satellite network, controlled by Elon Musk, the US tech oligarch. This raises suspicion of coordinated pressure to tip the scales in Russia’s favour after many months when Mr Putin’s forces have failed to deliver significant advances and his country’s economy has been suffering from the effect of Ukrainian missile and drone counterstrikes.Mr Trump is unhappy with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. He claims that this is the cause of high energy prices afflicting American consumers and threatening Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections. The domestic imperative to keep pump prices down led Mr Trump to do a grubby deal toimport dieselfrom Russia, in flagrant breach of international sanctions.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy.Photograph: Dan Bashakov/APThe real driver of global energy prices is notUkrainedefending itself from Russian attack, but Mr Trump’s failing war against Iran. However, the US president is incapable of admitting any fault. Blaming Mr Zelenskyy enables him to deny his own culpability and, with malevolent encouragement from Mr Putin, to revive the preposterous notion that Ukrainian intransigence rather than Russian aggression is the reason why his promise to broker a peace deal remains unfulfilled.Disrupting Mr Trump’s pro-Russian delusions is not easy, but it has been done before. It is not agratifying diplomatic taskto indulge the monstrous vanity of the US president by trying to impress upon him a view of his country’s national interest, that Mr Putin is not an ally of his country or his personal friend, which is self-evident to any rational observer.Mr Burnham rightly resists invitations to denounce the US president in public. He recognises that Ukraine’s cause and, by extension, also the cause of European democracy more widely, is better served by making the case in private. The best response to Mr Trump’s perfidy is for Mr Zelenskyy’s friends to reaffirm their support, as Mr Burnham has done, thereby signalling that Ukraine will not be beaten by deals between the Kremlin and the White House.Russia is failing to achieve its war aims because the invasion was conceived in delusional hatred for the very idea of independent Ukrainian nationhood, which routinely underestimates that country’s will to resist. That is a flaw in Mr Putin’s plans that no amount of collusion with Mr Trump can fix.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
