Content: The increasing use of houses of multiple occupancy  as part of the government’s plans to phase out the use of hotels to house asylum seekers has given some activists a new target.Photograph: Dan Chung/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe increasing use of houses of multiple occupancy  as part of the government’s plans to phase out the use of hotels to house asylum seekers has given some activists a new target.Photograph: Dan Chung/The GuardianSocial media‘English nationalist’ content creators film themselves in asylum seekers’ houseVideo posted online shows men entering home through unlocked door and claiming to be looking for paperworkDiane TaylorandBen QuinnWed 14 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Home Office accommodation provider has launched an investigation after “English nationalist” content creators posing as contractors filmed themselves entering a property housing asylum seekers.The video, titled “HMO Hunting in Leicestershire”, was posted to the Truthhurts101UK YouTube account, which describes itself as being run by an “English nationalist citizen journalist” and claims to cover “immigration, demographic change, policing and stories others overlook”. The footage was also posted to the associated TH101UK’s X account, where is has been viewed more than 300,000 times.The video shows three men accessing the back entrance of a house in Leicestershire accommodating asylum seekers. The men enter via an unlocked back door and move through several rooms of the house, including the kitchen, where they examine the contents of the fridge. They repeatedly claim to be looking for “paperwork”, searching through a pile of letters near the front door and boxes discarded in the back garden. The man filming, who narrates the video, claims he is the first to “document” this property.When the men filming encounter three men, who are believed to be asylum seekers living at the property, in the kitchen they tell them they are contractors sent to assess the property for repairs. They ask one man living at the property whether the property is run bySerco, a Home Office contractor used for asylum seeker accommodation, which the man confirms, and whether he has “paperwork”, which he says he does not.When the man living at the property asks the man filming for his ID he briefly shows him a lanyard. It is unclear what information it shows.In the footage, the man filming specifically names the street and the village where the house is located, and shows the exterior of the property and its surroundings, making it clearly identifiable.A Serco spokesperson said: “We are aware of this post. We take issues of this nature extremely seriously and are investigating.”A Home Office spokesperson said: “The safety and security of those housed in asylum accommodation, staff who work there and local communities are of the upmost importance to the government. We engage extensively with contractors, local authorities and the police and expect any instances of criminality to be taken seriously.”A TH101UK spokesperson defended the footage, accused the asylum seekers of being “ticking timebombs” and questioned why the Guardian, which they described as “irrelevant” and a “rag”, was “scrutinising independent journalism”.They added: “Don’t worry, I’ll keep asking the questions you should be.”In recent years, there has been an increase of self-styled “auditors”, and far-right activists have attempted to gain access to hotels and other forms of accommodation housing asylum seekers, sometimes under the guise of wanting to carry out “inspections”.When challenged, often by private security outside hotels, some have attempted to confuse the issue by quoting supposed “common law” principles, which have been taken up by members of the far right as a legal recourse that supersedes statutory laws.However, the increasing use of houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs) as part of the government’s plans to phase out the use of hotels to house asylum seekers has given some of these activists a new target, with some obtaining addresses from publicly available documents and sharing details with one another in online groups.TH101UK entered another asylum seeker property in Norfolk several months ago and posted footage online.After the Guardian brought the footage to the attention of YouTube, a spokesperson confirmed that it breached its standards, and said that it had been removed from the platform.A YouTube spokesperson said:“Harassment and cyberbullying are not allowed on YouTube and as part of this, we do not allow content that reveals someone’s personally identifiable information. Upon review, we have removed the flagged video for violating ourharassment and cyberbullyingpolicies.”Louise Calvey, the executive director of Asylum Matters, expressed concern about the video. She said: “This is a premeditated invasion into someone’s home for clicks and attention. The people that court this are the very worst of us, they’re the ones the pose a threat – barging into people’s homes, filming in people’s private spaces. The audacity and sense of entitlement is breathtaking.“Government must urgently take steps to improve protections, remove the details of shared accommodation sites of all descriptions from the public domain, support people accommodated as victims of crimes, and escalate quicker police responses.”Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaImmigration and asylumSercoHousingCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says | Ilhan Omar | The Guardian
description: Federal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraud
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Federal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraud
Content: Ilhan Omar, a frequent target of Donald Trump’s anti-Somali rhetoric, said she would ‘not be silenced’ by the justice department’s investigation.Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersView image in fullscreenIlhan Omar, a frequent target of Donald Trump’s anti-Somali rhetoric, said she would ‘not be silenced’ by the justice department’s investigation.Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersIlhan OmarIlhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source saysFederal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraudUS politics live – latest updatesAssociated PressWed 14 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal authorities investigating the Minnesota representativeIlhan Omarseized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the inquiry.The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence inMinnesotaas federal authorities investigate potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington DC home on Monday just weeks before theNovember midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election.The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.Democrats rebuke federal raid of Ilhan Omar’s home: ‘rogue abuse of power’Read moreOn Tuesday, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also looking into issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests, which will determine control of the House and the Senate, was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the representative for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement”.“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”A phone message seeking comment was left on Wednesday with a representative for Omar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThough the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The justice department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s fifth district, including Minneapolis. She is part of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.Explore more on these topicsIlhan OmarTrump administrationUS justice systemUS politicsWashington DCMinnesotanewsShareReuse this content

title: Sally Rooney says she can no longer sell books in UK due to Palestine Action support | UK news | The Guardian
description: Irish writer of Normal People says she can no longer receive royalties from British sales and she cancelled UK trip due to fear of arrest
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Irish writer of Normal People says she can no longer receive royalties from British sales and she cancelled UK trip due to fear of arrest
Content: Sally Rooney said the fulfilment of contracts to publish her work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence.Photograph: David Levenson/GettyView image in fullscreenSally Rooney said the fulfilment of contracts to publish her work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence.Photograph: David Levenson/GettyUK newsSally Rooney says she can no longer sell books in UK due to Palestine Action supportIrish writer of Normal People says she can no longer receive royalties from British sales and she cancelled UK trip due to fear of arrestHaroon SiddiqueandGeorge Francis LeeWed 14 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action.The Irish novelist, whose books include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, said her public support for the direct action group meant she could no longer receive royalties from UK sales.After Palestine Action was banned last year, Rooney said shewould use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Supporting organisations banned under the Terrorism Act is an offence and she subsequently cancelleda trip to the UKto pick up an award, for fear of arrest.In a statement provided to the Guardian, the bestselling author said: “‘In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”Ina high court statement in support of the legal challengeto proscription, warning against its impact on freedom of expression, Rooney said her books could disappear from UK stores and the publication of new works in the UK could be prevented.Her books have been critically acclaimed – she has beendescribed as the voice of a generation– and hugely commercially successful in the UK. Normal People has sold more than 1m copies, while Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You have each sold more than 500,000. Normal People and Conversations With Friends were adapted by the BBC, and the former racked up 62.7m views, becoming the broadcaster’s most-streamed series of 2020.Rooney said last year that she had been advised by the independent producer of the TV dramatisations that any payment to her for those series, both broadcast before the ban, would be a breach of terrorism laws if it knew or suspected that she was using the royalties to fund Palestine Action.Section 15 of the Terrorism Act makes it an offence if a person “provides money or other property, and knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism”. It carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.Her UK and Ireland publisher, Faber, said: “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.“As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned in July last year, most for holding placards saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”About 2,500 people have been charged, although none have been tried as a legal challenge to the ban is continuing andwill be heard by the supreme courtnext month. Most arrests and charges have related to section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which carries a maximum jail term of six months.Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action who has brought the legal challenge against the ban, said: “Sally Rooney being unable to publish her work in the UK marks a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action …“[She] took a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced. She has refused to compromise her convictions, even at considerable personal and professional cost. Her work should be celebrated and widely available​, not driven off the shelves of British bookshops because she refuses to be complicit in the suppression of solidarity with the Palestinian people. No author should have to choose between their principles and their freedom to publish.​”Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said: “Whatever one’s views on Palestine Action, we should all be concerned when laws intended to combat terrorism end up silencing artistic freedom and the ability to engage in peaceful political dissent.“Writers should not find their books disappearing from shelves because of their political beliefs. Nor should people have to choose between expressing their conscience and pursuing their livelihoods.“Sally Rooney’s willingness to accept the personal consequences of her convictions deserves recognition. There is a real danger that others, seeing the price she has paid, will decide they cannot afford to speak out.”Rooney’s books were still on sale in central London on Wednesday afternoon, and Waterstones said that existing stock could still be sold.Gian Carlo, a bookseller at Henry Pordes Books, said the same, adding: “Nothing goes to Sally Rooney in this case. We sell books of all types, they’re not connected to the author. I can’t say I don’t agree with her.John Clegg, a bookseller at London Review Bookshop, said: “I ordered more as soon as I saw the news. I saw the number go down to zero, so I hope they go through. People are going to want them and we’re not going to be able to get them through Faber.“Good on her for taking a stand, it seems a ridiculous law. If this thing convinces the Home Office to move faster to get rid of it, I’m all for it.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers
Content: Simbarashe Kundizeza says the story is entirely his own work.View image in fullscreenSimbarashe Kundizeza says the story is entirely his own work.AI (artificial intelligence)Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning storyArticle in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writersRachel Savagein JohannesburgWed 14 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.Kundizeza’s storyThe Blue Fighterwas announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published anarticleby the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”Kundizeza responded in astatement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.“I look forward to continuing to work with theCaine prizeteam, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”View image in fullscreenJournalist Vauhini Vara said she had run Kundizeza’s story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost entirely AI generated.Photograph: Andrew AltschulSimilar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazirwon the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prizewith The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) wasremoved from the longlistof France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.The Caine prize said in astatementthat it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize listRead moreIn his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journalarticlethat found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Caine prizeThe AtlanticShort storiesAwards and prizesFictionZimbabwenewsShareReuse this content

title: SpaceX rocket launch causes stunning ‘jellyfish cloud’ visible off US east coast | Florida | The Guardian
description: Expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalized in the sky and reflected sunlight off frozen particles after Florida launch
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalized in the sky and reflected sunlight off frozen particles after Florida launch
Content: SpaceX rocket launch creates glowing 'space jellyfish' cloud – videoFloridaSpaceX rocket launch causes stunning ‘jellyfish cloud’ visible off US east coastExpanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalized in the sky and reflected sunlight off frozen particles after Florida launchRichard Luscombein MiamiWed 14 Oct 2026 14.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleASpaceXrocket provided a stunning pre-dawn display overFloridaas a egiant, luminescent “jellyfish cloud” spread for miles, caused by an expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalizing in the sky and reflecting sunlight off the frozen particles.The phenomenon occurred shortly after Tuesday’s 6.33am ET launch of the Falcon 9 rocket carrying cargo to the InternationalSpaceStation.The timing of the blastoff, 48 minutes before sunrise at Florida’s Cape Canaveral space force station, provided a perfect example of the colorful effect only fully visible from Earth during dusk and dawn launches.The rocket’s north-eastern trajectory over the Atlantic also allowed residents of eastern states fromGeorgia to New Yorkto enjoy the spectacle.Nasa posted photographs of the jellyfish cloudon X, the social media platform owned by the SpaceX chief executive, Elon Musk. Among the hundreds of replies were images taken by sky watchers across multiple states.Those who missed Tuesday’s dazzling celestial show have another opportunity to view one next Monday, 19 October, when another SpaceX Falcon 9 isscheduled to lift offfrom the same space force station pad.An hour-long launch window for the satellite-deployment mission opens at 6.30am ET, little more than a half-hour before the 7.01am sunrise.Explore more on these topicsFloridaNasaSpaceXSpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Plan unveiled to increase share of land farmed organically in England to 10% | Farming | The Guardian
description: Government says ambition for 2036 will be good for food and climate resilience, but concerns remain over funding
Author: Pippa Neill
Headline: Government says ambition for 2036 will be good for food and climate resilience, but concerns remain over funding
Content: Some producers said ministers needed to provide financial backing if they wanted to see a significant transition to organic farming.Photograph: Cultura Creative (RF)/AlamyView image in fullscreenSome producers said ministers needed to provide financial backing if they wanted to see a significant transition to organic farming.Photograph: Cultura Creative (RF)/AlamyFarmingPlan unveiled to increase share of land farmed organically in England to 10%Government says ambition for 2036 will be good for food and climate resilience, but concerns remain over fundingPippa NeillEnvironment reporterWed 14 Oct 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government has set an ambition to increase the share of English land farmed organically to 10% by 2036, but concerns remain over how the transition will be funded.Currently, just 3.4% of England’s agricultural land is farmed organically, one of the smallest shares in Europe. France, for example, farms 10.4% of its land organically, and aims to increase this to 18% by 2027.Rob Haward, the chief executive oforganic veg box company Riverford, said it was a reflection of organic farming having political backing in the EU. Whereas in England, the lastorganic farming planwas published more than two decades ago.The government’snew plan, which has been more than three years in the making, sets out a vision for growth in the organic sector, with public procurement – in schools and hospitals, for example – cited as a significant opportunity. The government already has a long-term ambition for 10% of public sector food spend to meet higher environmental production standards. The plan states that the organic sector can play a vital role in achieving this.The environment secretary,Angela Eagle, said the plan was about “opening up opportunities across the sector, from backing farmers already producing organic food to helping others decide whether it could work for their businesses”.She added: “Organic farming should not be treated as a niche. More people are looking closely at where their food comes from, how it is produced and whether it meets standards they value.”Haward said public procurement was “impenetrable” for small organic farms, but hoped the plan would be a “catalyst for growth”. However, he said the sector now needed proper backing from the government, including grant funding.In September,thousands of farmerswere left empty-handed after the government’s sustainable farming incentive 2026 (SFI) funding was spent in just six hours. This meant that some farmers who might have been planning to use the funding to transition to organic farming may have missed out.“SFI needs to be reliable, successful and secure to enable this transition,” said Haward. “It’s hard for any farm to invest in their business if things change, we need some consistency.”Gareth Morgan, the head of farming policy at the Soil Association, said there had been a lot of discussions with Defra about funding, but in the end “there has been a compromise”.‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food securityRead more“There is now an urgent need to reopen SFI to enable farms to move to organic farming,” he said.Morgan added that increasing the share of land farmed organically could bring down the price of organic food for consumers. “Currently the price of food is subsidised and we don’t pay for the environmental impact. If organic food becomes more mainstream, the price difference will become less,” he said.Martin Lines, the chief executive of the Nature FriendlyFarmingNetwork, said farmers could not rely on government funding alone to make this transition, and said there needed to be “real investment from the supply chain and the private sector, along with fairer prices for farmers for their goods and stronger domestic markets for homegrown produce”.The National Farmers’ Union, whose members include organic and non-organic farms, said the plan signified a “really positive step forward … for the wider supply chain”.“Supporting domestic production will strengthen the resilience of our food supply chains and ensure British farmers and growers benefit from opportunities, rather than increasing our reliance on imports,” said Paul Tompkins, the deputy president of the union.In the plan’s foreword, Eagle said: “Across England, organic farmers, growers and food businesses play an important role in producing high-quality food while caring for soils, wildlife and the rural communities they are part of. In doing so, they also help advance wider goals for nature recovery, cleaner water and greater climate resilience.”This year has been challenging for farmers because of crop-destroying heat and drought alongside soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran. Organic farms have been found to bemore resilientin the face of these extreme weather conditions and are also not affected by rising fertiliser costs.“Organic farmers are much less exposed to these risks,” Morgan said, adding that the plan was a sign that the government was thinking hard about the pathway for food security.Explore more on these topicsFarmingEnglandAngela EagleOrganicsFoodClimate crisisRural affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year | Mountains | The Guardian
description: Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate
Content: The Aiguille du Midi cable car traverses the slopes of Mont-Blanc in Haute-Savoie, France.Photograph: Design Pics Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Aiguille du Midi cable car traverses the slopes of Mont-Blanc in Haute-Savoie, France.Photograph: Design Pics Inc/AlamyMountainsMont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a yearPeak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climateAjit NiranjanEurope environment correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWestern Europe’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.Chartered surveyors from the Union Nationale des Géomètres-Experts (UNGE) and the Ordre des Géomètres-Experts, who have regularly monitored the peak since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain, and drones to create a detailed model of the snow and ice cap.The summit has shrunk back by 3.43 metres since a high of 4,810.90 metres in 2007, the data shows.The experts cautioned against linking fluctuations in height from year to year to the rapid loss of Alpine ice being caused by fossil fuel pollution.“Regarding ice mass, it is essential to distinguish between changes in surface altitude and changes in the total volume or mass of ice,” a UNGE spokesperson said. “An increase in summit altitude does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained ice mass, nor does it contradict the documented retreat of Alpine glaciers.”Climate breakdown was a factor in western Europe’s hottest summer on record this year, scarring Alpine regions and melting ice at dizzying speed. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an “explosion of melt rates” after confirming that one-fifth of the country’s ice had been lost in the past five years, and 5.5% of volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.Jean des Garets, the president of the Haute-Savoie departmental chamber of surveyors and the leader of the Mont Blanc expedition, said the warming trend could be seen with the naked eye in the rest of the Alpine massif but that “for the moment, climate change doesn’t seem to have the same impact above 4,000 metres”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When we climb, we pass by the Brigade Blanche hut before the Tête-Rousse glacier,” he said in comments reported by the French television channel TF1 on Wednesday. “We’ve seen that the glacier has moved up. It has literally melted before our very eyes and now in some places we’re crossing a stream instead of a glacier.”Explore more on these topicsMountainsFranceGlaciersEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Businesses could be barred from non-essential water use amid supply threat | Water | The Guardian
description: Golf clubs, private schools and car washes may face tighter rules from water companies as England’s drought continues
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Golf clubs, private schools and car washes may face tighter rules from water companies as England’s drought continues
Content: Wimbleball reservoir in Exmoor, Somerset, is currently at less than a quarter of its capacity after the dry spring and summer heatwaves.Photograph: Paul Silvers/BNPSView image in fullscreenWimbleball reservoir in Exmoor, Somerset, is currently at less than a quarter of its capacity after the dry spring and summer heatwaves.Photograph: Paul Silvers/BNPSWaterBusinesses could be barred from non-essential water use amid supply threatGolf clubs, private schools and car washes may face tighter rules from water companies as England’s drought continuesSandra LavilleWed 14 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 06.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThree water companies are seeking to impose severe restrictions on businesses as the drought continues across most ofEngland, putting rivers and wildlife under huge pressure.Golf clubs and private schools could be barred from using mains water to irrigate playing fields and courses, and commercial car washes stopped from operating, under “non-essential use bans” being sought by the companies.Eleven areas of England are still in drought, rivers are suffering from low flows, groundwater levels are declining and reservoir levels are at 54% – 21% below what is expected in the autumn.Yorkshire was the latest area to move into drought status on 9 October. Parts of Wales are experiencing the first signs of drought recovery after the whole country was declared in drought in July.An illustration showing areas of England in droughtNineteen reservoirs or reservoir groups in England and Wales are less than 50% full, and eight are exceptionally low, up fromfive in August.The Met Office says above-average rainfallis needed over a sustained seven-month period to bring all areas out of drought. But last month England received about 65% of its typical September rainfall, with eastern and southern areas experiencing the greatest deficit.View image in fullscreenDepleted water levels at Ardingly reservoir in West Sussex.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersBusinesses in drought-hit areas have been excluded from thehosepipe restrictionsimposed on the public for the past three months. But South East, Southern and South West Water have applied to extend restrictions on water use to businesses via non-essential use bans in parts of their regions. If granted, water restrictions can be placed on golf clubs, private schools and commercial car washes to cut water use. Power hoses in car washes can use up to 25 litres of water per minute.Permission from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) is required, but the government has yet to respond to the water companies’ requests.An area showing reservoirs in England and WalesPressure on wildlife and the environmentfrom the drought is continuing. River flows in seven areas in England are exceptionally low, according to the latest Defra figures, affecting habitats, fish and wildlife. They include the River Derwent in the north-east, the rivers Yare and Ely Ouse in east England, and the River Tone and the Hampshire Avon catchments in south-west England.When river flows fall tolow flow levelsthey can take years to recover, with potentially severe effects on fish spawning and river health.Mark Owen, the head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said: “When rivers and fish are suffering from the ongoing effects of a severe drought, the Angling Trust supports further restrictions on non-essential water use, alongside urgent action to reduce huge leakage from water companies and unsustainable abstraction from rivers.“We must continue to reduce unnecessary demand for water. It makes little sense to ban people from washing cars at home while commercial car washes can continue operating.”In Hampshire, where the chalk aquifer is exceptionally low, Southern Wateris seeking a drought orderthat would allow it to draw water from an internationally prized chalk stream and rare salmon habitat, even at levels below what is deemed ecologically safe. Southern said it was applying for the permit for the River Test owing to “a clear threat to supplies” in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe company is seeking a non-essential use ban on commercial premises and businesses to reduce demand as it seeks to draw more water from the Test at levels that were previously deemed unacceptable.As they seek permission to put restrictions on businesses’ water use,South East Waterand South West Water have been allowed to alter the amount of water they draw from rivers to try to conserve water in their reservoirs.The Ardingly reservoir, near Haywards Heath in West Sussex, which serves 280,000 people, is exceptionally low, holding 1.05bn litres of water. Its total capacity is 5.2bn litres.In the south-west, Colliford reservoir on Bodmin Moor, which serves 255,000 households in Cornwall, is 37% full, holding 10.68bn litres against a total capacity of 28.5bn litres. Wimbleball in Somerset, which provides water for 390,000 people, is 18% full, with 3.8bn litres against a total capacity of 21.3bn litres.Sam Bottomley, South West Water’s director for drinking water services, said the region was entering a critical phase of an exceptionally prolonged drought.“Every day we continue to draw on our reservoirs to keep water flowing to homes, businesses and communities while river flows remain below the levels needed to support public water supply,” he said.“Many people understandably think a drought is over once it starts raining. In reality, recovery takes much longer.“Some rivers still remain at their lowest levels and with no significant rain forecast for the coming weeks, the immediate challenge is reducing demand and preserving enough stored water to maintain supplies until river flows and reservoir levels recover.”Explore more on these topicsWaterDroughtWater industryRiversSouth East WaterEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scale back on hake and coley, seafood charity tells shoppers | Fishing | The Guardian
description: Declining stocks and increased fishing pressure have led to lower sustainability ratings for two popular cod alternatives
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: Declining stocks and increased fishing pressure have led to lower sustainability ratings for two popular cod alternatives
Content: European hake caught in the North Sea, Celtic Seas, or Bay of Biscay have been moved from green to amber by the MCSPhotograph: VictorHuang/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenEuropean hake caught in the North Sea, Celtic Seas, or Bay of Biscay have been moved from green to amber by the MCSPhotograph: VictorHuang/Getty Images/iStockphotoFishingScale back on hake and coley, seafood charity tells shoppersDeclining stocks and increased fishing pressure have led to lower sustainability ratings for two popular cod alternativesZoe WoodWed 14 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK shoppers have previously been urged toavoid UK-caught codand to buy European hake or coley instead – but now these fish are in trouble, too.The MarineConservationSociety (MCS), an environmental charity, publishes its Good Fish Guide to help consumers and businesses make sustainable seafood choices. It uses a traffic-light system to rate seafood according to the health of fish stocks and environmental impact.On Wednesday, the MCS downgraded the ratings forEuropean hake caught in the North Sea, Celtic Seas, or Bay of Biscay from green to amber owing to declining stocks and increased fishing pressure.Meanwhile, the rating on coley caught around the UK (North Sea, West of Scotland, Rockall and Skagerrak) has fallen from amber to red – theworst rating– meaning it is a “fish to avoid”. Of the 10 coley fisheries rated by the guide, two are still green while the other eight are amber.Kerry Lyne, the Good Fish Guide manager, said the “status of fish stocks are continuously changing” and a “fish that was a good choice a few years ago is not necessarily a good choice everywhere today”.Most of the seafood consumed in the UK is made up of just a few different species, known as the big five: cod, haddock, salmon, tuna and prawns. This puts a lot of pressure on a handful of wild stocks.Cod populations have been in decline since 2015. The main cause is overfishing, although changing sea temperatures and other ecosystem pressures have affected breeding and juvenile survival.“The best thing we can all do if we eat seafood is diversify our seafood choices and avoid those most under threat,” Lyne added.With that in mind, the charity has suggested wild-caught sea bass from around the UK as a more ocean-friendly alternative to cod. Similar to cod, sea bass is a mild white fish with a flaky texture that can be swapped like-for-like in any recipe.The guide is updated twice a year and of the 727 ratings, the latest review has 29 downgrades and 11 upgrades.On the good news front, UK Atlantic bluefin tuna, which has shown huge signs of apopulation recovery, has a brand new green rating. Chris Graham, the charity’s head of ocean regeneration and sustainable seafood, said one of the factors behind the resurgence was better fisheries management brought in more than 20 years ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest sharkRead more“We’re pleased to see a small, well-managed fishery in place, but caution must prevail, and this iconic species must be monitored closely so the health of the UK population can continue to improve,” Graham said.Lyme Bay“disco-pot” scallopswere another new entry, with an amber rating. LED lights inside the pots to attract scallops mean the new technology has a much lower impact on the seabed than traditional dredging.Explore more on these topicsFishingFoodAnimalsConservationWildlifeMarine lifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Palantir and Sadiq Khan drop legal battle over Met contract | Palantir | The Guardian
description: Dispute related to claims London mayor blocked US tech firm from £50m police deal because of concerns over its values
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Dispute related to claims London mayor blocked US tech firm from £50m police deal because of concerns over its values
Content: Sadiq Khan said Palantir ‘makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital’.Photograph: Justin Tallis/ReutersView image in fullscreenSadiq Khan said Palantir ‘makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital’.Photograph: Justin Tallis/ReutersPalantirPalantir and Sadiq Khan drop legal battle over Met contractDispute related to claims London mayor blocked US tech firm from £50m police deal because of concerns over its valuesRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePalantir and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, have called off theirlegal fightover claims the Labour mayor was blocking the US tech company from signing a contract with the Metropolitan police because of its values and ethics.Palantir and the mayor’s office for policing and crime (Mopac) announced on Wednesday they had withdrawn allegations against each other, heading off a high court trial scheduled for January.Palantir sued Mopac in June after Khanstepped into block it from awarding Palantir a two-year, £50m deal for Scotland Yard to use AI to process intelligence in criminal investigations in a system called unified operational analytics (UOA), citing a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules.With Palantir also working for the Israeli military and for the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, Khan has previously said Londoners only wanted to see public money being paid to companies that “share the values of our city”.Louis Mosley, who heads Palantir in the UK and Europe, responded by accusing Khan of politicising procurement and said he was “putting politics above public safety”. He said: “What Londoners value is not being mugged, not being raped by a serving police officer.”The agreement to drop the claims against each other comes a month after Palantirhired Tom Watson, the former Labour party deputy leader, as a full-time lobbyist. The firm was concerned that if public authorities were able to block it from winning contracts due to objections over the values of its senior leadership, it would undermine its ability to operate in the UK.Palantir is facing a battle to retain its £330m NHS medical data contract amid a vociferous campaign from parts of the public and some MPs for it to be replaced by a less controversial company.Palantir and Mopac said in a joint statement that Mopac’s decision in May to block the contract “was not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company”.“Mopac recognises Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the mayor’s spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision,” it said.“Mopac’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners.”Khan said: “London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organisations across the UK and beyond.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWatson said: “The mayor and his team have recognised their actions could have created the impression that the decision to block the UOA contract was based on Palantir’s values. I’m very pleased that they have today corrected any such impression, and that even in the face of extreme provocation from highly organised pressure groups, decisions about deploying technology can still be made on their merits and in the public interest.”A new procurement process for the £50m police tech deal is under way and Mopac has agreed to treat Palantir “fairly and equally” if it bids, as expected. Equally, Mopac is not bound to agree to Palantir’s appointment.Each side is covering its own legal costs, no admissions of liability are made and no damages have been paid.Explore more on these topicsPalantirSadiq KhanLondon politicsMetropolitan policeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Archers cast ‘angry’ at BBC decision to scrap new Birmingham studio | BBC | The Guardian
description: Ben Norris says cost-cutting measure that means show will be recorded outside its home city risks ‘extraordinary burden’ for crew
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Ben Norris says cost-cutting measure that means show will be recorded outside its home city risks ‘extraordinary burden’ for crew
Content: The Archers has been based in Birmingham since its first episode in 1951.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Archers has been based in Birmingham since its first episode in 1951.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBBCThe Archers cast ‘angry’ at BBC decision to scrap new Birmingham studioBen Norris says cost-cutting measure that means show will be recorded outside its home city risks ‘extraordinary burden’ for crewMichael SavageMedia editorWed 14 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA cast member ofThe Archershas said its actors have been angered by the BBC’s decision to axe the show’s new studio, in a move that could lead to it being recorded away from its home in Birmingham.Ben Norris, who plays Ben Archer in the world’s longest-running soap opera, said the decision risked having a real impact on the quality of the show and placing an “extraordinary burden” on its crew.Norris told the Guardian that current plans, which would involve production staff working in a separate location to the actors recording the show, represented “classic short-termism and doesn’t represent value for money for the licence fee payer”.“This isn’t us actors being averse to change,” he said. “It’s very much us wanting to stand in solidarity with our colleagues in production, us wanting to ensure the continued highest quality of the programme for the listeners, the continued heritage of the show, its connection toBirmingham, and also for the BBC not to go back on many promises it made to the region.View image in fullscreenBen Norris, who plays Ben Archer, said the actors wanted to stand in solidarity with colleagues in production.Photograph: Steve Ullathorne“It’s a combination of all those things that has left us feeling as angry as we are.”Staff were informed last week that the BBC, as part of its £500m cost-cutting drive, hadditched plans for a new radio drama theatreat the Tea Factory in Digbeth, the corporation’s new Birmingham headquarters.While production staff will still move to the facility, the broadcaster is now looking for an existing UK studio where the show could be recorded. The West Midlands is included in the search, but there is no guarantee The Archers will be recorded in the region in which it has been based since its launch 75 years ago.Cast members met on Monday to discuss the announcement. Norris said there were practical problems with the new plan, including the need for last-minute script discussions and specific facilities.“The Archers is recorded in a very specific way that is unlike almost all other audio drama,” he said. “There are very few other studios that have those facilities, and none that are up to the same specifications as our current setup.“[The current studio setup] would need transporting, building and striking with any new space we travel to, placing an extraordinary burden on the technical team and incurring extra financial drain.“I also think it’s a totally false economy. I’ve been told that the additional cost of shipping those people to wherever we ended up would cancel out what it costs to build the new studio within five years, so it’s classic short-termism and doesn’t represent value for money for the licence fee payer at all.”He said that while actors were based in different places, there was a “big Midlands connection within the cast – either people who grew up or trained there or people who live there now”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year historyRead more“For day players, of which the Archers has many – coming in to play somebody’s midwife, somebody’s mechanic – those roles often go to local actors and should go to local actors because it’s one of the places that people can start their careers,” he said. “It’s the same for the writing team and the production team.“This decision flies completely in the face of theBBCand the government’s commitment to pursue as much regionality as possible and to have culture and the economy thriving in every postcode.”Norris feared listeners would eventually notice the impact.“We’re worried about the sustainability of this way of working,” he said. “We are worried about the relationship between cast and crew, but also their energy levels, their wellbeing … Maybe we’d get away with it for a bit, but we think at some point the show would suffer and the listeners would perceive that.”The performing arts union Equity has said it will oppose the BBC’s plans.Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, said hemet the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, on Wednesday to explore opportunities to continue to record the show in the region once it left Birmingham.Explore more on these topicsBBCThe ArchersBirminghamRadioRadio dramaRadio 4newsShareReuse this content

title: Family of man killed by tiger criticise online content after Trump reposts video | South Yorkshire | The Guardian
description: Relatives of William Chapman say footage of attack shared online ‘deeply offensive’ and causing them ‘severe distress’
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Relatives of William Chapman say footage of attack shared online ‘deeply offensive’ and causing them ‘severe distress’
Content: William Chapman, who was mauled to death when he entered the tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, had suffered from mental illness, his family said.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenWilliam Chapman, who was mauled to death when he entered the tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, had suffered from mental illness, his family said.Photograph: PASouth YorkshireFamily of man killed by tiger criticise online content after Trump reposts videoRelatives of William Chapman say footage of attack shared online ‘deeply offensive’ and causing them ‘severe distress’Mark BrownNorth of England correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 08.48 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family of a man killed by a tiger at a wildlife park in the UK have spoken about their “severe distress” at the circulation of online media afterDonald Trumpreposted a video of the incident.William Chapman, 23, was mauled to deathafter entering an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, on Saturday.His family described him as “bright, warm and engaging” and suffering from severe mental illness. They said online footage being shared was “deeply offensive” and causing them “severe distress”.One of those to circulate footage was the US president who posted a video clip of the tiger attack to 13 million followers on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday.The clip showed the tiger biting and clawing Chapman as he was sitting in the enclosure. At one point he wags his finger at the animal.Trump signed the footage with: “Don’t ever mess with nature! President DJT.” It did not show Chapman being killed.Later the president posted an AI-generated video of himself grinning and having fun by chasing and play fighting with the tiger. It is accompanied by the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight by The Tokens. It features Trump copying the pointing gesture made by Chapman and ends with him and the tiger hugging.Will Travers, the executive president of theBorn Free Foundation,said the AI post was “not only incredibly insensitive”, but also reckless.“It increases the risk to the lives of humans and captive wild animals,” he said. “Such images and videos can encourage individuals to seek out direct, unrealistic and high-risk contact with captive wild animals.”Relatives of Chapman, in a statement released on Tuesday evening, said: “The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened. The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this.“The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did.”The statement continued: “William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back. Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication.“It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death.“We would ask everybody to respect that process.”As a child, Chapman appeared in ITV’s 2009 comedy drama May Contain Nuts and in BBC Learning’s True Stories series,according to IMDb.He previously attended Jackie Palmer stage school in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, whichpaid tribute on Facebookand posted a picture of Chapman as a child student.The school said it was “deeply saddened” by Chapman’s death, adding: “We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer. It was a privilege to be part of his journey and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him.“William will be truly missed, and he will always hold a special place in our hearts. Rest in peace, William.”The wildlife park has said the Amur (Siberian) tiger called Altai, who was in the enclosure, will not be euthanised. The park has remained closed since the weekend and Doncaster city council, which is responsible for licensing the park, said it had started a health and safety investigation.An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster coroner’s court on Thursday morning.Explore more on these topicsSouth YorkshireDonald TrumpOnline abuseMental healthHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Boy, 17, accidentally shot dead with air rifle at Hampshire house party, inquest told | Hampshire | The Guardian
description: Connor Bell died of his injuries after his friend Jack Beechey, 18, pulled the trigger, mistaking it for the safety catch
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Connor Bell died of his injuries after his friend Jack Beechey, 18, pulled the trigger, mistaking it for the safety catch
Content: Connor Bell was described by his father at the inquest as ‘cheeky and mischievous but so kind and caring’.Photograph: Family handout/Solent NewsView image in fullscreenConnor Bell was described by his father at the inquest as ‘cheeky and mischievous but so kind and caring’.Photograph: Family handout/Solent NewsHampshireBoy, 17, accidentally shot dead with air rifle at Hampshire house party, inquest toldConnor Bell died of his injuries after his friend Jack Beechey, 18, pulled the trigger, mistaking it for the safety catchJamie GriersonWed 14 Oct 2026 10.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 17-year-old boy died after he was accidentally shot in the head with an air rifle by his friend at a house party, an inquest has been told.Connor Bell had been drinking at a friend’s house in Basingstoke,Hampshire, on 8 November last year when Jack Beechey fired the fatal shot by mistaking the trigger for the safety catch, the inquest heard.The boys were shooting the weapon out of the conservatory into the garden at targets such as bottles.Beechey, 18, accidentally pulled the trigger when he was trying to put the safety catch on the air rifle while it was pointed towards Bell’s head.Connor, from Tadley, Hampshire, was taken to Southampton general hospital but he died two days later from a severe brain injury.The inquest at Winchester coroner’s court was told that the crank air rifle was stored in the cupboard under the stairs in the home of Connor’s friend Joshua Brown, now 18.Paying tribute to his son at the inquest, Robert Bell said: “He was cheeky and mischievous but so kind and caring. He never took himself too seriously and had a wicked sense of humour.“He also enjoyed a variety of sports, especially football. He was often the driving force in his friends, going out to play football or just doing stuff together.“He was doing a sports course at college, and he had done a work placement at our local leisure centre in Tadley, and the manager there said as soon as he has got his certificate come back to us.”Brown, who was 17 at the time of the incident, gave evidence at the inquest, saying his father had shown him how to safely use the gun on two occasions.Talking about what his father told him, he said: “Not to point it at people.”When asked if he had thought about putting the gun away after shooting in the garden, before his friends came over, he said: “I wanted my friends to use it. I just thought it would be fun.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe inquest was told that Beechey was arrested by the police after the accidental shooting but no further action was taken.Giving evidence on Wednesday, Beechey said he had been drinking cider and vodka at the party and he was “a little bit drunk”.The Hampshire area coroner Jason Pegg ruled that Connor’s cause of death was a gunshot wound to the head and he died from cardiac arrest from a brain injury. He concluded that it was an accident.Pegg said: “Connor was just 17 years of age at the time of his death. It is quite clear to me, having heard from [Connor’s family], that he was a son, grandson and a friend. He was a young man who had aspirations in the physical fitness field and had a life planned ahead of him. He was full of life and had a cheeky side and had much to live for.”He added: “This demonstrates the real risk when you have a group of young people drinking alcohol. This is a deeply tragic case.”Explore more on these topicsHampshireEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lawyers for man shot by ICE in New York City say agent did not identify himself | New York | The Guardian
description: Account by Oscar Belgal differs sharply from that of DHS agents, who fired into vehicle with young boy in back seat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Account by Oscar Belgal differs sharply from that of DHS agents, who fired into vehicle with young boy in back seat
Content: Eyewitness footage shows Oscar Belgal being detained by ICE agents in the Bronx borough of New York City, on 8 October.Photograph: Pedro Almarez/ReutersView image in fullscreenEyewitness footage shows Oscar Belgal being detained by ICE agents in the Bronx borough of New York City, on 8 October.Photograph: Pedro Almarez/ReutersNew YorkLawyers for man shot by ICE in New York City say agent did not identify himselfAccount by Oscar Belgal differs sharply from that of DHS agents, who fired into vehicle with young boy in back seatAssociated PressWed 14 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son inNew YorkCity said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers”.The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal’s release, said he had picked up his son from school and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way,” Belgal’s lawyers wrote. “Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.Whatever happened next didn’t appear on the NYPD’s security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal’s damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.DHS didn’t comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal’s lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and now has impaired hearing.The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US immigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: I went to a Jamaican Patois class. Why was I so scared to speak it? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Centuries of historical baggage surrounds this form of speech. But I’m vowing to overcome shame and connect with this part of my culture
Author: Micha Frazer-Carroll
Headline: Centuries of historical baggage surrounds this form of speech. But I’m vowing to overcome shame and connect with this part of my culture
Content: ‘As a child, I would only hear my relatives fleetingly lapse into Creole’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘As a child, I would only hear my relatives fleetingly lapse into Creole’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe Long WaveLife and styleI went to a Jamaican Patois class. Why was I so scared to speak it?Centuries of historical baggage surrounds this form of speech. But I’m vowing to overcome shame and connect with this part of my cultureDon’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereMicha Frazer-CarrollWed 14 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRecently, my sister sent me and my mum a graphic promoting a Jamaican Patois (or Patwa) class on Instagram, organised by British teacher and authorNaia Lewis. It was unlike anything I’d ever seen before – Patois and other Caribbean Creole forms of speech are rarely treated as legitimate languages.As a descendant ofCaribbeanmigrants to the UK, I grew up surrounded by Patois, but had never practised speaking it.I wanted to go, but felt terrified of embarrassing myself. This week, I conquered that fear and explored why learning Patois and other Creole languages is so fraught and controversial across the diaspora.View image in fullscreenHard to pin down … there is sometimes a stigma that follows Caribbean Creole languages.Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian“In Jamaica, when it comes to speaking Patois, it’s seen as ‘chatting bad’,” says Naia Lewis, who runs classes in the language aimed at a beginner level. Patois developed during the transatlantic slave trade and functioned as a means for enslaved people to speak to one another and their slavers, combining African, Indigenous Caribbean, European and later, Chinese languages. Still broadly associated with the lower classes, it isoften dismissedas a form of “broken English”, and regulations stillprohibit Jamaican MPsfrom speaking the language in their parliament. “It’s seen as a lesser form of communication,” Lewis tells me.Patois belongs to a broader family of Caribbean Creole languages, and after the Windrush generation of Caribbean people migrated to Britain, many of their children weretold off or mockedfor speaking in them. This stigma and silence around these languages has trickled down to subsequent generations – I know some young British Caribbeans who mainly engage with Patoisin the form ofisolated slang words. As a child, I heard Creole in music, but would only hear my relatives fleetingly lapse into it when they wanted to express something particularly passionate, to impersonate their parents, or to cuss someone out.A widespread perception that Creoles are illegitimate languages also makes them hard to pin down. For example, I have Antiguan and Jamaican heritage, and grew up around descendants from numerous other Caribbean islands – who likely spoke in a mix of different Caribbean Creoles. But Jamaican Patois is the best known, and in Britain – where a large proportion of post-war Caribbean migrants were of Jamaican heritage – it is often used as a catch-all term.With centuries of cultural and historical baggage surrounding the Patois language, I notice I am very scared to try speaking it, and that the threshold for shame and embarrassment feels high. In Lewis’ class, it dawns on me that I have never actually uttered more than a word or two – and now I am doing it in front of a group of strangers.Finding the courage to speakView image in fullscreenMortifying … the way I hear sounds in my head is notably different to the way they come out of ‘mi mout’.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianI don’t say this lightly: due to my lack of language skills, there are moments in this class that are among the most mortifying of my life. I realise, only after I join the Zoom call with four others, that this is going to be incredibly interactive, and I am called on within the first five minutes for an exercise on prepositions – translating “on” to “pan” and so on.“Weh yuh fuon de?” (where is your phone?) prompts my teacher, followed by“Weh yuh remote deh?” (where is your remote?). I pass, knowing that I’m only safe for so long.We move on to phonics, and are presented with some clear rules for pronunciation in Patois. In words that begin “sk”, you broadly drop the “s” – we practise sayingkininstead of “skin”,kratchfor “scratch”. The same goes for words beginning “sp” in English. Try sayingpongeinstead of “sponge”,paidainstead of “spider”.This is harder than I thought it would be. I notice that years of family exposure means I can understand almost everything, but the way I hear sounds in my head is notably different to the way they come out ofmi mout. I am frustrated by how heavily my English accent inflects my speech, and I feel that I should be better at this than I actually am.Then comes the improvisation portion, and my time is truly up.Yu jos kom ina di ruum an evribadi jos staat fi ak wierd(you’ve just walked into a room and everyone has started acting weird). Our job is to have a conversation with one other person, in front of the group, to establish why everyone is behaving strangely in this imaginary scenario.When I’m called on, I buckle – telling Lewis that I don’t think I can do it off the cuff. She swaps with the student who is paired with me, asks me a question in front of the group:wagwan? There is a long, excruciating silence. I mentally scramble around for any of the phrases or terms I would hear my mum use around the house. But the problem is that I don’t know how to construct a full sentence with them. I smile blankly, and my face flushes.Then, I remember a previous exercise onduppies(or ghosts) – and ad lib that I’ve seen a ghost in the room. The following couple of minutes are painful, but we get through them, and no one laughs at me, or even really flinches. We’re all in the same boat here, self-conscious and exposed.Should we all be learning Afro-Creole languages?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘The more you practise, the easier things get’ … consuming Patois from family interactions is not enough.Illustration: Alexis Chivir-ter Tsegba/The GuardianAfter the class, I notice there are unexpected moments in which I feel a huge amount of anger and grief. The resentment is not so much about the loss of my people’s language to colonialism and enslavement. It’s the fact that, all these years, I hadn’t even thought that I had a language – that when people would speak to me in my people’s native tongues, it didn’t even register as a possibility to speak it back. Now, when I am asked to, I draw a blank.Still, I come away from the class feeling that more of us should be engaging with our native Creole languages – and that consuming them through music, or listening to family members, isn’t enough. “The more you practise, the easier things get,” Lewis says. “The more you make a sound, the easier your brain knows how to make that sound.”“Learning Patois is important so we don’t feel like a deer in headlights when people speak Jamaican Patois to us,” Lewis tells me. Whether it’s in the Caribbean or the UK, most of us encounter Patois speakers in our lives but, as Lewis says:“Some people don’t know how to respond appropriately, or don’t want to offend by saying it wrong, or get laughed at.”This shaming and discouragement sometimes even comes from people across the Caribbean diaspora who are proponents of the language and embrace it. While the adverts for Lewis’ classes received a broadly positive and excited response from those interested in learning, the reaction from fluent speakers was more mixed. “Some people have said that I’m exposing the language to too many people,” she tells me. While Lewis understands this perspective, she sees it as a form of gatekeeping of languages that are already precarious and policed.Mind your languageView image in fullscreenOn a mission … Naia Lewis teaches Caribbean Creole classes at beginner level.Photograph: Naia Lewis“There need to be people who can speak and teach Patois, so that people do not take advantage of the Jamaican culture and language and use it in inappropriate ways,” Lewis says. “When you don’t have any teachers of the language who are teaching the correct way of how to speak it, and the correct way of showing respect to Jamaican Patois as a language, then people will take it for a joke, or take it for dress up.” Lewis points to the fact that the Patois words that are the best-known among non-speakers are often swear words, used as a punchline.There is a real risk here of words falling out of use – phrases losing their meaning through co-option and parody by those who don’t truly respect our communication and culture. As Afro-Creole linguist Ìfẹ́ Shakur has pointed out, the silence, taboo and shaming around the language, which is so entrenched even within Caribbean communities, is “doing the work of the coloniser”. I vow to go back, and to be embarrassed again.To receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Tap inWhat is your relationship to Caribbean Creole languages? Share your thoughts by replying to this, or emailing us atthelongwave@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Long WaveCaribbeanLanguageBlack British culturenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Judge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiry | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Blow for Trump administration as Dawn and Taag hail ‘important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime’
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Blow for Trump administration as Dawn and Taag hail ‘important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime’
Content: The international criminal court in The Hague, which is investigating war crimes in Gaza.Photograph: Pierre Crom/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe international criminal court in The Hague, which is investigating war crimes in Gaza.Photograph: Pierre Crom/Getty ImagesTrump administrationJudge blocks US sanctions on rights groups helping ICC Gaza war crimes inquiryBlow for Trump administration as Dawn and Taag hail ‘important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime’Anna Bettsin New YorkWed 14 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US federal judge has temporarily blocked theTrump administrationfrom placing sanctions on two US-based human rights groups for working to help the international criminal court’s (ICC) investigations into war crimes in Gaza.In a30-page orderissued on Tuesday, Jesse M Furman, a judge at the US district court for the southern district of New York, granted a preliminary injunction to the two groups, Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn) and Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag).The two organizations sued the Trump administrationthis summer, challenging anexecutive order issuedin February 2025 that imposed sanctionsagainst the ICC.The order warned the US government would “impose tangible and significant consequences” on people involved in investigations that Washington saidthreatened the national securityof the US or its allies, including Israel.The order came after the ICCissued arrest warrantsfor the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defense minister Yoav Gallant, accusing them of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
