Both menhaverejectedaccusations against them, and the US government alsoopposedthe court’s decision to issue the warrants.In his opinion, Furman noted that last year two law professors brought a separate lawsuit challenging the 2025 executive order, and that the court had held that the order “violated those plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constituted a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and did not survive strict scrutiny”.Furman said that this lawsuit brought by Dawn and Taag – groups he described as “American advocacy organizations” – raised a “substantially similar challenge”. He wrote that the groups were challenging the 2025 order on “both statutory and constitutional grounds, re-upping many of the arguments made in the earlier cases”.Dawn and Taag are rights groups that had worked to gather information for the ICC as it investigatedallegations of war crimes against Palestinians.“The court concludes that the 2025 order likely violates plaintiffs’ first amendment rights because it constitutes a content-based regulation of their speech-based activities and cannot survive strict scrutiny,” Furman wrote.However, the judge stopped short of declaring the executive order “facially unconstitutional” and rejected the groups’ request to “enjoin the president and to enter a ‘universal’ injunction barring enforcement of the 2025 order against anyone”.The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian on the ruling.A spokesperson for the US state department said in a statement to the Guardian that “we do not comment on pending litigation” but added: “The Trump administration has been clear: the ICC poses an intolerable threat to US sovereignty.”Joseph Pace, a lawyer for Dawn and Taag, described Tuesday’s decision as “a victory for the first amendment and an important step in unraveling the ICC sanctions regime”.And in astatement, Omar Shakir, Dawn’s executive director, said: “Today, a US federal court has put the brakes in a major way on the Trump administration’s efforts to shield from justice the Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide and their US backers.”Dawn also said that it would “immediately resume” its advocacy with the ICC “to prosecute Israeli and American perpetrators of grave crimes”.The ruling comes just days after the USimposed financial sanctionson the ICC.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationInternational criminal courtGazaWar crimesUS politicsPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Student protests in Albania turn violent as demonstrators clash with police | Albania | The Guardian
description: Dozens of people detained after government building and two banks set on fire as tens of thousands march over education costs and corruption
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dozens of people detained after government building and two banks set on fire as tens of thousands march over education costs and corruption
Content: 1:14Anti-government student protests in Albania turn violent – videoAlbaniaStudent protests in Albania turn violent as demonstrators clash with policeDozens of people detained after government building and two banks set on fire  as tens of thousands march over education costs and corruptionGuardian staff and agencies in TiranaWed 14 Oct 2026 19.19 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTens of thousands of students have taken to the streets of Tirana, the Albanian capital, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and ⁠corruption.Police responded with water ⁠cannon and teargas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned bins and smashed the fronts of local businesses. A branch of Raiffeisen Bank near the education ministry also caught fire.Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were being treated for injuries and that 35 people had been detained.President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, adding: “The constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception.”The protests are the most violent outburst yet against Edi Rama, ⁠the prime minister, who won a fourth term in office in May last year but has since faced ​growing discontent at perceived graft surrounding top ‌officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures ‌as unpalatable alternatives.View image in fullscreenProtesters clash with police in central Tirana.Photograph: Adnan Beci/AFP/GettyThe unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by theproposed development ‌of a luxury resortalong Albania’s pristine southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has been caught up in legal disputes.“This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns,” said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name as she threw rocks at the police.Others chanted “resignation” and “police of crime”.Student ‌organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation.The unrest is part of a ​broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France,high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockadesdemanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests had spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodër.The government ⁠condemned the violence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA government building and two banks were set on fire during the protests.Photograph: Florion Goga/ReutersAlbana Koçiu, the deputy prime minister of Albania, said on Facebook: “Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used ​as an excuse for violence, city ​destruction or ugly fighting in the middle ​of the road. I call on ​students and every ‌honest citizen who believes in ​the right to ​protest: distance yourself from violence and vandalism!”The police issued a statement calling for calm. “Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed,” they said.Meanwhile, the EU, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the “violent escalation at the protest in Tirana”.A statement by the EU delegation in Tirana said: “We take note of the allegations of excessive violence by the police against protesters and journalists,”Calling for a prompt investigation, the delegation encouraged “all sides to de-escalate the tension”.Explore more on these topicsAlbaniaProtestEuropeStudent politicsStudentsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns | European Union | The Guardian
description: Ola Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competition
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Ola Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competition
Content: A production line at the Mercedes-Benz factory in Rastatt, Germany.Photograph: Christoph Steitz/ReutersView image in fullscreenA production line at the Mercedes-Benz factory in Rastatt, Germany.Photograph: Christoph Steitz/ReutersEuropean UnionExcluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warnsOla Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competitionLisa O’Carrollin BrusselsWed 14 Oct 2026 09.57 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLocking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.It is mainly aimed atChina, which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December.Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors.But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this wasnot on the cardsat the moment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EURead moreThe ACEA is also lobbying for anurgent suspension of plans to introduce 10% tariffs on UKelectric vehicles (EVs) imported to the EU, and EU EVs exported to the UK.“We are getting very anxious about it. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director.The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car.Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year.The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time.The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently.Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to anagreement on Friday between Beijing and Brusselsto reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years.One official said the time to rebalance trade by increasing EU exports was gone. “No amount of champagne [exports] is going to revitalise the relationship [with China],” a senior EU official told a separate trade policy briefing in Brussels.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionAutomotive industryManufacturing sectorBrexitAndy BurnhamEuropeInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sir Trevor Phillips urges CBS News colleagues to give critics blunt riposte | CBS | The Guardian
description: Phillips sought to buck up his fellow London bureau colleagues during a contentious staff meeting on Tuesday
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Phillips sought to buck up his fellow London bureau colleagues during a contentious staff meeting on Tuesday
Content: Sir Trevor Phillips attends a debate on immigration on 10 September 2025 in Birmingham, England.Photograph: Dave Benett/Tracey Welch/Getty Images for Sky NewsView image in fullscreenSir Trevor Phillips attends a debate on immigration on 10 September 2025 in Birmingham, England.Photograph: Dave Benett/Tracey Welch/Getty Images for Sky NewsCBSSir Trevor Phillips urges CBS News colleagues to give critics blunt ripostePhillips sought to buck up his fellow London bureau colleagues during a contentious staff meeting on TuesdayJeremy Barrin WashingtonWed 14 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe veteran British broadcaster Sir Trevor Phillips had some strong words of advice for hisCBS Newscolleagues when facing off against critics who question the editorial integrity of the network: “Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?”Phillips made his blunt suggestion during a contentious meeting of the network’sLondonbureau on Tuesday, during which the foreign editor, Shayndi Raice, went on a lengthy tirade criticizing unnamed staffers for suggesting that editorial oversight amounted to “interference” and informing colleagues that disobeying editors would be insubordination and “legal grounds for firing”.Phillips’s decision to join CBSwas announced in June. It came after its billionaire owner, David Ellison, installed the opinion journalist and broadcast newcomer Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief in a move thatshook staff.David Ellison denies he has ‘politicized’ Skydance despite close Trump linksRead moreThe Guardian,which first reportedthe Tuesday meeting, reviewed an audio recording of the contentious session that rattled staffers. A CBS News spokesperson and Phillips declined to comment on the meeting.Phillips spoke up initially to defend Raice, saying that the message she was delivering was common sense. “I’m genuinely surprised that you had to say anything that you just said in the last 15 minutes,” he said during the meeting. “It just seems to be axiomatic in any organization … I did want to say that I’m kind of surprised that in an organization of this vintage and capability, with the clever people I’ve met around here, that any of this actually has to be said.”He then turned to outside opinion about CBS, telling colleagues that he faced criticism after it was announced he was leaving his perch at Sky News to serve as the network’s senior global affairs correspondent. Phillips is also a contributor to CBS’s flagship news show 60 Minutes, andvoiced a short pieceon Sunday on protests in Europe. Since CBS parent Paramount Global was acquired by Ellison’s Skydance Media in the summer of 2025, the company’s leadership has faced accusations of tilting the editorial scales in a more conservative-friendly direction.“I could spend the next hour telling you the number of people when it was announced that I was coming here, the number of people who told me for all of the reasons you just explained, why this is the end of my career and how I was going to destroy everything that I’ve ever created, and all of that bollocks,” Phillips said.He continued: “I think we’re in a new game now, actually, where we are now players as journalists. And what people are constantly trying to do is to knock us off – to frighten us, essentially, into doing this or doing that. It puts a premium on two things – one is our objectivity, and two: having each other’s backs. I think the worst thing that can happen now is if we start to go about telling people, ‘Well, I would have done this if the higher-ups hadn’t told me to do that.’ That’s exactly what everybody wants us to get into the game of. That’s how we become vulnerable. That’s how we start adjusting our copy according to somebody else’s lines outside of here … I think what you said is really, really important, but it points me in the direction of us having the mentality – forgive my French here – of telling everybody, ‘Why don’t you just fuck off and let us do our jobs?’”Explore more on these topicsCBSTrevor PhillipsThe news on TVUS television industryLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Done family took £30m dividend from Betfred before warning of job cuts | Gambling | The Guardian
description: Money was withdrawn from gambling firm before founder warned chancellor against doubling machine games duty
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Money was withdrawn from gambling firm before founder warned chancellor against doubling machine games duty
Content: Fred Done, the founder of Betfred, has previously spoken out against the tax his family pays.Photograph: John Walton/PA Wire/PA ImagesView image in fullscreenFred Done, the founder of Betfred, has previously spoken out against the tax his family pays.Photograph: John Walton/PA Wire/PA ImagesGamblingDone family took £30m dividend from Betfred before warning of job cutsMoney was withdrawn from gambling firm before founder warned chancellor against doubling machine games dutyRob DaviesWed 14 Oct 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe billionaire Done family took a £30m dividend from their Betfred gambling empire, before warning that they would close hundreds of bookies and cut jobsif the government increases tax on high-street slot machines.The chancellor,John Healey, is understood to be considering proposals to double machine games duty in the upcoming budget, a move that the Social Market Foundation thinktank has said could boost state coffers by up to £460m.Industry figures, led by the Betfred boss, Fred Done, argue that such a move would result in the closure of vast swathes of the bookmaking and casino sector.On Wednesday, Done was among industry signatories who signed a last-ditch letter to Healey, warning that the policy could trigger up to 1,470 betting shop closures, 34 casino closures and 15,900 job losses.The plea, first reported by Sky News, came as Betfred’s holding company filed its accounts at Companies House.The Warrington-based betting firm won a record £996m from British punters in the year to the end of March 2026, the accounts show, booking a pre-tax profit of £64m.The strong performance allowed Betfred to pay its shareholders – mainly a series of trusts benefiting the Done family – an interim dividend of £30m, taking the value of shareholder payouts to more than £105m since 2022.The money is understood to have been reinvested into other Done family businesses, including their burgeoning property empire.Last month, Fred Done, who founded his first bookies in 1967 and went on to become one of Britain’s richest men, lamented that he “would not wish to be reborn” in the UK.“They keep saying those with the broadest shoulders should be paying more tax,” he told the Financial Times. “Well, how broad do my shoulders have to be? We paid £400m in taxes as a family last year.”The Done family, who are collectively worth about £3bn, remain the UK’s biggest taxpayers, according to the Sunday Times Tax List.Of the £400m they are estimated to have contributed last year, £54m came from machine games duty (MGD), according to the accounts for Betfred Group Holdings Limited.In theory, that sum would double if Healey follows through with plans to increase the duty rate from 20% to 40%.However, Done has said such an increase would render hundreds of bookmakers unprofitable at a stroke, forcing him to close them and ultimately reducing the Treasury’s tax take. Casinos have also warned of mass closures.It is not the first time that Done has threatened mass closures in response to government policy.Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?Read moreSince 2019, the company has threatened to close nearly 1,000 in response to higher taxes or tougher regulation, including the introduction of a £2 cap on fixed-odds betting terminals.Over that time, the company’s bookmaking estate has shrunk from about 1,620 to 1,293, a decrease of nearly 330. The decline has coincided with a broader shift towards online gambling, with Fred Done appearing in TV adverts urging customers to visit betfred.com.Campaigners supporting an increase in MGD have focused less on bookies and more on high-street slot machine venues known as adult gaming centres (AGCs), most of which are open 24 hours.Amid a broader decline in high-street gambling, with the number of bookies steadily shrinking, AGCs havethrived thanks to lax planning and licensing laws, targeting deprived areas in particular fornew shop openings.Andy Burnham has been a vocal critic of AGCs. In August, the prime minister announced measures designed to make it easier for councils to block new venues.However, some gambling industry figures have warned that AGCs are best-placed to survive a rise in MGD because they have lower overheads than casinos and bookies.In theory, this means that a rise in the duty could even benefit the sector as rival machine operators retrench. Merkur, the UK’s second-largest AGC operator, has already bid for some of 132 shops that Betfred put up for sale earlier this year.The Done family declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsGamblingTax and spendingJohn HealeySport bettingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Merry squishmas: £10 squeezy banana on list of top festive season toys | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Social media-driven craze puts ‘squishies’ up there with evergreen favourites such as Lego and Barbie, Hamleys says
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: Social media-driven craze puts ‘squishies’ up there with evergreen favourites such as Lego and Barbie, Hamleys says
Content: The Big Squij range of toys comes in a variety of food and animal shapes filled with a flour-based compound.Photograph: David Goymer/HamleysView image in fullscreenThe Big Squij range of toys comes in a variety of food and animal shapes filled with a flour-based compound.Photograph: David Goymer/HamleysRetail industryMerry squishmas: £10 squeezy banana on list of top festive season toysSocial media-driven craze puts ‘squishies’ up there with evergreen favourites such as Lego and Barbie, Hamleys saysZoe WoodWed 14 Oct 2026 10.03 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA cartoonish banana so addictively squidgy that it is “really difficult to put down” is tipped to be among the must-have toys thisChristmas, according to expert buyers at Hamleys.The £10 “slow-rise, squeezable, sensory” fruit taps into the “squishies” craze that is fuelling a high street boom in toy sales. In the coming weeks, Hamleys expects to sell thousands of the Big Squij toys, which come in a variety of food and animal shapes filled with a flour-based compound.Their popularity has been supercharged by social media and a growing army of child and adult collectors. There are more than 260,000TikTok postsand more than 600,000 on Instagram tagged #squishies. The most popular official brand, NeeDoh, has 1.1m TikTok followers.Victoria Kay, the head of buying and merchandising at Hamleys, said the “squishy craze is only really just getting going”.“The demand is huge. There is a wonderful simplicity to their power whether you are a young child or an adult.Literally once you squeeze one, it’s really difficult to put it down.”Squishies are the biggest toy trend of the year, according to Andrew Murphy, who runs The Entertainer, the UK’s largest chain of toy shops. Some theories suggest their viral success is because of their stress-relieving powers or simplicity, but he suggests the “degree of fanaticism from kids under 10 for these products is not explainable in any rational way. It’s just a real, deep desire”.The squishies craze is good news for independent toy shops, he said: “It will be increasing sales in total by minimum of 30%. Most of their costs are fixed so they’ll probably be doubling the profit for the year.”View image in fullscreenOne for J-Pop fans. The collectible figurine of the computer-generated pop-starHatsune Miku.Photograph: HamleysThe craze has been a shot in the arm for UK toy sales this year, which by the end of August were up 13% by value and 19% by volume, according the market research company Circana. Sales of toys that cost under £10 are growing fastest, with an extra £100m worth of these so-called “pocket money” items sold during the period thanks to the clamour for World Cup stickers and squishies.As forChristmas– still 72 days away – Hamleys says this week is when shopping for the festive season “officially” starts, according to a poll of consumers. With that in mind it has produced its annual shortlist of toys to please toddlers through to teenagers and older. At £10, the Big Squij toys are the cheapest. while the remote-controlled flying Thunder Unicorn” is the most expensive at £75.The list of 15 items includes evergreen favourites such as Lego, Barbie, Peppa Pig and PlayDoh. With the upcoming Marvel superhero extravaganzaAvengers: Doomsdayon the horizon it features two Doctor Doom toys – a £45 Lego bust and a £30 action figure.There is also something for J-Pop fans with a collectible figurine of the computer-generated pop-starHatsune Miku. The 16-year-old vocaloid – her “voice” comes from music software – is playing London’s O2 arena next month.Hamleysfestive 15Hamleys Movers & Shakers interactive pet£35Hamleys Thunder Unicorn£75Barbie Nutcracker doll£30PlayDoh Stamp & Spin Pizza playset£20Articulate Under Pressure£25skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPrimal Hatch Megalodon£55Doctor Doom action figure£30Hamleys ScorpiX RC transforming car£50Hatsune Miku figure£28Big Squij£10Numberblocks sing and record music player£27Lego Doctor Doom bust£45Ready, Pedal, Go interactive Peppa Pig£30Hamleys Wooden London taxi£25Hamleys Magic 3D Track set£60Explore more on these topicsRetail industryToysChristmasShops and shoppingShoppingLegonewsShareReuse this content

title: Stevie Wonder review – playing ​his greatest album in full, he knocks everyone sideways | Stevie Wonder | The Guardian
description: The opening night of Wonder’s tour marking the 50th anniversary of Songs in the Key of Life leaves jaws on the floor, thanks to sumptuous tracks carrying still-urgent messages
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The opening night of Wonder’s tour marking the 50th anniversary of Songs in the Key of Life leaves jaws on the floor, thanks to sumptuous tracks carrying still-urgent messages
Content: Extraordinary … Stevie Wonder at Birmingham’s Utilita Arena.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/Getty Images for ABAView image in fullscreenExtraordinary … Stevie Wonder at Birmingham’s Utilita Arena.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/Getty Images for ABAStevie WonderReviewStevie Wonder review – playing ​his greatest album in full, he knocks everyone sidewaysUtilita Arena, BirminghamThe opening night of Wonder’s tour marking the 50th anniversary of Songs in the Key of Life leaves jaws on the floor, thanks to sumptuous tracks carrying still-urgent messagesAlexis PetridisWed 14 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeated amid a bank of keyboards,Stevie Wonderaddresses the audience at the first date of his tour celebrating the 50thanniversary of Songs in the Key of Life, his most celebrated album. He says playing it in full like this was a longstanding ambition: the issue was that it needed so many people to bring it to fruition. He actually fulfilled that ambition a decade ago in North American arenas in 2014 and 2015, gigs from which the 50th anniversary shows take their cue – complete with Superstition added as an encore – but that said, you have to take his point about the number of people involved.There really are a lot of musicians up there: three percussionists, a string section, five brass players, six backing vocalists, two guitarists, three keyboard players, including Wonder himself, who variously plays a bank of synthesisers both vintage and modern, a grand piano, an upright tack piano and, on Ngiculela/Es Una Historia/I Am Singing, a bizarre stringed instrument called a harpejji that wasn’t actually invented when Stevie Wonder last released an album, let alone when Songs in the Key of Life was made. Harpejii or not, that very much counts as scaling things down dramatically compared to the album’s actual sessions. Made by a man who could pretty much do everything himself, its recording nevertheless involved 108 musicians: eight people are credited forhandclaps.Its lavishness spoke volumes both about the commercial expectations placed upon it, and the artistic challenge involved in capping what Wonder had recently achieved. Having threatened to retire from music entirely prior to its making, Wonder reconsidered and wound up signing what was, in 1975, the biggest recording contract in history, worth around $230m in today’s money. And in the space of barely two years, he’d released Music of My Mind, Talking Book, Innervisions and Fulfillingness’ First Finale, a bravura display of talent so overwhelming that, when Paul Simon won the 1976 best album Grammy, his acceptance speech thanked Wonder for not releasing anything in the preceding year and thus giving everyone else a chance.View image in fullscreenLavish … Wonder with his sizeable band.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/Getty Images for ABAThe remarkable thing about the Songs in the Key of Life live show is not that it reminds you how extraordinary the ensuing album was, and is – given that everyone from Michael Jackson to Elton John to George Michael has called it the greatest album ever made, it hardly needs highlighting – but that it embellishes it. Not because of the expanded arrangements, lovely though they are: it’s a moot point as to whether Village Ghetto Land is much improved when played by live strings rather than Wonder’s stacked synthesisers, as the studio version was pretty incredible to start off with. It’s because it is resolutely a live performance, rather than a perfect recreation.Wonder fluffs his harmonica solo on Easy Goin’ Evening (My Mama’s Call) and insists the band restart Isn’t She Lovely, dissatisfied with the initial version (“Stop!” he cries. “Sue me!”). He also stretches songs out at will, the band locking into the tough funk of All Day Sucker and Black Man, and adds to the album’s already teeming tracklisting. Its first half now comes with another instrumental as well as the knotty, jazz-fusion influenced Contusion. You could, at a push, call it a jam, replete with call-and-response audience participation, but that feels like underselling its dramatic, symphonic soul.Stevie Wonder releases four unheard songs from Songs in the Key of Life sessionsRead moreFor all its peerless reputation, there’s a certain risk involved in performing Songs in the Key of Life live, more or less in order (and including the four songs from the A Something’s Extra EP that was bundled with the original album). Risky because the album opens in relatively understated style: Love’s In Need of Love Today, Have a Talk With God and Village Ghetto Land are incredible songs by any metric, but they’re downbeat, sombre, frequently desperate in tone, reflective of someone so disheartened by mid-70s America he was strongly considering relocating to Ghana and devoting himself to charity work, hardly the big razzle-dazzling opening you might expect from an arena show. On the night, it doesn’t matter, perhaps because the audience know what to expect, perhaps because the lyrics depicting a US desperately lacking empathy, mired in hideous inequality and governed by people whose ostensible devotion to Christianity seemed to have no bearing whatsoever on their actions might as well have been written in 2026.They’re received ecstatically, although not quite as ecstatically as the reliably joy-bringing Sir Duke and I Wish. Indeed, you spend a lot of the show with your jaw on the floor. Even given its reputation, Songs in the Key of Life still has the ability to knock you sideways with the astonishing level of quality it maintains throughout: it’s an album on which the deep cuts would be anyone else’s showstoppers: Saturn, Knocks Me Off My Feet, Joy Inside My Tears. As the deep soul of the latter finally dies away, an earnest voice pipes up from the rear of the arena. “That,” it cries, audibly gobsmacked, “wasreallygood”.Stevie Wonder plays 3Arena, Stockholm, 22 October; returning to tour the UK 3-11 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStevie WonderPop and rockSoulR&Blive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I must continue until I die’: inside the fight to bring Iran’s thriving art scene to the world | Art | The Guardian
description: Amid economic sanctions and ongoing conflict, a new initiative is returning Iran’s artists to the international spotlight
Author: David Smith
Headline: Amid economic sanctions and ongoing conflict, a new initiative is returning Iran’s artists to the international spotlight
Content: Untitled, Aryan Dabbagh, 2021. Digital photography. 30cm x 45 cm.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Aryan Dabbagh, 2021.View image in fullscreenUntitled, Aryan Dabbagh, 2021. Digital photography. 30cm x 45 cm.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Aryan Dabbagh, 2021.Art‘I must continue until I die’: inside the fight to bring Iran’s thriving art scene to the worldAmid economic sanctions and ongoing conflict, a new initiative is returning Iran’s artists to the international spotlightDavid SmithWed 14 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the call came early one morning, Tehran residentElham Issariknew it must be urgent. The voice on the line was offering something precious. “Miss Elham,” he said excitedly, “I have a single tube of white paint! It’s overpriced and I know it’s overpriced but, if you want it, you have to buy it right now because there’s this other guy in this other city who wants it and you have to tell me within the next five minutes.”The tube of white paint would have cost Issari 5m tomans (about $36), she recalls. “I was like, I don’t think so, because that’s overpriced, and the next thing you know is it’s 4am and I’m onYouTubewatching how to make lead white in your backyard without getting lead poisoning.”‘What could be discovered? What is new there?’: blockbuster exhibition celebrates Roy LichtensteinRead moreIt is a revealing slice of life in Iran these days. Since the US and Israellaunched joint airstrikes and combat operationson 28 February, and turned the screws on Iran’s economy, thousands of visual artists have been plunged into economic and professional limbo.The sudden onset of war shuttered commercial galleries in central Tehran, cancelled scheduled solo exhibitions, severed shipping channels and destroyed the fragile domestic market that allows creators to pay rent and sustain studio practices.But it was out of this systemic breakdown that Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran was born. The initiative connects contemporary artists living and working inside Iran with international audiences, collectors and institutions through a dedicated platform atiranartistrelief.org.The project owes its existence toDario Duran, a Canadian-Iranian curator and founder of Duran Art Projects. Born in Shiraz, but raised in Canada, Duran holds degrees in photography, art history and curatorial studies. Six years ago, driven by nostalgia and a desire to connect with his heritage, he moved to Iran, where he fell in love with the dynamism of the domestic art scene.View image in fullscreenMariam Rasti and Dario Duran.Composite: Courtesy of Continuum: Artist Relief for IranWhen war broke out, Duran found himself caught directly in its crosshairs. “I was displaced,” the 38-year-old explains from Shiraz inIran. “My mom and dad were visiting from Canada and we had to flee Shiraz because Shiraz was being hit pretty hard every day. It was becoming unbearable. We went by ground to the north of the country, where it was relatively quiet.”In the north, Duran encountered dozens of other displaced cultural workers who had fled bombed urban centers such as Tehran and Isfahan. He linked up there withMariam Rasti, co-founder of Duran Art Projects, who had also fled the capital.“We were in constant communication with the artists,” Duran recalls. “One thing we saw over and over again was that, like never before, the artists were losing hope. Cancelled exhibitions, galleries closing, not being able to find materials, artists being displaced – every single person was going through the exact same uncertainty of what happens tomorrow.”Iran’s contemporary art world operates inside a structural bubble, isolated from international banking networks. Typically, an artist works for one or two years to prepare a body of work, relying on a single gallery showcase to generate enough sales to survive for the next two years. When conflict brought that domestic cycle to a dead halt, creators faced immediate ruin.Duran says: “We realised that at this moment, exhibition making, curation, archiving – these things do not matter. What matters, more than anything else, is simply sales. These artists were not able to pay their rent.“One artist put up his paintbrushes and paint tubes for sale on Divar [a classifieds site] just to carry on. Another artist told me: ‘I’m going to go work in a coffee shop for the time being because I have no idea if this art thing is going to work out for me’.”Determined to make a difference, Duran bought a couple of gigabytes of internet access so he could get on WhatsApp. From his laptop in the north, he drafted an open letter to international collectors, museum directors and gallerists across the diaspora, laying bare the plight of creators inside Iran.The response was immediate and overwhelming. Gallerists and curators in London, New York, Paris, Dubai, Toronto and Mumbai wrote back, eager to assist. What had originally been planned as a modest PDF catalogue featuring a dozen imperilled acquaintances rapidly transformed into a nationwide initiative.‘Each artist on their own terms’: why Lee Krasner was every bit the equal to husband Jackson PollockRead moreOver five months of feverish development, Duran, Rasti and a coalition of domestic galleries built Continuum. The digital platform brings together more than 500 original artworks by over 200 contemporary artists living and working inside Iran.Eleven commercial galleries across Iran agreed to voluntarily waive 100% of their sales commissions.Duran Art Projectscharges no platform fees. As a result, 100% of every completed artwork sale goes directly to the artist. To make acquisitions realistic for global buyers during an economic downturn, prices were capped across three accessible tiers: up to $500; $500–$2,500; $2,500–$5,000.While the online front end of Continuum offers a catalogue of striking abstract canvases, delicate line drawings and minimalist photography, the back-end operation is a masterclass in guerrilla logistics. Delivering physical artworks out of a country under heavy military bombardment and stringent international sanctions requires ingenuity bordering on subversion.“The logistics of it – we thought about this ad nauseam,” Duran says with a weary laugh. “Currently, this matter is changing on an hourly basis. The sanctions obviously have been very disruptive.”View image in fullscreenUntitled, Shayan Sajadian, 2024. Digital photography. 80cm x 80cm.Photograph: Shayan Sajadian/Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Shayan Sajjadian, 2024.Initially, Continuum relied on two domestic courier services capable of flying artwork packages from Tehran to shipment hubs in Dubai and Istanbul, where international carriers could take over. But as geopolitical tensions soared, regional airspace closed and commercial flight paths dissolved.Duran explains: “The flight connections through the UAE were cancelled so the couriers told us that UAE is off the table. But the second UAE comes off the table, they figure out another way. There is a man who had a courier company that was forced to shut down. In order to keep his business going, he is now using the ground borders, moving overland from Iran into Armenia. He goes by the land border, carries the artworks into Armenia and ships them out from there with full insurance.”To manage expectations, Continuum informs international buyers that delivery may take three to six months. Yet collectors worldwide, ranging from private patrons in North America to major European institutions, have shown extraordinary patience.For Duran, the real tragedy of the current crisis lies in the indiscriminate cruelty of international economic sanctions, which target ordinary citizens while doing nothing to alter political outcomes. “These sanctions are not putting much pressure on the government,” he observes. “It’s mostly punishing everybody that’s trying to live a life here. Everyone’s complaining but we’re trying to find solutions.”Among the artists trying to make a way out of no way isMehrdad Jafari, 43, who grew up in the northern province of Mazandaran, where his relatives worked as sculptors and painters. Speaking from Tehran through a Farsi interpreter, he says: “Growing up, I always had the dream that one day I would be in Tehran and have an art studio in this city, to create work and fully realise my potential.“My entire life has been dedicated, and continues to be dedicated, to my work. In fact, my existence is connected to my work. I have no other way of being. I must continue until I die.”View image in fullscreenUntitled, Mehrdad Jafari, 2026. Oil on Cardboard. 40 x 30 cm.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Mehrdad Jafari, 2026.As the father of a three-year-old child, Jafari’s experience of the war is filtered through the anxieties of parenthood. His artwork, which centres on the complex emotional tapestry of human relationships and community interactions, has had to adapt to severe material deprivations.“Because of the effect of sanctions, we’ve had to be a lot more imaginative in order to decide what materials we use,” Jafari explains. “Materials are quite difficult to find right now. But what I’ve had to do, and what others are doing, is replace this lack of materials with imagination. We use alternative materials to carry on.”Jafari views this enforced improvisation as a double-edged sword. “In one way we use our imaginations more, creating a more creative space and ways of thinking. But on the other hand, of course, we would love to be part of the global system and have access to the things everybody else has access to. That’s just not available to us right now.”For Jafari, Continuum’s launch during a time of active military conflict carries symbolic resonance. “It’s an extraordinary moment. It’s a bridge for us to connect with an international audience. For me personally, it brings a sense of calm – that we are not forgotten. Because of Continuum, I am more invigorated than ever to work. It gives us hope that life can carry on.”From the outset, Duran and Rasti insisted that the initiative would not function as an exhibition about war, nor would it force artists to turn their pain into visual entertainment for foreign viewers.Duran argues: “Iranian contemporary art doesn’t look like any one thing. Iran is not a style, and the Iranian identity is not a medium. An artist living in Shiraz shouldn’t have to make work that visually announces ‘Iran’ before an international audience is willing to take it seriously. We wanted the work to be encountered first as art, not as evidence about a country.”‘Curious and circumspect creatures’: the artist making sculptures for the rats of New York CityRead moreWhile some participating artists choose to directly address conflict, Continuum refused to make political commentary or suffering a requirement for inclusion.“There is a difference between giving artists visibility during a crisis and asking artists to make the crisis visible,” Duran adds. “I definitely didn’t want crisis to become the reason their work deserves attention. Context should deepen our understanding of an artwork; it shouldn’t imprison the artwork.”The breadth of work included on the platform bears out this philosophy. Across 500 pieces, viewers encounter delicate geometric abstraction, haunting figurative portraiture, avant-garde photography, experimental printmaking and sculpture.The financial relief generated by Continuum is already providing vital support to Iran’s artistic ecosystem. In a country where currency devaluation has eroded savings, a single $500 artwork sale can provide significant income towards studio rent or much-needed pigments.Issari, 38, reflects: “It creates a chain. If an artist is not so worried about their income, maybe they can continue teaching. If they can continue to teach, kids can continue to learn. The whole chain does not stop and we don’t fall into this pit of absolute hopelessness.”View image in fullscreenAzargun, Elham Issari, 2020. Oil on canvas. 24cm x 30 cm.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Elham Issari, 2020.Issari could not bring herself to work during the first weeks of heavy bombardment in Tehran. “I was here for the whole show. Hearing explosions five times, six times per day, every day – having to gather the cats and run to your safe place and count to 10. Then, as soon as it’s over, pick up the phone, check if your father is alive, if your mother’s alive, if your loved ones are OK. On repeat. It does a number on you.”The trauma was physical as much as psychological. “I didn’t touch a brush,” she recalls. “Actually, I did once, and my hands were shaking so badly that I literally just put it down. I was like, ‘I am not going to do this right now.’ And that’s OK, because I’m just not there.”While Issari, who studied art in London, is hopeful her paintings on Continuum will find homes in international collections, the initiative’s primary gift is emotional validation. “Even if you don’t sell, it’s that feeling of being seen,” she says with quiet determination. “For me, it’s tremendous. It’s easy to feel like you’re a pariah and you’re invisible. Just the fact that you’re being seen means a lot.”She adds: “I always have faith in the fact that art will survive, regardless of everything and anything. Artists are the best. If problem-solving were an Olympic sport, we would win a gold medal every time. We will find a way.”Explore more on these topicsArtIranPaintingPhotographyExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Girls is back: why it’s the perfect time for more of Lena Dunham’s millennial Sex and the City  | Girls | The Guardian
description: HBO’s era-defining comedy is set for a new five-episode series. Its bleakness and warmth couldn’t be more welcome
Author: Louis Staples
Headline: HBO’s era-defining comedy is set for a new five-episode series. Its bleakness and warmth couldn’t be more welcome
Content: Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Lena Dunham and Zosia Mamet in HBO’s Girls, 2012.Photograph: HBO/AllstarView image in fullscreenAllison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Lena Dunham and Zosia Mamet in HBO’s Girls, 2012.Photograph: HBO/AllstarGirlsGirls is back: why it’s the perfect time for more of Lena Dunham’s millennial Sex and the CityLouis StaplesHBO’s era-defining comedy is set for a new five-episode series. Its bleakness and warmth couldn’t be more welcomeWed 14 Oct 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTShareIt’s a pop culture emergency. A millennial-quake that shook my social feed to its core.Girls, the HBO show that stole the zeitgeist in the early Instagram era and madeLena Dunhama generational star, is returning for a five-episode revival series. The project was announced via amock video callwith some of the original cast: Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells. They’re all returning for the reboot, which will pick up the story 10 years after the 2017 finale.Lena Dunham’s Girls returning for limited run at HBORead moreGirls captured such a specific era when it premiered in 2012. Social media still felt new and exciting,Barack Obamawas president and so-called “woke 1” felt like it was going to be the new normal. The show’s characters navigated that terrifying twentysomething period when you’re searching for an identity, where it feels like everyone has it figured out but you. Dunham’s realistic approach to sex scenes – sticky, awkward, unflinching – made the show one of the first to be “discoursed” on social media, spawning endless think-pieces and Twitter threads. She was declared the voice of her generation, but she also became a figure of controversy who didn’t always seem suited to such intense, era-defining fame.For Dunham, theGirlsrevival comes at a time where she’s taking a victory lap. Following a string of successful TV projects and the release of Famesick – her New York Times best-selling memoir, which lifted the lid on her time filming Girls while living with chronic pain – she is in the ascendency once again. But given that reboots tend to have, ahem, amixedsuccess rate, the big question is: can Lena’s lightning strike twice?As a dyed-in-the-wool millennial who came of age on a cultural diet of Glee, unironic #hashtags and BuzzFeed quizzes, Girls really was my generation’s answer to Sex and the City. The shows similarly star four white women navigating life in New York, and the characters are rendered with such specificity and consistency that fans can endlessly argue about whether they’re “a Hannah” or “a Carrie”. (I’m a Miranda in SATC, and a Marnie in Girls.)The news that Girls is returning draws inevitablecomparisonswithAnd Just Like That, the post-Covid reboot that took us back into Carrie Bradshaw’s world in her 50s. Over three toe-curling seasons, AJLT became a case study in hownotto do a reboot. The show lost so much of the original’s astute, bitingcynicismand often seemed more concerned with atoning for its past, such as its glaring lack of diversity and a handful of offensive “early 2000s” storylines that aged poorly. Some of the characters – especially Miranda Hobbes, whose snarky realism was a vital leveller to Carrie’s delusional romanticism – were changedbeyond recognition.View image in fullscreenWilliams and Dunham in Girls’ sixth and final season, 2017.Photograph: Mark Schafer/HBOPersonally, I wouldn’t be against a Che Diaz cameo in Girls 2.0, but there’s a few factors that make it easier for Dunham to take her revival in a very different direction. Since Girls wrapped, she seems to have been in constant conversation with the characters. In 2023, when IinterviewedAllison Williams, the real-life Marnie Michaels told me that she and Dunham had spoken on the phone during Covid, where they discussed how they would have handled the pandemic. “Marnie would have 100% wrapped herself in cellophane, Hannah would have pretended to do the same, but would have been living very riskily in secret,” she said. “One of the powers of the specificity of those characters is that it’s quite easy to imagine.”Lena Dunham on going to rehab: ‘It was like the first day of college, except many of the people had a problem with heroin’Read moreThen there’s timing. While it’s expected that the “girls” of Girls will have evolved into adult women, 10 years is a smaller gap than thewaveof2000srebootswe’ve seen, which have often been tasked with filling in the blanks of two decades. The 2010s was certainly a different time – pre-Trump and pre-pandemic – but Hannah Horvath had an iPhone and posted attention-seeking tweets. Her world wasn’t totally unrecognisable, which should make it easier for Dunham to stay true to the parts of the characters that made fans love them.View image in fullscreenThe cast of Girls at the sixth season’s premiere in New York on 2 February 2017.Photograph: Evan Agostini/APTiming might also ask the deeper questions at the heart of the revival. Girls became a hit because of its relatable combination of warmth and bleakness. The show was aspirational in some ways, by nature of following four attractive, privileged women in the big city, but it also saw them sharing small apartments with friends whose big dreams were colliding with the reality of the post-recession economy. And if this was a story about any other generation, you’d expect for the characters to have graduated beyond the economic precarity and self-doubt of their 20s. But for millennials, it’s not so simple. The revival would do well to tap into how muchhasn’tchanged for the generation who are the first to be worse off than their parents. So many millennials are still navigating housing and job insecurity, and have that creeping feeling that they’re not progressing in life. This frustration could be very fruitful for Dunham, who has a particular talent for zoning in on wider generational anxieties as they’re happening.Netflix’s Mike Tyson docuseries offers an incomplete portrait of a troubling figure | Andrew LawrenceRead moreAt the heart of Girls is, of course, its polarising creator. Unlike SATC, which was mostlyreappraisedas too white and privileged after the original series concluded, Girls faced intense criticism at the time for its lack of diversity. Ten years on, without the noise of unforgiving social media discourse and think-pieces, the satirical genius of the show – and how it skewered the ridiculousness of its characters – is easier to see. Dunham wasfar from perfect, but it now seems clear that she was derided in a way that was plainly disproportionate, which often had more to do with her body and gender than the show, or even her own propensity to put her foot in it (thenapologise). Now, following the success of her memoir,Famesick, we’re in a period of Dunham-aissance, which might be why she’s choosing this moment to return to her most beloved work.Ten years on, the revival’s key challenge is unlikely to be the confessional subject matter, which feels more commonplace today because of the wave of female-fronted shows that came next, like Fleabag, Catastrophe and I May Destroy You. Instead, Dunham is tasked with meeting the expectations of diehard fans who have very strong views about the characters and have spent years creating their own theories on what they’re doing now. Reboots often struggle because they fail to grasp what fans loved about the original. But if there’s one person who is perceptive and daring enough to understand what the audience wants from her, Dunham may well be that girl.Explore more on these topicsGirlsUS televisionLena DunhamDramaTelevisionTV comedyComedycommentShareReuse this content

title: Winter of the Crow review – Lesley Manville magnificently on edge in intriguing cold war thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: Manville’s academic psychologist finds herself trapped in a tower block wasteland in 1980s Warsaw. Bizarre and surreal details add to the sinister vibe
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Manville’s academic psychologist finds herself trapped in a tower block wasteland in 1980s Warsaw. Bizarre and surreal details add to the sinister vibe
Content: No way out? … Lesley Manville as Professor Andrews in Winter of the Crow.Photograph: Danny James/Courtesy of Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenNo way out? … Lesley Manville as Professor Andrews in Winter of the Crow.Photograph: Danny James/Courtesy of Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewWinter of the Crow review – Lesley Manville magnificently on edge in intriguing cold war thrillerManville’s academic psychologist finds herself trapped in a tower block wasteland in 1980s Warsaw. Bizarre and surreal details add to the sinister vibePeter BradshawWed 14 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePart cold war thriller, part Kafkaesque reverie, this movie takes us back to the sinister drear of Poland in 1981, when General Jaruzelski has just introduced martial law in reaction to the dangerous new mood of freedom occasioned by the Solidarity trade unions. The director is Kasia Adamik, daughter of The Green Border’s Agnieszka Holland; the film is adapted from a story byOlga Tokarczuk, called Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw.Lesley Manville plays Professor Andrews, an academic clinical psychologist (like Tokarczuk) from Britain with testy, peremptory mannerisms; her indulgence is a fondness for taking Polaroid photos. She has attained a certain level of celebrity for a book on dreams, despite claiming that she never dreams herself. Andrews has been invited to give a lecture in Warsaw, during which she begins to outline views on mental illness not unlike those of Laing or Foucault; but her speech is chaotically disrupted by students shouting that Poland itself is an oppressive asylum.The chief protester’s sister Alina (Zofia Wichlacz) happens to be the postgrad student tasked with showing Professor Andrews around, but from the very first, there is confusion. Andrews loses her bag, then has to give her passport to Alina so she can go back to the airport and look for it; she can’t go to a hotel and must stay at a flat in a sketchy area, belonging to relatives of Alina. And when she awakens the next morning, Andrews sees a tank in the wretched and surreally deserted tower block wasteland. The clampdown has begun, murderous secret police are everywhere and she has no passport. Perhaps Andrews had better get used to staying inPolandfor the foreseeable future – or maybe for ever.It is an intriguing and disquieting movie, though one whose storytelling impulse slows a little, and perhaps the film could have benefited from closer editing – although this might have meant losing some of the bizarre and surreal details, like the live carp that people queue up to buy for food and keep in the bath.Winter of the Crow is in UK cinemas from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsThrillersPolandOlga TokarczukLesley ManvillereviewsShareReuse this content

title: VisionQuest review – Marvel’s latest TV show feels like it could have been made by a computer | Television | The Guardian
description: Paul Bettany stars in a WandaVision spinoff that’s a visually striking, genre-bending package – of fighting and tediously wordy dialogue. What an odd confection
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: Paul Bettany stars in a WandaVision spinoff that’s a visually striking, genre-bending package – of fighting and tediously wordy dialogue. What an odd confection
Content: Sparring partners … James Spader (left) as Ultron and Paul Bettany as The Vision in VisionQuest.Photograph: Marvel. All Rights ReservedView image in fullscreenSparring partners … James Spader (left) as Ultron and Paul Bettany as The Vision in VisionQuest.Photograph: Marvel. All Rights ReservedTV reviewTelevisionReviewVisionQuest review – Marvel’s latest TV show feels like it could have been made by a computerPaul Bettany stars in a WandaVision spinoff that’s a visually striking, genre-bending package – of fighting and tediously wordy dialogue. What an odd confectionRachel AroestiWed 14 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMartin Scorsese compared them to theme parks. Nicolas Cage likened them to WWE. The products of theMarvelCinematic Universe – 38 films, 18 television shows and counting – are not generally well regarded as works of art. This is understandable: they are derivative, corporate and also somewhat mechanical – not just in their CGI-heavy production or phased rollouts, but in their preoccupations, with robotics, technological combat, complex webs of association. This is not the cinema, per Scorsese, “of human beings trying to convey emotional, psychological experiences to another human being.”The MCU doesn’t just gravitate towards cliche in this area, it barely features actual humans at all. And yet – like a superhero searching for a special stone – you get the sense that Marvel will not rest until such profundity is within its grasp. Unlike rollercoasters or wrestling, the MCU can be quite intellectually demanding: why shouldn’t it be capable of illuminating truths about the human condition as well?VisionQuest, Marvel’s latest TV offering, seems to harbour such ambitions. It sees The Vision, a synthezoid, reckoning with the concept of selfhood: what does it mean to be humanesque? It’s a timely question, and VisionQuest is a visually striking, formally experimental and eclectically genre-bending package for it. Yet it is also a shouty, fighty blockbuster that retains everything – particularly the labyrinthine plotting – that has long made comic book fare such an artistic turn-off.View image in fullscreenSpader (left) as ‘evil-ish’ Ultron and Bettany as ‘nicely beta’ Vision.Photograph: MarvelFor a start, it is mired in lore. Scrolling through Disney+ a couple of weeks ago, I was warned that I needed to watch seven different films and TV shows to prepare for VisionQuest’s release. It’s a lot of homework (the dog ate mine), but there really is no point tuning in without having seen its direct prequel,WandaVision. That’s OK because the 2021 series – the MCU’s most creatively successful offering – is a bit of a masterpiece; a beautiful and thrilling psychological portrait of the Scarlet Witch, whose grief for her vanquished paramour Vision leads her to magically resurrect him via a chronologically evolving pastiche of American sitcoms.Inevitably, even WandaVision had to descend into standard superhero drivel at some point. VisionQuest is a spin-off with roots in such drivel, which involved Wanda’s Vision battling a reassembled version of his original body called The Vision (great name for a slick-fringed 1980s synthpop band). But then they made friends, and magical Vision planted his memories into his replacement, who duly fled.To, we discover, an Edinburgh pub, which Vision once frequented with Wanda. Desperate to connect with his forebear who he sees as more human, The Vision (Paul Bettany, doing a nicely beta English gent thing) now works at said boozer in his visually mortal form. But instead of going home at night, he slips into the walk-in fridge and reverts to his real robot self. And then we go inside his mind.Or whatever the AI equivalent of a mind is. Here it’s a houseshare with five other AIs, each given humanoid form and each with a specialism that helps The Vision, including social secretary Friday and defence expert E.D.I.T.H. We also have a wildly bearded James Spader as Ultron, Vision’s evil-ish maker who previously attempted to wipe out humanity.WandaVision review – Marvel’s sitcom superheroes are a retro joyRead moreThis is the basic setup. Now for the story. A bounty hunter is after The Vision (in a laughably unlikely twist, his hacker-style assistant is played by Diane Morgan) and, in order to lure him into his clutches, tracks down a teenager called Thomas who claims to be possessed by the spirit of one of Wanda and Vision’s magical twins. The Vision and Thomas meet and flee together, meaningful father-son bond still pending.That’s about one quarter of the plot. VisionQuest goes on to merge the fallout from WandaVision with an Ultron deep dive and an entirely different narrative about another robot. A huge amount of exposition is involved, and the AI-on-AI dialogue is tediously wordy (Ultron could get permanent residency in Pseuds Corner; at one point he marvels at “the unalgorithmic alacrity with which [humans] wobble”). Technically, that’s to the script’s credit – this is essentially a show about computer systems in conversation – but it still feels off-puttingly uncanny, like something AI really could manifest in the near future. The fusion of indie road trip movie, Matrix-like thriller, murder mystery and irreverent superhero dramedy, meanwhile, also feels like a computer’s idea of interesting art.VisionQuest is sometimes entertaining and always clever, yet if it does have anything to say about human nature, it is drowned out by dizzying plot particulars and the need for a big brawl every episode. Yet what’s really missing is actual jeopardy: it turns out to be quite difficult to emotionally invest in lines of code that exist in the “head” of an android. This isn’t dumb, mindless entertainment, but VisionQuest is still closer to the Big Dipper than GoodFellas.VisionQuest is on Disney+ nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewMarvelreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mistura review – ice queen brings Peruvian culinary drama to a gentle simmer | Movies | The Guardian
description: Bárbara Mori stars in tepid tale of a high-society wife who opens a restaurant in her home after her husband leaves her
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Bárbara Mori stars in tepid tale of a high-society wife who opens a restaurant in her home after her husband leaves her
Content: Chanelling Jackie Onassis … Bárbara Mori (Norma) in Mistura.Photograph: Seine PicturesView image in fullscreenChanelling Jackie Onassis … Bárbara Mori (Norma) in Mistura.Photograph: Seine PicturesMoviesReviewMistura review – ice queen brings Peruvian culinary drama to a gentle simmerBárbara Mori stars in tepid tale of a high-society wife who opens a restaurant in her home after her husband leaves herCath ClarkeWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 06.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat you expect from a film about a fancy high-end restaurant is a certain amount of heat: the roiling intensity of staff pushed to their absolute limits in the pursuit of gastronomic perfection. But this 1960s-set Peruvian drama instead maintains a gentle simmer, sedate and elegant. Perhaps it’s too elegant given the circumstances of its chef-proprietor, a high-society trophy wife with no catering experience who makes a high-stakes gamble on opening a successful restaurant.Bárbara Mori is Norma, a glacial beauty who cultivates a kind of Jackie Onassis chic: huge sunglasses, massive blow-dry, makeup thickly applied like armour. One night, Norma’s husband humiliatingly leaves her for a beauty queen. You’d be sympathetic if Norma wasn’t so foul to the staff, lashing out at housekeeper Rosa (Hermelinda Luján) and chauffeur Oscar (Cesar Ballumbrosio). It’s Oscar (who is a bit in love with Norma) who suggests she opens a restaurant in the house to pay the mortgage. Norma’s father was the French ambassador to Peru, and she has picked up his passion for gastronomy. Although the script is a bit inconsistent on this, since Oscar also says he’s never seen her so much as light the oven.The restaurant has four months to succeed before the bank repossesses the house. And still, there’s no sense of Norma, or the film, breaking into a sweat. She hires a Japanese Peruvian sous-chef in the kitchen; Oscar is front of house. But the early reviews are tepid, describing the French cuisine as a bit trad, and the restaurant is half empty. There are lessons to come about how teamwork makes the dream work, and embracing Peru’s cultural diversity. The trouble is that, before that, Norma is such an insufferable snob; it’s a bit too long to hold your nose and stick with her.Mistura is in UK and Irish cinemas from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsRestaurantsPeruFoodAmericasreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best books to read in October: new paperbacks from Zadie Smith, Thomas Pynchon and Francis Spufford | Books | The Guardian
description: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some brilliant new paperbacks, from a time-travelling fantasy novel to an eclectic essay collection
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some brilliant new paperbacks, from a time-travelling fantasy novel to an eclectic essay collection
Content: View image in fullscreenThis month's best paperbacksBooksThe best books to read in October: new paperbacks from Zadie Smith, Thomas Pynchon and Francis SpuffordLooking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some brilliant new paperbacks, from a time-travelling fantasy novel to an eclectic essay collectionWed 14 Oct 2026 10.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTShareFictionFictionShadow TicketThomas PynchonView image in fullscreenEverything is connected in Shadow Ticket, Thomas Pynchon’s fleet-footed noir fiction about a lindy-hopping detective in prohibition-era Wisconsin. The homemade bomb connects to the runaway cheese heiress, the cheese heiress to the federal agents, and the feds to the pro‑Nazi leagues at the bowling lanes outside town. Early-30s Milwaukee, in turn, is connected to powder-keg central Europe, where paramilitary groups have pitched camp on the Hungaro-Croatian border and guest speakers wax lyrical about “our immense fascist future”. Most likely it connects to the current moment as well, albeit wryly and slyly, with a nonchalant swing. That’s the implied final move of this merry dance of a book: the point where the past links its hands with the present.Shadow Ticket is a Pynchon novel – the 88-year-old’s first in 12 years; his ninth overall – and so it naturally connects to the man’s back catalogue, too, and its abiding fascination with conspiracy, chaos and the churn of American pop culture. Specifically it relates back to his two previous works –Inherent ViceandBleeding Edge– in that the story comes tailored as a dime-store whodunnit, complete with red herrings, plot twists and reams of hard-boiled dialogue. But classifications, like people, are never entirely to be trusted. Pynchon inhabits the genre like a hermit crab inside a mollusc shell, periodically peeking out from the gloom to remind us that he’s there.Xan Brooks£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionNonesuchFrancis SpuffordView image in fullscreenSpufford’s fourth work of fiction in a genre-spanning oeuvre, Nonesuch is a historical fantasy set during the second world war, every paragraph of which is packed with authorial zest. The novel opens in London, August 1939: war has been declared, but hasn’t yet made its reality felt in the city’s streets, and Iris Hawkins, an ambitious office clerk, makes her way through the sun-baked West End in a slinky dress. One half of a disastrous date later, she’s being whisked away to a DIY surrealist film club in bohemian Bloomsbury – not her scene at all – and two extremely fateful introductions: the first to Geoffrey Hale, a sweetly apprehensive BBC television engineer; and the second to the object of Geoffrey’s guileless infatuation, one Lady Lalage Cunningham, an icy aristocratic beauty with amazing hair and worrisome political sympathies. Cue chaos. Nonesuch follows the bolshy Iris from her seedy summer’s night through a regrettable Hampstead hook-up, and, eventually, neck-deep into a time-travelling plot by “magical fascist lunatics” to assassinate Winston Churchill. The novel is a pleasing pasticcio of romance, occultism, non-Euclidean geometry and airborne adventure across the blitz-stricken rooftops of London. It is difficult to imagine it would hold together quite so well in other hands than Spufford’s.AK Blakemore£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionBeasts of the SeaIida TurpeinenView image in fullscreenIn November 1741 Georg Wilhelm Steller, “theologian, naturalist, and curious man”, was shipwrecked on an island between Alaska and Russia. There he found, floating in the shallow waters, a vast sirenian,Hydrodamalis gigas,nine feet long and soon to be known as Steller’s sea cow. Having made it through the winter, largely by eating the sea cows, the following August Steller and the remaining survivors of the Great Northern Expedition left the island. Within 30 years, Steller’s sea cow was hunted to extinction.Having described these events, Finnish author Iida Turpeinen’s debut novel goes on to describe the lives of other historical figures, each of whom are touched in some way by the sea cow, now reduced to bones. There is Hampus Furuhjelm, governor of Alaska, in search of a complete skeleton, and his sister Constance, who finds peace and intellectual autonomy among her taxidermy collection. Later, there’s Hilda Olson, a scientific illustrator, and John Grönvall, specialist in the reconstruction of birds’ eggs, who is tasked with preparing a sea cow’s relics for exhibition.Turpeinen writes in a flowing present tense, moving seamlessly from one character to another, drawing us gently but firmly onwards. Emotional detail is astutely rendered. The result is a book that is almost hypnotically readable; it’s been much garlanded in Finland and it’s easy to see why.Jessie Greengrass£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionOther People’s FunHarriet LaneView image in fullscreenRuth, the narrator of Harriet Lane’s third novel, Other People’s Fun, is corroded by envy. Alone, her marriage over, her daughter grown and her freelance work as dull as it is low paid, she is that most dangerous of characters: an overlooked middle-aged woman with nothing to lose. When she bumps into beautiful, stupid and entitled Sookie at a school reunion, she reconnects with her teenage self “and all her violent desires”. Having flown under the radar as a pupil, noticed by Sookie only because she lent her her essays, she has perfect recall of her own petty humiliations, now amplified by the fact that she can stalk her contemporaries’ “best lives” on social media, while almost none of them remember her.The best comedy is sharpened by pain, and what Lane has pinpointed in her flint-sharp novel is something that has a highly modern resonance as the world of the haves and have-nots becomes increasingly polarised and toxic. When Ruth gets her revenge, it is as nasty as it is total. You will, I fear, howl with satisfaction.Amanda Craig£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionAbsenceIssa QuincyView image in fullscreenIn Quincy’s novel, the narrator is charmed by a poem first read to him as a child by his mother, which then follows him through his life. He’s stirred by memories and emotions as he is confronted by letters and photographs, phantoms and secrets, all of which make up a life that has been affected by generations of profound familial tragedy. Quincy’s prose is deftly lyrical and imaginative; I’ve had the pleasure of hearing him read from Absence at a literary salon in London and it was entrancing. He observes the fragility of memory, and what remains after our encounters, however fleeting, with people, say a schoolteacher or an estranged aunt; you might think of him as a counterpart to the novelists Rachel Cusk and Teju Cole.Jason OkundayeAbsenceis published by GrantaShort storiesShort storiesThe Land of Sweet ForeverHarper LeeView image in fullscreenThe Land of Sweet Forever is a collection of Lee’s unpublished short stories and previously uncollected essays. However, like most such books, it has little to offer to those who aren’t diehard fans.The short stories, written in Lee’s youth, are all badly underdeveloped. Most fail to work even as vignettes. One centres on trying to find a place to unload a truck in Manhattan; another on a temporary change to the way the doxology is sung in a Methodist church. A slender piece about the quirks of New York movie audiences is categorised as a story, but feels more like a newspaper sketch.The young Lee seems to have little sense of what a story is.On the positive side, there is already wit and charisma in the voice. One narrator, returning to her southern home town, recognises “a tall young man whose face belonged to the Wade family, but whose body showed extensive Talbert influence. He was Talbert Wade, of course.” This may be slight, but it’s elegantly done. There are also hints of iconoclastic anger struggling to get out, especially in The Water Tower, where a 12-year-old Mississippi girl erroneously thinks she is pregnant. Understanding that being an unwed mother would wreck the lives of her whole family, she decides the only way to save them is to destroy her shameful body.If we regard this book as literature, it is an unqualified failure. But it’s more properly seen – and will surely be read – for the light it sheds on Lee’s life. As such, it’s obliquely fascinating, largely because it radiates repression. Often there’s a sense that we’re seeing the side ofHarper Leethat wasn’t exceptional, but representative of a generation of women who were mostly muzzled.Lee writes in The Cat’s Meow (perhaps the strongest story in the collection): “I suppose a lot of people like me have mastered the first lesson of living at home these days: if you don’t agree with what you hear, place your tongue between your teeth and bite hard.” We feel those painfully gritted teeth on every page of this book. In a time of rising censorship, it’s salutary to be reminded that an author as important as Harper Lee came so close to being entirely silenced.Sandra Newman£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopEssaysEssaysDead and AliveZadie SmithView image in fullscreenDead and Alive bundles various odds and ends from the past nine years: speeches, opinion pieces, criticism and eulogies for departed literary heroes – Philip Roth, Martin Amis, Hilary Mantel.In Some Notes on Mediated Time – one of three completely new essays in the collection – Smith recalls how the “dreamy, slo-mo world” of her 1980s childhood gave way, within a generation, to the “anxious, permanent now” of social media. If you lived through that transition, you don’t have to be very old to feel ancient. When this estrangement is compounded by the ordinary anxieties of ageing, cultural commentary becomes inflected with self-pity. Smith’s identification with the protagonist ofTodd Field’s Tár, a once revered conductor who finds herself shunned by the younger cohort, takes on existential proportions: “Our backs hurt, the kids don’t like Bach any more – and the seas are rising!”Smith steers a sensible middle course on the vexed debate around “cultural appropriation” in fiction. There is more to people than their identity – “we can, sometimes, forget the mystery that lies at the heart of all selfhood”. The point is well made in a thoughtful piece on James Baldwin and the craft of writing, originally a lecture delivered to creative writing students over Zoom during the pandemic. Smith reminds her students that the essence of Baldwin’s brilliance was his ability to process politics through personal experience: he “submitted to his consciousness first and then re-examined what that might mean for his conscience”.
