This is sound advice, and Smith’s positions on the politics of creativity are beyond reproach, albeit commonsensical – amounting, essentially, to a caution against overcorrection and incuriosity.When it comes to actual politics, she is less assured. Her New Yorker op-ed on the war in Gaza, published in May 2024, was widely interpreted as unhelpfully equivocal, and seemed to conflate anti-war protesters with antisemites. She has since added her signature toan open letter acknowledging Israel’s actions as genocidal. The New Yorker piece, reprinted here with a new preamble hailing the protesters as “heroic”, is an intriguing artefact: the prose is mealy mouthed, heavy on the passive voice – all the more conspicuous since Smith’s writing is normally so clear and crisp.Houman Barekat£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopMemoirMemoirFly, Wild SwansJung ChangView image in fullscreenRemarkable success notoriously brings its own problems. Wild Swans, first published in 1991 and written by Jung Chang with the help of her husband, Irish-born historian and writer Jon Halliday, had a global impact few authors dare to dream of. It told the story of three generations of women in 20th-century China – Chang’s grandmother, her mother and herself – and became one of the most popular nonfiction books in history, selling more than13m copies in 37 languagesand collecting a fistful of awards and commendations. For any author, following that would be a challenge. Now, Fly, Wild Swans returns to the story, picking it up after Chang’s own departure from China in 1978, and revisiting episodes from the earlier work with added detail.Few can match Chang’s ability to bring Chinese history and politics to life through deeply felt personal narrative, and few have shaped western understanding of China as broadly. Nearly 35 years on from the book that made her name, this story of suffering and success has the air of a closing chapter, a reckoning with both her achievements and the cost of the path she chose.Isabel Hilton£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopMemoirWingsPaul McCartneyView image in fullscreenAfter splitting up, The Beatles faced an unprecedented challenge: how to be an ex-Beatle? McCartney yearned to play before audiences again, which he hadn’t since the Beatles stopped touring in 1966. But he couldn’t face doing it solo, the spotlight trained on him alone. So he asked Linda to help him put together a new group. This authorised, illustrated oral history, edited by cultural historian Ted Widmer, tells the story ofone of the most successful bands of the 1970s – and one of the strangest.It’s based on interviews (given for a new documentary on the band) with McCartney and former band members, as well as archive material. Widmer does an expert job of stitching this into a compelling narrative that includes cultural context – like what else was in the charts at the time – and plenty of photographs, many previously unseen. The result is a portal into a more eccentric age of pop, a fable about the tension between celebrity and creativity, and a story with elements of Spinal Tap and Wacky Races.Ian Leslie£19.80 (RRP £22) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

title: The Steps by Sylvester Stallone review – the inside story of Rocky | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The star takes us back to 70s New York to recount his breakthrough, and it’s a great yarn – but it’s laced with anger
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: The star takes us back to 70s New York to recount his breakthrough, and it’s a great yarn – but it’s laced with anger
Content: Sylvester Stalone on the set of Rocky II.Photograph: Sunset Boulevard/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSylvester Stalone on the set of Rocky II.Photograph: Sunset Boulevard/Corbis/Getty ImagesBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewThe Steps by Sylvester Stallone review – the inside story of RockyThe star takes us back to 70s New York to recount his breakthrough, and it’s a great yarn – but it’s laced with angerXan BrooksWed 14 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Philadelphia Museum of Art contains a 14th-century Buddhist temple, a one-acre sculpture garden and works by Picasso, Renoir and Van Gogh. Its most famous attraction, however, is a flight of stone steps that draws several million tourists every year. These are the so-called “Rocky Steps”, immortalised bySylvester Stallonein his 1976 movie about an underdog boxer who needs to build up his strength. The climb is a lung-busting challenge, but if unremarkable Rocky can sprint all the way to the top, he gives hope and encouragement to everyone down below.It’s not just the fans who relate to Rocky Balboa. So too does Stallone, whose entertaining rags-to-riches memoir paints the creator and his creation as all but indivisible, each an extension of the other. Stallone was flat broke and beaten down when he wrote his film about “the forgotten man”, the blue-collar schlub with a good heart and firm chin. Everyone knows that Rocky is being set up as a fall guy. He can’t possibly defeat Apollo Creed, the dazzling, charismatic, undefeated heavyweight champion of the world. Except that Rocky doesn’t care, he only wants to be seen, and in scripting an unlikely redemptive arc for his hero, Stallone wound up transforming his own fortunes as well.The Steps talks us through how he did it – or how he likes to tell people he did it – and how we might go about doing something similar in our own lives. Believe in yourself, he advises. Roll with the punches. Never throw in the towel. His memoir reads like a breakneck self-help manual in which the author is variously cast as guide, guru and crash-test dummy. Stallone – a keen student of narrative structure – knows that failure packs more dramatic punch than success, and shrewdly wraps up his account just as his film storms the Oscars. The man loses every round but the last, which is of course all that matters.double quotation markHe hates the snobs who write him off and the suits who feed him a diet of scrapsThe messaging can be cheesy and several of the stories feel fishy, but he spins a good yarn, plonking himself centre stage. He’s the raw, gauche outsider in Midnight Cowboy-era New York, earning a crust as an usher and cleaning cages at the zoo. He’s a striving Martin Eden in mid-70s California, trying and failing to get his scripts off the ground. Stallone writes in an authoritative conversational style, as though he’s leaning in close and draping his arm around your shoulder. He says, “I don’t know if you know anything about dogs,” and, “You might be asking, why doesn’t he go to a laundromat,” and, “If you’ve never been in a lion’s cage, let me tell you, it isverypungent,” and the effect is charming, companionable and ever so slightly oppressive.There is no side to Rocky – what you see is what you get. His creator, by contrast, feels more guarded and controlled. He presents himself as a sweet innocent – monastic and almost sexless – but there is an anger to his memories that burns on every page. He hates the snobs who write him off and the suits who feed him a diet of scraps. Francis Ford Coppola makes him wait several hours to audition; Richard Gere drips chicken grease on his trousers. Most of all he hates his mum and dad, who never wanted him to begin with and have left him with a desperate, mechanistic hunger to succeed. “If they’d been sweet and loving, like parents you see in a TV show, would I even be here?” he asks. They broke him and made him: it’s a complicated relationship.In a fair and just world, Stallone might have sold his labour-of-love screenplay about the life of Edgar Allan Poe. But now he’s down to his last $80 and his first child’s on the way and so he writes the first draft of Rocky in three days flat, pouring out a decade’s worth of humiliations and frustrations. Producers offer him a fortune to hand over the script, but he sticks to his guns and insists on playing the lead. The suits are in uproar; his agent’s having kittens. Except that our hero is proved right, his brinkmanship paying dividends. Rocky – a rousing old-school melodrama with a little 70s grit in its gloves – is cobbled together for a measly $900,000. It goes on to earn $225m.How true is this laundry list of hard knocks and life lessons? True enough. Stallone’s early struggles are well documented and largely verified. As for his origin tale about the making of Rocky, some see it as a foundational myth, heavily salted and spun. “The press feeds on the underdog story,” Gabe Sumner, United Artists’ former marketing boss, said back in 2006. Stallone’s claim that he faced down the studio, Sumner added, was “horseshit”, part of a “tremendous marketing campaign” in the run-up to the Oscars.The Steps asks us to accept the author as a real-world Rocky, the lowly everyman who hauled his way to the summit. That’s not a lie; it’s a life story to be proud of. But he is also Apollo Creed, the wily showboater and self-promoter, who knows that a David and Goliath story is good for business and that the best American heroes are self-directed, self-made and still a little rough around the edges.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Steps, by Sylvester Stallone is published by Seven Dials (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsAutobiography and memoirBook of the daySylvester StallonereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ply by Hernan Diaz review – Pulitzer winner’s dry vision of far-future America | Fiction | The Guardian
description: There are shades of JG Ballard in this tale of survival in a decaying metropolis, but big ideas and lengthy exposition crowd out the human drama
Author: Marcel Theroux
Headline: There are shades of JG Ballard in this tale of survival in a decaying metropolis, but big ideas and lengthy exposition crowd out the human drama
Content: Challenging language … Hernan Diaz.Photograph: TT News Agency/AlamyView image in fullscreenChallenging language … Hernan Diaz.Photograph: TT News Agency/AlamyFictionReviewPly by Hernan Diaz review – Pulitzer winner’s dry vision of far-future AmericaThere are shades of JG Ballard in this tale of survival in a decaying metropolis, but big ideas and lengthy exposition crowd out the human dramaMarcel TherouxWed 14 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHernan Diaz’s last novel, the formally inventiveTrust, narrated the biography of a successful financier from four different viewpoints to investigate themes of memory, representation, fiction and the fictitiousness of money. It was both critically and commercially successful and won the Pulitzer prize. His latest book, Ply, is a speculative epic set in a decaying city. While the time and location are never spelled out, the evidence strongly suggests a version of New York City several centuries into the future. A series of upheavals have depopulated this “shipwrecked world of dilapidated bygone grandeur”.There is more than a flavour of JG Ballard’s The Drowned World in the way the rewilded city is depicted: the lynx and deer stalking the streets, “the downtown swamp where the blind limbs and tendrils of trees and climbers have been at work for ages pulling the last line of collapsing buildings down into the spongy soil under the water”. Somewhere beyond the city, a more technologically sophisticated life endures. The evidence for this are the monopolistic companies Flow and Tensor, which control water and electricity respectively; and CTS, an unexplained acronym for a private security company that protects their interests and “holds a monopoly over monitoring and patrolling of the streets”.At street level, the city’s resourceful inhabitants live on their wits, bartering recycled goods, trading stimulants, food and other products. The novel’s narrator-protagonist is a pincher, someone who steals electricity from the grid. Like the city, she is never given a name. This is a strange bit of reticence in a novel that is generally eager to explain everything.Raised by her parents in a second-hand bookshop – “one of the last shops of its kind in town” – the narrator loses first her father and then her mother, though not before her mother, a tinker, trains her in the art of recycling broken objects. In a world of scarcity, these skills are much in demand. Like much in the book, the details of the narrator’s apprenticeship manage to be simultaneously lengthy and vague. She lovingly recalls her mother creating “spectacularly time-consuming and comically complex contraptions”. At one point, she also repairs a blender.double quotation markPly is a very dry biscuit, with lots of exposition but little in the way of narrative energyForced to fend for herself, the narrator spends time with gentle druggie Nelson, then utopian visionary Acevedo, who supervises her training as a tinker until she leaves to follow her doomed love interest Sol and find her true calling as a pincher.Interspersed with chapters of backstory, the real action of the book follows the narrator as she makes a living supplying stolen electricity to the city’s thriving independent music scene. On one of her regular pinching expeditions, she realises she’s being followed. It turns out that her technical accomplishments have caught the eye of Pola, a lone female scientist.Heraclitus-quoting Pola lives in the basement of what is probably the Metropolitan Museum of Art and is “convinced that we need to reconsider the meaning, reach and very nature of reason itself”. Pola, like the narrator’s mother, is an inspiring intellectual who is fascinated by machines. She is at work on something that she claims will “alter the fabric of reality itself”. There are many long explanations of how this laser plasma particle accelerator might work: “if we managed to entangle this particle with countless others in an ever-expanding arborescence, we could play with these superpositions and reorganise spacetime with total deliberation”. As far I understand it, Pola’s machine is basically another blender: one that will turn spacetime into a primordial smoothie, where there’s no distinction between subject and object, you and me, past and present.The second half of the book becomes, broadly speaking, a heist in which the narrator tries to figure out a way to steal a massive amount of power from the grid to fire up Pola’s machine. The plot is complicated by the appearance of a young girl called Ines; the machinations of two baddies called Kenneth and Leslie; evil scientist Casey; a scenester called Harlow, who’s a nod at Andy Warhol; and Anton, a trader from Bulgaria who talks like a character in an Oscar Wilde play. There is also some variation between third- and first-person narration as Diaz teases us with the notion that, through her involvement with Pola’s machine, the narrator has broken through to a non-dual perception of reality where the boundary between self and other dissolves.The step up to willing suspension of disbelief is a steep one in speculative and dystopian fiction. Where it works – I’m thinking of Russell Hoban, Michel Faber, Emily St John Mandel – there’s a constellation of things that seduce the reader: credible human relationships; a sense of grief at the changes that have come upon the world; curiosity; puzzlement; and a reticence that allows the reader to infer more than they’re actually told.The challenging language of Hoban’s Riddley Walker might not be to everyone’s taste – that broken English in which he laments the loss of a world he can’t begin to understand: “O what we ben! And what we come to!” But the narrative voice of Ply is, to my mind, off-puttingly knowing and verbose.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are a few selective gaps in the narrator’s understanding of the world – a shaky grasp of history and geography, no placenames, days of the week, or dates. Yet she can marshal a mysterious abundance of implied knowledge to describe an old salt shed: “The structure, an off-kilter polygon with planes intersecting at unexpected angles, rose like a hyper-augmented rendition of one of the billions of grains it once used to contain.”Big ideas – quantum mechanics, political economy, non-duality – crowd out the human drama that would give the story life. Characters make long speeches and die suddenly. And there’s something simplistic and complacent in the narrator’s view that some form of human progress is being hatched by the community struggling to live in the depopulated city. These convictions are never put under pressure. We never leave the city to see what life is like elsewhere. We never get to meet the faceless bureaucrats of Tensor or Flow. The novel’s antagonists are one-dimensional villains, not human beings pursuing their own idea of the good life. A writer with a more tragic view of human nature might suspect that, given the right incentives, most of us could find plausible-sounding reasons to say that two and two make five or take a job at CTS.The biggest problem of all is that Ply is a very dry biscuit, with lots of exposition but little in the way of narrative energy. In one of her rare moments of doubt, the narrator looks at Pola’s machine and wobbles as she sees “an abstract monument to an incomprehensible idea”. It’s an accurate summation of this novel.Ply by Hernan Diaz is published by Picador (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era | Games | The Guardian
description: The kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changer
Content: Evolutionary Link … The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenEvolutionary Link … The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2.Photograph: NintendoGamesThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K eraThe kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changerMatthew CastleWed 14 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen beloved art is revisited and revised, a familiar cry is often heard: “You’re ruining my childhood!” But with Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time, there are also livelihoods at risk: specifically, the man running the shooting gallery in Castle Town. In the original 1998 version of the game, he’d rip off players as they funnelled rupees and fudged the then still novel analogue-stick aiming. But in 2026 we have more responsive frame rates and a motion-controlled slingshot that allows precision adjustments. His targets tumble on the first go, and with them his entire business model. Even in Hyrule, the death of the high street seems inevitable.Bad news for him but great news for Link, a child of the forest who, as in 1998, steps into a vast fantasy kingdom to vanquish a great evil, but now does so with a number of improvements. The boy can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies to zip across grassy plains. He has a manual jump, free-rotating camera, a scrolling inventory bar that replaces menu screen faff and, crucially, a fatter wallet for holding all those gems he fleeces from struggling shooting gallery owners. Yes, we are being asked to applaud features that have been the norm for decades elsewhere, but it’s undeniably striking to enter familiar territory with a hero who feels this different under the thumbs.View image in fullscreenLink can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies.Photograph: NintendoThe dilemma facing any remake, let alone of a game recognised as a genre-defining classic, is how closely you hew to the past. As withthis year’s Star Fox revamp, Ocarina of Time finds Nintendo in a celebratory mode. It’s a polished victory lap for a game with little to prove. For newcomers it means seeing what the fuss is about without having to scrutinise the N64 original on unflattering flatscreen TVs. I doubt Hyrule Field – once a byword for video-game freedom – will ever conjure the awe it did in 1998, but seeing the sun catch in puddles and grass growing from the floor helps mask what is an obviously artificial pen, compared toBreath of the Wild’s sprawling continent.For some returning fans, the more controlled shape is precisely the appeal. After the “make your own adventure” ethos of Switch’s open-world Zeldas, there is comfort in slipping into traditional dungeons, where every room has a characterful beast to chop up or a mechanism to unpick with a growing kitbag of tools. My great fear was that some of the puzzles are simply too iconic to be forgotten and solved again. Yet here I am, sweatily hunting ghosts around the Forest Temple, and surreptitiously peering at my neighbour’s demo pod to remind myself that, yes, you have to … [redacted for your benefit]. Given that, in 1998, these were many designers’ first attempts at a 3D level, it is astonishing how fiendish they are and how you’re expected to hold complex architecture in your head to get the run of them.Also worth assigning headspace for: the newly orchestrated soundtrack. Melodies that fought through compressed N64 instrument samples to burn into the brain are given their own galloping freedom. I love the tentative brass when you lock an enemy into a duel – the musical equivalent of gnawing your lip.Link’s look is more contentious. Where Hyrule is prettied up with expected detail – swaying nettles in a forest home, marbled sunlight on a riverbed – its hero is radically made over. His large glassy eyes, and fat cheeks which reflect the light as if varnished, have led critics to accuse Nintendo of crudely pursuing a textbook next-gen sheen. Bells and whistles for the sake of filling 4K TVs with surface detail, rather than honouring the original artistic intent. In the past, some eager fans attempted to remake Zelda in more capable game engines and were ridiculed for mistaking technological grunt for artistry, and as evolving hardware opens those graphical avenues to Nintendo itself, it would be ironic if it fell for the same allure.In truth, Ocarina of Time looks coherent in motion on Switch 2. If anything, the layer of 4K specificity evokes another Zelda game, Twilight Princess, itself an attempt to apply a more mature, realistic lens to Hyrule. And could Link, with those overblown features, perhaps be nodding to another cultural pastime? As some corners of the internet scoffed at our newly “yassified” hero, the Nintendo veteran and former Legend of Zelda art director Takaya Imamura wondered if the character model drew from Zelda creator Shigeru Miyamoto’s own tastes. “[His] love ofningyogeki(puppet drama) is strongly reflected here,” Imamurawrote on X. Porcelain doll skin would certainly explain the uncanny sheen.View image in fullscreenIt is astonishing how fiendish the puzzles designed in 1998 still are.Photograph: NintendoWhile we can only guess at tight-lipped Nintendo’s intent, writer and translator Paul McQuade explains it is not an impossible leap. “In Japan, puppetry is not considered an art form strictly for children, which is largely how it’s perceived elsewhere,” he says. “It’s a rich art and is highly respected.” He thinks Miyamoto could easily have been influenced by puppet shows aired byJapanese broadcaster NHKin the Shōwa postwar era.And besides, there is something poetic about the notion. “It’s doll-like and intentionally juvenile,” McQuade says of Link’s chubby features and blushing nose. “It captures the essence of that forest where the children don’t ever grow up. Miyamoto, as a fan of puppetry, would of course draw on the vocabulary of dolls to make characters in that mould.”I like the idea of Nintendo honouring a community frozen in time in this way, while also acknowledging that time has moved on outside the game. With that passing comes an opportunity to tweak and massage. In an adventure where a boy can magically become a man and back again with the toot of his ocarina, it makes sense for timelessness and timeliness to be in conversation. With virtual bones this strong, it would be difficult to argue that anything has been truly ruined. Unless you run the shooting gallery, of course.The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is released for Switch 2 on 5 November.Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendo Switch 2NintendoThe Legend of ZeldafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth | Games | The Guardian
description: After years of sprawling, never-ending games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of shorter, more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming?
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: After years of sprawling, never-ending games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of shorter, more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming?
Content: Classic … video game arcades are finding new audiences.Photograph: Andrew Cline/AlamyView image in fullscreenClassic … video game arcades are finding new audiences.Photograph: Andrew Cline/AlamyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesReady player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirthAfter years of sprawling ‘forever’ games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming?Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 14 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s an important semi-nostalgic movement happening in games, and I’m excited about where it’s heading. But I don’t want to get ahead of myself here.Over the last five years, major publishers, obsessed with the success of “forever games” such as Fortnite, Minecraft and Roblox, have been throwing hundreds of millions of dollars into their own sprawling, endlessly updating, battle-pass-infested mega franchises – each designed to take all our time and money. The result has been astounding failures such asConcord, Mindseye and Tales of the Shire. Even the good games – Crimson Desert, Path of Exile 2, Blood of the Dawnwalker – are so bloated they have become the unyielding masters of our precious few hours of free time.It’s a relief, then, to see a growing number of mainstream titles heavily inspired by arcade design conventions, and intended as discreet, contained experiences. Along with the excellent driving game Star Wars Galactic Racer, which I rave about below, there’sAce Combat 8: Wings of Theve, an unreconstructed air-combat shooter that doesn’t want to become your whole life. You don’t have to romance your F/A-18F Super Hornet (although that does sound sort of cool), you don’t have to build your own airbase. You fly, you shoot things, there’s a story in the background, the end. It’s been equally lovely to see the success of Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls, a demanding 2D fighting game with complex interlocking power-up systems – the sort of thing my friends and I might have played in the arcades in 1993 before buying it on imported £100 Neo Geo carts.View image in fullscreenA quick round … in an age of endless online games, the appeal of the arcade is enduring.Photograph: B Christopher/AlamyAll of this points to one inevitable, socio-ludological phenomenon: the rebirth of the games arcade. Yes, I know there are already a few brilliant retro arcades dotted about, and plenty of chain bars and cafes such as Continue and NQ64 offering classic coin-ops alongside themed cocktails. There’s alsoArcade Arena, a new “immersive experience” venue in London that lets you play physical versions of Pac-Man and kart racers. But a growing number of players are interested in arcade-game design, and don’t necessarily want to play a few rounds of Time Crisis while downing a mojito.What I’m hoping to see is a more refined take on the coin-op arcade, something akin to the rise of the independent bookshop, with carefully curated collections of both new and classic experiences, and interesting events.This, I am pleased to discover, is happening. “The popularity of gaming bars and cafes is demonstrating that there is a sustainable business model in out-of-home gaming here in 2026,” says games journalist and arcade obsessive Will Freeman. “I wouldn’t go as far as to call it a boom, but there are a handful of smaller set-ups taking an approach that feels comparable to independent bookshops and record stores.”He mentions NQ Japan, which is about to open in London’s Soho. “While it is a cafe, there’s a firm focus on imported Japanese coin-op cabinets – covering newer games and cult classics that carry weight in the arcade community,” he tells me. “It really looks to be serving an authentic, arcade experience, bringing back that anticipation of getting your hands on exotic games from the cultural centre of arcade gaming.”View image in fullscreenHigh-end joy … the arcade gaming industry is booming.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianThe retro gaming industry is booming, with specialist manufacturers such as Analogue and Evercade producing high-end consoles that play original carts or new emulated collections of rare and sought-after titles. People are willing to spend money on an authentic arcade-style experience, just as they are now spending money on DVDs and vinyl records. A growing number of us want to have experiences that mega corps can’t provide through sleek, glassy devices.But while it is lovely that people are rediscovering foundational game mechanics through Ace Combat and Marvel Tōkon, there is much more to discover. The joy of arcades in the 1970s and 80s was that they were social hives as well as gaming spaces – you made friends, you learned from better players – and each game created its own community. Crucially, you went in with a handful of coins and could have a handful of very different experiences. A new era of boutique arcades could bring that back.“Something is under way, even if it is quietly,” says Freeman, pointing to smaller independent arcades with curated games libraries, such as Pixel Bunker in Milton Keynes. “I think we might see more independent arcades open up that drop the established ‘gaming cafe’ model to various degrees, and bring that feeling of local experts who really know their arcade culture, and want to build venues that draw in enthusiast communities.”Modern video games are bringing the arcade back into our homes. Perhaps now it is time to bring arcades back to our rapidly emptying high streets.What to playView image in fullscreenExcitingly familiar …. Star Wars Galactic Racer.Photograph: Fuse Games/Secret ModeIt feels like ages since we’ve seen an exciting mainstream racing game with a traditional linear structure rather than a vast open world. EnterStar Wars Galactic Racer– where you pilot landspeeders, speeder bikes and other outlandish Star Wars vehicles through intense circuits on excitingly familiar planets. As you progress, you unlock new parts and abilities, and plot your own route through a branching series of events. But crash out from a race and you have to go right back to the beginning of the season – a really clever implementation of rogue-lite design sensibilities in what is essentially a modern day take on Wipeout.What a joy it is to zoom through the wreckage-strewn canyons of Jakku and the icy tundras of Ando Prime, hitting the ramjet button to scorch past other vehicles at hundreds of miles-per-hour while a John Williams-adjacent symphonic score adds to the thrill. There hasn’t been a Star Wars racing title since Star Wars: Racer Revenge in 2002, which was, um, not a great game. I hope this is the beginning of a beautiful new era.Available on:PC, PS5, XboxEstimated playtime:20 hours plusskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenAI first? … Epic Games’ new approach to its forthcoming film adaptation.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAsreported in Bloomberg, it seems that the Fortnite creatorEpic Gameshas ordered an “AI-first” approach to developing a forthcoming Disney title. “Progress on the title has allegedly been slower than expected, partly because Epic underestimated how many staff it would require,”writes VGC. The team has apparently been told to use tools such as Anthropic’s Claude AI.GamesIndustry.Biz adds: “In an internal message seen by Bloomberg, one of the game’s directors told staff: ‘No more hand-written code.’ The director also said all of the game’s art would be ‘generated with full AI workflows.’” How do the developers feel? Stunned is the most widely reported reaction.There is a lot of interest in the subject ofgames industry unionisation, partly because ofthe most recent Xbox lay-offsand partly due to theongoing legal battlebetween Rockstar and a group of ex-employees fired, they contend, because they were seeking to unionise. Kotaku hasan interesting and enlightening story, this time about a failed attempt to unionise at the veteran studio Double Fine and the ongoing ramifications.The latest novel by Guardian games contributor,Sarah Maria Griffinis out.Strange Is the Lightis a gothic thriller about a group of friends whose lives are torn apart by a live-action role-playing game they invented as children.What to clickCastlevania: Belmont’s Curse – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled | ★★★☆☆End of Abyss – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenHigh Score … Gail Tilden, who led Nintendo of America to multimillion-selling success.Photograph: Netflix/Courtesy of NetflixA great question this week fromTrudyvia email:“I’m really into documentaries at the moment. Could you recommend any that deal with video games and the gaming industry?”There are a few absolute classics that really defined the genre – among them areThe King of Kong, about the competitive Donkey Kong players Steve Wiebe and Billy Mitchell, andIndie Game: The Movieabout a community of indie devs in the early 2010s. I’d also recommend the Netflix seriesHigh Score,the bizarreAtari: Game Over, about the burial and excavation of hundreds of ET carts in the early 80s, and the self-explanatoryRubber-Keyed Wonder: The Story of the Sinclair ZX Spectrum. For online documentaries, you definitely need to visit the excellent YouTube channelsNoClipandPeople Make Games– they have done fascinating, important work. I also enjoyed Travis “Samox” Beauchamp’s charmingly idiosyncraticseries,The Smash Bros. Finally, I have to do this – tryAnAlternative Reality: The Football Manager Documentary, which features an insightful video game journalist you may well recognise.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterArcade gamesRetro gamesGames consolesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Mary Wallopers review – legs and pints go flying to the sound of rowdy folk ragers | Music | The Guardian
description: Irish six-piece embark on their biggest tour yet, turning grisly old stories into a knees-up with politically astute, spit-and-sawdust energy
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Irish six-piece embark on their biggest tour yet, turning grisly old stories into a knees-up with politically astute, spit-and-sawdust energy
Content: Gets the room bouncing … Charles Hendy of the Mary Wallopers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGets the room bouncing … Charles Hendy of the Mary Wallopers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMusicReviewThe Mary Wallopers review – legs and pints go flying to the sound of rowdy folk ragersCorn Exchange, EdinburghIrish six-piece embark on their biggest tour yet, turning grisly old stories into a knees-up with politically astute, spit-and-sawdust energyKatie HawthorneWed 14 Oct 2026 06.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not often you see crowd surfing during folk songs, let alone songs about murderers-for-hire who targeted priests in the early 1700s. But so it is at a Mary Wallopers show, the Irish trad group with a passionate following for their rowdy folk ragers.Legs and pints go flying as the six-piece, playing banjo and tin whistle, set about Seán na Sagart, a new track which turns a grisly old story into a knees-up. By its breathless conclusion, the hitman is dead and his victims and clients alike get it in the neck from the band. Singer Charles Hendy grins, savouring the punchline: “You can’t trust the clergy with their holy little bits / And ya won’t be thanked by any god for workin’ with the Brits.”View image in fullscreenIn rude health … the Mary Wallopers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe Dundalk band are kicking off their biggest tour yet, in honour of third album Paddywhackery – a record that finds the group in rude health and confronting criticism that they are “too Irish, or whatever”, according to founding members Charles and Andrew Hendy.The new material is often furiously fast, with politics and humour both sharply deployed. Frenzied single The Big Mixer has the room bouncing to cutting lyrics about greasing the machinery of capitalism, while the hedonistic Kit Kat Club sounds like a hangover before the night’s even over, with sour vocal harmonies and Catriona Gribben’s wonderful, wheezing accordion.View image in fullscreenCatriona Gribben on accordion.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBut the band can also hold the room in silence. “Someone put a border in Ireland. It’s a pain in the hole,” Andrew deadpans, before a sparse, serious version of folk tune Smuggling the Tin, sung over a buzzing drone from Finnian O’Connor’s uilleann pipes. Original song Landlord’s Demise is just as transfixing; a slow, strange march performed by Andrew while drumming the bodhrán, as the crowd claps and stamps. “Any landlords here tonight?” Charles shouts, scanning the room. “Fuckin’… good!”Closing on Frost Is All Over, a roughly 300-year-old jig, they lend the skipping tune an almost clubby feel: strobes firing, hands in the air. The Wallopers make an urgent case for folk’s continued relevance with their spiky, spit-and-sawdust takes on tradition – whether that tradition likes it or not.The Mary Wallopers play O2 City Hall, Newcastle upon Tyne, 14 October; then touring UK and Ireland to 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicFolk musicPop and rocklive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Appl/Baillieu: Lines of Life review – gifted baritone blends Kurtág and Schubert  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: A perfect example of the Oxford International Song festival’s creative programming, Benjamin Appl’s unforced but focused recital was full of profoundly beautiful music
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: A perfect example of the Oxford International Song festival’s creative programming, Benjamin Appl’s unforced but focused recital was full of profoundly beautiful music
Content: Poetic instincts … baritone Benjamin Appl and  pianist James Baillieu performing at the Holywell Music Room in Oxford.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPoetic instincts … baritone Benjamin Appl and  pianist James Baillieu performing at the Holywell Music Room in Oxford.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianClassical musicReviewAppl/Baillieu: Lines of Life review – gifted baritone blends Kurtág and SchubertHolywell Music Room, OxfordA perfect example of the Oxford International Song festival’s creative programming, Benjamin Appl’s unforced but focused recital was full of profoundly beautiful musicClive PagetWed 14 Oct 2026 05.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver 25 years, the Oxford International Song festival has adopted a creative approach to programming. Benjamin Appl’s pairing of Schubert lieder with spiny miniatures by György Kurtág was a perfect example. Your Schubert crowd isn’t necessarily yourKurtágcrew, and yet the 280-year-old Holywell Music Room was packed to the rafters.Ellen Mawhinney and Daniel Silcock, one of the festival’s Young Artist duos, kicked things off with an aquatic-themed recital that showed off Mawhinney’s powerful soprano and Silcock’s poetic instincts at the piano. From the inspiriting Scottish ballad Kishmul’s Galley to Hamilton Harty’s impassioned Sea Wrack, their smartly curated 15 minutes paved the way for Appl and James Baillieu’s equally satisfying programme, Lines of Life.TheGerman British baritoneis a gifted communicator, binding together songs that could easily have rubbed each other the wrong way. It helps that he has worked intensively with Kurtág. As he explained from the stage, sometimes he’d spend an entire morning on the first line of a song before returning after lunch ready to work on line two, only to have the exacting composer say, “Well, shall we start from the beginning?” His unforced delivery of these concentrated musical nuggets, many of them unaccompanied, was intently focused.View image in fullscreenA gifted communicator … Appl.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianThe Six Hölderlin-Gesänge set gnomic poetry that is hard enough to grasp before the composer ups the ante with notes and rhythm. Appl took on board their frenetic gasps and growls, and yet at other times, Kurtág’s melismatic writing came across as profoundly beautiful.The Schubert selection was bound together by common themes of love, longing and loss. The nihilistic Totengräbers Heimweh brought out a brittle, sardonic quality that found echoes in the melancholy Schäfers Klagelied and the otherwise jaunty Die Taubenpost.There was vocal beauty too, in Viola for example, one of Schubert’s loveliest songsabout a jilted violetthat in the wrong hands could have turned saccharine. Baillieu’s dramatically astute accompaniment drove the narrative here as it did throughout. Just occasionally, when pulling back to soften the tone, Appl’s voice didn’t quite go where he wanted it to, but such moments were few and far between in a rewarding musical journey that segued seamlessly from start to finish.Oxford International Song festivalcontinues until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicMusic festivalsFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It put me in a fever dream’: Philip Venables on turning Sarah Kane’s 4.48 Psychosis into a shocking opera | Opera | The Guardian
description: A decade after the premiere of his work setting Kane’s hard-hitting play, it’s returning to the Royal Opera House. The composer remembers its fevered beginnings, the sweat and tears shed along the way, and how it changed his life forever
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A decade after the premiere of his work setting Kane’s hard-hitting play, it’s returning to the Royal Opera House. The composer remembers its fevered beginnings, the sweat and tears shed along the way, and how it changed his life forever
Content: ‘By opening night, our noses were so close to the grindstone that nobody had really thought about how it might be received… the overwhelming audience response felt like a huge release of tension, a euphoria borne from sweat and tears shed along the way.’The premiere staging of 4.48 Psychosis at the Lyric Hammersmith theatre.Photograph: © ROH/Stephen CummiskeyView image in fullscreen‘By opening night, our noses were so close to the grindstone that nobody had really thought about how it might be received… the overwhelming audience response felt like a huge release of tension, a euphoria borne from sweat and tears shed along the way.’The premiere staging of 4.48 Psychosis at the Lyric Hammersmith theatre.Photograph: © ROH/Stephen CummiskeyOpera‘It put me in a fever dream’: Philip Venables on turning Sarah Kane’s 4.48 Psychosis into a shocking operaA decade after the premiere of his work setting Kane’s hard-hitting play, it’s returning to the Royal Opera House. The composer remembers its fevered beginnings, the sweat and tears shed along the way, and how it changed his life foreverPhilip VenablesWed 14 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn January 2015, I was on an overnight flight coming back from New York, having attended Prototype, a festival of new opera. I didn’t sleep a wink, but worked without stopping in a packed, dark, sleepy cabin, reading and annotating a book and furiously making notes on my laptop. As if in a fever dream, my mind whirled with text, music, dramaturgy, theatre.Those six nocturnal hours were some of the most creatively fertile of my life. The book was 4.48 Psychosis; the annotations became the blueprint for an opera. Sarah Kane’s text had unlocked something in me, a fervour, a deluge of ideas. I could barely keep up, noting every impulse, every fantasy, as my mind pinballed around.I landed back home, back to real life, with a thud. That year turned out to be tough: a messy and protracted relationship breakup and a threat of bankruptcy and losing my house, a victim of rogue builders. I broke out in a bleeding stress rash, and, for the first time in my life, suffered insomnia. I was not composing. Time slipped by.View image in fullscreenPhilip Venables: ‘my mind whirled with text, music, dramaturgy, theatre.’Photograph: Charl MaraisIn late summer, I managed to pull myself together. I dusted off those notes from the flight, made some spreadsheets (always!), counted the days I had to write each scene and set to work. The opera was written at breakneck speed in six months, in something of a trance. My personal life remained fraught, but the opera, and Kane’s world, became a refuge, an escape, a joy. Writing flowed.I followed my blueprint almost without deviation. I wrote the most straightforward scenes first, out of order, in their matching groups: the patient-doctor dialogues, the serial sevens, the positive and negative affirmations. Slowly, a patchwork opera emerged, until only the most challenging scenes remained. Then I returned to the text; it had an uncanny ability to reveal more ideas, more music, like layers peeled back successively. I reminded myself to follow my instincts. I held on to sage advice from fellow composer James Weeks: “You want people to come out afterwards and say ‘that wasn’t an opera’.”double quotation markKane’s text was a libretto just waiting to be set, full of musicRehearsing the opera was demanding. I delivered the score late (something I’ve learned never to repeat) and I’d unwittingly written something that did not align with a standard production: swathes of complex ensemble singing that had to be learned together; lots of recorded material to be prepared; scenes requiring millisecond precision between light, sound and video. This was difficult material on every level, and the creative team, producers and cast rolled up their sleeves and met the challenges with grit and dedication. I owe a huge debt of gratitude to that heroic cast and the producer, Sarah Crabtree.By opening night in May 2016, our noses were so close to the grindstone that nobody had really thought about how it might be received. There was simply relief and astonishment that we had made it to the stage. So the overwhelming audience response felt like a huge release of tension, a euphoria borne from sweat and tears shed along the way.View image in fullscreenA rare and precious thing … Gweneth Ann Rand and Susanna Hurrell in 4.48 Psychosis, Lyric Hammersmith, 2016.Photograph: © ROH/Stephen CummiskeyA number of critics noted that the text was clear and present in the opera, that it “seems to emanate from everywhere”. This was my proudest achievement. Kane’s text was a libretto just waiting to be set, full of music. Aside from passages of dense poetry, there are song forms, conversations, extracts from psychological tests, prosaic medical notes, descriptions of dreams – and, streaked throughout, the darkest of humour. I tried to find musical equivalences: love songs, musical humour, percussion dialogues to grasp the banality of psychiatry, contrasted with moments of deeply expressive, impassioned opera. I threw as many ideas at it as I could, and the text reciprocated … it opened floodgates of imagination. A text such as this is a rare and precious thing.Over the following months I began to process the experience. Aside from the confidence boost, the success of 4.48 kickstarted another period of creative abundance: my close collaboration and friendship with director Ted Huffman. We wanted to make more, as quickly as possible. We talked every day about new projects, we watched shows, shared links, read, fantasised, critiqued. We applied for residencies, wrote pitches, talked to everyone we could. Since 4.48we have made three operasand a handful of smaller pieces, for vocalists, instrumentalists, choirs, even schoolchildren; doubtless we will make more. It is joyous.double quotation markSarah Kane has taught me more about opera than any opera ever has.Reflecting on this as I prepare for the 10th anniversary revival at theRoyal Opera Housemakes me realise how Kane’s text has for ever shaped the way I think about and make my work. These days I better understand those gut instincts that led me to her text and guided me through composing. I can now articulate the questions it provoked, the questions that I still ask of any new project: What is the relationship between character and performer? Who is speaking, and to whom? What does singing or speaking mean? How do we create a frame for performers to tell our story to an audience directly, without artifice? How do we create community on stage? Above all, I cherish Kane’s creation of a theatre of the imagination, not a theatre of representation. Tell, but don’t show.View image in fullscreenColin Shay and Sally Swanson in The Faggots and Their Friends Between Revolutions by  Philip Venables, directed by Ted Huffman, part of Manchester International festival 2023.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianKane has taught me more about opera than any opera ever has. It saddens me that, more than 25 years after the publication of her text, post-dramatic or formally experimental work graces British opera stages so rarely. We’re hung up on dramatisation, on representation, on the suspension of disbelief. There are so many other ways to skin a cat.While the opera has had several other performances and productions in the US, France and Germany, coming back to our original production and watching a new cast tackle it afresh has been a real pleasure – and also underlines the unique achievement of the original cast. Alongside, I’m writing and directing my first music theatre piece without Ted, The Alonetimes, a collaboration with Jennifer Walshe, which has its UK premiere on 19 October at the Schwarzman Centre in Oxford. A brand new adventure and returning to where I began, all in the same week. I’m incredibly lucky, and I owe it to that meeting with 4.48 Psychosis, all those years ago.4.48 Psychosis is at theLinbury theatre, London from 17-25 OctoberExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicRoyal Opera HouseSarah KaneShareReuse this content

title: Jessie Buckley suggests film industry gives too much weight to Oscar campaigns | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor, who won the Academy Award for best actress this year, was speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: The actor, who won the Academy Award for best actress this year, was speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards
Content: ‘I feel so proud being part of this community’ … Jessie Buckley.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/Invision/APView image in fullscreen‘I feel so proud being part of this community’ … Jessie Buckley.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/Invision/APMoviesJessie Buckley suggests film industry gives too much weight to Oscar campaignsThe actor, who won the Academy Award for best actress this year, was speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awardsNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJessie Buckley has questioned whether the film industry places too much emphasis on Oscar campaigns at the expense of nurturing emerging talent, suggesting there may be greater potential in supporting film-makers at grassroots level.Speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards in London, the actor was responding to comments by John Malkovich, who saidOscar campaigns were now the only way to get audiences into cinemas.“I think there’s truth in that,” Buckley told the Guardian. “You’ve got to take responsibility for sharing your work. It would be so easy to just go and film and then hide. I wish we could all do that. But I don’t think that’s how it works any more.”Buckley, who has made predominantly independent films, said the industry’s reliance on film promotion affected not just actors and directors but the wider workforce.“I feel so proud of being part of this community – this affects so many people’s lives. Crews, marketing, everybody. And if you don’t support it, you’re not going to have a job,” she said.“Maybe we’ve given that too much weight. I wonder if there’s more potential in nurturing at a grassroots level than giving so much weight to a marketing Oscar campaign.”Four emerging UK film-makers were named recipients of this year’sBFIand Chanel film-makers awards, each receiving £20,000 to develop their work.They were announced at a ceremony at Claridge’s in London on Wednesday, with Buckley and Gwendoline Christie joining a jury that also included BFI CEO Ben Roberts, Edward Enninful and Marie-Louise Khondji.double quotation markWe need to support the next generation. I want to know what they’ve got to say, what their world looks likeBuckley called for greater support for film-makers working outside established industry structures, pointing to the success of films “made on shoestring budgets”, includingObsessionandBackrooms.“People went to see them because of their quality, not because of the IP or what was deemed successful beforehand,” she said.“It’s essential that we support up-and-coming young film-makers. It would be completely selfish if we didn’t. At some point we want to pop off this earth, and we need to support the next generation. I want to know what they’ve got to say, what their world looks like.”The four winning films explored subjects including political protest, racial profiling, female solidarity and family trauma.View image in fullscreenJury members Gwendoline Christie and Jessie Buckley (centre) with, from left: Rich Felgate, Olive Nwosu, Imran Perretta and Rachel Taparjan.Photograph: James D KellyRich Felgate, director, producer and cinematographer of We, the Hated, was recognised for his documentary about Just Stop Oil protesters and the personal consequences of participating in a polarising movement. The jury described the film as “urgent and brave”.Buckley said it had prompted her to reconsider the role of protest in society. “In our world at the moment, protest seems like such a dangerous act, when historically it’s been essential to democracy,” she said.“It realigned me and reminded me of how important protest is, and how we can misunderstand the people within that. That we need to understand more and need films like that more.”Olive Nwosu won for Lady, her feature debut set in Lagos, which follows one of the city’s few female taxi drivers as she becomes drawn into the world of a childhood friend who has become a sex worker. The jury praised Nwosu’s cinematic ambition and her handling of challenging material.Imran Perretta was recognised forIsh, a black-and-white coming-of-age film set in Luton’s South Asian and Middle Eastern community. It follows two 12-year-old best friends whose relationship is tested after a police stop and search.The jury praised its exploration of racial profiling and the experience of being British while being treated as an outsider.Rachel Taparjan won for Something Familiar, her debut feature documentary about her search for her missing sisters after being adopted from Romania and brought to the UK as a child. The jury praised the film’s “naked, unselfconscious revelation of self”, saying it had stayed with them longest.Christie said the strength of this year’s field meant the jury had concluded it “couldn’t just select three winners”.The awards, which celebrate creative audacity and ambition, have run since 2022. Previous recipients include Harry Lighton, whose filmPillionwon best British independent film at the British independent film awards in 2025, and Savanah Leaf, who received the 2024 Bafta for outstanding debut by a British writer, director or producer.Explore more on these topicsFilmAwards and prizesJessie BuckleyFilm industryBFInewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s terrified, panicked, can’t sleep’: the tragic, lonely death of Beatles manager Brian Epstein | Music | The Guardian
description: Spandau Ballet’s Gary Kemp paid £10k at auction for Epstein’s address book. He then used it to co-author a thrilling account of the swinging 60s – and an intimate portrait of a tormented man whose life was unravelling
Author: Simon Harper
Headline: Spandau Ballet’s Gary Kemp paid £10k at auction for Epstein’s address book. He then used it to co-author a thrilling account of the swinging 60s – and an intimate portrait of a tormented man whose life was unravelling
Content: ‘He could not find a relationship’ … the Beatles with Epstein, right, at the premiere for A Hard Day’s Nightin 1964.Photograph: John Rodgers/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘He could not find a relationship’ … the Beatles with Epstein, right, at the premiere for A Hard Day’s Nightin 1964.Photograph: John Rodgers/RedfernsMusic‘He’s terrified, panicked, can’t sleep’: the tragic, lonely death of Beatles manager Brian EpsteinSpandau Ballet’s Gary Kemp paid £10k at auction for Epstein’s address book. He then used it to co-author a thrilling account of the swinging 60s – and an intimate portrait of a tormented man whose life was unravellingSimon HarperWed 14 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe email from Sotheby’s might easily have gone unread. Despite his deep appreciation for the musical heroes who came before him,Gary Kempis not a collector of rock memorabilia. But there, among the auction lots, was something that caught his eye: a 160x100mm black Twinlock binder that once belonged to the Beatles’ manager, Brian Epstein.The listing detailed 57 pages containing 404 entries, many handwritten by Epstein himself, cataloguing the social and business network of the Liverpudlian impresario in 1967, the year of his death. Kemp immediately recognised this was much more than simply an address book: it was a who’s who of 60s London at its swinging peak, from David Bailey and David Frost to most of the Rolling Stones. “I just thought, ‘I’ve got to have this. I’ve got to hold it,’” he says. “It’s got DNA on it.”double quotation markHis contract was up with the Beatles – and they’d stopped playing live, which gave him less purposeOn the day of the auction, Kemp, the songwriter and guitarist of Spandau Ballet, was in a recording studio bidding by phone. As the price quickly soared, so too did his determination. “I’m still pressing the yes button,” he remembers, “thinking, ‘My wife’s going to kill me for this!’”After bidding £10,710, Kemp became the book’s fifth owner. After Epstein’s death, it had passed to his brother, then his nephew, and then one more sale before reaching the auction at Sotheby’s. For Kemp, owning it felt like the culmination of a lifelong fascination with the Beatles and a long-held admiration for Epstein, the man who discovered the group at The Cavern in late 1961.View image in fullscreen‘There’s such a strong sense of the gay community in his book’ … Gary Kemp.Photograph: Simon EmmettKemp is talking from his study in an elegant five-storey Georgian townhouse he attributes, in part, to the inspiration and opportunities the Beatles gave him. “If it hadn’t been for Paul meeting John, I wouldn’t be living in this house,” he says. “But really, if it hadn’t been for Brian walking down those steps that November lunchtime, I wouldn’t be in this house either.”One visitor to Kemp’s home shortly after he’d acquired Epstein’s address book was art film-maker Simon Halfon, a friend since the 90s. He was just leaving when Kemp thought to show him his latest purchase. “I was obviously thrilled to look at it,” says Halfon. “An address book in many ways is a very personal thing. It’s not a diary, but it tells you who your friends are, your family, your business acquaintances, the places you hang out. It’s quite telling of an individual’s personality.”Halfon was an auspicious person to show it to. He had spent years fascinated by Epstein, developing a biopic of the manager with Jude Law attached to star, but it never came to fruition. Now, confronted with Epstein’s address book, and the revelatory list of contacts within, he saw a different story waiting to be told. “I called him on the way home,” says Halfon. “I said, ‘Christ, Gary, this is a book.’ And he was up for it straight away.”“I realised,” says Kemp, “the only way to do this is to tell Brian’s story through his contacts. This was Brian 360.”What followed was an exhaustive piece of detective work. Name by name, Kemp scoured books, newspapers, magazines and online archives, trying to establish not only who each person was, but why they had crossed paths with Epstein. Meanwhile, Halfon was tasked with sourcing corresponding imagery. Some names proved straightforward, while others were little more than shadows they’d futilely chase.The result is 1967: The World of Brian Epstein and the Beatles – not a biography in the traditional sense, but an alphabetical list of fragments that, read in sequence, reveals an unexpectedly intimate picture of a complex man unravelling in the last months of his life. Through the people he knew, it captures Epstein juggling the increasingly elaborate business affairs of the Beatles within an international set of artists, managers and lawyers, while wrestling with the more tormenting aspects of his own life. And because these are the people who surrounded him in 1967, the book also depicts the circumstances closing in around him.“It was really a key year for Brian,” Kemp explains. “His contract is up with the Beatles. And the Beatles have stopped playing live, which gives him less purpose.”This sense of unease permeates the book. Struggling to keep pace with his expanding empire, that January Epstein merged his NEMS Enterprises with Robert Stigwood’s agency to ease the workload, causing friction with the Beatles. “He’s terrified,” says Kemp. “He finds these boys who he transforms into the biggest phenomenon the world has seen, but then it starts to run away from him. And we’re at this stage now where he is panicked. He can’t sleep. He’s taking uppers and downers.”View image in fullscreen‘It was nice to push Brian to the foreground’ … at Abbey Road in 1967.Photograph: David Magnus/ShutterstockEpstein’s drug use exacerbated an already precarious mental state. The book traces his encounters with addiction doctors, the gambling dens he frequented, and his stints in rehab at The Priory in London. His Jewishness often made him feel like an outsider, and he was gay at a time when it was still a criminal offence – part of the complicated landscape he privately navigated.“There’s such a strong sense of the gay community within the book,” says Kemp, “whether it’s Brian’s lawyer, David Jacobs, the people he brought down from Liverpool … or people in the book, like Robin Maugham, Somerset Maugham’s nephew, who all had gay relationships that were quite open in that they lived together.”What’s striking about this book is that despite reconstructing the remarkable breadth of Brian’s orbit, he emerges as a lonely, isolated figure. “He couldn’t find a relationship,” says Kemp, who uncovers in these pages a handful of likely liaisons – men who passed briefly through Brian’s life.The most disturbing of these is John “Dizz” Gillespie, an aspiring American actor with whom Brian had a volatile, on-off affair. The last time they’d met, in August 1966, Dizz had stolen Brian’s attache case from his Los Angeles hotel room, making off with $20,000, contracts, incriminating photographs, and – perhaps – his previous address book. The betrayal, distress and persistent threat of blackmail and/or exposure sent Brian into a downward spiral.It is startling, therefore, to find Dizz’s name here at all, whether Brian included it out of guilt, desperation or lingering hope. Gillespie left almost no trace of himself. “There’s not even a mugshot,” says Halfon, “which you’d think there would be, because he was a bit of a villain in his own way.” Finally, Halfon discovered a signed copy of John Lennon’s A Spaniard in the Works, inscribed to Dizz with a characteristically acerbic note. “That was at least something,” he continues, “to prove his existence and interweave it into Brian’s world.”Epstein was alone when he died, aged just 32, of an accidental overdose of sleeping pills, on 27 August. He’d spent the bank holiday weekend at his country house in Sussex, but a guest he’d hoped to see failed to show, and a disappointed, drunk Epstein drove home to London that same night, locking himself in his Chapel Street bedroom.Kemp imagines Epstein there, withdrawn and despondent, reaching for his address book in need of friendly reassurance. “It was almost certainly on his bed when he was found dead,” Kemp says, “because he was calling people, and he would have been calling people using that book.”The reward for months of scrutiny into Epstein’s short life was, for Kemp, a closeness with the man himself. “I came out knowing him more. I felt I’d walked with him down different streets,” he says. “Because the book has addresses in it, you see it geographically as well.”View image in fullscreenA lonely, isolated figure … Brian Epstein in 1966 when homosexuality was still illegal.Photograph: C Maher/Getty ImagesThose locations are vital in bringing the physical world Epstein inhabited so vividly alive in the book. London sparkles with references to its clubs, offices, restaurants and homes, while further afield, the feverish nightclub culture of New York and the glamorous Hollywood scene (via Dean Martin, Colonel Tom Parker, Orson Welles) crackle with the same electricity. Epstein feels present throughout, fluttering through the worlds of music, theatre, business and bohemia, constantly making new connections along the way.Together, those details create an evocative, three-dimensional portrait of a man often overshadowed by the towering legends of his most famous charges. “It’d just be nice to push Brian slightly to the foreground,” says Halfon. “It’s very hard to stand in front of the Beatles in a way, as a character, because they’re so larger than life. But people can say, ‘Well, this was the guy who made their dream come true.’”But what of the Fab Four themselves? Anyone flicking through the pages expecting to spot John, Paul, George or Ringo’s names will be sorely disappointed. Their exclusion, Kemp suggests in the introduction, may be down to security reasons – particularly in light of Dizz Gillespie’s thieving. But appearances, as readers will find out, can be deceiving.It’s been a voyage of intrigue that Kemp seems reluctant to end. “Maybe I’ve started a thing now,” he laughs. “Frank Sinatra’s got an address book out there somewhere.”1967 – The World of Brian Epstein and The Beatles by Gary Kemp and Simon Halfon (HarperCollins, £25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMusicGary KempThe BeatlesMusic booksBiography booksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s vibe is lady who lounges - not lunches | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Think boucle jackets with low-waisted jeans, silk blouses with masculine trousers, pencil skirts with wellies …
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Think boucle jackets with low-waisted jeans, silk blouses with masculine trousers, pencil skirts with wellies …
Content: Video: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Melanie WilkinsonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashionFashionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s vibe is lady who lounges - not lunchesThink boucle jackets with low-waisted jeans, silk blouses with masculine trousers, pencil skirts with wellies …Jess Cartner-MorleyWed 14 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt always makes me feel a tiny bit queasy when looking “ladylike”, as a trend or a vibe or whatever, comes into fashion. How does it make sense to spend our hard-earned paychecks cosplaying as women of lunches and leisure?You can’t deny these clothes are cute, though. A boucle jacket can make you feel as if the Eiffel Tower might come into view around the next corner, even though you are in the wrong country. A mini-heel lets you imagine you might be having a glass of sancerre with your lunch, when in reality a can of San Pellegrino is as exciting as it is going to get. There is an air of gentle charm, of courtesy, to lady-adjacent style that can take the edge off a tough day.So I am cautiously, provisionally, glass-half-full about this season’s ladylike-with-a-twist trend. Call it the lady who lounges, not the lady who lunches. The lady who lounges has the jacket and the heels and maybe even the pearls, but she wears jeans and she’s definitely not in a pussy bow. Same DNA, different agenda. The allure of ladylike dressing is about the delicious fantasy of ease, of life lived off the clock. This is not real life, no. But maybe it doesn’t hurt to dream a little.double quotation markSlept-in hair or a bare-ish face are a useful counterpoint to pearls and tweedMatthieu Blazy’sChanelis the mother ship for this mood. Chanel is where much of the visual language of ladylike comes from: the neat little jacket, the chain bag, the two-tone shoe, the pearls. Blazy has been ruffling Coco’s bob, throwing masculine tailoring in against the house’s more buttoned-up instincts, redoing bags with a crumpled, lived-in slouch. This is Coco getting dressed from a boyfriend’s wardrobe rather than a boutique. There were clues at Miu Miu’s autumn show, too, which Miuccia Prada described in terms of “gentleness” and “romance”, and where pencil skirts were worn with wellies, and bow-trimmed minidresses with walking boots.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianThis is ladylike with its shoes kicked off, and it probably starts with a textured jacket and jeans. The jacket should sit on your shoulders rather than pin them into position. The jeans have an ease to them – a lower waist, rather than mom jeans, helps knocks the primness out of the jacket. Underneath, try a crisp shirt or a plain white vest. Or swap jeans for a pencil skirt, but wear a big jumper rather than a neat cardigan. A silk blouse wants a masculine trouser; a brooch wants a battered old coat.You need something in your outfit that turns up with its elbows on the table. A look where every element is saying the same thing feels robotic and cookie-cutter. Personal style has the odd raw edge. Don’t underestimate the power of hair and makeup. Or rather, the power of a little less hair and makeup than the clothes seem to expect. Slept-in hair or a bare-ish face are a useful counterpoint to pearls and tweed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: pair a little skirt with a chunky jumper for the perfect balancing actRead moreTrends are a buffet rather than a tasting menu these days. If a fancy pair of jewel-coloured leather gloves make you feel fabulous, go for it; if they make you feel as though you should be waving from a carriage, steer clear. Ladylike accessories work best when they look as if they wandered into the wrong outfit, so pin a brooch to denim or wear a silk scarf with a sweatshirt. This isn’t about making casual clothes smarter or fancy clothes more laid-back exactly, but more about making the outfit hard to pigeonhole. We can play with the fantasy of being a lady without having any intention of taking on the job full-time.The old ladylike trend felt like performing a life you didn’t have. This one lets you live your real life, only in such a nice jacket that people will wonder where you are going for dinner. Have the boucle. Have the pearls. Have the sancerre, should the opportunity arise. Then put those kitten heels back on and get back to business.Stylist: Melanie Wilkinson.Model: Imogen May at Milk.
