title: Is the modern economic system broken? These urban beekeepers think so – and this is their solution | Bees | The Guardian
description: At Bybi in Copenhagen, a dedicated group of staff and volunteers have built a community for all centred on the production of honey – much of which is given away for nothing. Could it be replicated elsewhere?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: At Bybi in Copenhagen, a dedicated group of staff and volunteers have built a community for all centred on the production of honey – much of which is given away for nothing. Could it be replicated elsewhere?
Content: Hive of activity … Aref Haboo(left), Bybi’s principal beekeeper, with Mohammed, a fellow apiarist.Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHive of activity … Aref Haboo(left), Bybi’s principal beekeeper, with Mohammed, a fellow apiarist.Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The GuardianEuro visionsBeesIs the modern economic system broken? These urban beekeepers think so – and this is their solutionAt Bybi in Copenhagen, a dedicated group of staff and volunteers have built a community for all centred on the production of honey – much of which is given away for nothing. Could it be replicated elsewhere?Zoe WilliamsWed 14 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe bees at Bybi,a collective of beekeepers in Copenhagen, live on the roof. Their home is a complex of Victorian buildings, right in the centre of the city, that looks like an idealised vision of the modern social enterprise, ennobled by the architecture of the past. It’s a place of cottage industry in concert with nature, where the marginalised are brought in from the fringes and corporations stand waiting to help, where jobs happen but a lot of the work is done by volunteers, and where – this bit is important – a lot of time is spent discussing ideas.Oliver Maxwell, Bybi’s 48-year-old founder, encourages me to examine the buildings more closely. They were once a prison, a workhouse and a hospital; their functions today – a homeless shelter, a young offender institution and, until recently, a job centre – are not so different. Denmark’s Victorian transformation, from “agricultural backwater to industrialised agriculture”, was reflected in how they treated people, Maxwell says.In the middle of it all is the collective, which looks like a lot of things – a commune, a kitchen-table business, an art space. Everything smells of honey. Long drapes in earthy colours frame the entrance to a space where volunteers jar honey by hand. Small pots are stacked against a window in what appears to be a random formation, but this turns out to be a stylistic map of the city: each jar is from a particular street, with its own shade and its own taste, thanks to “the flowers people planted, the weather, the bees’ own decisions and choices”, as Maxwell puts it.“Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection, a place asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?” he says. Between 40 and 50 volunteers come in and out throughout the year, with a core team of 15 undertaking practical, honey-related tasks and events.They have 80 to 100 colonies, not just on this rooftop, but all over the city, on businesses and conference centres, schools, municipal buildings, restaurants. They produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year. How that turns into money really depends.Sometimes they give it away, at weddings and festivals. “Honey is an invitation,” Maxwell says. “It wants you to come in as a co-creator, with a joint responsibility for its health. We ask that you share it with someone you care for. And you plant a flower to help the bees.”View image in fullscreen‘Honey is an invitation’ … jarring up at Bybi.Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The GuardianSometimes they sell it in the old-fashioned way, at a couple of boutique delicatessens around the city. Sometimes they ask people how much they want to pay; some are generous, some are not. Sometimes they discuss it in a reverse haggle, sitting in a group where they, as sellers, start low; the bidders tend to drive the price higher by thinking deeply about what went into the honey.Maxwell, an anthropologist, is originally from the UK. He spent time in Vietnam doing forest protection, some more in Brighton training social enterprises, then arrived in Denmark in 2007, setting up Bybi along similar lines in 2010. The plan was to employ homeless and other marginalised people, who would then be absorbed back into society. Honey would be made at the same time. Bybi also employed a social worker, “who was always a really nice person”.The problem is, “it just doesn’t work”, he says. “The bottom half of the jobs market has fallen out and everyone else has to run faster and faster. The moment you make contact with the market economy, everyone just melts. We’re sitting here with a crisis of community,a loneliness crisis, a crisis in the meaning and purpose of work. People need to do stuff – we’ll find stuff to do. But the labour theory of value, where you create worth with your time, your boss takes it and gives you some back that you can live on? That does not work.”They abandoned the “giving homeless people jobs” agenda. Now, people come because they want to, not because they’ve been forced to by the job centre. Five or so people are employed, with more in the summer; there are scores of volunteers, including disabled people who pack flower seeds. “They do it as slowly as they like and we give most of the seeds away for free,” Maxwell says. “It’s outside the logic of work.”View image in fullscreen‘The moment you make contact with the market economy, everyone just melts’ … Oliver Maxwell, the founder of Bybi, and Anne-Louise Krogh Hornbech Jensen, who runs its projects and research.Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The GuardianAnd yet jobs are found. Maybe that, like the honey, is a byproduct of the bees. Back on the roof, 53-year-old Aref Haboo, the principal beekeeper, is looking for the queen amid sheets of honeycomb. The Syrian Kurd, who came to Denmark in 2014, finds her first time with an instinct gleaned from 18 years doing this job in the Afrin province of northern Syria, before he was displaced by Islamic State.Bees can recognise faces, apparently; they can also count and maybe even dream.Anne-Louise Krogh Hornbech Jensen, 34, who wrote her dissertation on Bybi and now works here, says she always sticks by Haboo around the bees because then she doesn’t get stung, which is as much proof as a bee could give you that they recognise faces. Haboo says Danish honeybees are less aggressive and more productive than Syrian bees.This haphazard income stream isn’t the only thing keeping Bybi afloat. Its partners include universities, architects and corporations such as L’Oréal, which took some bees for the land at the back of a distribution centre.“The director became fascinated and stopped cutting the grass,” says Maxwell. “He got bat boxes, bird boxes, hedgehog boxes. They sponsored our work with schools. Employees collected the seeds and took them home, so the biodiversity of the field was spreading through the city. The director discovered a kestrel was nesting there when he found a dismembered rabbit.”View image in fullscreen‘You have to be OK with saying: “Our primary interest is not humans”’ … Haboo tends to his colony.Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The GuardianWhen rewilding, says Nicolas Hansen, a 27-year-old volunteer and nature management student, “you have to be OK with saying: ‘Our primary interest is not humans.’ You have to give nature its space.”Those various sponsorships support schools programmes at Bybi, plus they collaborate with a lot of artists. People sometimes write messages to the bees, just catching them up with the news, recalling a preindustrialised era when many households would keep a hive or two and talk to the bees.Refugees also work here, while people on incapacity benefits volunteer, but no one would call this a project for employing refugees or refurbishing the economically inactive. “We also have corporate refugees volunteering,” Maxwell says breezily, describing the volunteers burnt out by their high-flying jobs. Andrew Japp, a 52-year-old from Scotland, says: “I’d call myself more of a transient.”Every society projects their image on to honeybees. Ancient Egyptians said they were the tears of the sun god Ra, to reinforce the divine right of the pharaoh, who was given the title Nesut-Bity, “he of the sedge and the bee”. To Aristotle, bees were the first “political animals”, organised in city states. In Manchester, the birthplace of modern capitalism, there is a bee on every lamp-post. All the language we use about them – hives, colonies, workers, queens – makes them not just capitalism’s mascot, but an attempt to reconcile the contradictions of the new, self-correcting market economy into a coherent picture, modelled in the natural world.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We layer this industrious language on them, but it’s completely wrong,” Maxwell says. “The relationship they have with a flower isn’t toil – it’s sexual. It’s the reproduction of life in a language of touch, taste, smell, dance, colour; the hair they have on their eyeballs, the way they can hear through their feet. It’s an intense sensory experience and it can only be understood as pleasure. They’re not obeying an order. They’re obeying their senses telling them it’s gorgeous.”View image in fullscreen‘Today’s conditions are full of possibilities for improbable collaborations across people, plants and animals’ … employees and volunteers at Bybi.Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The GuardianBybi’s mission is sometimes described as “degrowth” or “regeneration”. Both apply, but neither captures the sense of urgency, that “we’re all living with this cognitive dissonance all the time, that everything bad is being hyperscaled, from AI toEl Niño, yet we’re meant to exist as if everything works and nothing has changed,” says Maxwell. “The problem here is that we need to change metaphors.”Often, when it makes a decision, Bybi will deploy what the philosopher Bruno Latour called the “parliament of things”– a bid to expand democracy to take in nonhuman agents such as animals, rivers and plants. “Stay with the trouble,” is Maxwell’s watch‑phrase, or one of them, referencing Donna Haraway’s 2016 book, in which she argues that, in the face of ecological crisis, we shouldn’t wait in despair to be rescued: instead, form bonds of care and fight like hell.Madeline Pugh, 26, is a student volunteer from the US. She says Denmark is the perfect sandbox for this experiment: “As a culture, it really appreciates and finds beauty in slow processes, taking time to build something with good intentions.” But it’s not a sweet story of easy integration and togetherness. Haboo’s life outside the bees is precarious – he got a speeding ticket the other day that could have jeopardised his citizenship application, even though he has been in Denmark for 12 years and his wife and children are here, too.“Danish society makes out it’s all about sourdough and pretty girls on bicycles, but it’s incredibly racist. It wins all the prizes for being livable, but not if you’re brown,” Maxwell says.View image in fullscreen‘Bees’ relationship with a flower isn’t toil – it’s sexual’ … a swarm of insects at Bybi.Photograph: Valdemar Ren/The GuardianThere is a raging debate about honeybees in Denmark, which is a kind of nativism with the sting removed (ironically): there are 293 species of bee in the country, but only one makes honey; all the others are, to varying degrees, endangered. People make the argument that honeybees aren’t properly Danish, that they are taking work from wild bees, that they are sexually promiscuous, that they spread diseases and that they are a conspiracy of the EU and industrial agriculture. Honeybees are so connected with industrial agriculture that they have become a lightning rod for rural communities who feel trampled by it, who see themselves as the disenfranchised wild bee in this equation.As much as honey is all around, Bybi isn’t taking the honeybee’s side in this culture war – it wants to introduce a relationship with bees that enriches conditions for all pollinating insects. That means more flowers planted and more spaces left to be rewilded, but also, on a deeper level, more people engaging with the interdependence between our activities and the ecosystems that sustain us.But there is pushback to what Bybi does. Some say it shouldn’t be getting into bed with corporations, although Japp says the relationship with businesses is more: “We don’t subscribe to your bullshit, but you should subscribe to ours.” People say it’s not scalable: they ask how it’s going to feed the world and point to the reliance on volunteers as a sign that it’s not a viable concern that could stand on its own two feet. “As if there’s a spot on Earth where capitalism doesn’t exist,” Maxwell says, exasperated. “We have to start in the conditions that exist today, which are messy and compromised, but also full of possibilities for improbable collaborations across people, plants and animals.”As part of an internship at Gehl,a design consultancythat specialises in urban transformation and community-building, Pugh is doing a project on the eight components of awe, as defined in Dacher Keltner’s 2023 book, Awe. These are moral beauty (other people’s kindness or courage); collective effervescence (bees are good at this); nature; music; art; spiritual and religious experience; life and death (being present at one); and epiphanies. “A lot of people here are keepers of awe,” she says.There is no blueprint that could replicate the precise alchemy of people, place and nature found at Bybi. But an experiment in cooperating across species and within our own – to bring in everyone from the suits to the left-behind – to foster a sense of common purpose and imagine a post-industrial future? That must be scalable.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The best electric heaters in the UK, from traditional stove-style units to modern smart models – tested | Interiors | The Guardian
description: Want to heat just one room without firing up the boiler? We cosied up to 12 electric heaters to find the best for your home
Author: Pete Wise
Headline: Want to heat just one room without firing up the boiler? We cosied up to 12 electric heaters to find the best for your home
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterInteriorsReviewThe best electric heaters in the UK, from traditional stove-style units to modern smart models – testedWant to heat just one room without firing up the boiler? We cosied up to 12 electric heaters to find the best for your homeThe best hot-water bottlesPete WiseWed 14 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAre you in need of a stopgap stand-in for your central heating? Or perhaps you’re looking for an efficient appliance to heat a small space. If so, investing in one of the best electric heaters can rid your home of the cold.Electric heaters range from compact, fast-acting fan-powered models to oil-filled radiators and wall-mounted panels. Some also have smart functionality, so you can ask Alexa to turn up the heat, and other advanced features such as air purification and adaptive heating. But which are best?I cosied up to some of the most popular models from makers including Russell Hobbs, Everhot, Dreo and Mill. Here’s my roundup of the best electric heaters, including models that are cheap to run, high-powered and capable of warming a large room, alongside smart electric devices with app-assisted functionality.At a glanceBest electric heater overallDreoPTC fan heater Solaris 718£118.99 at AmazonBest budget electric heaterRussell HobbsOscillating ceramic 2kW heater£41.99 at WayfairBest stove-style electric heaterEverhotElectric heater£1,369 at Peter Tyson ElectricalsBest efficient electric heaterMillWifi max portable heater 1,500W£157 at AmazonWhy you should trust meProduct reviews should be fair, useful and unflinchingly geeky – something I keep in mind when getting to grips with each new batch of items I test.I’ve reviewed hundreds of products, ranging from fridges and fans to combi drills and pressure washers, since 2017. My favoured approach to reviews is in-depth exploration that prioritises hands-on testing and attention to detail.How I testedView image in fullscreen‘Sauna-like conditions’: each heater was tested at its maximum temperature.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianStaying warm matters, so I dug deep to test the models featured in this guide.I set up each model in my living room and blasted them at the maximum temperature. I measured the room’s air temperature using a digital thermometer at regular intervals to see how powerfully each heater was warming the space. Bravely risking sauna-like conditions, I took each measurement from the centre of the room and kept the windows and door shut during each heater’s test.Of course, temperature gain isn’t the only measure of an electric heater’s quality. I also assessed each model’s noise levels from the same position at regular intervals, and used an infrared thermometer after each test to judge whether the heater would be safe to touch. To gauge energy efficiency, I plugged the heaters into a power usage meter during testing.I was keen to try each heater’s special features, so I tested extras such as timed heating and smartphone operability. I ended up testing 12 heaters, and I believe that the eight models listed below are worthy of your consideration.Some brands did not want the heaters I tested back, so those will be donated for fundraising toCat Action Trust 1977, a small national charity dedicated to the welfare of feral cats.The best electric heaters in 2026Best electric heater overall:Dreo PTC fan heater Solaris 718DreoPTC fan heater Solaris 718from£118.99£139.99 at Dreo£118.99 at AmazonWhat we loveQuieter operation than most fan models, despite its powerWhat we don’t loveRelatively high energy usageView image in fullscreen£139.99 at Dreo£118.99 at AmazonI was instantly impressed with this obelisk-shaped fan heater from Dreo. Within a few seconds of activation, it had begun to make a chilly room feel cosy. And after five minutes of heating at the highest of the five available settings, my jumper was well and truly off.Why we love itFor a powerful fan model (drawing up to 2,000W), this is an impressively quiet heater, producing a deep, rushing sound as opposed to a harsh roar. I measured the noise at 46dB while using the highest setting – far quieter than any other fan heater I’ve tested. Operation is simple, with either the remote control or the on-unit buttons tapping into timed heating, lateral oscillation and a child lock. You can also use this as a towerfan for cooling, with three settings to choose from.The Solaris 718 has some heat-sensitive features to guide or control your usage. The Eco mode automatically chooses a heat setting to keep the room at a specified temperature, and there’s an LED indicator ring on the top that glows different colours to tell you whether the room is cold or hot (how Dreo defines these states, we know not).It’s a shame that …it’s quite energy-intensive on a high heat setting, and the elaborate grilles on the front and back of the heater are not the easiest to clean.Temperature increase during testing:5.9CAverage noise level:46dBEnclosure temperature after an hour:40.2CRunning cost an hour on maximum:52pSize:75.4 x 20.1 x 20.1cm (HWD)Weight:3.6kgDreoPTC fan heater Solaris 718from£118.99£139.99 at Dreo£118.99 at AmazonWhat we loveQuieter operation than most fan models, despite its powerWhat we don’t loveRelatively high energy usageBest budget electric heater:Russell Hobbs oscillating ceramic 2kW heaterRussell HobbsOscillating ceramic 2kW heaterfrom£41.99£41.99 at Wayfair£41.99 at AmazonWhat we loveQuality and performance are great for the priceWhat we don’t loveIts on-unit controls are a trifle clunkyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£41.99 at Wayfair£41.99 at AmazonAlthough it’s compact and affordably priced, the Russell Hobbs oscillating ceramic 2kW heater promises the kind of powerful, efficient heating you might expect from a more expensive model. It has some higher-end features, too, including oscillation (the heater rotates) and an Eco mode that adapts heating to the room temperature.Why we love itWithout a doubt, this is one of the best budget-friendly heaters I’ve tested. It spreads warm air throughout the room, even when used in its static mode. Activating oscillation with a press of a button on the remote control (or the on-unit control panel) only makes the effect more pronounced. The air directly in front of the heater felt very hot when I used a high temperature setting.This heater has quite a low-pitched operating noise, and while it’s a little loud, I find this more agreeable than the high-pitched whine you get with some fan heaters. I also appreciated its small footprint, bleep-free option (perfect for timer-based heating at night) and safety features, which include automatic shut-off if the heater were to topple over.It’s a shame that …the on-unit control buttons are a little tricky to press. But I’m splitting hairs here – this is a brilliant heater for the price.Temperature increase during testing:6.3CAverage noise level:51dBEnclosure temperature after an hour:59.1CRunning cost anhour on maximum:49pSize:33.5 x 15.5 x 14.8cm (HWD)Weight:1.9kgRussell HobbsOscillating ceramic 2kW heaterfrom£41.99£41.99 at Wayfair£41.99 at AmazonWhat we loveQuality and performance are great for the priceWhat we don’t loveIts on-unit controls are a trifle clunkyBest stove-style electric heater:Everhot electric heaterEverhotElectric heaterfrom£1,369£1,369 at Peter Tyson Electricals£1,369 at Cooks & CompanyWhat we loveBeautiful looks and top-notch cast iron constructionWhat we don’t loveYou’ll need plenty of floor space to accommodate itView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£1,369 at Peter Tyson Electricals£1,369 at Cooks & CompanyThis cast-iron model is surely the nicest-looking electric heater of them all. It would make a fabulous addition to most interior schemes – especially if you have an empty fireplace or alcove that needs filling.Why we love itFar from just a talking point, Everhot’s heater serenely produces 1.5kW of heating power via its stove-top vent. It warmed the space effectively and near-silently during my testing, resulting in a gradual increase in room temperature.The controls are simple, with just a power switch and heat-setting dial to master. Both components have a lovely finish, in keeping with the generally outstanding quality of the appliance.While the door on this model is non-functioning, you can geta similar model with an integrated ovenand a working door, which understandably comes at a higher price.One note of caution: the top of this stove gets extremely hot during and after use, so this heater may be unsuitable in households with pets or children.It’s a shame that …the price of this heater is too high for most buyers, especially if you’ll use it only occasionally. With that said, if you’re looking for an electric stove to use regularly, this one’s for you.Temperature increase during testing:3.8CAverage noise level:34dBEnclosure temperature after an hour:105.2CRunning cost anhour on maximum:41pSize:50.8 x 48.7 x 41cm (HWD)Weight:~40kg (each model is handmade, so some variation is inevitable)EverhotElectric heaterfrom£1,369£1,369 at Peter Tyson Electricals£1,369 at Cooks & CompanyWhat we loveBeautiful looks and top-notch cast iron constructionWhat we don’t loveYou’ll need plenty of floor space to accommodate itBest efficient electric heater:Mill wifi max portable heater 1,500WMillWifi max portable heater 1,500Wfrom£157£169 at Currys£157 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s effective and energy efficientWhat we don’t loveTakes up more floor space than expectedView image in fullscreen£169 at Currys£157 at AmazonNorwegian brand Mill promotes this heater’s wifi operability first and foremost – but I believe its real strength is its near-silent, highly efficient heating. Barely detectable by a sound meter, it subtly heated my cold living room to a comfortable temperature in less than 10 minutes while using less electricity than any comparable model.Why we love itThere are two ways to operate the heater: via theMill Norwaysmartphone app, or using a dial and LED display on the side of the unit. The app brings some fancier functionalities such as remote operation and weekly heating programmes, but the control that will really matter to most users is the on-unit dial, which effortlessly adjusts the thermostat to temperatures up to 35C.Unusually for a heater, this model is bathroom suitable with IPX4 moisture resistance. That means it can withstand the occasional spray of water, although it definitely shouldn’t be used too close to the bath or shower. The oval-shaped base – which requires assembly using your own screwdriver – feels stable and is gentler on flooring than feet or casters.It’s a shame that …the heater takes up quite a lot of floor space, and setting up wifi operation via the app proved fiddly.Temperature increase during testing:7CAverage noise level:26dBEnclosure temperature after an hour:65.8CRunning cost an hour on maximum:39pSize:38.5 x 62 x 24.5cm (HWD)Weight:5.5kgMillWifi max portable heater 1,500Wfrom£157£169 at Currys£157 at AmazonWhat we loveIt’s effective and energy efficientWhat we don’t loveTakes up more floor space than expectedThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘I had it set up and appreciably warming my living room within about 30 seconds’: the Swan 700W plug-in mini fan heater.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianSwan 700W plug-in mini fan heaterSwan700W plug-in mini fan heaterfrom£14.89£14.99 at Swan£14.89 at AmazonWhat we loveA useful option for warming up at close quartersWhat we don’t loveNoisy operation and relatively limited heating powerView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£14.99 at Swan£14.89 at AmazonBest for:small rooms too short on space for a conventional heaterThis tiny power socket heater from Swan is designed to plug straight into an outlet and deliver warmth in your direction of choice. I had it set up and appreciably warming my living room within about 30 seconds.In terms of extra features, Swan has kept this heater straightforward and practical. Using the controls on the top, you can adjust the output temperature and set a timed heating duration between one and 12 hours. Selected settings are shown clearly on the digital display.You can also use the plug rotation button (on the right-hand side) to switch the heater’s position, which partly makes up for the restriction of using it only in a place where it can be plugged in.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s noisy. This heater would be best suited to people who spend a lot of time wearing headphones.Temperature increase during testing:2.4C;average noise level:56dB;enclosure temperature after an hour:60.4C;running cost anhour on maximum:17p;size:14 x 11 x 12cm (HWD);weight:0.63kgSwan700W plug-in mini fan heaterfrom£14.89£14.99 at Swan£14.89 at AmazonWhat we loveA useful option for warming up at close quartersWhat we don’t loveNoisy operation and relatively limited heating powerDuux Threesixty 2 ceramic heaterDuuxThreesixty 2 ceramic heaterfrom£89.99£89.99 at Duux£119 at CurrysWhat we loveEfficient, temperature-sensitive heatingWhat we don’t loveFlawed connectivity proves an obstacle to smart featuresView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£89.99 at Duux£119 at CurrysBest for:powerful heating with a small footprintLooking like the defiantly well-adjusted love child of a smart speaker and an air purifier, the Duux Threesixty 2 is clearly the techiest heater on our list. Its minimalist design and pleasing packaging positively beg you to feature it in a social media unboxing video. On a more practical note, the Threesixty 2 delivers heated air in all directions, and has a PTC element that delivers temperature-appropriate heating thanks to its electronic properties (the element’s electrical resistance is such that it heats up intensely when the air is cold, and warms gently in milder conditions).I felt the warming effect of this compact fan heater pretty much straight after turning it on. There are three on-unit temperature settings, giving you some control over the heat level – but less than you’d get with most heaters. As a simple, manual fan heater, the Threesixty 2 works great, thoroughly warming the space while making less noise than your standard fan model.It didn’t make the final cut because …controlling this smart heater via smartphone or smart assistant is difficult. I found the Duux app too buggy to use.Temperature increase during testing:7.6C;average noise level:54dB;enclosure temperature after an hour:58.3C (lid);running cost anhour on maximum:48p;size:30 x 22 x 22cm (HWD);weight:2.4kgDuuxThreesixty 2 ceramic heaterfrom£89.99£89.99 at Duux£119 at CurrysWhat we loveEfficient, temperature-sensitive heatingWhat we don’t loveFlawed connectivity proves an obstacle to smart featuresDevola 1500W wifi-enabled smart glass panel electric heaterDevolaWifi-enabled smart glass panel electric heaterfrom£119.99£119.99 at Devola£119.99 at B&QWhat we loveIts sleek, contemporary designWhat we don’t loveElevated risk of breakage during assemblyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Pete Wise/The Guardian£119.99 at Devola£119.95 at AmazonBest for:extensive smart functionality at an affordable priceThis smart-assistant-compatible glass-panel heater from Devola is as sleek as they come, with a well-integrated digital on-unit display and controls. Plus, connect it to your wifi and smartphone, and you’ll have access to advanced features, including voice control and timed heating. During my testing, it operated quietly and heated the space steadily.A little assembly is required before use, with the exact steps depending on whether you wish to use the heater as a freestanding or wall-mounted unit. I chose the freestanding configuration and had the plastic feet attached to the bottom within a few minutes (taking great care during handling, as dropping this glass-panelled heater could be disastrous).It didn’t make the final cut because …operating the heater with the remote control isn’t exactly intuitive. You need to go into its settings menu and set a temperature for each of the three operating modes, rather than raising or lowering the heat manually. Smartphone app operation proves easier.Temperature increase during testing:6.4C;average noise level:34dB;enclosure temperature after an hour:44.6C;running cost anhour on maximum:48p;size:‎47 x 65 x 8cm (HWD);weight:7.68kgDevolaWifi-enabled smart glass panel electric heaterfrom£119.99£119.99 at Devola£119.99 at B&QWhat we loveIts sleek, contemporary designWhat we don’t loveElevated risk of breakage during assemblyVonHaus small oil-filled radiator 1,500WVonHausSmall oil-filled radiator 1,500Wfrom£47.99£47.99 at Robert Dyas£49.99 at VonHausWhat we loveIt costs little and works quietlyWhat we don’t loveModest heat outputView image in fullscreen£47.99 at Robert Dyas£49.99 at VonHausBest for:those on a strict budgetThis small, portable, inexpensive oil-filled radiator is a practical choice for occasional use. There are just two controls to master: a power selection switch (which toggles between 600W, 900W and 1,500W) and a thermostat dial.I found this radiator produced enough heat to make a chilly room comfortable, and it used relatively little electricity to do so. You can use the thermostat dial to set the desired temperature at which the heater will maintain the room – saving you from overheating and overspending on energy.The heater is quiet, except for the occasional quiet gurgling of oil, which is quite a pleasant sound in my opinion.It didn’t make the final cut because …it heats only moderately. While this model does a good enough job in a small space, it’s not suitable for heating a medium-sized or large room.Temperature increase during testing:2.7C;average noise level:33dB;enclosure temperature after an hour: 70.6C;running costan hour on maximum:23p;size:62 x 33.5 x 24cm (HWD);weight:6.9kgVonHausSmall oil-filled radiator 1,500Wfrom£47.99£47.99 at Robert Dyas£49.99 at VonHausWhat we loveIt costs little and works quietlyWhat we don’t loveModest heat outputWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenAn electric heater costing under £100 should be appropriate for many people’s needs.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianHow much should you spend on an electric heater?Electric heaters vary wildly in price, from less than £50 to £500 and beyond. Swanky ones can cost more than £1,000.How much you spend should depend, above all, on how much you intend to use it. For many users, an electric heater is an occasional-use item to warm you up in out-of-the-ordinary circumstances – such as when we can’t use the central heating due to home improvement work or a malfunction. If this sounds like you, then an electric heater costing under £100 should be appropriate for your needs.However, some buyers want an electric heater to use more regularly. You may use yours to heat just one room in your home, thus avoiding the need to use central heating or install a wood-burning stove. In such cases, spending more could give you a more attractive design and advanced features, such as smart operability.For reference, the total cost of adding a new plumbed-in radiator to an existing heating system tends to run between £200 and £600.Are electric heaters cheap to run?In a word, no. Electricity costs more than gas in the UK, relative to the power delivered to appliances. If an electric heater and a boiler-powered radiator had the same efficiency, it would cost more to produce the same level of heat with the electric unit.That said, using an electric heater in one room could prove more cost-effective than turning on central heating throughout the home. If you’re willing to experiment with your heating habits to reduce your energy costs, an electric heater could be part of the cost-saving combination.Some electric heaters cost less to run than others. In particular, models with a lower wattage, simple functionality and efficient design tend to have lower running costs.Which is the most efficient electric heater?Based on our testing, the cheapest electric heater to run is the Swan 700W plug-in mini fan heater.However, assessing an electric heater’s efficiency also requires us to consider its capability to heat a room adequately. This is tricky to define, as the heating performance needed depends on factors including the size of the space and your preferred ambient temperature.Of the models featured in this guide, I would consider the Mill wifi max portable heater 1,500W to be the most efficient electric heater for medium to large rooms, while the VonHaus small oil-filled radiator 1,500W is the most efficient electric heater for small rooms (provided you’re happy with moderate heating).Ceramic, fan and infrared heaters: which is better?If you’re choosing a new electric heater, there’s a good chance you’ll settle on a ceramic, fan or infrared heater. These three popular types have contrasting pros and cons.Ceramic heatershave heating elements made from – you guessed it – a ceramic material. Models of this type, such as the Duux Threesixty 2, use fans to distribute warm air quickly, while others radiate heat more gradually. Noise levels vary depending on the design.Fan heaterstake in air, heat it up rapidly and push it out into the room. They start producing heat almost instantly, and then quickly cool down after deactivation, as was the case with the Dreo PTC Solaris 718 during testing. Most fan heaters are relatively noisy, but on the plus side, they often have nice-to-have features such as oscillation and cooling modes for warmer weather.Infrared heaters emit infrared light that warms people and objects directly, rather than heating the air first. These heaters can work efficiently when used for targeted heating.The main drawbacks are that the direct warmth disappears quickly after deactivation, and heating can be patchy.Ultimately, ceramic, fan and infrared heaters can all do a fine job of keeping you warm. Ceramic models tend to be quieter, although fan-assisted models can be noisy. Fan models can heat up quickly, and infrared heaters provide targeted warmth.What to do with your old electric heaterElectric heaters have a shelf life, with warranty periods often in the range of two to five years. Many models stay in good condition for longer, but when faults occur with components, such as the heating element or thermostat, it may prove more economical to replace your heater than it is to repair it.We would urge you to explore having a broken electric heater repaired, especially if it’s under warranty. However, when buying a new model is unavoidable, there are some disposal options that will minimise the environmental impact.The best solution in most cases is to take the electric heater to your local recycling centre (the Recycle Now website will help you find one), where it can be processed as Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment. Alternatively, you could try listing the heater for free on local marketplace websites as a “spares or repairs” item.For more:The best electric blankets and heated throwsThe best hot-water bottles for comfort and cosinessThe best heated clothes airers to save time and money when drying your laundryPete Wise is ajournalist based in Leeds, withmore than a decade’s experience coveringeverything from global development and social causes to technology and music. As a home renovator and music studio renter, Pete has spent countless hours hunkering over electric heaters, little knowing that each tweak of the thermostat was a small step towards writing this articleThis article was originally published on 7 November 2024. description: Brown betty is a thrifty and delicious crumble-like autumnal treat
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Brown betty is a thrifty and delicious crumble-like autumnal treat
Content: Tom Hunt’s apple ,maple and blackberry brown betty.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s apple ,maple and blackberry brown betty.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notDessertHow to use stale bread to make a classic British pudding – recipeA thrifty and delicious crumble-like autumnal treat, a bit like a cobbler … or a buckle … or a grunt …Tom HuntWed 14 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe have a family tradition of making our daughter a fruit pie of some sort for her first day of school each September. Last year, it was a simple apple pie, but we intend to make our way through the myriad heritage desserts, from crumbles and crisps to cobblers,buckles,pandowdys,grunts,slumpsandsonkers. This year, we made a brownbetty, a wonderful, crumble-like dessert made with stale bread. We kept things seasonal with apples and blackberries from the garden, but any combination of fruit works really. I sweetened this one with maple syrup, but use your sweetener of choice: each adds its own unique flavour.Apple, maple and blackberry brown bread bettyA brown betty is easier to make than crumble; it’s also arguably even tastier, and it saves waste, too. I used three brown bread crusts left over frommy wholemeal bread taste test, which, when stale, make perfect and flavourful breadcrumbs. The topping should be good enough to eat even before cooking – totally delicious, salty sweet with maple syrup, and crunchy with seeds – so taste and adjust as you see fit with more salt, sweetener, nuts and seeds. The addition of sea salt is a gamechanger that really brings out the sweetness of the maple syrup.Serves4-64 apples100g blackberries70-80g maple syrup, or brown sugar or another sweetener1 tsp vanilla essence50ml water, or brandy75g butter, 50g of it melted, or extra-virgin olive oil3 slices wholemeal bread(about 85g), torn into pieces50g mixed seeds, or roughly chopped nuts (optional)½ tsp sea salt1 tsp ground cinnamonYoghurt, or cream, ice-cream or custard, to serveCut the cored apples into rough cubes (compost the cores, orturn them into pectin jelly) and toss with the blackberries, 40g of the maple syrup (or other sweetener), the vanilla essence and 50ml water (or brandy; the alcohol will cook off, and leave behind a lovely, complex flavour). Tip into a roughly 20cm-wide skillet or ovenproof dish, then dot with 25g of the butter (or extra-virgin olive oil).Tear the bread into pieces, then pulse-blend into chunky breadcrumbs. Stir in the remaining 30-40g sweetener, the melted butter (or extra-virgin olive oil), the mixed seeds or nuts, if using, the sea salt and ground cinnamon. Scatter this mix over the top of the fruit, then bake in a 200C (180C)/390F/gas 6 oven for 40-45 minutes, until golden brown and bubbling.Remove, leave to rest on the counter for 10 minutes, then serve with yoghurt, cream, ice-cream or custard.Explore more on these topicsDessertWaste notFoodFood wasteBreadFruitBakingAutumn food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cheese tart, corn salad, squash with ’nduja, radicchio salad: Joe Otway’s recipes for early autumn | Food | The Guardian
description: Celebrate seasonal British-grown produce with four easy dishes guided by a natural ingredient in its prime
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Celebrate seasonal British-grown produce with four easy dishes guided by a natural ingredient in its prime
Content: Joe Otway’s roast winter squash with ’nduja.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/Photographs: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian, food Styling: Rosie Reynolds, prop styling: Florence BlairView image in fullscreenJoe Otway’s roast winter squash with ’nduja.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/Photographs: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian, food Styling: Rosie Reynolds, prop styling: Florence BlairFoodCheese tart, corn salad, squash with ’nduja, radicchio salad: Joe Otway’s recipes for early autumnCelebrate seasonal British-grown produce with four easy dishes guided by a natural ingredient in its primeJoe OtwayWed 14 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly autumn is one of the most generous and comforting times of year to cook with British produce: sweetcorn is at its peak, squash begins to sweeten as the weather cools and bitter leaves such as radicchio provide balance to the season’s abundance. Today’s recipes are simple celebrations of British ingredients, using just a handful of carefully chosen components to let each vegetable shine. Whether it’s a buttery cheese tart for sharing; a fresh, herby corn salad; sweet roast squash with warm, spicy ’nduja; or bitter leaves lifted with a floral dressing, they all rely on cooking with ingredients at their seasonal peak and allowing nature to guide the menu.Cheese tartView image in fullscreenMade for sharing: Joe Otway’s cheese tart.Prep10 minChill30 min+Cook1 hrMakes4individual tarts90g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing120g plain flour, plus extra for dusting110g mature cheddar, finely grated70g whole eggs25ml whole milk10g ready-made English mustard, or to taste110ml double creamSea salt andblack pepperFirst, make the pastry. Rub the butter into the flour until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs, then add 60g of the grated cheddar and knead gently until the mix comes together into a dough. Divide into four, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes.Meanwhile, make the custard. Blend the eggs, milk, remaining 50g grated cheddar and mustard until smooth, then stir in the cream by hand and season to taste.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and grease and line four individual 8-10cm tart tins. Lightly flour a work surface, roll out each piece of pastry, then use to line the tins. Line each pastry base with baking paper, fill with baking beans or similar, then blind bake for 15 minutes, until lightly golden. Lift out the paper and beans, then return the tarts to the oven for a further five minutes, until the bases are crisp and golden.Carefully pour the custard into each tart case until they’re almost full, then bake for another 15-25 minutes, depending on your oven (the actual temperature of domestic ovens varies a fair bit, after all), until the custard is lightly browned and just set with a slight wobble in the centre.Leave to cool to room temperature, then serve, either with a bitter leaf salad or with one of the following two sides.Corn salad with soured cream and oreganoView image in fullscreenJoe Otway’s corn salad with soured cream and oregano.Prep5 minCook15 minServes4Sea salt andblack pepper4 fresh sweetcorn cobs, or 1 400g tin good-quality sweetcorn150g soured cream100ml extra-virgin olive oilJuice of ½ lemonSea salt20g fresh oregano leaves, plus extra to garnish30g parmesan, shavedBring a large pan of salted water to a boil, drop in the corn cobs, cook for four or five minutes, until tender, then drain and refresh. Once the cobs are cool enough to handle, cut off the kernels and put in a bowl (if you’re using tinned corn, skip the blanching stage and simply drain the water from the can).Mix the soured cream with 20ml of the olive oil, the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Blend the oregano with the remaining olive oil until fragrant. Dress the sweetcorn with the oregano oil, then season generously with salt and a little more lemon juice, if needed.Spread the soured cream mix over a platter, spoon the dressed corn on top, scatter over a few more oregano leaves and finish with generous shavings of parmesan and a final twist of black pepper.Roast winter squash with ’ndujaView image in fullscreenJoe Otway’s roast winter squash with ’nduja.Prep10 minCook45 minServes41kg winter squash(uchiki kuri is ideal, although butternut works well too), halved, deseeded and cut into skin-on wedges5 tbsp olive oilSea salt20g pumpkin seeds120g ’nduja2 tbsp good-quality honey150g Greek yoghurt1 tbsp lemon juice1 small handfulflat-leaf parsley, leaves picked and roughly choppedHeat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Toss the squash wedges with two tablespoons of the olive oil and a generous pinch of salt, then arrange on an oven tray and roast for 30-40 minutes, turning every 10 minutes, until tender and caramelised. Add the pumpkin seeds to the tray for the final 10 minutes of cooking.Meanwhile, in a small saucepan gently warm the ’nduja, honey and the remaining olive oil until the mix comes together into a loose dressing. In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.Spread the yoghurt on a platter, arrange the squash wedges and toasted pumpkin seeds on top, then spoon over the warm ’nduja dressing. Finish with the parsley and serve.Radicchio with elderflower vinaigretteView image in fullscreenJoe Otway’s radicchio with elderflower vinaigrette.Yes, elderflower is an early-summer flavour, but that’s why they invented cordial, so we can enjoy that gentle fragrance all year round.Prep10 minServes43 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil2 tbsp elderflower cordial2 tbsp white-wine vinegar1 tsp dijon mustardSea salt and black pepper2 heads bitter leaves– radicchio, treviso, chicory or endive will all work well here40g hard sheep’s cheese, or pecorinoIn a small bowl, whisk the oil, cordial, vinegar, mustard, and salt and pepper to taste, until lightly emulsified.Trim the bases off the radicchio heads, then separate the leaves and put them in a medium bowl. Dress the leaves generously with the vinaigrette, then season with a little more salt and pepper if needed. Leave to marinate for five to 10 minutes, so the leaves soften slightly and absorb the dressing, then arrange on a serving plate and finish with generous shavings of the cheese.Joe Otway is chef/co-owner ofHigher Ground,Bar ShrimpandFlawd, all in Manchester.Explore more on these topicsFoodCheesePieBakingPastryEggsVegetablesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Energy bills through the roof? Five signs your house is leaking heat | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: From finding draughts to buying a thermal leak detector – there are simple, cost-effective ways to start sorting heat loss
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: From finding draughts to buying a thermal leak detector – there are simple, cost-effective ways to start sorting heat loss
Content: A thermal imaging camera shows heat loss through the roof and windows of a house.Photograph: ivansmuk/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenA thermal imaging camera shows heat loss through the roof and windows of a house.Photograph: ivansmuk/Getty Images/iStockphotoEnergy billsEnergy bills through the roof? Five signs your house is leaking heatFrom finding draughts to buying a thermal leak detector – there are simple, cost-effective ways to start sorting heat lossHow to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fencesZoe WoodWed 14 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1. Cold draughts around windows, doors and loft hatchesPick a day when there is a good breeze, and heat the house to its usual temperature. Then wander around with a candle or smoke pen (about £20). Alternatively, buy a thermal leak detector. This flashes blue for cold, green for normal and red for warm.2. Water trapped between window panes“Misting or water trapped between the panes of double glazing can point to a failed sealed unit,” says Antony Heath, the marketing and development director at Glevum Windows. “Once the seal has broken, the window may no longer insulate as effectively.”3. Condensation on windowsCondensation on the inside of windows, particularly first thing in the morning, can indicate cold surfaces where heat is escaping, says Oliver Novakovic, technical and innovation director at Barratt Redrow. It can have several causes, including poor ventilation. Older single-glazed windows allow more heat loss, which exacerbates the problem.View image in fullscreenRadiators with surplus air are a sure sign of inefficient heating.Photograph: kelvinjay/Getty Images/iStockphoto4. The heating is always on, but your house still feels coldIf your home struggles to maintain a comfortable temperature, it may be losing heat through walls, floors or the roof. Uneven room temperatures can also be a sign that radiators are not working or heat is escaping faster in some areas. “The better a home is at retaining warmth through good insulation and airtightness, the less energy is needed to keep it comfortable,” Novakovic says.5. Snow melts faster on your roofIf snow melts quickly on your roof while nearby properties remain blanketed – or it is a hotspot for birds – this can be a sign that heat is escaping. An older or uninsulated home can lose 25% of its heat through the roof.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsHousehold billsConsumer affairsEnergy industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vitamin patches have their grip on the wellness industry: but is the fad only skin deep?  | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Experts peel back the evidence to see whether any of the health claims about vitamin patches stick – or whether it’s the placebo effect at work
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Experts peel back the evidence to see whether any of the health claims about vitamin patches stick – or whether it’s the placebo effect at work
Content: ‘One of the big fundamental problems of vitamin patches is that most vitamins are water soluble. What doesn’t get through the skin? Stuff that’s water soluble,’ says Prof Nial Wheate.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘One of the big fundamental problems of vitamin patches is that most vitamins are water soluble. What doesn’t get through the skin? Stuff that’s water soluble,’ says Prof Nial Wheate.Composite: Getty ImagesAntiviralHealth & wellbeingVitamin patches have their grip on the wellness industry: but is the fad only skin deep?Donna LuExperts peel back the evidence to see whether any of the health claims about vitamin patches stick – or whether it’s the placebo effect at workRead more in theAntiviral seriesWed 14 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTShareFeeling fatigued and listless? Searching for an energy boost? Want to improve your mood and motivation? The solution may be, according to a proliferation of online articles and wellness TikToks, not to seek medical advice but to whack on a vitamin patch.Wearers purport to feel more focused or energised when adorned with the patches, some of which look like transparent squares, and others which are cuter and more colourful, resembling stickers or temporary tattoos.The adhesives, also called wellness or supplement patches, contain tiny amounts of vitamins, minerals such as iron and magnesium, as well as other compounds such as caffeine and ginger extract.Magnesium is essential for health. But can supplements really help with digestion, muscle pain, anxiety and sleep? | AntiviralRead moreDo any of the claims about vitamin patches stick, or are they merely a Band-Aid solution?Can vitamins actually get through the skin?Very few medicines are available as patches, says Nial Wheate, a professor of pharmaceutical chemistry at Macquarie University. “There’s a reason we don’t have paracetamol and aspirin patches.”The key issue is that the skin is a very effective protective barrier: the structure of its outermost layer, the stratum corneum, blockswater, bacteria and most drugsfrom getting through.“It doesn’t mean the right medicines can’t be delivered that way,” Wheate says. “The things that do get through the skin tend to be what we call lipophilic” – fat soluble. For this reason, skin patches are often used to deliver opioid medications, hormone replacement therapy and nicotine, which are all lipophilic.For example, the advantage of a nicotine skin patch for smoking cessation, Wheate says, is that it gives a slow, sustained release “where you’re continuously releasing that drug into the bloodstream”, as opposed to an oral tablet which leads to a higher initial spike of the drug and more rapid clearance from the body.However, he says: “One of the big fundamental problems of vitamin patches is that most vitamins are water soluble. What doesn’t get through the skin? Stuff that’s water soluble.”Some wellness patches market themselves as bypassing the “unwanted side effects” of oral supplements – constipation is a commonly reported side-effect of iron tablets, for example.But iron, and other vitamins and minerals commonly used in patches, such as vitamin B12 and magnesium – cannot properly cross the skin barrier.And if any amountdoesmake it through the skin, “the other issue is the amount of drug you can load into a patch is very, very small”, Wheate points out. “So what you get is microdosing of any of those vitamins.“The biggest effect [wearers] would get is a placebo effect.”One patch available in Australia, marketed for immunity, for example, contains 1mg of vitamin C. The clinical signs of scurvy, by comparison, appear whendaily vitamin C intakedrops below 7 to 8mg.More ‘bang for your buck’ in the fruit and veg sectionThe average person can get theirrecommended intakeof vitamins (such as vitamin C and vitamin B12) and minerals (elements such as iron, zinc and iodine) from diet alone, without the need for supplements – in oral or patch form.“There’s definitely cases when people need [supplemental] vitamins and minerals,” says Clare Collins, professor of nutrition and dietetics at the University of Newcastle. This includes people with specific deficiencies, such as those with low iron or vegans who are at higher risk of vitamin B12 deficiency. Pregnant women, too, have a higher nutritional requirement for folate, iodine and vitamin D.“The nutrients that are more likely to be absorbed [through the skin] are ones that dissolve in fat,” Collins says. “But they don’t necessarily go all the way into your bloodstream, which is why [vitamin patches] are not that effective.”There have been few studies in humans into how well fat-soluble vitamins – vitamins A, D, E and K – are absorbed into the skin, Collins says. Onesmall 2019 studylooked at the effect of multivitamin patches in patients after gastric bypass surgery for weight loss, who are at higher risk of nutrient deficiencies. Patch users, it found, were “more likely to have vitamin D deficiency and lower serum concentration of various vitamins and minerals” than patients taking oral supplements.Multivitamins promise glowing skin, better sleep and a longer life. But who do supplements really benefit? | Donna LuRead more“The patches were not able to replace oral supplements and that’s a very specific group where food intakes are markedly reduced,” Collins says. “In the current day, that would still apply to bariatric surgery, but that would also apply to people taking GLP-1 [weight-loss drugs].”Given the lack of evidence for their effect, Collins suggests people save the money they would otherwise expend on vitamin patches and “spend it in the fruit and veg section … you’ll get more bang for your buck”.Unlike patches, Collins says fresh fruit and vegetables will also provide a variety ofphytonutrients– plant-based chemicals that occur naturally in foods – which have numerous benefits including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. “You get the nutrients that improve your insulin sensitivity, and all the range of fibres that promote bowel health and promote a diverse microbiome.”For people considering a vitamin supplement or a patch, Collins suggests “having a think about what the underlying issues are”.“If you’re just feeling run-down, then go and get yourself a check-up with your GP.”Donna Lu is an assistant editor, climate, environment and science at Guardian AustraliaAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsShare your experienceShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
