title: Winter warmers: 10 of Britain’s best heated lidos | Swimming | The Guardian
description: From an infinity pool with sauna in Scotland to a restored Victorian gem in Bristol, here are 10 great spots where you can swim in comfort year-round
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: From an infinity pool with sauna in Scotland to a restored Victorian gem in Bristol, here are 10 great spots where you can swim in comfort year-round
Content: The leisure centre at Portavadie in Argyll is believed to have the biggest heated outdoor infinity pool in Scotland.Photograph: portavadie.comView image in fullscreenThe leisure centre at Portavadie in Argyll is believed to have the biggest heated outdoor infinity pool in Scotland.Photograph: portavadie.comSwimmingWinter warmers: 10 of Britain’s best heated lidosFrom an infinity pool with sauna in Scotland to a restored Victorian gem in Bristol, here are 10 great spots where you can swim in comfort year-roundRachel DixonWed 14 Oct 2026 03.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortavadie, ArgyllPortavadie, on the banks of Loch Fyne on the west coast of Scotland, was originally earmarked as an oil rig, but plans fell through. Today it is a marina with holiday homes, a restaurant and bar, a gift shop, and a leisure centre with what is believed to be the biggest heated outdoor infinity pool in Scotland. There are also outdoor spa pools and a sauna, an indoor pool and a gym; treatments such as massages and facials are available. The facilities are powered by a woodchip biomass generator, and have views across the loch and over to the Isle of Arran.£14for a90-minute swim, sauna and hot tubBeccles Lido, SuffolkView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Adam White/Beccles LidoSwimmers have long taken dips in the Waveney, and in 1894 an enclosed “bathing place” was dug out of the river at Beccles, a market town on the southern edge of the Broads national park. In 1959, this was replaced by an unheated riverside pool, which 50 years later became a three-pool lido. This year, the pools will be heated to 28C in winter for the first time, initially until 3 January, then, if popular, through to the end of March. The 30-metre main pool has a springboard and slide; there are also toddler and splash pools, a wood-fired sauna and a cafe. The timetable is yet to be finalised but there will be lane swimming, family fun swims and aquacise classes.From£7.40adultsHathersage Swimming Pool, DerbyshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Danny Lawson/PAIn July, the Peak District village of Hathersage celebrated the 90th anniversary of its 30-metre outdoor pool. It was given to the village by a local philanthropist, George Lawrence, who was killed in the Sheffield blitz. The original coke boiler, which heated the water to a maximum of 20C, has been replaced with a modern renewable heating system (temperature at time of writing: 27C). It is open daily year-round – hours are reduced from November to March – with hot poolside showers, and a sauna from October. There are regular night swims with live music, and a cafe serving hot drinks and homemade food.£8 adultsThames Lido, Reading, BerkshireView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Andre PattendenThe riverside pool on King’s Meadow, Reading was fed by the Thames when it opened in 1902, originally for ladies only. It was converted to mains water in the 1950s, closed in the 70s, and finally reopened after a three-year restoration in 2017. Today, the 25-metre pool is heated to 20-24C year-round; there is a hot tub (38-40C), sauna and steam room, and a cold-water drench bucket and “ship funnel” shower. Swimmers can also book a massage. The high-end poolside restaurant opens at 9am for breakfast (homemade granola, bacon butties, Turkish-style eggs) and serves lunch and dinner daily (such as crab tagliatelle or Ibérico pork).From£25 for a two-hour swim, sauna, steam and hot tubChesham Moor, BuckinghamshireView image in fullscreenThe pool at Chesham Moor sports centre is believed to have begun as a deep puddle used for bathing in the 1890s. Today it is a 25-metre spring-fed lido, upgraded in 2023, with a Nasa-designed ionisation unit, which keeps chlorine levels low. It has solar panels and is heated to 27C year-round, although in very cold weather it may be a little cooler. It is open daily for a mix of lane and general swimming, plus aqua fitness sessions and swim masterclasses. There are also outdoor circuit classes and tennis courts, a nearby riverside walk, and a cafe serving hot drinks, sausage rolls, sandwiches and cake.From £7adultsSea Lanes, Brighton, East SussexView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Carlos Jasso/ReutersThis “stepping stone to the sea” opened in 2023: a 50-metre, six-lane, beachfront swimming pool. It is heated to a minimum of 19C year-round. Coaching is available for all levels, from beginners learning to swim to open-water swimmers and triathletes. For a post-training refuel, Fika serves brunch and coffee, Wood x Coal cooks lunch and dinner over fire, and Bison Beer has 14 draught beers plus wine and cocktails. Just four miles along the seafront isSaltdean Lido, a 40-metre, crescent-shaped modernist masterpiece (built in 1938). This winter, it opens only for the month of December, when it is heated to 19C; there is alsoa sauna(run separately).£11.90 adultsskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHampton Pool, LondonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Gee/AlamyBuilt in 1922, this 36-metre pool next to Bushy Park in south-west London is now run by a charity. It is open 365 days a year and heated to a tropical 28C. There is also a 12.5-metre learner pool, gym, fitness classes and Sundeck Cafe (porridge, soup, jacket potatoes), and regular events such as moonlight and festive swims. Londoners are spoiled for choice when it comes to heated outdoor pools – other options includeLondon Fields Lido(50 metres, 24C),Oasis Sports Centrein central London (27.5 metres, 26C and a sauna),Charlton Lido(50 metres, 22C),Pools on the Parkin Richmond (33 metres, 25C) andPark Road Lidoin Crouch End (50 metres, 22-24C).Taking a deep dive in Helsinki’s subterranean cityRead moreLido Ponty, Rhondda Cynon TafView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Ceri Breeze/AlamyThe National Lido of Wales, in Pontypridd, opened in 1927 – swimmers over the years include a young Tom Jones. It reopened in 2015 after a £6.3m restoration, and today has three heated pools: a main pool, an activity pool and a splash pool. The pools are heated to 28C in the summer, but in winter the heat is turned down to a bracing 14-15C. These cool-water swims are avaiable at weekends from 24 October to 28 November, for ages 16 and over. There are hot outdoor and indoor showers, and heated indoor changing rooms. Some swimmers may prefer to wait for the Boxing Day and New Year’s Day swims, when the heat is cranked back up to a steamy 28C.£4 adultsBristol LidoView image in fullscreenThis Victorian outdoor swimming pool opened in 1850, closed in 1990 and was almost redeveloped into flats. Instead, it was bought and restored by Arne Ringner, the businessman who later bought Thames Lido (see above), and reopened in 2008. The 24-metre pool is heated to 20-24C year-round. There is a sauna, steam room and hot tub, and a poolside restaurant and bar that runs regular supper clubs. Upcoming events include synchronised swimming shows, Christmas lunches and dinners (three courses £35/£50) and a New Year’s Eve party (£135 for a two-hour swim and five-course dinner).From£25for atwo-hour session – swim, sauna, steam and hot tubFaversham Pools, KentFaversham Pools comprises three heated outdoor pools – a 33-metre lido with three diving boards (1, 3 and 5 metres), a fun rapids pool and a toddler pool with slides – plus a 25-metre indoor pool and whirlpool bath. While the smaller pools are open only from April to September, the lido is open year-round, albeit with reduced hours from September to April (4-7pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays and 8-11am on Sundays). These winter outdoor sessions are lane swimming only, for over-16s.Tides Cafeserves warming homemade food, such as soup (perhaps Thai butternut squash or Egyptian lentil), toasties, macaroni cheese and curries.£8.50adultsExplore more on these topicsSwimmingFitnessDay tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: worried about hair loss? Here’s a treatment that actually works | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Many products claim to stop age-related thinning, but this one really works
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: Many products claim to stop age-related thinning, but this one really works
Content: Spectacles courtesy of Cubitts.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSpectacles courtesy of Cubitts.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sali Hughes on beautyBeautySali Hughes on beauty: worried about hair loss? Here’s a treatment that actually worksMany products claim to stop age-related thinning, but this one really worksSali HughesWed 14 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m 51, perimenopausal, and somewhere between the newly distended stomach and the urge to pick fights with fellow passengers on public transport (why have people stopped wearing headphones?), came hair thinning. Brilliant.It’s not as though I could claim an abundance in the first place. However, hair-loss products were at least something I could explore professionally, so I tested and tested, figuring there must be a column in there somewhere. There wasn’t.In the end, I did what I’d previously told my closest friends to do: I signed up toHair+Me, a £34.99 monthly subscription service, staffed by clinicians dispensing proved hair-loss medications such as Minoxidil (prescribed across genders) and Finasteride and Dutasteride (for biological men only) in tablet or ointment form.double quotation markAfter two months, new hair is visibly growing – as well as on my chin, so I’ve upped my tweezingI knew it could work. I’d got my best friend, Cait, on to it when she, who’d always prided herself on an enormous thatch, stopped hair-washing because the sight of large clumps on the shower floor ruined the next week. She signed up, uploaded her photos and their nightly tablets (topical ointment is not usually prescribed to pet owners as it’s toxic to some animals), performed near miracles. Within a couple of weeks, baby hairs were forming, the shedding had slowed to normal and Cait was herself once more. Ditto two other girlfriends who followed my same advice.Aside from my very different base level (my hair has always been thin and flat), my trajectory on Hair+Me/Minoxidil has been identical. After two months, new hair is visibly growing (as well as on my chin, a common side-effect, so I’ve upped my tweezing).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: the best undereye concealers for over-35sRead moreI tell you all this not by way of medical advice (I’m not qualified to give it), but to explain thatreal, evidence-backed help – not rosemary shampoos and dubious tech gadgets promoted uncritically online – is out there. Even for free via your GP, if s/he is sympathetic. In which case, my congratulations. But with appointment times shaved to the bone (assuming they can be secured at all), it may save time and tears to explore a paid subscription for the same treatment.Anxiety around hair loss is not some frivolous, vain “champagne problem”. It can be a misery at a time when our plates are already too full. Even friends who barely wear moisturiser, let alone engage with any non-invasive cosmetic treatments such as Botox, have found age-related thinning to be their line in the sand and opted to shed the guilt, not the hair.Explore more on these topicsBeautySali Hughes on beautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Children are naturally drawn to beauty’: the head of the ‘Issey Miyake’ preschool on their pleated uniforms | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Ms Lam Montessori’s head of school reveals teachers wear a different Japanese designer after their chic clothes drew online envy
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: Ms Lam Montessori’s head of school reveals teachers wear a different Japanese designer after their chic clothes drew online envy
Content: Teachers at the Brooklyn school went viral after a Redditor questioned its policy that staff wear pleated uniforms.Photograph: Ms Lam MontessoriView image in fullscreenTeachers at the Brooklyn school went viral after a Redditor questioned its policy that staff wear pleated uniforms.Photograph: Ms Lam MontessoriFashion‘Children are naturally drawn to beauty’: the head of the ‘Issey Miyake’ preschool on their pleated uniformsMs Lam Montessori’s head of school reveals teachers wear a different Japanese designer after their chic clothes drew online envyHannah MarriottWed 14 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Does anyone know what the deal is Ms Lam Montessori … and why all their employees wear Issey Miyake … every day … I’m confused and a bit jealous,” asked one commenter on the Williamsburg subreddit last week, sparking a unexpected viral moment for a chain of Brooklyn Montessori preschools.The poster was responding to photos on the Montessori’s website of the teachers’ uniforms: raspberry, cobalt and apple green dresses in plissé fabric. They appeared to be from the Pleats Please line by Japanese designer Issey Miyake. It seemed an avant-garde choice for staff posing in front of the abachi and blond wood toys of their preschool classroom.On X, those pictures were screen grabbed and viewed 3.5m times, with most comments reading along the lines of “only in Brooklyn”.So was it Issey Miyake?Over email from Taiwan, Ms Lam Montessori head of school, Stephanie Woo – a vision in chartreuse pleated fabric and matching hexagonal-framed glasses on the nursery’s website – explains that the dresses are actually by a more affordable Japanese designer, Yamasaki Takashi (they are priced around a 10th of the $700 one might pay for a Pleats Please frock), and are worn at all of the company’s locations. Ms Lam is a Mandarin immersion school and was originally founded in Taipei, Taiwan, where it has 14 branches, as well as its five in Brooklyn.double quotation markWe believe young children should be surrounded by beautyStephanie WooWoo is herself a “huge fan” of Issey Miyake, and owns “a couple of pieces that I bring out for special events at the school”. She adds: “Issey Miyake clothing is of course stunning, but we chose Yamasaki for its understated designs, comfort, durability and price. Those qualities made it a particularly good fit for everyday life in our classrooms,” she writes, adding that the clothes wash well and “hold their color and shape beautifully. Even after we’ve washed it 100 times, they still come out of the dryer looking much the same.”She adds that the outfits were originally her mother’s idea – the original Ms Lam – who, according to the company’s website, was the first person to bring Montessori to Taiwan. Staff in Taiwan have been wearing them for 12 years and in Brooklyn for eight. Uniforms are important, she says, working with children from the age of one to six: “They help a young child recognize, even on a busy campus, this adult can help me.”One of the reasons the Issey Miyake-esque outfits so delighted the internet is that the Pleats Please line, which launched in 1993, is having a fashion resurgence.View image in fullscreenModels walk the runway during the Issey Miyake womenswear spring/summer 2023 show as part of Paris fashion week on 20 September 2022.Photograph: Richard Bord/Getty ImagesOne particular garment – the Madame T stole, a large piece of plissé fabric with a diamond-shaped neck hole, which comes with an instruction booklet for the many ways it can be folded around the body – has recently become asocial media fascination. In August, the shopping platform Lystranked itamong the hottest products of the summer, and reported a 100% rise in demand for Issey Miyake quarter-on-quarter.That said, Issey Miyake – which was launched in 1970 in Tokyo – and its more affordable Pleats Please line has never really been uncool. Miyake was the first of the wave of Japanese designers – followed by Yohji Yamamoto and Rei Kawakubo’s Comme des Garçons – to break through into European fashion.‘It gives Shein’: how did polyester become the world’s most-hated material?Read moreMiyake developed his then revolutionary near-permanent pleats in the late 1980s, by constructing garments first, flat, at a much larger size than they would eventually fold down to, then heat-pleating afterwards. Most Pleats Please garments are 100% polyester, and their popularity comes despite a largerpolyester backlash. Unlike fast-fashion polyester, Pleats Please are high quality, the designs timeless – and the construction of the garments makes specific use of polyester’s thermoplastic properties to hold shape, rather than using cheap polyester to make throwaway knockoffs of natural fibers.Pleats Please’s practical, technical and arty associations – the focus is on the garment, and its own silhouette, rather than the body beneath – has made it popular with accomplished creative women for decades. Zaha Hadid, Solange Knowles, Meryl Streep, Tessa Thompson and Joni Mitchell are among its longtime fans, while Lorde, who wore a neon pink Pleats Please crop top at Lollapalooza Doja Cat have been spotted wearing the designer more recently.In the west, says Dr Sasha Raspopina, the course leader for the fashion marketing and journalism BA at London Metropolitan University, Pleats Please has a kind of “if you know you know” appeal. She has noticed its adoption in east London among young people, who are perhaps “trying to signal that they are creative”. Given that context, Raspopina thought the Montessori image was a meme at first because the garment seemed to speak of an “alternate universe” to that of the kindergarten teacher.View image in fullscreenMeryl Streep wears a pleated Issey Miyake jacket at a Into the Woods screening gala in London in 2015.Photograph: David M Benett/WireImageThe use of a Pleats Please-inspired garment may land differently for an east Asian audience, says Prof Wessie Ling, a visiting professor of transcultural arts and design at the University of Bologna (who, as a fashion scholar, knew the dresses weren’t genuine Miyake the moment she saw the photo: “the materials, and how it drapes on the body isn’t quite there,” she says).She says that the link between Japanese design and Taiwan is very deep, given the colonial history (Taiwan was under Japanese colonial rule from 1895 until 1945). In east Asia more broadly, she says, there is a profound “admiration for Japanese designers, specifically the first generation of Japanese designers”. Miyake was the first to open a boutique in Paris, in the 1970s, nearly 10 years before Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto. This was at a time when “absolutely no other non-white designers made it into the fashion capital. So he represents something.” In east Asia, she says. Miyake is “the signature Japanese designer” and the first designer brand a woman would turn to if they reached executive level.Ling had not heard of the brandYamasaki Takashi, but she has noticed many younger, independent east Asian designers, including those based in South Korea and Vietnam, recently using pleats similar to Miyake’s. She doesn’t necessarily consider them to be copycats. “Obviously it is a kind of Miyake because it’s pleats – but they also create different patterns, colors and silhouettes, and they are putting some thought into the pleats they are trying to create.”As Woo adds over email, the aesthetic of the garments certainly matters, even at school: “The truth is, we believe young children should be surrounded by beauty. From birth to age six, children have what Montessori calls the ‘Absorbent Mind’ – they effortlessly absorb so much from their surroundings,” she says. “They are naturally drawn to beauty, and by making it part of their daily lives, we hope to nurture their appreciation for it and their desire to care for the spaces and things around them.”Explore more on these topicsFashionSchoolsSchool brandingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: I learned to read and write – at 42 | Books | The Guardian
description: I had worked for 25 years, married and started a family. But a crisis at the supermarket reminded me there was something missing from my life
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: I had worked for 25 years, married and started a family. But a crisis at the supermarket reminded me there was something missing from my life
Content: Peter Lloyd with his Read Easy coach, Alison Hollinrake.Photograph: Supplied imageView image in fullscreenPeter Lloyd with his Read Easy coach, Alison Hollinrake.Photograph: Supplied imageA moment that changed meBooksA moment that changed me: I learned to read and write – at 42I had worked for 25 years, married and started a family. But a crisis at the supermarket reminded me there was something missing from my lifePeter Lloyd as told toAmmar KaliaWed 14 Oct 2026 01.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2021, at 42 years old, I had the reading age of a four-year-old. I had spent my life up to that point not being able to read and write, navigating the world with careful planning and the help of my wife. During the Covid lockdowns, however, the world turned upside down and my usual way of going through life exploded. My wife was home-schooling our 10-year-old son and I was ashamed to not be able to help; my usual work as a lorry driver was put on hold, and even simple tasks like shopping had become incredibly difficult.I became overwhelmed one day in the supermarket aisles trying to find a milk that my wife and son could drink, since they are both allergic to dairy and soy. I worried I might poison them. It hit me that the way I had been living my life previously could not continue.I didn’t want to tell my wife, because she was dealing with enough already, but once I got home it just came out that I was struggling. She then told me she had found an organisation that might be able to help me. Since leaving school, I had tried multiple times to learn how to read – nothing had worked. I didn’t think it was worth trying again but she convinced me to do it for her. That moment changed my entire life.I was born partially deaf, and things were difficult growing up in Lancashire. I could hear people talking to me but I often became overwhelmed by noises, which meant I couldn’t follow what the teacher was saying at school. At six years old I was transferred to a special school, but there, things got worse. Each student was dealing with their own special educational needs or behavioural issues, so it was even harder to concentrate. At the same time, I had several operations on my ears, which meant my hearing came back, but by then I had been told to sit at the back of the class and keep quiet. When I left school at 16, I had no qualifications, I had a bad stammer from anxiety and I couldn’t read or write.I managed to get a job working on a nearby farm through a friend, and after a year I decided to go to college to learn how to read. My parents discouraged me as they thought it was better I earn a living and contribute to the household costs while I was still living at home. Thankfully, I was able to pass my driving test because there wasn’t a theory portion and I could memorise what the road signs meant. I realised I was good at visualising and could map out a route in my head.Eventually, when I moved out, I applied for my lorry licence. Using those visualising skills, I began working as a lorry driver at 22 years old. I got by through memorising motorway numbers and routes. The invention of talking satnavs was a great help. Yet I still couldn’t read.In 2010, I was convinced by a friend to try college again but, once more, it didn’t work – I didn’t have the foundations of literacy to understand what they were trying to teach. However, it was there that I met my wife. Once we were together, it was a huge relief for me, as she would step in to help whenever reading or writing was involved. I didn’t feel judged by her.We carried on like this, working as a team, for the next decade until Covid hit and I reached crisis point. After the milk incident, my wife suggested I get in touch with the Read Easy charity, andI organised an initial meeting with one of its volunteers, Alison.I had a meltdown before we even met, since I couldn’t figure out how to pay at the car park, but once I finally made it inside, Alison put me completely at ease. She said we would need to start small but that she would be by my side, working through a series of reading manuals created by the Shannon Trust.View image in fullscreen‘ I can’t believe how beautiful reading is’ … Peter Lloyd.Photograph: Supplied imageMy goal was to read the first Harry Potter book, since I had heard they were wonderful and I could identify with Harry as an outsider because of my deafness. Over the next three years we met twice each week and the world completely opened up to me. I finished the Harry Potter book, and even though I missed out on reading to my son when he was younger, we can now do other things together – such as cooking, because I can read and follow a recipe he’s chosen.Today, I’m an ambassador for Read Easy, since I think it’s important to encourage others in my situation to seek help, especially men who might be too ashamed to talk. I also want to take my GCSE in English and I’d like to change careers to keep helping others. I have three books on the go at the moment – I can’t believe how beautiful reading is!Peter’s story features inThe Book That Changed My Life, which airs on 14 October on BBC Two and iPlayerExplore more on these topicsBooksA moment that changed meShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: This is Dorset’s worst-located stone circle – but Nine Stones is well worth a visit | Environment | The Guardian
description: Winterbourne Abbas: These bronze age megaliths have hosted rituals and seen off electricity pylons. Today they endure by the side of an A-road
Author: Sara Hudston
Headline: Winterbourne Abbas: These bronze age megaliths have hosted rituals and seen off electricity pylons. Today they endure by the side of an A-road
Content: The Nine Stones at Winterbourne Abbas, Dorset.Photograph: Sara HudstonView image in fullscreenThe Nine Stones at Winterbourne Abbas, Dorset.Photograph: Sara HudstonCountry diaryEnvironmentCountry diary: This is Dorset’s worst-located stone circle – but Nine Stones is well worth a visitWinterbourne Abbas: These bronze age megaliths have hosted rituals and seen off electricity pylons. Today they endure by the side of an A-roadSara HudstonWed 14 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 03.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Nine Stones at Winterbourne Abbas have an inglorious setting. Hard by the A35, there are only slim iron railings and a small ditch to shield the circle from the heavy traffic rumbling west. And for about six months of the year the ditch flows with water (the winter bourne), often overspilling and flooding the road.Yet the surroundings used to be even less picturesque. Until a few years ago, a line of high‑voltage electricity pylons looped across the valley, humming and sizzling a few hundred metres from the monument.In 2022, the lines were buried out of sight. Today, the path to the circle crosses the underground cables, passing two small enclosures, each containing a pair of grey metal cabinets. Stern and mysterious, connected to hidden power, these modern installations echo the bronze age megaliths beyond.View image in fullscreenA close-up of the Nine Stones stone circle, showing chunks of pink flint, an unusual colour caused by iron elements present when the stone formed.Photograph: Sara HudstonThecircle itselfsits in a wooded glade, which would be peaceful were it not for the lorries clattering by. The individual stones are markedly different from each other, varying in size from knee-high to 1.5m, some squat, some broad, and one like a tall, cloaked figure. An old beech tree stump, rotted and streaked with moss, acts as a tenth, more temporary, marker.From a distance, the monoliths look like typical sandstone sarsens found across southern chalk downland, grey and slightly bulbous. Viewed up close, a surprise reveals itself. The largest are made of a conglomerate of pebbles, flint and quartz held together with fine-grained sediment. It’s hard to believe that this mix – known locally as “puddingstone” – occurred naturally because it looks uncannily like a rough aggregate stirred into concrete.Some of the chunks of flint are flushed pink, an unusual effect caused by the presence of iron elements. The colour is diffused through layers of rock flakes, like strawberry juice frozen in ice. This oddity offers a clue about where the sarsens came from. Less than two miles away is theValley of Stones, a scattering of large boulders left at the end of the last ice age, many of which contain the same rosy flint nodules. Material from there was used locally in other ritual settings from the Neolithic onwards.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsEnvironmentCountry diaryRural affairsHistoryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine is littered with landmines on a scale last seen in Vietnam. How can they be removed? | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Faced with deadlier threats, demining groups are coming up with new ways of working using drones and AI
Author: Artem Mazhulin
Headline: Faced with deadlier threats, demining groups are coming up with new ways of working using drones and AI
Content: A Halo Trust deminer working in a field.Faced with deadlier threats, demining groups are coming up with new ways of working using drones and AIByAmy Hawkinsin Kharkiv region. Photographs byJulia KochetovaWed 14 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCrouched over on her hands and knees in a field of weeds, Olena Kabanova is digging into the ground. With a shovel and a steady hand, the 58-year-old digs out a neat square around the spot where a mine detector has sensed a suspicious object.Four years ago, this field in easternUkrainewas occupied by Russian soldiers. Now back under Ukrainian control, it is littered with landmines. Civilians such as Kabanova are trying to make the land usable again.Landminesare a scourge of conflict zones. Littered across contested territory, they leave land unusable for years after a war has ended. Removing them is an expensive and dangerous job. And the use of long-range drones in Ukraine, which is often described as the most mine-contaminated country in the world, is increasing the scale of the problem.View image in fullscreenDifferent types of ammunition presented at the Halo Trust office in Kharkiv.“What we’re now seeing is the massive increase in the use of drone-delivered munitions,” says Paul Heslop, senior mine action advisor for the United Nations in Ukraine. “What already was a very high-intensity battle area is now potentially, through the use of drones on both sides, becoming a much wider area of contamination and a scale that we haven’t seen since the Americans were dropping cluster munitions on the Ho Chi Minh trail.”View image in fullscreenOlena Kabanova, a deminer with the Halo Trust, working at the site in the Kharkiv region.The task of clearing landmines from Ukraine is replete with challenges. Drone and missile attacks make working outdoors unsafe; humanitarian workers are sometimes directly targeted. And newer, deadlier threats are also appearing. They include the POM-3, a small cylindrical mine used by Russian forces that could be mistaken for an abandoned vacuum flask. It is detonated by the vibrations of approaching footsteps.POM-3 mines mean there are “specific villages that we just completely avoid”, says Anda Riza, a unit commander of the Halo Trust, the largest international humanitarian demining organisation in Ukraine, which employs Kabanova in the field in Kharkiv. The types of landmines are “constantly developing and evolving”, says Valeriia Shumska, Riza’s colleague.View image in fullscreenValeriia Shumska, an operations support manager with the Halo Trust, at the site in the Kharkiv region.But the technological innovation that is emerging from the conflict is also helping deminers to come up with new ways of working, which they hope are quicker and safer than the traditional hands-and-knees approach. The advances are being supported by the $1.5bn funding that has poured into Ukraine’s demining sector since the start of the full-scale invasion.Take Kabanova’s job. Digging out a patch of land could take up to 45 minutes. But a new machine can do it in five. Called the DMR-7, it is a small, tank-like vehicle fitted with a hosepipe that shoots out jet flows of compressed air.The tank is operated by a human using a remote controller who stands at a safe distance away. The operator manoeuvres the tank into place and then, with a loud mechanical whirring and plumes of dirt billowing skywards, the DMR-7 uses the force of compressed air to blast away a small patch of soil. It is a bulky, expensive alternative to a shovel, but it’s one that deminers hope can make one of the most dangerous parts of the demining process quicker and safer.View image in fullscreenUsing a remote control, an operator moves a grenade found at the demining site.The DMR-7 is just one of a host of new pieces of kit that the Halo Trust is experimenting with in Ukraine. Other technologies include AI-powered image analysis, ground-penetrating radar and devices that can detect explosive material, not just metal.Just as drones have transformed the battlefield, they have also created new opportunities for humanitarians. Before 2022, much of Halo’s surveillance work – looking for signs of explosives – was done with binoculars and maps. Now it is done with drones, and satellite imagery, which can be analysed with the help of AI.But war has also led to innovations in anti-drone technology. Drone jamming systems, used by both Russian and Ukrainian forces, can interfere with humanitarian work. Halo has lost several drones to jamming and spoofing attacks.And the advances in new technology are not spread equally between providers.In a field adjacent to one that Kabanova is working in, staff from the state emergency services are also clearing mines. Under the glare of the late summer sun, Mykyta Shulzhenko, the head of the mechanised demining unit, says his colleagues have started using drones for surveillance. But they are not yet able to use AI to analyse the drone-captured imagery. “I really hope this kind of technology will be implemented soon in our work,” he says.View image in fullscreenMykyta Shulzhenko, the head of the mechanised demining unit of the state emergency service of Ukraine, at a demining site in the Kharkiv region.The Halo Trust alone spent nearly £50m in Ukraine in the year to 31 March 2025, dwarfing the state’s annual budget of £28.6m for a programme to clear agricultural land of mines and unexploded ordnance. And there are dozens of other demining organisations with overlapping responsibilities and approaches. Responsibility for the sector is split across multiple government agencies. Attempts to reform the country’s mine action law to bring it in line with international standards have faltered.Ihor Bezkaravainyi, a deputy economy minister who leads the country’s work on demining, wants to streamline the policymaking process to create one cabinet-level office to oversee the whole sector. But progress has been slow. Asked why, he offers a weary shrug: “Because, people.”View image in fullscreenIhor Bezkaravainyi, a deputy economy minister, leads work on demining in Ukraine.“When we’re talking about a new law, it will mean that some government bodies will lose responsibility, and, they think, power,” Bezkaravainyi says.One person who has worked in Ukraine’s demining sector puts it more bluntly: “The biggest barrier to demining Ukraine is the government of Ukraine.”Bezkaravainyi says: “When we’re talking about an ordinary situation with mine action … the conflict has ended, and the government does not exist … in Ukraine, it’s the opposite situation.”That leads to a host of regulatory and bureaucratic barriers. For example, deminers are often prevented from using vehicles that are driven directly by a person, with health and safety standards requiring that the vehicles are operated remotely. Riza says: “We know for a fact that doing it remotely is much slower than having a person in the cab. That continues to be our biggest challenge.”View image in fullscreenA deminer operating remotely behind a protective shield.Heslop argues that the Ukrainian authorities are overly broad in their categorisation of land as being contaminated by mines, an approach that risks wasting time and money on clearing land that wasn’t dangerous in the first place. “Just because it was occupied by the Russians doesn’t necessarily mean it was contaminated,” he says. “Land is only contaminated if it’s got fucking explosives in it.”But deminers across the sector agree that technological advances will accelerate their ability to release Ukraine’s richly fertile land for civilian use at a much faster rate than has been possible in the past.“This is the cutting edge of technology,” says Heslop. “This is where the humanitarian mine action sector is going through the biggest pivot in the last 30 years.”Additional research by Illia Dyadik and Artem MazhulinThis article was amended on 14 October 2026. Paul Heslop is senior mine action advisor for the United Nations in Ukraine, not programme manager for mine action at the UN Development Programme in Ukraine as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineLandminesWeapons technologyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state | Global development | The Guardian
description: Drawing on dozens of interviews with intelligence and police officers across two continents, a Guardian investigation reveals the murderous cost of our insatiable appetite for cocaine
Author: Mark Townsend
Headline: Drawing on dozens of interviews with intelligence and police officers across two continents, a Guardian investigation reveals the murderous cost of our insatiable appetite for cocaine
Content: Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian DesignBloodlinesGlobal developmentHow Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco stateDrawing on dozens of interviews with intelligence and police officers across two continents, a Guardian investigation reveals the murderous cost of our insatiable appetite for cocaineRead more:Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’Explainer:What is state capture and why does it matter?Supported byAbout this contentMark TownsendWed 14 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTShareAs abductions go, few have been more brazen. Alan Jalloh was with two friends outside Goodies supermarket, frantic as usual with late afternoon shoppers. Rush hour in downtown Freetown, Sierra Leone’s capital, was under way with familiar gusto.A black Toyota Rav4 forced its way through the Peninsula highway traffic. Witnesses describe burly white men leaping out, yanking on balaclavas. Jalloh, 40, seemed to freeze. As did his two friends, one a famous Freetown footballer. All three were dragged into the waiting SUV. None of them have been seen since.Two days later, on 25 October 2025, another three men disappeared. Within a week, nine people had been seized from the city’s streets, most in broad daylight. They were dismembered, police sources were told. At least one was beheaded. An officer investigating Jalloh’s abduction, says: “They were exterminated to hide the truth.”No bodies have been found.Five months after Jalloh disappeared, an ageing cargoship, the Arconian, left Freetown. By May, it was navigating savage seas 100 miles off the coast of Morocco when Spanish civil guards boarded. Lucas Fernández*, clutching his assault rifle on the ship’s lower deck, stumbled across figures in the Arconian’s darkened cargo hold.View image in fullscreenThe largest cocaine seizure ever, taken from the Arconian by the Spanish civil guard in May.Photograph: Courtesy Guardia CivilFernández raised his gun, finger on the trigger. A man pointed an assault rifle back at him. Time stood still. Fernández says the man became agitated, yelling in English, incomprehensible above the storm outside. “It was crazy,” Fernández says.Within minutes, he and his fellow officers had disarmed six gunmen found hiding in the bowels of the ship. Nearby, were 1,279 bales of cocaine wrapped in plastic; weighing between 30 and 45 tonnes, it isthe largest amountof the drug ever seized.Cocaine bales are lifted out of the Arconian’s hold and lined up on the dockSeventeen days later, the audience at Oxford University rose to applaud the guest speaker. Julius Maada Bio had nailed it once again.His address– eulogising robust leadership – was the latest in a whirlwind year for the president of Sierra Leone.The chair of Ecowas – theEconomic Union of West African States, a region home to more than 400 million people, Bio is among the most influential African voices in the UN. The EU sees Bio as one of its most reliable allies in Africa and has a long history of showering the impoverished country with aidstretching back more than 45 years.But the most important figure in Sierra Leone is not this ambitious politician, but the man who ordered the abduction of Jalloh; the man responsible for the Arconian’s monumental cocaine stash. A man calledJos Leijdekkers. He also happens to be Bio’s son-in-law.What is state capture and why does it matter?Read moreAt 35, Leijdekkers isEurope’s pre-eminent cocaine baron. Intelligence assessments credit the Dutchman with importing volumes vast enough to repeatedly crash Europe’s cocaine market. Last year, he halved the drug’s wholesale price. Multiple intelligence sources confirm he has also transformed Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco state.“It is state capture by a criminal network on a scale never seen,” says a western official.View image in fullscreenPresident Julius Maada Bio delivering his address on African leadership at the 2026 Oxford University Africa Society conference in May.Photograph: Courtesy of Julius Maada BioAt least 14 people have been killed inside Sierra Leone on Leidjekkers’ orders. High-ranking police are believed to have been murdered on his say-so. Officers have fled the country fearing they will be next.“If you get in his way, he wipes you out,” says an intelligence source.Like most, they spoke on condition of anonymity, aware of Leidjekkers’ capacity to reach those who cross him.Sierra Leone’s fate is a tale of western duplicity. Despite detailed intelligence of the extraordinary volumes of cocaine being exported toEurope, the EU continued to woo Bio and his government. The UN did the same: overlooking its own evidence.And intelligence sources warn that Leijdekkers’ network is rapidly expanding. “The entire westAfricaregion is at risk,” says a Dutch official.Leijdekkers’ prodigious transcontinental network brings deadly violence.Dozens of his gunmen descended on a sleepy Dutch village last month intent on retribution. A European police source said: “We’ve had cocaine disputes before, but nothing like this. We’ve entered a new era.”View image in fullscreenCCTV footage of masked and armed men in Overasselt, a village near the Dutch-German border, in what transpired to be an attack on a warehouse by Leijdekkers’ gang.Photograph: HandoutThe first recorded sighting of Leijdekkers in west Africa came in October 2022. A six-vehicle convoy thundered down Aberdeen Road, towards Lumley beach, leaving Freetown traffic police baffled. No one had briefed they were expecting VIPs. “‘The convoy was bigger than our president’s,” says one officer.Unaware of Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker, Freetown police were sufficiently concerned to begin surveillance on the mysterious convoy, which had stopped outside theSky Bar, a nightlife institution in the city.At 4am, the group were trailed to a waterfront house near Hamilton beach. There, the covert surveillance team were stunned: revellers included their own bosses.At the time, western intelligence agencies had no idea of Leijdekkers’ whereabouts. One of Europe’smost wanted menhad simply vanished. For years, authorities had tracked his rise in the Dutch underworld, watching how the local hitman from the well-heeled town of Prinsenbeek accrued key contacts for transatlantic cocaine shipments.View image in fullscreenA poster issued by Europol in 2022 appealing for information that would lead to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers.Photograph: EU Most WantedWhen Dutch intelligence traced Leijdekkers to Sierra Leone in 2024, he had created something remarkable: a sprawling cocaine empire from scratch.“He’s very adept at adaptation, cultivating ties,” says an official. “A new country, but he won over its most influential people.”That included marrying the president’s daughter, Agnes Bio, and starting a family. Sierra Leone’s top officials partied with the moneyed new guy. Immigration chiefs secured him a diplomatic passport. The person whose job it was to investigate cocaine traffickers became a drinking buddy.Leijdekkers’ wealth corrupted. According to intelligence, he was generating a $150m (£113m) monthly profit – greater than the running cost of Sierra Leone’s entire state.Hundreds of people were on his payroll, say sources, including senior military and police figures. But what Leijdekkers coveted most was Freetown’s seaport: the Queen Elizabeth II Quay, perfectly sited between cocaine-producing South America and Europe’s booming markets.View image in fullscreenCovertly filmed footage of Leijdekkers at Lor restaurant in Freetown attending the birthday party of Alusine Kanneh, the former chief immigration officer of Sierra Leone. Kanneh was later sacked by the president.Photograph: HandoutIn August 2023, his wife’s uncle, Yankuba Bio, became head of the port. Yankuba Bio denies a close relationship with “any individual called or identified as Jos Leijdekkers”.Sources, though, say port officials on Leijdekkers’s payroll make $2,000 a month – more than 30 times thenational average.In January 2025,the Dutch sent an extradition request to Sierra Leone for the fugitive, who had been sentenced in absentia to more than 100 years in prison for crimes including attempted murder.Sierra Leone denied knowing the man. For Leijdekkers, it was a defining moment: he had state protection. His confidence culminated in the arrival into Freetown’s port on 18 April of the Arconian, a green cargo vessel the length of a football pitch. Over the next four days, about 30 tonnes of cocaine were hauled onboard, according to western intelligence.“From experience, the maximum you can hide is eight tonnes. Thirty tonnes says you’re operating in plain sight,” says a UN agent. Yankuba Bio says such claims are “false, completely untrue and without foundation” adding that the port “does not engage in or facilitate the export” of cocaine.View image in fullscreenFreetown’s industrial port, perfectly sited between cocaine-producing South America and Europe’s booming markets.Photograph: Amazing Aerial/AlamyOn 26 April, a cryptic tip-off electrified European investigators. An unidentified vessel had left west Africa carrying 18 tonnes of cocaine, the second-largest such cargo identified in Europe.Within 70 hours, the Arconian had been identified. At 8pm on 1 May, with the vessel pitching in brutal, black seas, Fernández, of Spain’s civil guardcentral operational unit, was first onboard.Having arrested the 23-strong Filipino crew, the officer spotted a gun lying on the deck. “We started to search more deeply,” says Fernández.After his team stumbled across the six-strong paramilitary detail guarding the cocaine, it became chillingly evident the gunmen had orders to kill anyone who threatened Leijdekkers’ drugs. They had no idea Fernández was a police officer.Route of the Arconian from Sierra Leone“They thought we were an organisation come to rob the drugs,” he says. “It was very tense. Anyone – them, us – might have fired.”It took interminable seconds for Leijdekkers’ men to appreciate the truth. “They knew then it would be worse to open fire.”The Arconian seizure shattered previous understanding of cocaine trafficking. Firstly, Leijdekkers appeared certain that his €812m (£687m) cargo would reach Europe. No attempt was made to conceal the drugs. “There was a 60-metre-long corridor full of it,” says Fernández.Map of the route of the ArconianSuch nonchalance corroborated intelligence assessments that Leijdekkers had repeatedly flooded Europe with shipments, utilising a vast narco fleet and driving the wholesale cocaine price to a record low.In the weeks before the raid, the Arconian completely changed its identity. Analysis for the Guardian by the maritime AI companyWindwardtracked at least three “suspicious” vessels from Freetown in the months before the Arconian. All rebranded themselves before leaving Sierra Leone.In January this year, a cargo boat changed its registration details just before arriving in Freetown. After a month, it left for an unspecified destination. On 15 March, the vessel loitered off the Canary Islands for four hours. Investigators say the Arconian intended to linger off the Spanish archipelago, offloading the cocaine to aflotilla of speedboats.View image in fullscreenSpanish police at the port of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Spain, in January, guarding the record seizure of the drug.Photograph: Ramón de la Rocha/EPALast Christmas Eve, another suspicious ship altered its name, flag and identifying traits when anchored off Freetown. With no destination declared, it left on Christmas Day. Approaching the Canary Islands on 9 January, it slowed and remained there for 13 hours before heading to Libya, which was also the Arconian’s stated destination.Exactly the same pattern was observed with a ship leaving Freetown on 15 December, too.Anothereight vesselswith near-identical traits to the Arconian have departed Freetown for Libya via the Canary Islands since 2024.These include the White Labeille, which left Freetown in November 2024, was tracked off the Canary Islands and later “went dark”, switching off locator devices. Four months earlier, theWhite Eagledeparted Sierra Leone before going dark off Morocco and being mysteriously abandoned. On the same day, another vessel – the White Arrow – was discarded in Libya with its Filipino crew, weeks after leaving Freetown.Other ships were found abandoned close to Freetown. One trawler, Sky 777, ran aground on Lumley Beach last year. No one has claimed it.Months later, theAgios Basseterredrifted on to nearby Hamilton beach. Witnesses described white men hurriedly retrieving packages from the boat. It, too, was never claimed.As investigators pored over the Arconian, Sierra Leonean authorities claimed its cargo originated from a mystery maritime transfer. However, analysis for the Guardian of its final voyage byLloyd’s List Intelligenceconfirmed that the ship’s speed was consistent. There were no stops for a ship-to-ship transfer.View image in fullscreenThe Sky 777, a trawler that ran aground on Freetown’s Lumley Beach last year, is still unclaimed.Photograph: HandoutSomething else did not seem right. Usually, the loss of even a modest cocaine cargo unleashes a wave of underworld violence. Intelligence agencies waited for the bloodshed.Two days after the Arconian’s seizure, Leijdekkers chaired a Freetown summit to pinpoint what had gone wrong. Who gave the tip-off? Did he have a mole?But no violence followed. “Mind-boggling amounts of cocaine had gone,” says a police source, “but Leijdekkers behaved like nothing had happened. Extraordinary.”Perhaps Alan Jalloh underestimated Leijdekkers? Or maybe he was blinded by greed? Either way, intelligence indicates he was seen to have “betrayed” the Dutch fugitive over a cocaine deal.Policeinvestigating the kidnapping made a swift breakthrough. Officers tracked down the black Toyota SUV. “We recognised it from our surveillance work on Leidjekkers,” says one.Three kidnappers were arrested, but before they could be questioned, senior officers intervened. “They were released the same day,” says a source.The investigating team’s caseload snowballed. Two days later, inquiries prompted a police raid on a Freetown warehouse. Inside were two teenagers and the property owner, guarding blocks of cocaine.Halfway through the arrest, 40 armed troops turned up. At gunpoint, police were ordered to release the suspects. “Officers were told to leave everything with the military. Nobody saw those boys again,” says a police source.View image in fullscreenSierra Leonean soldiers patrol in Freetown in June 2023. A day earlier, police fired teargas at crowds at the main opposition party’s headquarters.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/GettyOver the following days, other people went missing, including the owner of a Lumley beach bar. A name linking the disappeared kept cropping up: Leijdekkers. Detectives, though, felt their inquiry was increasingly thwarted. The lead investigator was abruptly transferred: Jalloh’s family could no longer contact them.Nine people had disappeared, yet not a single police statement was issued. Such silence is even more striking because Jalloh, a shopkeeper, was related to Sierra Leone’s vice-president, and kidnapped alongsideAlusine “Bokay” Koroma, a lauded Sierra Leonean international footballer.Asked for details of its investigation, Sierra Leone police did not respond. The military also declined to comment. Westernintelligence reports, though, are unequivocal: Leijdekkers’ enforcers murdered Jalloh. “His mercenaries were supported by the police and military,” says one report.Witness statements reveal that hours before he was abducted, troops visited Jalloh’s FreetownLiquor Martand looted its contents. Some of those kidnapped, police learned, were buried at Freetown’s police cemetery.“Reliable sources say they were sliced with a power saw while alive. A pit was dug, the bodies dissolved with chemicals and concreted over,” said a Sierra Leonean police officer. Another source with knowledge of the burials informed investigators that a “head was missing”.View image in fullscreenAlan Jalloh, opening his Liquor Mart store in Freetown. He has not been seen since he was abducted.Photograph: Alan Jalloh/LinkedinOther deaths occurred, such as John Conteh, who worked at Freetown’s port, checking container seals at the quayside. Intelligence sources reveal Conteh began “monitoring and inspecting containers” linked to Leijdekkers.At about 1am on 2 June 2024,Conteh was crushedin work machinery. In the commercially sensitive heart of one of west Africa’s most critical ports, his death was apparently not caught on CCTV.Conteh, who worked forMediterranean Shipping Company(MSC), the world’s largest shipping group, is the only MSC employee to have died in Freetown since it started operations there 14 years ago.Eight days after Conteh’s death, Sierra Leonean authorities concluded the incident was a “work-related accident”.MSC declined to comment, referring to port authority statements. Sierra Leone police similarly chose not to respond. Western intelligence believe Conteh died in “suspicious circumstances”.View image in fullscreenA covert picture of Leijdekkers, allegedly taken last year in the Aberdeen area of FreetownEven high-ranking police officers are at risk. On 8 April 2023, Supt Matthew “Boyka” Banya was in a marked police car near Makeni’s famous clock tower. Banya was adjusting to the northern city, having been ousted from Freetown after allegedly falling foul of Leijdekkers’ network.Anassassin shot Banyain his vehicle at point-blank range.“Boyka wanted to expose Leijdekkers so an assailant was sent,” a Sierra Leonean police source claims.The president himself urged police action but no killer was caught. “There was no proper investigation. They let it go,” added the source. Justice campaigners claim they were “obstructed” by the authorities. Police would not comment.Such unsolved killings have chilled the country. Residents describe a climate of fear. “Targeted assassinations, cover-ups and impunity. We are terrified,” says one local politician.Most feared are the “commandos”, Leijdekkers’ Turkish, Dutch and Serbian bodyguards, armed with pistols and assault rifles.Journalists attempting to document Leijdekkers risk arrest, as happened to the Dutch reporterSophie van Leeuwen, who travelled to Freetown last year.A 24/7 police surveillance operation was instigated. At one point, officers watched her drive past Leijdekkers as he drank in the Sky Bar.On her sixth day in Freetown, she was detained for several days onspying charges before being released. Her media files were deleted.Politicians are similarly silenced. Abdul Kargbo, leader of the opposition, alleges that he was threatened after raising trafficking concerns. “They sent people to advise me to stay off [the issue],” he says.View image in fullscreenThe reporter Sophie van Leeuwen, held in Freetown on spying charges.Photograph: OwlpressLeidjekkers shows little sign of lying low, openly enjoying his favourite nightspots, Scarlet, Lor and the Sky Bar.But observers report an increase in security; more armed guards, more lookouts and increasingly rigorous counter-surveillance. Drivers are frequently rotated. His fleet of vehicles are routinely changed. When Leijdekkers makes a journey, reconnaissance teams are dispatched 24 hours in advance. “He seems more paranoid,” says a source.His caution might be valid. Twice, Dutch special forces have been positioned off the west African coast preparing to seize him. Aborted at the last minute, the operations will have jangled nerves. “His biggest fear is a mole,” says a Sierra Leonean source.Several trusted lieutenants aside, Leijdekkers’ business is largely a one-man show. “It makes his network difficult to infiltrate; it can absorb the arrest of senior figures while easily getting rid of juniors.”His willingness to eradicate any perceived weak links can be seen, sources allege, in the deaths of a specialist police unit. Leijdekkers, they claim, feared the team knew too much, including where Jalloh was buried. Two months after the shopowner disappeared, a police vehicle crashed, killing three officers. The officialaccount was that it was an accident.View image in fullscreenA Sierra Leonean organised crime squad officer carries a box of the powerful opioid tapentadol, found on a shipment from India at Freetown terminal in March.Photograph: Saidu Bah/AFP/GettyDays later, a fourth officer of the unit was found hanged. “His family knows their son would not hang himself. No investigation was mounted,” says a police source.Leijdekkers’ arrival has also brought a surge in cocaine’s popularity among Freetown’s middle classes, particularly the Lumley beach nightclubs. The drug’s street price is the lowest in west Africa.Abubakar Sesay, 32, a cocaine addict in Freetown, says dealers operate with political protection: “The bulk is mainly for export to Europe, but a small quantity is sold locally through criminal networks facilitating the trafficking trade.”Experts already warn that cocaine poses a serious public health concern, particularly if processed into cheaper crack cocaine. “We’re already seeing overdoses,” says a drugs campaigner.Despite its relatively low street price, the drug’s wider popularity in Sierra Leone is still limited by its cost, as nearlyhalf of the population live in extreme poverty.View image in fullscreenSlums in Freetown. Nearly half of the country’s population live in extreme poverty.Photograph: Robert Harding/AlamyVery few people benefit from Leijdekkers’ largesse, with sources estimating only a “few hundred” of the country’s nine million people share in the profits. Yet cocaine has warped the country’s economy.One dishat Lor restaurant can cost £270 – five months’ pay for the average Sierra Leonean.A slew of luxury car showrooms line Wilkinson Road; new apartments abound. “My driver showed me a huge multi-storey building built by a police officer. Not a regional commander – a traffic cop!” says the politician.Fresh construction linked to Leijdekkers is emerging across west Africa. Operating bases have been established within Liberia, Guinea Bissau and now Ghana. Using diplomatic passports, Leijdekkers and his men roam the region with ease. Witnesses describe Liberian police applauding his convoy as it crossed the border.On 21 July, thebiggest drugs bust in Liberia’s historywas announced when almost 4 tonnes of Leijdekkers’ cocaine, worth £235m, was found near its capital, Monrovia.Liberia destroys nearly 4.2 tonnes of cocaine seized in two major operationsThe previous day, sources say Leijdekkers returned to Freetownfrom Liberia. They also recognised the man arrested with the Monrovia cocaine, who was seen with Leijdekkers in Freetown.Leijdekkers “frequently” visits Guinea Bissau, courting the junta that seized power last November.There is scrutiny, too, in Ghana where last month several of Leijdekker’s network were arrested.As gifts go, they caught the eye. On 23 June 2026,EU officials gavetwo sleek speedboats to Bio’s government at a ceremony in Freetown. The vessels were for the same military co-opted by Leijdekkers to help tackle drug trafficking – one of many EU offerings made despite detailed warnings over Leijdekkers’ influence in Sierra Leone.View image in fullscreenOne of two speedboats given to the Sierra Leonean navy through the EU-funded Support to West Africa Integrated Maritime Security programme.Photograph: Courtesy of EU in Sierra LeoneIn a deal signed before Leijdekkers arrived in Freetown, Brussels sanctioned a€352m aid packagerunning until 2027. So far, €245m has been paid.In August 2024 – weeks after Dutch intelligence confirmed Bio’s government was harbouring Europe’s chief cocaine importer – the EU agreed to givean extra €90mto Sierra Leone.In January 2025,another €35mwas unlocked at a Freetown meeting with EU officials. Other deals involved tens of millions of EU taxpayers’ money paid directly into Sierra Leone’s treasury.After the Arconian seizure, on 9 June 2026,Brussels opened the European chamber of commerce in Freetownto boost investment. Its inaugural president was the Sierra Leonean head of the shipping company whose employee John Conteh died at Freetown’s port.Strengthening democracy was a core ambition of European investment in Sierra Leone. Since Leijdekkers arrival, the EU hasspent €5.6mon the issue: not enough to prevent recent allegations that he financed $100,000 bribes in an attempt tocorrupt its electoral system.The Dutch justice minister,David van Weel, exasperated with Bio’s refusal to extradite Leijdekkers, wants Brussels to freeze development aid to Freetown. To date, just€18m of funding has been suspended.View image in fullscreenAgnes Bio, Leijdekker’s wife, addressing the UN security council in 2024.Photograph: UNIn summer 2024, as evidence indicated that Bio’s government was protecting Leijdekkers, Sierra Leone assumed the rotatingpresidency of the UN security council.In June 2025, after becoming chair of Ecowas, Bio led a committee demanding apermanent African seaton the security council. The UN body, which is mandated to impose sanctions on a country controlled by a drug lord, seems unwilling to target one of its lamentably few African voices.“There was no appetite. Leidjekkers never came up,” says a European diplomat.Bio doubled down on his statesman persona. Ten days after the Arconian was seized, he met the French president, Emmanuel Macron, before flying to London for his speech at Oxford.In September, Bioaddressed world leadersat the UN general assembly with a speech on “restoring trust”. A New York meeting with Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, saw Bio’seconomic policies feted. Anti-narcotics investigators were gobsmacked.Even Leijdekker’s 32-year-old wife, Agnes, is accredited to Sierra Leone’s UN mission in New York.Julius Maada Bio addresses the UN general assembly in SeptemberIn London, whereBio’s wife, Fatima, until recently had a council flat, a dedicated team is investigating Leijdekkers’ sprawling UK connections.Sharing daily briefings with their Dutch counterparts, Britain’sNational Crime Agencyhas identified interlinked trafficking networks. “Intelligence is telling us that he’s linked to an awful lot of things. We have a number [of UK cocaine importations] we think he was involved in,” said a UK source.The British government has not aired any concerns over Bio’s government.It resembled ascene from Sinaloa, the Mexican region where drug cartels use brazen violence to subjugate the state and send a show of force. It was the quiet Dutch village of Overasselt where, on 1 September this year, dozens of heavily armed men descended. Leijdekkers’ hastily assembled “narco-army” opened fire on a rural warehouse, killing a security guard and, when police arrived, seriously wounding two officers.Hooded men carrying guns stop in their tracks in video from Overasselt sourced by De TelegraafIn thepre-dawn chaos, 34 of the narco trafficker’s foot soldiers were arrested. A cache of high-velocity weapons was found nearby.For Europe’s police, it was the realisation of a long-dreaded nightmare: Latin America’s cartel-style violence had arrived.Leijdekkers attack on Overasselt was completely out of character. Intelligence updates had long chronicled a trafficking network characterised by meticulous paperwork and finely tuned logistics to remain under the radar. Overasselt was the precise opposite. “He’s getting desperate,” a Dutch police source believes.Having lost €812m on the Arconian, the Overassalet raid was prompted by the loss on 29 August of 1.2 tonnes of cocaine near the French-Spanish border.Leijdekkers believed a rival had nabbed it. Within two days, he and associates had recruited for this outlandish raid. But Leijdekkers was wrong. It was police, in fact, who had intercepted the €50m cargo.View image in fullscreenStills from an online video in which men threaten to kill the family of a man accused of stealing cocaine. The banner says in Dutch: ‘Threatening video surfaces following raid on Jan G’s farm in the Netherlands’Days later, the fugitive faced another egregious blow when police officers confirmed they had caught Leijdekkers’ chief financier, a senior operator in a clandestine money transfer system dubbed “Dubai bank”.Since the Arconian was intercepted, Leijdekkers has lost up to 12 shipments – and the wholesale price of cocaine in Europe has risen from€12,000 to €22,000 a kilo.His cumulative losses, police believe, have left him in debt to the ColombianCali cartel.He also faces a gigantic monthly payroll inside Sierra Leone. A cornered Leijdekkers is a dangerous proposition. Having outlasted former accomplices, such as the alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan, recentlyextradited from Dubai to Ireland, and the convicted Moroccan-Dutch traffickerRidouan Taghi, sentenced to life in prison in 2024, Leijdekkers retains extensive influence within the sprawling criminal ecosystem in north Africa and Europe, the so-called Mocro mafia.Police sources, who once insisted Freetown would “never, ever” extradite their wealthy guest, are now wondering if that might change. And for the Bio family, international pressure is escalating. Van Weel, the Netherlands’ justice and security minister, said work was under way to “sanction” individuals linked to Leijdekkers. The president’s office declined to comment, though there is no suggestion he is implicated in any suspected illegal activity linked to Leijdekkers.View image in fullscreenA social-media video showing Leijdekkers attending church in Tihun, Sierra Leone, in January 2025.Photograph: Fatima Maada Bio/Facebook/ReutersLeijdekkers’ lawyer dismissed the allegations as “politically driven”. A subsequent statement read: “My client wants you to know that the information you got from anonymous sources is complete nonsense, probably nourished by the Dutch authorities and therefore not fit for publication.”Sierra Leone stands on the brink, along with the rest of west Africa. A regional narco-economy, where fragile states are overwhelmed by entrenched corruption and ruthless criminal networks, remains a distinct possibility.Like Jalloh, Leijdekkers may disappear from Freetown. He will probably surface elsewhere to assemble a fresh empire.“There’s no sign of him retiring,” says a police source. “Every day, the guy’s growing his wings, expanding his network.”

title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers
Content: Simbarashe Kundizeza says the story is entirely his own work.View image in fullscreenSimbarashe Kundizeza says the story is entirely his own work.AI (artificial intelligence)Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning storyArticle in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writersRachel Savagein JohannesburgWed 14 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.Kundizeza’s storyThe Blue Fighterwas announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published anarticleby the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”Kundizeza responded in astatement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.“I look forward to continuing to work with theCaine prizeteam, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”View image in fullscreenJournalist Vauhini Vara said she had run Kundizeza’s story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost entirely AI generated.Photograph: Andrew AltschulSimilar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazirwon the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prizewith The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) wasremoved from the longlistof France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.The Caine prize said in astatementthat it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize listRead moreIn his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journalarticlethat found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Caine prizeThe AtlanticShort storiesAwards and prizesFictionZimbabwenewsShareReuse this content

title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns | Guinea-Bissau | The Guardian
description: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr
Content: The trial would withhold hepatitis B vaccines from thousands of newborns in a country where the disease is widespread.Photograph: Phanie/Sipa Press/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe trial would withhold hepatitis B vaccines from thousands of newborns in a country where the disease is widespread.Photograph: Phanie/Sipa Press/AlamyGuinea-BissauGuinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newbornsHealth minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK JrMelody SchreiberWed 14 Oct 2026 09.16 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuinea-Bissauhas not approved the controversialhepatitis Bstudy in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed byRobert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials inGuinea-Bissauhad approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at apress briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-BissauRead more“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have beencalled into questionin the past year.The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny.
