You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.”When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”.“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS toldReutersin a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.At least four members of the Danish committeeresignedafter approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life.Hepatitis Bis widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”.Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira,saidin February.The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a Februarystatementpushing back on the trial.Explore more on these topicsGuinea-BissauHepatitis BVaccines and immunisationRobert F Kennedy JrChildren's healthAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Joni Mitchell becomes US citizen: ‘A journey that began 62 years ago’ | Joni Mitchell | The Guardian
description: Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to Instagram
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to Instagram
Content: Joni Mitchell at her US citizenship ceremony.Photograph: InstagramView image in fullscreenJoni Mitchell at her US citizenship ceremony.Photograph: InstagramJoni MitchellJoni Mitchell becomes US citizen: ‘A journey that began 62 years ago’Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to InstagramBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 14 Oct 2026 04.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, along with a photo of her next to an American flag, accompanied by the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.”It means that Mitchell can now vote in US elections, something that she had complained she wasn’t able to do.At a concert in 2024, Mitchell said: “Fuck Donald Trump, I love that song,” referring to the rap track by YG. She added: “I wish I could vote ... I’m a Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants.”Mitchell was born in Fort Macleod, Alberta, in 1943, and eventually settled with her family in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Her earliest gigs were at folk clubs there, followed by Calgary and Toronto, where she met US folk singer Chuck Mitchell. They married in 1965 and Mitchell moved to the US. The marriage didn’t last, ending two years later, but by that time Mitchell had established herself as a mellifluous, original voice on the vibrant US folk music circuit.View image in fullscreenFolk original … Joni Mitchell in 1968.Photograph: Jack Robinson/Getty ImagesShe released her debut album in 1968, and soon after, using the album’s royalties, moved to Los Angeles’ Laurel Canyon where she recorded her first gold-selling album, Ladies of the Canyon. She remained based in California and currently lives in Santa Barbara.Joni Mitchell: where to start in her back catalogueRead moreMitchell’s most recent studio album is Shine, from 2007. After that she spent a number of years out of the public eye, suffering a brain aneurysm in 2015 that required extensive recovery. But she returned to live performance in 2022 with an unannounced set at the Newport folk festival, and has since performed a number of all-star “Joni Jam” concerts.A biopic about her is being prepared by director Cameron Crowe, who began work on it in the early 2020s. Earlier this year, record executive Clive Davis announced at a party thatMeryl Streep would play Mitchellin the film.Explore more on these topicsJoni MitchellPop and rockFolk musicCanadaAmericasCelebritynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: International alliance of China-sceptic legislators warns of risks inherent in misjudging bilateral relationship
Author: Rebecca Bailey
Headline: International alliance of China-sceptic legislators warns of risks inherent in misjudging bilateral relationship
Content: Past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised, the report says.Photograph: Florence Lo/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenPast engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised, the report says.Photograph: Florence Lo/Pool Reuters/APForeign policyUK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report saysInternational alliance of China-sceptic legislators warns of risks inherent in misjudging bilateral relationshipRebecca BaileyChina correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s approach toChinais “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads.The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU marketsRead moreIt cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, says Ipac, pointing to budget cuts as an additional problem.Ipac counts almost 50 MPs among its members, including from Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National party, the Greens and Reform.Ipac member and former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.A UK government spokesperson said that while working with China presented opportunities, “we are also clear-eyed about the threats China poses, and national security is the first duty of government”.“We will cooperate with China where we can while meeting any challenges head-on,” they added.The Chinese embassy in London said Ipac’s “sole agenda is to manufacture falsehoods, mislead the public, and undermine China’s relations with other countries”.The report “distorts the facts” and “is not even worth refuting”, it added.While the Ipac report accepts that “disengagement is not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights.The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.Emerging technologies such as AI represent “another front we’re potentially facing”, Labour’s Dame Meg Hillier said at the launch, with the report identifying areas of concern such as disinformation and surveillance capabilities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.The government conducted its own audit of the UK-China relationship in late 2024 but has said it cannot publish most of the detail for fear of damaging national interests.But Evan Fowler, author of the Ipac report, said that a public audit was important “because engagement with China doesn’t just happen at the government level”.It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”Explore more on these topicsForeign policyChinaTrade policyEspionageAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying | Russia | The Guardian
description: FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences
Content: The arrest comes amid a spike in tensions between Russia and Japan following Vladimir Putin’s August trip to the Kuril islands, the Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that is claimed by both countries.Photograph: artaxerxes_longhand/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe arrest comes amid a spike in tensions between Russia and Japan following Vladimir Putin’s August trip to the Kuril islands, the Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that is claimed by both countries.Photograph: artaxerxes_longhand/AlamyRussiaRussia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spyingFSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defencesJustin McCurryin TokyoTue 13 Oct 2026 21.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of spying, in the latest sign of rising tensions between Moscow and Tokyo.Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai, from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, adding that he had been accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.Japan’s foreign ministry summoned the Russian ambassador in Tokyo, Nikolay Nozdrev, over the arrest later on Wednesday.Imai, a reporter at the newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin, was reportedly preparing to return to Japan when he was arrested for allegedly collecting information on Russia’s defence capabilities, according to Russia’s Tass news agency.Russia’s FSB security agency claimed the journalist had intended to pass the information on to Japanese intelligence.The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him. The man was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention. It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred. The charges carry up to 20 years in prison.Japan’s foreign ministry urged Moscow to extend “fair and impartial treatment” to the detained journalist. “The Japanese embassy … in Moscow and the consulate general in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk lodged a request with the Russian authorities for the prompt provision of information, as well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” an official told Agence France-Presse.The Hokkaido Shimbun said in a statement that it was aware of the announcement by Russian authorities but it was “still confirming the details”.“Ensuring the safety of the journalist is our top priority, and we are responding accordingly,” it said.Imai’s arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and alongstanding disputeover sovereignty of islands belonging to the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido.Russia regards Japan as an “unfriendly” country because it has joined western sanctions over its war ⁠in Ukraine. Russia has arrested several citizens of “unfriendly” countries in recent years, accusing them of working for western intelligence services.In 2023, US journalistEvan Gershkovich was arrestedon espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before beingreleased in a 2024 prisoner swap.The Kuril Islands: how a visit from Putin reignited a 150-year-old dispute between Japan and RussiaRead moreThe FSB said it had “opened a criminal case against the Japanese national”, and that he had been placed in pre-trial detention, Russian news agencies reported, citing the agency.Russian media reported he would remain in custody until 12 December.“Attempts by Tokyo to use its correspondents in Russia … to gather information aimed at undermining the security of our state is regrettable,” Zakharova said, alleging this was “not an isolated case”.The Kurils have been under Russian control since the end of the second world war, when Soviet forces seized the islands in the final days of the conflict, forcing about 17,000 Japanese citizens to leave and, over time, replacing them with a similar number of Russians.In 2022, Moscow scrapped a programme that allowed former residents to travel to the islands to visit the graves of their ancestors in protest at Japan’s support for Ukraine.Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, visited one of the disputed islands in August,causing an ​uproar in Japan. Tokyo has ‌said it would continue ​implementing sanctions against ​Russia and supporting Ukraine.With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsRussiaJapanAsia PacificEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX | Wyoming | The Guardian
description: Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege
Content: Aili Wang was arrested at Los Angeles airport as she allegedly sough to return to China.Photograph: Mark Gomelsky/APView image in fullscreenAili Wang was arrested at Los Angeles airport as she allegedly sough to return to China.Photograph: Mark Gomelsky/APWyomingGraduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAXMicrobiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allegeAssociated PressTue 13 Oct 2026 20.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAWyomingmicrobiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return toChina. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.Wang remained jailed without bail on Tuesday in Los Angeles. She allegedly bought a chemical, acrylamide, over eBay, and it was first detected when the alleged victim’s wife and others tested water from the coffee maker he used to brew tea.US officials for years have accused China of stealing intellectual property from American universities.The microbiology professor overseeing both graduate students, Mark Gomelsky, said the accusations left him reeling. He was uncertain if the victim will fully recover.“It’s been disheartening, to say the least, to see that one of your students’ lives is in jeopardy and another student may be responsible for that,” Gomelsky told the Associated Press. “That was one of the worst shocks in my professional career.”Wang had no attorney listed in court documents. The AP tried to reach her via email and LinkedIn messages.The police investigation began after the victim, identified in court documents as “KT”, began experiencing symptoms and his wife and others allegedly isolated the chemical in the coffee maker water. The victim and campus police then set up surveillance cameras in the office space he shared with Wang at the university in Laramie.Wang allegedly was recorded 27 September going through the alleged victim’s desk. On 1 October, she was recorded “taking photos and manipulating notebooks” on his desk, as well as rinsing out his mug with a liquid from her own mug, a University of Wyoming campus police officer’s affidavit said.Wang and the alleged victim, who did not share research areas, did not get along, according to the affidavit.The alleged victim began experiencing extreme tiredness, inability to sleep and other unexplained symptoms soon after attending a prestigious conference in August, Gomelsky said.He also noticed a strange taste in the tea that he made with a small coffee maker on his desk, Gomelsky said. When he washed the coffee maker, Gomelsky said, the taste would go away.Suspecting someone in their shared office could be poisoning the graduate student, Gomelsky said a chemistry professor tested the water and identified acrylamide.Wang faces a felony aggravated assault and battery charge in Wyoming punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine.It is not clear when she could be extradited to the state, where Albany county circuit court judge Robert Sanford granted prosecutors’ request and raised bond to $1.5m cash-only.Wang allegedly asked eBay to delete her account after she bought acrylamide over the online retail site twice last summer, police said.Explore more on these topicsWyomingChinaAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Paddington: The Musical is coming to Sydney in 2027 | Australian theatre | The Guardian
description: Hugely successful West End show will open at Capitol Theatre in September 2027, with dates in other Australian cities yet to be announced
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Hugely successful West End show will open at Capitol Theatre in September 2027, with dates in other Australian cities yet to be announced
Content: Paddington: The Musical in London. The show, based on Michael Bond’s 1958 book A Bear Called Paddington, has won numerous theatre awards, and is coming to Sydney in 2027.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenPaddington: The Musical in London. The show, based on Michael Bond’s 1958 book A Bear Called Paddington, has won numerous theatre awards, and is coming to Sydney in 2027.Photograph: Johan PerssonAustralian theatrePaddington: The Musical is coming to Sydney in 2027Hugely successful West End show will open at Capitol Theatre in September 2027, with dates in other Australian cities yet to be announcedGet our weekend culture and lifestyle emailSian CainWed 14 Oct 2026 19.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia, prepare to start guarding your marmalade reserves: the award-winning Paddington: The Musical is on its way.The acclaimed theatre production, which has been running in London’s West End since 2025, will land inSydneyin September 2027, where it will be performed at the Capitol Theatre for 10 weeks.Dates in any other Australian cities have yet to be announced, as has the cast.Paddington: The Musical review – they’ve looked after this bear quite splendiferouslyRead moreSydney is a long way from London’s Paddington Station, where the clumsy but lovable bear from Peru is taken in by the Brown family and wins over the whole neighbourhood.The show, based on Michael Bond’s 1958 book A Bear Called Paddington as well as the hit film adaptations over the last decade,has received many five-star reviews,includingin the Guardian.Much has been made of the state-of-the-art animatronic puppet used to portray Paddington, which was designed by costume designer Tahra Zafar. In London, the bear is played by a duo: James Hameed provides the voice and is the remote puppeteer, while Arti Shah performs wearing the furry costume.Sign up for the fun stuff with our rundown of must-reads, pop culture and tips for the weekend, every Sunday morningPaddington: The Musical won seven Olivier awardsearlier this year, tying for the record for the most wins for any musical, including best new musical, a joint best actor in a musical award for Hameed and Shah, and best set design. It also won a record nine WhatsOnStage awards and the Critics’ Circle award for best new musical.Paddington: The Musical will continue to be performed in London until at least 2028 andis opening on Broadway in April 2027.In a statement, the show’s producers, Sonia Friedman and Eliza Lumley, said they were “thrilled” the show would go to Sydney due to the city’s “extraordinary appetite for world-class musical theatre and the affection Australians have long held for Paddington”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSaved for SundayEase your Sunday scaries with the best of Guardian Australia’s culture and lifestyle journalism.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“From the outset, we have wanted Paddington The Musical to open only in cities where it can be produced with the same ambition, care and theatrical scale as in London. Paddington’s journey across the world in search of a new home – and his discovery that home can be found through kindness, acceptance and a sense of belonging – feels particularly resonant for Australian audiences.”The show’s composer, Tom Fletcher, said it had been “the greatest adventure of my career”.“I’ve made many happy memories writing, recording and touring Australia over the years and I am so excited to have the opportunity to bring our show to Sydney and share this very rare and special bear with Australian audiences,” he added.Explore more on these topicsAustralian theatreSydneyPaddingtonMichael BondChildren and teenagersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Illegal tobacco increasingly hard to spot, with some fakes in plain packaging featuring Australian health warnings  | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Government warned that counterfeit tobacco produced by criminal organisations in south-east Asia is becoming more sophisticated
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Government warned that counterfeit tobacco produced by criminal organisations in south-east Asia is becoming more sophisticated
Content: Cigarettes in Australian-style plain packaging are being counterfeited at factories in Cambodia, according to intelligence provided to the federal government.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenCigarettes in Australian-style plain packaging are being counterfeited at factories in Cambodia, according to intelligence provided to the federal government.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAAustralia newsIllegal tobacco increasingly hard to spot, with some fakes in plain packaging featuring Australian health warningsGovernment warned that counterfeit tobacco produced by criminal organisations in south-east Asia is becoming more sophisticatedGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressWed 14 Oct 2026 19.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 20.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe black-market tobacco trade continues to thrive as sellers turn to counterfeit packaging to skirt bans, prompting calls for the urgent passing of tougher laws.Intelligence provided to the federal government shows cigarettes in plain Australian-style packaging are being produced illegally at an industrial scale in south-east Asian warehouses.Experts weigh in on how to tackle illicit tobacco – and why an 80% excise cut is not on their listRead moreFactories owned and operated by criminal syndicates, primarily based in Cambodia, are pumping out increasingly sophisticated fake products that replicate common brands.Some of the counterfeit packaging is even branded with Australian health warnings.View image in fullscreenJulian Hill has urged parliament to pass laws giving authorities new powers to target the illicit tobacco trade.Photograph: ABF MediaThe production has prompted the customs minister, Julian Hill, to urge parliament to pass tough laws as soon as possible.A new bill on the tobacco trade is expected to be debated in the Senate on Thursday. It would give law enforcement stronger powers to detect and disrupt illegal tobacco trade lines, including choking off criminal profits.But Hill was concerned the sophisticated overseas production of cigarettes was becoming increasingly hard to detect or stop.“Serious and organised criminal syndicates have weaponised the cheap oversupply of tobacco globally and will do anything to make a buck,” he said.“The crooks will continue to adapt their tactics.“This highlights the urgency of equipping state, territory and commonwealth authorities with these new powers to go after anyone involved in the illegal tobacco trade, including the supply chains and retail outlets,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSeveral states and territories have been cracking down on enforcement measures, including blitzes of black-market shopfronts. Queensland has taken the hardest line and legal cigarette sales have grown as a result.NSW police closed 10 retailers across the state last week, including eight in south-west Sydney.Across just two days on 6 and 7 October, NSW health inspectors seized 420,000 illegal cigarettes, about 60kg of loose-leaf tobacco and thousands of illicit vapes – small numbers compared with the 2.4 tonnes of tobacco confiscated since the start of the year.Some shops have been closed for more than 90 days as the NSW government ramps up enforcement.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsSmokingOrganised crimeCrime - AustraliaTobacco industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Student protests in Albania turn violent as demonstrators clash with police | Albania | The Guardian
description: Dozens of people detained after government building and two banks set on fire as tens of thousands march over education costs and corruption
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dozens of people detained after government building and two banks set on fire as tens of thousands march over education costs and corruption
Content: 1:14Anti-government student protests in Albania turn violent – videoAlbaniaStudent protests in Albania turn violent as demonstrators clash with policeDozens of people detained after government building and two banks set on fire  as tens of thousands march over education costs and corruptionGuardian staff and agencies in TiranaWed 14 Oct 2026 19.19 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTens of thousands of students have taken to the streets of Tirana, the Albanian capital, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and ⁠corruption.Police responded with water ⁠cannon and teargas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned bins and smashed the fronts of local businesses. A branch of Raiffeisen Bank near the education ministry also caught fire.Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were being treated for injuries and that 35 people had been detained.President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, adding: “The constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception.”The protests are the most violent outburst yet against Edi Rama, ⁠the prime minister, who won a fourth term in office in May last year but has since faced ​growing discontent at perceived graft surrounding top ‌officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures ‌as unpalatable alternatives.View image in fullscreenProtesters clash with police in central Tirana.Photograph: Adnan Beci/AFP/GettyThe unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by theproposed development ‌of a luxury resortalong Albania’s pristine southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has been caught up in legal disputes.“This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns,” said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name as she threw rocks at the police.Others chanted “resignation” and “police of crime”.Student ‌organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation.The unrest is part of a ​broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France,high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockadesdemanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests had spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodër.The government ⁠condemned the violence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA government building and two banks were set on fire during the protests.Photograph: Florion Goga/ReutersAlbana Koçiu, the deputy prime minister of Albania, said on Facebook: “Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used ​as an excuse for violence, city ​destruction or ugly fighting in the middle ​of the road. I call on ​students and every ‌honest citizen who believes in ​the right to ​protest: distance yourself from violence and vandalism!”The police issued a statement calling for calm. “Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed,” they said.Meanwhile, the EU, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the “violent escalation at the protest in Tirana”.A statement by the EU delegation in Tirana said: “We take note of the allegations of excessive violence by the police against protesters and journalists,”Calling for a prompt investigation, the delegation encouraged “all sides to de-escalate the tension”.Explore more on these topicsAlbaniaProtestEuropeStudent politicsStudentsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery ‘progressing as planned’  | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Pontiff has begun walking in his hospital room and is eating normally after operation to remove growth, doctors say
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Pontiff has begun walking in his hospital room and is eating normally after operation to remove growth, doctors say
Content: Pope Leo talks to his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, before his admission to hospital on Tuesday.Photograph: Ciro De Luca/ReutersView image in fullscreenPope Leo talks to his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, before his admission to hospital on Tuesday.Photograph: Ciro De Luca/ReutersPope Leo XIVPope Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery ‘progressing as planned’Pontiff has begun walking in his hospital room and is eating normally after operation to remove growth, doctors sayAngela Giuffridain RomeWed 14 Oct 2026 18.31 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leo’s recovery from a lung cancer operation is progressing as planned, his doctors have said, as the pontiff received good wishes from around the world, including from Britain’s King Charles.Leo, who had acancerous mass removed from his right lunglate on Tuesday, began walking in his hospital room after respiratory therapy on Wednesday. He was eating normally, his doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritoria said in a statement issued by the Vatican.A blood test and chest X-ray showed “normal post-operative progress” and the results were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”, they said.The operation at Rome’s Gemelli hospital confirmed that Leo, 71, has the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma. The Vatican has not yet disclosed the results of further tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.The cancer diagnosis for Leo, who was elected as the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church in May 2025, has come as a shock.In a rare moment of Vatican transparency, the pope announced during his angelus prayer on Sunday that doctors had found a small nodule on his lung during a checkup and that it was “well-contained” and had been detected early.Messages have been sent from around the world. King Charles, who is also being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer, would write to Leo privately, a source told Agence France-Presse. Charles and Queen Camilla met the pope when they travelled to the Vatican in October last year.Donald Trump, the US president, said: “I want to see Pope ‌Leo get well. I just want ⁠to wish him ​well, get ​better ​fast.”Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, wished Leo a full and swift recovery in a message posted on X and said the pontiff was “a source of hope and inspiration for billions around the world”.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said he and his wife, Jeanette, were praying for Leo. The couple met the pontiff at the Vatican in May.The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, wrote on X that Leo’s serenity and strength were an inspiration for all. “We hope for his full and speedy recovery,” she wrote.Before the operation, all of Leo’s appointments until 20 October were cancelled. He went on a papal trip to France in September and is scheduled to go to South America in November for a 12-day trip covering 10 cities.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVThe papacyCatholicismEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Throttling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holds
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Throttling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holds
Content: A Ukrainian couple and their baby daughter outside a bombed building in Kyiv on Tuesday.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APView image in fullscreenA Ukrainian couple and their baby daughter outside a bombed building in Kyiv on Tuesday.Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/APUkraineAnalysisIn Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death tollDan SabbaghDefence and security editorThrottling of mobile internet system will affect Kyiv’s air defences more than its strikes on oil refineries. Now Zelenskyy must be hoping that US intel holdsWed 14 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.55 EDTShareInUkrainethe situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a Russian missile attack in Kyiv on Wednesday.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersThe immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal withRussia.However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with theunexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.Russia has bombed twobridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy,on a visit to Londonon Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.Explore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeKyivTrump administrationForeign policyVolodymyr ZelenskyyElon MuskanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restricted | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Launch of Russian ballistic missiles on Ukraine, with no US warning, coincides with outage of Starlink managed by Musk’s SpaceX
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Launch of Russian ballistic missiles on Ukraine, with no US warning, coincides with outage of Starlink managed by Musk’s SpaceX
Content: Smoke rises over Kyiv after Russian strikesUkraineUkrainian military’s access to Starlink satellite internet suddenly restrictedLaunch of Russian ballistic missiles on Ukraine, with no US warning, coincides with outage of Starlink managed by Musk’s SpaceXAndrew Rothin KyivWed 14 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 04.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUkraine’s military has suddenly had its access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as theTrump administrationhas increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.The terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy.The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukrainewithout any advance warning from the USfor a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing withUkraine. Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.Ukraine did not receive any warning beforeRussialaunched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force. But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.Musk said that Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons, and that the Ukrainian military was linked to a separate network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government. “This is not underSpaceXcontrol,” Musk wrote.Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”View image in fullscreenA firefighter works at the site of a food store hit by a Russian attack on Lutsk on 14 October.Photograph: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/ReutersLimiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.“With their actions our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals has been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected. The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Zelenskyy to be replaced as Ukraine’s leader – an extraordinary act of political interference against a wartime ally – as a personal feud between the two presidents has burst into the open.The reports that Starlink was being throttled on the frontlines were interpreted by some as further pressure on Ukraine to end the fighting and make a deal with Russia at any cost.Serhii Sternenko, a political activist with close ties to the military, first reported the outage and later said that the speeds at which the loss of connectivity occurred had fallen even lower. “It is likely that the company ‘SpaceX’ resorted to such measures at the request of the Trump administration,” he said. “Ordinary satellite communication terminals are currently operational.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUkraine war briefing: Zelenskyy decries ‘absolutely unjust’ lack of warning from allies after Kyiv plant strikeRead moreTrump has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say that the closure of the strait of Hormuz has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.Zelenskyy had suggested, though not said, that the US was intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine about impending Russian missile strikes.Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.“The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” Zelenskyy said. “Russia does not consider the American president’s statements strong.”At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become even more widespread.Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed by either side. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”Ukraine is observing a short-term moratorium on striking Russian refineries while Kyiv seeks to show that it is ready for talks with Russia. Zelenskyy arrived in London on Wednesday to meet Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister. He will also be received by King Charles.Zelenskyy is seeking new negotiations with the US. He has sent proposals to the Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, saying Ukraine was ready to work towards a ceasefire and “Russia must also be part of this agreement”.Explore more on these topicsUkraineSpaceXTrump administrationRussiaElon MuskUS politicsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year | Mountains | The Guardian
description: Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climate
Content: The Aiguille du Midi cable car traverses the slopes of Mont-Blanc in Haute-Savoie, France.Photograph: Design Pics Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Aiguille du Midi cable car traverses the slopes of Mont-Blanc in Haute-Savoie, France.Photograph: Design Pics Inc/AlamyMountainsMont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a yearPeak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climateAjit NiranjanEurope environment correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWestern Europe’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.Chartered surveyors from the Union Nationale des Géomètres-Experts (UNGE) and the Ordre des Géomètres-Experts, who have regularly monitored the peak since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain, and drones to create a detailed model of the snow and ice cap.The summit has shrunk back by 3.43 metres since a high of 4,810.90 metres in 2007, the data shows.The experts cautioned against linking fluctuations in height from year to year to the rapid loss of Alpine ice being caused by fossil fuel pollution.“Regarding ice mass, it is essential to distinguish between changes in surface altitude and changes in the total volume or mass of ice,” a UNGE spokesperson said. “An increase in summit altitude does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained ice mass, nor does it contradict the documented retreat of Alpine glaciers.”Climate breakdown was a factor in western Europe’s hottest summer on record this year, scarring Alpine regions and melting ice at dizzying speed. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an “explosion of melt rates” after confirming that one-fifth of the country’s ice had been lost in the past five years, and 5.5% of volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.Jean des Garets, the president of the Haute-Savoie departmental chamber of surveyors and the leader of the Mont Blanc expedition, said the warming trend could be seen with the naked eye in the rest of the Alpine massif but that “for the moment, climate change doesn’t seem to have the same impact above 4,000 metres”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When we climb, we pass by the Brigade Blanche hut before the Tête-Rousse glacier,” he said in comments reported by the French television channel TF1 on Wednesday. “We’ve seen that the glacier has moved up. It has literally melted before our very eyes and now in some places we’re crossing a stream instead of a glacier.”Explore more on these topicsMountainsFranceGlaciersEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel blocks construction of key Gaza base created by Trump peace board | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Israel has not permitted US-led project to house 150 international troops to move forward
Author: Aram Roston
Headline: Exclusive: Israel has not permitted US-led project to house 150 international troops to move forward
Content: Trump, with Board of Peace representatives, shows the group’s founding charter at a meeting at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump, with Board of Peace representatives, shows the group’s founding charter at a meeting at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January.Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesUS foreign policyIsrael blocks construction of key Gaza base created by Trump peace boardExclusive: Israel has not permitted US-led project to house 150 international troops to move forwardAram Rostonin WashingtonWed 14 Oct 2026 15.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 18.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.In early August, the Board of Peace, the international organization authorized in 2025 by the UN and chaired by the US president, issuedits first construction contract for Gaza: Louisiana-based Arkel International would construct a military outpost for 150 international troops that would be the vanguard of an international stabilization force.Two months later,Israelhas still not permitted the contract to move forward, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. Contractors and trucks are not being allowed to cross into Gaza and begin the work. “Israel won’t open the border,” they said.Trump’s Board of Peace plans to grant itself sweeping immunity, documents showRead moreA Board of Peace spokesperson declined to comment. The Israeli Defense Forces and the Israeli government declined tocomment.Israel’s war in Gaza is one of the eight wars Trump claims to have resolved. Helisted it again last week in a screedon social media, protesting that it was unfair he had not won the Nobel peace prize.The Board of Peace, formed in the wake of an October 2025 ceasefire inGaza, is central to Trump’s claims to have ended the conflict.Arkel’s planned “mission support site temporary outpost” is decidedly rudimentary: a fortified position of about 100 meters by 100 meters, at a site that was once part of the controversial and now defunct Gaza Humanitarian Foundation project, according to the person familiar with the matter. The US-backed GHF operated in Gaza from May 2025 till October 2025 to deliver aid protected by private contractors.The base would host short rotating deployments of a well-armed force of 150 troops in Gaza, the person said. They would come from a larger component of 500 sent already from Morocco and Kosovo.But without this contract, the source said, the rest of the Board of Peace program cannot launch. Israel’s refusal to allow Arkel, the contractor, to build the base, essentially cuts the Board of Peace off at the legs.“You can’t get in without [an international stabilization force (ISF)]. You can’t rebuild,” the person said. “There’s no security. There’s no deliveries of construction equipment. You can’t even start putting utilities. You can’t start putting in basic life-support facilities you know because without the ISF you can’t go in.”The person familiar with the matter said the Board of Peace believes that Israel’s government will let the project proceed after the Israeli elections, which are scheduled for 27 October.The controversial Board of Peace has a unique structure. Trump is designated as chair for life. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, is an executive board member, as is real estate developer Steve Witkoff, whom Trump has appointed as a mediator in various international disputes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThough many western democracies have kept their distance from the Board of Peace, 28 countries joined as founding members earlier this year. Kushner has unveiled renderings of a futuristic vision of Gaza, where the city was envisioned as a pristine luxury waterfront resort city with hi-tech skyscrapers looking out over the Mediterranean.On 23 September the group unveiled what it said was a six-month, $2.45bn plan, as the first step towards reconstruction with a 10-year estimated cost of $71bn.There were lofty promises and requests for contributions. “Today we can point to real progress,” announced Witkoff.A US senior adviser to the board, Aryeh Lightstone, announced a new fund would be started. “Your high net-worth donations will go directly to the Palestinian people,” he said. Lightstone has traveled in Trump circles since the president’s first term. He officiated as a rabbi at the 2020 wedding of Trump adviser Stephen Miller to Katie Miller.Israel has continued strikes in Gaza since the October ceasefire, killing about1,400people over that time, according to Gaza health authorities.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyIsraelGazaDonald TrumpPalestineTrump administrationMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Two container ships sink near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: Vessels were hit by missiles as rise in strikes suggests Iran is trying to close waterway before US midterm elections
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Vessels were hit by missiles as rise in strikes suggests Iran is trying to close waterway before US midterm elections
Content: People walk past an anti-US billboard in Tehran depicting an IRGC member placing his foot on an unmanned underwater US vehicle.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople walk past an anti-US billboard in Tehran depicting an IRGC member placing his foot on an unmanned underwater US vehicle.Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAStrait of HormuzTwo container ships sink near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacksVessels were hit by missiles as rise in strikes suggests Iran is trying to close waterway before US midterm electionsPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 13.05 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo container ships near the strait of Hormuz have ⁠sunk after being struck by missiles, amid the sharpest rise in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war withIran.The increase in attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in an attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.TheTrump administrationhas been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.On Wednesday, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.The Singapore-flagged ​container ‌ship GFS Pride sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day. Hours later, the Antigua- and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, having been hit by a ​projectile ​on 23 September, according to data from ‌the ‌International Maritime Organization.Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship had sunk after hitting a naval mine while making an unauthorised passage through the strait.State television quoted a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that said the ship was travelling on an “illegal and dangerous route” when it hit the mine.The ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.View image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz near Bandar Abbas, Iran. UKMTO reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours.Photograph: Razieh Poudat/ReutersHowever, UKMTO suggested that both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles, raising questions over Tehran’s account.Iran has repeatedly warned ships against trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The US military has beenguiding ships through the waterwayon a route nearer to Oman’s coast.Ships in the area were reporting an intense series of attacks in recent days, with six vessels attacked on Sunday alone, according to UKMTO’s monitoring.Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October. Of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers and two others were crude oil tankers.The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop-off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Trump launched his war on Iran, and the Republican party is bracing for punishment at the polls.View image in fullscreenUS fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Donald Trump launched his war on Iran.Photograph: Bizuayehu Tesfaye/Las Vegas Review-Journal/APAccording to two Iranian officials, Iran has recently begun using new tactics against vessels it considers to be in violation of its restrictions. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being ⁠to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials told Reuters.The decision to adopt the new ​strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ‌ruling system, the officials added.A US military official, ‌speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Tehran had changed tactics in one significant way. After the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to ‌identify potential targets, including American naval vessels, the official said.Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzUS-Israel war on IranIranTrump administrationOilShipping industryMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Global human rights commitments adopted by government extend reach to enablers of unlawful activity
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Global human rights commitments adopted by government extend reach to enablers of unlawful activity
Content: Bilboards for Israel’s elections seen in the West Bank on 8 October. Bids for a new settlement in the West Bank are open and contracts for it could be signed before a potential change of government on 27 October.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAView image in fullscreenBilboards for Israel’s elections seen in the West Bank on 8 October. Bids for a new settlement in the West Bank are open and contracts for it could be signed before a potential change of government on 27 October.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAForeign policyNew UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlementsGlobal human rights commitments adopted by government extend reach to enablers of unlawful activityPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorWed 14 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners.The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person.Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation.The Israeli governmentclosed the UK consulatelast week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government.The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it.Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement.Burnham sees sanctions against Israeli settlements as an electoral assetRead moreThe proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications.A new urgent procedure will allow ministers to mirror designations already made by the EU, US, Canada or Australia for up to 112 days while a specific separate UK case is prepared.The new global sanctions regime will come into force on Thursday but will need endorsement by MPs and peers within 28 days.The foreign secretary,Ed Miliband, is pushing through the measures at speed because the Israeli government has vowed to press ahead with an E1 settlement containing 1,234 homes in the West Bank – a development that many observers say would sever a contiguous, viable Palestinian state, so making the so-called two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict near impossible.The E1 bids close on 19 October but the Israel Land Authority has confirmed that the tender box will not be opened, nor the bids considered, before 19 November, which is after the Israeli election on 27 October.The British Palestinian Project said the Israeli deferral “does not remove the need to deter commitments being made now, since bidders and their backers commit on 19 October, contracts could still be signed before a new Israeli government is formed”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe project welcomed the addition of the right to liberty and security of person in the new laws, saying it opens a route tosanctionsfor serious arbitrary or unlawful detention, including of Palestinian children, and of those responsible for or enabling it. Save the Children estimated in November 2023 that 10,000 Palestinian children had passed through Israeli military detention over the preceding 20 years.A UN 2026 report on children and armed conflict verified that 981 Palestinian children were detained by Israeli forces in 2025 and 180 of them remained in administrative detention without charge or trial at the year’s end.Will UK sanctions have any impact on Israel’s ‘settler terrorists’ in West Bank?Read moreThe UK has already applied sanctions designations for restrictions on humanitarian aid in Sudan and South Sudan but this is the first time this general power is being applied as part of a new worldwide regime including Israel.Refusing permits or blocking convoys will be sufficient grounds to apply sanctions, without requiring the obstruction to constitute a formal breach of international humanitarian law – thereby lowering the threshold for action.Separate work is under way by UK officials in conjunction with European partners on how to outlaw British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyIsraelPalestineEd MilibandLabourMiddle East and north AfricaInternational lawnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iranian woman handed death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media post | Global development | The Guardian
description: Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year
Content: Najmeh Amini appealed from prison for international intervention. She was also sentenced to more than 12 years for ‘acting against national security’ and ‘spreading propaganda’View image in fullscreenNajmeh Amini appealed from prison for international intervention. She was also sentenced to more than 12 years for ‘acting against national security’ and ‘spreading propaganda’Women in prisonGlobal developmentIranian woman handed death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media postRights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this yearSupported byAbout this contentDeepa ParentWed 14 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHuman rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death sentences and executions in Iran, after reports that a 23-year-old woman, Najmeh Amini,has been sentenced to death for blasphemyover a social-media post.Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court.A source close to Amini’s family told the US-based Human Rights Activists inIran(HRAI) that Amini was sentenced to death on charges of “sab ol-nabi” (insulting the prophet). She was reportedly arrested following online monitoring by Iran’s Cyber Police (Fata). The exact content of her posts has not been publicly disclosed.In the second case, Amini was sentenced to 12 years, six months and one day on charges including acting against national security and spreading propaganda against the regime.Amini was arrested by security forces duringJanuary’s nationwide protests, which were suppressed with a deadly crackdown. Thousands were reported killed, while the HRAI news agency, Hrana, said more than 50,000 people were arrested.In an audio recording released last month and attributed to Amini, she appealed for international intervention, calling on the UN, lawyers and rights groups to investigate her case.“I do not want to make a hero out of myself today. I only want one thing: be my voice,” she said.“I am an innocent young girl with so many hopes and dreams,” Amini said. “I have parents who are waiting for me. A family that every night, with the fear of losing me, turns their night into morning.”Rights groups warn that the Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to instil fear and suppress dissent. According to the Oslo-based Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), more than 600 executions have already been carried out this year.View image in fullscreenIranians block a Tehran street during nationwide protests in January, which were sparked by the weak economy but became political and anti-regime.Photograph: Mahsa/Middle East Images/AFPMahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of IHRNGO, said Amini’s case should be seen as a serious warning.“Sentencing a young woman to death for what she posted on social media risks normalising the use of the death penalty against peaceful expression and pushing the boundaries of the death penalty even further,” he said.Amiry-Moghaddam added that the Iranian authorities were testing the international community’s “tolerance” towards capital punishment. “If the international community does not respond firmly now, cases like this could become far more common,” he said.Under article 262 of Iran’s Islamic penal code, insulting the prophet Muhammad or revered Shia figures is punishable by death. However, article 263 provides exemptions for statements made while intoxicated or without deliberate intent, although offenders may still face up to 74 lashes in certain circumstances.According to the Iranian newspaper Khorasan, which confirmed the judicial proceedings, Amini told the court she had posted the remarks while hallucinating after taking psychedelic mushrooms with friends and her defence argued it was a “slip of the tongue”.The presiding judge rejected her defence, reportedly asking: “Why, in that same hallucinatory state, did you not insult other individuals or opponents of the regime, such as America and Israel?”Amini’s death sentence is not final and remains subject to appeal before Iran’s supreme court.Family of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for helpRead moreThe student’s sentencing comes at a time when Iranian lawmakers are seeking tocriminalise contact with all foreign media,including posts on social media deemed to be financed by another country.Elnaz*, 24, who took part in the protests in Tehran in January and was arrested over social-media posts at the height of the war in March, said she lived in constant fear of surveillance.“I was arrested even though my social-media account was private. So it’s not just the regime’s cyber-police we have to worry about. There’s also this constant mistrust, this feeling that someone is watching me all the time, even when I’m alone in my room.“I’m scared to post anything on social media … but after everything they’ve put us through, do we really have anything left to lose? They can kill us even if we don’t post anything on social media.”Although executions in Iranhave surged in recent years, reaching their highest level in three decades, death sentences for blasphemy remain relatively rare. The last documented case was on 8 May 2023, whenYousef Mehrad and Sadrollah Fazeli-Zare were executedafter being convicted of blasphemy-related offences tied to social-media activity.*Name has been changed to protect her identityExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentWomen in prisonCapital punishmentHuman rights (Global development)ProtestIranMiddle East and north AfricaSocial medianewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown – The Latest | India | The Guardian
description: A fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government, raising concerns that India is constricting voter freedoms and sliding further into autocracy. Lucy Hough speaks to South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Author: Lucy Hough
Headline: A fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government, raising concerns that India is constricting voter freedoms and sliding further into autocracy. Lucy Hough speaks to South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Content: 00:00:0000:00:00Today in FocusIndiaIndia’s cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown – The LatestA fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government and the closure of a historic protest site in Delhi. Two of the movement’s leaders have been imprisoned for five days for violating suppression measures. The protests, which began over frustration about education and unemployment, are now focused on voting rights. Modi’s government denies claims it is seeking to disenfranchise millions of voters.
