But its treatment of protesters has been criticised by the UN and Amnesty International and raised concerns that India is sliding further into autocracy. title: Leaders of India’s Cockroach party jailed for violating ban on protest site | India | The Guardian
description: Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das will spend spend five days in prison for entering Delhi’s Jantar Mantar – a historic protest site that has been closed by authorities
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das will spend spend five days in prison for entering Delhi’s Jantar Mantar – a historic protest site that has been closed by authorities
Content: Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, co-conveners of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), have been jailed for five days in Delhi.Photograph: Kabir Jhangiani/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAshutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, co-conveners of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), have been jailed for five days in Delhi.Photograph: Kabir Jhangiani/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIndiaLeaders of India’s Cockroach party jailed for violating ban on protest siteAshutosh Ranka and Saurav Das will spend spend five days in prison for entering Delhi’s Jantar Mantar – a historic protest site that has been closed by authoritiesWhy Indian voters are on the streetsHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiWed 14 Oct 2026 01.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against thebrutal crackdown on youth protestersin Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.11:32India's cockroach protesters defy Modi's crackdown - The Latest“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar todemand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.The CJP,alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.’How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’ Why Indian voters are on the streetsRead moreThe election commission has ​denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters ‌can re-enrol.Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed asweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight.View image in fullscreenDelhi police inspect vehicles near the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi on Tuesday.Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty ImagesIn the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”Ranka and Das ‌were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”.“Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi.The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.Kiran Stacey contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsIndiaProtestSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streets | India | The Guardian
description: Anger at electoral roll changes has boiled over, sparking a crisis for Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Anger at electoral roll changes has boiled over, sparking a crisis for Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government
Content: Protesters in Jammu and Kashmir call for the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.Photograph: Faisal Khan/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenProtesters in Jammu and Kashmir call for the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.Photograph: Faisal Khan/NurPhoto/ShutterstockIndia‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streetsAnger at electoral roll changes has boiled over, sparking a crisis for Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist governmentLeaders of India’s Cockroach party jailedHannah Ellis-PetersenandShaikh Azizur RahmanTue 13 Oct 2026 22.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.The 38-year-old migrant worker, born into a poor Muslim family, was not alone. Since last year, 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – have been removed from India’s electoral roll through a process known as SIR, or special intensive revision. In the nearly eight decades since India’s independence, never have the voter rolls shrunk by such a huge amount over such a short time.View image in fullscreenShahida Fakir is staying in a village in Bangladesh after she was detained on suspicion of being an illegal immigrant and pushed across the border.Photograph: SuppliedThe Narendra Modi government has called SIR a legitimate exercise to clean up the electoral rolls. Overseen by the election commission, tens of millions of dead and duplicate names have been removed. Yet so have the names ofmillions of living Indian citizens.Critics allege that the pledge to “purify” India’s voter roll of illegal immigrants has instead been used for more sinister purposes – disenfranchising tens of millions of Muslims, other minorities, and poor and lower caste communities, who are largely not BJP voters.In a matter of weeks, nationwide anger at SIR has boiled up and spilled out on to the streets of India’s biggest cities, presenting a formidable challenge to the government. Over the weekend, Delhi was transformed into a high-security fortress of barricades, roadblocks and tens of thousands of police and paramilitaries whodetained thousands of people, as they attempted to stop youth-led protests calling for the man who oversaw SIR, the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down immediately.11:32India's cockroach protesters defy Modi's crackdown - The LatestOn Monday, opposition parties – who have decried SIR as a “weapon for vote theft” by the Modi government –drew tens of thousands of supportersas they marched through the capital and presented a petition to the supreme court, demanding Kumar’s resignation. The youth-led Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, who were behind the call for Saturday’s action,have vowed to “fight on”in their protests against SIR.Opposition and civil society leaders allege that SIR has already given the BJP an electoral advantage in states such as Bihar and West Bengal, claims the party denied. Others say the exercise has had even more concerning implications: under changes to SIR unilaterally implemented by Kumar, the election commission has become the arbiter of Indian citizenship, a sweeping overreach of its remit.The consequences are already playing out in West Bengal, where Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) recently came to power and began a crackdown on “illegal” immigrants, complete with several new detention centres. Civil society groups say Muslims excluded by SIR are being targeted.Fakir was among them. Just three months after the voter list was published – and while her hearing to challenge her exclusion was pending – she was picked up by police and accused of being an illegal Bangladeshi immigrant.In July she was pushed over the border to Bangladesh, a country she had never been to nor had any connection with, and remains stuck there. “I have all the documents to prove I am an Indian citizen,” she said in a tearful phone call from the Bangladesh border village where she has been sheltering. “I fell on their feet and begged the police not to send me to Bangladesh but they pushed me over the border.”View image in fullscreenA protest march in Dhaka, Bangladesh, against India’s ‘push-ins’ of Muslims at the border in June.Photograph: Mamunur Rashid/NurPhoto/ShutterstockA Bangladesh border guard officer confirmed Fakir’s account. “We checked all her documents and are convinced that she is an Indian citizen,” they said. In September, her family submitted a petition to the supreme court challenging her deportation. The Indian government was given a month to respond.“All I want is to return to my family and my home in India. I am waiting desperately for that day,” she said. The backlog of millions of voters in West Bengal challenging their exclusion means it could be years before Fakir’s case is heard.Those across West Bengal who have been stripped of their votes speak of their terror of being accused of being an alien in their own land. Some have had benefits taken away. Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui, 80, from the North 24 Parganas district, said his grandfather had been a freedom fighter for Indian independence and three generations of his family were on the voter rolls. Yet after SIR, Siddiqui described his “humiliation” on finding his name gone.“With my name erased from the voter list, I am in constant terror. What if they send me to a detention camp?” he said. “I cannot bear to think about being separated from my children and grandchildren at this age, especially when all my ancestors have been buried in India.”View image in fullscreenSitting at his home in the village of Nehalpur in West Bengal, Mohammad Hedayet Ullah Siddiqui says that he has voted in all Indian elections since 1972.Photograph: Shaikh Azizur Rahman/The GuardianCritics say the problems began in 2023, when the Modi government changed the process for appointing the three-body election commission, giving majority control to the government for the first time. Within a matter of months, the Modi-led panel had appointed Kumar as the election commissioner in spite of opposition objections.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“For decades, the election commission was one of our more credible, independent bodies, but now that has been eroded,” said Ronojoy Sen, a senior fellow at the South Asian Studies Programme, National University of Singapore.By the following year, the new election commission body had begun SIR, starting in Bihar, where it immediately raised concerns among human rights groups after more than 6 million names were removed. Not long after the revisions, the BJP won a landslide victory in the Bihar state elections.Despite concerns over SIR rumbling on for months, it did not spark national protests until the Indian Express newspaper last month revealed that two members of the election commission had raised 14 objections to how voters were being excluded from the rolls, but they were unilaterally overruled by Kumar.“India has always been a flawed democracy but at least citizens felt they had the right to vote and that elections were regular and fair,” said Sen. “SIR has taken away that right. From how it has been conducted, it’s difficult to see how the motive was anything other than to enhance the election prospects of the BJP.”View image in fullscreenBJP supporters celebrate during vote counting at state elections in West Bengal in May 2026.Photograph: Dibyangshu Sarkar/AFP/Getty ImagesThree former election commissioners have openly criticised SIR as a “hostile exercise” that has undermined the sanctity of the country’s electoral rolls by focusing on the exclusion – rather than inclusion – of voters. OP Rawat, a former chief election commissioner, described changes to the voter registration form as “wrong and illegal”.Ashok Lavasa, who was an election commissioner between 2018 and 2020, called for the SIR to be scrapped. “An unfair procedure has been imposed on millions of people in the country, and you have the judiciary which has validated that,” he said last month. “How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?”None have been more vehement in their opposition than SY Qureshi, who was chief election commissioner between 2010 and 2012. “This is a national harassment exercise designed to throw Muslims off the electoral roll,” he claimed. “The only way to restore the credibility of India’s elections is to restore those deleted voters.”The BJP has denied any political involvement or motive in the SIR process, accusing the opposition Congress party of “jealousy” over its recent electoral victories and saying any deleted voters can simply re-enrol. The BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedisaid the allegations were “disinformation” and part of an opposition campaign “being orchestrated to create an atmosphere of division and anarchy”.Nonetheless, the election commission has appeared to accept some flaws in the process. Late last week, it belatedly put a cap on the number of voter deletion forms – which allow people to submit objections on behalf of others – after incidents in which people submitted thousands of forms targeting legitimate Muslim voters.Public anger, meanwhile, has continued to build. In Delhi, where the SIR exerciseleft millions of people off the draft list, protests are expected to continue this week.A Delhi resident for 30 years, Prashant Tandon, 60, said he could not believe it when a notice came to his door, questioning his life as a voter. “If someone doubts my citizenship, they should produce evidence against me,” he said furiously, adding that he would be protesting alongside the young people. “I should not have to prove that I am an Indian citizen.”Additional reportingAakash HassanExplore more on these topicsIndiaSouth and central AsiaNarendra ModiHuman rightsBangladeshnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stopping Pip for ADHD or autism would not make big savings, says thinktank | Benefits | The Guardian
description: Resolution Foundation says ‘crude changes’ to benefits system would probably make it harder for people to work
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Resolution Foundation says ‘crude changes’ to benefits system would probably make it harder for people to work
Content: The number of Pip claimants has gone up rapidly in recent years, particularly among younger people with mental health issues, ADHD or autism.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe number of Pip claimants has gone up rapidly in recent years, particularly among younger people with mental health issues, ADHD or autism.Photograph: Johner RF/Getty ImagesBenefitsStopping Pip for ADHD or autism would not make big savings, says thinktankResolution Foundation says ‘crude changes’ to benefits system would probably make it harder for people to workPatrick ButlerSocial policy editorWed 14 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBanning people with anxiety, ADHD or autism from claiming disability benefits would not deliver major financial savings and would probably make it harder for them to get or stay in a job and participate in society, a leading thinktank has warned.TheResolution Foundationsaid any proposals to make certain mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions ineligible for personal independence payments (Pip) would be “crude changes” aimed at hitting unrealistic savings targets.But it warned that Pip was “failing on several fronts” and called for a major overhaul to keep a lid on costs – currently rising at an “unsustainable” rate – and restore public trust in a benefit widely seen as unfair and dysfunctional.Young people’s Pip claims for ADHD and autism ‘rising fastest in affluent areas’Read moreAbout £4.4bn a year could be saved if Pip support was better targeted, it said. Cash support could be removed from an estimated one in six working-age Pip claimants (670,000) who report having no extra costs as a result of their disability.However, it added that any reforms should proceed with caution because of the success of Pip in ensuring high numbers of disabled and ill people were able to participate in “economically valuable” activities, such as work, caring, training or volunteering, that they would not be able to do otherwise.Official concern over Pip has soared in recent years, in part because of the rapidly rising number of claimants, particularly among young people, with much of that sharp increase linked to claims for mental health, ADHD and autism.Spending on Pip in England and Wales has risen in real terms by 183% since it was introduced in 2014. This year the bill is expected to be £28bn, rising to £34bn by the end of the decade, according to official forecasts.Attempts by the previous Labour administration under Keir Starmer to push through £5bn of crude savings to Pip collapsed last year amid a rebellion of backbench MPs. His successor, Andy Burnham, has said renewed attempts to reform benefits would not involve “crude cuts”.Welfare officials, who are awaiting anofficial review of Pip by welfare minister Stephen Timmsand the Milburn review of the youth jobs crisis, are understood to beconsidering proposalsto exclude under-25s from the Pip system.Pip has also found itself at the heart of culture war rows, with some, such asthe Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, arguing it should not be paid to claimants with so-called “mild” conditions that were not disabling or likely to incur higher daily living costs.The Resolution Foundation said attempting to link Pip awards to particular conditions was simplistic and impractical as most claimants reported multiple conditions – often combining physical, mental and behavioural conditions.Burnham has a chance to overhaul Pip. Here’s what a truly progressive system could look like | Frances RyanRead moreLindsay Judge, the thinktank’s research director, said: “Pip is a vital benefit for disabled people that enables them to participate in society and live fuller and more active lives. But the current system is failing on several fronts – claimants don’t trust it, awards don’t fully reflect the nature of disability today and spending is rising unsustainably.“As well as continuing to provide cash awards to help with ongoing additional costs, a reformed Pip system should focus on supporting disabled people to participate in society. A system more attuned to people’s needs would also mean that around one in six current Pip recipients who don’t face significant limitations or additional costs because of their disability would no longer qualify for cash support.“There is no perfect system of disability support, but one that better reflects the fact that people often have multiple and fluctuating conditions must target greater support and engagement where it’s needed, and avoid waste where it’s not.”A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “Pip is awarded based on a functional assessment that determines how a condition impacts a person’s day-to-day needs. But as the Timms Review report made clear, Pip is no longer fit for purpose and the recommendations from its final report will lay the foundation for sustainable reform.”Explore more on these topicsBenefitsMental healthNeurodiversityResolution FoundationState benefitsWelfareDisabilitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Volodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink access | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president accused US president of picking the other side after four years of war
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Ukrainian president accused US president of picking the other side after four years of war
Content: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham in London.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Pool/APView image in fullscreenUkraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham in London.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/Reuters Pool/APUkraineVolodymyr Zelenskyy feels ‘betrayed’ by Donald Trump over Starlink accessUkrainian president accused US president of picking the other side after four years of warDan Sabbagh,Jessica ElgotandAndrew Rothin KyivWed 14 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has said he feels personally betrayed by Donald Trump after it emerged that Ukraine’s military has had its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite squeezed, raising doubts about long-term US support for Kyiv.The Ukrainian president, on a visit to London, accused Trump of picking the other side after more than four years of war, risking a breakdown in relations already strained by theUS agreeing to buy diesel from Moscow.Ahead of a meeting with prime ministerAndy Burnhamin Downing Street, Zelenskyy appeared in a TV interview where he was asked whether the sudden restriction of Starlink was deliberate and if he felt betrayed by Trump.“Really, yes … but it’s a little bit more complicated ⁠than just my emotions or my feelings,” the Ukrainian president replied, adding: “It’s a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner.”Overnight, Ukraine’s military reported that, without explanation, the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, wasno longer working at speeds greater than 100mph.That effectively rendered most of the drones used byUkraineto strike behind the frontlines inoperable – and, it later emerged, affected the most effective air defence system to stop Russian jet-powered attack drones bombing Kyiv.“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely. Because it was 1am at night, Starlink was blocked by SpaceX and the United States,” Zelenskyy said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukrainewithout any advance warning from the USfor a second night. For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.Trump denied that his administration had cut intelligence sharing on Tuesday, but Zelenskyy said in an interview with US broadcaster NPR, aired on Wednesday, that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited in the future.The US president has demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, which he has blamed for the high cost of diesel, although most analysts say the closure of the strait of Hormuz after the US-Israel attack on Iran has had a far larger impact on global energy prices.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham greeted Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, warmly at No 10.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/ReutersThe two leaders fell out in the spring of 2025 during a disastrous visit by Zelenskyy to the Oval Office, where the US president said: “You don’t have the cards” to win the war. The row was followed by a brief pause in intelligence sharing and a desperate scramble by European allies to calm the row.Burnham met Zelenskyy in Downing Street on Wednesday, hours after he promised MPs that the Ukrainian president “would not leave empty-handed” and that he had tasked officials with drawing up further sanctions and options for speeding up military aid.As the pair met at No 10, he promised that Britain’s support for Ukraine would remain constant. “You have seen the solidarity and the support you have got from everybody here in Britain. We are behind you and that will not change,” he said.Zelenskyy had met King Charles in Buckingham Palace earlier on Wednesday.In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death tollRead moreIn brief remarks to reporters, Zelenskyy said he hoped to raise access to Starlink and intelligence sharing in his meeting with the British prime minister.Burnham pledged that he would accelerate the supply of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which the country uses to counter Russian drone strikes and said they were looking for “all possible avenues” of further support.The prime minister also said he was prepared to discuss the ceasefire proposed by Trump on attacks on energy infrastructure but acknowledged that Moscow had not abided by it.“Sadly, what we have seen from Russia is further attacks on critical national infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.Earlier Burnham told MPs at PMQs that he wanted to be “careful” about potential criticism of Trump that might risk exacerbating tensions, saying he was “laying the ground” for a reconciliation: “I will listen to President Zelenskyy carefully, but he won’t be going away from Britain today empty-handed.”The UK is also set to give £17m in funding towards repairs to the protective roof over the destroyed Chornobyl nuclear power plant which was damaged by Russian drone strike last year.The meeting, which lasted just over an hour, began as Burnham greeted Zelenskyy with a hug on Downing Street, before the pair walked to the door of No 10 and posed for photographs, flanked by Irish Guards in full ceremonial uniform.Musk said the decision to curtail Starlink was not one made by him. The communications system is not directly licensed to clients who are using weapons, and the Ukrainian military was linked to a related network called Starshield, which is operated by the US government.“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Trump.Terminals travelling at more than 100mph and using a version of Starlink for the military and other national security agencies suddenly lost connectivity, said Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser on military technology to Zelenskyy, in what appeared to be a targeted outage meant to disrupt military operations.“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” said Beskrestnov, who is also a popular military blogger. “It’s clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | EditorialRead moreLimiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s air defences because it is being used, according to Beskrestnov, in “the most current effective solution”: interceptors that target the jet-powered Shahed drones now deployed in large numbers to bomb Ukraine.“With their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend ourselves,” he added in a follow-up post. Shahed interception rates had already dropped from more than 90% to about 60% when Russia upgraded its engines to jet power in the early summer.It also complicates Ukraine’s use of medium-range, mid-strike drones for hitting targets in its territories occupied by Russia. But, ironically, it would have no impact on Ukraine’s deep strike bombing of oil refineries because Kyiv is banned from using Starlink to hit targets inside of Russia.Russia carried out a massive strike against Ukrainian energy infrastructure late on Tuesday evening, Zelenskyy said, launching 39 ballistic missiles and 120 attack drones against Kyiv and Kharkiv. The strikes hit five big power plants, key substations and other infrastructure that sustains major cities including Kyiv.At least 600,000 people were now without power, he said, adding that outages could become more widespread.Trump last week announced an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine that has not been confirmed. Zelenskyy said he had not heard of the deal until Trump announced it on his Truth Social site, and the Kremlin on Wednesday claimed it was abiding by the ceasefire because Trump had not specified which energy infrastructure it included.Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin’s spokesperson, told reporters: “The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified in detail, so it cannot be claimed that Russia is failing to observe it.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineAndy BurnhamVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK hospitality sector to offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people out of work | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Restaurants and pubs such as Nando’s and Fuller’s will create placements for 18- to 24-year-olds under DWP-backed scheme
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Restaurants and pubs such as Nando’s and Fuller’s will create placements for 18- to 24-year-olds under DWP-backed scheme
Content: The scheme is intended to help young people ‘get their first step on the ladder’ and build their careers.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe scheme is intended to help young people ‘get their first step on the ladder’ and build their careers.Photograph: AzmanL/Getty ImagesYouth unemploymentUK hospitality sector to offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people out of workRestaurants and pubs such as Nando’s and Fuller’s will create placements for 18- to 24-year-olds under DWP-backed schemeAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBars, clubs and restaurants will offer up to 100,000 jobs to young people not in employment, education or training (Neet) over the next three years in an effort to give them a first step on the ladder into work.The move comes before the publication of a report on Neets by the former health secretary Alan Milburn, who has warned that the number of young people not in work or education in the UKcould rise to 1.25 millionover the next five years unless ministers intervene.His full review into Britain’s crisis in youth unemployment, including recommendations to the government about how to tackle the crisis, is expected soon after the autumn budget on 28 October.Working with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), hospitality businesses including the restaurant chains Wagamama, Nando’s andBurger King, the hotel chain Premier Inn and pub chains including Fuller’s and Mitchells & Butlers will offer Neets aged 18 to 24 placements of up to four weeks to gain “the skills and confidence needed to take their first step into work”.The initiative, which will be launched by Andy Burnham during a visit to a hospitality venue on Thursday, comes after the DWPannounced a similar scheme for retailersincluding Marks & Spencer, Asda, Pets at Home and the John Lewis Partnership last month.The work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, said the scheme would help young people “get their first step on the ladder” and build their careers. “With the UK employment rate now the second highest in the G7, this will unlock 100,000 jobs and connect young people with employers ready to take them on and help them build a brighter future,” he said.Lucy Powell, the education secretary, is expected to announce a review of school exclusion changes, after research showed that students who are persistently absent from school are nearly four times more likely to end up unemployed and not in education or training.A consultation will gather views on measures to support students at risk of exclusion, improve integration into the classroom and help children stay engaged in the classroom.Powell said: “Absence and exclusion are too often a path to disengagement, with increased risks of becoming Neet. Too many young people who fall out of education risk being permanently left on the sidelines of work and opportunity.”Milburn has signalled that Britain’s benefits system should be overhauled, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships. Ministers are understood to be considering sweeping changes to the welfare system, includingscrapping a critical disability benefitfor under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.Milburn has previously argued that a national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work.The chancellor, John Healey, has indicated a readiness to curtail the government’s rising benefits bill, while McFadden has said there isa moral and economic caseto shake up the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has made demands for cuts to welfare a central plank of her attacks on the government, telling Burnham in prime minister’s questions (PMQs) on Wednesday that he should cut welfare to fund higher defence spending.But ministers will be wary of going head to head with Labour MPs, and will hope to avoid a repeat of thewelfare rebellionthat forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentLabourHospitality industryBurger KingMitchells & ButlersUnemploymentYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and extreme comments | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Party faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist views
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Party faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist views
Content: Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, was filmed calling Asian homeowners ‘parasites’.Photograph: ITVView image in fullscreenAlan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, was filmed calling Asian homeowners ‘parasites’.Photograph: ITVReform UKReform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and extreme commentsParty faces fresh crisis as three councillors quit after ITV undercover filming exposed violence, misogyny and racist viewsBen QuinnPolitical correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 15.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 17.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and election candidates for the party were caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views.Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from an ITV undercover investigation that aired on Wednesday.Reform leaderNigel Faragehas postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex on Thursday morning as the party tries to contain the fallout expected to come from further revelations in the coming days. That will include revelations from undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters.Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election.However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites,” and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.View image in fullscreenChris Whelan resigned from Reform UK on 12 October.Photograph: ITVFeeney won seats on Birmingham city council and Solihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”.Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues.Feeney was filmed with other candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, talking about where a local mosque might be built. After they make extreme racist comments in the discussion, Feeney says: “Oh god, we’re all going to end up in the papers”.Reform donations scandal: the final blow for Farage? – The LatestRead moreChris Whelan announced he had resigned from Reform on 12 October “on personal and health grounds”. Campbell is still in post.Dean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed separately making a range of comments during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection, including when he discussed what he would do with illegal immigrants crossing the Channel.Reform has been attempting to pre-empt the impact from the ITV investigation, which will potentially be at its most damaging when footage from inside Reform’s London HQ airs.The party used a statement issued on Wednesday night to accuse ITV and Hardcash Productions of “extreme methods of deception”.“They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees,” it said.The party said that this came at a time when Farage and other members of Reform were “being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation”.View image in fullscreenDean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed making comments about illegal immigrants during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection.Photograph: ITV“They have not included this in their report, despite being on notice since March this year. There is currently an ongoing police investigation relating to security breaches against Mr Farage, as is well known,” it added.Reform said that not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK, adding: “Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.”The latest crisis to hit the party comes at a time when it has been stalling in the polls and faces problems including the fallout from a different undercover investigation which filmed senior officials discussing a potential way tosecure foreign donations to the party.The outcome is also awaited of a parliamentary standards commissioner investigation into whether Farage should have declared a £5m gift from thecrypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.Bridget Phillipson MP, chair of the Labour party, said: “The extreme racism and appalling behaviour exposed by this investigation is truly sickening. Nigel Farage can’t shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples. Every Reform councillor, council candidate or party member found to have made such despicable comments must be thrown out of Reform UK immediately.”Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on 18 October at 10.20pm on ITV1, ITVX, STV & STV PlayerExplore more on these topicsReform UKLocal governmentNigel FarageLocal politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annually | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares
Content: OpenAI is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1.1tn.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1.1tn.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annuallyAccounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last yearRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings,according tothe Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped andhacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this monthone of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.Booming AI salaries have already had asignificant effect on housing pricesin San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIChatGPTAI (artificial intelligence)LondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of Chicago | US universities | The Guardian
description: Alleged assault follows report of gang-rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Alleged assault follows report of gang-rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism online
Content: The AEPi fraternity house near the University of Chicago campus in Chicago, where an alleged sexual assault was reported at a weekend party.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APView image in fullscreenThe AEPi fraternity house near the University of Chicago campus in Chicago, where an alleged sexual assault was reported at a weekend party.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APUS universitiesSexual assault reported at frat house near University of ChicagoAlleged assault follows report of gang-rape at frat house at Cornell, which ignited national uproar and criticism onlineUwa Ede-OsifoWed 14 Oct 2026 19.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 21-year-old woman reported being sexually assaulted last weekend at a fraternity house near the University ofChicago, as Greek life nationwide faces renewed scrutiny for recurrent misconduct.The incident allegedly took place on Sunday at about 1.50am at the off-campus Alpha Epsilon Pi residence,accordingto a university daily crime log.In a police reportobtainedby the Chicago Sun-Times, the woman said she was “not fully conscious” when she was found partially undressed inside a bathroom with a man, who was also semi-nude.Fraternities are the most likely place for unwanted sexual contact. Should they be shut down?Read moreShe told police, according to the report, that a group had blocked her friends, at first, from entering the bathroom.A person of interest has been identified, according to university officials.The individual is not a student and has been banned from campus, theyannouncedon Wednesday.No one is in custody, Chicago police said on Wednesday afternoon, adding that an investigation remains ongoing.Jonathan Pierce, a spokesperson for the fraternity, said on Wednesday there was no evidence its members had participated in the assault or were aware of it.“When AEPi members (there were several “sober monitors” during the party, including the chapter’s safety officer) became aware of the victim’s report, they offered assistance by providing food and water and even loaned a shirt to the victim as she reported being cold while she waited outside for emergency response,” Pierce said.“We are pleased that the alleged assailant has been identified and hope that the victim can find some solace in knowing that justice is being done.”The alleged assault follows a harrowing report of a gang-rape at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024. Recent news of the purported attack ignited national uproar and criticism of the Ivy League school’s perceived leniency toward the alleged offenders.New York state prosecutors havereopenedan investigation into the report.Under mounting backlash, Cornell has alsosuspendedall fraternity parties for the remainder of the academic year, as it assesses the safety of its Greek societies.Last week, the University of Arizona took a similar move, halting all fraternity activity in the wake of several hazing and physical assault allegations, includingaccusationsof a Greek organization coercing recruits into binge drinking and swallowing live goldfish.Explore more on these topicsUS universitiesRape and sexual assaultUS crimeHigher educationChicagoFraternities and sororitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lawyers for man shot by ICE in New York City say agent did not identify himself | New York | The Guardian
description: Account by Oscar Belgal differs sharply from that of DHS agents, who fired into vehicle with young boy in back seat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Account by Oscar Belgal differs sharply from that of DHS agents, who fired into vehicle with young boy in back seat
Content: Eyewitness footage shows Oscar Belgal being detained by ICE agents in the Bronx borough of New York City, on 8 October.Photograph: Pedro Almarez/ReutersView image in fullscreenEyewitness footage shows Oscar Belgal being detained by ICE agents in the Bronx borough of New York City, on 8 October.Photograph: Pedro Almarez/ReutersNew YorkLawyers for man shot by ICE in New York City say agent did not identify himselfAccount by Oscar Belgal differs sharply from that of DHS agents, who fired into vehicle with young boy in back seatAssociated PressWed 14 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLawyers for a man wounded by an immigration officer while driving with his young son inNew YorkCity said in a court filing Wednesday that the agent who shot him never identified himself before he ran up to the car, smashed one of its windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.The account by lawyers for Oscar Belgal contrasted sharply with the version of events outlined by Department of Homeland Security officials. They have said officers opened fire only after Belgal smashed his car into two government vehicles and “accelerated toward other officers”.The Legal Aid Society, in a petition filed in Brooklyn federal court seeking Belgal’s release, said he had picked up his son from school and was stopped in front of a fire hydrant, looking for a parking spot, when “an anonymous, masked man” stormed up to the vehicle with his gun drawn, followed by other masked men with guns.“The men did not identify themselves, show any documents or otherwise communicate with Oscar in any substantive way,” Belgal’s lawyers wrote. “Instead, without identifying himself, the first man struck and shattered Oscar’s window and began firing a pistol into Oscar’s car while his son cowered in the back seat. One of those bullets struck Oscar in the neck and he immediately began to bleed.”New York City police security camera footage released by the department last week shows some of the encounter but doesn’t conclusively resolve the dispute about how the shooting happened.The video shows a man wearing a sweatshirt and a red hat running up to the car with his gun pointed at Belgal, then immediately using the barrel of his gun to bash the driver’s side window. The window shatters on the second blow.A second officer comes into view alongside the car and draws his gun. Belgal then pulls into the street, away from the two officers. The car pulls out of view of the camera, with the officer in the red hat in pursuit.Whatever happened next didn’t appear on the NYPD’s security cameras, but the chase ended just a moment later, with Belgal’s damaged car resting against a concrete barrier with bullet holes in its windshield and a rear window.Video from bystanders and NYPD body camera footage show that ICE officers handcuffed Belgal and tended to a gunshot wound to his neck as he sat on the pavement outside the car. NYPD officers took Belgal to a nearby hospital.DHS didn’t comment Wednesday on the claims by Belgal’s lawyers, saying the incident remains under investigation. But DHS officials have maintained that ICE officers fired their weapons because they believed their lives were in danger.Belgal’s lawyers said he didn’t learn the men were ICE officers until he awoke later in the hospital. They say he remains detained at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, where he has yet to receive surgery to remove the bullet lodged in his neck. They also say he has lost sensation on the left side of his face and now has impaired hearing.The Federal Bureau of Prisons, which manages the jail, didn’t immediately comment.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US immigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ilhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source says | Ilhan Omar | The Guardian
description: Federal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraud
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Federal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraud
Content: Ilhan Omar, a frequent target of Donald Trump’s anti-Somali rhetoric, said she would ‘not be silenced’ by the justice department’s investigation.Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersView image in fullscreenIlhan Omar, a frequent target of Donald Trump’s anti-Somali rhetoric, said she would ‘not be silenced’ by the justice department’s investigation.Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/ReutersIlhan OmarIlhan Omar’s phone seized and relatives subpoenaed in criminal inquiry, source saysFederal authorities issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas in inquiry into potential immigration fraudUS politics live – latest updatesAssociated PressWed 14 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal authorities investigating the Minnesota representativeIlhan Omarseized the Democratic lawmaker’s phone and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to a person briefed on the inquiry.The subpoenas were issued for a grand jury collecting evidence inMinnesotaas federal authorities investigate potential fraud in Omar’s immigration paperwork, said the person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss an ongoing investigation. The investigation led to federal agents searching Omar’s Washington DC home on Monday just weeks before theNovember midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election.The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Markwayne Mullin, has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork.Democrats rebuke federal raid of Ilhan Omar’s home: ‘rogue abuse of power’Read moreOn Tuesday, Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, said in a Fox News interview that “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and that her office is also looking into issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.“If there was a crime that was committed, it will be prosecuted,” Pirro said.The search of Omar’s home so close to next month’s midterm contests, which will determine control of the House and the Senate, was swiftly condemned by Democrats, who accused the administration of targeting the representative for political purposes. Omar, in a statement on X, called the search an “attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement”.“For 10 years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation,” she said. “I will not be silenced.”A phone message seeking comment was left on Wednesday with a representative for Omar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThough the Republican focus on Omar’s background dates back years, the search notably took place three weeks before the November midterms, in which Omar is seeking re-election. The justice department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.Omar, who was first elected to the House in 2018, represents Minnesota’s fifth district, including Minneapolis. She is part of “the Squad” of progressive lawmakers who are a vibrant political force on the left wing of Congress but have also endured repeated attacks from Trump, dating back to his first term. She was one of the first two Muslim American women in the House and the first African refugee to be elected to Congress.Explore more on these topicsIlhan OmarTrump administrationUS justice systemUS politicsWashington DCMinnesotanewsShareReuse this content

title: US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms | Inflation | The Guardian
description: Final inflation report before voters go to polls comes amid widespread anger over cost of living under Trump
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Final inflation report before voters go to polls comes amid widespread anger over cost of living under Trump
Content: An employee arranges vegetables at a Whole Foods in Los Angeles.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn employee arranges vegetables at a Whole Foods in Los Angeles.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesInflationUS inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midtermsFinal inflation report before voters go to polls comes amid widespread anger over cost of living under TrumpSend us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm electionsGaya GuptaWed 14 Oct 2026 10.29 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRepublicansare entering the midterm elections with the highest rate ofinflationsince the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7%in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with theTrump administrationover the cost of living.Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%.Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.Price increases this year have largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record high last month.September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990.inflation chartThe economy has consistently been cited as a top issue for American voters, as rising gasoline prices and persistent inflation have eaten into household budgets. Higher energy prices from the Iran war have cost Americans more than $1,020 per household, according toBrown University, and a total of $133bn for all US consumers.Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for inflation that is outpacing their earnings, including 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump.In recent weeks, Trump has attempted to downplay his administration’s role in price increases, pointing to the Iranian government as the cause of the squeeze. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest inflation report.On Tuesday, Trump posted on social media that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate effort to affect the upcoming elections.“They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran … in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE,” he wrote.Later on Tuesday, Trump defended his record on the economy during a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, saying that his support for families has been “substantial”. “Every time they want to try and get me, they say ‘affordability’,” he said.Heightened inflation will put more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates, its tool to cool prices. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing elevated prices. Higher rates affect the cost of borrowing money, including mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate, applied to the most commonly used loans for home ownership, is up to 7.40%.“Inflation in the US has come in higher than expected, in a blow toDonald Trumpahead of November’s midterms,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, in a statement. “The president has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.”Explore more on these topicsInflationTrump administrationUS economyDonald TrumpUS-Israel war on IranEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn for money-laundering failures | Bank of America | The Guardian
description: Third-largest fine in US treasury’s history, due to failure to report suspicious activity, may affect third-quarter earnings
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Third-largest fine in US treasury’s history, due to failure to report suspicious activity, may affect third-quarter earnings
Content: The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Bank of America’s failings exposed ‘the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks’.Photograph: Arlyn McAdorey/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said Bank of America’s failings exposed ‘the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks’.Photograph: Arlyn McAdorey/ReutersBank of AmericaBank of America fined $1.2bn for money-laundering failuresThird-largest fine in US treasury’s history, due to failure to report suspicious activity, may affect third-quarter earningsReutersWed 14 Oct 2026 07.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBank of America(BAC.N), has been fined $1.21bn by US regulators for widespread failures to detect ‌potential money laundering and other illicit activity, a penalty the bank said will hurt third-quarter earnings.The US treasury department said the fine, the third-largest in department history, is due to the bank’s failure to report more than $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, including $1bn that posed national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks.“Financial institutions are on the ​front lines of protecting our economic and national security,” the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said in a statement. “When a bank of this size ​fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the ⁠entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks.”The treasury said the bank “prioritized its revenues” in building compliance programs, and overly relied on inquiries ​from outside parties such as law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls.The consent order requiresBank of Americato hire an ​independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity that the bank failed to detect at the time and report those transactions to the treasury department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network.Bank of America settles Epstein survivors’ lawsuitRead more“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” said a Bank of America spokesperson in a statement. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of ​employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised ​by our regulators.”The spokesperson added that the bank’s third-quarter results due for release on Wednesday would include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2bn, which will reduce quarterly net income ‌by approximately ⁠17 cents a share.Analysts have estimated adjusted earnings per share of $1.10, according to mean estimates compiled by LSEG, but that excludes one-offs like this fine.Shares were down 2.7% in after-hours trading after closing the day down 1.1%.The penalty is likely to add to negative investor sentiment and raise concerns about higher expenses and whether Bank of America can maintain its roughly $6bn quarterly share buyback pace, the UBS analyst Erika Najarian said in a note.With earnings due ​on Wednesday, “we think shares likely underperforming at ​open”, she said.She noted there ⁠was no asset cap, a regulatory penalty that would limit how large the bank could grow.As part of the fine, the treasury department’s office of the comptroller of the currency levied a $750m civil ​penalty against the lender, the largest ever for the regulator, citing failures to address shortcomings in its anti-money ​laundering programs that were ⁠identified as part of a 2024 cease-and-desist order from the watchdog.The regulator said the bank’s compliance program was “deficient and ineffective”, and its transaction monitoring system caused the bank to delay filing suspicious activity reports on billions of dollars of transactions.In addition, the bank paid an $11.6m fine to the treasury department’s office of foreign ⁠assets control ​for more than 400 apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs. The treasury said the bank mistakenly ​processed millions of dollars in payments that violated sanctions programs targeting countries including Russia and Iran.The fine comes days after American Expresswas also hit with a $350m penaltyfor similar anti-money ​laundering shortcomings.Explore more on these topicsBank of AmericaBankingRegulatorsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: District court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after Trump administration blocked access to three outlets last month
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: District court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after Trump administration blocked access to three outlets last month
Content: Katie Zacharia holds her first press briefing at the White House in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenKatie Zacharia holds her first press briefing at the White House in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersTrump administrationJudge extends White House access to banned media outlets CNN, MS Now and PoliticoDistrict court judge Timothy Kelly was ruling after Trump administration blocked access to three outlets last monthJeremy Barrin WashingtonWed 14 Oct 2026 00.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge ordered the White House on Tuesday to continue allowing journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico to access the building as the media coalition’s lawsuit against theTrump administrationplays out.Timothy Kelly, a district court judge, had on 24 Septembergranted a 14-day reprievefor the news organizations, whichsix days earlier had been bannedby the president in an extraordinary move from entering the White House grounds “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”.US justice department investigating TV networks over Trump pool coverageRead more“Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House ‘hard pass’ press credentials held by employees ofCNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO, thereby maintaining the status quo since the Court’s entry of a temporary restraining order on September 24, 2026,” the judge wrote in granting a preliminary injunction requested by the plaintiffs.The organizations filed a lawsuit on 21 September seeking to overturn the ban as a violation of their rights under the US constitution. But that temporary restraining order expired on Tuesday, bringing the media companies into court late last week to ask for a preliminary injunction that would lift the ban during the duration of the lawsuit, which could take months.During arguments at the E Barrett Prettyman federal courthouse in Washington,Kelly seemed inclined to lift the ban indefinitely, telling a lawyer for the federal government that his side had “a notice problem” that was “probably the biggest hurdle” they had to overcome.The Trump White House gave no advance notice to the media companies affected to say that they were at risk of losing their press badges, which the news organizations have said are essential to their ability to cover the administration. While the White House sent letters to the media companies informing them of the ban, they did so post-hoc, after building access had already been cut off, in violation of binding court precedent.In his ruling on Tuesday, Judge Kelly wrote that the plaintiffs “are likely to succeed not only on their due process claim, but also on their two First Amendment claims”. While access to the White House is not guaranteed, court precedent dictates that once it is provided to journalists, it cannot be taken away for editorial or viewpoint-based reasons.During arguments for a preliminary injunction on 8 October, media lawyer Theodore J Boutrous told the judge that Trump had offered a “confession” – in a Time magazine interview last week – that he was banning the media companies explicitly because of the content of their reporting, not because of any other considerations, such as national security.“The case has gotten stronger for the plaintiffs thanks to President Trump,” Boutrous told the judge.The judge seemed to agree. “President Trump’s own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes to alter their reporting on him, bolstering the case that his action here is sufficient to deter a reporter of ordinary firmness from reporting in the same way she had before,” he wrote.Although the White House has largely adhered to the judge’s prior ruling restoring access on a temporary basis, journalists for CNN and Politico have on occasion been prevented from performing “pool duty” – covering the daily activities of the president – because the administration has interpreted the judge’s temporary restraining order to solely require access to the White House complex, not smaller spaces like Air Force One or the Oval Office.The judge required the media plaintiffs to post a bond of $1.In a statement, Boutrous said of the judge’s ruling: “When the President issued his ‘ban on the free press,’ he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment. Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn’t like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers.”The court, he added, “was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this ‘unconstitutional ban on the free press’ for the foreseeable future”.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationCNNMS NowDonald TrumpUS politicsUS television industryUS press and publishingnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annually | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares
Content: OpenAI is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1.1tn.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1.1tn.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annuallyAccounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last yearRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings,according tothe Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners. The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped andhacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this monthone of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.Booming AI salaries have already had asignificant effect on housing pricesin San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIChatGPTAI (artificial intelligence)LondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Quickfire Doué and Dembélé inspire PSG to thrilling win at Manchester City | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Désiré Doué and Ousmane Dembélé struck early as Paris Saint-Germain ran out 4-2 winners against a stunned Manchester City despite Erling Haaland’s double
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Désiré Doué and Ousmane Dembélé struck early as Paris Saint-Germain ran out 4-2 winners against a stunned Manchester City despite Erling Haaland’s double
Content: Désiré Doué (left) and Ousmane Dembélé savour the moment PSG open the scoring.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDésiré Doué (left) and Ousmane Dembélé savour the moment PSG open the scoring.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianChampions LeagueQuickfire Doué and Dembélé inspire PSG to thrilling win at Manchester CityDavid Hytnerat the Etihad StadiumWed 14 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 18.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA penny for Pep Guardiola’s thoughts. The legendaryManchester Citymanager was back at the Etihad Stadium for the first time since his departure at the end of last season and, well, the announcement of you-know-what.Sporting a flat cap, Guardiola took his seat in the stands behind the City chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, and the chief executive, Ferran “Not” Soriano, and, certainly, the TV director seemed intent on scrutinising him – if the number of cutaway shots to him were any guide.Jackson and Barkley doubles sink feeble Fenerbahce in record Aston Villa winRead moreEverybody knows where Guardiola stands onthe great City scandal; the numerous guilty verdicts handed down to them on the 100-plus charges they have facedfor breaking the Premier League’s financial rules. He has backed his former employers to somehow disprove them. But what did he make of his old team here against the might of the defending European champions, Paris Saint-Germain?Not much in the first half would have been a reasonable conclusion. PSG played football from a higher plane and they might have led by more thanthe three unanswered goals they scored. But if defiance has been the theme for City – and it fed into Guardiola’s presence here – they produced plenty more of it during a thrilling second half.City refused to accept the inevitable. They threw everything at PSG. Erling Haaland ran on adrenaline as City created a flurry of openings. The No 9 was unplayable at times; he finished with two goals and a few near misses. City were a goal away from worrying PSG.The problem for them was the one that Maghnes Akliouche scored to put PSG 4-1 in front. It meant that City’s dream of an astonishing fightback was only an illusion. What a terrible concession it was for Gianluigi Donnarumma – and not for the first time.View image in fullscreenThe former City manager Pep Guardiola takes his seat at the Etihad.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianIt was a spin and blast from Akliouche on the edge of the area and Donnarumma appeared to have palmed the ball up and away. Except that it dropped all the way back down – quite a way back down – and into the net. How did it happen? It was one of many head-scratchers; the sheer weight of chances was difficult to process. PSG even threw in a late penalty fail by Ferran Torres, who came on as a substitute; his kick was weak and too close to Donnarumma. Are you missing it all, Pep?City must play under a cloud, certainly until their appeal against the charges is completed, and they ran into a PSG team that shimmered with menace.
