Luis Enrique’s starting XI featured seven players who are on the 30-strong Ballon d’Or shortlist. The manager had another three from it among his substitutes, including João Neves and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.PSG bristled with their trademark assurance on the ball; the beautifully grooved combinations. It does not matter how tight the spaces are. They back themselves to get out of them. Witness the opening goal and a scintillating piece of team play that began deep on the right-hand side of their defensive third.In the blink of an eye, PSG were surging up the flank and then opening out the move, Fabián Ruiz playing the final pass to Désiré Doué on the left. The winger cut inside and shot low for the near corner from outside the area. It was the precision that did for Donnarumma, although the former PSG goalkeeper had to do better at his post.View image in fullscreenOusmane Dembélé doubles PSG’s lead in the first half.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianWhen PSG landed the follow-up punch just 75 seconds later, City were reeling, the home crowd stunned. It was a goal that featured two crosses, the first from Ousmane Dembélé out to Doué on the left. He took the ball down and crossed back for Dembélé, who stole in behind Marc Guéhi. The run was too cute, the header  straightforward.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was no exaggeration to say that PSG could have had five by the interval. City had no defence to their cut and thrust; the sheer pace of it, the positional fluidity too. Achraf Hakimi appeared to be playing almost anywhere but right-back. He popped up inside the six-yard box in the 32nd minute only to send a free header against the post, but City were swiftly disabused of the notion that the danger had passed.View image in fullscreenVitinha sweeps home PSG’s third before the interval.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianPSG won the ball back and went for the jugular once again. Akliouche was involved, there was a lovely backheeled assist from Warren Zaïre-Emery and Vitinha lashed home a low drive. When Hakimi blew a one-on-one with Donnarumma on 39 minutes, it felt as though his team were toying with City.Enzo Maresca made a triple change at the interval, introducing Matheus Nunes, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Iliman Ndiaye – and the effect was immediate. City played with devil-may-care abandon. Their toothless first half was forgotten. Enzo Fernández blew a gilt-edged headed opportunity and Ndiaye worked Matvey Safonov before Haaland pulled one back. It was a whipped ball in from Ndiaye, which Haaland sent into the far corner with a flex of the neck muscles. He was not close in, either.Could City take the lifeline? Antoine Semenyo ran through and dinked against the crossbar. The offside flag was raised, although he looked to have been level. City needed the next goal to make it interesting. Instead, they lost the initiative after another Donnarumma lapse.It was the prompt for a whirlwind finale. Josko Gvardiol saw a header cleared off the line by Nuno Mendes, Fernández rattled the outside of a post and Haaland looped a header against the top of the crossbar before he scored again – a low finish after good work from Bouaddi. Haaland was denied the hat-trick when he stretched to prod at Nunes’ cross at goal – it was an excellent save by Safonov – and City finished with 27 shots and 52 touches in the opposition box. Those numbers would be enough for victory on most nights. Just not this one.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueManchester CityParis Saint-Germainmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I expect more’: the key questions from Martínez’s Manchester United broadside | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: From Jason Wilcox’s role to the views of the rest of the squad, we tackle the major talking points at Old Trafford after the defender’s outburst
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: From Jason Wilcox’s role to the views of the rest of the squad, we tackle the major talking points at Old Trafford after the defender’s outburst
Content: Michael Carrick is under pressure at Manchester United while Lisandro Martínez has launched a verbal attack on the club’s director of football Jason Wilcox.Composite: Getty, ReutersView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick is under pressure at Manchester United while Lisandro Martínez has launched a verbal attack on the club’s director of football Jason Wilcox.Composite: Getty, ReutersManchester UnitedAnalysis‘I expect more’: the key questions from Martínez’s Manchester United broadsideJamie JacksonFrom Jason Wilcox’s role to the views of the rest of the squad, we tackle the major talking points at Old Trafford after the defender’s outburstWed 14 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.32 EDTShareAfter Manchester United’s 2-0 loss at Atlético Madrid,Lisandro Martínez teed offat the director of football, Jason Wilcox, and the rest of the executive. “We don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams,” said the defender. “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox] … Really poor [the Atlético defeat] – I have to control myself a lot but something is a reflection of the mirror of how our club is at the moment.” Here we consider the key questions emerging from Martínez’s explosive remarks.Jason Wilcox: ‘best eyes’ at Manchester United or promoted too far and too fast?Read moreIs Martínez’s view reflective of the squad generally?Yes is the short answer. The Guardian has been told the decision to target three midfielders in Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Carlos Baleba caused bemusement in the squad that no other areas were strengthened in the summer. Carrick led United to third last term after the side only had 17 league games remaining when he took over in January, having been eliminated from the other competitions. The need for defensive reinforcements is particularly acute because the back four of Diogo Dalot, Martínez, Harry Maguire and Luke Shaw has been together since 2022. Martínez is out of contract next summer and it is thought the 28-year-old may not be offered a new deal or have his one-year option triggered by the club, so teammates are conscious his outburst also came because he expects to leave.How culpable is Wilcox?As United’s director of football the 55-year-old wields near-unilateral power on football decisions, with only Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who controls sporting policy, above him. If the buck stops with the executive, the most recent transfer window was Wilcox’s responsibility. This was the latest in a line of missteps on his United record. One concerns when Dan Ashworth (Wilcox’s predecessor) was ongardening leave from Newcastle in the first half of 2024, Wilcox interviewed potential replacements for Erik ten Hag before, oddly, deemingthat the head coach should stay. The Dutchman signed a fresh contract butwas sacked that autumn. Another involves Wilcox’s major falling out with the man he hired as the Dutchman’s successor, Ruben Amorim, after which the Portuguese said the director of football hadtold him he should change his favoured 3-4-3 shape. “I came here to be the manager of Manchester United – not to be the coach of Manchester United,” said Amorim, aftera 1-1 draw at Leedson 4 January (his job title was head coach). He was sacked the next day. Wilcox worked with Omar Berrada, United’s chief executive, at Manchester City, where Berrada rose to become chief football operations officer, and Wilcox became academy director. Wilcox moved to Southampton and became director of football from summer 2023 until April 2024,when he joined United, having been identified by Berrada, so there is scrutiny of his experience at elite level.View image in fullscreenLisandro Martínez’s post-match interview has exposed the divisions at Manchester United.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesHow much blame is Carrick’s?The 45-year-old’s ability to prosper is related to the quality of Wilcox’s work, primarily in the market, so he cannot be solely responsible for a dire six points from six league games and two victories in all competitions all season. Yet by definition his role as head coach demands Carrick do the best with his resources, and that progress is made on the training ground. On matchdays there is scant excuse for United’s disjointedness, inferior running stats and inability, twice, to take advantage against 10 men: the 1-0 loss to City andSaturday’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham. How is Carrick viewed by his players? According to Santos they back him. “We believe in the manager, we believe in the whole staff, we believe in [ourselves as] players,” he said after the Atlético game. “We are in a bad moment but we have to work to change this result.”.Is United’s unity and discipline crumbling?For further evidence see Amad Diallo’s Snapchat post after the defeat by Atlético: “Fucking disgrace; I have no words.” So United have a World Cup-winner, Martínez, aiming shots at Wilcox and by implication Ratcliffe and Berrada, and a fellow senior player, Diallo, cursing but in ambiguous fashion, adding to the sense of meltdown at the club because it is unclear whether the “disgrace” meant the performance, Martínez’s diatribe, the squad his teammate referred to as not good enough, or something else. All of this is mirrored on the pitch, where United’s 671.4km run in the Premier League is the fifth-lowest (Arsenal’s 716.2 is the highest), and their 581 sprints the fourth-lowest (Brentford’s 765 the most).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick has support from his squad but Manchester United’s form has dropped significantly this season.Photograph: Susana Vera/ReutersWhere are the Glazers in all this?In mitigation Wilcox can point to the six American siblings, who remain majority owners and whose family has placed an eye-watering £1.1bn-plus debt on the club that severely restricts the transfer budget. Wilcox oversaw a £155m summer outlay and a net spend of about £100m in a summer when City’s corresponding figures were £457.5m and about £175m. City buying players such as Enzo Fernández (for a British record-equalling £125m), Elliot Anderson (£115m), Ayyoub Bouaddi (£81m) and Iliman Ndiaye (£65m) showed their greater financial muscle, helped by being much better sellers of talent. How they have reached this point has, though, been thrown into sharp focusby last month’s verdictthat they have serially cheated.Are there positives for United?Any straw should be clutched at so Carrick and his staff can view the first 97 minutes of Baleba’s United career as a rosy augury. After entering on 59 minutes against Spurs, a cute swivel and deft chip to Bruno Fernandes was a moment as impressive as the rest of his debut, and at Atlético the 22-year-old hunted down opponents and crunched into tackles, suggesting his game contains energy, muscularity and skill. It’s early days but perhaps if Baleba had been fit to start the campaign (he was recovering from an ankle problem) he might have affected one or more of the defeat at Hull, the 2-2 draw at Everton when Ainsley Maitland-Niles equalised late, the 1-0 loss to City when Phil Foden was sent off after 23 minutes or the Carabao Cup elimination by Brighton.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Finding Renée Richards: the complicated past and present of a trans sports pioneer | Tennis | The Guardian
description: A new book explores the story of the tennis player who sued to play in the US Open after transitioning and, fifty years later, supports bans on trans athletes
Author: Rich Tenorio
Headline: A new book explores the story of the tennis player who sued to play in the US Open after transitioning and, fifty years later, supports bans on trans athletes
Content: Renée Richards successfully sued the USTA to play in the 1977 US Open women’s draw.Photograph: Focus On Sport/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRenée Richards successfully sued the USTA to play in the 1977 US Open women’s draw.Photograph: Focus On Sport/Getty ImagesTennisFinding Renée Richards: the complicated past and present of a trans sports pioneerIn 1977, Richards sued to play in the US Open after transitioning. Now she supports bans on trans athletes in women’s sports. A new biography explores a complex legacyRich TenorioWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a story that dominated tennis headlines back in 1977: Dr Renée Richards, an ophthalmologist who excelled as a male amateur player before a sex-change operation, was suing for the right to play in the women’s draw of the US Open. Where did Richards go for legal assistance? None other than Roy Cohn.Better known for prosecuting suspected communists during the red scare andmentoringDonald Trump, Cohn turned his attention to fighting for Richards’s inclusion. His firm successfully argued the case – part of the narrative of a new biography, Finding Renée Richards: The Groundbreaking Story of Tennis’s Trans Pioneer by Julie Kliegman.“The lawsuit was really significant,” Kliegman says. “Obviously, clearly, it was very significant for Renée. But the decision was limited to her, as opposed to setting a precedent for trans people going forward.”For Kliegman –a sports journalist who is trans and non-binary– the project offered a chance to reexamine a 50-year-old cause célèbre and the topic of inclusion for trans people, in sports and in wider society, then and now.“There are a lot of parallels,” Kliegman says. “What struck me the most is that if anything, the conversation and dynamics between athletes are amplified today by the hostility [that is] more powerful than anything Renée would have faced.”Kliegman researched the story, in part, by accessing her subject’s multiple autobiographies as well as interview transcripts from another memoir project that never got published. They also interviewed Richards, now 92, in person multiple times. On one occasion, Richards showed Kliegman photo after photo of the celebrities who had posed with her over the years. Another time, the two met for lunch at the golf club where Richards still comes by regularly for a ladies’ day on the links.These meetings also gave Kliegman a chance for some back-and-forth with their subject over trans rights.“Renée today believes that trans women and girls should not be allowed to play girls and women’s sports unless they have not undergone so-called male puberty,” Kliegman says, describing this as a 180-degree shift from the lawsuit Richards filed in 1977. “She does not, overall, believe most trans athletes should be allowed to play girls and women’s sports. It was an interesting point of tension between me and Renée.”View image in fullscreenRenée Richards, center, attends the 2018 US Open.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/GC ImagesRichards “cites research that shows trans girls and women may have an advantage over cisgender peers,” Kliegman says. “My impression is that the research isn’t conclusive enough.”In writing the book, the author made a decision that went against their journalistic training but was in accordance with Richards’s wishes.“In recent years, you usually don’t refer to someone by their former name, former pronouns, when they change it,” Kliegman says, “even when referring to past points of their life. I came to understand [using their birth name when talking about their early life] was really important for [Richards] to fully depict the back and forth, the push and pull, Dick [Richards was formerly called Richard Raskind] and Renée.”The decision to use he/him pronouns in referring to Raskind, and she/her pronouns when it came to Richards, “was a tough one for me,” Kliegman says. “It goes against the journalistic norms I understand.” Yet, the author adds, “[Richards] felt I could not describe it accurately without ‘he’ and ‘her’ pronouns … So much in the book, Renée did not have any say over. It’s a journalistic project, not an authorized biography. Just about the only thing I think she needed a say over was [to] describe her respectfully.”As the book tells it, Raskind grew up in a Jewish-American family in New York City. His father was an orthopedic surgeon, and his mother was a psychiatrist. According to the book, Raskind was bullied by his older sister, who made him wear her clothing. As he entered young adulthood, matriculating at Yale University, he voluntarily began wearing women’s clothing in private, and presenting as a female on visits to Greenwich Village. All the while, he played men’s tennis. After medical school at the University of Rochester, he became an ophthalmologist in New York, and joined the Navy, where he competed in service tennis tournaments and worked aboard submarines. Throughout college, med school and beyond, he dated women. Yet for a time, he discussed his conflict over his gender identity with several psychoanalysts.“At the time, it was really, really difficult to get the care you needed as a trans person,” Kliegman says. “Also, on top of this, Renée was uncertain she was a woman. Certainly, she was a trans woman. Certainly, she was Renée. But there were also these other pressures encouraging her in the direction to present as Richard Raskind, whether it be for his career, for his love life, different forces.”In the late 1960s, Raskind traveled to a clinic in Morocco that performed sex-change operations, yet decided against surgery. He subsequently met and married Barbara Mole, the woman who would become his wife and the mother of their son, Nicholas. After the marriage ended, Raskind decided to undergo a sex-change operation, this time in his home town of New York, in 1975. He chose the new first name Renée, French for “reborn”.It was a new start in many ways: a new gender, a new name and a cross-country relocation to California. Yet Richards’s old love of tennis remained. She began competing as a woman, and having success.“As Richard Raskind, he was a great tennis player,” Kliegman says. “He ranked as high as the top 10 in the eastern region of 35-and-over players. He was quite good, with a powerful lefty serve that people would talk about and recognize. Dick became Renée – and she remained a very good tennis player.”Then she was outed – by broadcast journalist Richard Carlson, father of Tucker. With her background now public, Richards’s right to play women’s pro tennis was challenged by the United StatesTennisAssociation (USTA). The organization questioned whether Richards was “genetically female”, as quoted in the book. Officials demanded a test to see whether Richards had “the conventional XX sex chromosomes”, according to the book. Eventually, Richards sued.“Tennis is sort of the through line, one of the through lines of her life,” Kliegman says. “At any age, she could contribute to it … It sustained her through difficult times in her life. I think it’s what prompted the lawsuit – ‘Why I can’t I have this, this lifeline for me, a constant throughout my life, I should be able to play tennis, do the thing I love.’”After a judge ruled in Richards’s favor, she was allowed to compete in the US Open. In singles, Richards lost in the first round to the defending Wimbledon champion, Virginia Wade. In doubles, Richards had more success, joining Betty Ann Stuart to reach the final, where they lost to Martina Navratilova and Betty Stöve.View image in fullscreenBillie Jean King, left, advocated for Renée Richards to play on the women’s tennis tour in the 1970s.Photograph: Newsday LLC/Newsday/Getty ImagesThe difficulties for Richards did not end. Some female competitors treated her with hostility. The book credits Billie Jean King with convincing most of the women’s tennis world to let Richards play.“Billie Jean King was a huge part of Renée’s story,” Kliegman says. “She took a little while to make up her mind. She was quiet on the issue for so many years, but I understand why … She ended up calling doctors, asking them questions. She was not super familiar with the concept of trans people at the time.“She also met with Renée, which I think was really crucial … It convinced [King] that [Richards] was a woman like any other, who deserved a place on the tour. Billie Jean King showed support by playing doubles alongside Renée … which was huge, I think.”After retiring from professional tennis, she was ranked at No 20 in singles at her peak, Richards went on to coach Navratilova in what the book describes as a successful but sometimes bumpy partnership. Richards also returned to practicing ophthalmology for a long career, with a list of clients that included sports and politics journalist Keith Olbermann. There was a late-in-life tragedy for Richards: her son Nicholas died by suicide at age 47 in 2019.“It’s still raw for her,” Kliegman says. “I don’t think the tragedy of losing a child is something most people ever get over.”As Kliegman has gotten to know Richards, the author reflects that there is a little less daylight between their positions on trans rights, in part because of anti-trans policies of the Trump administration.“If I did not see her views on trans athletes themselves evolve, what I did see was that she now understands restrictions on trans athletes … are connected to this broader project the right wing has to try to eliminate trans people from public life,” Kliegman says. “It’s not a distinction she was making, and was comfortable with, before Trump was reelected.”Explore more on these topicsTennisLGBTQ+ rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Removing political speech from MLS fans is untenable – just ask Austin FC | MLS | The Guardian
description: The protests around an anti-ICE T-shirt show that politics can never be separated from sports, especially now
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The protests around an anti-ICE T-shirt show that politics can never be separated from sports, especially now
Content: Austin FC fans at a game on 9 September.Photograph: Scott Wachter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustin FC fans at a game on 9 September.Photograph: Scott Wachter/Getty ImagesMLSRemoving political speech from MLS fans is untenable – just ask Austin FCLeander SchaerlaeckensThe protests around an anti-ICE T-shirt show that politics can never be separated from sports, especially nowWed 14 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 16.47 EDTShareOn 26 September, Daniela Silva was expelled from Austin FC’s match with San Diego FC for wearing a T-shirt reading “Abolish ICE”.She saysshe was banned from Q2 Stadium for a year (Austin FC said that the ban was issued by the Austin Police Department, not the club, and that they offered to rescind it but that Silva declined).This happened, really, truly, and you cannot make this up, during Austin FC’s Hispanic Heritage Night. It also happened six days afterImmigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents shot a Venezuelan delivery driver, 28-year-old Wilber Garcés Pérez, in the torso in Austin, sparking protests in the city.The club’s Hispanic Heritage Night includedfolk dancesand highlighted local nonprofits serving the Hispanic community. “For Austin FC, celebrating Hispanic Heritage Month means celebrating the many cultures and communities that help make Austin what it is,”the club’s website still declares.And yet, a fan sporting a T-shirt with a very reasonable response to the ongoing assault on the Hispanic community of Austin, and indeed the nation, was banished.The club referred to Q2 Stadium policy, the wording of which is an exact copy of Major League Soccer’s fan code of conduct. Both prohibit, among other things, “Displaying signs, symbols or images for commercial purposes or for electioneering, campaigning or advocating for or against any candidate, political party, legislative issue, or government action.” It’s the same policy MLS has cited inseveral other instances, though an MLS spokesperson said on Wednesday that the league policy does not govern articles of clothing, but that a stadium policy would, hence why Silva was removed under the stadium policy.Regardless of which policy was responsible, Austin FC supporter groups Los Verdes and La Murga de Austin took issue, releasinga joint statement. “Opposition to ICE is not an abstract political debate for many of our members and neighbors,” it read. “It is about what is happening here, in our community, and about their safety, dignity, and ability to move through it without fear. In the days since, members of our community have questioned whether they feel safe and welcome returning to Q2. That should matter to Austin FC. The club has a responsibility to communicate clearly that our Hispanic and immigrant communities are welcome and safe at Q2.”At the club’s home game on Saturday, a 4-1 loss to runaway league leaders Nashville SC, La Murga de Austinwalked out in protestof Silva’s ejection, clearing out much of the supporters section. Its banner, reading “NO ICE IN THIS MELTING POT”, was taken down.“We love this club. But love is not silent,” La Murgasaid in a statement. “We are asking Austin FC to speak out – publicly, with conviction – against the injustice ICE is inflicting on the communities of Austin. The same communities the club says it supports. The same communities whose faces fill your marketing, whose voices fill your stadium, whose hands and hearts make this place what it is.”The club told the Guardian it is engaging with supporters on the topic of rules around political messaging in stadiums. But those rules are unjustifiable and, in this climate, possibly even untenable.MLS and its clubshave priorswhen it comes to these ideological confrontations with its own fans. In 2015, it ordered the removal of “Refugees welcome” banners at Toronto FC games. In 2019, the leaguehad to walk backits ban on the Iron Front symbol, first used by anti-Nazi paramilitaries in the 1930s and since broadly appropriated by the antifa movement – which has always been more of an idea than an actual organization but was nevertheless deemed to be political by the league. At the other end of the ideological spectrum, a man in a Make America Great Again hat was ejected from St Louis City’s stadium during a game last year.In the weeks after the war between Israel and Hamas began in 2023,MLS banned both Israeli and Palestinian flagsin its stands as a measure it called “temporary” but which, three years on, remains in place. A carveout exists, however, for Columbus Crew fans, who wereawarded an exemptionto fly a single Palestinian flag after the club signed Palestinian striker Wessam Abou Ali. Fans of the teams who field the league’s eight Israeli players can fly a single Israeli flag.Meanwhile, when Latino Nashville fans stayed away from their stadium in drovesfor fear of ICE arrestson their way home from games, the league did permit a banner reading “We’re not all here” to note their absence. The subtext was self-evident.Herein lies the trouble. The rules feel squishy because there is no one way to coherently and consistently keep political speech out of stadiums. The notion of apolitical sports, idealized by some as a kind of how-things-used-to-be paradigm that never existed, is a fantasy.MLS isn’t alone in trying to make it a reality. Most of the other American major leagues try just as hard to stay neutral in any matter that may cost them a few dollars by upsetting fans, or draw the ire of their overwhelmingly conservative owners. Then again, few sports seem to have hardcore fans as politically engaged as those in American soccer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’d also argue that the approach is counterproductive. An MLS stadium banning T-shirts with mainstream messages draws far more attention than just treating fans as adults with a worldview, who don’t need to be policed.MLS loves to highlight its hardcore fans when it sells itself to new audiences. Yet it also wants to sanitize them, rather than just accepting that most of them skew progressive and will proclaim their values accordingly.A league cannot cleanse itself of the inconveniences of reality outside its facilities, especially when that reality is expressly hostile to as many as 30% of its fans, per its own count. Pretending that it can only leads to ugly episodes like the one in Austin. Not to mention a disillusioned and mistrusting fanbase.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.This article was amended on 14 October to reflect MLS’s clarification that, though the wordings of the league’s fan code of conduct and the Q2 Stadium fan code of conduct are identical, the league’s does not govern articles of clothing while a stadium’s may.Explore more on these topicsMLSAustin FCUS sportsFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: NFL star Tyreek Hill’s estranged wife awarded $500,000 damages in battery trial | NFL | The Guardian
description: A jury found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro, ending a high-profile civil trial
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A jury found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro, ending a high-profile civil trial
Content: Tyreek Hill has played for the Dolphins and Chiefs.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APView image in fullscreenTyreek Hill has played for the Dolphins and Chiefs.Photograph: Rebecca Blackwell/APNFLNFL star Tyreek Hill’s estranged wife awarded $500,000 damages in battery trialReceiver liable for two counts, not liable on eight othersLakeeta Vaccaro alleged abuse by NFL receiverAssociated PressWed 14 Oct 2026 08.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Miami jury on Tuesday found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro – ending the high-profile civil trial involving theNFLwide receiver and his estranged wife.Hill, who has played for the NFL’s Kansas City Chiefs and Miami Dolphins, was found liable for two counts of battery – one stemming from an incident in January 2024, and another from April 2025. The jury awarded Vaccaro $500,000 in compensatory damages but did not award her punitive damages.The jury found Hill, 32, not liable for eight other counts that included battery, assault and continuing domestic violence.The trial involved allegations of abuse made by Vaccaro, 30, who on the stand described instances in which Hill allegedly pulled her hair and “treated me like I was, just, a man.” The jury was also shown a photo Vaccaro took of markings on her chest that she says were made during an argument between the pair. Hill took the stand last week and mostly denied what he called “false allegations” made by his estranged wife, while saying in one instance he shoved Vaccaro and “created a hole in the wall.”Hill embraced one of his attorneys and shook hands with others following the verdict before leaving the courtroom by himself.Vaccaro’s lawyer, Paul Schwiep, had asked the jury to “restore her dignity” and was seeking $8m in damages from Hill.“Money doesn’t undo the harm, but it’s just how our civil justice system works,” Schwiep said.Christi Bright said Hill was thankful after the trial.“Mr Hill was very pleased that he was able to get his story out and to be able to tell the world what he’s not been able to speak about,” Bright told reporters. “He’s very grateful.”Hill is still working his way back from a dislocated knee and torn ligaments suffered in September 2025 while he was with the Dolphins, but his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, has indicated that his client wishes to return to the NFL.Explore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Peralta shines as Rays seize on Ramírez error to level ALCS against Guardians | MLB | The Guardian
description: Freddy Peralta pitched six scoreless innings as Tampa Bay capitalized on a costly José Ramírez error to beat Cleveland 3-1 and level the ALCS at 1-1
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Freddy Peralta pitched six scoreless innings as Tampa Bay capitalized on a costly José Ramírez error to beat Cleveland 3-1 and level the ALCS at 1-1
Content: Tampa Bay pitcher Freddy Peralta celebrates after recording the final out of the fifth inning against Cleveland during Game 2 of the ALCS on Tuesday night in St Petersburg, Florida.Photograph: Mike Stobe/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTampa Bay pitcher Freddy Peralta celebrates after recording the final out of the fifth inning against Cleveland during Game 2 of the ALCS on Tuesday night in St Petersburg, Florida.Photograph: Mike Stobe/Getty ImagesMLBPeralta shines as Rays seize on Ramírez error to level ALCS against GuardiansFreddy Peralta pitches six scoreless innings in 3-1 winJosé Ramírez error opens door to three-run fourthALCS heads to Cleveland at 1-1 for Thursday’s Game 3AgenciesTue 13 Oct 2026 23.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFreddy Peralta pitched six innings of four-hit ball, Liam Hicks lined a two-run single after a fielding error by José Ramírez and the Tampa Bay Rays beat theCleveland Guardians3-1 on Tuesday night to level the American League Championship Series at 1-1.Game 3 of the best-of-seven series is Thursday night in Cleveland.Ramírez, whose two-run homer in Game 5 of the AL Division Series against Chicago helped the Guardians become just the 11th team to overcome a 2-0 deficit in a best-of-five series, misplayed a grounder in the fourth inning that led to three unearned runs against rookie left-hander Parker Messick.Junior Caminero walked to start the inning and Victor Mesa Jr grounded into a forceout that was originally ruled a double play. The Rays challenged the calls at both first and second base, and Mesa was ruled safe after a video review overturned first-base umpire Mark Ripperger’s decision.After Jonny DeLuca struck out, Chandler Simpson beat out a high chopper to shortstop, and Mesa reached third standing up when Ramírez failed to cover the bag.Ben Williamson followed with a grounder that scooted under Ramírez’s glove and between his legs after the ball hit the edge where the artificial turf met the infield dirt. The third baseman played back rather than charging.Williamson reached second and Simpson advanced to third. Hicks drove the next pitch to right-center for a 3-0 lead, electrifying the towel-waving, cowbell-ringing crowd of 32,125 at Tropicana Field.Peralta and three relievers needed no more support.With fans chanting “Freddy! Freddy! Freddy!”, Peralta struck out six to earn the win. He was fired up as he walked off the mound in the sixth after striking out Petey Halpin swinging on a full-count changeup.Kevin Kelly recorded two outs in the seventh, retiring Ramírez on a fly ball to center with two runners on.Left-hander Ian Seymour replaced him, and Chase DeLauter lined an RBI double into the right-field corner.View image in fullscreenRays teammates Taylor Walls and Richie Palacios celebrate after their 3-1 win over the Guardians in Game 2 on Tuesday night.Photograph: Julio Aguilar/Getty ImagesSeymour struck out Jo Adell swinging on a changeup, stranding runners at second and third. He pitched a perfect eighth before Bryan Baker retired the side in order in the ninth for his fourth postseason save.Acquired by the Rays from the Mets at the trade deadline, Peralta turned his season around in Tampa Bay, going 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts after posting a 4.99 ERA for New York.Messick, who grew up attending Rays games at Tropicana Field, took the loss after allowing six hits and three unearned runs in five innings.Cleveland had won four straight postseason games for the first time since winning their first six playoff games in 2016 on their way to a World Series berth.The 98-win Rays swept the New York Yankees in the Division Series before losing Monday’s ALCS opener 7-3.Explore more on these topicsMLBTampa Bay RaysCleveland GuardiansBaseballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: USWNT returnees earn 2-2 draw against Spain, an early World Cup wake-up call | USA women's football team | The Guardian
description: The US were on the verge of losing two straight at home, but second-half goals from Ashley Sanchez and Mallory Swanson salvaged a draw
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: The US were on the verge of losing two straight at home, but second-half goals from Ashley Sanchez and Mallory Swanson salvaged a draw
Content: Ashley Sanchez marked closed her USWNT comeback with a goal.Photograph: Drew Hallowell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAshley Sanchez marked closed her USWNT comeback with a goal.Photograph: Drew Hallowell/Getty ImagesUSA women's football teamUSWNT returnees earn 2-2 draw against Spain, an early World Cup wake-up callThe US were on the verge of losing two straight at home, but second-half goals from Ashley Sanchez and Mallory Swanson salvaged a drawPablo Iglesias Maurerat Subaru ParkTue 13 Oct 2026 21.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was nearly time for the panic button. Maybe not to press it, but to acknowledge that it’s within reach. A listless, shorthanded US women’s national team were struggling against Spain, down 2-0, and facing the ignominy of two straight losses at home after being badly exposed inSaturday’s 2-0 defeat in Washington DC.Then two players who had just returned to the team after long absences turned the tide. Ashley Sanchez and Mallory Swanson, after international goal droughts of 1,648 days and 801 days respectively, each scored in the second half to earn a 2-2 draw with the reigning World Cup champions.The result may have avoided the worst-case scenario, but the way it unfolded will give US fans pause. Just 255 days from the 2027 World Cup, these two defeats to Spain raise fresh questions before the side’s return to World Cup qualification in late November. But of course, there are caveats. Both teams were missing key players, and with the World Cup still nine months away there’s plenty of time to course correct.USWNT exposed by ruthless Spain as early goals settle heavyweight friendlyRead moreRather, the matches served as a helpful reminder of what many – including USWNT head coach Emma Hayes – already knew: Spain, the top-ranked team in the world, are the first side in decades who can legitimately outclass the US women, long the international standard bearers for the sport.“They are world class. We are still in progress,” Hayes said after Tuesday’s match. “I didn’t learn anything I didn’t already know.”Hayes made four changes from the starting lineup she rolled out against Spain on Saturday, handing Manchester United goalkeeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce the start in goal, tapping Claire Hutton in midfield, slotting Sanchez on the wing and attempting to shore up her backline with Angel City full-back Gisele Thompson.The US fared better in the game’s opening 10 minutes than they did for much of Saturday’s decisive loss, but were once again nearly undone by an early defensive lapse. Around the 15-minute mark, Spain attacker Clara Pinedo easily split US defenders Emily Fox and Kennedy Wesley with a perfectly timed run, and her close-range effort from the far side of the box challenged Tullis-Joyce but did not find the back of the net.Spain’s pair of goals came on opposite sides of the half-hour mark. The first came courtesy of two-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas, who made easy work of a tap-in at the near post. The ball arrived at her feet after a lovely, patient nine-pass sequence by the Spaniards; Barcelona midfielder Clara Serrajordi’s ensuing cross traversed the six-yard box, was deftly stepped over by Pinedo and found Putellas alone to finish her 43rd international goal.Six minutes later, the US handed Spain another goal. Under duress, Tullis-Joyce played a pass through her own central defenders and directly to Putellas, who strode forward and threaded an angled ball to OL Lyonnes midfielder Salma Paralluelo, who smashed her effort off the underside of the crossbar and into the goal, silencing the 18,648 in attendance in Chester, Pennsylvania.Once again missing center-back Naomi Girma and midfielder Sam Coffey, the US were exposed badly in defense; Spain, despite missing three-time Ballon d’Or winner Aitana Bonmatí and a host of others, were rarely challenged – at least not until the game reached its closing stages, and substitutions turned the tide.“We see the importance of the squad depth and how are players are developing, especially the less-experienced ones,” Hayes said, referring to the changes for both sides.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US finally found the back of the net at the 50th minute on the counterattack. Lindsey Heaps collected the ball in the US box and played it upfield to Sophia Wilson, who did well to fight off a defender and sprint upfield, eventually playing across to Sanchez, who rounded her defender and struck an inch-perfect finish past Spain keeper Misa Rodríguez. Sanchez was consistently in dangerous spots for the US.The Americans finally managed to seize a bit of control in the dying moments, after both teams made wholesale changes, with the equalizer coming again on the counterattack. Debutant Kate Del Fava did well to gain possession in her own half and found Michelle Cooper with a 40-yard, lofted ball. Cooper crossed to Swanson, who did well to finish from the top of the area. Improbably, midfielder Lily Yohannes very nearly won the game for the US in the final minute of stoppage time, with her effort parried just wide by Rodríguez.“I don’t think the group coming in the second half did themselves any harm,” Hayes said. “They were fearless.”The US continue to struggle against Spain, and are winless againstLa Rojain three matches over the last six years. In the interim, Spain have emerged as a dominant force, sharing the same possession-based, positional-play style the Spanish men have employed for decades. Spanish clubs have been rapidly professionalized over the last decade and those same clubs have pumped millions into youth development, populating the national team with a steady stream of young prospects.The US women look ahead now to a match against a much lesser opponent, albeit in a contest with much higher stakes: they’ll meet El Salvador in the quarter-finals of the Concacaf W Championship on 27 November in Mansfield, Texas, with direct qualification to the 2027 World Cup on the line.Explore more on these topicsUSA women's football teamSpain women's football teamWomen's footballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gianni Infantino faces grilling at potentially ‘explosive’ Fifa council meeting | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over the World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and the peace prize
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over the World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and the peace prize
Content: Gianni Infantino (left) will meet critics including Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin (right).Photograph: Mark Pain/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino (left) will meet critics including Uefa’s president, Aleksander Ceferin (right).Photograph: Mark Pain/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.FifaGianni Infantino faces grilling at potentially ‘explosive’ Fifa council meetingWorld Cup sell-off, Balogun and peace prize on agendaOpponents will press home need for independent reviewMatt Hughesin ZurichWed 14 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over his involvement in the abortedWorld Cup sell-off plan, theFolarin Balogun affairand the decision toaward Donald Trumpthe inaugural Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting at the world governing body’s headquarters on Thursday.TheFifapresident rejected repeated calls for an extraordinary general meeting of council in the summer after the emergence of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposals, but will meet his critics for the first time since then in Zurich, with one attender predicting that the talks could be “explosive”.Aleksander Ceferin, Victor Montagliani and Sheikh Salman Bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, the presidents of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation respectively, all of whom have called for Infantino to resign, will be present to press home demands for anindependent review of Fifa’s governance.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.In response to letters from Ceferin, Montagliani and Salman sent last month Infantinopledged to commissionan external review of Fifa’s future governance, but no details have been forthcoming, and there is scepticism over whether it will be truly independent.In addition to FFE, Balogun and the peace prize, which featured on an agenda circulated by Fifa last month, Infantino is also likely to face questions about a report in the Times this week that he received a “second salary” of about £1.3m in 2024, on top of the £3.9m declared in Fifa’s accounts.US Internal Revenue Service filings show a Fifa subsidiary in charge of running last summer’s World Cup paid Infantino $1.76m, that was not mentioned in Fifa’s annual report, in which his salary is recorded as 4.27m Swiss francs (£3.86m).Fifa statutes state that “the individual compensation of the Fifa president … shall be made public”. The governing body has denied wrongdoing.“Fifa does not pay a second salary to the Fifa president and complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation,” it said. “The Fifa president’s annual compensation, as well as other contractual benefits, are decided by the independent compensation subcommittee.“Fifa strongly rejects any claims that it has failed to disclose any financial information and has violated Fifa’s statutes. Fifa accounts are independently audited, and all declarations are in line with tax regulations in Switzerland, the United States and elsewhere.”Despite these controversies, and the public opposition of the European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations, Infantino is on course to be re-elected unopposed in March’s election.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMontagliani has rejected calls to standagainst Infantino to focus on being re-elected as Concacaf’s president and Uefa has yet to find an alternative candidate despite tentatively sounding out high-profile footballing figures including Arsène Wenger and Michele Kang, who owns clubs including London City Lionesses.The deadline for candidates to declare their intention to stand is 18 November, with the election due to be held at Fifa congress in Rabat on 18 March.Infantino is expected to put forward a £2.6bn increase in the amount of money Fifa hands out for global football development at the meeting in Zurich, using cash from the governing body’s reserves to do so. The hike, covering funding from 2027 to 2030, would take the total Fifa spend on football development for the period to £4.83bn.Explore more on these topicsFifaGianni InfantinoFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jackson and Barkley doubles sink feeble Fenerbahce in record Aston Villa win | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Nicolas Jackson and Ross Barkley each scored twice in Aston Villa’s 6-0 thrashing of Fenerbahce in the Champions League for their biggest European win
Author: Peter Lansley
Headline: Nicolas Jackson and Ross Barkley each scored twice in Aston Villa’s 6-0 thrashing of Fenerbahce in the Champions League for their biggest European win
Content: Ross Barkley shares a high-five with fellow goalscorer Nicolas Jackson after Aston Villa’s fifth goal.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoss Barkley shares a high-five with fellow goalscorer Nicolas Jackson after Aston Villa’s fifth goal.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersChampions LeagueJackson and Barkley doubles sink feeble Fenerbahce in record Aston Villa winPeter Lansleyat Villa ParkWed 14 Oct 2026 17.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 18.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt may be a bit early for the pantomime season but the Holte End enjoyed acclaiming their heroes and villains asAston Villawon at home for the first time this season with their biggest victory in European competition. Every touch for Mason Greenwood, playing his first game in England since January 2022, was booed, but even louder applause was reserved for Aston Villa’s rediscovered attacking prowess.Johan Manzambi celebrated his 21st birthday by opening the scoring on his firstChampions Leagueappearance, before Nicolas Jackson took the game beyond Fenerbahce’s reach with two more goals before half-time to help banish any fears about playing in front of the demolished North Stand.With Prince William cheering on from the stands, Ross Barkley made this a night to remember as he scored twice, the first goal from a penalty earned by Manzambi, and Tammy Abraham helped Villa score six in a game for the first time since beating Brighton in 2023. No team has won more games (15) in European competition since the start of last season.Bradley Barcola’s clinical hat-trick inspires Liverpool to 6-3 rout of LaskRead moreVilla’s supposed hex about playing in front of the empty North Stand was put to bed as they scored three times at the end of the ground that is being redeveloped this winter. “Greenwood, Greenwood, what’s the score,” echoed around the three packed stands at Villa Park. Chants of a less salubrious nature were also given regular renditions. This was the former England forward’s first game in this country since he played inManchester United’s 1-0 win against West HamUnited in nearly five years ago.View image in fullscreenJohan Manzambi scores his deflected goal for the opener.Photograph: Tim Keeton/EPAGreenwood was charged in 2022 with attempted rape, controlling and coercive behaviour and assault occasioning actual bodily harm. The Crown Prosecution Servicediscontinued the case in February 2023after key witnesses withdrew their involvement and new material came to light. The player had denied the charges.He had played for Marseille in a friendly against Villa 14 months ago, when he allegedly spat at Amadou Onana. So it was no surprise when his name was booed as the teams were announced and at every subsequent involvement.Far more palatable was the freedom with which Villa played. Jackson now has five goals for Unai Emery’s teamsince signing from Chelseafor £65m in the summer while Manzambi, a £59.5m capture from Freiburg, was a joy to watch in the No 10 role, combining deft touch with wiry physicality. “My first Champions League game and my first goal, on my birthday,” he said. “My family are here. That’s very nice for me.”The Switzerland international composed himself to score after Mattéo Guendouzi had inadvertently headed on John McGinn’s cross following a short corner.Zion Suzuki twice saved well from Vedat Muriqi but Villa created umpteen chances themselves. Jackson, collecting Boubacar Kamara’s pass, struck home cleanly from the edge of the penalty area just after the half-hour mark before repeating the trick six minutes before the interval. In between, Oguz Aydin shot against the Villa bar, but, truth be told, Villa’s 11th successive home win in European competitions was already safely banked.Villa’s free-scoring spell is in stark contrast to their start to the season, when they only managed one goal in their opening four games. Now they have scored at least three times in four of their past six matches.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShould they beat Viking here next Wednesday, Villa would be well on their way to qualifying from the league stage with nine points from three games. “We are being ambitious,” Unai Emery, the Villa manager, said. “We want to be protagonists in the Champions League.”View image in fullscreenNicolas Jackson drills the ball between Nathan Aké’s legs to score Aston Villa’s third.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersManzambi was tripped by Ismail Yuksek midway through the second half for the penalty from which Barkley made it 4-0, even if Jackson admitted he had fancied the chance to keep the match ball. “Yeah I wanted to take it but the most important thing is we win,” the striker told TNT Sports. “Hopefully next time I’ll get the hat-trick.”The cheers that followed that goal were promptly matched by the jeers for Greenwood as he was substituted. The pantomime was over as a contest.Barkley swiftly added a fifth with a deflected shot. But even before Abraham turned in Alysson’s cross for the sixth goal, some Villa minds were turning to Saturday evening’s trip to Newcastle United and the perennial autumnal challenge of resurrecting a difficult start to the league season. In Emery they trust.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueAston VillaFenerbahcematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Bradley Barcola’s clinical hat-trick inspires Liverpool to 6-3 rout of Lask | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Bradley Barcola opened his account for Liverpool with a hat-trick in their 6-3 win against Lask of Austria in the Champions League
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Bradley Barcola opened his account for Liverpool with a hat-trick in their 6-3 win against Lask of Austria in the Champions League
Content: Bradley Barcola celebrates his hat-trick goal for Liverpool as Andoni Iraola’s side turned on the style.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBradley Barcola celebrates his hat-trick goal for Liverpool as Andoni Iraola’s side turned on the style.Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueBradley Barcola’s clinical hat-trick inspires Liverpool to 6-3 rout of LaskAndy Hunterat Raiffeisen ArenaWed 14 Oct 2026 14.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 18.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiverpool cleansed themselves from the stains of defeat by Manchester City at the earliest opportunity. A rampant display in Austria saw Bradley Barcola ignite his Liverpool account with the first hat-trick of his professional career and Andoni Iraola’s team devastate Lask’s big night in theChampions League. The major surprise was how the hosts managed to score three.Iraola’s pre-match faith in the big-money signings Barcola and Florian Wirtz was repaid as the pair helped dismantle limited opponents. But it was not all about the money and the £123m signing from Paris Saint-Germain scoring the first goals of hisLiverpoolcareer. Lewis Koumas registered his first goal in the competition and replaced Steven Gerrard as the youngest player to score and assist in a Champions League game for Liverpool. A total of 26 shots equalled Liverpool’s record in a Champions League away game.“I’m really happy for Bradley,” said the Liverpool head coach. “Yesterday you were asking me a lot about his numbers, and also Flo [Wirtz], and both of them played really well. They made a difference. Apart from the hat-trick Bradley was a threat one-v-one, helped us control the game and defended the pockets. It will do their confidence good for sure.”Lask v Liverpool: Champions League – liveRead moreThe home end was full and in strong voice over an hour before kick-off as Lask supporters came to savour their club’s first home game in the Champions League proper. The Lask team proved to be much less impressive though, in fairness to the Austrian crowd, their support rarely wavered even as a rout unfolded before their eyes. Liverpool revelled in their superiority and the invitation to recover fromSunday’s first defeat of the season.Iraola rested Virgil van Dijk, delaying the defender’s 200th game as Liverpool captain, and Alexis Mac Allister as he managed workloads ahead of Saturday’s visit to Brentford. A new-look central defence of Ronald Araújo and Jérémy Jacquet were given a physical test by theLaskstrikers Samuel Adeniran and Krystof Danek but handled the host’s rudimental approach comfortably.View image in fullscreenBradley Barcola slides the ball into the bottom corner to score his second in the first half.Photograph: Dénes Erdős/APLiverpool were utterly dominant against an opponent that struggled to retain possession in all areas of the pitch. The breakthrough was inevitable but also a result of a mix-up in the Lask defence between Alemão and the goalkeeper, Lukas Jungwirth. From the second corner that followed their error, Araújo towered above his marker to head home Kostas Tsimikas’s delivery. It was the Uruguay international’s first Liverpool goal and the start of an onslaught.Merely 96 seconds later it was 2-0 as Barcola also scored his first Liverpool goal. The summer recruitfound himself under scrutinyahead of the game, along with Wirtz, having gone six appearances for his new club without a goal or an assist. That issue was put to bed when Rio Ngumoha weaved in from the right and Koumas laid the ball back to the lurking winger. Barcola swept a first-time shot inside Jungwirth’s far post. Liverpool were enjoying themselves.Wirtz soon found himself with a much-needed assist for Barcola’s second goal. The Germany international has looked more at home for Liverpool in the Champions League than Premier League and this was no exception. Wirtz picked out Barcola’s run into the Lask area and the winger rolled a cool finish beyond the exposed keeper.Lask could have been seriously embarrassed before half-time. Koumas had a fine finish disallowed for offside and, following another neat exchange between Wirtz and Barcola, Ryan Gravenberch’s shot kissed the inside of the far post. Liverpool’s 19 attempts on goal were the most by an away side in the first half of a Champions League game since records began in 2003-04.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLiverpool’s Lewis Koumas jumps for joy after opening his Champions League account.Photograph: Michael Zemanek/ShutterstockThere would be no letup from Iraola’s team after the interval. Jeremie Frimpong morphed into an old-fashioned centre-forward to rise above Yvan Dibango and bury a textbook header into the bottom corner from Tsimikas’s cross. Koumas had a second goal disallowed for offside before Alisson’s clean sheet was ruined by the Lask substitute Robert Ljubicic sweeping home inside his near post. Barcola was presented with his hat-trick when Ngumoha released Frimpong and the full-back flashed a low cross through the Lask six-yard box. Barcola applied a simple finish at the back post.Frimpong also supplied the assist for Koumas’s deserved goal, converted from close range after the home side were caught playing out from the back. The Lask substitute Florian Flecker brought a touch of respectability to the scoreline with two goals in four minutes, both set up by Dibango, but there was no disguising the emphatic manner of Liverpool’s victory nor the surge of confidence it should give to Barcola.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueLiverpoolLaskmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Champions League: Mourinho’s Real Madrid stage wild comeback on Roma return | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Real Madrid scored three late goals to come back from 3-1 down to beat Roma while Bodø/Glimt kept up their home form against Borussia Dortmund
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Real Madrid scored three late goals to come back from 3-1 down to beat Roma while Bodø/Glimt kept up their home form against Borussia Dortmund
Content: Antonio Rüdiger scored Real Madrid’s late winner on his return to his former club.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersView image in fullscreenAntonio Rüdiger scored Real Madrid’s late winner on his return to his former club.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersChampions LeagueChampions League: Mourinho’s Real Madrid stage wild comeback on Roma returnMourinho’s side score three late goals from 3-1 deficitDortmund latest team beaten in Norway by Bodø/GlimtAgenciesWed 14 Oct 2026 17.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosé Mourinho enjoyed aRomareunion to remember asReal Madridcompleted an astonishing comeback by scoring three late goals to claim a 4-3 away win in theChampions Leagueon Wednesday.Marten de Roon gave the hosts a deserved opener before Kylian Mbappé struck back on his 100th Champions League appearance to level the scores at the break. Two Donyell Malen strikes in the space of six minutes early in the second half seemed to take the game away from the 15-time European champions asRomaran rampant.Quickfire Doué and Dembélé inspire PSG to wild win at Manchester CityRead moreBut Madrid scored three goals in the final six minutes, all stemming from corners, to turn the game on its head as Carlos Espí, Endrick and the former Roma defender Antonio Rüdiger struck at a stunned Stadio Olimpico.Mourinho was a popular figure as he led Roma to the Conference League title and Europa League final during two-and-a-half years in charge. The Portuguese coach was honoured with banners and chants by the home crowd in Roma’s first home Champions League match in more than seven years.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho is given a hero’s welcome on his return to Roma.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APTheReal Madridwinger Vinícius Júnior, who featured in the win, was handed a four-match ban for pulling an opponent’s hair during Saturday’s league win over Villarreal. The decision was announced shortly before the game kicked off in Rome – a situation that left Mourinho furious with Spain’s football authorities.“They do things shamelessly now,” Mourinho said. The cat is out of the bag now. Two hours before the match, a player must know he has a four-match suspension. Couldn’t they do it now? Couldn’t they do it tomorrow morning? Do we have to come by bus and almost arrive at the stadium when we find out?”Fredrik Sjøvold’s 52nd-minute strike secured a 1-0 victory forBodø/GlimtoverBorussia Dortmund, extending the Norwegian side’s remarkable home record against Europe’s elite.Bodø were a cut above the 2024 Champions League runners-up and took the lead through Sjøvold just after the break. Dortmund improved in the final half hour but were unable to strike back, despite a late chance for Felix Nmecha.“There’s nothing we can complain about, we deserved to lose,” said the Dortmund coach, Niko Kovac. “We didn’t bring enough passion today – that’s something Bodø did much better. They took the lead and after that we woke up, but by then it was too late.”View image in fullscreenFredrik Sjøvold celebrates after scoring what proved to be the winner for Bodø/Glimt.Photograph: NTB/ReutersDortmund join Manchester City, Inter and Sporting as recent big-name scalps on the artificial turf of Bodø’s Aspmyra Stadium. Bodø’s run to the last 16 last season was underpinned by an excellent record at their 8,200-capacity home, officially the smallest venue in this year’s competition.Nomadic Ukrainian championsShakhtar Donetskcelebrated moving into their new Champions League “home” at Stamford Bridge by storming back to beatAEK Athens3-1.The Greek side took the lead in the 28th minute through Lovro Majer but Pedrinho levelled confidently from the penalty spot just six minutes later. With about 10 minutes of normal time to go, Vinicius Tobias found the net from a tight angle and the substitute Gleiker Mendoza made the game safe, smashing home after cutting in from the left.Shakhtar, from the east of Ukraine,are using Chelsea’s groundas the base for their European fixtures this season, with the Londoners absent from continental competition.View image in fullscreenShakhtar Donetsk fans make themselves at home at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/APSince the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the UK has provided refuge to 265,000 Ukrainians, according to the Ukrainian embassy in London. Fans from the expat population turned out in force on Wednesday, swelling the crowd to 29,000.Isco scored the winner and Abde Ezzalzouli netted a contender for goal of the week asReal BetisdefeatedPorto3-2 in a bad-tempered game in Seville.Ezzalzouli struck the ball from the corner of the penalty area into the top corner at the far post after the break. Gabriel Veiga equalised with a fine free-kick and set off a kerfuffle between rival players with his celebration. Three players were booked.ThePortosubstitute Samu Aghehowa – a Spain international – scored just two minutes after coming on, only for Cucho Hernández – another substitute – to equalise in the 74th. Isco got the winner late with a penalty.Stuttgartcontinued their 100% record in this season’s league phase with a 3-0 win againstSlovan Bratislavain Slovakia. Earlier, Anis Hadj Moussa scored twice as the Dutch leaders,Feyenoord, came from behind to beat visitingComo3-2.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueReal MadridRomaBodø/GlimtBorussia DortmundShakhtar DonetskAEK AthensnewsShareReuse this content

title: Championship roundup: Soucek doubles up as West Ham hit nine-man Lincoln for six | Championship | The Guardian
description: Tomas Soucek netted two late goals to round off an emphatic 6-0 win for West Ham at Lincoln after red cards for Tom Hamer and Conor McGrandles, while Portsmouth won a seesawing match against Sheffield United
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tomas Soucek netted two late goals to round off an emphatic 6-0 win for West Ham at Lincoln after red cards for Tom Hamer and Conor McGrandles, while Portsmouth won a seesawing match against Sheffield United
Content: Tomas Soucek (left) is congratulated by his teammates after scoring the first of his two goals late on against Lincoln.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenTomas Soucek (left) is congratulated by his teammates after scoring the first of his two goals late on against Lincoln.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAChampionshipChampionship roundup: Soucek doubles up as West Ham hit nine-man Lincoln for sixTomas Soucek rounds off big victory after two redsPortsmouth strike late to beat 10-man Sheffield UnitedPress AssociationWed 14 Oct 2026 17.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWest Hamreturned to winning ways as they cruised to a 6-0Championshipvictory against nine-manLincolnat the ProAmpac Stadium.The hosts had Tom Hamer sent off after just three minutes and Conor McGrandles followed him off the pitch 20 minutes later, with Konstantinos Mavropanos heading West Ham ahead on the stroke of half-time.Championship roundup: Swansea’s win at Millwall marred by alleged racist abuse of Eom Ji-sungRead moreThe second half was dominated by West Ham, with further goals coming from Edvin Austbø, Jarrod Bowen, Pablo and Tomas Soucek, who scored twice, as the beleaguered home side desperately tried to keep the score down.“I credit Lincoln as even with one man down, they were in the game and still creating a lot of problems for us,” said the West Ham manager, Nuno Espírito Santo, after watching his club’s biggest away win for 103 years.“I think we made mistakes in terms of trying to rush things,” Nuno added. “It changed after the second goal and we played much better, in terms of being patient, recycling the ball and being clinical.”Southamptonrecordedtheir second hard-fought 1-0 win in the space of four daysas they condemned their hosts,Norwich, to a fourth successive league defeat.Tonda Eckert’s side followed up Sunday’s victory over their local rivals, Portsmouth, with their first away win of the campaign in the league, with Kuryu Matsuki scorijng what proved to be the winner early in the second half.Southampton are now well-placed in the top half of the table after 10 games, despite starting the campaignwith a four-point deduction, while Norwich remain too close to the bottom for comfort after another disappointing display.“To be fair there have been some good performances away from home when we just needed to finish better, ” Eckert said. “Tonight we have put in another good performance and on this occasion, we have got our reward. I am very happy for the boys because they worked very hard out there.”Ebou Adams scored an 89th-minute winner asPortsmouthrecovered after giving away a 2-0 lead to beat 10-manSheffield United3-2 at Fratton Park.The hosts had been in cruise control after Zak Swanson’s stunning blast into the top corner and Adrian Segecic’s tap-in either side of Hamza Choudhury’s dismissal for two bookings. But Japhet Tanganga and Tom Cannon levelled the score and the visitors were somehow hunting back-to-back victories for the first time this season.View image in fullscreenSouthampton manager Tonda Eckert celebrates with his players after their 1-0 win at Norwich.Photograph: Nigel French/PAAdams had the last word when he jumped off the bench to convert with a minute to go to give Portsmouth their third win of the campaign. After the game, Sheffield United manager Chris Wilder criticised referee Oliver Langford for his decision to send Choudhury off.“There were a number of decisions which were incredibly frustrating,” Wilder said. “That is three players that have been sent off in the last two games he [Langford] has refereed us. Where are the young and up-and-coming referees who would be refereeing in the Championship now, instead of the ones that are just surviving?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“No doubt we will have another survivor ref on Saturday. Where is the quality? Where are the ones coming through?” Wilder added. It is a tough one for the players, but there is more frustration and anger towards somebody. We have to deal with it.”The Portsmouth head coach, John Mousinho, was frustrated by his team’s display despite their late winner. “I am happy that we won the game but the nature and circumstances of it … we have a large amount to learn and a long way to come.“There was a little bit of relief when the winner went in, but there was fury through the game and I still am furious,” he added. “I think the players are on the same page as me and that is why there was muted celebrations at the end.”QPRcontinued their impressive early season form with a thumping 4-1 win at home to strugglingDerby. Three of the goals came in the first half, with Alfie Lloyd scoring, Nicolas Madsen tucking away a penalty and Harvey Vale adding the third.Paul Smyth made it four with a deflected effort midway through the second half before Lars-Jørgen Salvesen scored a late consolation goal for Derby. Rangers’ victory was marred by a potentially serious knee injury to defender Amadou Mbengue, who was carried off on a stretcher late on.Derby have now gone six league games without a win but their head coach, John Eustace, remains optimistic despite increasing pressure. “It’s a long season. We’ve had some difficult moments and I’m confident we’ll come through it,” Eustace said. “I don’t think the players will need picking up. I think they’ll be angry and ready to go for the next game.”PosTeamPGDPts1Swansea109232Middlesbrough106213West Ham1017194Birmingham106175QPR106176West Brom102177Southampton1011168Stoke101169Blackburn1021510Wolverhampton921411Millwall1001412Bristol City10-21413Charlton10-31414Bolton10-31315Sheff Utd1001216Portsmouth9-11117Wrexham10-41118Lincoln City10-101119Cardiff1011020Norwich10-3921Burnley10-4822Watford10-11823Derby10-10624Preston North End10-124Explore more on these topicsChampionshipWest Ham UnitedLincoln CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City staff invited on government trade trip to India | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig invited City representative on trade trip organised by business secretary
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig invited City representative on trade trip organised by business secretary
Content: Bev Craig, Andy Burnham’s successor, said east Manchester had felt the benefits of the club’s investment.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBev Craig, Andy Burnham’s successor, said east Manchester had felt the benefits of the club’s investment.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianManchester CityManchester City staff invited on government trade trip to IndiaExclusive: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig invited City representative on trade trip organised by business secretaryKiran StaceyandMatt HughesWed 14 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA club representative from Manchester City was invited on a government-backed trade delegation to India this week, despite the clubbeing found guiltyof 114 breaches of Premier League rules.Andy Burnham’s successor as Manchester mayor Bev Craig took a representative from the club to Delhi and Mumbai on a trip organised by business secretary Jonathan Reynolds,where she and other northern mayors have been promoting British trade and tourism.She defended the decision to invite City even as the prime minister came under fire for his own contacts with the club, telling the Guardian it had played a vital role in helping build infrastructure in her city.“If a football club has broken the rules, a football club should be punished for breaking the rules, and that is pretty clear in an independent process,” she said.“I think what can also be true at the same time though, if you ask residents in eastManchester, have they benefited from a new library, a new leisure centre, a new sixth-form college, infrastructure investment, the job opportunities that come from them being a good employment charter signee and an early adopter of the real living wage – then they will have felt that benefit.”City, which says it is innocent of the charges and has appealed against them, declined to comment.The revelation comes as Burnham faced pressure over his relationship with City’s owners during his time as mayor ofGreater Manchester. The prime minister was forced to clarify on Wednesday that he had two additional dinners with the club chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium, having previously declared those only as matchday hospitality.Speaking at PMQs, Burnham said no one from the club had raised the Premier League charges with him.Craig’s defence of the club came as her mayoral authoritypublished detailsof Burnham’s contacts with City officials when he was mayor.The release showed the prime minister had attended a formal meeting with al-Mubarak, chatted to him in the stands at a player’s testimonial game and was accompanied by staff from the club on official overseas visits.But theSun newspaper revealed later on Mondaythat Burnham had twice attended a pre-match dinner with the chair, which was declared in now-deleted council paperwork. No 10 said it was routine for the records to be deleted when a new mayor was in place.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with Khaldoon al-Mubarak.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PABurnham’s initial response to the findings against City had drawn criticism after he said he would be“really concerned”if its Abu Dhabi owners sold the club in the wake of the Premier League findings, calling them a “huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”.As the prime minister came under fire for his comments, Downing Street clarified that he believed where wrongdoing had been established, those responsible should face the consequences.City attended the trade delegation alongside several other northern sports and leisure organisations, including Lancashire cricket club and Visit Lake District. While in India, the football club took part in an event in Delhi promoting British tourism.The Great North – a coalition of mayors from the north ofEnglandwhich organised the India event – said its aim was “to shine a spotlight on the great tourism products across the north of England”.​skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Greater Manchester mayoral authority said on Tuesday that representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would “routinely join business delegations” on international visits during Burnham’s time as mayor.Burnham’s defence of City and its owners has focused attention not only on his links to the club but on how reliant he was on investment from Abu Dhabi to power Manchester’s strong growth rates when he was mayor.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with Bev Craig after her victory in the Greater Manchester mayoral election.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAOther senior politicians on this week’s trade delegation include Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, Douglas Alexander, the Scotland secretary, and Angela Eagle, the environment secretary.Reynolds took part in a Premier League event on Tuesday, where he met schoolchildren being taught by British-trained coaches. He denied afterwards that the charges against City had tainted the league’s reputation.
