It is otherwise one of Britain’s most successful cultural exports.“The brand of the Premier League – one of the UK’s most important brands … that is incredibly powerful,” he said.Asked whether it was appropriate for City to have been invited, given the charges it faced, he said: “That’s a Greater Manchester issue, and obviously they are a major participant in the economy in Greater Manchester.“I understand the interest – the relationship between Manchester andManchester City– but in terms of the allegations, their appeal, that is a football matter.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityBev CraigGreater ManchesterAndy BurnhamLocal governmentManchesterEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Millwall’s Alex Neil criticised for his comments on stoppage for alleged racism | Millwall | The Guardian
description: The Millwall head coach, Alex Neil, has been criticised by Kick It Out after claiming the stoppage in Tuesday’s loss to Swansea ‘killed momentum’
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The Millwall head coach, Alex Neil, has been criticised by Kick It Out after claiming the stoppage in Tuesday’s loss to Swansea ‘killed momentum’
Content: Alex Neil has faced criticism for his response after Millwall’s game against Swansea was briefly suspended due to alleged racial abuse.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenAlex Neil has faced criticism for his response after Millwall’s game against Swansea was briefly suspended due to alleged racial abuse.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAMillwallMillwall’s Alex Neil criticised for his comments on stoppage for alleged racismKick It Out statement: managers should ‘set the tone’Head coach said delay in Swansea game ‘killed momentum’Guardian sportWed 14 Oct 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Millwall head coach, Alex Neil, has been criticised by the anti-racism campaign group Kick It Out after complaining that a stoppage in play over alleged racist abuse “killed the momentum” in Tuesday’s home defeat toSwansea City.TheChampionshipfixture was suspended for around seven minutes after reports of abusive chants being aimed at the Swansea midfielder Eom Ji-sung. The referee, Edward Duckworth, halted the match in the 65th minute before speaking with both teams’ managers, the fourth official and a safety officer.Championship roundup: Swansea’s win at Millwall marred by alleged racist abuse of Eom Ji-sungRead moreAfter the game, Neil toldBBC Radio London: “I understand, obviously, there’s been an incident. That’s not something I’m going to get involved in, that’ll be for the authorities to deal with. But the fact that it stops the game, I just don’t see the point.“The referee was wanting to speak to whoever the safety officer is, and when he spoke to him [the game] restarted. That’s partly my frustration. I want to get the game restarted, I want to get the game played. It needs to get dealt with … [but] stopping the game doesn’t deal with anything. All it does is kill the momentum.”In a statement published on social media,Kick It Outsaid: “Player welfare should always take precedence over the momentum or flow of a match, and it’s essential that managers and all leaders recognise this and set the tone with their language so that everyone can stand up to discrimination.“We’re disappointed to hear reports of racist abuse towards Swansea’s Eom Ji-sung during Tuesday’s Championship game atMillwall. Both clubs have condemned the incident, and it’s positive that Millwall and match officials followed the right protocols so that action can be taken to identify any individual responsible.”The statement added: “Protocols are in place to help match and security officials respond appropriately. That ensures players are protected and key details are captured so that accountability can follow, regardless of how long it takes.”View image in fullscreenThe match referee, Edward Duckworth, speaks to both managers during the break in play.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAMillwall have not responded to the Kick it Out statement, but said on Tuesday: “The club operates a zero-tolerance policy towards any form of discriminatory abuse. Any individual found to have engaged in such behaviour will face the strongest possible action.“The club is working alongside the relevant authorities to establish the facts and is unable to comment further as tonight’s alleged incident is the subject of an ongoing police investigation, which the club fully supports.”Swansea won the game 1-0, with Ronald scoring a late winner after the restart, and Neil admitted afterwards: “If we score, I probably don’t feel this way.” The 45-year-old added that the alleged abuse “has been reported and it’s not acceptable.”The Swansea head coach, Vítor Matos, praised the referee and Millwall’s club staff for their responses to the incident. “The referee followed the protocol for these sort of situations, they did the right thing,” he said.“Millwall did the right thing by announcing there is no place for this sort of thing. I’m happy with how it was handled, but really sad that it happened.”Explore more on these topicsMillwallKick It OutRaceSwansea CityChampionshipnewsShareReuse this content

title: Enzo Maresca insists Manchester City are ‘close’ to PSG despite home defeat | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Enzo Maresca said he enjoyed facing the Champions League holders and denied the Premier League charges had an impact on his players
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Enzo Maresca said he enjoyed facing the Champions League holders and denied the Premier League charges had an impact on his players
Content: Enzo Maresca said he ‘really likes’ to play against PSG after Manchester City’s 4-2 loss.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca said he ‘really likes’ to play against PSG after Manchester City’s 4-2 loss.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAManchester CityEnzo Maresca insists Manchester City are ‘close’ to PSG despite home defeatLuis Enrique admits ‘luck was on our side’ in 4-2 winMaresca denies players were affected by guilty verdictsDavid Hytnerat the Etihad StadiumWed 14 Oct 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca felt Manchester City proved they were close to the level ofParis Saint-Germainafter losing out to them in a Champions League thriller at the Etihad Stadium.City trailed 3-0 at half-time against the defending champions and the damage might have been heavier. But they threw caution to the wind in the second half, creating a host of chances and hinting at a remarkable comeback before going down 4-2.Maresca’s team, who were watched by their former manager, Pep Guardiola, had won all of their previous matches this season – apart from the Community Shield loss to Arsenal. They continue to play under the cloud of their guilty verdicts for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules over a nine-year period from 2009. But on the field against PSG, Maresca suggested City were unlucky – an assessment with which his opposite number,Luis Enrique, agreed.Quickfire Doué and Dembélé inspire PSG to wild win at Manchester CityRead more“I really like to play against PSG,” Maresca said. “They are brave. I know the way they want to press, they go man to man, they are quite dynamic and I think we are there … my feeling is we are close. It was a bit of a strange game because we concede two goals in two minutes [early in the first half] and that created some problems for us. In the second half, we did enough to deserve something more. Luis told me at the end they had been quite lucky.”It was the proverbial game of two halves, with PSG excellent in the first period. They were pushed back after the interval, City finishing with 27 shots, albeit the PSG substitute Ferran Torres did miss a penalty at the end for 5-2.Maresca was asked whether the guilty verdicts on the Premier League charges plus the emotion of Sunday’s 3-0 win at Liverpool had affected his players in the first half. “No, I don’t think so,” he replied.Luis Enrique said: “City created a huge amount of problems for us. The team that lost were perhaps a bit unlucky. I think the luck was on our side. It’s obvious what happened – a team losing 3-0 took risks. I knew they would really come out and go for it. They left one man in defence, they pushed everyone else forward into attack and it is really difficult to manage that. In the first half, we were almost perfect in our pressing game.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityEnzo MarescaParis Saint-GermainLuis EnriqueChampions LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United teammates widely share Martínez view that Wilcox is failing | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Lisandro Martínez’s view that Jason Wilcox is failing as Manchester United’s director of football reflects the dressing room’s general frustration at recruitment and squad depth
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Lisandro Martínez’s view that Jason Wilcox is failing as Manchester United’s director of football reflects the dressing room’s general frustration at recruitment and squad depth
Content: Lisandro Martínez joined Manchester United from Ajax in 2022.Photograph: Alvaro Medranda/Quality Sport Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLisandro Martínez joined Manchester United from Ajax in 2022.Photograph: Alvaro Medranda/Quality Sport Images/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedManchester United teammates widely share Martínez view that Wilcox is failingDefender challenged, though, by at least one playerLater insists on social media: ‘I believe in teammates’Jamie JacksonWed 14 Oct 2026 18.17 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLisandro Martínez’s view thatJason Wilcox is failingas Manchester United’s director of football reflects wider dressing-room frustration over recruitment and squad depth, although the outburst caused at least one teammate to challenge the defender to identify who he believes is not good enough for the side.Martínez may face internal ­disciplinary action over extensive criticism of the hierarchy made in two broadcast interviews after Tuesday’s 2-0 Champions Leaguedefeat at Atlético Madrid. The players had Wednesdayyesterday off so any action would not be taken before their return to training on Thursdaytoday.Football Daily | Martínez lets rip as United’s dirty laundry gets a very public airingRead moreMartínez directed his anger at Wilcox and what he referred to as “the top” of the club, saying not enough players had been signed and questioning the scale of investment, and that “more ambition” was needed. He said: “We don’t have the best squad at the moment compared with other top teams.”Martínez’s comments prompted a challenge from at least one teammate before the flight back to ­Manchester and caused a heightening of tension. The Argentinian did not appear to explicitly call out his teammates, saying merely that “as players we have to do more”, and claimed that last season the squad had “created the base to build an amazing team”.Although the sway of dressing-room opinion is with Martínez, his remarks are also seen as the centre-back considering his future, because he is out of contract next summer.Defeat at Atlético left United with two wins this season, having taken six points from their first six Premier League matches, the club’s poorest league start for 40 years. The run of form has put the head coach Michael Carrick under pressure, but Martínez took aim at Wilcox and the rest of the hierarchy. “Tonight it is easy to say the coach, easy to say the players, but also we have to see other areas,” he said, pointing upwards.“I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. I have to be honest, as players we have to do more, but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.”Graphic showing top net spends since Jason Wilcox took main responsibility for Manchester United’s transfersWilcox, the executive in charge of transfers, oversaw £155m of spending in the last window onYouri Tielemans,Andrey SantosandCarlos Baleba. The decision to recruit three midfielders while not strengthening other areas has been met with puzzlement among the squad, particularly as Wilcox was looking for a left-back, with Newcastle’s Lewis Hall the prime target.Luke Shaw is United’s only senior player in that position and his 12-year career at the club has been plagued by injury. The 31-year-old missed the defeat by Atlético and owing to a muscular problem. The lack of depth at left-back reflects the prevailing view among players that Carrick has been left without the resources to challenge. United wereeliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brightonafter making eight changes.Although Carrick led United to third last season, this came after he took over as caretaker in mid-January with only 17 league games to play with the team out of all the other competitions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMartínez is understood to favour a move to an elite European club outside the Premier League.On Wednesday night, Martínez released a statement on social media in an attempt to clarify his comments, writing: “I know that, first and foremost, it’s us, the players, who have to deliver, and I put myself at the front of that responsibility.”He added: “I believe in my teammates, our manager and everyone working to help this club move forward.” Yet he still maintained his post-match comments “reflect how I feel and how much I want to see this club competing for the biggest honours”.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitednewsShareReuse this content

title: Kevin Pietersen tells ECB he will not promote gambling site while on England duty | Kevin Pietersen | The Guardian
description: Kevin Pietersen has told the England and Wales Cricket Board that he will not promote betting while on duty as England’s specialist mentor despite signing a lucrative deal with an online gambling company
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Kevin Pietersen has told the England and Wales Cricket Board that he will not promote betting while on duty as England’s specialist mentor despite signing a lucrative deal with an online gambling company
Content: England specialist mentor Kevin Pietersen holds a broken bat as Harry Brook and Brendon McCullum look on.Photograph: John Walton/PAView image in fullscreenEngland specialist mentor Kevin Pietersen holds a broken bat as Harry Brook and Brendon McCullum look on.Photograph: John Walton/PAKevin PietersenKevin Pietersen tells ECB he will not promote gambling site while on England dutySpecialist mentor signed lucrative deal with online firmBoard’s strict code prohibits betting across cricketExclusive byMatt HughesWed 14 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKevin Pietersen has told the England and Wales Cricket Board he will not promote betting while on duty as England’s specialist mentor. Pietersen signed a lucrative contract as a brand ambassador for an online gambling company this week.The former England batter is contracted to work withBrendon McCullum’s white-ball teamfor around 150 days over the next 13 months until the conclusion of the 50-over World Cup co-hosted by South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. Pietersen’s betting ­interests create a potential headache for his employers.The Spin | The sleepy English hotel where Bradman and Australia left cricket memories galoreRead moreThe ECB’s anti-corruption code bans participants from “directly or indirectly soliciting, inducing, enticing, instructing, persuading, encouraging, facilitating or authorising any other party to enter into a bet in relation to the result, progress, conduct or any other aspect of any match or competition.”The ECB does not take advertising revenue from gambling companies, has banned Hundred franchises from sponsorship deals with betting firms from next year and its regulations state that any counties accepting commercial gambling income must demonstrate that the proceeds are reinvested into infrastructure projects or community programmes.All participants in cricket are also prohibited from betting, a rule that led to the England fast bowlerBrydon Carse being given a 16-month ban– 13 of which were suspended – two years ago for placing 303 bets between 2017 and 2019.Pietersen announced he is joining the Philippines-based Dafabet on Monday. The 46-year-old is understood to have reassured the ECB, however, that he will not promote Dafabet while on England duty, which given the extent of his commitments over the next year will prove restrictive.While Pietersen is not travelling to Pakistan for a 50-over tri series also featuring Sri Lanka that starts next week, he will play a full part in the winter tours of Australia and South Africa, as well as all England’s domestic white-ball matches next summer leading into the World Cup.The ECB previously hadissues regarding McCullum’s betting interestsafter the then Test coach joined the Cyprus-based company 22bet as an ambassador three years ago. He went on to promote its Indian Premier League betting markets on Facebook and YouTube.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe ECB concluded that McCullum was not in breach of its anti-corruption code, althoughhe opted to terminate his relationship with 22betanyway. Unlike 22bet, which is licensed offshore in Curacao, Dafabet has a licence to operate in the UK.Explore more on these topicsKevin PietersenEngland cricket teamECBCricketGamblingnewsShareReuse this content

title: University of Maryland club tennis team suspended over racist imagery sent to other schools | Maryland | The Guardian
description: Image of state flag incorporating KKK hoods was sent to other schools participating in regional tennis tournament
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Image of state flag incorporating KKK hoods was sent to other schools participating in regional tennis tournament
Content: The University of Maryland on 28 July in College Park, Maryland.Photograph: Al Drago/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe University of Maryland on 28 July in College Park, Maryland.Photograph: Al Drago/Getty ImagesMarylandUniversity of Maryland club tennis team suspended over racist imagery sent to other schoolsImage of state flag incorporating KKK hoods was sent to other schools participating in regional tennis tournamentMarina DunbarWed 14 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe University ofMaryland(UMD) has indefinitely suspended its club tennis team after a graphic featuring Ku Klux Klan imagery was circulated to other universities before a regional tournament, prompting widespread condemnation.The controversy erupted after Toni Rachal, president of Howard University’s club tennis team, spotted the offensive material in a shared Google document sent to participating schools before last weekend’s tournament,WUSA9reported.The graphic features an altered Maryland state flag incorporating images of Ku Klux Klan hoods. Rachal discovered the image while examining a Google document that had been emailed to the tournament’s participating tennis clubs.Minnesota professor linked to series of bizarre incidents involving urine at universityRead moreIn a letter addressed to UMD, Rachal described the imagery as “associated with racial hatred and intimidation” and called for “meaningful accountability” following the incident, WUSA9 reported.The tennis club atHoward, a historically Black university in Washington DC, released astatementon social media describing the image as “a recognizable symbol associated with the Ku Klux Klan”. It questioned how the image made its way into official tournament materials.The University of Maryland’s president, Darryll J Pines, said the tennis club “distributed programming material with a graphic containing racist imagery directed at people who are Black or African American”, according to a universitystatement.While the incident “may have directly involved only a few student team members”, the university’s recreation and wellness department moved to suspend the entire club indefinitely “pending an administrative investigation by the office of student conduct”, the statement said.The university’s police department and office of civil rights and sexual misconduct have also launched investigations into the incident.Bryant Reed, president of the Black student union at UMD, said in a phone interview that Black students at UMD are “extremely disturbed” by the “blatant act of racism” from the school’s tennis club.“Nobody is comfortable with the fact that something like that happened so openly and so blatantly, and there are some people that are on the tennis team that didn’t know that this was happening that are also extremely disturbed in general about the situation,” he said.Reed also said that he believes this is just one more incident in a longstanding pattern of racism that Black students at the institution face.“This is definitely not an isolated incident,” he said. “Here at UMD, people often report things like micro-aggressions or just a general feeling of isolation as Black students.“I can share about a specific instance where a friend of mine was sitting in a residence hall and someone said to him: ‘Oh, you’re the diversity admit,’ and it was blatant, it was random. He didn’t know that person. This is the sort of thing that happens all the time,” he added.The isolation Black students feel at UMD is reflected even in its demographics. According to theUS census, 31% of Maryland residents identify as Black, yet Black students at UMD only make upabout 14%of the undergraduate student body.Aniya Baker, vice-president of the Black student union at UMD, said she feels that officials at the university are not taking the steps necessary for any meaningful change to occur.“Any time an issue has been brought up on campus where it’s specifically targeting Black students, I do not feel like our concerns were actually taken seriously,” Baker said.She gave an example of a Black student facing discrimination last year, saying the union responded by informing the institution’s student government association (SGA), which Baker said would not even release a public statement to students acknowledging the situation. “That’s just one of many instances where Black students were just being ignored,” she said.And unlike the SGA, the Black student union does not have a relationship with the university’s administration, which she said puts the organization “at a disadvantage when it comes to issues that are surfacing in the Black community because we do not readily have access towards our administrators, which I feel is extremely unfair”.Reed said that the university making an effort to involve itself more in the spaces of Black students is the first step at improving conditions. The institution’s vice-president of student affairs did reach out to the union immediately following news of the incident, which the union said it appreciated, but still feels more concrete action needs to be taken for things to get better.The tennis tournament proceeded with the remaining participating teams, but Maryland’s team withdrew from competition and forfeited its matches. Howard’s club tennis team went on to reach the tournament semi-finals, marking its strongest performance in the event since the organization was established in 2021.The Maryland club remains suspended indefinitely as university officials investigate the distribution of the racist image.Explore more on these topicsMarylandRaceUS universitiesUS educationTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netflix’s Mike Tyson docuseries offers an incomplete portrait of a troubling figure  | Documentary | The Guardian
description: The once heroic boxer showcases a frankness in this compelling new series but also an unwillingness to take accountability for his darkest moments
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: The once heroic boxer showcases a frankness in this compelling new series but also an unwillingness to take accountability for his darkest moments
Content: Mike Tyson isn’t the first rehabilitation project to feature the disgraced heavyweight champion.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenMike Tyson isn’t the first rehabilitation project to feature the disgraced heavyweight champion.Photograph: NetflixDocumentaryNetflix’s Mike Tyson docuseries offers an incomplete portrait of a troubling figureAndrew LawrenceThe once heroic boxer showcases a frankness in this compelling new series but also an unwillingness to take accountability for his darkest momentsWed 14 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.21 EDTShareMike Tysonnever envisioned old age. And yet here he still is, having outlived his parents, Brooklynites of ill repute who died when he was a teenager, and the Brownsville tough guys who teased him for being scrawny and having a lisp. Here he is after doing hard time for rape in his prime, winning and losing great fortunes and battling addiction to drink, drugs and fame. Here he still is, 60 years old and a grandfather now, mixing it up withJake Paul in the ring, opening up tomanosphere-adjacent podcasters, bobbing into an impromptu White House press briefing – Māori face-tattoounmistakably in the frame– while on a DC visit to buck up his old pal as his party faces a bleak midterm forecast. “I don’t have to exist,” the champ says in Tyson, the latest four-part vanity project on his turbulent life and times. “Some reason, something allowed me to exist.”Tyson review – deeply icky … and that’s before Trump shows upRead moreIn his heyday, Tyson was a mesmerizing sporting event unto himself – the ruthless knockout machine who struck fear into opponents at first sight, felled them in seconds and looked back on the carnage with cool nonchalance. His darkest episodes –the combustive relationship with actor Robin Givens, the six-year prison sentence for rape, biting off Evander Holyfield’s ear – only deepened the public fascination with him, adding to the lore of boxing’s baddest man. In the winter of his life, Tyson’s self-reflection, so deep it tips into self-parody, is the enthralling spectacle now. And if generations of Black comedians have proved anything, it’s that the appetite forMike Tyson impersonationsis inexhaustible.This new Netflix docuseries isn’t the first rehabilitation project to feature the disgraced heavyweight champion: in 2008, there was the HBO documentary he produced with since#MeToo-d director James Toback; in 2012, the one-man Broadway show featuring Tyson and director Spike Lee. In between, there were Tyson’s cameos in The Hangover, which reframed his erratic behavior as campy mischief. But even as this kinder, gentler Iron Mike was invited back on to the chatshow circuit to promote his latest ventures, after being dropped as a major pitchman in the wake of abuse and rape allegations, the charm offensive could never quite gloss over his ugliest moments on camera – like the time hethreatened to eat Lennox Lewis’s children.Tysonbiting off Holyfield’s earin their 1997 title fight remains one of the most bizarre incidents in sport, a forever freeze-frame of a competitor come totally unhinged. “I was horrified by it,” Bill Clinton said at the time, “and I think the American people are.” When reminded of that quip in the Netflix doc, Tyson took offense, asking what Clinton – of all presidents – knew from scandal.Donald Trump promoted a number of Tyson’s fights at his Atlantic City casino and went to bat for him in the press after Tyson split with manager Don King. Director Floyd Russ, who previously helmeda forensic OJ Simpson documentary, sits down with Trump at the White House for the Netflix doc, but the interview isn’t much of a coup. Mostly, Trump looks old and tired and makes the interview about himself. “The media was rough on Mike, but it just made Mike hotter,” he says. “They’re rough on me, and I’m president!” The assault allegations aren’t brought up – perhaps because they might hit too close to home.Givens and Desiree Washington are the glaring omissions from Netflix’s Tyson – but not for lack of effort, the documentary hastens to note. In the case of the pageant contestant – who was 18 when she accused then 25-year-old Tyson of rape – all Russ has to go by is the 1992 interview Washington gave to Barbara Walters, in which she said she wasoffered $1m to recant her story. “Just a lying, reptilian, monstrous, young lady” is how Tyson characterized Washington ina 2003 interview with Fox’s Greta Van Susteren, adding that, with his reputation as a rapist already established, he might as well “rape her and her fuckin mama”.Ultimately, Tyson – who has even outlived fellow rogues Simpson and Tupac, an ardent supporter the boxer still remembers for visiting him in prison – dismisses Washington in the documentary as another opponent he overcame. “Whatever bad she tried to do, she lost,” he tells Russ. “What did she get, a million and a half bucks? I came out of prison with 400m bucks, so you tell me. I’m invincible.”Of course, longtime Tyson watchers might be inclined to dismiss that as more tough talk, given how entrenched his vulnerabilities are in media canon. Over the years, Tyson has spoken at length about how growing up poor and Black in Brownsville, amid abuse at home and bullying on the streets, followed him into adulthood. The death of Cus D’Amato, the mythic boxing trainer who nurtured his talent and brought stability to his life, continues to cast a long shadow. The timing of that loss, just as Tyson was on the verge of becoming the youngest heavyweight champion in history, remains a source of tremendous pain. In 2009, his four-year-old daughter was playing on a treadmill when she became entangled in the machine’s emergency-stop safety tether andaccidentally strangled herself. In those tough moments, you really feel for the guy.And yet there is something unnerving about Tyson’s candor, his willingness to revisit the darkest chapters of his life with the same openness as his triumphs – like sitting down with a storybook monster and finding him eager to explain the horrors without actually having to take any accountability for them. And while the Netflix doc captures Tyson seemingly without pretense – eavesdropping on his therapy sessions and joining in on hishallucinogenic Toad-venom 5-MeO-DMT trip– the fighter is never completely unguarded. He knows the cameras are there, and that Netflix will take it easy on him. Tyson, a producer on this project too, invited them in after all. If anything, the doc makes clear Tysonlivesfor the camera and redemption is never the point –andthat the gawkers will keep showing up, even though most already know what is in store. “This camera, to me, is a narcotic,” he says. “I’m so overwhelmed and overpowered by this narcotic, I’ll make a fool out of myself. It’s just that addicting.”Explore more on these topicsDocumentaryMike TysonBoxingNetflixTelevisionFactual TVUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: The eyes have it: Reform politician’s ‘smart glasses’ prompt calls for ban in Westminster | Wearable technology | The Guardian
description: Jason O’Connell’s suspected use of the specs to aid his speech in Senedd reignites debate over AI-enabled devices
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Jason O’Connell’s suspected use of the specs to aid his speech in Senedd reignites debate over AI-enabled devices
Content: Reform UK politician appears to use smart glasses as teleprompter in debateWearable technologyThe eyes have it: Reform politician’s ‘smart glasses’ prompt calls for ban in WestminsterJason O’Connell’s suspected use of the specs to aid his speech in Senedd reignites debate over AI-enabled devicesRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 12.43 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a flowing speech packed full of precise statistics – but Jason O’Connell, aReform UKSenedd member, was not quite the gifted orator he had first appeared. The periodic flashing in his spectacles seemed to give the game away as he spoke for five minutes in the Senedd chamber without a glance at his notes.“Cardiff reviewed 192 roads, following 933 requests, and only four routes have returned to 30mph,” he said as he led the party’s charge to abolish 20mph traffic zones. “£38.3m wasted to implement this policy and up to £8.9bn in an act of economic self-harm.”It was probably no feat of memory – rather, the Reform member for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr was suspected of using smart glasses that turned his lenses into tiny teleprompters.In the days afterwards, Senedd members said the issue of smart glasses – popularised by Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta – needed to be dealt with at pace, with explicit guidance developed on their use.There was no suggestion that O’Connell’s glasses were recording. But it has prompted a fresh debate about the increasingly popular technology, with theHouse of Commonsfacing calls to ban smart glasses at Westminster.The Liberal Democrats wrote to Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, on Wednesday urging him to act amid the “increasing use of smart glasses” on the parliamentary estate. They warned that with Christmas coming, even more people could start using the AI-enabled devices in 2027.Norway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public placesRead moreThe technology has myriad implications. Anna Sabine, the Liberal Democrat spokesperson for culture, media and sport, said smart glasses could lead to debates becoming increasingly “managed”.“How much is the quality of what an MP is saying actually down to what they’re getting through the AI glasses?” she said. “It’s a really interesting question.”She said she had not yet identified anyone wearing smart glasses in parliament but added: “This is the problem: I wouldn’t necessarily know.” A law would help to keep the estate and the work MPs did “private and secure”.Sabine added: “Smart glasses can record video and take photographs discreetly … creating a particular risk to the existing rules on the parliamentary estate [limiting recording and photography].“I am regularly in meetings with documents or talking about important, private matters on behalf of my constituents. I am sure you will agree that the details of such cases should never be at risk of being shared because someone is filming or taking pictures discreetly.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Because smart glasses look like ordinary glasses, and increasingly their recording indicator lights can be covered or disabled, filming could easily go unnoticed by security teams, putting private information at risk.”A spokesperson for the UK parliament said it was reviewing its policy on the use of camera-equipped smart glasses, as well as other forms of wearable technology, on the parliamentary estate.The senior deputy speaker of the House of Lords, Lord Ponsonby, told parliament last month that the review “is considering the implications of these emerging technologies and whether additional guidance is required”.He added: “This work will bring together expertise from those responsible for filming and photography policy, physical and information security, privacy and data protection compliance and accessibility and reasonable-adjustment requirements, ensuring that any future approach appropriately balances security, privacy, operational needs and accessibility considerations.”O’Connell has been contacted for comment. On Sunday heposteda picture on X of himself wearing a pair of comedy large pink glasses for a breast cancer charity, with the message: “Trialling some new glasses for the chamber this week. Apparently my last ones caused quite a stir.”Explore more on these topicsWearable technologyWelsh politicsReform UKTechnology policyHouse of CommonsPrivacyWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remain
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remain
Content: Research workers in a lab in Irkutsk, Russia.Photograph: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/APView image in fullscreenResearch workers in a lab in Irkutsk, Russia.Photograph: The Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East/APAI (artificial intelligence)ExplainerCould AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remainIan SampleScience editorWed 14 Oct 2026 13.34 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his annual speech on threats to the nation, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of the UK’s intelligence service,MI5, warned that AI had the potential to “change the stakes” on existing and even new bioweapons. Here we look at how AI might help in the development of bioweapons and the hurdles that remain.How could AI help people make bioweapons?It depends on who wants to make them. One risk is the rogue, unskilled bad actor or terrorist group that works from a garage laboratory. AI chatbots could help them skill up, by compiling relevant information, planning experiments and troubleshooting problems. It’s likely the work would focus on using existing pathogens and toxins.The other risk comes from well-resourced organisations and nation states that have plenty of skilled scientists, high containment laboratories and all of the equipment and reagents needed to work on bioweapons safely. AI tools could help researchers identify genetic tweaks to make existing pathogens more lethal, for example. This is the more immediate concern, according to Dr Filippa Lentzos, a reader in science and international security at King’s College London. “Here, AI does not remove the need for expertise, it amplifies expertise that is already there,” she says.A more distant risk comes from highly skilled groups using AI to design completely new pathogens and toxins that are resistant to drugs or have no antidotes.Have people tried using AI to make bioweapons?Last year, police in India uncovered a suspected bioterrorism plot in which a doctor and several others drew on AI chatbot queries and AI-driven search, allegedly to help them make ricin, a deadly toxin, using kitchen tools. It is unclear whether the AI’s responses helped, but other accounts suggest the tools can provide relevant and dangerous information.The AI company Anthropic raised further concerns in September when itreportedfive cases of scientists in unnamed countries trying to use its Claude chatbot for what may have been dangerous work on viruses or toxins. One red flag, the company said, was that after being blocked, the scientists found workarounds.UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing InstituteRead moreIn one case, Anthropic said researchers used the chatbot to plan experiments that would introduce mutations in a highly pathogenic bird flu virus to make it adapt and spread more easily in mammals. The work, and the other cases, could signify attempts to make pathogens more dangerous, but such studies are also done in legitimate labs to help researchers spot future pandemics and develop vaccines and drugs to treat disease.What else has raised concerns?A flurry of studies has shown how AI tools can provide potentially dangerous information on bioweapons. In arecent exerciseat MIT, non-science students were asked if they could get an AI chatbot to help them unleash a pandemic. Within an hour, the chatbots listed four potential pandemic pathogens, explained how to make them from synthetic DNA, and supplied names of DNA synthesis companies that were unlikely to screen their orders. It is easier said than done, however.In another case, the Stanford University researcher Dr David Relman described how an AI explained how to modify a pathogen to make it resistant to treatment. Another scientist revealed that an AI chatbot had explained how to use a weather balloon to release biological weapons from the sky.The dual-use nature of biological research can make it hard to distinguish valuable work that could protect health from attempts to develop bioweapons. In 2025, scientists at Los Alamos National Laboratorytrained an AIto predict how exceptionally potent neurotoxins from marine snails latch on to human cells, work that could help in the development of antidotes. But the US government became concerned when Chinese researchers drew on the work to develop their own tool todesign new toxins. The Chinese researchers said the work was aimed solely at developing drugs.In April, scientists raised further concerns when they madethe first viruses designed by AI. The viruses are a particular type that only invade bacteria, and the work could lead to new medicines, but experts warned that it raised “urgent biosafety and biosecurity questions”.What hurdles make it difficult?Most work on bioweapons is beyond the reach of unskilled groups: as well as being highly technical, it is extremely dangerous. While AI chatbots might be prompted to give information on bioweapons, a list of instructions is not enough. “Information is only one part of the problem,” says Lentzos. “Tacit expertise, access to biological materials and equipment, experimental validation, scale-up and delivery all remain substantial barriers.”Sonia Ben Ouagrham-Gormley, the deputy director of the biodefense programme at George Mason University in Virginia says tacit knowledge – the unwritten knowhow that an AI is unlikely to help with – has been key in the success of historical state-run bioweapons programmes.Prof Martin Pačesa at the University of Zurich said access to material was critical. “Any graduate physicist could sketch up plans for a potentially more effective nuclear bomb, but where is he going to get a lump of uranium from? Same for bioweapons. If you have access to material and facilities capable of producing them, then AI is not going to make too much difference if you want to do harm.”What extra measures are needed?Some AI companies are taking steps to prevent people from using their tools to develop bioweapons, but the majority are not announcing what, if anything, they are doing, says Prof Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We have no formal government policies in place in any country yet to protect against this kind of misuse,” he says.He wants formal independent evaluations of new AI models before they are released, with any dangers eliminated before the models are made public. And high-risk biological data, such as information on how pathogens might spread more easily, should be restricted. Meanwhile, companies that make genetic material for researchers must screen orders to ensure they are not for the creation of novel, highly dangerous viruses. Some screening already happens, but it is largely voluntary, and can be sidestepped if researchers use AI to design new, harmful genetic sequences that companies are not checking for.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChatbotsInfectious diseasesMI5AnthropicUK security and counter-terrorismBiologyexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Palantir and Sadiq Khan drop legal battle over Met contract | Palantir | The Guardian
description: Dispute related to claims London mayor blocked US tech firm from £50m police deal because of concerns over its values
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Dispute related to claims London mayor blocked US tech firm from £50m police deal because of concerns over its values
Content: Sadiq Khan said Palantir ‘makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital’.Photograph: Justin Tallis/ReutersView image in fullscreenSadiq Khan said Palantir ‘makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital’.Photograph: Justin Tallis/ReutersPalantirPalantir and Sadiq Khan drop legal battle over Met contractDispute related to claims London mayor blocked US tech firm from £50m police deal because of concerns over its valuesRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePalantir and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, have called off theirlegal fightover claims the Labour mayor was blocking the US tech company from signing a contract with the Metropolitan police because of its values and ethics.Palantir and the mayor’s office for policing and crime (Mopac) announced on Wednesday they had withdrawn allegations against each other, heading off a high court trial scheduled for January.Palantir sued Mopac in June after Khanstepped into block it from awarding Palantir a two-year, £50m deal for Scotland Yard to use AI to process intelligence in criminal investigations in a system called unified operational analytics (UOA), citing a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules.With Palantir also working for the Israeli military and for the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, Khan has previously said Londoners only wanted to see public money being paid to companies that “share the values of our city”.Louis Mosley, who heads Palantir in the UK and Europe, responded by accusing Khan of politicising procurement and said he was “putting politics above public safety”. He said: “What Londoners value is not being mugged, not being raped by a serving police officer.”The agreement to drop the claims against each other comes a month after Palantirhired Tom Watson, the former Labour party deputy leader, as a full-time lobbyist. The firm was concerned that if public authorities were able to block it from winning contracts due to objections over the values of its senior leadership, it would undermine its ability to operate in the UK.Palantir is facing a battle to retain its £330m NHS medical data contract amid a vociferous campaign from parts of the public and some MPs for it to be replaced by a less controversial company.Palantir and Mopac said in a joint statement that Mopac’s decision in May to block the contract “was not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company”.“Mopac recognises Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the mayor’s spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision,” it said.“Mopac’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners.”Khan said: “London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organisations across the UK and beyond.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWatson said: “The mayor and his team have recognised their actions could have created the impression that the decision to block the UOA contract was based on Palantir’s values. I’m very pleased that they have today corrected any such impression, and that even in the face of extreme provocation from highly organised pressure groups, decisions about deploying technology can still be made on their merits and in the public interest.”A new procurement process for the £50m police tech deal is under way and Mopac has agreed to treat Palantir “fairly and equally” if it bids, as expected. Equally, Mopac is not bound to agree to Palantir’s appointment.Each side is covering its own legal costs, no admissions of liability are made and no damages have been paid.Explore more on these topicsPalantirSadiq KhanLondon politicsMetropolitan policeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tool and target: US law enforcement grapple with AI-enabled terrorism and anti-tech extremism | Technology | The Guardian
description: From the FBI to local police departments, US authorities are increasingly warning of would-be terrorists using AI to plan attacks and anti-datacenter extremism
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: From the FBI to local police departments, US authorities are increasingly warning of would-be terrorists using AI to plan attacks and anti-datacenter extremism
Content: A previously unreported cache of law enforcement and intelligence agency documents show that law enforcement agencies have, since 2021, considered AI both a tool and a target of would-be terrorists.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA previously unreported cache of law enforcement and intelligence agency documents show that law enforcement agencies have, since 2021, considered AI both a tool and a target of would-be terrorists.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesTechnologyTool and target: US law enforcement grapple with AI-enabled terrorism and anti-tech extremismFrom the FBI to local police departments, US authorities are increasingly warning of would-be terrorists using chatbots to plan attacks and anti-AI extremist threatsJohana BhuiyanandNick Robins-EarlyWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.38 EDTShareIn May 2025, a 25-year-old mandetonateda car bomb outside a Palm Springs fertility clinic, killing himself and injuring four others. For many, it was a wake-up call about the threats to reproductive care facilities. For the FBI, though, it was also a sign of what the agency had feared for years: bad actors were using generative AI to plan and execute terror plots.The suspect used an unnamed generative AI tool that failed to detect his request for bomb-making instructions, law enforcement officers wrote in a previously unreported document reviewed by the Guardian. The privacy of his conversation with the AI chatbot hindered alerting police that someone was looking up how to make a bomb, according to the memo.FBI officers fear the scenario is set to repeat itself: “Threat actors will likely increase their use of GenAI tools for attack planning,” said the memo, which was distributed by the bureau’s Los Angeles division in May 2026. “Current built-in GenAI safeguards are insufficient to prevent illicit use as malicious actors successfully employ ‘jailbreaking’ techniques to access dangerous information.”AI executives and staff at leading AI companies have focused their public remarks on potential doomsday scenarios, a long-term, hypothetical harm of the technology they are developing. Law enforcement officers, by contrast, have been grappling with what they fear are the present-day threats that AI enables, including violent crimes.A previously unreported cache of law enforcement and intelligence agency documents show that law enforcement agencies have, since 2021, considered AI both a tool and a target of would-be terrorists. Law enforcement has been trying to keep pace with the ways bad actors may be using AI for harm, concerned that the rapidly evolving technology may supercharge new and existing types of crimes.At the same time, as public sentiment over AI and its impacts on society and the environment has soured, agencies have sought to protect AI infrastructure. The documents show police and intelligence officers are closely monitoring online opposition to datacenters among various groups with what they describe as extremist ideologies.US police fear Meta smart glasses could be used to secretly record themRead moreThe Guardian exclusively reviewed more than 80 documents and memos that were distributed among a nationwide network of federal, state and local law enforcement offices – including the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the FBI and the New York City police department (NYPD) – between 2021 and 2026. They were obtained by the government transparency non-profit Property of the People and shared with the Guardian.In these documents, officers discussed:How extremists could use AI to devise attacks and recruit new membersHow AI could be used to disseminate and produce everything from deepfakes to election misinformation and child sexual abuse material (CSAM)How people seeking information on how to make weaponry or bombs could use AI to circumvent police detectionHow to ensure that officers could take advantage of AI tools in policing, for things like social media monitoring, while managing public concern over the use of these toolsMonitoring social media for opposition to AI and potential extremist attacks on datacentersThe FBI did not respond to detailed questions on its monitoring of anti-AI sentiment and use of AI, but pointed to a general fact sheet on the agency’s use of the technology.The NYPD stated that its threat analysis report on artificial intelligence was related to the “AI 2027” project – an influential forecast from several AI researchers that speculated about the technology’s rapid growth and the threats it could present. In one of the project’s possible futures, it predicted bioweapon-armed drones wiping out humanity.“This NYPD Intelligence Analysis Report contained a summary and assessment of AI 2027,” the NYPD said. “It was distributed to appropriate NYPD members and partners for their awareness, as part of the Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau’s mission of analyzing developments and trends that have implications for public safety and national security.”The DHS said it “prioritizes the safety and security of Americans and remains committed to mitigating all forms of ideologically-motivated violence”, and regularly shares intelligence with state and local law enforcement related to threats from violent extremists.“DHS threat assessments draw on available intelligence, law-enforcement information, and other reporting to inform partners of evolving threats,” the DHS said in a statement. “DHS assesses that malicious actors may seek to use artificial intelligence to enhance existing harmful activities, including cyber-enabled activity, fraud schemes, and the production or dissemination of violent extremist propaganda”.Tech-enabled terrorism and anti-tech extremismLaw enforcement agencies’ concerns over AI and extremism fall into two broad categories, the documents show. One focuses on the burgeoning threat of extremists using new tools such as generative AI to plot attacks or promote their ideology. The other involves extremists targeting the modern technology that underpins society and has a long history within far-right movements.Before mainstream, widespread opposition to datacenters swept the US, there was a strain of violent extremism that targeted tech facilities and other critical infrastructure, hoping such terrorism could lead to the collapse of society and instigate a race war.Law enforcement officers expressed concern over the threat these militias posed to datacenters’ security before the 2022 launch of ChatGPT. Several bulletins, such as an October 2021 joint threat analysis from DHS, National Counterterrorism Center and FBI, highlighted a plot by Seth Pendley, a January 6 rioter andfar-right militiamember, to blow up an Amazon Web Services facility.“Pendley believed a successful attack on the Amazon facility would disrupt 70 percent of Internet service, expose perceived abuses of power, and lead to revolution,” the bulletin said. Pendley pleaded guilty to a charge of malicious attempt to destroy a building with an explosive and was sentenced in 2021 to 10 years in prison for plotting the attack.Although law enforcement agencies have long trackedextremist militia threats to infrastructurelike Pendley’s, the documents show that in the years since the generative AI boom began, agencies more frequently expressed concern over anti-tech and anti-datacenter sentiment. Multiple fusion centers – law enforcement hubs for collecting information and coordinating between agencies – around the US warned of growing threats from domestic violent extremists – pointing to posts across social media platforms, messaging apps and forums like 4chan in which commenters vowed to destroy datacenters.“I bring a sort of ‘tannerite and gasoline’ vibe to ai data centers,” an account associated with a white supremacist posted on Facebook last year, according to a 2025 Philadelphia police department intelligence bulletin. Combining gasoline with Tannerite, a brand of well-known explosive compound, produces a large and fiery detonation.On some far-right forums, users discussed killing CEOs of AI companies and local officials who support datacenters, agents warned, as well as arson and bombing attacks against data facilities.Law enforcement agencies also monitored real-world anti-datacenter incidents or protests, including a demonstration in Michigan in March where the documents said that three people allegedly associated with a white supremacist group held a banner opposing what they called a “Jewish data center” being built in the state.As opposition to artificial intelligence and datacenters have become more widespread, however, questions have arisen over how law enforcement agencies’ tracking anti-datacenter and anti-tech ideology may bleed over into surveillance of non-violent protest movements. Distrust of the AI industry and mobilization against datacenters has now become so prevalent that it is a mainstream issue of the midterm elections, far from an extremist position.The documents show agencies casting a wide net as they track opposition to the tech industry, including broadly monitoring public social media and opposition such as proposed legislation against datacenters. In a Nevada Threat Analysis Center report from April 2026, law enforcement officials cited alocal city council hearingon a datacenter moratorium as part of a trend of increased negative sentiment towards the facilities.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators hold signs during a protest against artificial intelligence outside Open AI’s headquarter offices in San Francisco, California, on 11 July 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images“The Reno City Council heard a strong public opposition to data center development in the area. The concerns focused on water consumption, rising utility costs, pollution, and long-term climate impacts,” the document said.Some experts and activists have expressed concern that asmobilization against datacenters grows, peaceful anti-AI organizations could face surveillance from authorities.“There’s nothing extreme about not wanting to lose your livelihood to AI, your drinking water to AI datacenters, your privacy to ubiquitous AI surveillance or your life to runaway rogue AI,” said Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People. “What’s extreme is law enforcement treating these legitimate objections as threats to be neutralized.”The ‘rising threat’ of AIIn the months after OpenAI introduced ChatGPT in 2022, law enforcement agencies across the US began to pay attention to the way the novel technology was being used. Even in its infancy, the tool could produce images that were indistinguishable from “authentic images”, according to one May 2023 law enforcement document. Police in Minnesota and in California worried that function could exacerbate problems with child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes and “terrorist propaganda materials”.At the time, many of these risks were largely theoretical in the eyes of law enforcement, the documents show. In one memo distributed by two California intelligence centers, officials warned that officers should remain vigilant because they predicted AI may one day make it easier to circumvent CSAM detection methods, that it may be used to produce and disseminate deepfakes and that it may increase the volume of propaganda.But as generative AI expanded in both its capabilities and reach, so too did law enforcement concerns about the types of crimes it could enable. By April 2024, the DHS’s intelligence department sent out a memo suggesting, without citations or evidence, that foreign terrorist organizations and domestic violent extremists who were “presumably US based persons” had “successfully bypassed generative Al guardrails” in order to generate bomb-making instructions and “general tactics for conducting attacks against the United States”.Warnings about the ways violent extremists exploit AI grew in their intensity in 2025. Individuals and malicious groups across the US were weaponizing AI tools “to spread hate speech, recruit new members, and radicalize online supports more efficiently”, according to a memo from the Orange County Intelligence Assessment Center. In one example the memo cited, users of rightwing social media platform Gab created an Adolf Hitler chatbot that was programmed to say that the Holocaust was exaggerated, climate change was a scam and the 2020 election was rigged. Other examples had less evidence. The intelligence center wrote that a 17-year-old student who opened fire in Antioch, Tennessee, in January 2025 was “likely influenced by the vast amounts of extremist content readily available through the AI-enhanced web”. The source the center cited in this example included no mentions of AI.A few months later, in April 2025, the Joint Regional Intelligence Center (JRIC), a Los Angeles-based DHS fusion center and the largest such facility in the country, published a five-part series issuing a stern warning: the misuse of generative AI for nefarious purposes was on the rise. Among the concerns was the surge in AI-created CSAM. The National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), a child protection non-profit, received more than 7,000 child exploitation reports involving GenAI between 2023 and 2025, the memo said.Child sexual abuse content growing online with AI-made images, report saysRead moreBy 2026, the documents showed that law enforcement agencies were paying more attention to how AI could make their jobs harder. In April, New York state’s intelligence center warned that AI-generated images were being used to prank people, including officers. In March, a man was arrested in Florida for showing an officer an AI-generated video of his patrol car being broken into. That same month, a man in New York was arrested for using AI to create false evidence that his car was damaged by police.“This activity involving a patrol car represents a form of law enforcement harassment,” the memo said. “While often intended as humorous and not intentionally seeking to create dangerous situations, the prank can elicit an armed law enforcement response.”AI’s proliferation could also make it harder for police to be tipped off to planned violent attacks, officers’ memos warned. In an FBI public safety awareness report, the agency cautioned that the private nature of AI models made it easier for bad actors to evade any “tripwires” or anything that would trigger an alert – like posting in an open forum with bystanders who might report them to the authorities. In the memo, the FBI encouraged agencies to develop relationships with AI companies to streamline “reporting avenues”.Law enforcement agencies have grown wary of the ways AI could be used against them – even if they also use those very same tools for their police and investigative work. As the Guardian previously reported,police have warned that Meta’s AI-enabled smart glasses could be used to surreptitiously record their activities. In an August 2025 NYPD memo, police warned that law enforcement agencies needed to keep pace with AI advancements so they were prepared to respond “to increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, other Al-enabled crime, and advanced malign influence campaigns”. But they also worried about the public questioning police use of AI including for social media monitoring.“Law enforcement organizations may also face the challenge of calming public fears over the extent of the use of Al in policing, including rumors surrounding surveillance, the loss of privacy, and even the future integration of humanoid robots into the police force,” the memo said.In January, an officer from a Maine intelligence center warned that a new AI-enabled software in Amazon Ring and other video doorbells could be used to monitor and alert residents of police activity. Several companies have implemented a feature that sends alerts about activity that the doorbell cameras detect, describing what’s happening outside using AI. Police and law enforcement have a long history of obtaining and accessing Amazon Ring footage as part of their investigations.“This notification feature can compromise officer safety, as it could provide advanced warning of an officer’s presence, tactics, formations, equipment, and could expose officers to increased risks,” the memo said.

title: Nvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety research | Nvidia | The Guardian
description: Pledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risen
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Pledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risen
Content: Nvidia says most of the money will ‘support the wider UK AI safety and security research community’.Photograph: Manami Yamada/ReutersView image in fullscreenNvidia says most of the money will ‘support the wider UK AI safety and security research community’.Photograph: Manami Yamada/ReutersNvidiaNvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety researchPledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risenDan MilmoGlobal technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 06.10 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmakerNvidiais donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research.The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models,will be able to examine cutting-edge technologydeveloped by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released.Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”.Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents hadattacked Hugging Face, a tech startup.Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London.The computing power will be delivered via UK-based datacentres using Nvidia chips.“The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.”Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”.On Monday Narayan confirmed that AISI was conducting tests on US-developed AI models before they are released, after reports that the White House had restricted access.The AI minister also warned that the UK faces agentic attacks similar to the one carried out by OpenAI agents on Australia’s healthcare system this year.“It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached,” said Narayan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot,warned of a new AI safety threat on Mondayafter it published a blogpost stating its models could soon become self-replicating. They find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart ovens and lawnmowers, the company said.Under such a scenario the models could power themselves without datacentres, and instead could use a “botnet” of interconnected devices, Anthropic said, adding that the world should prepare for a future where such botnets were here to stay.“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” Anthropic’s researchers wrote.Explore more on these topicsNvidiaAI (artificial intelligence)Technology sectorComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Eight states accuse OpenAI of coaching children to harm themselves in lawsuit | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: US states sue ChatGPT maker and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young users
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: US states sue ChatGPT maker and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young users
Content: Eight US states sued OpenAI, alleging the ChatGPT maker is harming children en masse.Photograph: izusek/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEight US states sued OpenAI, alleging the ChatGPT maker is harming children en masse.Photograph: izusek/Getty ImagesOpenAIEight states accuse OpenAI of coaching children to harm themselves in lawsuitUS states sue ChatGPT maker and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young usersDara KerrandBlake MontgomeryWed 14 Oct 2026 17.50 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight US states sued OpenAI Wednesday, alleging theChatGPTmaker is harming children en masse.Kansas, Arizona, Montana, Iowa and four others allege the company’s products carried out “willful, dangerous, reckless and unlawful conduct” by coaxing children into harming themselves.“OpenAI is hurting kids and they are lying to Iowans,” Brenna Bird, the attorney general for Iowa, said in a statement. “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide – all while pretending to be their fake friend.”All eight states accuse OpenAI of violating consumer protection laws and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young users. They are additionally seeking monetary damages, and asking the court to halt OpenAI from developing artificial intelligence models that can improve upon themselves until the company shows those models are in line with human values.This is the first time several US states have banded together in a coordinated legal action against an AI company.Drew Pusateri, a spokesperson for OpenAI, said the company had“built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack”.“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” Pusateri continued. “We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company.”The lawsuits allege that OpenAI has been misleading the public into believing that ChatGPT is a safe tool and that the company puts safety first. The states say that in reality, the chatbot has been designed to be “overly agreeable and feign human compassion”. The attorneys point to examples of ChatGPT being dangerous to vulnerable users, like children, and coaching people to commit suicide or harm others.This comes after a groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI andother tech companiesalleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has beensued in seven separate casesthat blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”.Dozens of cases have also been filed against OpenAI over ChatGPT’s alleged role in mass shootings. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI ofconcealing safety risksafter a mass shooting at Florida State University. The company has also beensued by the families of 37 victimsof the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting in Canada, who allege ChatGPT induced the shooter to carry out the attack.The eight states that filed suit on Wednesday say there is a growing body of research that allegedly shows ChatGPT can harm critical-thinking skills, encourage paranoia and delusions, offer dangerous medical advice and promote unhealthy behavior.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe lawsuits also note that the recent examples of OpenAI’s models going rogue, with its AI agentshacking into other companiesandgovernment entities, show that the technology is prone to deceiving human users.Pusateri said OpenAI had strengthened its safeguards in regards to those episodes and would “continue sharing information about the extensive steps we’ve taken in response to incidents of misalignment”.The eight states are suing OpenAI independently in their state courts and include Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIChatGPTAI (artificial intelligence)ChildrenChildren's techChatbotsLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI accuses employee who left for Apple of leaking plans for unreleased device | Apple | The Guardian
description: Hours before Apple and the ChatGPT maker were due to face off in court, a new allegation delayed the showdown
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hours before Apple and the ChatGPT maker were due to face off in court, a new allegation delayed the showdown
Content: Apple has said it has policies and procedures to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenApple has said it has policies and procedures to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers.Photograph: Andrew Harnik/Getty ImagesAppleOpenAI accuses employee who left for Apple of leaking plans for unreleased deviceHours before Apple and the ChatGPT maker were due to face off in court, a new allegation delayed the showdownReutersWed 14 Oct 2026 16.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn ⁠OpenAIemployee who left theChatGPTmaker forApplesent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal ⁠account and later ⁠made a presentation ​about the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership, a new filing in the lawsuit between OpenAI and Apple alleges.In the filing ⁠in US federal court in San Jose, California,OpenAIalleged that the presentation happened months ago and that Apple is now making ⁠AI products of its own, citing the release of Apple’s HomeView product this week.“OpenAI ​is very concerned that its trade ‌secret and confidential information is ‌now circulating insideApple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s ‌confidential and innovative work,” OpenAI said in its filing.The two companies were due to face off in court on Wednesday in an ongoing trade secrets lawsuit, but the new allegation delayed the showdown. OpenAI said it may file a countersuit based on the new claim.Apple said that it has policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers and that it has found no evidence to support OpenAI’s allegations.The document, filed on Tuesday, is part of a trade secret dispute ‌filed by Apple earlier this year against OpenAI. The iPhone maker alleged its own employees left and took confidential information to OpenAI’s hardware ​division. OpenAI has denied those allegations.Earlier this week, US district court judge Edward Davila granted part of Apple’s request for early access to digital files from OpenAI in the suit.Davila said Apple could gather data from some of its former employees’ devices and ⁠sit three of them for depositions on a sped-up schedule, including the ​two defendants in ​the case – Chang Liu, a former ​senior system electrical engineer, and Tang Yew Tan, a former vice-president of product ‌design for iPhone and ​Apple Watch.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe case ​is likely to go to trial in October 2027, though OpenAI has said in court filings that it could be ready for trial as soon as June 2027.Explore more on these topicsAppleOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)Intellectual propertyChatGPTnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annually | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares
Content: OpenAI is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1.1tn.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1.1tn.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersOpenAIOpenAI’s London staff receive average of £2.3m per person annuallyAccounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last yearRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 14 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.The earnings amount to 58 times the median UK full-time employee earnings,according tothe Office for National Statistics. An OpenAI worker on an average package could expect to take home about £1,000 an hour in salary and equity before tax.But there is understood to be a wide discrepancy between the highest and lowest earners.
