The biggest compensation packages are reserved for AI researchers who help build the San Francisco company’s cutting-edge models such as Astra.The figures relate to 2025, when there was a talent war and OpenAI’s rival, Meta, was reported to be offering multi-year packages running into several hundred million dollars.OpenAI’s London base reflects the UK capital’s status as an important hub for AI talent with some of the brightest machine-learning experts and AI researchers coming out of universities such as Cambridge. Google DeepMind is also based in King’s Cross.The company declined to comment on the figures, which come after a series of AI safety crises involving its models. This summer AI agents, under training, escaped andhacked into an unrelated company website, Hugging Face, while this monthone of its safety leaders quit, saying that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.OpenAI’s London office has been established as its largest international research hub but it also houses a government affairs team and sales and marketing functions – responsible for selling licences to companies and organisations. George Osborne, the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer, joined last December as the company’s head for countries.The earnings were a big jump on the previous year, when the average pay and equity package was £1.1m.Booming AI salaries have already had asignificant effect on housing pricesin San Francisco, where the average one-bedroom property now rents for $4,400 per month, a figure that is up more than 25% from last year and is nearly three times the US average. Landlords have been trying to capitalise on the boom, particularly in areas closest to the offices of the biggest AI companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.In London, OpenAI UK Ltd recorded a more than trebling of its turnover in 2025 to £293m, on which it made a £20.3m profit.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIChatGPTAI (artificial intelligence)LondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers
Content: Simbarashe Kundizeza says the story is entirely his own work.View image in fullscreenSimbarashe Kundizeza says the story is entirely his own work.AI (artificial intelligence)Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning storyArticle in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writersRachel Savagein JohannesburgWed 14 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.Kundizeza’s storyThe Blue Fighterwas announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published anarticleby the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”Vara said that she had run the story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The exception, she said, was an epigraph from what is described as an unpublished poem by the South African writer Vangile Gantsho.Vara said that when she read the story, she “was struck by the proliferation of language that is common in AI-produced writing: the not x, but y sentence constructions; the glut of metaphors; the platitudinous aphorisms”.She said: “Taste is subjective, but trust me, this story is bad – maudlin and full of tired tropes.”Kundizeza responded in astatement on X: “For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote ‘The Blue Fighter’. I did not use generative AI to write it. It is entirely my own work.“I look forward to continuing to work with theCaine prizeteam, and to celebrating this recognition with the people who helped bring this story into the world. Most importantly, I will continue to write.”View image in fullscreenJournalist Vauhini Vara said she had run Kundizeza’s story through the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, and it had deemed the story to be almost entirely AI generated.Photograph: Andrew AltschulSimilar claims have been made recently about other literary prize winners. In July, the Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazirwon the Commonwealth Foundation’s short story prizewith The Serpent in the Grove, despite critics on social media claiming it had “obvious markers” of AI writing.Last month, the Canadian-Haitian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça Ou Mourir (It Was That or Die) wasremoved from the longlistof France’s most prestigious literary prize, the Goncourt, after an anonymous online account alleged the book was “almost entirely” written by AI.The Caine prize said in astatementthat it was reviewing the allegations that Kundizeza had used AI. It said: “When such claims are made, it is our responsibility to look into them. We aim to do this by taking a human-centred approach, ensuring that writers are supported and cared for during the process.”Its chair questioned the reliability of AI-detection software itself.Ellah Wakatama told the BBC’s Front Row radio show: “As someone who chairs a prize, I’m obviously not against AI, but what I am against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case, regardless of what the Atlantic says, because they have already proclaimed our winner to be a cheater without investigating it properly.“I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready.”Vara said in her article, and repeated in an interview with Front Row, that she had read a 2021 story by Kundizeza that was tonally and stylistically different from The Blue Fighter.Novelist accused of using AI to write book removed from French prize listRead moreIn his statement, he responded: “To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing.”Vara pointed to Pangram’s own research that found that false positives were rare, including for non-native English speakers writing in English, as well as a peer-reviewed journalarticlethat found Pangram had “strong accuracy” when assessing mock academic papers created fully, partly or with no AI. However, she acknowledged to the BBC that there was “relatively little third-party research” on the accuracy of AI detection software.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Caine prizeThe AtlanticShort storiesAwards and prizesFictionZimbabwenewsShareReuse this content

title: Was this Mark Zuckerberg’s first – and last – taste of Guinness? | Beer | The Guardian
description: The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half full
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half full
Content: Mark Zuckerberg savours the flavour of a pint of Guinness.Photograph: YouTube/Cheeky PintView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg savours the flavour of a pint of Guinness.Photograph: YouTube/Cheeky PintPass notesBeerWas this Mark Zuckerberg’s first – and last – taste of Guinness?The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half fullWed 14 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Guinness.Age:Arthur Guinness began brewing porter in the 1770s. Guinness draft was first poured in 1959.Appearance:Espresso martini in a pint glass.But it’s beer.It’s stout, yeah. Irish stout.Sort of an old man’s drink, isn’t it?Not these days. Fans of Guinness include Kim Kardashian, Olivia Rodrigo, even the Princess of Wales.That’s just a bunch of celebrities pretending to like Guinness either because they’re visiting Ireland or it’s Saint Patrick’s Day. Or both.Some of them have actually tasted it:Mark Zuckerberg, for example.I wouldn’t have guessedZuckerbergdrinks Guinness.He has drunk it – and apparently for the first time – on a recent instalment of the Irish billionaire John Collison’s Cheeky Pint podcast, which is set in a pub.How did he like it?He didn’t say.What makes you think it was his first time?The look on his face.Did he look as if he was enjoying it?He looked as if he might be allergic to it.What do you mean?At the start of the podcast, while discussing his new Muse AI app, theMetafounder picks up the full pint in front of him and takes a sip.Like a regular person, you mean.Close enough, up to that point. But his subsequent reaction went viral.What did he do?He looked surprised, for a start. Then as if he was having trouble swallowing. He pursed his lips, squirmed in his seat and seemed to be looking around for the nearest exit.Oh my.After that he clutched at his shirt collar a bit. He even tried smiling briefly before realising he’d selected the wrong human facial expression from the dropdown menu. Eventually he managed to power down and reset himself.Did he at leastfinish the pint?He kept at it, but by the 1 hour 20 minute mark he’d only managed about half.Then what happened?There was an apparent break in filming, and when they resumed he had another full pint in front of him.His worst nightmare! Still, I suppose Guinness can manage withoutZuckerberg’s endorsement.You would have thought so – it sells 1.88bn pints a year globally, withsales continuing to rise, while the overall beer market declines. And Guinness 0.0 is the No 1 non-alcoholic beer in the UK.So what made Zuckerberg think he ought to pretend to like it?Well, he didbuy a castle in Irelandlast month for €20m (£17m), so maybe he’s planning on popping down to his local more often?Do say:“Guinness is an acquired taste, and I’m in the process of acquiring it in the same way I’ve acquired many startups and competitors. Was this answer helpful?”Don’t say:“Then, when my new AI model kills everyone, I’ll drink what I like.”Explore more on these topicsBeerPass notesMark ZuckerbergFood & drink industryMetaAlcoholfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like being in a vortex’: US report details extent of ‘devastating’ dating-app scams | US politics | The Guardian
description: Congress calls for Match Group and others to do more to help victims like Mary, who lost $100,000 to app scammer
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Congress calls for Match Group and others to do more to help victims like Mary, who lost $100,000 to app scammer
Content: Senator Maggie Hassan in Washington in 2020. Hassan said there was ‘still more that Match needs to do’.Photograph: Alexander Drago/ReutersView image in fullscreenSenator Maggie Hassan in Washington in 2020. Hassan said there was ‘still more that Match needs to do’.Photograph: Alexander Drago/ReutersUS politics‘Like being in a vortex’: US report details extent of ‘devastating’ dating-app scamsCongress calls for Match Group and others to do more to help victims like Mary, who lost $100,000 to app scammerAnna BettsWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMary met a man on the dating app Plenty of Fish in 2024. She told the Guardian she had been looking for a connection, but instead became the victim of a romance scam that cost her almost $100,000.“There was a lot of conversation, and then it started with the constant contact, pressure and repeated asks for money,” Mary, who asked that her last name be withheld, said in an interview on Tuesday. “It just escalated really, really quickly.”Mary was one of several people who spoke to staffers from the US Congress’s joint economic committee as part of an investigation by Senators Maggie Hassan, Democrat of New Hampshire, and Marsha Blackburn, Republican of Tennessee, into romance scams on dating platforms owned by Match Group. Match Group operates apps such as Tinder, Hinge, Plenty of Fish, Match (formerlyMatch.com) and others.“Romance scams, in which fraudsters form relationships to induce money or gifts from victims, have become a leading form of financial fraud in the United States and cost Americans at least $1.3bn annually,” the senators noted upon the investigation’s launchlast September.On Tuesday,a reportdetailing the results of that investigation was published.Internal documents provided by Match Group showed that “as of the second half of 2025, Tinder had not updated most of its machine learning models in years” and “as a result, Tinder detected scammers and other bad actors less reliably and struggled to keep pace with emerging threats”, per the report.Data provided by Match Group also showed that through the third quarter of 2025 in the US, nearly 1.5m scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge had “matched with at least one other user”. The report also showed that nearly 500,000 of those accounts “exchanged contact information with another user”.Mary told the Guardian that she tried to establish whether the scammer she spoke with was real. He would contact her constantly, she said, and knew where she lived. She said that the man told her he needed money for work-related things and medical emergencies.“They never leave you alone,” she said. “I call it like being in a vortex. You don’t even realise what’s happening. You’re sending money, and it’s adding up, but each one of those times that you send money, it’s, like, not connected to the other times. But finally when I realized how much money I lost, I was like: ‘Whoa.’”In total, Mary said she sent the man about $100,000 in cryptocurrency payments. After realizing he was a scammer, she blocked his number. He would then switch phone numbers and contact her again.Mary has since sought to identify the people behind the fraud and discovered other Plenty of Fish profiles using the same photos as the man she had talked to. She has reported them to the platform.“If you knew me, you would say she would never do that,” Mary said, adding that she struggles to understand how it all happened, but believes it’s “really a lot about force of control”.Tuesday’s report noted that since the launch of the investigation last September, Match Group had “introduced and expanded important measures designed to combat scams” includinga facial verification featureon the Tinder app across the US, “requiring all new Tinder users to complete a video selfie verification process”.In anews releaseon Tuesday, Hassan and committee Democrats added that Match Group also “instituted new efforts designed to remove harmful accounts more effectively” including in the first half of 2025, a “new AI model” that examines profiles and other information to detect scammers and other bad actors.“It is encouraging that following committee outreach, Match Group introduced new AI models,” the report states. However, those “changes came after a prolonged period during which scams continued to proliferate on Tinder”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn response to the report on Tuesday, Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice-president of trust and safety said in a statement: “We’re grateful the committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.”He said: “That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already complete. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history. Trust and safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.”Much of the safety work, including face check, was already under way before the committee’s investigation, Match Group toldNBC News.In June, Hassanintroduced legislationalongside with the Republican senator Rick Scott, that would establish a central portal for Americans to report scams “and get the help they need from law enforcement and agencies”.Hassan, in a statement along with the release of the report on Tuesday, described romance scams as “devastating – both financially and emotionally – to people who are looking for connection and instead find themselves targeted and exploited by global criminal enterprises”.“During the course of our investigation, Match Group made progress in combating scammers – but it shouldn’t have taken so long, and there’s still more that Match needs to do,” she said.“As criminal networks use AI to supercharge their scams, dating apps and all companies must quickly and proactively keep their scam defenses up to date. Companies must stay vigilant and prioritize comprehensive scam prevention at every level to protect consumers and block fraudsters from infiltrating online platforms.”Explore more on these topicsUS politicsDatingAppsUS CongressDemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth | Games | The Guardian
description: After years of sprawling, never-ending games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of shorter, more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming?
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: After years of sprawling, never-ending games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of shorter, more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming?
Content: Classic … video game arcades are finding new audiences.Photograph: Andrew Cline/AlamyView image in fullscreenClassic … video game arcades are finding new audiences.Photograph: Andrew Cline/AlamyPushing Buttons newsletterGamesReady player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirthAfter years of sprawling ‘forever’ games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming?Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 14 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s an important semi-nostalgic movement happening in games, and I’m excited about where it’s heading. But I don’t want to get ahead of myself here.Over the last five years, major publishers, obsessed with the success of “forever games” such as Fortnite, Minecraft and Roblox, have been throwing hundreds of millions of dollars into their own sprawling, endlessly updating, battle-pass-infested mega franchises – each designed to take all our time and money. The result has been astounding failures such asConcord, Mindseye and Tales of the Shire. Even the good games – Crimson Desert, Path of Exile 2, Blood of the Dawnwalker – are so bloated they have become the unyielding masters of our precious few hours of free time.It’s a relief, then, to see a growing number of mainstream titles heavily inspired by arcade design conventions, and intended as discreet, contained experiences. Along with the excellent driving game Star Wars Galactic Racer, which I rave about below, there’sAce Combat 8: Wings of Theve, an unreconstructed air-combat shooter that doesn’t want to become your whole life. You don’t have to romance your F/A-18F Super Hornet (although that does sound sort of cool), you don’t have to build your own airbase. You fly, you shoot things, there’s a story in the background, the end. It’s been equally lovely to see the success of Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls, a demanding 2D fighting game with complex interlocking power-up systems – the sort of thing my friends and I might have played in the arcades in 1993 before buying it on imported £100 Neo Geo carts.View image in fullscreenA quick round … in an age of endless online games, the appeal of the arcade is enduring.Photograph: B Christopher/AlamyAll of this points to one inevitable, socio-ludological phenomenon: the rebirth of the games arcade. Yes, I know there are already a few brilliant retro arcades dotted about, and plenty of chain bars and cafes such as Continue and NQ64 offering classic coin-ops alongside themed cocktails. There’s alsoArcade Arena, a new “immersive experience” venue in London that lets you play physical versions of Pac-Man and kart racers. But a growing number of players are interested in arcade-game design, and don’t necessarily want to play a few rounds of Time Crisis while downing a mojito.What I’m hoping to see is a more refined take on the coin-op arcade, something akin to the rise of the independent bookshop, with carefully curated collections of both new and classic experiences, and interesting events.This, I am pleased to discover, is happening. “The popularity of gaming bars and cafes is demonstrating that there is a sustainable business model in out-of-home gaming here in 2026,” says games journalist and arcade obsessive Will Freeman. “I wouldn’t go as far as to call it a boom, but there are a handful of smaller set-ups taking an approach that feels comparable to independent bookshops and record stores.”He mentions NQ Japan, which is about to open in London’s Soho. “While it is a cafe, there’s a firm focus on imported Japanese coin-op cabinets – covering newer games and cult classics that carry weight in the arcade community,” he tells me. “It really looks to be serving an authentic, arcade experience, bringing back that anticipation of getting your hands on exotic games from the cultural centre of arcade gaming.”View image in fullscreenHigh-end joy … the arcade gaming industry is booming.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianThe retro gaming industry is booming, with specialist manufacturers such as Analogue and Evercade producing high-end consoles that play original carts or new emulated collections of rare and sought-after titles. People are willing to spend money on an authentic arcade-style experience, just as they are now spending money on DVDs and vinyl records. A growing number of us want to have experiences that mega corps can’t provide through sleek, glassy devices.But while it is lovely that people are rediscovering foundational game mechanics through Ace Combat and Marvel Tōkon, there is much more to discover. The joy of arcades in the 1970s and 80s was that they were social hives as well as gaming spaces – you made friends, you learned from better players – and each game created its own community. Crucially, you went in with a handful of coins and could have a handful of very different experiences. A new era of boutique arcades could bring that back.“Something is under way, even if it is quietly,” says Freeman, pointing to smaller independent arcades with curated games libraries, such as Pixel Bunker in Milton Keynes. “I think we might see more independent arcades open up that drop the established ‘gaming cafe’ model to various degrees, and bring that feeling of local experts who really know their arcade culture, and want to build venues that draw in enthusiast communities.”Modern video games are bringing the arcade back into our homes. Perhaps now it is time to bring arcades back to our rapidly emptying high streets.What to playView image in fullscreenExcitingly familiar …. Star Wars Galactic Racer.Photograph: Fuse Games/Secret ModeIt feels like ages since we’ve seen an exciting mainstream racing game with a traditional linear structure rather than a vast open world. EnterStar Wars Galactic Racer– where you pilot landspeeders, speeder bikes and other outlandish Star Wars vehicles through intense circuits on excitingly familiar planets. As you progress, you unlock new parts and abilities, and plot your own route through a branching series of events. But crash out from a race and you have to go right back to the beginning of the season – a really clever implementation of rogue-lite design sensibilities in what is essentially a modern day take on Wipeout.What a joy it is to zoom through the wreckage-strewn canyons of Jakku and the icy tundras of Ando Prime, hitting the ramjet button to scorch past other vehicles at hundreds of miles-per-hour while a John Williams-adjacent symphonic score adds to the thrill. There hasn’t been a Star Wars racing title since Star Wars: Racer Revenge in 2002, which was, um, not a great game. I hope this is the beginning of a beautiful new era.Available on:PC, PS5, XboxEstimated playtime:20 hours plusskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenAI first? … Epic Games’ new approach to its forthcoming film adaptation.Photograph: Costfoto/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAsreported in Bloomberg, it seems that the Fortnite creatorEpic Gameshas ordered an “AI-first” approach to developing a forthcoming Disney title. “Progress on the title has allegedly been slower than expected, partly because Epic underestimated how many staff it would require,”writes VGC. The team has apparently been told to use tools such as Anthropic’s Claude AI.GamesIndustry.Biz adds: “In an internal message seen by Bloomberg, one of the game’s directors told staff: ‘No more hand-written code.’ The director also said all of the game’s art would be ‘generated with full AI workflows.’” How do the developers feel? Stunned is the most widely reported reaction.There is a lot of interest in the subject ofgames industry unionisation, partly because ofthe most recent Xbox lay-offsand partly due to theongoing legal battlebetween Rockstar and a group of ex-employees fired, they contend, because they were seeking to unionise. Kotaku hasan interesting and enlightening story, this time about a failed attempt to unionise at the veteran studio Double Fine and the ongoing ramifications.The latest novel by Guardian games contributor,Sarah Maria Griffinis out.Strange Is the Lightis a gothic thriller about a group of friends whose lives are torn apart by a live-action role-playing game they invented as children.What to clickCastlevania: Belmont’s Curse – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled | ★★★☆☆End of Abyss – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenHigh Score … Gail Tilden, who led Nintendo of America to multimillion-selling success.Photograph: Netflix/Courtesy of NetflixA great question this week fromTrudyvia email:“I’m really into documentaries at the moment. Could you recommend any that deal with video games and the gaming industry?”There are a few absolute classics that really defined the genre – among them areThe King of Kong, about the competitive Donkey Kong players Steve Wiebe and Billy Mitchell, andIndie Game: The Movieabout a community of indie devs in the early 2010s. I’d also recommend the Netflix seriesHigh Score,the bizarreAtari: Game Over, about the burial and excavation of hundreds of ET carts in the early 80s, and the self-explanatoryRubber-Keyed Wonder: The Story of the Sinclair ZX Spectrum. For online documentaries, you definitely need to visit the excellent YouTube channelsNoClipandPeople Make Games– they have done fascinating, important work. I also enjoyed Travis “Samox” Beauchamp’s charmingly idiosyncraticseries,The Smash Bros. Finally, I have to do this – tryAnAlternative Reality: The Football Manager Documentary, which features an insightful video game journalist you may well recognise.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter –email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterArcade gamesRetro gamesGames consolesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era | Games | The Guardian
description: The kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changer
Content: Evolutionary Link … The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenEvolutionary Link … The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2.Photograph: NintendoGamesThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K eraThe kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changerMatthew CastleWed 14 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen beloved art is revisited and revised, a familiar cry is often heard: “You’re ruining my childhood!” But with Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time, there are also livelihoods at risk: specifically, the man running the shooting gallery in Castle Town. In the original 1998 version of the game, he’d rip off players as they funnelled rupees and fudged the then still novel analogue-stick aiming. But in 2026 we have more responsive frame rates and a motion-controlled slingshot that allows precision adjustments. His targets tumble on the first go, and with them his entire business model. Even in Hyrule, the death of the high street seems inevitable.Bad news for him but great news for Link, a child of the forest who, as in 1998, steps into a vast fantasy kingdom to vanquish a great evil, but now does so with a number of improvements. The boy can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies to zip across grassy plains. He has a manual jump, free-rotating camera, a scrolling inventory bar that replaces menu screen faff and, crucially, a fatter wallet for holding all those gems he fleeces from struggling shooting gallery owners. Yes, we are being asked to applaud features that have been the norm for decades elsewhere, but it’s undeniably striking to enter familiar territory with a hero who feels this different under the thumbs.View image in fullscreenLink can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies.Photograph: NintendoThe dilemma facing any remake, let alone of a game recognised as a genre-defining classic, is how closely you hew to the past. As withthis year’s Star Fox revamp, Ocarina of Time finds Nintendo in a celebratory mode. It’s a polished victory lap for a game with little to prove. For newcomers it means seeing what the fuss is about without having to scrutinise the N64 original on unflattering flatscreen TVs. I doubt Hyrule Field – once a byword for video-game freedom – will ever conjure the awe it did in 1998, but seeing the sun catch in puddles and grass growing from the floor helps mask what is an obviously artificial pen, compared toBreath of the Wild’s sprawling continent.For some returning fans, the more controlled shape is precisely the appeal. After the “make your own adventure” ethos of Switch’s open-world Zeldas, there is comfort in slipping into traditional dungeons, where every room has a characterful beast to chop up or a mechanism to unpick with a growing kitbag of tools. My great fear was that some of the puzzles are simply too iconic to be forgotten and solved again. Yet here I am, sweatily hunting ghosts around the Forest Temple, and surreptitiously peering at my neighbour’s demo pod to remind myself that, yes, you have to … [redacted for your benefit]. Given that, in 1998, these were many designers’ first attempts at a 3D level, it is astonishing how fiendish they are and how you’re expected to hold complex architecture in your head to get the run of them.Also worth assigning headspace for: the newly orchestrated soundtrack. Melodies that fought through compressed N64 instrument samples to burn into the brain are given their own galloping freedom. I love the tentative brass when you lock an enemy into a duel – the musical equivalent of gnawing your lip.Link’s look is more contentious. Where Hyrule is prettied up with expected detail – swaying nettles in a forest home, marbled sunlight on a riverbed – its hero is radically made over. His large glassy eyes, and fat cheeks which reflect the light as if varnished, have led critics to accuse Nintendo of crudely pursuing a textbook next-gen sheen. Bells and whistles for the sake of filling 4K TVs with surface detail, rather than honouring the original artistic intent. In the past, some eager fans attempted to remake Zelda in more capable game engines and were ridiculed for mistaking technological grunt for artistry, and as evolving hardware opens those graphical avenues to Nintendo itself, it would be ironic if it fell for the same allure.In truth, Ocarina of Time looks coherent in motion on Switch 2. If anything, the layer of 4K specificity evokes another Zelda game, Twilight Princess, itself an attempt to apply a more mature, realistic lens to Hyrule. And could Link, with those overblown features, perhaps be nodding to another cultural pastime? As some corners of the internet scoffed at our newly “yassified” hero, the Nintendo veteran and former Legend of Zelda art director Takaya Imamura wondered if the character model drew from Zelda creator Shigeru Miyamoto’s own tastes. “[His] love ofningyogeki(puppet drama) is strongly reflected here,” Imamurawrote on X. Porcelain doll skin would certainly explain the uncanny sheen.View image in fullscreenIt is astonishing how fiendish the puzzles designed in 1998 still are.Photograph: NintendoWhile we can only guess at tight-lipped Nintendo’s intent, writer and translator Paul McQuade explains it is not an impossible leap. “In Japan, puppetry is not considered an art form strictly for children, which is largely how it’s perceived elsewhere,” he says. “It’s a rich art and is highly respected.” He thinks Miyamoto could easily have been influenced by puppet shows aired byJapanese broadcaster NHKin the Shōwa postwar era.And besides, there is something poetic about the notion. “It’s doll-like and intentionally juvenile,” McQuade says of Link’s chubby features and blushing nose. “It captures the essence of that forest where the children don’t ever grow up. Miyamoto, as a fan of puppetry, would of course draw on the vocabulary of dolls to make characters in that mould.”I like the idea of Nintendo honouring a community frozen in time in this way, while also acknowledging that time has moved on outside the game. With that passing comes an opportunity to tweak and massage. In an adventure where a boy can magically become a man and back again with the toot of his ocarina, it makes sense for timelessness and timeliness to be in conversation. With virtual bones this strong, it would be difficult to argue that anything has been truly ruined. Unless you run the shooting gallery, of course.The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is released for Switch 2 on 5 November.Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendo Switch 2NintendoThe Legend of ZeldafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The most important US midterm trends I’m seeing | Molly Jong-Fast | The Guardian
description: The one I worry about most is voter anger – which both parties are not taking seriously enough
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The one I worry about most is voter anger – which both parties are not taking seriously enough
Content: ‘Voters seem mad that the establishment isn’t elevating their concerns enough.’Photograph: Saul Loeb/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Voters seem mad that the establishment isn’t elevating their concerns enough.’Photograph: Saul Loeb/ReutersOpinionUS politicsThe most important US midterm trends I’m seeingMolly Jong-FastThe one I worry about most is voter anger – which both parties are not taking seriously enoughWed 14 Oct 2026 14.47 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTShareThat chill in the air you are feeling is not the weather, it is theRepublicansfreaking out about the 2026 midterm elections. Midterms are always referendums on the incumbent, though the party in power usually would rather they weren’t.This midterm feels less like a referendum on Trumpism than a dirge. It’s easy to see how Republicans got here, lulled into thinking that their guy, Donald Trump, could once again defy political gravity. Trump certainly thought he could.When it became clear he couldn’t, Trump tried to defy political gravity by federalizing elections and messing with mail-in voting (many would call this cheating) or redrawing the map to gain seats in states like Texas (many would also call this cheating).Even Trump at his peak couldn’t defy diesel at $6.50 a gallon, and Trump is no longer the deft faux populist he was in his first term. Bored, his eyelids often droop and his mouth often becomes slack during his PM meetings.The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too | EditorialRead moreIn a political environment like this whereDemocratshave about a nine-point advantage, even some of the redder parts of the country seem very much in play. Even some of those redrawn seats in Texas may stay in Democratic hands.Trump’s mail-in voting plan has been foiled by six and half supreme court justices, the political reality is beginning to sink in and that political reality is looking like a doozy. Turns out doing the exact opposite of what you campaigned on is not that popular. Here are some of stories I have noticed emerging this midterm election cycle.Hyper-local inflationOne of the things I noticed when interviewing political candidates for my podcast Fast Politics was that the cost-of-living crisis looks different in different places. In Maine, a candidate for the second congressional district, Matt Dunlap, told me his voters were worried about heating oil prices. That’s because diesel hit a record national average of $6.51 this week and both diesel and heating oil use a very similar chemical compound.Maine also starts getting cold in October, so heating oil is a major expense for residents. Bobby Pulido, a Texas congressional candidate and Tejano singer, told me that one of the things that voters in his 15th congressional district are worried about was beef prices, which are about $7 a pound. But Texas cattle ranchers are also not happy about the administrationimporting beef from South America.Bernie-DogsI’ve seen more than a few internet fights about the left v center divide in the Democratic party but there are candidates who represent both the left and the center. These are candidates who have been endorsed bythe Blue dogs and Bernie Sanders.They are populist moderates running in purple(ish) districts. I’ve talked to a lot of Democratic candidates who describe a political atmosphere which fueled by voter rage is not left v right as much as down v up.These candidates include Pennsylvania’s Bob Brooks, Wisconsin’s Rebecca Cooke, Montana’s Sam Forstagand Ohio’s Brian Poindexter. All these candidates are either very involved in their unions or, in the case of Cooke, in a union family. They are centrists and populists, something that at least theoretically shouldn’t coexist.EnvironmentalIowa has two major elections this cycle – in both the Democratic candidates are polling ahead, and in both the Democrats are running in an “up v down” framing. But the reason that Iowa, a state Trump won by 13.2 points in 2024 and 9.4 points in 2016, is so deeply in play this cycle may have more to do with environmental contamination than inflationary pressures. Iowa is in the middle of a cancer crisis; it has the second highest rate of cancer in the US. For people over the age of 50, it’s10% higher than the national average.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Medhi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCulture warsThomas Frank wrote about how Republicans in Kansas used culture war issues to get working-class people to vote for Republicans, who then enacted pro-oligarch legislation. Well, weirdly, Kansas has emerged as a focal point this cycle.The Wall Street Journal reported Roger Marshall, a Republican senator, was met with boos, hisses and jeering at the Kansas state fair Senate debate. He is running against Adam Hamilton, a popular Democrat and mega-church pastor. Recent reporting details Marshall’s predatory behavior regarding debt collectionsfor his gynecological practice. The Cook Political Report recently shifted the race fromlikely Republican to lean Republican, which for a state Trump won by more than 16 points is kind of striking.DesperationIn less than two years Republicans have gone from shocking bravado to desperately begging for votes. Vance went on the rightwing tech-bro podcast all in to ask voters to“give us another chance, or give us another couple of years, to continue to work on the amazing things that we’ve been doing for the past two years”.In Iowaat a rally for Republicans where Senate candidate Ashley Hinson didn’t show up, Vance pleaded with the crowd. “Whenever you hear me talk during this midterm campaign, I’ll say Rome was not built in a day because we know there’s a lot of work to do.”And on X, Matt Gaetz, a former Republican congressman,posted: “Bro we need your vote. I hate the war too. But the Democrats want to trans your kids.” It was such a clear distillation of the Republican closing message of these midterms: we didn’t do any of the stuff you elected us to do but Democrats want to … and then you can insert any of the culture warrior tropes that the party has bantered about.There are other trends, I’m seeing. The one that I worry the most about is voter anger. In 2018, we saw a rejection of Trumpism but voters didn’t seem as furious. It feels like both parties aren’t taking voter anger seriously enough.Sure, voters want to kick out Republicans, we can see this in the polls, but voters seem mad that the establishment isn’t elevating their concerns enough. Datacenters and government corruption are issues that 80% of voters support action on. If the establishment fails to address these issues with authenticity and zeal, both parties are going to have real problems.Molly Jong-Fast is the host of the Fast Politics pod, contributing writer for the times and an analyst for MS NowExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionRepublicansDemocratsUS midterm elections 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Removing political speech from MLS fans is untenable – just ask Austin FC | MLS | The Guardian
description: The protests around an anti-ICE T-shirt show that politics can never be separated from sports, especially now
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: The protests around an anti-ICE T-shirt show that politics can never be separated from sports, especially now
Content: Austin FC fans at a game on 9 September.Photograph: Scott Wachter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustin FC fans at a game on 9 September.Photograph: Scott Wachter/Getty ImagesMLSRemoving political speech from MLS fans is untenable – just ask Austin FCLeander SchaerlaeckensThe protests around an anti-ICE T-shirt show that politics can never be separated from sports, especially nowWed 14 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 16.47 EDTShareOn 26 September, Daniela Silva was expelled from Austin FC’s match with San Diego FC for wearing a T-shirt reading “Abolish ICE”.She saysshe was banned from Q2 Stadium for a year (Austin FC said that the ban was issued by the Austin Police Department, not the club, and that they offered to rescind it but that Silva declined).This happened, really, truly, and you cannot make this up, during Austin FC’s Hispanic Heritage Night. It also happened six days afterImmigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents shot a Venezuelan delivery driver, 28-year-old Wilber Garcés Pérez, in the torso in Austin, sparking protests in the city.The club’s Hispanic Heritage Night includedfolk dancesand highlighted local nonprofits serving the Hispanic community. “For Austin FC, celebrating Hispanic Heritage Month means celebrating the many cultures and communities that help make Austin what it is,”the club’s website still declares.And yet, a fan sporting a T-shirt with a very reasonable response to the ongoing assault on the Hispanic community of Austin, and indeed the nation, was banished.The club referred to Q2 Stadium policy, the wording of which is an exact copy of Major League Soccer’s fan code of conduct. Both prohibit, among other things, “Displaying signs, symbols or images for commercial purposes or for electioneering, campaigning or advocating for or against any candidate, political party, legislative issue, or government action.” It’s the same policy MLS has cited inseveral other instances, though an MLS spokesperson said on Wednesday that the league policy does not govern articles of clothing, but that a stadium policy would, hence why Silva was removed under the stadium policy.Regardless of which policy was responsible, Austin FC supporter groups Los Verdes and La Murga de Austin took issue, releasinga joint statement. “Opposition to ICE is not an abstract political debate for many of our members and neighbors,” it read. “It is about what is happening here, in our community, and about their safety, dignity, and ability to move through it without fear. In the days since, members of our community have questioned whether they feel safe and welcome returning to Q2. That should matter to Austin FC. The club has a responsibility to communicate clearly that our Hispanic and immigrant communities are welcome and safe at Q2.”At the club’s home game on Saturday, a 4-1 loss to runaway league leaders Nashville SC, La Murga de Austinwalked out in protestof Silva’s ejection, clearing out much of the supporters section. Its banner, reading “NO ICE IN THIS MELTING POT”, was taken down.“We love this club. But love is not silent,” La Murgasaid in a statement. “We are asking Austin FC to speak out – publicly, with conviction – against the injustice ICE is inflicting on the communities of Austin. The same communities the club says it supports. The same communities whose faces fill your marketing, whose voices fill your stadium, whose hands and hearts make this place what it is.”The club told the Guardian it is engaging with supporters on the topic of rules around political messaging in stadiums. But those rules are unjustifiable and, in this climate, possibly even untenable.MLS and its clubshave priorswhen it comes to these ideological confrontations with its own fans. In 2015, it ordered the removal of “Refugees welcome” banners at Toronto FC games. In 2019, the leaguehad to walk backits ban on the Iron Front symbol, first used by anti-Nazi paramilitaries in the 1930s and since broadly appropriated by the antifa movement – which has always been more of an idea than an actual organization but was nevertheless deemed to be political by the league. At the other end of the ideological spectrum, a man in a Make America Great Again hat was ejected from St Louis City’s stadium during a game last year.In the weeks after the war between Israel and Hamas began in 2023,MLS banned both Israeli and Palestinian flagsin its stands as a measure it called “temporary” but which, three years on, remains in place. A carveout exists, however, for Columbus Crew fans, who wereawarded an exemptionto fly a single Palestinian flag after the club signed Palestinian striker Wessam Abou Ali. Fans of the teams who field the league’s eight Israeli players can fly a single Israeli flag.Meanwhile, when Latino Nashville fans stayed away from their stadium in drovesfor fear of ICE arrestson their way home from games, the league did permit a banner reading “We’re not all here” to note their absence. The subtext was self-evident.Herein lies the trouble. The rules feel squishy because there is no one way to coherently and consistently keep political speech out of stadiums. The notion of apolitical sports, idealized by some as a kind of how-things-used-to-be paradigm that never existed, is a fantasy.MLS isn’t alone in trying to make it a reality. Most of the other American major leagues try just as hard to stay neutral in any matter that may cost them a few dollars by upsetting fans, or draw the ire of their overwhelmingly conservative owners. Then again, few sports seem to have hardcore fans as politically engaged as those in American soccer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’d also argue that the approach is counterproductive. An MLS stadium banning T-shirts with mainstream messages draws far more attention than just treating fans as adults with a worldview, who don’t need to be policed.MLS loves to highlight its hardcore fans when it sells itself to new audiences. Yet it also wants to sanitize them, rather than just accepting that most of them skew progressive and will proclaim their values accordingly.A league cannot cleanse itself of the inconveniences of reality outside its facilities, especially when that reality is expressly hostile to as many as 30% of its fans, per its own count. Pretending that it can only leads to ugly episodes like the one in Austin. Not to mention a disillusioned and mistrusting fanbase.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.This article was amended on 14 October to reflect MLS’s clarification that, though the wordings of the league’s fan code of conduct and the Q2 Stadium fan code of conduct are identical, the league’s does not govern articles of clothing while a stadium’s may.Explore more on these topicsMLSAustin FCUS sportsFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: How we lost our appetite for eat-the-rich satire | Movies | The Guardian
description: Tom Cruise’s latest film could lose $250m (£190m) – could one reason be that audiences are tired of Hollywood telling them what they already know about the super-rich
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tom Cruise’s latest film could lose $250m (£190m) – could one reason be that audiences are tired of Hollywood telling them what they already know about the super-rich
Content: Up in smoke … Digger director Alejandro González Iñárritu (left) and Tom Cruise at the film’s Japanese premiere in Tokyo on 6 October.Photograph: Keizo Mori/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenUp in smoke … Digger director Alejandro González Iñárritu (left) and Tom Cruise at the film’s Japanese premiere in Tokyo on 6 October.Photograph: Keizo Mori/UPI/ShutterstockMoviesHow we lost our appetite for eat-the-rich satireAlastair RyderTom Cruise’s latest film could lose $250m (£190m) – could one reason be that audiences are tired of Hollywood telling them what they already know about the super-rich?Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.34 EDTShareIt seems as if nobody can decide who should shoulder most of the blame for the recent box office flop ofDigger.Was it the oustedWarner Brosfilm executives Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, whose love of big-budget auteur cinema usually came with a hefty price tag? Or was it the marketing team, who were responsible for hiding the movie’s biggest swing from all trailers, ensuring many viewers would be left alienated from its early meta-reveal onwards?The truthful answer is that the film’s fate was sealed long before anybody could point fingers over its failure. In the past year it’s become clear that audiences have grown tired of the worn-out cinematic trend Digger is a part of: the eat-the-rich satire.There was a brief moment when audiences couldn’t get enough movie takedowns of the uber-wealthy, with the breakout success of Parasite inspiring Hollywood to seize upon its class-conscious themes and drag them into the west. The sustained fallout from the Covid pandemic brought issues of wealth inequality further into the spotlight, and titles as varied asGlass Onion,Saltburn,Triangle of SadnessandThe Menuall spoke to the zeitgeist with their distinct, controversial takedowns of the 1%.On the small screen, Succession and The White Lotus rapidly increased their audiences after acclaimed first seasons, thanks to the promise of darkly comic social commentary skewering those at the top of the food chain. Audiences were more than ready to eat the rich, but their appetites were satiated long before Hollywood had even considered switching up the menu.Digger is the most high-profile casualty of this trend running its course, with some reports predicting it could lose a staggering $250m (£190m) during its cinema run. The divisive reviews and audience reactions are easy to blame, but perhaps it would have been better received had audiences not grown exhausted by constant cinematic reminders about how much they’ve been screwed over by the rich and powerful.The theme hasn’t grown any less urgent, but interest in movies that hold a cracked mirror up to this reality has waned. Already this year, two action-revenge movies pitting lower-class protagonists against the super-rich in fights to the death –Ready or Not 2andThey Will Kill You– belly-flopped at the box office, and even arthouse audiences seem to be exhausted by this brand of topical satire, if receipts forRosebush PruningandI Love Boostersare anything to go by.On the small screen, the return of anthology series Beef,an awards sensation and streaming hit in its first run, failed to register as it pivoted to this familiar class satire, barely cracking Netflix’s daily top 10 before disappearing entirely.Later this week, Romain Gavras’s Sacrifice will debut on Netflix with no fanfare, more than a year after its hotly anticipated festival premierelanded with a thud. It’s a tale of shallow but self-righteous celebrities at a fundraising gala infiltrated by violent activists, boasting an A-list cast including Chris Evans, Anya Taylor-Joy and John Malkovich. It echoes many of the previously mentioned titles’ themes about the tension between the wealthy and their commitment to political causes. And even with its starry ensemble and clear cultural relevance, it took several months to find a distributor, and this paragraph may be the first you’re hearing of it.The strangest thing about the death of this trend in movies is that many of its ideas are finding more ground in the mainstream. Even the most vanilla tax on higher earners is supported by 75% of Britons,according to YouGov, and a clear majority of60% in the US. People are becoming more openly critical of the super-wealthy, so it is strange that pop culture taking aim at their unsustainable lifestyles is being met with fatigue.We’re living through a time when the world’s richest man is also one of the most widely disliked, and the real-estate mogul US president keeps hitting new lows in approval ratings. Despite the not-so-secret allegiances of some studio heads –Skydance CEO David Ellisonis an enthusiastic Trump backer – Hollywood creatives are aware of how detested among the public these figures are beyond their bases, and studios haven’t been shy in greenlighting movies with a satirical disdain for everything they represent, politically and culturally. Why has it stopped striking a chord?Tom Cruise’s Digger has flopped spectacularly – but I think it is a misunderstood masterpieceRead moreThe most obvious explanation is pure exhaustion. Doomscrolling has become a daily activity for millions, so why would anybody need to part with their money to see a movie satirising the people responsible for the state of the world when they could get sharper, more topical gags on their timeline for free?In trying to speak to the times without the responsibility of reacting to more specific headlines, the eat-the-rich movie often winds up preaching the obvious, late to the joke even if the sentiment remains relevant. It’s the Stewart Lee routine about political satire – “Was it funny? No, but I agreed the fuck out of it” – blown up to blockbuster scale, and nobody is spending their hard-earned cash to politely nod along to a movie they should be laughing at.The irony of Digger being the final movie released by Warner Bros as an independent studio hasn’t been lost, with its theme of billionaires trying to control the narrative foreshadowing the arrival of a new studio owner with an interest in appeasing the president.We might become nostalgic for this brand of movie very quickly if the worst assumptions about Ellison’s studio takeover come true, as well as being thankful that a movie of this kind could have ever been greenlit at this level. Unfortunately, no passage of time will make this and every other late-stage capitalism satire become laugh-out-loud funny.Explore more on these topicsFilmDiggerWarner BrosClass issuesDonald TrumpParamount PicturesSaltburncommentShareReuse this content

title: The raid on Ilhan Omar’s house is dangerous political theater | Moira Donegan | The Guardian
description: The raid is meant to cast an air of suspicion and criminality over Democratic candidates who, like Omar, are facing the voters in a matter of weeks
Author: Moira Donegan
Headline: The raid is meant to cast an air of suspicion and criminality over Democratic candidates who, like Omar, are facing the voters in a matter of weeks
Content: ‘It was meant to make the president seem strong and appease the racist impulses of his base.’Photograph: Tim Evans/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘It was meant to make the president seem strong and appease the racist impulses of his base.’Photograph: Tim Evans/ReutersOpinionIlhan OmarThe raid on Ilhan Omar’s house is dangerous political theaterMoira DoneganThe raid is meant to cast an air of suspicion and criminality over Democratic candidates who, like Omar, are facing the voters in a matter of weeksWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.55 EDTShareOn Monday, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security raided the Washington DC area home of Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota congresswoman and a progressive Democrat, in the latest instance of Donald Trump’s effort to weaponize the national security state to harass, punish and embarrass his political opponents.The raid, which was approved by a judge after a reportedly extensive back-and-forth with federal security officials, was nominally carried out in connection with a spurious criminal investigation into Omar’s childhood immigration to the US.In reality, the episode is best understood as a bit of political theater. It was meant to embarrass Omar, a Black, immigrant Muslim woman in Congress whose ascent to national political prominence has become a symbol to the Maga right of the resentments and threats posed by pluralism.It was meant to cast an air of suspicion and criminality over the Democratic candidates who, like Omar, are facing the voters in a matter of weeks.Trump calls me ‘crooked as hell’. That’s rich coming from him | Representative Ilhan OmarRead moreIt was meant to make the president seem strong and appease the racist impulses of his base as his party faces down what is expected to be a trouncing in November’s midterm elections.And it was meant to convey, both to this wavering base and to the nation at large, the Maga movement’s vision of law and citizenship, which the president views not as guarantors of dignity in a liberal democracy, but as tools to enforce racial hierarchy within a much narrower and more punitive white nationalist project.Let’s be clear: there is no evidence to support the allegation, which the raid on Monday was nominally meant to investigate, that Omar or her family committed immigration fraud when they came to the US as refugees in the late 1980s, when Omar was a child.But just because something isn’t true has never stopped the Maga movement from repeating it. Both the conspiracist cesspool of the far-right internet and its denizens who now have places of prominence in the Republican party have repeatedly and falsely claimed that Omar is not a legitimate citizen.“We actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud,”said JD Vance, the vice-president– who once claimed, falsely, that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating neighbors’ pets, and then defended his tendency to “create stories” about immigrants – on a podcast.For his part, Trump seems to be particularly repulsed by Omar, the first Somali-American in Congress, and has been smearing, attacking and threatening her for the better part of a decade.He has lately expanded his hate toall of Omar’s fellow Somali immigrants, complaining just days before the raid on Omar’s home that “the once great state of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali immigrants” and calling on non-Somali Minnesotans to “fight back”. Omar has previously faced threats and attacks in the wake of Trump’s comments about her.The raid is probably intended to make the Trump administration seem fearsome and all-powerful, prompting acquiescence from institutions and frenzied satisfaction from his base in the style that was seen in the first months of 2025, immediately following Trump’s return to power.This, at least, seems to be the idea behind Trump’s repeated attacks on Omar at campaign rallies this week; at one, the crowd responded to the president’s jeers about Omar by chanting “Deport! Deport! Deport!”The scene evoked the signs at the 2024 Republican national convention, where Trump’s party rallied delegates with promises of mass ethnic cleansing and members of the crowd held signs aloft reading “MASS DEPORTATION NOW.”But it’s unclear whether this promise of racist libidinal gratification will be enough to motivate Trump’s 2024 supporters to get out to the polls in November – especially since many of them will have to pay upwards of $5 a gallon for the gas they need to get there.But if we can interpret the Trump administration’s decision to raid Omar’s home as a cynical campaign tactic, the evident weakness of the ploy should not confuse us to the seriousness and degradation of Trump’s moral project.Omar, after all, is not just a congresswoman: to the Trump world, she is a symbol. Born in Mogadishu, Somalia, in 1982, Omar was barely out of infancy when her family fled the Somali civil war for a Kenyan refugee camp, and was still small when they settled in Minneapolis, the city that Omar now represents in Congress.One would be hard pressed to find a more aggressively wholesome and picturesque story of the promise of American equality: that a child from a faraway country can come here and become a full and valued member of her community, can in fact come to represent her city in Congress on an equal footing as those who were born here – that their citizenship has no caveats or conditions on account of their race or origin – is both America’s greatest achievement and also the reality that the Trump movement emerged to eradicate.If there’s a “fraud” that Trump and his cronies see in Omar, it might not be a literal immigration violation, as they claim, but something more abstract and spiritual. The “fraud” to them, is in Omar’s claim to the dignity of equal citizenship; in the idea that a woman, born in Somalia, might be as equally and powerfully American as they are.Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsIlhan OmarOpinionDonald TrumpUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: AI overlords say they want to democratise their technology. Here’s how | Richard Wilson and Clara Long | The Guardian
description: A fight over a datacentre in Utah has been a testing ground for citizens’ assemblies, paving the way to oversight
Author: Clara Long
Headline: A fight over a datacentre in Utah has been a testing ground for citizens’ assemblies, paving the way to oversight
Content: ‘Sam Altman was right: decisions of this magnitude cannot remain inside laboratories in San Francisco.’Photograph: Erik Isakson/Getty Images/Tetra images RFView image in fullscreen‘Sam Altman was right: decisions of this magnitude cannot remain inside laboratories in San Francisco.’Photograph: Erik Isakson/Getty Images/Tetra images RFOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI overlords say they want to democratise their technology. Here’s howRichard WilsonandClara LongA fight over a datacentre in Utah has been a testing ground for citizens’ assemblies, paving the way to oversightWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.41 EDTShareWhat’s your “(p)doom” – the percentage chance that rogue AI will create an existential catastrophe? Judging by their recent warnings, it is rising among tech bosses.On 25 September, OpenAI paused training of its latest frontier models as reports of AI agents going rogue mounted. A day later, Australia’s Senate asked the bosses ofOpenAI and Anthropicto appear before an inquiry after rogue OpenAI agents broke into US government websites and an Australian health portal. Both declined.Bill Gates, meanwhile, has warned that AI in the wrong hands could “cause a billion deaths”. “No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he said.Days before, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, the chief executives of Anthropic and OpenAI,appeared before the UN security council. Amodei warned that AI could become “a risk to humanity as a whole”. Altman said that “if AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone”.On this, he’s right.Doomsday scenarios aside, AI is already disrupting schools, workplaces and public services, with the most marginalised often feeling the impacts harder and faster. If democracy is to matter in this era of tech power, surely we must try to democratise AI. But how?Utah offers a glimpse. Proposals for a datacentre more than twice the size of Manhattan provoked a furious backlash over energy use and the potential impact on the state’s stressed water supplies and Great Salt Lake ecosystem, all while people felt excluded from having a say.On 18 and 19 September, Utah Common Ground convened38 residents selected by civic lotteryto consider what role the public should have in shaping decisions about AI technology and infrastructure.Despite their political differences, participants overwhelmingly agreed on the need for greater public control. Their 10 recommendations included public hearings and independent environmental assessments for hyperscale datacentres, community-led AI literacy programmes and tighter transparency rules. Every recommendation received at least 82% support. In a polarised state, that is a mandate legislators should struggle to wave away.Globally, there have beenmore than 80 public participation projects focused on AIover the past five years, involving more than 200,000 people in more than 95 countries. In Switzerland, acitizens’ assemblydemanded privacy, transparency and meaningful human control. ABelgian citizens’ panelcalled for AI that serves everyone and leaves nobody behind.At present, however, this work is fragmented and largely ignored by decision-makers in government and the labs. TheCitizens’ Track on AI, a decentralised network of assemblies rooted in communities but connected to the institutions where consequential decisions about AI are being made, intends to change that.TheBloom Project, which helped convene the Utah assembly, is building one part of that network: a series of US local and state assemblies intended to feed into a national citizens’ assembly on AI in 2028. At the global level, the ambition is to connect assemblies across countries into the UN’s emerging processes for AI governance, while also creating direct lines of accountability to the AI companies.A bridge built by the powerful can be withdrawn by them. That is why Utah matters. Its forum was rooted in civic groups that will outlast the forum itself, though it has no guaranteed hearing yet. Durable civic power needs both: communities that keep convening and decision-makers who have to answer them.The same principle underpinsproposals published last week for a standing global citizens’ assembly on AI: combining the independent moral authority of globally representative, self-governing citizens with legislated powers to hold AI companies accountable for their safety and alignment practices.None of this is easy. Yet deliberation need not be slow: Taiwan went from citizens’ panel to law in months in an effort to address scam advertising. It is also hard to buy: lobbyists can buy policy influence, not the outcome of a citizens’ assembly.Can any of this protect us against AI being used to launch a cyber-attack, develop a biological weapon or escape human control altogether? Not by itself. But how much risk society should accept isn’t an engineering question – it’s a political one. Citizens’ assemblies can give governments the mandate, and the cover, to impose the testing, red lines and stop buttons that companies won’t impose on themselves.The danger is not only that AI may escape human control. It is whether the humans controlling it are a tiny group of elite executives, investors and politicians vulnerable to corporate capture.Altman was right: decisions of this magnitude cannot remain inside laboratories in San Francisco. But moving them into closed meetings between powerful states would not make AI democratic either.Imagine instead every school, workplace and community connecting into this process: shaping what the AI companies do, but also becoming proactive in the face of the AI onslaught. A trulyglobal citizens’ assemblyrooted in the communities that understand the impacts of datacentres and labour displacement. Something large enough to counter the AI arms-race narrative that dominates debate and paralyses political action.The key question, then, is not whether democratising AI is realistic, but whether AI can realistically be governed without it.Democracy is not an optional restraint on this technology. It may be our only means of keeping its development and deployment under meaningful human control.Richard Wilson is the CEO of Iswe Foundation and Clara Long is the co-executive director of the Bloom ProjectExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSam AltmanDario AmodeiOpenAIAnthropicUtahDatacentrescommentShareReuse this content

title: Why are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Airports’ TSA staff have been stripped of their chairs in the name of ‘professionalism’. Most supermarket staff have never had them. Meanwhile, Donald Trump is seated at his desk – and apparently snoozing, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Airports’ TSA staff have been stripped of their chairs in the name of ‘professionalism’. Most supermarket staff have never had them. Meanwhile, Donald Trump is seated at his desk – and apparently snoozing, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: ‘Please don’t be seated’ … TSA staff have been deprived of their chairs.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Please don’t be seated’ … TSA staff have been deprived of their chairs.Photograph: Myung J Chun/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesOpinionUS politicsWhy are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president?Arwa MahdawiAirports’ TSA staff have been stripped of their chairs in the name of ‘professionalism’. Most supermarket staff have never had them. Meanwhile, Donald Trump is seated at his desk – and apparently snoozingWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTShareGreat news for everyone who is soon to fly via a US airport: the Trump administration has just elevated the travel experience. You still risk getting arrested by immigration agents andthrowninto a detention centre, but never mind that! Instead, luxuriate in the fact that none of the poorly paid Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff with whom you interact will be sitting down. The government recentlygot rid of all the chairsat travel document checking stations, arguing that “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism” and strengthens “our security posture and … commitment to hospitality”. Funnily enough, border patrol and customs officers have not adopted the same policy. Perhaps because their job tends to involve being as inhospitable as possible.TSA agents aren’t the only US workers getting sore calf muscles during their shifts. Unlike their European and British counterparts, cashiers at US supermarkets have traditionally been forced tostand while working. The US’s upright obsession seems to be down to a Protestant work ethic and a lack oflabour laws. Sitting apparently conveys laziness to the discerning American consumer. Over the years there have been numerousright-to-sitlawsuits pushing back on mandatory standing but, while things are shifting slightly, seated supermarket cashiers are still unusual. One exception is Aldi, which has beenexpandingaggressively in the US. Cashiersget chairs at Aldibecause (surprise) it’s more efficient when your workers’ feet aren’t aching all the time.While seated cashiers and TSA agents may be looked down on by the US establishment, it’s a different story for high-flyers. Rather than “maintaining a standing posture” to “reinforce professionalism”, the US president often looks as if he issnoozingat his desk. Which, to be fair, is probably because he regularly stays up all night posting extremely important memes on the internet.Having their chairs seized isn’t the only indignity that TSA agents have faced recently: along with other federal employees, they had towork without payfor several weeks during government shutdowns in Trump’s second term. Members of Congress on the other hand? They could continue to collect their generous salaries during the shutdown unless they explicitlychose not to. Americans should not take this injustice sitting down.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
