title: Violent and abusive language is seeping into our political debate. We have Donald Trump to blame  | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: Liberal MP Angie Bell’s rhetoric and Warren Mundine’s joke about murder at CPAC are part of a dangerous trend
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: Liberal MP Angie Bell’s rhetoric and Warren Mundine’s joke about murder at CPAC are part of a dangerous trend
Content: The small business minister, Anne Aly, says she received 19 death threats on social media in the past week and Angie Bell’s comments ‘should never have been said’.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPView image in fullscreenThe small business minister, Anne Aly, says she received 19 death threats on social media in the past week and Angie Bell’s comments ‘should never have been said’.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPOpinionAustralian politicsViolent and abusive language is seeping into our political debate. We have Donald Trump to blamePaul DaleyLiberal MP Angie Bell’s rhetoric and Warren Mundine’s joke about murder at CPAC are part of a dangerous trendGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastWed 14 Oct 2026 17.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 17.53 EDTShareAt some point, though it’s hard to pinpoint precisely when, the language of supposedly civilised public discourse started to become imbued with a dark malevolence.Given the long history of American influence on pretty much all things culturally Australian, it seems inevitable that Maga’s violent and abusive rhetoric would make its way into our politics. And it’s pretty fair to say the current US president has led the western populist way when it comes to saying out loudthe ugly and violent thingsthat might once have remained internal.Yes, the frog of public expectation has boiled pretty quickly in recent years, to the point where the land of the free must now debate the hideouswhys and whereforesof the Trump administration’s proposal to turnexecution into livestreamed public entertainment.Anne Aly reveals she has received 19 death threats in the past week aloneRead moreIs it any wonder that the hard Australian populist right has picked up on the vibe that thinking your violent thoughts aloud – and aiming them at political opponents – has somehow become de rigueur?There’s a couple of prime – if exceedingly ugly – examples to parse in almost as many days. Let’s begin on Monday this week and work backwards.Monday – that was when a federal Liberal National MP from Queensland, Angie Bell, talking about the fracas over the tax office’s acceptance of credit card payments, said that small business minister, Anne Aly, and the prime minister should be“stoned in the square”.Here is exactly what Bell – forced to withdraw the comments – said in parliament: “This minister and this prime minister should be absolutely shamed and stoned in the square.”For the uninitiated, this comment connotes – deliberately or otherwise – the communal squares in places where people (usually women) have been publiclyexecuted by stoning.In a social media response to Bell’s comments, Aly made plain the potential implications of such violent rhetoric: “I don’t usually comment about these sorts of things but I feel like I have to. This past week alone I’ve had 19 death threats on my social media. And in the past I’ve had death threats that are couched in that exact same language: stone her.”She continued: “We are a country that proudly stands against violence against women and against regimes that use brutal methods like stoning against women. This is not just something that we should just turn away from. It is racist. It is misogynistic. And it should never have been said.”Which begs the question: if elected officials and other public figures reckon it’s OK to enunciate such brutal intent against opponents, might some unidentified others in the public square feel licensed/enabled to do likewise – or worse?Just asking.Bell later conceded she’d used a “poor choice of words” and confirmed deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume’s claim that the Liberal National MP had “reached out” to Aly. Bell also said Aly’s comments amounted to “deflecting” – which is kind of tantamount to the classic footy player’s – “if-I’ve-offended-anyone’’ – qualified apology-cum-double-down. Hume, meanwhile, said that while Bell’s comments were maybe a bit “clumsy” they amounted to “a storm in a teacup”. Thequeen of personal political invective, Pauline Hanson, meanwhile urged everyone to “just calm down” over Bell’s comments that were simply “made in the heat of the moment”.Well we’re all good then. Say what you like in the heat of the political moment. Then move right along.Or perhaps let’s go back to last Saturday’s opening of the Australian Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC). The term “conservative” was used pretty loosely for this jamboree of the hard political right. But then again, a fair bit of the language bandied around was also less than conservative and liberally seasoned with personal invective.Australian politics live: Liberal MP ‘reached out’ to Anne Aly after saying she should be ‘shamed and stoned’, Hume saysRead moreTake the opening warm-up speech of the CPAC chair, Warren Mundine, in which he decorously revved up the net-zero-hungry crowd with a lash at the energy and climate change minister, Chris Bowen.Mundinereportedly saidthat Bowen’s name alone gave him “chills” while recounting his visceral reaction to encountering the minister in Canberra.“I looked at him [Bowen] and my body language gave me away,”Mundine said.“My mate had to grab me to say, ‘It doesn’t go well on your CV if you murder a federal minister.’”It’s great – just in case you need one – to have on hand a mate who can remind you of such niceties.Anyway, the audience guffawed at this little gag about murder and the minister.Which goes to show, perhaps, that there’s a broadening political marketplace – maybe more than just at the darker edges of the public square – for such outlandish rhetoric. At least under the banner of conservatism.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsAustralian politicsOpinionLabor partyDonald TrumpCoalitionLiberal National partycommentShareReuse this content

title: For the future of green politics, look beyond the Green party | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Environmentalists of all political hues must find the language and ideas that turn passion for climate action into impetus, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Environmentalists of all political hues must find the language and ideas that turn passion for climate action into impetus, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Climate protesters outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, London, 6 October 2026.Photograph: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenClimate protesters outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, London, 6 October 2026.Photograph: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionClimate science scepticism and denialFor the future of green politics, look beyond the Green partyZoe WilliamsEnvironmentalists of all political hues must find the language and ideas that turn passion for climate action into impetusWed 14 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.55 EDTShareThe future of Green politics is under constant discussion after theHolborn and St Pancras byelection, but a much heavier clash – in meaning, symbolism and portent – happened earlier this summer, in King’s Lynn and West Norfolk. The council declared a climate emergency in 2021, along with hundreds of others, and while it was under Conservative control. It is now controlled by independents, and a Reform UK councillor, Austen Moore, moved to scrap the declaration.It was the end of June, and the meeting had to be called off, because of the extreme heat in the King’s Lynn council chamber. A lot of people paused to grimly remark on that irony, but not Moore, who simply rescheduled the motion for the following week, where it was voted down (by 33 to seven). A local scientist and member of Extinction Rebellionliveblogged that debate, adding helpful maps, such as how much of the county was already below the annual flood level – most of it, including King’s Lynn itself. If this all sounds like a cheerful take home, numerous other Reform-led councils have had the same debate and Reform has prevailed. Their arguments can be terrifyingly illiterate. In Kent, councillor Linden Kemkaran asserted that climate change is fine because the worldwas warmer in Roman times, and as “carbon dioxide … is a trace gas essential for life on Earth”, to try to cut carbon emissions would itself be dangerous.If you’re waiting for reality to knock some sense into politics, you will wait too long. There is no heatwave, no flood, no El Niño, no omnicrisis, that will divert rightwing populism from its crusade against action on climate.The question isn’t what the Green party alone could do to create an eco-populist wave of equal volume. A party that could single-handedlyrepresent the 68% of peoplewho want action on climate change doesn’t exist in modern British politics. The question is, how do you turn that strength of feeling into something more concrete, so it isn’t constantly being ram-raided by unshameable, unscientific chancers? Environmentalists in every party, leaders of every party (apart from the Conservatives, who seem hellbent on chasing Reform, despite thestated valuesof their supporters), need to find the language and ideas that turn passion for the environment into impetus.In theirrecent report, Caroline Lucas and the green philosopher Rupert Read make the case for “eco-popularism” rather than eco-populism: a way of thinking that doesn’t try to hotwire its way into people’s emotional circuitry with invigorating binaries, but, rather, describes actions that would genuinely change lives for the better, and therefore be popular.Rightwing populists have a set of arguments against climate action that are taking hold more generally and are self-fulfilling: the more they’re repeated, the more they win at local level, the more people come to believe that these views are generally held. Those narratives are that climate action of any sort – be it ultra-low emission zones, 15-minute cities or, most importantly, net zero – is too expensive at this time; that net zero itself is a luxury belief of the comfortable elite who don’t care about ordinary people’s living conditions (Lucas and Read paraphrase from aNigel Farage columnlast year).This so-called “Manichean” framing, the noble masses betrayed by a corrupt elite, is dog obvious, but to point to Farage and say “you, the guy in receipt of £5m from a non-domiciled crypto billionaire,you’rerepresenting the masses against the elites?” is tempting but fruitless. No case for climate action will take hold unless it addresses the conditions that populists exploit – the cost of living, of course, but also the sense of precariousness and active fear of the future that climate events intensify.A prime minister freezing bus fares or taking the VAT off heating doesn’t address those brute realities and deep anxieties: if anything, it shores up a sense that central government is no longer capable of building the resilience and adaptation a chaotic world demands. People need to know there’s a plan for cheaper, greener energy, food security and extreme weather events. Local, tangible actions should be supported, broadcast and celebrated, in political debate and in the media; a discussion held in abstract terms of global patterns and borderless looming disaster doesn’t just foster despair. It plays back into the hands of populists, whose incredibly proximal enemies – small boats, asylum seekers – and standing street armies create the opposite impression, of agency and might. It doesn’t matter that it’s specious and vindictive – it matters that it lands and there is no answering call to arms. One of the many paradoxes of the climate debate is that the far right talks as though disaster is not real, but acts as though it’s imminent. The left does the opposite, talking of catastrophe but acting as if there’s time to lose.Without a change of direction, even those of us who are constitutionally not susceptible to rightwing populism will still give in to its echo, which is hopelessness. Coherence is desperately needed: to promise defence spending at the expense of heat pumps, or high-quality jobs with the downside of new fossil-fuel exploration, is simply to reinforce a sense of impotence, nationally and individually.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKing’s Lynn and West Norfolk’s debate in July had an interesting pivot from Reform: they had started to magpie the language of “resilience building”, in place of climate action. But they didn’t mean it to describe peat and wildlife restoration, or food cooperatives, or retrofitted housing, or community-owned wind power. They weren’t interested in solar panels or sustainable drainage or civic infrastructure. It was the broadest possible false promise: spend less on climate, therefore less has been spent, therefore your community is more resilient. Councillors from all the other parties united to defeat them, and politics national and local can learn from that unity; but no party can afford to wait for an opponent to unite against.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Vitamin patches have their grip on the wellness industry: but is the fad only skin deep?  | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Experts peel back the evidence to see whether any of the health claims about vitamin patches stick – or whether it’s the placebo effect at work
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Experts peel back the evidence to see whether any of the health claims about vitamin patches stick – or whether it’s the placebo effect at work
Content: ‘One of the big fundamental problems of vitamin patches is that most vitamins are water soluble. What doesn’t get through the skin? Stuff that’s water soluble,’ says Prof Nial Wheate.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘One of the big fundamental problems of vitamin patches is that most vitamins are water soluble. What doesn’t get through the skin? Stuff that’s water soluble,’ says Prof Nial Wheate.Composite: Getty ImagesAntiviralHealth & wellbeingVitamin patches have their grip on the wellness industry: but is the fad only skin deep?Donna LuExperts peel back the evidence to see whether any of the health claims about vitamin patches stick – or whether it’s the placebo effect at workRead more in theAntiviral seriesWed 14 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTShareFeeling fatigued and listless? Searching for an energy boost? Want to improve your mood and motivation? The solution may be, according to a proliferation of online articles and wellness TikToks, not to seek medical advice but to whack on a vitamin patch.Wearers purport to feel more focused or energised when adorned with the patches, some of which look like transparent squares, and others which are cuter and more colourful, resembling stickers or temporary tattoos.The adhesives, also called wellness or supplement patches, contain tiny amounts of vitamins, minerals such as iron and magnesium, as well as other compounds such as caffeine and ginger extract.Magnesium is essential for health. But can supplements really help with digestion, muscle pain, anxiety and sleep? | AntiviralRead moreDo any of the claims about vitamin patches stick, or are they merely a Band-Aid solution?Can vitamins actually get through the skin?Very few medicines are available as patches, says Nial Wheate, a professor of pharmaceutical chemistry at Macquarie University. “There’s a reason we don’t have paracetamol and aspirin patches.”The key issue is that the skin is a very effective protective barrier: the structure of its outermost layer, the stratum corneum, blockswater, bacteria and most drugsfrom getting through.“It doesn’t mean the right medicines can’t be delivered that way,” Wheate says. “The things that do get through the skin tend to be what we call lipophilic” – fat soluble. For this reason, skin patches are often used to deliver opioid medications, hormone replacement therapy and nicotine, which are all lipophilic.For example, the advantage of a nicotine skin patch for smoking cessation, Wheate says, is that it gives a slow, sustained release “where you’re continuously releasing that drug into the bloodstream”, as opposed to an oral tablet which leads to a higher initial spike of the drug and more rapid clearance from the body.However, he says: “One of the big fundamental problems of vitamin patches is that most vitamins are water soluble. What doesn’t get through the skin? Stuff that’s water soluble.”Some wellness patches market themselves as bypassing the “unwanted side effects” of oral supplements – constipation is a commonly reported side-effect of iron tablets, for example.But iron, and other vitamins and minerals commonly used in patches, such as vitamin B12 and magnesium – cannot properly cross the skin barrier.And if any amountdoesmake it through the skin, “the other issue is the amount of drug you can load into a patch is very, very small”, Wheate points out. “So what you get is microdosing of any of those vitamins.“The biggest effect [wearers] would get is a placebo effect.”One patch available in Australia, marketed for immunity, for example, contains 1mg of vitamin C. The clinical signs of scurvy, by comparison, appear whendaily vitamin C intakedrops below 7 to 8mg.More ‘bang for your buck’ in the fruit and veg sectionThe average person can get theirrecommended intakeof vitamins (such as vitamin C and vitamin B12) and minerals (elements such as iron, zinc and iodine) from diet alone, without the need for supplements – in oral or patch form.“There’s definitely cases when people need [supplemental] vitamins and minerals,” says Clare Collins, professor of nutrition and dietetics at the University of Newcastle. This includes people with specific deficiencies, such as those with low iron or vegans who are at higher risk of vitamin B12 deficiency. Pregnant women, too, have a higher nutritional requirement for folate, iodine and vitamin D.“The nutrients that are more likely to be absorbed [through the skin] are ones that dissolve in fat,” Collins says. “But they don’t necessarily go all the way into your bloodstream, which is why [vitamin patches] are not that effective.”There have been few studies in humans into how well fat-soluble vitamins – vitamins A, D, E and K – are absorbed into the skin, Collins says. Onesmall 2019 studylooked at the effect of multivitamin patches in patients after gastric bypass surgery for weight loss, who are at higher risk of nutrient deficiencies. Patch users, it found, were “more likely to have vitamin D deficiency and lower serum concentration of various vitamins and minerals” than patients taking oral supplements.Multivitamins promise glowing skin, better sleep and a longer life. But who do supplements really benefit? | Donna LuRead more“The patches were not able to replace oral supplements and that’s a very specific group where food intakes are markedly reduced,” Collins says. “In the current day, that would still apply to bariatric surgery, but that would also apply to people taking GLP-1 [weight-loss drugs].”Given the lack of evidence for their effect, Collins suggests people save the money they would otherwise expend on vitamin patches and “spend it in the fruit and veg section … you’ll get more bang for your buck”.Unlike patches, Collins says fresh fruit and vegetables will also provide a variety ofphytonutrients– plant-based chemicals that occur naturally in foods – which have numerous benefits including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. “You get the nutrients that improve your insulin sensitivity, and all the range of fibres that promote bowel health and promote a diverse microbiome.”For people considering a vitamin supplement or a patch, Collins suggests “having a think about what the underlying issues are”.“If you’re just feeling run-down, then go and get yourself a check-up with your GP.”Donna Lu is an assistant editor, climate, environment and science at Guardian AustraliaAntiviralis a fortnightly column that interrogates the evidence behind the health headlines and factchecks popular wellness claimsShare your experienceShare your experienceWhat health trend do you want examined?Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. title: I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis | Anonymous | The Guardian
description: Insurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequences, says an anonymous modeller and whistleblower
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Insurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequences, says an anonymous modeller and whistleblower
Content: Flooded streets in Brechin, Scotland, in the aftermath of Storm Babet in October 2023.Photograph: Iain Masterton/AlamyView image in fullscreenFlooded streets in Brechin, Scotland, in the aftermath of Storm Babet in October 2023.Photograph: Iain Masterton/AlamyOpinionInsurance industryI work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisisAnonymousInsurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequencesWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTShareIwork for a major insurer, assessing the risk posed by natural disasters on properties around the world, from family homes to schools, government offices and multibillion-dollar commercial centres. The world is facing greater risk than ever from extreme weather. We are not prepared – and that inaction could have profound consequences for the global financial system.In the face of ever more extreme and unpredictable climate risks, I am coming under pressure to cut my forecasts for the losses that disasters will cause in order to make insurance more affordable – and get my employer more business. In some instances, the questioning of our numbers and models is justified. But too often, it is not being done to produce more accurate models, but to artificially lower prices. If this is happening at my firm, which is struggling to compete with rivals’ prices, it’s happening elsewhere.Our sector is carrying more risk than we realise. The warming global climate has caused more frequent high-intensity storms, rising sea levels, flooding, wildfires and drought. While the immediate impact of these events is plain to see, the long-term effects will be compounded as insurers withdraw from affected areas, leaving the economy in freefall and people’s day-to-day lives in ruins.As a modeller, it is my job to look objectively and scientifically at the data to calculate an expected loss from a natural disaster, which affects the price of the premium for a given policy. Our industry says it holds those numbers as sacrosanct, but as my analysis shows higher and more volatile risk, the price rises with it and we lose customers.So modellers like me are coming under pressure to reduce their projected losses. In the most basic terms, we are collectively fudging the numbers and taking on more risk than we should for a lower price than the expected loss demands. Sometimes I will forecast losses that would normally be seen as much too risky for us to insure, but we offer the policies anyway. This will eventually lead to a sector built on “competitively priced” contracts that underestimate risk, leaving gaping holes in the safety net that insurance is supposed to provide.For example, if subsidence – which is made worse by drought – damages a number of homes in your area, insurers may exclude this from your policy, so you won’t be covered if subsidence then hits your house.When that happens to an entire community, businesses leave, investment dries up and the local economy tanks. Now imagine this happening in multiple towns around the country, at the same time. And subsidence is just one such issue, alongside wildfires, coastal erosion, wind and floods – and that’s just in the UK.I have respect for underwriters who are just doing their jobs, and I know that no single individual is responsible. My concern lies with the attitude of much of the industry towards modellers, actuaries and researchers: there is a sense that we are an inconvenience to the deal-making process, rather than an essential part of risk management. We are the failsafe that stops our industry from reckless gambling.At the largest scale, misquoted insurance can damage insurers, companies, their employees and the communities that rely on them. The upshot is that our customers are likely to be much more exposed to climate-related risks than they realise. People are not budgeting for a major increase in their insurance premiums or planning for their homes becoming uninsurable, but many of them absolutely should be.If the worst happens, the insurance industry may not have the money to pay every claim when a major disaster hits. That would have profound consequences for the economy as a whole – businesses could go bankrupt, the housing market could seize up and, if people couldn’t pay their mortgages, banks would fail.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs natural catastrophes continue to become less predictable and more severe, the foundations of our entire economy will only become more fragile. Our customers deserve to know.The writer is a modeller working in the insurance industry. title: This civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan Liew | The Guardian
description: Don’t be fooled by its bickering leaders. Their calibrated fake fighting will probably end in coalition, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: Don’t be fooled by its bickering leaders. Their calibrated fake fighting will probably end in coalition, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Liew
Content: Kemi Badenoch is congratulated by Robert Jenrick after winning the Conservative party leadership contest, 2 November 2024.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch is congratulated by Robert Jenrick after winning the Conservative party leadership contest, 2 November 2024.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionConservativesThis civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than everJonathan LiewDon’t be fooled by its bickering leaders. Their calibrated fake fighting will probably end in coalitionWed 14 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTShareKapow! In a warmly received conference speech, Kemi Badenoch turns her fire on Reform UK, describing it as “weird”, and ruling out an electoral pact. Slap! Not to be outdone, her former colleague Robert Jenrick derides Badenoch as a champion of the wealthy, which is quite rich for a guy who looks like he’s just accidentally ingested a bundle of £50 notes through his sphincter. Bosh! Reform’s Richard Tice and Restore’s Rupert Lowe clash online over the result of acouncil byelectionin Derbyshire, in which the Greens profited from a split rightwing vote. “Vote Restore get Islamists,” Tice chides. “Vote Reform, get some random Bangladeshi bloke,” Lowe responds.Meanwhile, theConservativesare back. The Kemibounce is real. The Keminaissance is true. We’ve all got a severe case of the Kemirrhoids. And you may wonder why much of the media are talking about a Badenoch revival in a year where her party lost 563 councillors and 40% of its councils, remains about four points below its apparent nadir of 2024, and in which the leader herself appears incapable of doing a broadcast interview without looking like a restaurant diner who received exactly what she ordered and is inexplicably furious at it. The point is that the Conservatives are a serious party of government again, and thereasonis that we all said so.And even if we take into account Badenoch’s curiouslyresilient personal polling, this does feel like a largely arbitrary volte-face. There was a soft-focus interview in the Financial Times, a warm editorial in the Sun, and generally positive coverage of the Tory conference in the rest of the rightwing press. Tom Tugendhat, the new shadow foreign secretary and once regarded as a party moderate, had a sympathetic platform in the Observer to defend the party’s opposition to net zero and the European convention on human rights.One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy | Jane MartinsonRead moreFrom a safe distance, it is possible to regard these realignments in a fairly optimistic light. The right is tearing itself to shreds, potentially allowing a leftwing alternative – or failing that, Labour – to clean up. And in the continuing scrap between Lowe and Nigel Farage, or the series of aggressive Telegraph editorials aimed atRestore Britain, it is tempting to glimpse a reassertion of basic, consensual values in which, for all our many disagreements, certain voices will always be beyond the pale.Occasionally you will even hear it said on the progressive left that a strong centre-right is a necessary, welcome bulwark against the extremist far right. That while we can disagree strongly and vehemently with Badenoch’s party, we can also recognise the ways in which a moderate right can act as a kind of cordon sanitaire against the nativists, ethnonationalists and race theorists who may otherwise get their hands on the levers of government. All of which would probably be true, if that were actually what was happening. But is it?Let’s start with the Tories, who appear to be rapidly pivoting towards a demographic that one insider has described as “Waitrose Woman”: affluent, socially liberal, turned off by culture-war rhetoric but laser-focused on tax and the economy. “We have done a ton of opinion research over the last 18 months,” a Conservative source told the Mail on Sunday. “You do have to appear reasonable.” Or, as one shadow cabinet ministertold the Guardian: “We have outsourced our toxicity to Reform.”But in the real world, beyond superficial branding, how different are the two platforms? Shadow cabinet member Nick Timothy called Islamic prayers in Trafalgar Squareun-British, “an act of domination”, “straight from the Islamist playbook”, andBadenoch backed him. Badenoch advocates a ban on pro-Palestine marches, but argued Tommy Robinson should not receive the same treatment. Another shadow cabinet member, Katie Lam, advocated mass deportations of legally settled immigrants in order to make Britain a “culturally coherent group of people”.The Conservative police and crime commissioner Donna Jones responded to the masked vigilante protests in Portsmouth byblaming the governmentfor failing to control our borders. Aformer neo-Nazi activistwas selected as a local election candidate for the Tories, and subsequentlyappointed as an adviser. In the Telegraph, Badenoch wrote that anyone committed to net zero targets is no longer welcome in the party.As for Reform, Monday’s announcement that it wouldimmediately suspend the UK asylum systembrought the party further in line with Restore, both of whom advocate ICE-style raids, the stripping of citizenship from people who thought they were here permanently, and the cessation of aid and visas to countries who refuse to take back migrants. Suella Braverman, a former Tory, now says she can “understand why some people are drawn to Restore”, and suggests people of colour cannot be English.Indeed, you can argue that net zero, welfare, tax cuts, Israel, Brexit, defence spending, trans rights, Donald Trump, the obsession with grooming gangs and Islam, immigration and, most importantly, their common enemies, there is barely a sheet of nori to separate the three parties. And yet at the same time we are expected to believe that these parties engaged in an eternal blood feud, rather than three heads of the same army, pursuing different strategies towards a common cause.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRobert Jenrick launches scathing broadside against ‘Kensington Kemi’Read moreNaturally Westminster will fall for this narrative wholesale, focused as it is on divisions over alliances, personalities over ideas. The Conservatives will be allowed to carry on decontaminating their brand without decontaminating their platform. Farage will continue as flag bearer for the movement, sweeping up donor money and airtime. Meanwhile Restore serves an equally important role as the engine of change, the pressure group, the brains trust: shifting the rhetorical window to the right while allowing Badenoch and Farage to look reasonable in comparison.The civil war on the right is in fact a charade, a fake fight being enacted for our benefit. The right bloc is now a single basic substance, responsive and carefully calibrated to the different audiences it needs to capture. Reform, already in informal talks with Restore, can now tailor its offering to the post-industrial north, Midlands and Wales, leaving the rehabilitated Conservatives – the acceptable face of the project – to concentrate on their southern and rural heartlands. And if, after all the bickering and infighting, a coalition should be required? Do we really expect a Conservative party founded entirely on the gain and exercise of power to suddenly turn it down?To those on the left, the idea of a rightwing meltdown feels vaguely reassuring. But in reality nothing here is being repudiated. The personalities may butt heads for our entertainment, but the ideas and politics are largely common among them all. The parts are being divvied out, but ultimately the production remains the same.Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsConservativesOpinionReform UKRestore BritainKemi BadenochNigel FarageRichard TiceFar rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George Monbiot | The Guardian
description: Tom Watson has said ‘mob rule’ must not decide public contracts. Perhaps he should take a look at his new employer, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Author: George Monbiot
Headline: Tom Watson has said ‘mob rule’ must not decide public contracts. Perhaps he should take a look at his new employer, says Guardian columnist George Monbiot
Content: The then defence secretary, John Healey, with the Palantir CEO, Alex Karp, after signing an investment deal in London, September 2025.Photograph: Lucy North/PAView image in fullscreenThe then defence secretary, John Healey, with the Palantir CEO, Alex Karp, after signing an investment deal in London, September 2025.Photograph: Lucy North/PAOpinionPalantirPalantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influenceGeorge MonbiotTom Watson has said ‘mob rule’ must not decide public contracts. Perhaps he should take a look at his new employerWed 14 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 07.06 EDTShareWhat a world we live in. Imagine: gangs dragging civil servants off commuter trains and beating them up because they handed government data jobs to the wrong contractor – and the government is changing its procurement decisions as a result. Well, OK, it might not have happened yet, but it’s only a matter of time. As the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watsonasks: “Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?” No, I absolutely don’t want the latter, and it’s always good to get ahead of trouble.But then I remember there are two common meanings of mob rule. One is intimidation by crowds of thugs. The other is a pejorative term for democracy. And while I’ve yet to see government procurement practices in the UK determined by pitchforks and flaming torches, democratic transparency could be a genuine threat to certain contractors. One might have hoped that Watson, who oncetook on the Murdoch empire, would have recognised the distinction. But then again, one might have hoped that Watson would not havetaken a jobas a senior vice-president at Palantir.Over the past few years, this US company has been worming its way into the British state. It has landed contracts worth hundreds of millions with the Ministry of Defence, several police forces, the Financial Conduct Authority, the atomic weapons establishment and the NHS. Its superpower, according to adeep investigationby Peter Geoghegan and Lucas Amin in the London Review of Books, is that it is “willing to spend more on securing political access than almost all of its British and continental competitors”. It made abundant use of Peter Mandelson’s company Global Counsel, which seems, in turn, to have madeabundant useof the UK’s remarkably flimsy lobbying laws. Watson is one of more than 30 former UK ministers and officials Palantirnow employs.Recent lobbyist for Palantir had key role in helping Andy Burnham become PMRead morePalantir’s contracts might have been awarded lawfully, but some of us might question the ways in which doors were opened for it. These include anunrecorded meetingbetween Boris Johnson, Dominic Cummings and the co-founder of Palantir, Peter Thiel, in Downing Street in 2019. It was invited back to Downing Street when the Covid-19 pandemic began a few months later, and was working in the NHS within days, on a contract for which it chargedonly £1. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan,has criticisedsuch loss-leaders, which can quickly lead to reliance on a company, at which point it can name its price.Another controversial meeting was brokered by Mandelson in 2025, when he was UK ambassador to the US. Keir Starmer visited Palantir’s showroom in Washington, where he met the company’s global and UK chief executives, Alex Karp and Louis Mosley. They talked about defence spending. No 10, Geoghegan and Amin tell us, “refused to say whether Starmer knew that Palantir was a client of Global Counsel, in which Mandelson still held a stake of around a fifth at the time. The meeting was never declared on transparency registers.” A few months later, Palantirsecureda £241m contract with the Ministry of Defence, without an open tender.Now we learn that Martha Dalton, a key player in Andy Burnham’s campaign to win the Makerfield byelection, enabling him to become prime minister, was onunpaid leavefrom the lobbying company she co-founded, Lodestone. Lodestone had done extensive work for Palantir. And the Financial Timesreportsthat Samantha Jones, then the lead non-executive director on the board of the health department, was an adviser to one of Palantir’s partners when the company was bidding for its huge and controversial NHS contract. Now she is permanent secretary in the same department.There have beenrepeatedallegations that some of Palantir’s products arerubbish. But, as the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committeewarns, government agencies can quickly succumb to “vendor lock-in”: once you start using them, it can be very hard to stop.Thiel,has claimed that“the NHS makes people sick”, and that we should “just rip the whole thing from the ground and start over”. The company is deeply embedded in the Trump administration, where it supplies software that helps ICE findundocumented people. It also works for the Israeli government on identifying targets in Gaza. When Karp was confronted by a protester who told him that “Palantir kills Palestinians”,he replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”This is the company handling our critical information. After official denials, itturns outthat NHS England has granted Palantir “unlimited access” to patient data. This is ahuge issue. Identifiable patient data is supposed to be visible only to people directly involved in a patient’s care, or who have received the patient’s informed consent. There arewidespread concernsabout how this and otherdatasetsmight be used.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow Palantir got into the NHS - podcastRead moreSo, as Palantir runs intoever-greater controversy, it’s not hard to see why it might have hired Watson, who, with Burnham, was a minister in Gordon Brown’s government. I wouldn’t presume to speculate about what attracted Watson to the multibillion-dollar company.In July, the government’s ethics and integrity commissionrecommendeda major shake-up, enabling us to see all the encounters between lobbyists and ministers, aides and senior officials. I’ve heard this call many times before. The pattern is always the same: a scandal, followed by a call to action, followed by … little or nothing.Before he became prime minister, David Cameronnotedthat lobbying “has tainted our politics for too long”. He would shine “the light of transparency” on it. Instead, he oversaw an act that was “more loophole than law”. It did nothing to protect us from lobbying by people such as Cameron –pulling strings, once out of office, among his old colleagues, to try to drum up government business for the bankGreensill.You could almost believe that the real purpose of government was to do the bidding of corporations, foreign states and the ultra-rich. You could almost believe that some government ministers may have an eye on future opportunities when they resist effective reform.So this is another key test for Burnham. Will he allow the mob rule of private business to keep dominating our lives, or will he ensure that government is for the people?George Monbiot is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsPalantirOpinionLobbyingTom WatsonAndy BurnhamPeter ThielNHScommentShareReuse this content

title: In Germany the mood is dark. But the Weimar narrative is a far right trap | Klaus Brinkbäumer | The Guardian
description: The final season of the TV epic Babylon Berlin is taking us back to 1933. Our confidence is falling apart, but that’s where the parallels end, says the German journalist Klaus Brinkbäumer
Author: Klaus Brinkbäumer
Headline: The final season of the TV epic Babylon Berlin is taking us back to 1933. Our confidence is falling apart, but that’s where the parallels end, says the German journalist Klaus Brinkbäumer
Content: Liv Lisa Fries as Charlotte Ritter and Volker Bruch as Gereon Rath in Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Christine Schroeder/X Filme CreaView image in fullscreenLiv Lisa Fries as Charlotte Ritter and Volker Bruch as Gereon Rath in Babylon Berlin.Photograph: Christine Schroeder/X Filme CreaOpinionGermanyIn Germany the mood is dark. But the Weimar narrative is a far right trapKlaus BrinkbäumerThe final season of the TV epic Babylon Berlin is taking us back to 1933. Our confidence is falling apart, but that’s where the parallels endWed 14 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 06.48 EDTShareThere is one experience we in Germany can all find mildly satisfying this autumn, as we watch the dark and terrifyingfinal season of the hit TV series Babylon Berlin. We know everything those fearless (a few of them) or frightened (many more) and opportunistic (the majority) people on the screen do not. We know their future.Made by the public broadcaster ARD, Babylon Berlin has run for over 10 years, brilliantly fictionalising howGermanysleepwalked into nazism and the second world war. The fifth and last season begins in January 1933 with Adolf Hitler appointedReichskanzler.Our funny and beautiful police detective superheroine Charlotte Ritter and the also beautiful, less funny and slightly more dubious detective Gereon Rath – both fictional – are still arguing and falling in and out of love as they chase criminals and Nazis, who are becoming synonymous. Berlin is still singing, dancing. loving. Newspapers are still being printed. Trains still run. The Jewish lawyer Hans Litten – a historical figure – still believes in German laws and German integrity (the real Litten ended up killing himself in Dachau in 1938).Watching the show 93 years after the events being depicted, I constantly want to shout at the screen: turn left here – you can kill Hitler at this dinner, and the Reichstag won’t burn, and it will all end differently. Wake up, I want to scream at the opportunistic majority – don’t you understand what is happening?They don’t, of course. They turn the other way and fail to kill Hitler. Because facts are facts. The dramatists are accurately describing February 1933 as the month in which German society was radically torn apart at an extraordinary speed because of mistakes made by party leaders and others who could still have stopped it all. ⁠View image in fullscreenThe Nazis take hold in Babylon Berlin’s fifth season.Photograph: Frédéric Batier/X Filme CreativeThe timing could hardly be more apt. Babylon Berlin began streaming in 2017, the year the extreme-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) entered the Bundestag for the first time with 12.6 % of the vote. Nine years on, the AfD has become my country’s dominant political force. In September it won 44% of the vote in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and 38.3% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the latter contest, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU dropped to 4.9% and didn’t even garner enough votes to enter the state parliament – an unprecedented humiliation.It is, therefore, quite tempting to watch Babylon Berlin and see ourselves in those historic times. But does it make sense? It does, but not in the way you might expect.There are not millions of desperate unemployed people on today’s German streets, nor paramilitary armies fighting heated battles. There is no Versailles trauma and the last global financial crisis was in 2008. There is no German president systematically replacing parliamentary government with emergency rule.The German men’s football team coach, Jürgen Klopp, recentlyadvised the nation to look at its strengthsrather than constantly stare at what is not working, so let’s start there. Germany has a strong constitutional court system and powerful federal states; it has, with help from its partners, created and maintained European integration, along with an established democratic culture and institutions designed explicitly because of the lessons of Weimar. Our European Germany in 2026 is not Weimar Germany in 1933.But there is another connection between Babylon Berlin and us as German spectators today – an echo that is more subtle and more interesting. It lies in this conviction that everything is falling apart. Here the wonderfully tongue-breaking termselbsterfüllende Prophezeiung(self-fulfilling prophecy) comes into play.Germany excels at the one thing no country should aspire to be good at. We are constantly describing ourselves as a country in terminal decline. Just spend an evening watching political talkshows or listening to people around you, and you will conclude that we are witnessing the final collapse of a failed state.The trains are all late. Bridges and streets are crumbling. Schools are failing and German childrenlagging behind in Pisa rankings.Bureaucracy is suffocating business and taxes are sky-high, plus ineffectively used. Isn’t energy too expensive and our pension system unsustainable? Immigration is out of control. Our digital transformation is a joke. And as for our car industry, that is on its knees. Plus, we lost to Ecuador and Paraguay at the World Cup. And the government cannot agree on how to fix any of this because support for the two big mainstream parties (the centre-right CDU and the centre-left SPD) is shrinking, and coalitions between parties that hate each other have become ever more complicated and fragile.Some of this is true – painfully so.View image in fullscreenAfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund embraces co-leader Alice Weidel after the party won 44% of the vote in the Saxony-Anhalt state elections, September 2026.Photograph: Thilo Schmülgen/ReutersI started writing these lines on a train from Hamburg to Tübingen via Stuttgart which was delayed by two hours. Someone in the hierarchy of Deutsche Bahn (or an AI, of course) then decided that, as we were already this late, the train would terminate in Mannheim. I had to cancel my plans and instead turn around and go back home. This is how you spend a day in modern Germany.Something much larger than my individual problem has arisen, however: our national narrative of failure has developed a disturbing relationship with reality. Germany’s seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed back above 3 million in September and inflation reached 3.3%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWithin the world of public broadcasting, talk about reform has been imminent for more than a decade – but instead of building the strongest and most robust system possible, which then might actually withstand the shocks, there are simply more meetings, and more reports, and more commissions of inquiry.The biggest problem, though, is Germany’s belief in the enormity of its problems. And this is exactly where Babylon Berlin and its look at 1933 becomes a more relevant companion to 2026 than the “Weimar is back” cry suggests .Democracies become vulnerable when people cease to believe that democracy can deliver. The destruction of Weimar was preceded by such a loss of faith. The circumstances were and are fundamentally different now. But one political mechanism is recognisable: the extreme right has a brief and simple story to tell.Close the borders. Deport those people we don’t know. Ignore Brussels. Stop paying Ukraine. Bring back cheap Russian energy and abolish stupid climate rules. Put Germany first.Our society seems scared and exhausted from years of crisis after crisis, and from the alarming talk of never-ending crises of tomorrow. The AfD understands this and knows how to turn every minor and unresolved problem into evidence that “das System” is rotten. My cancelled train is no longer just that, but proof of national doom. The brilliance of declinism lies in the fact that it is self-confirming. Once you have accepted that the country is collapsing, you see nothing but evidence for it.Would we recognise the end of our democracy if it were happening today, and to us? Or, instead, would we recognise the strength of our democracy if it were not ending?There is a danger in catastrophising so much that we cease to notice resilience, and progress, and that many things work just fine. German angst becomes German cynicism; cynicism turns to contempt; and, finally, contempt will make the AfD’s promise of destruction sound like the renewal we all need.We can and must tell the other, true story, of a country that has found trusted friends and partners and hence a peace that has lasted for 80 years, and economic and political, cultural and scientific successes most nations dream of – even in football (although it has become increasingly difficult to remember those days).This is not 1933 revisited, but it is a serious moment. And a good moment to for a reminder that, in dangerous times, a democratic coalition needs to govern as decisively, effectively and empathetically as it possibly can.Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is a podcast and TV host in Germany and has published nine booksExplore more on these topicsGermanyOpinionEuropeAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightcommentShareReuse this content

title: The IMF says we need to make ‘urgent choices’. But are they choices the Albanese government is willing to make? | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: The IMF is not a body that needs to worry about elections or the political cost of interest rates or inflation
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: The IMF is not a body that needs to worry about elections or the political cost of interest rates or inflation
Content: Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese. Greg Jericho writes Albanese’s government will ‘thank the IMF for confirming that the best way for a government to lower inflation is to lower prices of things such as energy and petrol’.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenJim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese. Greg Jericho writes Albanese’s government will ‘thank the IMF for confirming that the best way for a government to lower inflation is to lower prices of things such as energy and petrol’.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPGrogonomicsAustralian economyThe IMF says we need to make ‘urgent choices’. But are they choices the Albanese government is willing to make?Greg JerichoThe IMF is not a body that needs to worry about elections or the political cost of interest rates or inflationGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTue 13 Oct 2026 22.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 22.16 EDTShareThe IMF on Tuesday released its latest World Economic Outlook, suggesting“Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices”. But the choices are ones a government wishing to win an election would likely ignore.The IMF, as a rule, always sees a need to cut spending and lower taxes. Given its history of lending money to countries in severe debt, that’s no shock, and, even if the austerity it prescribed ruined lives, the IMF is very much in the Margaret Thatcher “the medicine is harsh but the patient requires it” mould.That’s important given what it thinks are “urgent choices”.But first we always get a sense of how the IMF see the world when we look at the titles of its outlook. A year ago, it wasGlobal Economy in Flux, Prospects Remain Dim, followed byGlobal Economy: Steady amid Divergent Forces. That,as I suggested at the time, was an extraordinary way to describe a world where Donald Trump was threatening Greenland and had just launched an insurgency into Venezuela.Since then, of course, there has been nothing “steady”, and the IMF outlooks went fromGlobal Economy in the Shadow of WartoGlobal Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology.Now apparently all is resilient despite the strain.For Australia the update slightly downgrades forecasts for economic growth over the next couple years. The big downgrades, though, came last October, before the US and Israel’s war on Iran:Click here if this graph does not displayThe downgrades since April are all margin of error stuff.The forecast for economic growth this year has Australia in the top half of the advanced nations of the OECD, and only behind the US among the G7 nations:Click here if this graph does not displaySimilarly, the forecast for inflation is not much changed from April – up a bit, but the IMF still thinks inflation will be below 3% by next year:Click here if this graph does not displayThere has beena report thatthis will mean Australia’s inflation is among the highest across the OECD next year. But, to be honest, so long at it is between 2% and 3%, arguing over who has the lowest is pretty silly.And yes, Australia is expected to see its unemployment rise by more than most OECD economies but it will remain lower here than three of the G7.Click here if this graph does not displayI also would happily take the IMF’s prediction for unemployment in 2026 of 4.4% and 4.7% next year, given currently (at least until Thursday) it is 4.6%.Over the next five years (at which point predictions get very ropey) the IMF sees pretty weak growth, inflation within the target range and unemployment not going above 4.8%Click here if this graph does not displayWould that be so bad? I’d prefer unemployment closer to 4% but, right now, given the ructions in the economy, steady inflation below 3% and unemployment lower than 4.8% is a pretty nice combination.These things never come true though (see above), so perhaps more relevant are the “urgent choices” that the IMF thinks needs to be made.One chapter of the outlook examines how governments respond to cost of living shocks such as the US-Israel war on Iran or Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.It notes government can either provide income support to (mostly) low-income households or it can suppress prices by, for example, cutting the fuel excise or subsidising energy costs (two policies the Albanese government undertook).The IMF found that (and prepare to be shocked) price-suppressing policies suppressed prices and thus lowered current inflation and also the inflationary expectations of the following year.By contrast, providing households with income support raised consumption by more (again not a shock) but it actually raised inflation not only in the current year but the expectation for inflation in the following year:Click here if this graph does not displayNow you might think that makes it obvious that if you want to lower the burden of inflation the best policy is to suppress prices and actually lower inflation.But no.The IMF says these figures show that “during cost-of-living crises, governments should preserve price signals and rely primarily on temporary, targeted income support for the most vulnerable”.And why? Well mostly because price suppression costs more, and the IMF hates government spending – especially if it increases a budget deficit.The IMF looked at measures by European countries in 2020 to 2023 and found income support helped the lowest 20% of households slightly more than price suppression – but the other 80% were all worse off.Click here if this graph does not displayI have some sympathy with the IMF not worrying too much about higher income households but this ignores the reality that cutting fuel excise or subsiding energy costs actually lowers inflation and thus helps keep interest rates lower.Does anyone really think the RBA would have kept rates down last year if the government increased income support and, as a result, increased inflation?The IMF is not a body that needs to worry about elections or the political cost of interest rates or inflation.As such, its advice is nice to consider but I suspect the Albanese government will look at the finding and thank the IMF for confirming that the best way for a government to lower inflation is to lower prices of things such as energy and petrol, and to do so again if needed.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyGrogonomicsLabor partyAnthony AlbaneseJim ChalmersInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)Australian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: President Zelenskyy’s allies must show the Russian president that American perfidy won’t alter the course of a war the Kremlin is losing
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: President Zelenskyy’s allies must show the Russian president that American perfidy won’t alter the course of a war the Kremlin is losing
Content: Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in August 2025. ‘Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Donald Trump in August 2025. ‘Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionUkraineThe Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechangingEditorialPresident Zelenskyy’s allies must show the Russian president that American perfidy won’t alter the course of a war the Kremlin is losingWed 14 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareWhen Donald Trump pledged to end the war in Ukrainewithin 24 hoursof re-entering the White House last year, no one with any depth of insight into the conflict believed him. But Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image as a master dealmaker. After a period when it seemed that Kyiv’s European allies had steered the US president away from pro‑Kremlin partisanship, he has reverted to the grotesque view that Ukrainian capitulation is a necessary precondition for peace.These are the perilous circumstances in which President Volodymyr Zelenskyymet Andy Burnhamon Wednesday in Downing Street. In recent days, the US president has called for a change of government in Ukraine. He claimed that apartial ceasefirehad been agreed, while Russia escalated its bombardments. According to Mr Zelenskyy, the latest missile strikes have come without the intelligence warnings from the US that have, in the past, facilitated self-defence. There have been reports of Ukrainian soldierslosing accessto the Starlink satellite network, controlled by Elon Musk, the US tech oligarch. This raises suspicion of coordinated pressure to tip the scales in Russia’s favour after many months when Mr Putin’s forces have failed to deliver significant advances and his country’s economy has been suffering from the effect of Ukrainian missile and drone counterstrikes.Mr Trump is unhappy with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. He claims that this is the cause of high energy prices afflicting American consumers and threatening Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections. The domestic imperative to keep pump prices down led Mr Trump to do a grubby deal toimport dieselfrom Russia, in flagrant breach of international sanctions.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy.Photograph: Dan Bashakov/APThe real driver of global energy prices is notUkrainedefending itself from Russian attack, but Mr Trump’s failing war against Iran. However, the US president is incapable of admitting any fault. Blaming Mr Zelenskyy enables him to deny his own culpability and, with malevolent encouragement from Mr Putin, to revive the preposterous notion that Ukrainian intransigence rather than Russian aggression is the reason why his promise to broker a peace deal remains unfulfilled.Disrupting Mr Trump’s pro-Russian delusions is not easy, but it has been done before. It is not agratifying diplomatic taskto indulge the monstrous vanity of the US president by trying to impress upon him a view of his country’s national interest, that Mr Putin is not an ally of his country or his personal friend, which is self-evident to any rational observer.Mr Burnham rightly resists invitations to denounce the US president in public. He recognises that Ukraine’s cause and, by extension, also the cause of European democracy more widely, is better served by making the case in private. The best response to Mr Trump’s perfidy is for Mr Zelenskyy’s friends to reaffirm their support, as Mr Burnham has done, thereby signalling that Ukraine will not be beaten by deals between the Kremlin and the White House.Russia is failing to achieve its war aims because the invasion was conceived in delusional hatred for the very idea of independent Ukrainian nationhood, which routinely underestimates that country’s will to resist. That is a flaw in Mr Putin’s plans that no amount of collusion with Mr Trump can fix.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
