title: ‘I must continue until I die’: inside the fight to bring Iran’s thriving art scene to the world | Art | The Guardian
description: Amid economic sanctions and ongoing conflict, a new initiative is returning Iran’s artists to the international spotlight
Author: David Smith
Headline: Amid economic sanctions and ongoing conflict, a new initiative is returning Iran’s artists to the international spotlight
Content: Untitled, Aryan Dabbagh, 2021. Digital photography. 30cm x 45 cm.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Aryan Dabbagh, 2021.View image in fullscreenUntitled, Aryan Dabbagh, 2021. Digital photography. 30cm x 45 cm.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Aryan Dabbagh, 2021.Art‘I must continue until I die’: inside the fight to bring Iran’s thriving art scene to the worldAmid economic sanctions and ongoing conflict, a new initiative is returning Iran’s artists to the international spotlightDavid SmithWed 14 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the call came early one morning, Tehran residentElham Issariknew it must be urgent. The voice on the line was offering something precious. “Miss Elham,” he said excitedly, “I have a single tube of white paint! It’s overpriced and I know it’s overpriced but, if you want it, you have to buy it right now because there’s this other guy in this other city who wants it and you have to tell me within the next five minutes.”The tube of white paint would have cost Issari 5m tomans (about $36), she recalls. “I was like, I don’t think so, because that’s overpriced, and the next thing you know is it’s 4am and I’m onYouTubewatching how to make lead white in your backyard without getting lead poisoning.”‘What could be discovered? What is new there?’: blockbuster exhibition celebrates Roy LichtensteinRead moreIt is a revealing slice of life in Iran these days. Since the US and Israellaunched joint airstrikes and combat operationson 28 February, and turned the screws on Iran’s economy, thousands of visual artists have been plunged into economic and professional limbo.The sudden onset of war shuttered commercial galleries in central Tehran, cancelled scheduled solo exhibitions, severed shipping channels and destroyed the fragile domestic market that allows creators to pay rent and sustain studio practices.But it was out of this systemic breakdown that Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran was born. The initiative connects contemporary artists living and working inside Iran with international audiences, collectors and institutions through a dedicated platform atiranartistrelief.org.The project owes its existence toDario Duran, a Canadian-Iranian curator and founder of Duran Art Projects. Born in Shiraz, but raised in Canada, Duran holds degrees in photography, art history and curatorial studies. Six years ago, driven by nostalgia and a desire to connect with his heritage, he moved to Iran, where he fell in love with the dynamism of the domestic art scene.View image in fullscreenMariam Rasti and Dario Duran.Composite: Courtesy of Continuum: Artist Relief for IranWhen war broke out, Duran found himself caught directly in its crosshairs. “I was displaced,” the 38-year-old explains from Shiraz inIran. “My mom and dad were visiting from Canada and we had to flee Shiraz because Shiraz was being hit pretty hard every day. It was becoming unbearable. We went by ground to the north of the country, where it was relatively quiet.”In the north, Duran encountered dozens of other displaced cultural workers who had fled bombed urban centers such as Tehran and Isfahan. He linked up there withMariam Rasti, co-founder of Duran Art Projects, who had also fled the capital.“We were in constant communication with the artists,” Duran recalls. “One thing we saw over and over again was that, like never before, the artists were losing hope. Cancelled exhibitions, galleries closing, not being able to find materials, artists being displaced – every single person was going through the exact same uncertainty of what happens tomorrow.”Iran’s contemporary art world operates inside a structural bubble, isolated from international banking networks. Typically, an artist works for one or two years to prepare a body of work, relying on a single gallery showcase to generate enough sales to survive for the next two years. When conflict brought that domestic cycle to a dead halt, creators faced immediate ruin.Duran says: “We realised that at this moment, exhibition making, curation, archiving – these things do not matter. What matters, more than anything else, is simply sales. These artists were not able to pay their rent.“One artist put up his paintbrushes and paint tubes for sale on Divar [a classifieds site] just to carry on. Another artist told me: ‘I’m going to go work in a coffee shop for the time being because I have no idea if this art thing is going to work out for me’.”Determined to make a difference, Duran bought a couple of gigabytes of internet access so he could get on WhatsApp. From his laptop in the north, he drafted an open letter to international collectors, museum directors and gallerists across the diaspora, laying bare the plight of creators inside Iran.The response was immediate and overwhelming. Gallerists and curators in London, New York, Paris, Dubai, Toronto and Mumbai wrote back, eager to assist. What had originally been planned as a modest PDF catalogue featuring a dozen imperilled acquaintances rapidly transformed into a nationwide initiative.‘Each artist on their own terms’: why Lee Krasner was every bit the equal to husband Jackson PollockRead moreOver five months of feverish development, Duran, Rasti and a coalition of domestic galleries built Continuum. The digital platform brings together more than 500 original artworks by over 200 contemporary artists living and working inside Iran.Eleven commercial galleries across Iran agreed to voluntarily waive 100% of their sales commissions.Duran Art Projectscharges no platform fees. As a result, 100% of every completed artwork sale goes directly to the artist. To make acquisitions realistic for global buyers during an economic downturn, prices were capped across three accessible tiers: up to $500; $500–$2,500; $2,500–$5,000.While the online front end of Continuum offers a catalogue of striking abstract canvases, delicate line drawings and minimalist photography, the back-end operation is a masterclass in guerrilla logistics. Delivering physical artworks out of a country under heavy military bombardment and stringent international sanctions requires ingenuity bordering on subversion.“The logistics of it – we thought about this ad nauseam,” Duran says with a weary laugh. “Currently, this matter is changing on an hourly basis. The sanctions obviously have been very disruptive.”View image in fullscreenUntitled, Shayan Sajadian, 2024. Digital photography. 80cm x 80cm.Photograph: Shayan Sajadian/Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Shayan Sajjadian, 2024.Initially, Continuum relied on two domestic courier services capable of flying artwork packages from Tehran to shipment hubs in Dubai and Istanbul, where international carriers could take over. But as geopolitical tensions soared, regional airspace closed and commercial flight paths dissolved.Duran explains: “The flight connections through the UAE were cancelled so the couriers told us that UAE is off the table. But the second UAE comes off the table, they figure out another way. There is a man who had a courier company that was forced to shut down. In order to keep his business going, he is now using the ground borders, moving overland from Iran into Armenia. He goes by the land border, carries the artworks into Armenia and ships them out from there with full insurance.”To manage expectations, Continuum informs international buyers that delivery may take three to six months. Yet collectors worldwide, ranging from private patrons in North America to major European institutions, have shown extraordinary patience.For Duran, the real tragedy of the current crisis lies in the indiscriminate cruelty of international economic sanctions, which target ordinary citizens while doing nothing to alter political outcomes. “These sanctions are not putting much pressure on the government,” he observes. “It’s mostly punishing everybody that’s trying to live a life here. Everyone’s complaining but we’re trying to find solutions.”Among the artists trying to make a way out of no way isMehrdad Jafari, 43, who grew up in the northern province of Mazandaran, where his relatives worked as sculptors and painters. Speaking from Tehran through a Farsi interpreter, he says: “Growing up, I always had the dream that one day I would be in Tehran and have an art studio in this city, to create work and fully realise my potential.“My entire life has been dedicated, and continues to be dedicated, to my work. In fact, my existence is connected to my work. I have no other way of being. I must continue until I die.”View image in fullscreenUntitled, Mehrdad Jafari, 2026. Oil on Cardboard. 40 x 30 cm.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Mehrdad Jafari, 2026.As the father of a three-year-old child, Jafari’s experience of the war is filtered through the anxieties of parenthood. His artwork, which centres on the complex emotional tapestry of human relationships and community interactions, has had to adapt to severe material deprivations.“Because of the effect of sanctions, we’ve had to be a lot more imaginative in order to decide what materials we use,” Jafari explains. “Materials are quite difficult to find right now. But what I’ve had to do, and what others are doing, is replace this lack of materials with imagination. We use alternative materials to carry on.”Jafari views this enforced improvisation as a double-edged sword. “In one way we use our imaginations more, creating a more creative space and ways of thinking. But on the other hand, of course, we would love to be part of the global system and have access to the things everybody else has access to. That’s just not available to us right now.”For Jafari, Continuum’s launch during a time of active military conflict carries symbolic resonance. “It’s an extraordinary moment. It’s a bridge for us to connect with an international audience. For me personally, it brings a sense of calm – that we are not forgotten. Because of Continuum, I am more invigorated than ever to work. It gives us hope that life can carry on.”From the outset, Duran and Rasti insisted that the initiative would not function as an exhibition about war, nor would it force artists to turn their pain into visual entertainment for foreign viewers.Duran argues: “Iranian contemporary art doesn’t look like any one thing. Iran is not a style, and the Iranian identity is not a medium. An artist living in Shiraz shouldn’t have to make work that visually announces ‘Iran’ before an international audience is willing to take it seriously. We wanted the work to be encountered first as art, not as evidence about a country.”‘Curious and circumspect creatures’: the artist making sculptures for the rats of New York CityRead moreWhile some participating artists choose to directly address conflict, Continuum refused to make political commentary or suffering a requirement for inclusion.“There is a difference between giving artists visibility during a crisis and asking artists to make the crisis visible,” Duran adds. “I definitely didn’t want crisis to become the reason their work deserves attention. Context should deepen our understanding of an artwork; it shouldn’t imprison the artwork.”The breadth of work included on the platform bears out this philosophy. Across 500 pieces, viewers encounter delicate geometric abstraction, haunting figurative portraiture, avant-garde photography, experimental printmaking and sculpture.The financial relief generated by Continuum is already providing vital support to Iran’s artistic ecosystem. In a country where currency devaluation has eroded savings, a single $500 artwork sale can provide significant income towards studio rent or much-needed pigments.Issari, 38, reflects: “It creates a chain. If an artist is not so worried about their income, maybe they can continue teaching. If they can continue to teach, kids can continue to learn. The whole chain does not stop and we don’t fall into this pit of absolute hopelessness.”View image in fullscreenAzargun, Elham Issari, 2020. Oil on canvas. 24cm x 30 cm.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran, presented by Duran Art Projects. © Elham Issari, 2020.Issari could not bring herself to work during the first weeks of heavy bombardment in Tehran. “I was here for the whole show. Hearing explosions five times, six times per day, every day – having to gather the cats and run to your safe place and count to 10. Then, as soon as it’s over, pick up the phone, check if your father is alive, if your mother’s alive, if your loved ones are OK. On repeat. It does a number on you.”The trauma was physical as much as psychological. “I didn’t touch a brush,” she recalls. “Actually, I did once, and my hands were shaking so badly that I literally just put it down. I was like, ‘I am not going to do this right now.’ And that’s OK, because I’m just not there.”While Issari, who studied art in London, is hopeful her paintings on Continuum will find homes in international collections, the initiative’s primary gift is emotional validation. “Even if you don’t sell, it’s that feeling of being seen,” she says with quiet determination. “For me, it’s tremendous. It’s easy to feel like you’re a pariah and you’re invisible. Just the fact that you’re being seen means a lot.”She adds: “I always have faith in the fact that art will survive, regardless of everything and anything. Artists are the best. If problem-solving were an Olympic sport, we would win a gold medal every time. We will find a way.”Explore more on these topicsArtIranPaintingPhotographyExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A dominatrix and her tightly bound client: Giada Ripa’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘Karen is a Japanese dominatrix and “rope artist” who ties up her clients in a way that echoes how samurai bound their prisoners. Clients are mostly men with high-pressure jobs’
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: ‘Karen is a Japanese dominatrix and “rope artist” who ties up her clients in a way that echoes how samurai bound their prisoners. Clients are mostly men with high-pressure jobs’
Content: ‘She is a therapeutic person for them – they talk to her’ … an image from The Yokohama Project by Giada Ripa.Photograph: Giada RipaView image in fullscreen‘She is a therapeutic person for them – they talk to her’ … an image from The Yokohama Project by Giada Ripa.Photograph: Giada RipaMy best shotArt and designA dominatrix and her tightly bound client: Giada Ripa’s best photograph‘Karen is a Japanese dominatrix and “rope artist” who ties up her clients in a way that echoes how samurai bound their prisoners. Clients are mostly men with high-pressure jobs’Interview byCharlotte JansenWed 14 Oct 2026 09.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTen years ago, my dad called to say he had found these amazing images hidden under piles of maps and stuff in an attic in our family home in Piemonte, northern Italy. He had come across a leather-bound album of 53 black and white photographs: portraits of Japanese “native types”, reflecting the 19th-century colonial way of representing people, cultures and views ofJapan.It turned out we had a treasure in our hands: it was an album of photographs byFelice Beato, the first foreign photographer to arrive in Japan in 1863 at the end of the Edo period and on the eve of the Meiji era.When Beato arrived, Japan was still largely closed to foreigners. He started accompanying British diplomatic and military delegations and later set up a portrait studio where he photographed geishas, fishers, samurai, teachers, government officials – creating a kind of visual encyclopedia of people, professions and ways of life. These were the first images of Japan that the western world saw.double quotation markMathilde Ruinart, one of our ancestors, rode through areas forbidden to foreigners and reportedly shot some bandits deadI have always worked with historical archives. Finding this album was amazing, but I couldn’t understand why it had ended up in our house. I needed to know and decided to look for clues. A year later, I found a 19th-century manuscript written by one of our ancestors,Mathilde Ruinart, an intellectual and a painter. She had married the first Italian ambassador to Japan, who was sent there in 1867 partly to help secure Japanese silkworms, as a disease was devastating the European silk industry. She had accompanied her husband – the journey took four months – and they stayed for four years. The manuscript was her diary, as well as letters, detailing her time there.I was so fascinated that I read it all in one night. While Beato is well known, no one had heard of this remarkable woman, who knew she was witnessing a major transition in Japan and wanted to leave a trace of her years there. She rode her horse through parts of the country forbidden to foreigners with a gun in her dress and reportedly once shot a group of bandits dead.I found as many of Mathilde’s descendants as I could and uncovered more of her archive, including hernetsukecollection, brought back from her time in Japan. I photographed her objects and belongings – I dedicated an entire year to her. She was the same age as Beato and in Japan at the same time, so it was obvious to me that they must have met there, and that she must have selected and bought the photographs from him, which is how they came to be in my house.From that cameThe Yokohama Project, a dialogue between the three of us – Beato, Ruinart and me – across 150 years. Three ways of seeing Japan, past and present, trying to understand and build a bridge. In the first chapter of the project I followed their footsteps, going to places they went, shooting on large-format film, echoing the slow process of observation. For the second chapter, I photographed about 40 Japanese professions, some still linked to those photographed by Beato, such as the geisha and theshamisen player, but also going beyond them to contemporary Japan. I invited people to a studio in Tokyo to present themselves in the ways they wanted to be seen. I photographed Lolita girls, anda fishmongerwho was like a movie star. In Tokyo fishmongers are superstars – he came with €1,000-worth of red snapper in a basket and told me we had 10 minutes or the fish would go bad, which is a problem shooting on large-format as it’s a very slow process.Karen, who appears in this portrait, describes herself as a BDSM dominatrix and a rope artist. She practisesshibariwith cross-dressing, tying and binding – a broader term than bondage. It is a visual and technical practice of tying the body with rope that can be erotic or not. It originates from the way samurai would bind their prisoners. Karen also practiseskinbaku, a specific term for tight binding. She uses it in an intimate way with her clients, who are mostly men with high social and professional pressures.Her practice allows them to step outside their day to day identities and express a side they can’t show elsewhere. She is a therapeutic person for them, and they talk to her – it’s not just a physical relationship but a cathartic experience. It allows her clients to transcend daily life. The man in this image is actually an assistant who worked on the project with me and agreed to be part of the picture. The two of them talked, and she decided how to tie him. He had never experienced it before – and he admitted afterwards that he enjoyed it.The Yokohama Projectby Giada Ripa is published byGost BooksView image in fullscreenPhotograph: courtesy Giada RipaGiada Ripa’s CVBorn:London, 1974High point:My first museum solo exhibition, Displacement, at the Moscow Museum of ModernArtin 2011Top tip:Follow what genuinely makes you curious. Research can give you the starting point, but it’s through looking, questioning and having a personal encounter with the subject that the work begins to come aliveExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotJapanPhotographyArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Baby review – Pearl Mackie is meticulous as an abuse survivor | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Gurpreet Kaur Bhatti’s compassionate solo play follows a young mother’s struggle to get life back on track after time behind bars
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: Gurpreet Kaur Bhatti’s compassionate solo play follows a young mother’s struggle to get life back on track after time behind bars
Content: ‘You believe me, right?’ … Pearl Mackie in Baby.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreen‘You believe me, right?’ … Pearl Mackie in Baby.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewBaby review – Pearl Mackie is meticulous as an abuse survivorBrixton House, LondonGurpreet Kaur Bhatti’s compassionate solo play follows a young mother’s struggle to get life back on track after time behind barsHolly O'MahonyWed 14 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlenty of abuse survivors don’t go on to commit terrible crimes, argues the titular Baby as she attempts to make sense of the cause-and-effect cycle that landed her in prison and saw her precious baby daughter forcibly removed. It’s a line that echoes the more merciless commentary surrounding the case of US death row inmate Christa Pike, whose failed execution last month led to global headlines.Produced by Clean Break, a theatre company built specifically for women in the sightlines of the criminal justice system, Gurpreet Kaur Bhatti’s compassionate solo play offers a holistic, cradle-to-grave look at its character’s life, while spotlighting a broken pipeline. Once you’ve fallen through the cracks and into a gutter of crime and drug dependency, it argues, it’s impossible to climb back out. Survive and you’ll become a number with a case file and a lack of agency, whose remaining years will be spent pinballing between probation officers and case workers.Baby is played meticulously by Doctor Who’s Pearl Mackie, who carries her character from a precocious child who is top of her class – despite playing carer to her mother behind the scenes – to a young woman who, having unknowingly got involved with an older criminal, ends up behind bars, then struggles to get back on track.View image in fullscreenMeticulous … Pearl Mackie.Photograph: Helen MurrayLike Pike, Baby may not fare well in the court of public opinion, but nor would a formal hearing be likely to present her full story, which she relays to us directly. “You believe me, right?” she implores us, eyes wide. We do.Though we see brief flashes of reasonable anger, Baby wears a beaming smile almost permanently under Milli Bhatia’s direction, and it can seem like trauma bounces off her too lightly. I longed for Baby to deliver a more guttural response to her turmoil, like Denise Gough in People, Places and Things, or Sophie Melville in Iphigenia in Splott.Her uncharacteristic sunniness unshackles her from stereotypes, and on Khadija Raza’s buttercup-yellow set, this is seemingly the point. But the details of her roughest ordeals are skipped over too, creating the sense we’re watching the diluted, censored version of a darker story.AtBrixton Houseuntil 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreWomenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Girls is back: why it’s the perfect time for more of Lena Dunham’s millennial Sex and the City  | Girls | The Guardian
description: HBO’s era-defining comedy is set for a new five-episode series. Its bleakness and warmth couldn’t be more welcome
Author: Louis Staples
Headline: HBO’s era-defining comedy is set for a new five-episode series. Its bleakness and warmth couldn’t be more welcome
Content: Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Lena Dunham and Zosia Mamet in HBO’s Girls, 2012.Photograph: HBO/AllstarView image in fullscreenAllison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Lena Dunham and Zosia Mamet in HBO’s Girls, 2012.Photograph: HBO/AllstarGirlsGirls is back: why it’s the perfect time for more of Lena Dunham’s millennial Sex and the CityLouis StaplesHBO’s era-defining comedy is set for a new five-episode series. Its bleakness and warmth couldn’t be more welcomeWed 14 Oct 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTShareIt’s a pop culture emergency. A millennial-quake that shook my social feed to its core.Girls, the HBO show that stole the zeitgeist in the early Instagram era and madeLena Dunhama generational star, is returning for a five-episode revival series. The project was announced via amock video callwith some of the original cast: Allison Williams, Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet and Andrew Rannells. They’re all returning for the reboot, which will pick up the story 10 years after the 2017 finale.Lena Dunham’s Girls returning for limited run at HBORead moreGirls captured such a specific era when it premiered in 2012. Social media still felt new and exciting,Barack Obamawas president and so-called “woke 1” felt like it was going to be the new normal. The show’s characters navigated that terrifying twentysomething period when you’re searching for an identity, where it feels like everyone has it figured out but you. Dunham’s realistic approach to sex scenes – sticky, awkward, unflinching – made the show one of the first to be “discoursed” on social media, spawning endless think-pieces and Twitter threads. She was declared the voice of her generation, but she also became a figure of controversy who didn’t always seem suited to such intense, era-defining fame.For Dunham, theGirlsrevival comes at a time where she’s taking a victory lap. Following a string of successful TV projects and the release of Famesick – her New York Times best-selling memoir, which lifted the lid on her time filming Girls while living with chronic pain – she is in the ascendency once again. But given that reboots tend to have, ahem, amixedsuccess rate, the big question is: can Lena’s lightning strike twice?As a dyed-in-the-wool millennial who came of age on a cultural diet of Glee, unironic #hashtags and BuzzFeed quizzes, Girls really was my generation’s answer to Sex and the City. The shows similarly star four white women navigating life in New York, and the characters are rendered with such specificity and consistency that fans can endlessly argue about whether they’re “a Hannah” or “a Carrie”. (I’m a Miranda in SATC, and a Marnie in Girls.)The news that Girls is returning draws inevitablecomparisonswithAnd Just Like That, the post-Covid reboot that took us back into Carrie Bradshaw’s world in her 50s. Over three toe-curling seasons, AJLT became a case study in hownotto do a reboot. The show lost so much of the original’s astute, bitingcynicismand often seemed more concerned with atoning for its past, such as its glaring lack of diversity and a handful of offensive “early 2000s” storylines that aged poorly. Some of the characters – especially Miranda Hobbes, whose snarky realism was a vital leveller to Carrie’s delusional romanticism – were changedbeyond recognition.View image in fullscreenWilliams and Dunham in Girls’ sixth and final season, 2017.Photograph: Mark Schafer/HBOPersonally, I wouldn’t be against a Che Diaz cameo in Girls 2.0, but there’s a few factors that make it easier for Dunham to take her revival in a very different direction. Since Girls wrapped, she seems to have been in constant conversation with the characters. In 2023, when IinterviewedAllison Williams, the real-life Marnie Michaels told me that she and Dunham had spoken on the phone during Covid, where they discussed how they would have handled the pandemic. “Marnie would have 100% wrapped herself in cellophane, Hannah would have pretended to do the same, but would have been living very riskily in secret,” she said. “One of the powers of the specificity of those characters is that it’s quite easy to imagine.”Lena Dunham on going to rehab: ‘It was like the first day of college, except many of the people had a problem with heroin’Read moreThen there’s timing. While it’s expected that the “girls” of Girls will have evolved into adult women, 10 years is a smaller gap than thewaveof2000srebootswe’ve seen, which have often been tasked with filling in the blanks of two decades. The 2010s was certainly a different time – pre-Trump and pre-pandemic – but Hannah Horvath had an iPhone and posted attention-seeking tweets. Her world wasn’t totally unrecognisable, which should make it easier for Dunham to stay true to the parts of the characters that made fans love them.View image in fullscreenThe cast of Girls at the sixth season’s premiere in New York on 2 February 2017.Photograph: Evan Agostini/APTiming might also ask the deeper questions at the heart of the revival. Girls became a hit because of its relatable combination of warmth and bleakness. The show was aspirational in some ways, by nature of following four attractive, privileged women in the big city, but it also saw them sharing small apartments with friends whose big dreams were colliding with the reality of the post-recession economy. And if this was a story about any other generation, you’d expect for the characters to have graduated beyond the economic precarity and self-doubt of their 20s. But for millennials, it’s not so simple. The revival would do well to tap into how muchhasn’tchanged for the generation who are the first to be worse off than their parents. So many millennials are still navigating housing and job insecurity, and have that creeping feeling that they’re not progressing in life. This frustration could be very fruitful for Dunham, who has a particular talent for zoning in on wider generational anxieties as they’re happening.Netflix’s Mike Tyson docuseries offers an incomplete portrait of a troubling figure | Andrew LawrenceRead moreAt the heart of Girls is, of course, its polarising creator. Unlike SATC, which was mostlyreappraisedas too white and privileged after the original series concluded, Girls faced intense criticism at the time for its lack of diversity. Ten years on, without the noise of unforgiving social media discourse and think-pieces, the satirical genius of the show – and how it skewered the ridiculousness of its characters – is easier to see. Dunham wasfar from perfect, but it now seems clear that she was derided in a way that was plainly disproportionate, which often had more to do with her body and gender than the show, or even her own propensity to put her foot in it (thenapologise). Now, following the success of her memoir,Famesick, we’re in a period of Dunham-aissance, which might be why she’s choosing this moment to return to her most beloved work.Ten years on, the revival’s key challenge is unlikely to be the confessional subject matter, which feels more commonplace today because of the wave of female-fronted shows that came next, like Fleabag, Catastrophe and I May Destroy You. Instead, Dunham is tasked with meeting the expectations of diehard fans who have very strong views about the characters and have spent years creating their own theories on what they’re doing now. Reboots often struggle because they fail to grasp what fans loved about the original. But if there’s one person who is perceptive and daring enough to understand what the audience wants from her, Dunham may well be that girl.Explore more on these topicsGirlsUS televisionLena DunhamDramaTelevisionTV comedyComedycommentShareReuse this content

title: Stevie Wonder review – playing ​his greatest album in full, he knocks everyone sideways | Stevie Wonder | The Guardian
description: The opening night of Wonder’s tour marking the 50th anniversary of Songs in the Key of Life leaves jaws on the floor, thanks to sumptuous tracks carrying still-urgent messages
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The opening night of Wonder’s tour marking the 50th anniversary of Songs in the Key of Life leaves jaws on the floor, thanks to sumptuous tracks carrying still-urgent messages
Content: Extraordinary … Stevie Wonder at Birmingham’s Utilita Arena.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/Getty Images for ABAView image in fullscreenExtraordinary … Stevie Wonder at Birmingham’s Utilita Arena.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/Getty Images for ABAStevie WonderReviewStevie Wonder review – playing ​his greatest album in full, he knocks everyone sidewaysUtilita Arena, BirminghamThe opening night of Wonder’s tour marking the 50th anniversary of Songs in the Key of Life leaves jaws on the floor, thanks to sumptuous tracks carrying still-urgent messagesAlexis PetridisWed 14 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeated amid a bank of keyboards,Stevie Wonderaddresses the audience at the first date of his tour celebrating the 50thanniversary of Songs in the Key of Life, his most celebrated album. He says playing it in full like this was a longstanding ambition: the issue was that it needed so many people to bring it to fruition. He actually fulfilled that ambition a decade ago in North American arenas in 2014 and 2015, gigs from which the 50th anniversary shows take their cue – complete with Superstition added as an encore – but that said, you have to take his point about the number of people involved.There really are a lot of musicians up there: three percussionists, a string section, five brass players, six backing vocalists, two guitarists, three keyboard players, including Wonder himself, who variously plays a bank of synthesisers both vintage and modern, a grand piano, an upright tack piano and, on Ngiculela/Es Una Historia/I Am Singing, a bizarre stringed instrument called a harpejji that wasn’t actually invented when Stevie Wonder last released an album, let alone when Songs in the Key of Life was made. Harpejii or not, that very much counts as scaling things down dramatically compared to the album’s actual sessions. Made by a man who could pretty much do everything himself, its recording nevertheless involved 108 musicians: eight people are credited forhandclaps.Its lavishness spoke volumes both about the commercial expectations placed upon it, and the artistic challenge involved in capping what Wonder had recently achieved. Having threatened to retire from music entirely prior to its making, Wonder reconsidered and wound up signing what was, in 1975, the biggest recording contract in history, worth around $230m in today’s money. And in the space of barely two years, he’d released Music of My Mind, Talking Book, Innervisions and Fulfillingness’ First Finale, a bravura display of talent so overwhelming that, when Paul Simon won the 1976 best album Grammy, his acceptance speech thanked Wonder for not releasing anything in the preceding year and thus giving everyone else a chance.View image in fullscreenLavish … Wonder with his sizeable band.Photograph: Katja Ogrin/Getty Images for ABAThe remarkable thing about the Songs in the Key of Life live show is not that it reminds you how extraordinary the ensuing album was, and is – given that everyone from Michael Jackson to Elton John to George Michael has called it the greatest album ever made, it hardly needs highlighting – but that it embellishes it. Not because of the expanded arrangements, lovely though they are: it’s a moot point as to whether Village Ghetto Land is much improved when played by live strings rather than Wonder’s stacked synthesisers, as the studio version was pretty incredible to start off with. It’s because it is resolutely a live performance, rather than a perfect recreation.Wonder fluffs his harmonica solo on Easy Goin’ Evening (My Mama’s Call) and insists the band restart Isn’t She Lovely, dissatisfied with the initial version (“Stop!” he cries. “Sue me!”). He also stretches songs out at will, the band locking into the tough funk of All Day Sucker and Black Man, and adds to the album’s already teeming tracklisting. Its first half now comes with another instrumental as well as the knotty, jazz-fusion influenced Contusion. You could, at a push, call it a jam, replete with call-and-response audience participation, but that feels like underselling its dramatic, symphonic soul.Stevie Wonder releases four unheard songs from Songs in the Key of Life sessionsRead moreFor all its peerless reputation, there’s a certain risk involved in performing Songs in the Key of Life live, more or less in order (and including the four songs from the A Something’s Extra EP that was bundled with the original album). Risky because the album opens in relatively understated style: Love’s In Need of Love Today, Have a Talk With God and Village Ghetto Land are incredible songs by any metric, but they’re downbeat, sombre, frequently desperate in tone, reflective of someone so disheartened by mid-70s America he was strongly considering relocating to Ghana and devoting himself to charity work, hardly the big razzle-dazzling opening you might expect from an arena show. On the night, it doesn’t matter, perhaps because the audience know what to expect, perhaps because the lyrics depicting a US desperately lacking empathy, mired in hideous inequality and governed by people whose ostensible devotion to Christianity seemed to have no bearing whatsoever on their actions might as well have been written in 2026.They’re received ecstatically, although not quite as ecstatically as the reliably joy-bringing Sir Duke and I Wish. Indeed, you spend a lot of the show with your jaw on the floor. Even given its reputation, Songs in the Key of Life still has the ability to knock you sideways with the astonishing level of quality it maintains throughout: it’s an album on which the deep cuts would be anyone else’s showstoppers: Saturn, Knocks Me Off My Feet, Joy Inside My Tears. As the deep soul of the latter finally dies away, an earnest voice pipes up from the rear of the arena. “That,” it cries, audibly gobsmacked, “wasreallygood”.Stevie Wonder plays 3Arena, Stockholm, 22 October; returning to tour the UK 3-11 NovemberExplore more on these topicsStevie WonderPop and rockSoulR&Blive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: How we lost our appetite for eat-the-rich satire | Movies | The Guardian
description: Tom Cruise’s latest film could lose $250m (£190m) – could one reason be that audiences are tired of Hollywood telling them what they already know about the super-rich
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tom Cruise’s latest film could lose $250m (£190m) – could one reason be that audiences are tired of Hollywood telling them what they already know about the super-rich
Content: Up in smoke … Digger director Alejandro González Iñárritu (left) and Tom Cruise at the film’s Japanese premiere in Tokyo on 6 October.Photograph: Keizo Mori/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenUp in smoke … Digger director Alejandro González Iñárritu (left) and Tom Cruise at the film’s Japanese premiere in Tokyo on 6 October.Photograph: Keizo Mori/UPI/ShutterstockMoviesHow we lost our appetite for eat-the-rich satireAlastair RyderTom Cruise’s latest film could lose $250m (£190m) – could one reason be that audiences are tired of Hollywood telling them what they already know about the super-rich?Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.34 EDTShareIt seems as if nobody can decide who should shoulder most of the blame for the recent box office flop ofDigger.Was it the oustedWarner Brosfilm executives Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, whose love of big-budget auteur cinema usually came with a hefty price tag? Or was it the marketing team, who were responsible for hiding the movie’s biggest swing from all trailers, ensuring many viewers would be left alienated from its early meta-reveal onwards?The truthful answer is that the film’s fate was sealed long before anybody could point fingers over its failure. In the past year it’s become clear that audiences have grown tired of the worn-out cinematic trend Digger is a part of: the eat-the-rich satire.There was a brief moment when audiences couldn’t get enough movie takedowns of the uber-wealthy, with the breakout success of Parasite inspiring Hollywood to seize upon its class-conscious themes and drag them into the west. The sustained fallout from the Covid pandemic brought issues of wealth inequality further into the spotlight, and titles as varied asGlass Onion,Saltburn,Triangle of SadnessandThe Menuall spoke to the zeitgeist with their distinct, controversial takedowns of the 1%.On the small screen, Succession and The White Lotus rapidly increased their audiences after acclaimed first seasons, thanks to the promise of darkly comic social commentary skewering those at the top of the food chain. Audiences were more than ready to eat the rich, but their appetites were satiated long before Hollywood had even considered switching up the menu.Digger is the most high-profile casualty of this trend running its course, with some reports predicting it could lose a staggering $250m (£190m) during its cinema run. The divisive reviews and audience reactions are easy to blame, but perhaps it would have been better received had audiences not grown exhausted by constant cinematic reminders about how much they’ve been screwed over by the rich and powerful.The theme hasn’t grown any less urgent, but interest in movies that hold a cracked mirror up to this reality has waned. Already this year, two action-revenge movies pitting lower-class protagonists against the super-rich in fights to the death –Ready or Not 2andThey Will Kill You– belly-flopped at the box office, and even arthouse audiences seem to be exhausted by this brand of topical satire, if receipts forRosebush PruningandI Love Boostersare anything to go by.On the small screen, the return of anthology series Beef,an awards sensation and streaming hit in its first run, failed to register as it pivoted to this familiar class satire, barely cracking Netflix’s daily top 10 before disappearing entirely.Later this week, Romain Gavras’s Sacrifice will debut on Netflix with no fanfare, more than a year after its hotly anticipated festival premierelanded with a thud. It’s a tale of shallow but self-righteous celebrities at a fundraising gala infiltrated by violent activists, boasting an A-list cast including Chris Evans, Anya Taylor-Joy and John Malkovich. It echoes many of the previously mentioned titles’ themes about the tension between the wealthy and their commitment to political causes. And even with its starry ensemble and clear cultural relevance, it took several months to find a distributor, and this paragraph may be the first you’re hearing of it.The strangest thing about the death of this trend in movies is that many of its ideas are finding more ground in the mainstream. Even the most vanilla tax on higher earners is supported by 75% of Britons,according to YouGov, and a clear majority of60% in the US. People are becoming more openly critical of the super-wealthy, so it is strange that pop culture taking aim at their unsustainable lifestyles is being met with fatigue.We’re living through a time when the world’s richest man is also one of the most widely disliked, and the real-estate mogul US president keeps hitting new lows in approval ratings. Despite the not-so-secret allegiances of some studio heads –Skydance CEO David Ellisonis an enthusiastic Trump backer – Hollywood creatives are aware of how detested among the public these figures are beyond their bases, and studios haven’t been shy in greenlighting movies with a satirical disdain for everything they represent, politically and culturally. Why has it stopped striking a chord?Tom Cruise’s Digger has flopped spectacularly – but I think it is a misunderstood masterpieceRead moreThe most obvious explanation is pure exhaustion. Doomscrolling has become a daily activity for millions, so why would anybody need to part with their money to see a movie satirising the people responsible for the state of the world when they could get sharper, more topical gags on their timeline for free?In trying to speak to the times without the responsibility of reacting to more specific headlines, the eat-the-rich movie often winds up preaching the obvious, late to the joke even if the sentiment remains relevant. It’s the Stewart Lee routine about political satire – “Was it funny? No, but I agreed the fuck out of it” – blown up to blockbuster scale, and nobody is spending their hard-earned cash to politely nod along to a movie they should be laughing at.The irony of Digger being the final movie released by Warner Bros as an independent studio hasn’t been lost, with its theme of billionaires trying to control the narrative foreshadowing the arrival of a new studio owner with an interest in appeasing the president.We might become nostalgic for this brand of movie very quickly if the worst assumptions about Ellison’s studio takeover come true, as well as being thankful that a movie of this kind could have ever been greenlit at this level. Unfortunately, no passage of time will make this and every other late-stage capitalism satire become laugh-out-loud funny.Explore more on these topicsFilmDiggerWarner BrosClass issuesDonald TrumpParamount PicturesSaltburncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘It put me in a fever dream’: Philip Venables on turning Sarah Kane’s 4.48 Psychosis into a shocking opera | Opera | The Guardian
description: A decade after the premiere of his work setting Kane’s hard-hitting play, it’s returning to the Royal Opera House. The composer remembers its fevered beginnings, the sweat and tears shed along the way, and how it changed his life forever
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A decade after the premiere of his work setting Kane’s hard-hitting play, it’s returning to the Royal Opera House. The composer remembers its fevered beginnings, the sweat and tears shed along the way, and how it changed his life forever
Content: ‘By opening night, our noses were so close to the grindstone that nobody had really thought about how it might be received… the overwhelming audience response felt like a huge release of tension, a euphoria borne from sweat and tears shed along the way.’The premiere staging of 4.48 Psychosis at the Lyric Hammersmith theatre.Photograph: © ROH/Stephen CummiskeyView image in fullscreen‘By opening night, our noses were so close to the grindstone that nobody had really thought about how it might be received… the overwhelming audience response felt like a huge release of tension, a euphoria borne from sweat and tears shed along the way.’The premiere staging of 4.48 Psychosis at the Lyric Hammersmith theatre.Photograph: © ROH/Stephen CummiskeyOpera‘It put me in a fever dream’: Philip Venables on turning Sarah Kane’s 4.48 Psychosis into a shocking operaA decade after the premiere of his work setting Kane’s hard-hitting play, it’s returning to the Royal Opera House. The composer remembers its fevered beginnings, the sweat and tears shed along the way, and how it changed his life foreverPhilip VenablesWed 14 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn January 2015, I was on an overnight flight coming back from New York, having attended Prototype, a festival of new opera. I didn’t sleep a wink, but worked without stopping in a packed, dark, sleepy cabin, reading and annotating a book and furiously making notes on my laptop. As if in a fever dream, my mind whirled with text, music, dramaturgy, theatre.Those six nocturnal hours were some of the most creatively fertile of my life. The book was 4.48 Psychosis; the annotations became the blueprint for an opera. Sarah Kane’s text had unlocked something in me, a fervour, a deluge of ideas. I could barely keep up, noting every impulse, every fantasy, as my mind pinballed around.I landed back home, back to real life, with a thud. That year turned out to be tough: a messy and protracted relationship breakup and a threat of bankruptcy and losing my house, a victim of rogue builders. I broke out in a bleeding stress rash, and, for the first time in my life, suffered insomnia. I was not composing. Time slipped by.View image in fullscreenPhilip Venables: ‘my mind whirled with text, music, dramaturgy, theatre.’Photograph: Charl MaraisIn late summer, I managed to pull myself together. I dusted off those notes from the flight, made some spreadsheets (always!), counted the days I had to write each scene and set to work. The opera was written at breakneck speed in six months, in something of a trance. My personal life remained fraught, but the opera, and Kane’s world, became a refuge, an escape, a joy. Writing flowed.I followed my blueprint almost without deviation. I wrote the most straightforward scenes first, out of order, in their matching groups: the patient-doctor dialogues, the serial sevens, the positive and negative affirmations. Slowly, a patchwork opera emerged, until only the most challenging scenes remained. Then I returned to the text; it had an uncanny ability to reveal more ideas, more music, like layers peeled back successively. I reminded myself to follow my instincts. I held on to sage advice from fellow composer James Weeks: “You want people to come out afterwards and say ‘that wasn’t an opera’.”double quotation markKane’s text was a libretto just waiting to be set, full of musicRehearsing the opera was demanding. I delivered the score late (something I’ve learned never to repeat) and I’d unwittingly written something that did not align with a standard production: swathes of complex ensemble singing that had to be learned together; lots of recorded material to be prepared; scenes requiring millisecond precision between light, sound and video. This was difficult material on every level, and the creative team, producers and cast rolled up their sleeves and met the challenges with grit and dedication. I owe a huge debt of gratitude to that heroic cast and the producer, Sarah Crabtree.By opening night in May 2016, our noses were so close to the grindstone that nobody had really thought about how it might be received. There was simply relief and astonishment that we had made it to the stage. So the overwhelming audience response felt like a huge release of tension, a euphoria borne from sweat and tears shed along the way.View image in fullscreenA rare and precious thing … Gweneth Ann Rand and Susanna Hurrell in 4.48 Psychosis, Lyric Hammersmith, 2016.Photograph: © ROH/Stephen CummiskeyA number of critics noted that the text was clear and present in the opera, that it “seems to emanate from everywhere”. This was my proudest achievement. Kane’s text was a libretto just waiting to be set, full of music. Aside from passages of dense poetry, there are song forms, conversations, extracts from psychological tests, prosaic medical notes, descriptions of dreams – and, streaked throughout, the darkest of humour. I tried to find musical equivalences: love songs, musical humour, percussion dialogues to grasp the banality of psychiatry, contrasted with moments of deeply expressive, impassioned opera. I threw as many ideas at it as I could, and the text reciprocated … it opened floodgates of imagination. A text such as this is a rare and precious thing.Over the following months I began to process the experience. Aside from the confidence boost, the success of 4.48 kickstarted another period of creative abundance: my close collaboration and friendship with director Ted Huffman. We wanted to make more, as quickly as possible. We talked every day about new projects, we watched shows, shared links, read, fantasised, critiqued. We applied for residencies, wrote pitches, talked to everyone we could. Since 4.48we have made three operasand a handful of smaller pieces, for vocalists, instrumentalists, choirs, even schoolchildren; doubtless we will make more. It is joyous.double quotation markSarah Kane has taught me more about opera than any opera ever has.Reflecting on this as I prepare for the 10th anniversary revival at theRoyal Opera Housemakes me realise how Kane’s text has for ever shaped the way I think about and make my work. These days I better understand those gut instincts that led me to her text and guided me through composing. I can now articulate the questions it provoked, the questions that I still ask of any new project: What is the relationship between character and performer? Who is speaking, and to whom? What does singing or speaking mean? How do we create a frame for performers to tell our story to an audience directly, without artifice? How do we create community on stage? Above all, I cherish Kane’s creation of a theatre of the imagination, not a theatre of representation. Tell, but don’t show.View image in fullscreenColin Shay and Sally Swanson in The Faggots and Their Friends Between Revolutions by  Philip Venables, directed by Ted Huffman, part of Manchester International festival 2023.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianKane has taught me more about opera than any opera ever has. It saddens me that, more than 25 years after the publication of her text, post-dramatic or formally experimental work graces British opera stages so rarely. We’re hung up on dramatisation, on representation, on the suspension of disbelief. There are so many other ways to skin a cat.While the opera has had several other performances and productions in the US, France and Germany, coming back to our original production and watching a new cast tackle it afresh has been a real pleasure – and also underlines the unique achievement of the original cast. Alongside, I’m writing and directing my first music theatre piece without Ted, The Alonetimes, a collaboration with Jennifer Walshe, which has its UK premiere on 19 October at the Schwarzman Centre in Oxford. A brand new adventure and returning to where I began, all in the same week. I’m incredibly lucky, and I owe it to that meeting with 4.48 Psychosis, all those years ago.4.48 Psychosis is at theLinbury theatre, London from 17-25 OctoberExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicRoyal Opera HouseSarah KaneShareReuse this content

title: Jessie Buckley suggests film industry gives too much weight to Oscar campaigns | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor, who won the Academy Award for best actress this year, was speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: The actor, who won the Academy Award for best actress this year, was speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards
Content: ‘I feel so proud being part of this community’ … Jessie Buckley.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/Invision/APView image in fullscreen‘I feel so proud being part of this community’ … Jessie Buckley.Photograph: Scott A Garfitt/Invision/APMoviesJessie Buckley suggests film industry gives too much weight to Oscar campaignsThe actor, who won the Academy Award for best actress this year, was speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awardsNadia KhomamiArts and culture correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 13.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJessie Buckley has questioned whether the film industry places too much emphasis on Oscar campaigns at the expense of nurturing emerging talent, suggesting there may be greater potential in supporting film-makers at grassroots level.Speaking at the BFI and Chanel film-maker awards in London, the actor was responding to comments by John Malkovich, who saidOscar campaigns were now the only way to get audiences into cinemas.“I think there’s truth in that,” Buckley told the Guardian. “You’ve got to take responsibility for sharing your work. It would be so easy to just go and film and then hide. I wish we could all do that. But I don’t think that’s how it works any more.”Buckley, who has made predominantly independent films, said the industry’s reliance on film promotion affected not just actors and directors but the wider workforce.“I feel so proud of being part of this community – this affects so many people’s lives. Crews, marketing, everybody. And if you don’t support it, you’re not going to have a job,” she said.“Maybe we’ve given that too much weight. I wonder if there’s more potential in nurturing at a grassroots level than giving so much weight to a marketing Oscar campaign.”Four emerging UK film-makers were named recipients of this year’sBFIand Chanel film-makers awards, each receiving £20,000 to develop their work.They were announced at a ceremony at Claridge’s in London on Wednesday, with Buckley and Gwendoline Christie joining a jury that also included BFI CEO Ben Roberts, Edward Enninful and Marie-Louise Khondji.double quotation markWe need to support the next generation. I want to know what they’ve got to say, what their world looks likeBuckley called for greater support for film-makers working outside established industry structures, pointing to the success of films “made on shoestring budgets”, includingObsessionandBackrooms.“People went to see them because of their quality, not because of the IP or what was deemed successful beforehand,” she said.“It’s essential that we support up-and-coming young film-makers. It would be completely selfish if we didn’t. At some point we want to pop off this earth, and we need to support the next generation. I want to know what they’ve got to say, what their world looks like.”The four winning films explored subjects including political protest, racial profiling, female solidarity and family trauma.View image in fullscreenJury members Gwendoline Christie and Jessie Buckley (centre) with, from left: Rich Felgate, Olive Nwosu, Imran Perretta and Rachel Taparjan.Photograph: James D KellyRich Felgate, director, producer and cinematographer of We, the Hated, was recognised for his documentary about Just Stop Oil protesters and the personal consequences of participating in a polarising movement. The jury described the film as “urgent and brave”.Buckley said it had prompted her to reconsider the role of protest in society. “In our world at the moment, protest seems like such a dangerous act, when historically it’s been essential to democracy,” she said.“It realigned me and reminded me of how important protest is, and how we can misunderstand the people within that. That we need to understand more and need films like that more.”Olive Nwosu won for Lady, her feature debut set in Lagos, which follows one of the city’s few female taxi drivers as she becomes drawn into the world of a childhood friend who has become a sex worker. The jury praised Nwosu’s cinematic ambition and her handling of challenging material.Imran Perretta was recognised forIsh, a black-and-white coming-of-age film set in Luton’s South Asian and Middle Eastern community. It follows two 12-year-old best friends whose relationship is tested after a police stop and search.The jury praised its exploration of racial profiling and the experience of being British while being treated as an outsider.Rachel Taparjan won for Something Familiar, her debut feature documentary about her search for her missing sisters after being adopted from Romania and brought to the UK as a child. The jury praised the film’s “naked, unselfconscious revelation of self”, saying it had stayed with them longest.Christie said the strength of this year’s field meant the jury had concluded it “couldn’t just select three winners”.The awards, which celebrate creative audacity and ambition, have run since 2022. Previous recipients include Harry Lighton, whose filmPillionwon best British independent film at the British independent film awards in 2025, and Savanah Leaf, who received the 2024 Bafta for outstanding debut by a British writer, director or producer.Explore more on these topicsFilmAwards and prizesJessie BuckleyFilm industryBFInewsShareReuse this content

title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s new press secretary: ‘Her reading is good for an 11-year-old’ | Late-night TV roundup | The Guardian
description: The host roasted Katie Zacharia after her awkward and confusing first press conference
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The host roasted Katie Zacharia after her awkward and confusing first press conference
Content: Jimmy Kimmel: ‘He hired a fourth-grader to be press secretary.’Photograph: YouTubeView image in fullscreenJimmy Kimmel: ‘He hired a fourth-grader to be press secretary.’Photograph: YouTubeLate-night TV roundupJimmy Kimmel on Trump’s new press secretary: ‘Her reading is good for an 11-year-old’The host roasted Katie Zacharia after her awkward and confusing first press conferenceGuardian staffWed 14 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJimmy Kimmelreacted to thedisastrous first dayat work of the new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia.Jimmy KimmelJimmy Kimmel opened Tuesday evening’s monologue with a rundown onDonald Trump’s new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, who held her first press conference that morning.“You know, Trump’s been president for quite a long time now,” Kimmel explained. “I think it’s been about, what, 50 or 60 years? And in order to keep him awake and interested every six months they bring in a new fawning blond dolt to add to the rotation.”But though Zacharia is afawning, blond conspiracy theorist, “things did not get off to a great start for Malibu Katie today,” Kimmel said. “Her first briefing was brief. It was only 14 minutes long, but even in that short time she accomplished exactly what she was brought in to do, which is slobber a whole tube of lip gloss all over the president’s behind.”Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s Nobel prize ‘snub’: ‘Thanks a lot, Norway. You made our baby cry’Read moreFor one, Zacharia opened the briefing by telling reporters that she wanted to work for Trump for “a very long time”.“She wanted to work for him for a very long time,” Kimmel repeated. “And really that’s all it takes nowadays. All it takes is that and dressing like you’re about to announce pre-boarding on a Delta Air Lines flight.”Kimmel then played another clip of Zacharia reading stiltedly from her notes. “Her reading is good for an 11-year-old!” be joked. “He hired a fourth-grader to be press secretary.”Zacharia, he noted, is “a real piece of work” who “made her name calling Democrats pedophiles on social media and giving weight to Pizzagate. So I’m sure she’ll immediately call for everyone named in the Trump-Epstein files to be punished to the full extent of the law.”Kimmel also showed numerous clips of Zacharia’s work as a talking head for various fringe rightwing outlets, including the claim that no one would see The Odyssey as it was a “woke movie”.“Well, that woke movie went on to make $1.8bn,” Kimmel retorted. “So we got a smart one here.”All in all, “Katie’s first outing was, as her boss might say, a total disaster,” he concluded. “I was impressed, though – you know how hard it is to become Trump’s worst press secretary that quickly?”To add to the embarrassment, after the briefing, Zacharia, allegedly a lawyer, responded to reporter questions about where she passed the bar exam with the unhelpful answer of “I moved to China.”Asked for clarification, the Trump administration refused to specify when or where Zacharia passed the bar exam.“I have a feeling the only bar she passed is from Dry Bar,” Kimmel quipped.Explore more on these topicsLate-night TV roundupJimmy KimmelTV comedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tinie Tempah says he will finally visit Scunthorpe after campaign by fans | Tinie Tempah | The Guardian
description: Rapper to visit Lincolnshire town 16 years after saying he had never been there in his hit Pass Out
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Rapper to visit Lincolnshire town 16 years after saying he had never been there in his hit Pass Out
Content: Tempah told a Scunthorpe-based fan he would visit the town in exchange for 5,000 pre-saves of his new album.Photograph: Marco Grey/PAView image in fullscreenTempah told a Scunthorpe-based fan he would visit the town in exchange for 5,000 pre-saves of his new album.Photograph: Marco Grey/PATinie TempahTinie Tempah says he will finally visit Scunthorpe after campaign by fansRapper to visit Lincolnshire town 16 years after saying he had never been there in his hit Pass OutHannah Al-OthmanNorth of England correspondentWed 14 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTFirst published on Wed 14 Oct 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rapper Tinie Tempah has said he will finally visit Scunthorpe – 16 years after he announced to the world that he had never been to the town in his number one hitPass Out.His decision follows a campaign by fans, led by Ben Johns, a Scunthorpe resident, who carried a cardboard cutout of the artist around theLincolnshiretown and encouraged people to pre-save Tempah’s new album.Johns had contacted Tempah on Instagram asking “what it would take” to get him to visit his home town, and the artist replied saying “I’ll do you a deal brother”, adding that he would pay a “long awaited visit” in return for 5,000 pre-saves of the album The Night’s Not Dead.On his TikTok account, Johns said it would be “an iconic moment in British music history, bringingTinie Tempahto Scunthorpe”.The 2010 single, with the lyrics “I been Southampton but I’ve never been to Scunthorpe” spent 65 weeks in the charts, with two weeks at number one.Johns’s cardboard cutout – with a QR code link to pre-save the album – toured Scunthorpe, visiting Scunthorpe United’s ground, John Leggott sixth form college, and going on a night out on the town, drumming up pre-saves along the way.In a video posted to social media, the London-based artist, whose work is a mix of rap, hip-hop and grime, said he would be holding up his end of the bargain and would be heading to Lincolnshire title: Joni Mitchell becomes US citizen: ‘A journey that began 62 years ago’ | Joni Mitchell | The Guardian
description: Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to Instagram
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to Instagram
Content: Joni Mitchell at her US citizenship ceremony.Photograph: InstagramView image in fullscreenJoni Mitchell at her US citizenship ceremony.Photograph: InstagramJoni MitchellJoni Mitchell becomes US citizen: ‘A journey that began 62 years ago’Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to InstagramBen Beaumont-ThomasWed 14 Oct 2026 04.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, along with a photo of her next to an American flag, accompanied by the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.”It means that Mitchell can now vote in US elections, something that she had complained she wasn’t able to do.At a concert in 2024, Mitchell said: “Fuck Donald Trump, I love that song,” referring to the rap track by YG. She added: “I wish I could vote ... I’m a Canadian. I’m one of those lousy immigrants.”Mitchell was born in Fort Macleod, Alberta, in 1943, and eventually settled with her family in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. Her earliest gigs were at folk clubs there, followed by Calgary and Toronto, where she met US folk singer Chuck Mitchell. They married in 1965 and Mitchell moved to the US. The marriage didn’t last, ending two years later, but by that time Mitchell had established herself as a mellifluous, original voice on the vibrant US folk music circuit.View image in fullscreenFolk original … Joni Mitchell in 1968.Photograph: Jack Robinson/Getty ImagesShe released her debut album in 1968, and soon after, using the album’s royalties, moved to Los Angeles’ Laurel Canyon where she recorded her first gold-selling album, Ladies of the Canyon. She remained based in California and currently lives in Santa Barbara.Joni Mitchell: where to start in her back catalogueRead moreMitchell’s most recent studio album is Shine, from 2007. After that she spent a number of years out of the public eye, suffering a brain aneurysm in 2015 that required extensive recovery. But she returned to live performance in 2022 with an unannounced set at the Newport folk festival, and has since performed a number of all-star “Joni Jam” concerts.A biopic about her is being prepared by director Cameron Crowe, who began work on it in the early 2020s. Earlier this year, record executive Clive Davis announced at a party thatMeryl Streep would play Mitchellin the film.Explore more on these topicsJoni MitchellPop and rockFolk musicCanadaAmericasCelebritynewsShareReuse this content

title: VisionQuest review – Marvel’s latest TV show feels like it could have been made by a computer | Television | The Guardian
description: Paul Bettany stars in a WandaVision spinoff that’s a visually striking, genre-bending package – of fighting and tediously wordy dialogue. What an odd confection
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: Paul Bettany stars in a WandaVision spinoff that’s a visually striking, genre-bending package – of fighting and tediously wordy dialogue. What an odd confection
Content: Sparring partners … James Spader (left) as Ultron and Paul Bettany as The Vision in VisionQuest.Photograph: Marvel. All Rights ReservedView image in fullscreenSparring partners … James Spader (left) as Ultron and Paul Bettany as The Vision in VisionQuest.Photograph: Marvel. All Rights ReservedTV reviewTelevisionReviewVisionQuest review – Marvel’s latest TV show feels like it could have been made by a computerPaul Bettany stars in a WandaVision spinoff that’s a visually striking, genre-bending package – of fighting and tediously wordy dialogue. What an odd confectionRachel AroestiWed 14 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMartin Scorsese compared them to theme parks. Nicolas Cage likened them to WWE. The products of theMarvelCinematic Universe – 38 films, 18 television shows and counting – are not generally well regarded as works of art. This is understandable: they are derivative, corporate and also somewhat mechanical – not just in their CGI-heavy production or phased rollouts, but in their preoccupations, with robotics, technological combat, complex webs of association. This is not the cinema, per Scorsese, “of human beings trying to convey emotional, psychological experiences to another human being.”The MCU doesn’t just gravitate towards cliche in this area, it barely features actual humans at all. And yet – like a superhero searching for a special stone – you get the sense that Marvel will not rest until such profundity is within its grasp. Unlike rollercoasters or wrestling, the MCU can be quite intellectually demanding: why shouldn’t it be capable of illuminating truths about the human condition as well?VisionQuest, Marvel’s latest TV offering, seems to harbour such ambitions. It sees The Vision, a synthezoid, reckoning with the concept of selfhood: what does it mean to be humanesque? It’s a timely question, and VisionQuest is a visually striking, formally experimental and eclectically genre-bending package for it. Yet it is also a shouty, fighty blockbuster that retains everything – particularly the labyrinthine plotting – that has long made comic book fare such an artistic turn-off.View image in fullscreenSpader (left) as ‘evil-ish’ Ultron and Bettany as ‘nicely beta’ Vision.Photograph: MarvelFor a start, it is mired in lore. Scrolling through Disney+ a couple of weeks ago, I was warned that I needed to watch seven different films and TV shows to prepare for VisionQuest’s release. It’s a lot of homework (the dog ate mine), but there really is no point tuning in without having seen its direct prequel,WandaVision. That’s OK because the 2021 series – the MCU’s most creatively successful offering – is a bit of a masterpiece; a beautiful and thrilling psychological portrait of the Scarlet Witch, whose grief for her vanquished paramour Vision leads her to magically resurrect him via a chronologically evolving pastiche of American sitcoms.Inevitably, even WandaVision had to descend into standard superhero drivel at some point. VisionQuest is a spin-off with roots in such drivel, which involved Wanda’s Vision battling a reassembled version of his original body called The Vision (great name for a slick-fringed 1980s synthpop band). But then they made friends, and magical Vision planted his memories into his replacement, who duly fled.To, we discover, an Edinburgh pub, which Vision once frequented with Wanda. Desperate to connect with his forebear who he sees as more human, The Vision (Paul Bettany, doing a nicely beta English gent thing) now works at said boozer in his visually mortal form. But instead of going home at night, he slips into the walk-in fridge and reverts to his real robot self. And then we go inside his mind.Or whatever the AI equivalent of a mind is. Here it’s a houseshare with five other AIs, each given humanoid form and each with a specialism that helps The Vision, including social secretary Friday and defence expert E.D.I.T.H. We also have a wildly bearded James Spader as Ultron, Vision’s evil-ish maker who previously attempted to wipe out humanity.WandaVision review – Marvel’s sitcom superheroes are a retro joyRead moreThis is the basic setup. Now for the story. A bounty hunter is after The Vision (in a laughably unlikely twist, his hacker-style assistant is played by Diane Morgan) and, in order to lure him into his clutches, tracks down a teenager called Thomas who claims to be possessed by the spirit of one of Wanda and Vision’s magical twins. The Vision and Thomas meet and flee together, meaningful father-son bond still pending.That’s about one quarter of the plot. VisionQuest goes on to merge the fallout from WandaVision with an Ultron deep dive and an entirely different narrative about another robot. A huge amount of exposition is involved, and the AI-on-AI dialogue is tediously wordy (Ultron could get permanent residency in Pseuds Corner; at one point he marvels at “the unalgorithmic alacrity with which [humans] wobble”). Technically, that’s to the script’s credit – this is essentially a show about computer systems in conversation – but it still feels off-puttingly uncanny, like something AI really could manifest in the near future. The fusion of indie road trip movie, Matrix-like thriller, murder mystery and irreverent superhero dramedy, meanwhile, also feels like a computer’s idea of interesting art.VisionQuest is sometimes entertaining and always clever, yet if it does have anything to say about human nature, it is drowned out by dizzying plot particulars and the need for a big brawl every episode. Yet what’s really missing is actual jeopardy: it turns out to be quite difficult to emotionally invest in lines of code that exist in the “head” of an android. This isn’t dumb, mindless entertainment, but VisionQuest is still closer to the Big Dipper than GoodFellas.VisionQuest is on Disney+ nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewMarvelreviewsShareReuse this content

Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: The Emmy-nominated Fellow Travelers follows the clandestine relationship between Hawkins Fuller and Tim Laughlin in 50s’ Washington. Plus: Louis Theroux on Portrait Artist of the Year. Here’s what to watch tonight
Content: Matt Bomer as Hawk and Jonathan Bailey as Tim in Fellow Travelers.Photograph: Ben Mark Holzberg/SHOWTIMEView image in fullscreenMatt Bomer as Hawk and Jonathan Bailey as Tim in Fellow Travelers.Photograph: Ben Mark Holzberg/SHOWTIMETV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: an Emmy-nominated US period drama finally lands on UK TVFellow Travelers follows the clandestine relationship between Hawkins Fuller and Tim Laughlin in 50s’ Washington. Plus: Louis Theroux on Portrait Artist of the Year. Here’s what to watch tonightHollie Richardson,Hannah J Davies,Jack SealeandAli CatterallWed 14 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFellow Travelers10pm, Channel 4From the makers ofHomeland, this suave, weighty, Emmy-nominated period drama finally lands on UK telly. It is both a romance and a thriller, following Hawk (Matt Bomer) and Tim (Jonathan Bailey) who meet in Washington DC during the height of McCarthyism, and develop a sexual relationship across the next three decades.Hollie RichardsonThe Repair Shop: Beyond the Barn8pm, BBC OneMore emotional tales from inside the workshop and across the UK. Will a record player with a connection to three continents be brought back to life? And is there any hope for a 1950s Rolleiflex camera that once snapped portraits of the royals, but is now in need of a highly delicate restoration?Hannah J DaviesPortrait Artist of the Year 20268pm, Sky ArtsView image in fullscreenLouis Theroux and Stephen Mangan take a closer look at an artist’s painting.Photograph: Chris Lobina/Chris Lobina / SkyLouis Theroux is the first brave celebrity to sit for his portrait in this week’s competition. “If you do splotches, that will be fine,” he assures them.
