title: The best books to read in October: new paperbacks from Zadie Smith, Thomas Pynchon and Francis Spufford | Books | The Guardian
description: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some brilliant new paperbacks, from a time-travelling fantasy novel to an eclectic essay collection
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some brilliant new paperbacks, from a time-travelling fantasy novel to an eclectic essay collection
Content: View image in fullscreenThis month's best paperbacksBooksThe best books to read in October: new paperbacks from Zadie Smith, Thomas Pynchon and Francis SpuffordLooking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some brilliant new paperbacks, from a time-travelling fantasy novel to an eclectic essay collectionWed 14 Oct 2026 10.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTShareFictionFictionShadow TicketThomas PynchonView image in fullscreenEverything is connected in Shadow Ticket, Thomas Pynchon’s fleet-footed noir fiction about a lindy-hopping detective in prohibition-era Wisconsin. The homemade bomb connects to the runaway cheese heiress, the cheese heiress to the federal agents, and the feds to the pro‑Nazi leagues at the bowling lanes outside town. Early-30s Milwaukee, in turn, is connected to powder-keg central Europe, where paramilitary groups have pitched camp on the Hungaro-Croatian border and guest speakers wax lyrical about “our immense fascist future”. Most likely it connects to the current moment as well, albeit wryly and slyly, with a nonchalant swing. That’s the implied final move of this merry dance of a book: the point where the past links its hands with the present.Shadow Ticket is a Pynchon novel – the 88-year-old’s first in 12 years; his ninth overall – and so it naturally connects to the man’s back catalogue, too, and its abiding fascination with conspiracy, chaos and the churn of American pop culture. Specifically it relates back to his two previous works –Inherent ViceandBleeding Edge– in that the story comes tailored as a dime-store whodunnit, complete with red herrings, plot twists and reams of hard-boiled dialogue. But classifications, like people, are never entirely to be trusted. Pynchon inhabits the genre like a hermit crab inside a mollusc shell, periodically peeking out from the gloom to remind us that he’s there.Xan Brooks£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionNonesuchFrancis SpuffordView image in fullscreenSpufford’s fourth work of fiction in a genre-spanning oeuvre, Nonesuch is a historical fantasy set during the second world war, every paragraph of which is packed with authorial zest. The novel opens in London, August 1939: war has been declared, but hasn’t yet made its reality felt in the city’s streets, and Iris Hawkins, an ambitious office clerk, makes her way through the sun-baked West End in a slinky dress. One half of a disastrous date later, she’s being whisked away to a DIY surrealist film club in bohemian Bloomsbury – not her scene at all – and two extremely fateful introductions: the first to Geoffrey Hale, a sweetly apprehensive BBC television engineer; and the second to the object of Geoffrey’s guileless infatuation, one Lady Lalage Cunningham, an icy aristocratic beauty with amazing hair and worrisome political sympathies. Cue chaos. Nonesuch follows the bolshy Iris from her seedy summer’s night through a regrettable Hampstead hook-up, and, eventually, neck-deep into a time-travelling plot by “magical fascist lunatics” to assassinate Winston Churchill. The novel is a pleasing pasticcio of romance, occultism, non-Euclidean geometry and airborne adventure across the blitz-stricken rooftops of London. It is difficult to imagine it would hold together quite so well in other hands than Spufford’s.AK Blakemore£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionBeasts of the SeaIida TurpeinenView image in fullscreenIn November 1741 Georg Wilhelm Steller, “theologian, naturalist, and curious man”, was shipwrecked on an island between Alaska and Russia. There he found, floating in the shallow waters, a vast sirenian,Hydrodamalis gigas,nine feet long and soon to be known as Steller’s sea cow. Having made it through the winter, largely by eating the sea cows, the following August Steller and the remaining survivors of the Great Northern Expedition left the island. Within 30 years, Steller’s sea cow was hunted to extinction.Having described these events, Finnish author Iida Turpeinen’s debut novel goes on to describe the lives of other historical figures, each of whom are touched in some way by the sea cow, now reduced to bones. There is Hampus Furuhjelm, governor of Alaska, in search of a complete skeleton, and his sister Constance, who finds peace and intellectual autonomy among her taxidermy collection. Later, there’s Hilda Olson, a scientific illustrator, and John Grönvall, specialist in the reconstruction of birds’ eggs, who is tasked with preparing a sea cow’s relics for exhibition.Turpeinen writes in a flowing present tense, moving seamlessly from one character to another, drawing us gently but firmly onwards. Emotional detail is astutely rendered. The result is a book that is almost hypnotically readable; it’s been much garlanded in Finland and it’s easy to see why.Jessie Greengrass£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionOther People’s FunHarriet LaneView image in fullscreenRuth, the narrator of Harriet Lane’s third novel, Other People’s Fun, is corroded by envy. Alone, her marriage over, her daughter grown and her freelance work as dull as it is low paid, she is that most dangerous of characters: an overlooked middle-aged woman with nothing to lose. When she bumps into beautiful, stupid and entitled Sookie at a school reunion, she reconnects with her teenage self “and all her violent desires”. Having flown under the radar as a pupil, noticed by Sookie only because she lent her her essays, she has perfect recall of her own petty humiliations, now amplified by the fact that she can stalk her contemporaries’ “best lives” on social media, while almost none of them remember her.The best comedy is sharpened by pain, and what Lane has pinpointed in her flint-sharp novel is something that has a highly modern resonance as the world of the haves and have-nots becomes increasingly polarised and toxic. When Ruth gets her revenge, it is as nasty as it is total. You will, I fear, howl with satisfaction.Amanda Craig£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionAbsenceIssa QuincyView image in fullscreenIn Quincy’s novel, the narrator is charmed by a poem first read to him as a child by his mother, which then follows him through his life. He’s stirred by memories and emotions as he is confronted by letters and photographs, phantoms and secrets, all of which make up a life that has been affected by generations of profound familial tragedy. Quincy’s prose is deftly lyrical and imaginative; I’ve had the pleasure of hearing him read from Absence at a literary salon in London and it was entrancing. He observes the fragility of memory, and what remains after our encounters, however fleeting, with people, say a schoolteacher or an estranged aunt; you might think of him as a counterpart to the novelists Rachel Cusk and Teju Cole.Jason OkundayeAbsenceis published by GrantaShort storiesShort storiesThe Land of Sweet ForeverHarper LeeView image in fullscreenThe Land of Sweet Forever is a collection of Lee’s unpublished short stories and previously uncollected essays. However, like most such books, it has little to offer to those who aren’t diehard fans.The short stories, written in Lee’s youth, are all badly underdeveloped. Most fail to work even as vignettes. One centres on trying to find a place to unload a truck in Manhattan; another on a temporary change to the way the doxology is sung in a Methodist church. A slender piece about the quirks of New York movie audiences is categorised as a story, but feels more like a newspaper sketch.The young Lee seems to have little sense of what a story is.On the positive side, there is already wit and charisma in the voice. One narrator, returning to her southern home town, recognises “a tall young man whose face belonged to the Wade family, but whose body showed extensive Talbert influence. He was Talbert Wade, of course.” This may be slight, but it’s elegantly done. There are also hints of iconoclastic anger struggling to get out, especially in The Water Tower, where a 12-year-old Mississippi girl erroneously thinks she is pregnant. Understanding that being an unwed mother would wreck the lives of her whole family, she decides the only way to save them is to destroy her shameful body.If we regard this book as literature, it is an unqualified failure. But it’s more properly seen – and will surely be read – for the light it sheds on Lee’s life. As such, it’s obliquely fascinating, largely because it radiates repression. Often there’s a sense that we’re seeing the side ofHarper Leethat wasn’t exceptional, but representative of a generation of women who were mostly muzzled.Lee writes in The Cat’s Meow (perhaps the strongest story in the collection): “I suppose a lot of people like me have mastered the first lesson of living at home these days: if you don’t agree with what you hear, place your tongue between your teeth and bite hard.” We feel those painfully gritted teeth on every page of this book. In a time of rising censorship, it’s salutary to be reminded that an author as important as Harper Lee came so close to being entirely silenced.Sandra Newman£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopEssaysEssaysDead and AliveZadie SmithView image in fullscreenDead and Alive bundles various odds and ends from the past nine years: speeches, opinion pieces, criticism and eulogies for departed literary heroes – Philip Roth, Martin Amis, Hilary Mantel.In Some Notes on Mediated Time – one of three completely new essays in the collection – Smith recalls how the “dreamy, slo-mo world” of her 1980s childhood gave way, within a generation, to the “anxious, permanent now” of social media. If you lived through that transition, you don’t have to be very old to feel ancient. When this estrangement is compounded by the ordinary anxieties of ageing, cultural commentary becomes inflected with self-pity. Smith’s identification with the protagonist ofTodd Field’s Tár, a once revered conductor who finds herself shunned by the younger cohort, takes on existential proportions: “Our backs hurt, the kids don’t like Bach any more – and the seas are rising!”Smith steers a sensible middle course on the vexed debate around “cultural appropriation” in fiction. There is more to people than their identity – “we can, sometimes, forget the mystery that lies at the heart of all selfhood”. The point is well made in a thoughtful piece on James Baldwin and the craft of writing, originally a lecture delivered to creative writing students over Zoom during the pandemic. Smith reminds her students that the essence of Baldwin’s brilliance was his ability to process politics through personal experience: he “submitted to his consciousness first and then re-examined what that might mean for his conscience”. This is sound advice, and Smith’s positions on the politics of creativity are beyond reproach, albeit commonsensical – amounting, essentially, to a caution against overcorrection and incuriosity.When it comes to actual politics, she is less assured. Her New Yorker op-ed on the war in Gaza, published in May 2024, was widely interpreted as unhelpfully equivocal, and seemed to conflate anti-war protesters with antisemites. She has since added her signature toan open letter acknowledging Israel’s actions as genocidal. The New Yorker piece, reprinted here with a new preamble hailing the protesters as “heroic”, is an intriguing artefact: the prose is mealy mouthed, heavy on the passive voice – all the more conspicuous since Smith’s writing is normally so clear and crisp.Houman Barekat£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopMemoirMemoirFly, Wild SwansJung ChangView image in fullscreenRemarkable success notoriously brings its own problems. Wild Swans, first published in 1991 and written by Jung Chang with the help of her husband, Irish-born historian and writer Jon Halliday, had a global impact few authors dare to dream of. It told the story of three generations of women in 20th-century China – Chang’s grandmother, her mother and herself – and became one of the most popular nonfiction books in history, selling more than13m copies in 37 languagesand collecting a fistful of awards and commendations. For any author, following that would be a challenge. Now, Fly, Wild Swans returns to the story, picking it up after Chang’s own departure from China in 1978, and revisiting episodes from the earlier work with added detail.Few can match Chang’s ability to bring Chinese history and politics to life through deeply felt personal narrative, and few have shaped western understanding of China as broadly. Nearly 35 years on from the book that made her name, this story of suffering and success has the air of a closing chapter, a reckoning with both her achievements and the cost of the path she chose.Isabel Hilton£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopMemoirWingsPaul McCartneyView image in fullscreenAfter splitting up, The Beatles faced an unprecedented challenge: how to be an ex-Beatle? McCartney yearned to play before audiences again, which he hadn’t since the Beatles stopped touring in 1966. But he couldn’t face doing it solo, the spotlight trained on him alone. So he asked Linda to help him put together a new group. This authorised, illustrated oral history, edited by cultural historian Ted Widmer, tells the story ofone of the most successful bands of the 1970s – and one of the strangest.It’s based on interviews (given for a new documentary on the band) with McCartney and former band members, as well as archive material. Widmer does an expert job of stitching this into a compelling narrative that includes cultural context – like what else was in the charts at the time – and plenty of photographs, many previously unseen. The result is a portal into a more eccentric age of pop, a fable about the tension between celebrity and creativity, and a story with elements of Spinal Tap and Wacky Races.Ian Leslie£19.80 (RRP £22) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

title: The Steps by Sylvester Stallone review – the inside story of Rocky | Autobiography and memoir | The Guardian
description: The star takes us back to 70s New York to recount his breakthrough, and it’s a great yarn – but it’s laced with anger
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: The star takes us back to 70s New York to recount his breakthrough, and it’s a great yarn – but it’s laced with anger
Content: Sylvester Stalone on the set of Rocky II.Photograph: Sunset Boulevard/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSylvester Stalone on the set of Rocky II.Photograph: Sunset Boulevard/Corbis/Getty ImagesBook of the dayAutobiography and memoirReviewThe Steps by Sylvester Stallone review – the inside story of RockyThe star takes us back to 70s New York to recount his breakthrough, and it’s a great yarn – but it’s laced with angerXan BrooksWed 14 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Philadelphia Museum of Art contains a 14th-century Buddhist temple, a one-acre sculpture garden and works by Picasso, Renoir and Van Gogh. Its most famous attraction, however, is a flight of stone steps that draws several million tourists every year. These are the so-called “Rocky Steps”, immortalised bySylvester Stallonein his 1976 movie about an underdog boxer who needs to build up his strength. The climb is a lung-busting challenge, but if unremarkable Rocky can sprint all the way to the top, he gives hope and encouragement to everyone down below.It’s not just the fans who relate to Rocky Balboa. So too does Stallone, whose entertaining rags-to-riches memoir paints the creator and his creation as all but indivisible, each an extension of the other. Stallone was flat broke and beaten down when he wrote his film about “the forgotten man”, the blue-collar schlub with a good heart and firm chin. Everyone knows that Rocky is being set up as a fall guy. He can’t possibly defeat Apollo Creed, the dazzling, charismatic, undefeated heavyweight champion of the world. Except that Rocky doesn’t care, he only wants to be seen, and in scripting an unlikely redemptive arc for his hero, Stallone wound up transforming his own fortunes as well.The Steps talks us through how he did it – or how he likes to tell people he did it – and how we might go about doing something similar in our own lives. Believe in yourself, he advises. Roll with the punches. Never throw in the towel. His memoir reads like a breakneck self-help manual in which the author is variously cast as guide, guru and crash-test dummy. Stallone – a keen student of narrative structure – knows that failure packs more dramatic punch than success, and shrewdly wraps up his account just as his film storms the Oscars. The man loses every round but the last, which is of course all that matters.double quotation markHe hates the snobs who write him off and the suits who feed him a diet of scrapsThe messaging can be cheesy and several of the stories feel fishy, but he spins a good yarn, plonking himself centre stage. He’s the raw, gauche outsider in Midnight Cowboy-era New York, earning a crust as an usher and cleaning cages at the zoo. He’s a striving Martin Eden in mid-70s California, trying and failing to get his scripts off the ground. Stallone writes in an authoritative conversational style, as though he’s leaning in close and draping his arm around your shoulder. He says, “I don’t know if you know anything about dogs,” and, “You might be asking, why doesn’t he go to a laundromat,” and, “If you’ve never been in a lion’s cage, let me tell you, it isverypungent,” and the effect is charming, companionable and ever so slightly oppressive.There is no side to Rocky – what you see is what you get. His creator, by contrast, feels more guarded and controlled. He presents himself as a sweet innocent – monastic and almost sexless – but there is an anger to his memories that burns on every page. He hates the snobs who write him off and the suits who feed him a diet of scraps. Francis Ford Coppola makes him wait several hours to audition; Richard Gere drips chicken grease on his trousers. Most of all he hates his mum and dad, who never wanted him to begin with and have left him with a desperate, mechanistic hunger to succeed. “If they’d been sweet and loving, like parents you see in a TV show, would I even be here?” he asks. They broke him and made him: it’s a complicated relationship.In a fair and just world, Stallone might have sold his labour-of-love screenplay about the life of Edgar Allan Poe. But now he’s down to his last $80 and his first child’s on the way and so he writes the first draft of Rocky in three days flat, pouring out a decade’s worth of humiliations and frustrations. Producers offer him a fortune to hand over the script, but he sticks to his guns and insists on playing the lead. The suits are in uproar; his agent’s having kittens. Except that our hero is proved right, his brinkmanship paying dividends. Rocky – a rousing old-school melodrama with a little 70s grit in its gloves – is cobbled together for a measly $900,000. It goes on to earn $225m.How true is this laundry list of hard knocks and life lessons? True enough. Stallone’s early struggles are well documented and largely verified. As for his origin tale about the making of Rocky, some see it as a foundational myth, heavily salted and spun. “The press feeds on the underdog story,” Gabe Sumner, United Artists’ former marketing boss, said back in 2006. Stallone’s claim that he faced down the studio, Sumner added, was “horseshit”, part of a “tremendous marketing campaign” in the run-up to the Oscars.The Steps asks us to accept the author as a real-world Rocky, the lowly everyman who hauled his way to the summit. That’s not a lie; it’s a life story to be proud of. But he is also Apollo Creed, the wily showboater and self-promoter, who knows that a David and Goliath story is good for business and that the best American heroes are self-directed, self-made and still a little rough around the edges.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Winter of the Crow review – Lesley Manville magnificently on edge in intriguing cold war thriller | Movies | The Guardian
description: Manville’s academic psychologist finds herself trapped in a tower block wasteland in 1980s Warsaw. Bizarre and surreal details add to the sinister vibe
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Manville’s academic psychologist finds herself trapped in a tower block wasteland in 1980s Warsaw. Bizarre and surreal details add to the sinister vibe
Content: No way out? … Lesley Manville as Professor Andrews in Winter of the Crow.Photograph: Danny James/Courtesy of Signature EntertainmentView image in fullscreenNo way out? … Lesley Manville as Professor Andrews in Winter of the Crow.Photograph: Danny James/Courtesy of Signature EntertainmentMoviesReviewWinter of the Crow review – Lesley Manville magnificently on edge in intriguing cold war thrillerManville’s academic psychologist finds herself trapped in a tower block wasteland in 1980s Warsaw. Bizarre and surreal details add to the sinister vibePeter BradshawWed 14 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePart cold war thriller, part Kafkaesque reverie, this movie takes us back to the sinister drear of Poland in 1981, when General Jaruzelski has just introduced martial law in reaction to the dangerous new mood of freedom occasioned by the Solidarity trade unions. The director is Kasia Adamik, daughter of The Green Border’s Agnieszka Holland; the film is adapted from a story byOlga Tokarczuk, called Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw.Lesley Manville plays Professor Andrews, an academic clinical psychologist (like Tokarczuk) from Britain with testy, peremptory mannerisms; her indulgence is a fondness for taking Polaroid photos. She has attained a certain level of celebrity for a book on dreams, despite claiming that she never dreams herself. Andrews has been invited to give a lecture in Warsaw, during which she begins to outline views on mental illness not unlike those of Laing or Foucault; but her speech is chaotically disrupted by students shouting that Poland itself is an oppressive asylum.The chief protester’s sister Alina (Zofia Wichlacz) happens to be the postgrad student tasked with showing Professor Andrews around, but from the very first, there is confusion. Andrews loses her bag, then has to give her passport to Alina so she can go back to the airport and look for it; she can’t go to a hotel and must stay at a flat in a sketchy area, belonging to relatives of Alina. And when she awakens the next morning, Andrews sees a tank in the wretched and surreally deserted tower block wasteland. The clampdown has begun, murderous secret police are everywhere and she has no passport. Perhaps Andrews had better get used to staying inPolandfor the foreseeable future – or maybe for ever.It is an intriguing and disquieting movie, though one whose storytelling impulse slows a little, and perhaps the film could have benefited from closer editing – although this might have meant losing some of the bizarre and surreal details, like the live carp that people queue up to buy for food and keep in the bath.Winter of the Crow is in UK cinemas from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsThrillersPolandOlga TokarczukLesley ManvillereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mistura review – ice queen brings Peruvian culinary drama to a gentle simmer | Movies | The Guardian
description: Bárbara Mori stars in tepid tale of a high-society wife who opens a restaurant in her home after her husband leaves her
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Bárbara Mori stars in tepid tale of a high-society wife who opens a restaurant in her home after her husband leaves her
Content: Chanelling Jackie Onassis … Bárbara Mori (Norma) in Mistura.Photograph: Seine PicturesView image in fullscreenChanelling Jackie Onassis … Bárbara Mori (Norma) in Mistura.Photograph: Seine PicturesMoviesReviewMistura review – ice queen brings Peruvian culinary drama to a gentle simmerBárbara Mori stars in tepid tale of a high-society wife who opens a restaurant in her home after her husband leaves herCath ClarkeWed 14 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 06.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat you expect from a film about a fancy high-end restaurant is a certain amount of heat: the roiling intensity of staff pushed to their absolute limits in the pursuit of gastronomic perfection. But this 1960s-set Peruvian drama instead maintains a gentle simmer, sedate and elegant. Perhaps it’s too elegant given the circumstances of its chef-proprietor, a high-society trophy wife with no catering experience who makes a high-stakes gamble on opening a successful restaurant.Bárbara Mori is Norma, a glacial beauty who cultivates a kind of Jackie Onassis chic: huge sunglasses, massive blow-dry, makeup thickly applied like armour. One night, Norma’s husband humiliatingly leaves her for a beauty queen. You’d be sympathetic if Norma wasn’t so foul to the staff, lashing out at housekeeper Rosa (Hermelinda Luján) and chauffeur Oscar (Cesar Ballumbrosio). It’s Oscar (who is a bit in love with Norma) who suggests she opens a restaurant in the house to pay the mortgage. Norma’s father was the French ambassador to Peru, and she has picked up his passion for gastronomy. Although the script is a bit inconsistent on this, since Oscar also says he’s never seen her so much as light the oven.The restaurant has four months to succeed before the bank repossesses the house. And still, there’s no sense of Norma, or the film, breaking into a sweat. She hires a Japanese Peruvian sous-chef in the kitchen; Oscar is front of house. But the early reviews are tepid, describing the French cuisine as a bit trad, and the restaurant is half empty. There are lessons to come about how teamwork makes the dream work, and embracing Peru’s cultural diversity. The trouble is that, before that, Norma is such an insufferable snob; it’s a bit too long to hold your nose and stick with her.Mistura is in UK and Irish cinemas from 16 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsRestaurantsPeruFoodAmericasreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned review – Brontë horror do-over is part Dracula, part Jeeves and Wooster | Movies | The Guardian
description: Emily Brontë’s classic is reimagined with extra stranglings, slashings and pitchfork impalings but plays it straight
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Emily Brontë’s classic is reimagined with extra stranglings, slashings and pitchfork impalings but plays it straight
Content: Grisly fate … Ross Townsend-Green as Mr Lockwood in Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned.Photograph: Courtesy of EMRJ EntertainmentView image in fullscreenGrisly fate … Ross Townsend-Green as Mr Lockwood in Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned.Photograph: Courtesy of EMRJ EntertainmentMoviesReviewWuthering Heights: The House of the Damned review – Brontë horror do-over is part Dracula, part Jeeves and WoosterEmily Brontë’s classic is reimagined with extra stranglings, slashings and pitchfork impalings but plays it straightPhil HoadWed 14 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 04.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhere pornography once trod, horror has now become the genre that infiltrates and apes all others. With a host of out-of-copyright cartoon characters recently grave-robbed for not-so-fresh IP, now classic literature is apparently fair game for a gruesome glow-up, in this case, Emily Brontë’s regular GCSE-botherer. But Becca Hirani’s laboured reworking makes the book’s gothic subtext crashingly, jugular-spurtingly textual.As in the novel, wide-eyed Mr Lockwood (Ross Townsend-Green) pays a courtesy call to his brooding landlord Heathcliff (Sky Cheema) at Wuthering Heights. But this time, his sojourn is more like Jonathan Harker’s at Dracula’s castle; everywhere he turns, the shrouded phantom of Heathcliff’s beloved Catherine Earnshaw (Elle O’Hara) is lurking, and she leaves an extra dollop of gore on the windowsill in her famous nocturnal apparition. The tetchy host doesn’t do much to put Lockwood at ease – even before he’s trapped in the house by a bubo-inflicting malady. Between the hallucinations, the surly servants, and the weird absence of Heathcliff’s rumoured son Linton, he begins freaking out that it’s a different kind of moors story he’s stumbled into.Hirani puts undeniable effort in getting her plot points to line up with Brontë’s – even if most of the characters, including poor old Lockwood’s horse, meet a much grislier fate. Rationed out in snippets of Catherine’s diary, the confidences of housekeeper Nelly (Nicola Wright) and more random supernatural flashbacks involving Lockwood, the manor’s backstory is rather garbled, though with the OTT hook of Heathcliff as an 18th-century Yorkshire Ripper. Rather than amping up the camp, as the likes of Kate Bush and Emerald Fennell did in their takes on the novel, Hirani plays it straight and dour, mystifyingly so, given the extra stranglings, slashings and pitchfork-impalings she’s chucked in.At the same time, diffident acting undermines the film’s claim as pure slasher fare: Townsend-Green’s jumpy turn feels as if he has strayed out of Jeeves and Wooster, while, despite the Rasputin looks, windy-voiced Cheema is too loose to convince as Byronic bad boy. For much of the runtime, we’re left with too little that makes his conversion to homicidal mania credible, until the last-minute lowdown on his Hellraiser-like scheme for his ward, Cathy (Anna Coupé). Reanimating the corpse of Brontë in this rickety way, this update not only feels pointless, but short on self-awareness or fun.Wuthering Heights: The House of the Damned is on digital platforms from 19 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsEmily BrontëreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Mary Wallopers review – legs and pints go flying to the sound of rowdy folk ragers | Music | The Guardian
description: Irish six-piece embark on their biggest tour yet, turning grisly old stories into a knees-up with politically astute, spit-and-sawdust energy
Author: Katie Hawthorne
Headline: Irish six-piece embark on their biggest tour yet, turning grisly old stories into a knees-up with politically astute, spit-and-sawdust energy
Content: Gets the room bouncing … Charles Hendy of the Mary Wallopers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGets the room bouncing … Charles Hendy of the Mary Wallopers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianMusicReviewThe Mary Wallopers review – legs and pints go flying to the sound of rowdy folk ragersCorn Exchange, EdinburghIrish six-piece embark on their biggest tour yet, turning grisly old stories into a knees-up with politically astute, spit-and-sawdust energyKatie HawthorneWed 14 Oct 2026 06.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s not often you see crowd surfing during folk songs, let alone songs about murderers-for-hire who targeted priests in the early 1700s. But so it is at a Mary Wallopers show, the Irish trad group with a passionate following for their rowdy folk ragers.Legs and pints go flying as the six-piece, playing banjo and tin whistle, set about Seán na Sagart, a new track which turns a grisly old story into a knees-up. By its breathless conclusion, the hitman is dead and his victims and clients alike get it in the neck from the band. Singer Charles Hendy grins, savouring the punchline: “You can’t trust the clergy with their holy little bits / And ya won’t be thanked by any god for workin’ with the Brits.”View image in fullscreenIn rude health … the Mary Wallopers.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe Dundalk band are kicking off their biggest tour yet, in honour of third album Paddywhackery – a record that finds the group in rude health and confronting criticism that they are “too Irish, or whatever”, according to founding members Charles and Andrew Hendy.The new material is often furiously fast, with politics and humour both sharply deployed. Frenzied single The Big Mixer has the room bouncing to cutting lyrics about greasing the machinery of capitalism, while the hedonistic Kit Kat Club sounds like a hangover before the night’s even over, with sour vocal harmonies and Catriona Gribben’s wonderful, wheezing accordion.View image in fullscreenCatriona Gribben on accordion.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBut the band can also hold the room in silence. “Someone put a border in Ireland. It’s a pain in the hole,” Andrew deadpans, before a sparse, serious version of folk tune Smuggling the Tin, sung over a buzzing drone from Finnian O’Connor’s uilleann pipes. Original song Landlord’s Demise is just as transfixing; a slow, strange march performed by Andrew while drumming the bodhrán, as the crowd claps and stamps. “Any landlords here tonight?” Charles shouts, scanning the room. “Fuckin’… good!”Closing on Frost Is All Over, a roughly 300-year-old jig, they lend the skipping tune an almost clubby feel: strobes firing, hands in the air. The Wallopers make an urgent case for folk’s continued relevance with their spiky, spit-and-sawdust takes on tradition – whether that tradition likes it or not.The Mary Wallopers play O2 City Hall, Newcastle upon Tyne, 14 October; then touring UK and Ireland to 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicFolk musicPop and rocklive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Appl/Baillieu: Lines of Life review – gifted baritone blends Kurtág and Schubert  | Classical music | The Guardian
description: A perfect example of the Oxford International Song festival’s creative programming, Benjamin Appl’s unforced but focused recital was full of profoundly beautiful music
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: A perfect example of the Oxford International Song festival’s creative programming, Benjamin Appl’s unforced but focused recital was full of profoundly beautiful music
Content: Poetic instincts … baritone Benjamin Appl and  pianist James Baillieu performing at the Holywell Music Room in Oxford.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPoetic instincts … baritone Benjamin Appl and  pianist James Baillieu performing at the Holywell Music Room in Oxford.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianClassical musicReviewAppl/Baillieu: Lines of Life review – gifted baritone blends Kurtág and SchubertHolywell Music Room, OxfordA perfect example of the Oxford International Song festival’s creative programming, Benjamin Appl’s unforced but focused recital was full of profoundly beautiful musicClive PagetWed 14 Oct 2026 05.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 05.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver 25 years, the Oxford International Song festival has adopted a creative approach to programming. Benjamin Appl’s pairing of Schubert lieder with spiny miniatures by György Kurtág was a perfect example. Your Schubert crowd isn’t necessarily yourKurtágcrew, and yet the 280-year-old Holywell Music Room was packed to the rafters.Ellen Mawhinney and Daniel Silcock, one of the festival’s Young Artist duos, kicked things off with an aquatic-themed recital that showed off Mawhinney’s powerful soprano and Silcock’s poetic instincts at the piano. From the inspiriting Scottish ballad Kishmul’s Galley to Hamilton Harty’s impassioned Sea Wrack, their smartly curated 15 minutes paved the way for Appl and James Baillieu’s equally satisfying programme, Lines of Life.TheGerman British baritoneis a gifted communicator, binding together songs that could easily have rubbed each other the wrong way. It helps that he has worked intensively with Kurtág. As he explained from the stage, sometimes he’d spend an entire morning on the first line of a song before returning after lunch ready to work on line two, only to have the exacting composer say, “Well, shall we start from the beginning?” His unforced delivery of these concentrated musical nuggets, many of them unaccompanied, was intently focused.View image in fullscreenA gifted communicator … Appl.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The GuardianThe Six Hölderlin-Gesänge set gnomic poetry that is hard enough to grasp before the composer ups the ante with notes and rhythm. Appl took on board their frenetic gasps and growls, and yet at other times, Kurtág’s melismatic writing came across as profoundly beautiful.The Schubert selection was bound together by common themes of love, longing and loss. The nihilistic Totengräbers Heimweh brought out a brittle, sardonic quality that found echoes in the melancholy Schäfers Klagelied and the otherwise jaunty Die Taubenpost.There was vocal beauty too, in Viola for example, one of Schubert’s loveliest songsabout a jilted violetthat in the wrong hands could have turned saccharine. Baillieu’s dramatically astute accompaniment drove the narrative here as it did throughout. Just occasionally, when pulling back to soften the tone, Appl’s voice didn’t quite go where he wanted it to, but such moments were few and far between in a rewarding musical journey that segued seamlessly from start to finish.Oxford International Song festivalcontinues until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicMusic festivalsFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era | Games | The Guardian
description: The kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changer
Content: Evolutionary Link … The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenEvolutionary Link … The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2.Photograph: NintendoGamesThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K eraThe kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changerMatthew CastleWed 14 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 14 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen beloved art is revisited and revised, a familiar cry is often heard: “You’re ruining my childhood!” But with Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time, there are also livelihoods at risk: specifically, the man running the shooting gallery in Castle Town. In the original 1998 version of the game, he’d rip off players as they funnelled rupees and fudged the then still novel analogue-stick aiming. But in 2026 we have more responsive frame rates and a motion-controlled slingshot that allows precision adjustments. His targets tumble on the first go, and with them his entire business model. Even in Hyrule, the death of the high street seems inevitable.Bad news for him but great news for Link, a child of the forest who, as in 1998, steps into a vast fantasy kingdom to vanquish a great evil, but now does so with a number of improvements. The boy can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies to zip across grassy plains. He has a manual jump, free-rotating camera, a scrolling inventory bar that replaces menu screen faff and, crucially, a fatter wallet for holding all those gems he fleeces from struggling shooting gallery owners. Yes, we are being asked to applaud features that have been the norm for decades elsewhere, but it’s undeniably striking to enter familiar territory with a hero who feels this different under the thumbs.View image in fullscreenLink can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies.Photograph: NintendoThe dilemma facing any remake, let alone of a game recognised as a genre-defining classic, is how closely you hew to the past. As withthis year’s Star Fox revamp, Ocarina of Time finds Nintendo in a celebratory mode. It’s a polished victory lap for a game with little to prove. For newcomers it means seeing what the fuss is about without having to scrutinise the N64 original on unflattering flatscreen TVs. I doubt Hyrule Field – once a byword for video-game freedom – will ever conjure the awe it did in 1998, but seeing the sun catch in puddles and grass growing from the floor helps mask what is an obviously artificial pen, compared toBreath of the Wild’s sprawling continent.For some returning fans, the more controlled shape is precisely the appeal. After the “make your own adventure” ethos of Switch’s open-world Zeldas, there is comfort in slipping into traditional dungeons, where every room has a characterful beast to chop up or a mechanism to unpick with a growing kitbag of tools. My great fear was that some of the puzzles are simply too iconic to be forgotten and solved again. Yet here I am, sweatily hunting ghosts around the Forest Temple, and surreptitiously peering at my neighbour’s demo pod to remind myself that, yes, you have to … [redacted for your benefit]. Given that, in 1998, these were many designers’ first attempts at a 3D level, it is astonishing how fiendish they are and how you’re expected to hold complex architecture in your head to get the run of them.Also worth assigning headspace for: the newly orchestrated soundtrack. Melodies that fought through compressed N64 instrument samples to burn into the brain are given their own galloping freedom. I love the tentative brass when you lock an enemy into a duel – the musical equivalent of gnawing your lip.Link’s look is more contentious. Where Hyrule is prettied up with expected detail – swaying nettles in a forest home, marbled sunlight on a riverbed – its hero is radically made over. His large glassy eyes, and fat cheeks which reflect the light as if varnished, have led critics to accuse Nintendo of crudely pursuing a textbook next-gen sheen. Bells and whistles for the sake of filling 4K TVs with surface detail, rather than honouring the original artistic intent. In the past, some eager fans attempted to remake Zelda in more capable game engines and were ridiculed for mistaking technological grunt for artistry, and as evolving hardware opens those graphical avenues to Nintendo itself, it would be ironic if it fell for the same allure.In truth, Ocarina of Time looks coherent in motion on Switch 2. If anything, the layer of 4K specificity evokes another Zelda game, Twilight Princess, itself an attempt to apply a more mature, realistic lens to Hyrule. And could Link, with those overblown features, perhaps be nodding to another cultural pastime? As some corners of the internet scoffed at our newly “yassified” hero, the Nintendo veteran and former Legend of Zelda art director Takaya Imamura wondered if the character model drew from Zelda creator Shigeru Miyamoto’s own tastes. “[His] love ofningyogeki(puppet drama) is strongly reflected here,” Imamurawrote on X. Porcelain doll skin would certainly explain the uncanny sheen.View image in fullscreenIt is astonishing how fiendish the puzzles designed in 1998 still are.Photograph: NintendoWhile we can only guess at tight-lipped Nintendo’s intent, writer and translator Paul McQuade explains it is not an impossible leap. “In Japan, puppetry is not considered an art form strictly for children, which is largely how it’s perceived elsewhere,” he says. “It’s a rich art and is highly respected.” He thinks Miyamoto could easily have been influenced by puppet shows aired byJapanese broadcaster NHKin the Shōwa postwar era.And besides, there is something poetic about the notion. “It’s doll-like and intentionally juvenile,” McQuade says of Link’s chubby features and blushing nose. “It captures the essence of that forest where the children don’t ever grow up. Miyamoto, as a fan of puppetry, would of course draw on the vocabulary of dolls to make characters in that mould.”I like the idea of Nintendo honouring a community frozen in time in this way, while also acknowledging that time has moved on outside the game. With that passing comes an opportunity to tweak and massage. In an adventure where a boy can magically become a man and back again with the toot of his ocarina, it makes sense for timelessness and timeliness to be in conversation. With virtual bones this strong, it would be difficult to argue that anything has been truly ruined. Unless you run the shooting gallery, of course.The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is released for Switch 2 on 5 November.Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendo Switch 2NintendoThe Legend of ZeldafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to use stale bread to make a classic British pudding – recipe | Dessert | The Guardian
description: Brown betty is a thrifty and delicious crumble-like autumnal treat
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Brown betty is a thrifty and delicious crumble-like autumnal treat
Content: Tom Hunt’s apple ,maple and blackberry brown betty.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s apple ,maple and blackberry brown betty.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notDessertHow to use stale bread to make a classic British pudding – recipeA thrifty and delicious crumble-like autumnal treat, a bit like a cobbler … or a buckle … or a grunt …Tom HuntWed 14 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe have a family tradition of making our daughter a fruit pie of some sort for her first day of school each September. Last year, it was a simple apple pie, but we intend to make our way through the myriad heritage desserts, from crumbles and crisps to cobblers,buckles,pandowdys,grunts,slumpsandsonkers. This year, we made a brownbetty, a wonderful, crumble-like dessert made with stale bread. We kept things seasonal with apples and blackberries from the garden, but any combination of fruit works really. I sweetened this one with maple syrup, but use your sweetener of choice: each adds its own unique flavour.Apple, maple and blackberry brown bread bettyA brown betty is easier to make than crumble; it’s also arguably even tastier, and it saves waste, too. I used three brown bread crusts left over frommy wholemeal bread taste test, which, when stale, make perfect and flavourful breadcrumbs. The topping should be good enough to eat even before cooking – totally delicious, salty sweet with maple syrup, and crunchy with seeds – so taste and adjust as you see fit with more salt, sweetener, nuts and seeds. The addition of sea salt is a gamechanger that really brings out the sweetness of the maple syrup.Serves4-64 apples100g blackberries70-80g maple syrup, or brown sugar or another sweetener1 tsp vanilla essence50ml water, or brandy75g butter, 50g of it melted, or extra-virgin olive oil3 slices wholemeal bread(about 85g), torn into pieces50g mixed seeds, or roughly chopped nuts (optional)½ tsp sea salt1 tsp ground cinnamonYoghurt, or cream, ice-cream or custard, to serveCut the cored apples into rough cubes (compost the cores, orturn them into pectin jelly) and toss with the blackberries, 40g of the maple syrup (or other sweetener), the vanilla essence and 50ml water (or brandy; the alcohol will cook off, and leave behind a lovely, complex flavour). Tip into a roughly 20cm-wide skillet or ovenproof dish, then dot with 25g of the butter (or extra-virgin olive oil).Tear the bread into pieces, then pulse-blend into chunky breadcrumbs. Stir in the remaining 30-40g sweetener, the melted butter (or extra-virgin olive oil), the mixed seeds or nuts, if using, the sea salt and ground cinnamon. Scatter this mix over the top of the fruit, then bake in a 200C (180C)/390F/gas 6 oven for 40-45 minutes, until golden brown and bubbling.Remove, leave to rest on the counter for 10 minutes, then serve with yoghurt, cream, ice-cream or custard.Explore more on these topicsDessertWaste notFoodFood wasteBreadFruitBakingAutumn food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cheese tart, corn salad, squash with ’nduja, radicchio salad: Joe Otway’s recipes for early autumn | Food | The Guardian
description: Celebrate seasonal British-grown produce with four easy dishes guided by a natural ingredient in its prime
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Celebrate seasonal British-grown produce with four easy dishes guided by a natural ingredient in its prime
Content: Joe Otway’s roast winter squash with ’nduja.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/Photographs: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian, food Styling: Rosie Reynolds, prop styling: Florence BlairView image in fullscreenJoe Otway’s roast winter squash with ’nduja.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/Photographs: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian, food Styling: Rosie Reynolds, prop styling: Florence BlairFoodCheese tart, corn salad, squash with ’nduja, radicchio salad: Joe Otway’s recipes for early autumnCelebrate seasonal British-grown produce with four easy dishes guided by a natural ingredient in its primeJoe OtwayWed 14 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly autumn is one of the most generous and comforting times of year to cook with British produce: sweetcorn is at its peak, squash begins to sweeten as the weather cools and bitter leaves such as radicchio provide balance to the season’s abundance. Today’s recipes are simple celebrations of British ingredients, using just a handful of carefully chosen components to let each vegetable shine. Whether it’s a buttery cheese tart for sharing; a fresh, herby corn salad; sweet roast squash with warm, spicy ’nduja; or bitter leaves lifted with a floral dressing, they all rely on cooking with ingredients at their seasonal peak and allowing nature to guide the menu.Cheese tartView image in fullscreenMade for sharing: Joe Otway’s cheese tart.Prep10 minChill30 min+Cook1 hrMakes4individual tarts90g unsalted butter, plus extra for greasing120g plain flour, plus extra for dusting110g mature cheddar, finely grated70g whole eggs25ml whole milk10g ready-made English mustard, or to taste110ml double creamSea salt andblack pepperFirst, make the pastry. Rub the butter into the flour until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs, then add 60g of the grated cheddar and knead gently until the mix comes together into a dough. Divide into four, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes.Meanwhile, make the custard. Blend the eggs, milk, remaining 50g grated cheddar and mustard until smooth, then stir in the cream by hand and season to taste.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and grease and line four individual 8-10cm tart tins. Lightly flour a work surface, roll out each piece of pastry, then use to line the tins. Line each pastry base with baking paper, fill with baking beans or similar, then blind bake for 15 minutes, until lightly golden. Lift out the paper and beans, then return the tarts to the oven for a further five minutes, until the bases are crisp and golden.Carefully pour the custard into each tart case until they’re almost full, then bake for another 15-25 minutes, depending on your oven (the actual temperature of domestic ovens varies a fair bit, after all), until the custard is lightly browned and just set with a slight wobble in the centre.Leave to cool to room temperature, then serve, either with a bitter leaf salad or with one of the following two sides.Corn salad with soured cream and oreganoView image in fullscreenJoe Otway’s corn salad with soured cream and oregano.Prep5 minCook15 minServes4Sea salt andblack pepper4 fresh sweetcorn cobs, or 1 400g tin good-quality sweetcorn150g soured cream100ml extra-virgin olive oilJuice of ½ lemonSea salt20g fresh oregano leaves, plus extra to garnish30g parmesan, shavedBring a large pan of salted water to a boil, drop in the corn cobs, cook for four or five minutes, until tender, then drain and refresh. Once the cobs are cool enough to handle, cut off the kernels and put in a bowl (if you’re using tinned corn, skip the blanching stage and simply drain the water from the can).Mix the soured cream with 20ml of the olive oil, the lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Blend the oregano with the remaining olive oil until fragrant. Dress the sweetcorn with the oregano oil, then season generously with salt and a little more lemon juice, if needed.Spread the soured cream mix over a platter, spoon the dressed corn on top, scatter over a few more oregano leaves and finish with generous shavings of parmesan and a final twist of black pepper.Roast winter squash with ’ndujaView image in fullscreenJoe Otway’s roast winter squash with ’nduja.Prep10 minCook45 minServes41kg winter squash(uchiki kuri is ideal, although butternut works well too), halved, deseeded and cut into skin-on wedges5 tbsp olive oilSea salt20g pumpkin seeds120g ’nduja2 tbsp good-quality honey150g Greek yoghurt1 tbsp lemon juice1 small handfulflat-leaf parsley, leaves picked and roughly choppedHeat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Toss the squash wedges with two tablespoons of the olive oil and a generous pinch of salt, then arrange on an oven tray and roast for 30-40 minutes, turning every 10 minutes, until tender and caramelised. Add the pumpkin seeds to the tray for the final 10 minutes of cooking.Meanwhile, in a small saucepan gently warm the ’nduja, honey and the remaining olive oil until the mix comes together into a loose dressing. In a small bowl, mix the yoghurt with the lemon juice and a pinch of salt.Spread the yoghurt on a platter, arrange the squash wedges and toasted pumpkin seeds on top, then spoon over the warm ’nduja dressing. Finish with the parsley and serve.Radicchio with elderflower vinaigretteView image in fullscreenJoe Otway’s radicchio with elderflower vinaigrette.Yes, elderflower is an early-summer flavour, but that’s why they invented cordial, so we can enjoy that gentle fragrance all year round.Prep10 minServes43 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil2 tbsp elderflower cordial2 tbsp white-wine vinegar1 tsp dijon mustardSea salt and black pepper2 heads bitter leaves– radicchio, treviso, chicory or endive will all work well here40g hard sheep’s cheese, or pecorinoIn a small bowl, whisk the oil, cordial, vinegar, mustard, and salt and pepper to taste, until lightly emulsified.Trim the bases off the radicchio heads, then separate the leaves and put them in a medium bowl. Dress the leaves generously with the vinaigrette, then season with a little more salt and pepper if needed. Leave to marinate for five to 10 minutes, so the leaves soften slightly and absorb the dressing, then arrange on a serving plate and finish with generous shavings of the cheese.Joe Otway is chef/co-owner ofHigher Ground,Bar ShrimpandFlawd, all in Manchester.Explore more on these topicsFoodCheesePieBakingPastryEggsVegetablesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Was this Mark Zuckerberg’s first – and last – taste of Guinness? | Beer | The Guardian
description: The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half full
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half full
Content: Mark Zuckerberg savours the flavour of a pint of Guinness.Photograph: YouTube/Cheeky PintView image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg savours the flavour of a pint of Guinness.Photograph: YouTube/Cheeky PintPass notesBeerWas this Mark Zuckerberg’s first – and last – taste of Guinness?The Meta boss looked traumatised when he sipped stout on the Cheeky Pint podcast. An hour later, his glass was still half fullWed 14 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Guinness.Age:Arthur Guinness began brewing porter in the 1770s. Guinness draft was first poured in 1959.Appearance:Espresso martini in a pint glass.But it’s beer.It’s stout, yeah. Irish stout.Sort of an old man’s drink, isn’t it?Not these days. Fans of Guinness include Kim Kardashian, Olivia Rodrigo, even the Princess of Wales.That’s just a bunch of celebrities pretending to like Guinness either because they’re visiting Ireland or it’s Saint Patrick’s Day. Or both.Some of them have actually tasted it:Mark Zuckerberg, for example.I wouldn’t have guessedZuckerbergdrinks Guinness.He has drunk it – and apparently for the first time – on a recent instalment of the Irish billionaire John Collison’s Cheeky Pint podcast, which is set in a pub.How did he like it?He didn’t say.What makes you think it was his first time?The look on his face.Did he look as if he was enjoying it?He looked as if he might be allergic to it.What do you mean?At the start of the podcast, while discussing his new Muse AI app, theMetafounder picks up the full pint in front of him and takes a sip.Like a regular person, you mean.Close enough, up to that point. But his subsequent reaction went viral.What did he do?He looked surprised, for a start. Then as if he was having trouble swallowing. He pursed his lips, squirmed in his seat and seemed to be looking around for the nearest exit.Oh my.After that he clutched at his shirt collar a bit. He even tried smiling briefly before realising he’d selected the wrong human facial expression from the dropdown menu. Eventually he managed to power down and reset himself.Did he at leastfinish the pint?He kept at it, but by the 1 hour 20 minute mark he’d only managed about half.Then what happened?There was an apparent break in filming, and when they resumed he had another full pint in front of him.His worst nightmare! Still, I suppose Guinness can manage withoutZuckerberg’s endorsement.You would have thought so – it sells 1.88bn pints a year globally, withsales continuing to rise, while the overall beer market declines. And Guinness 0.0 is the No 1 non-alcoholic beer in the UK.So what made Zuckerberg think he ought to pretend to like it?Well, he didbuy a castle in Irelandlast month for €20m (£17m), so maybe he’s planning on popping down to his local more often?Do say:“Guinness is an acquired taste, and I’m in the process of acquiring it in the same way I’ve acquired many startups and competitors. Was this answer helpful?”Don’t say:“Then, when my new AI model kills everyone, I’ll drink what I like.”Explore more on these topicsBeerPass notesMark ZuckerbergFood & drink industryMetaAlcoholfeaturesShareReuse this content
